"是，"催眠师说，"往下说。她多大？"

"十八。"

"危险的年纪。怎么样呢？"

===Original===
“Well: it seems that she has been indulging in these historical romances—excessively. Excessively. Even to the neglect of her philosophy. Filled her mind with unutterable nonsense about soldiers who fight—what is it?—Etruscans?”

“Egyptians.”

“Egyptians—very probably. Hack about with swords and revolvers and things—bloodshed galore—horrible!—and about young men on torpedo catchers who blow up—Spaniards, I fancy—and all sorts of irregular adventurers. And she has got it into her head that she must marry for Love, and that poor little Bindon—”

“I’ve met similar cases,” said the hypnotist. “Who is the other young man?”

Mwres maintained an appearance of resigned calm. “You may well ask,” he said. “He is”—and his voice sank with shame—“a mere attendant upon the stage on which the flying-machines from Paris alight. He has—as they say in the romances—good looks. He is quite young and very eccentric. Affects the antique—he can read and write! So can she. And instead of communicating by telephone, like sensible people, they write and deliver—what is it?”

“Notes?”

“No—not notes… Ah—poems.”

The hypnotist raised his eyebrows. “How did she meet him?”

“Tripped coming down from the flying-machine from Paris—and fell into his arms. The mischief was done in a moment!”

“Yes?”

===Chinese===
"怎么样呢：看样子她迷上了这些历史传奇——迷得不行。迷得不行。连哲学都荒废了。满脑子灌的全是些不堪入耳的胡话——什么兵士打仗——叫什么来着？——伊特鲁里亚人（Etruscans）？"

"埃及人（Egyptians）。"

"埃及人——多半就是。拿刀剑手枪之类一通乱砍——血流成河——可怕！——又是什么年轻人驾着鱼雷快艇去炸——大概是西班牙人（Spaniards）罢——还有诸如此类各种不守规矩的亡命之徒。她竟一头钻进了牛角尖，非要为爱情嫁人不可，而那个可怜的小宾登——"

"不——不是便条……呃——是诗。"

催眠师扬了扬眉。"她怎么遇上他的？"

"从巴黎来的飞行机器上下来时一脚踏空——扑进了他怀里。祸事就这么一瞬间铸成了！"

===Original===
“Well—that’s all. Things must be stopped. That is what I want to consult you about. What must be done? What *can* be done? Of course I’m not a hypnotist; my knowledge is limited. But you—?”

“Hypnotism is not magic,” said the man in green, putting both arms on the table.

“Oh, precisely! But still—!”

“People cannot be hypnotised without their consent. If she is able to stand out against marrying Bindon, she will probably stand out against being hypnotised. But if once she can be hypnotised—even by somebody else—the thing is done.”

“You can—?”

“Oh, certainly! Once we get her amenable, then we can suggest that she *must* marry Bindon—that that is her fate; or that the young man is repulsive, and that when she sees him she will be giddy and faint, or any little thing of that sort. Or if we can get her into a sufficiently profound trance we can suggest that she should forget him altogether—”

“Precisely.”

“But the problem is to get her hypnotised. Of course no sort of proposal or suggestion must come from you—because no doubt she already distrusts you in the matter.”

The hypnotist leant his head upon his arm and thought.

“It’s hard a man cannot dispose of his own daughter,” said Mwres irrelevantly.

“You must give me the name and address of the young lady,” said the hypnotist, “and any information bearing upon the matter. And, by the by, is there any money in the affair?”

Mwres hesitated.

“There’s a sum—in fact, a considerable sum—invested in the Patent Road Company. From her mother. That’s what makes the thing so exasperating.”

“Exactly,” said the hypnotist. And he proceeded to cross-examine Mwres on the entire affair.

It was a lengthy interview.

===Chinese===
"嗯——就是这样。这事非止住不可。这便是我想请教您的事。该怎么办？能怎么办？我自然不是催眠师；我所知有限。可您——？"

"催眠术可不是魔法，"那绿衣人说，把两臂都搁在桌上。

"哦，正是！可是——"

"人不经本人同意是无法被催眠的。她若能抗拒嫁给宾登，多半也能抗拒被催眠。可一旦她被催眠了——哪怕是被别人催眠——事便成了。"

"你能——？"

"哦，自然！一旦我们使她变得顺从，便能暗示她非嫁给宾登不可——说这是她的命；或者说那年轻人面目可憎，一见他便要头晕目眩、要昏倒，诸如此类的小手段。或者，要是我们能使她进入足够深的迷睡，便能暗示她把那人忘得一干二净——"

"正是。"

"但问题在于如何使她被催眠。当然，您这边绝不能有任何提议或暗示——因为此事上她无疑早已不信任您了。"

催眠师把头枕在臂上，想了想。

"做父亲的竟不能处置自己的女儿，这也太难了，"姆雷斯不着边际地说了一句。

"您得把这位小姐的姓名住址给我，"催眠师说，"以及与此事相关的种种情况。顺便问一句，这里头有钱财之事么？"

姆雷斯犹豫了一下。

"有一笔款子——其实是一笔可观的款子——投在专利道路公司（Patent Road Company）里。是她母亲那边来的。所以才叫人这么恼火。"

"原来如此，"催眠师说。接着他便就整桩事对姆雷斯细细盘问起来。

这一席谈话很长。

===Original===
And meanwhile “Elizebeθ Mwres,” as she spelt her name, or “Elizabeth Morris” as a nineteenth-century person would have put it, was sitting in a quiet waiting-place beneath the great stage upon which the flying-machine from Paris descended. And beside her sat her slender, handsome lover reading her the poem he had written that morning while on duty upon the stage. When he had finished they sat for a time in silence; and then, as if for their special entertainment, the great machine that had come flying through the air from America that morning rushed down out of the sky.

At first it was a little oblong, faint and blue amidst the distant fleecy clouds; and then it grew swiftly large and white, and larger and whiter, until they could see the separate tiers of sails, each hundreds of feet wide, and the lank body they supported, and at last even the swinging seats of the passengers in a dotted row. Although it was falling it seemed to them to be rushing up the sky, and over the roof-spaces of the city below its shadow leapt towards them. They heard the whistling rush of the air about it and its yelling siren, shrill and swelling, to warn those who were on its landing-stage of its arrival. And abruptly the note fell down a couple of octaves, and it had passed, and the sky was clear and void, and she could turn her sweet eyes again to Denton at her side.

Their silence ended; and Denton, speaking in a little language of broken English that was, they fancied, their private possession—though lovers have used such little languages since the world began—told her how they too would leap into the air one morning out of all the obstacles and difficulties about them, and fly to a sunlit city of delight he knew of in Japan, halfway about the world.

She loved the dream, but she feared the leap; and she put him off with “Some day, dearest one, some day,” to all his pleading that it might be soon; and at last came a shrilling of whistles, and it was time for him to go back to his duties on the stage. They parted—as lovers have been wont to part for thousands of years. She walked down a passage to a lift, and so came to one of the streets of that latter-day London, all glazed in with glass from the weather, and with incessant moving platforms that went to all parts of the city. And by one of these she returned to her apartments in the Hotel for Women where she lived, the apartments that were in telephonic communication with all the best lecturers in the world. But the sunlight of the flying stage was in her heart, and the wisdom of all the best lecturers in the world seemed folly in that light.

===Chinese===
与此同时，"伊丽莎白·姆雷斯"——她把自己名字拼作 Elizebeθ Mwres——按十九世纪人的写法便是"伊丽莎白·莫里斯"（Elizabeth Morris）——正静静地坐在巴黎来的飞行机器降落的巨大平台下方一处僻静的等候处。坐在她身旁的，是她那身材修长、面目俊美的恋人，正念着他在当班时写就的、献给她的诗。念完之后，两人静默地坐了一会儿；跟着，仿佛是专为给他们助兴，那台当日清晨从美洲穿过长空飞来的巨型机器，从天空中俯冲而下。

起初只是一个长长的小方点，在远处絮状的云层间隐约泛蓝；转瞬之间便大了、白了，越来越大、越来越白，直到他们能看清那层层叠叠的帆翼——每一层都有几百英尺宽——以及它们所撑起的瘦长身躯；到末了，连乘客们一排小点似的吊座也依稀可辨。它分明是在坠落，在他们眼里却像是沿着天空直冲上来；在城市一片屋顶的上方，它的影子朝他们跳了过来。他们听见它四周空气的呼啸，听见它尖厉而渐高的汽笛嘶鸣，那是在警告降落台上的人它到了。陡然之间，那声响跌下了两个八度，它已经掠过，天空重又澄澈、空空如也；她这才得以把她那双甜甜的眼睛重新转向身边的登顿（Denton）。

他们不再作声；登顿用一种破碎英语构成的小小语言对她说话——他们自以为是这语言独家的主人，虽说自从有了世界，恋人便一直用这种小语言——告诉她：他们总有一天早晨也要从眼前这一切障碍与艰难中纵身一跃，飞到半个地球之外、他熟知的一座日本（Japan）的、洒满阳光的欢乐之城去。

她爱恋这个梦，却畏惧那一跃；他每求她快些成行，她都用"总有一天的，最亲爱的，总有一天"来搪塞；末了一阵哨声尖啸而起，到了他该回到平台上当班的时分。他们分别了——千百年来，恋人的分别向来如此。她顺着一条通道走到一部电梯前，由此来到近世伦敦的一条街道上：所有的街道都从顶到脚用玻璃封起来挡风遮雨，到处是奔往城市各处的不间断的活动站台。她从其中一条回到了她所居住的"女子大旅馆"（Hotel for Women）的房间里——那房间与全世界最优秀的讲师都以电话相通。可飞行平台上的那片阳光仍在她心底，相形之下，全世界最优秀的讲师的种种学问，都成了痴人说梦。

===Original===
She spent the middle part of the day in the gymnasium, and took her midday meal with two other girls and their common chaperone—for it was still the custom to have a chaperone in the case of motherless girls of the more prosperous classes. The chaperone had a visitor that day, a man in green and yellow, with a white face and vivid eyes, who talked amazingly. Among other things, he fell to praising a new historical romance that one of the great popular storytellers of the day had just put forth. It was, of course, about the spacious times of Queen Victoria; and the author, among other pleasing novelties, made a little argument before each section of the story, in imitation of the chapter headings of the old-fashioned books: as for example, “How the Cabmen of Pimlico stopped the Victoria Omnibuses, and of the Great Fight in Palace Yard,” and “How the Piccadilly Policeman was slain in the midst of his Duty.” The man in green and yellow praised this innovation. “These pithy sentences,” he said, “are admirable. They show at a glance those headlong, tumultuous times, when men and animals jostled in the filthy streets, and death might wait for one at every corner. Life was life then! How great the world must have seemed then! How marvellous! They were still parts of the world absolutely unexplored. Nowadays we have almost abolished wonder, we lead lives so trim and orderly that courage, endurance, faith, all the noble virtues seem fading from mankind.”

And so on, taking the girls’ thoughts with him, until the life they led, life in the vast and intricate London of the twenty-second century, a life interspersed with soaring excursions to every part of the globe, seemed to them a monotonous misery compared with the daedal past.

At first Elizabeth did not join in the conversation, but after a time the subject became so interesting that she made a few shy interpolations. But he scarcely seemed to notice her as he talked. He went on to describe a new method of entertaining people. They were hypnotised, and then suggestions were made to them so skilfully that they seemed to be living in ancient times again. They played out a little romance in the past as vivid as reality, and when at last they awakened they remembered all they had been through as though it were a real thing.

===Chinese===
白天中段的时辰她在健身房里度过，与另外两个姑娘和她们共有的女伴一同吃了午饭——因为上等人家没了母亲的少女，照例仍需有位女伴相陪。那天那位女伴来了一位客人，一个穿黄绿衣裳的男人，脸色苍白、目光炯炯，说起话来着实惊人。说着说着，他便赞起了一部新出的历史传奇——出自当时一位极负盛名的通俗说书人之手。这部书，自然，写的是维多利亚女王那段恢宏的时代；作者除了一些讨巧的新花样之外，还在每一段故事之前加了一小段引子，模仿旧式书的回目款式：例如《平利科（Pimlico）的马车夫如何拦下维多利亚线的公共汽车，以及宫廷广场（Palace Yard）的大战》，又如《皮卡迪利（Piccadilly）的警察如何在值勤途中被杀》。那黄绿衣裳的人对这种创新赞不绝口。"这些短小精悍的句子，"他说，"实在是妙。一眼便能叫人看出那个横冲直撞、乱糟糟的时代——人与牲口在肮脏的街道上挤作一团，死神可能在每个角落等着你。那时的日子才叫日子！那时的世界在人们眼里，该有多么辽阔！多么不可思议！世上竟还有全然未曾涉足的地方。如今我们几乎消灭了惊奇，过着这般整整齐齐、井井有条的日子，连勇气、坚韧、信念，一切高尚的德行，似乎都正在从人身上消退。"

他这样一路讲下去，把姑娘们的思绪也一并带走——到末了，她们所过的日子，二十二世纪那座庞大而错综的伦敦里的日子，中间夹杂着飞往全球各地的远行——在她们看来，与那精巧繁复的过去一比，竟成了一种单调的苦刑。

起初伊丽莎白并不加入谈话，可过了一阵，这话题越发有趣，她也怯怯地插了几句嘴。可他说话时似乎全未留意到她。他接着描述起一种娱乐人们的新法子：先把人催眠了，再巧妙地向他们作出种种暗示，使他们仿佛又活到了古时。他们在往昔里活出一段小小的浪漫，栩栩如生一如真实；到末了醒来，回想起所经历的一切，便像真发生过一样。

===Original===
“It is a thing we have sought to do for years and years,” said the hypnotist. “It is practically an artificial dream. And we know the way at last. Think of all it opens out to us—the enrichment of our experience, the recovery of adventure, the refuge it offers from this sordid, competitive life in which we live! Think!”

“And you can do that!” said the chaperone eagerly.

“The thing is possible at last,” the hypnotist said. “You may order a dream as you wish.”

The chaperone was the first to be hypnotised, and the dream, she said, was wonderful, when she came to again.

The other two girls, encouraged by her enthusiasm, also placed themselves in the hands of the hypnotist and had plunges into the romantic past. No one suggested that Elizabeth should try this novel entertainment; it was at her own request at last that she was taken into that land of dreams where there is neither any freedom of choice nor will…

And so the mischief was done.

One day, when Denton went down to that quiet seat beneath the flying stage, Elizabeth was not in her wonted place. He was disappointed, and a little angry. The next day she did not come, and the next also. He was afraid. To hide his fear from himself, he set to work to write sonnets for her when she should come again…

For three days he fought against his dread by such distraction, and then the truth was before him clear and cold, and would not be denied. She might be ill, she might be dead; but he would not believe that he had been betrayed. There followed a week of misery. And then he knew she was the only thing on Earth worth having, and that he must seek her, however hopeless the search, until she was found once more.

He had some small private means of his own, and so he threw over his appointment on the flying stage, and set himself to find this girl who had become at last all the world to him. He did not know where she lived, and little of her circumstances; for it had been part of the delight of her girlish romance that he should know nothing of her, nothing of the difference of their station. The ways of the city opened before him east and west, north and south. Even in Victorian days London was a maze, that little London with its poor four millions of people; but the London he explored, the London of the twenty-second century, was a London of thirty million souls. At first he was energetic and headlong, taking time neither to eat nor sleep. He sought for weeks and months, he went through every imaginable phase of fatigue and despair, over-excitement and anger. Long after hope was dead, by the sheer inertia of his desire he still went to and fro, peering into faces and looking this way and that, in the incessant ways and lifts and passages of that interminable hive of men.

At last chance was kind to him, and he saw her.

===Chinese===
"这是我们多年来一直想做到的事，"催眠师说，"这其实便是一场人造的梦。如今我们终于摸到了门道。诸位想想它为我们展开了什么——阅历的丰盈，冒险的回归，还有从我们身处的这肮脏、尔虞我诈的生活中得以暂避的庇所！想想看！"

"您竟能做到！"女伴热切地说。

"这事终于办得到了，"催眠师说，"您尽可随心定做一场梦。"

女伴头一个被催眠了；她醒过来时说，方才那场梦，真是妙不可言。

另外两个姑娘受了她的鼓舞，也把自己交到催眠师手里，到那浪漫的旧世里神游了几番。没人提议伊丽莎白也来试试这新鲜玩艺儿；末了倒是她自己主动请求，才被带进那片梦之国度——在那里，既无所谓选择之自由，也无所谓意志……

祸事便这样成了。

一日，登顿照例下到飞行平台下那处僻静的座位去，伊丽莎白却不在她惯常所坐的地方。他大失所望，又有些恼。次日她没有来，再过一日也没有。他害怕起来。为了对自己隐瞒这份害怕，他埋头替她写起十四行诗来，等着她再来时给她……

三天里他借这消遣与恐惧相抗，随后那冷冰冰的事实便明明白白地摆在他眼前，再不容否认。她也许是病了，也许是死了；可他不肯相信自己竟被辜负了。随后是一周煎熬。再然后，他明白她才是这世上唯一值得一得的东西，他必须去找她，不管那寻找多么无望，直到再度把她找到。

他自己有一点小小的私财，于是辞去了飞行平台上的差事，专心去找这个终于成了他全世界的姑娘。他不知她住在何处，对她的境况也所知甚少；因为这段少女浪漫之情中有一桩乐处，便是他理应对她一无所知——不知他们身份上的差距。城市的条条道路在他面前向东、向西、向南、向北地敞开。即使在维多利亚时代，伦敦也是一座迷宫——那座区区四百万人的小伦敦；可他所探索的这座伦敦，二十二世纪的伦敦，却是一座三千万人之众的伦敦。起初他精力充沛、奋不顾身，连吃饭睡觉的工夫也不肯耽搁。他寻了几周又几月，走遍了所能想象的一切疲倦与绝望、过度兴奋与愤怒。希望早已死尽之后，单凭欲望的惯性，他仍在那座无边无际的人之蜂巢里那些绵延不绝的通道、电梯与走廊之间来来回回，端详着一张张脸，东张西望。

末了好运终于眷顾了他，他看见了她。

===Original===
It was in a time of festivity. He was hungry; he had paid the inclusive fee and had gone into one of the gigantic dining-places of the city; he was pushing his way among the tables and scrutinising by mere force of habit every group he passed.

He stood still, robbed of all power of motion, his eyes wide, his lips apart. Elizabeth sat scarcely twenty yards away from him, looking straight at him. Her eyes were as hard to him, as hard and expressionless and void of recognition, as the eyes of a statue.

She looked at him for a moment, and then her gaze passed beyond him.

Had he had only her eyes to judge by he might have doubted if it was indeed Elizabeth, but he knew her by the gesture of her hand, by the grace of a wanton little curl that floated over her ear as she moved her head. Something was said to her, and she turned smiling tolerantly to the man beside her, a little man in foolish raiment knobbed and spiked like some odd reptile with pneumatic horns—the Bindon of her father’s choice.

For a moment Denton stood white and wild-eyed; then came a terrible faintness, and he sat before one of the little tables. He sat down with his back to her, and for a time he did not dare to look at her again. When at last he did, she and Bindon and two other people were standing up to go. The others were her father and her chaperone.

He sat as if incapable of action until the four figures were remote and small, and then he rose up possessed with the one idea of pursuit. For a space he feared he had lost them, and then he came upon Elizabeth and her chaperone again in one of the streets of moving platforms that intersected the city. Bindon and Mwres had disappeared.

===Chinese===
那是一年节庆的日子。他饿着肚子，付过了通用的饭资，进了城里一处巨型公共食堂；他在桌椅间挤来挤去，全出于习惯，把经过的每一群人都细细打量一番。

他僵立当场，浑身动弹不得，眼睛瞪得大大的，嘴唇微张。伊丽莎白坐在离他不到二十码的地方，正目不转睛地盯着他看。她的眼睛对他来说，是那样冷硬——冷硬、毫无表情、毫无相识之色，宛如一尊塑像的眼睛。

她朝他看了一会儿，目光便越过他，投向了别处。

倘若只凭她的眼睛判断，他简直要怀疑这是不是伊丽莎白了；可他从她手的动作、从她侧首时飘到耳际那一缕俏皮小卷发的婀娜，认出了她。有人对她说了句什么，她转过脸去，宽容地朝身旁那个男人笑了笑——一个小个子男人，穿着滑稽的衣裳，那衣裳疙疙瘩瘩、刺刺棱棱，活像一只长着充气角的古怪爬虫——正是她父亲所选中的那位宾登。

登顿一时面无人色、双目圆睁；跟着一阵可怕的眩晕袭来，他在一张小桌前坐了下来。他背对着她坐下，有一阵子不敢再朝她看。待到他终于再看时，她与宾登以及另外两人已经起身要走。另外两人是她的父亲和她的女伴。

他坐着，仿佛动弹不得，直到那四道身影走远变小；这才站起身来，一心只想着追赶。有一阵子他怕跟丢了人，继而又在一条贯穿城市、铺着活动站台的街上，重新撞见了伊丽莎白和她的女伴。宾登和姆雷斯已不知去向。

===Original===
He could not control himself to patience. He felt he must speak to her forthwith, or die. He pushed forward to where they were seated, and sat down beside them. His white face was convulsed with half-hysterical excitement.

He laid his hand on her wrist. “Elizabeth?” he said.

She turned in unfeigned astonishment. Nothing but the fear of a strange man showed in her face.

“Elizabeth,” he cried, and his voice was strange to him: “dearest—you *know* me?”

Elizabeth’s face showed nothing but alarm and perplexity. She drew herself away from him. The chaperone, a little grey-headed woman with mobile features, leant forward to intervene. Her resolute bright eyes examined Denton. “*What* do you say?” she asked.

“This young lady,” said Denton—“she knows me.”

“Do you know him, dear?”

“No,” said Elizabeth in a strange voice, and with a hand to her forehead, speaking almost as one who repeats a lesson. “No, I do not know him. I *know*—I do not know him.”

“But—but… Not know me! It is I—Denton. Denton! To whom you used to talk. Don’t you remember the flying stages? The little seat in the open air? The verses—”

“No,” cried Elizabeth—“no. I do not know him. I do not know him. There is something… But I don’t know. All I know is that I do not know him.” Her face was a face of infinite distress.

The sharp eyes of the chaperone flitted to and fro from the girl to the man. “You see?” she said, with the faint shadow of a smile. “She does not know you.”

“I do not know you,” said Elizabeth. “Of that I am sure.”

“But, dear—the songs—the little verses—”

“She does not know you,” said the chaperone. “You must not… You have made a mistake. You must not go on talking to us after that. You must not annoy us on the public ways.”

“But—” said Denton, and for a moment his miserably haggard face appealed against fate.

“You must not persist, young man,” protested the chaperone.

“*Elizabeth!*” he cried.

Her face was the face of one who is tormented. “I do not know you,” she cried, hand to brow. “Oh, I do not know you!”

For an instant Denton sat stunned. Then he stood up and groaned aloud.

He made a strange gesture of appeal towards the remote glass roof of the public way, then turned and went plunging recklessly from one moving platform to another, and vanished amidst the swarms of people going to and fro thereon. The chaperone’s eyes followed him, and then she looked at the curious faces about her.

“Dear,” asked Elizabeth, clasping her hand, and too deeply moved to heed observation, “who was that man? Who *was* that man?”

The chaperone raised her eyebrows. She spoke in a clear, audible voice. “Some half-witted creature. I have never set eyes on him before.”

“Never?”

“Never, dear. Do not trouble your mind about a thing like this.”

===Chinese===
他按捺不住自己了。他觉得自己非立刻跟她说话不可，否则便要死了。他挤到她们就座的地方，在她们身旁坐了下来。他那张苍白的脸，因半歇斯底里的激动而扭曲着。

他把手搭在她的手腕上。"伊丽莎白？"他说。

她转过脸来，是全然由衷的惊愕。她脸上只有对一个陌生男子的恐惧。

"伊丽莎白，"他喊道，声音连自己听了都觉得陌生："最亲爱的——你认得我？"

伊丽莎白的脸上只显出惊慌与困惑。她从他手下挣开。那位女伴——一个头发花白、五官生动的小个子妇人——探身过来要干预。她那双明亮而坚定的眼睛打量着登顿。"你说什么？"她问。

"这位小姐，"登顿说——"她认得我的。"

"你认得他吗，亲爱的？"

"不，"伊丽莎白声音异样地说，一只手按着前额，说话的口吻几乎像在背一段功课。"不，我不认得他。我晓得——我不认得他。"

"可是——可是……竟不认得我！是我呀——登顿。登顿！你从前常和我说话的那个人。你不记得飞行平台了吗？露天的那个小座位？那些小诗——"

"不，"伊丽莎白喊道——"不。我不认得他。我不认得他。有什么东西……可我不知道。我只知道我不认得他。"她满脸都是无尽的痛苦。

女伴那双锐利的眼睛在姑娘和男子之间来回扫视。"您瞧？"她说，嘴角挂着一丝若有若无的笑意。"她不认得您。"

"我不认得您，"伊丽莎白说，"这一点我确信无疑。"

"可是，亲爱的——那些歌——那些小诗——"

"她不认得您，"女伴说，"您万万不可……您认错人了。事已至此，您不能再同我们说下去了。您不得在公共通衢上纠缠我们。"

"可是——"登顿说，一时之间，他那憔悴不堪的脸满含冤苦地向命运申诉。

"年轻人，您不能再纠缠下去，"女伴正色道。

"伊丽莎白！"他喊道。

她的脸是一个受着折磨的人的脸。"我不认得您，"她喊道，手按着额头，"哦，我不认得您！"

登顿一时呆坐在那里，如遭雷击。然后他站起身来，大声地呻吟了一下。

他做了一个古怪的手势，像是在向公共通道那遥远的玻璃穹顶申诉；转身便不顾一切地从一条活动站台跳到另一条，消失在站台上来来往往、摩肩接踵的人流里。女伴的眼睛追随着他，然后她看了看四周好奇的脸。

"亲爱的，"伊丽莎白握住她的手，动情至深，顾不得旁人的目光，"那个人是谁？那个人到底是谁？"

女伴扬了扬眉。她用清晰可闻的声音说："一个半痴不癫的家伙。我生平从未见过他。"

"从未？"

"从未，亲爱的。这种小事，不必挂在心上。"

===Original===
And soon after this the celebrated hypnotist who dressed in green and yellow had another client. The young man paced his consulting-room, pale and disordered. “I want to forget,” he cried. “I *must* forget.”

The hypnotist watched him with quiet eyes, studied his face and clothes and bearing. “To forget anything—pleasure or pain—is to be, by so much—*less*. However, you know your own concern. My fee is high.”

“If only I can forget—”

“That’s easy enough with you. You wish it. I’ve done much harder things. Quite recently. I hardly expected to do it: the thing was done against the will of the hypnotised person. A love affair too—like yours. A girl. So rest assured.”

The young man came and sat beside the hypnotist. His manner was a forced calm. He looked into the hypnotist’s eyes. “I will tell you. Of course you will want to know what it is. There was a girl. Her name was Elizabeth Mwres. Well—”

He stopped. He had seen the instant surprise on the hypnotist’s face. In that instant he knew. He stood up. He seemed to dominate the seated figure by his side. He gripped the shoulder of green and gold. For a time he could not find words.

“*Give her me back!*” he said at last. “Give her me back!”

“What do you mean?” gasped the hypnotist.

“Give her me back.”

“Give whom?”

“Elizabeth Mwres—the girl—”

The hypnotist tried to free himself; he rose to his feet. Denton’s grip tightened.

“Let go!” cried the hypnotist, thrusting an arm against Denton’s chest.

In a moment the two men were locked in a clumsy wrestle. Neither had the slightest training—for athleticism, except for exhibition and to afford opportunity for betting, had faded out of the Earth—but Denton was not only the younger but the stronger of the two. They swayed across the room, and then the hypnotist had gone down under his antagonist. They fell together…

Denton leaped to his feet, dismayed at his own fury; but the hypnotist lay still, and suddenly from a little white mark where his forehead had struck a stool shot a hurrying band of red. For a space Denton stood over him irresolute, trembling.

===Chinese===
此后不久，那位穿黄绿衣裳、鼎鼎大名的催眠师，又迎来了一位主顾。那青年在他的诊室里来回踱步，面色苍白，神情狼狈。"我要忘掉，"他喊道，"我一定要忘掉。"

催眠师静静地注视着他，端详他的脸、衣裳和举止。"忘掉任何东西——无论快乐还是痛苦——便意味着相应地少了一点——自己。不过，您的事您自己作主。我的收费很高。"

"只要我能忘掉——"

"您这倒不难。您本人情愿。我做过比这难得多的事。就在不久之前。那事我本来几乎没指望办到：那是在被催眠者本人不情愿的情况下做成的。一桩情事——和您的一样。一位姑娘。所以您大可放心。"

那青年走过来，在催眠师身边坐下。他的举止是强装的镇定。他直视着催眠师的眼睛。"我告诉你吧。当然，您会想知道是什么事。从前有个姑娘。她叫伊丽莎白·姆雷斯。这个嘛——"

他停住了。他看见了催眠师脸上霎时的诧异。在那一霎间，他明白了。他站起身来。他仿佛居高临下地俯视着身旁坐着的那人。他一把抓住那黄绿色的肩膀。有好一阵子他找不出话来。

"把她还给我！"他终于说道，"把她还给我！"

"您这是什么意思？"催眠师喘着气说。

"把她还给我。"

"把谁？"

"伊丽莎白·姆雷斯——那个姑娘——"

催眠师想挣开；他站起身来。登顿的手却抓得更紧。

"放手！"催眠师喊道，用一只臂膀去抵登顿的胸口。

一眨眼间两人便笨拙地扭作一团。两人都丝毫未受过训练——因为运动竞技，除了表演和供人下注之外，早已从地球上消退了——可登顿不仅更年轻，力气也更大。两人在屋里摇来晃去，跟着催眠师便被对手压倒在地。他们一同倒下去……

登顿跳起身来，被自己的暴怒吓坏了；可催眠师躺着不动了，忽然，从他额头撞上一张凳子的那个白色小伤口处，渗出了一道匆匆的血红。登顿在他身旁站了一会儿，犹豫不决，浑身发抖。

===Original===
A fear of the consequences entered his gently nurtured mind. He turned towards the door. “No,” he said aloud, and came back to the middle of the room. Overcoming the instinctive repugnance of one who had seen no act of violence in all his life before, he knelt down beside his antagonist and felt his heart. Then he peered at the wound. He rose quietly and looked about him. He began to see more of the situation.

When presently the hypnotist recovered his senses, his head ached severely, his back was against Denton’s knees and Denton was sponging his face.

The hypnotist did not speak. But presently he indicated by a gesture that in his opinion he had been sponged enough. “Let me get up,” he said.

“Not yet,” said Denton.

“You have assaulted me, you scoundrel!”

“We are alone,” said Denton, “and the door is secure.”

There was an interval of thought.

“Unless I sponge,” said Denton, “your forehead will develop a tremendous bruise.”

“You can go on sponging,” said the hypnotist sulkily.

There was another pause.

“We might be in the Stone Age,” said the hypnotist. “Violence! Struggle!”

“In the Stone Age no man dared to come between man and woman,” said Denton.

The hypnotist thought again.

“What are you going to do?” he asked.

“While you were insensible I found the girl’s address on your tablets. I did not know it before. I telephoned. She will be here soon. Then—”

“She will bring her chaperone.”

“That is all right.”

“But what—? I don’t see. What do you mean to do?”

“I looked about for a weapon also. It is an astonishing thing how few weapons there are nowadays. If you consider that in the Stone Age men owned scarcely anything *but* weapons. I hit at last upon this lamp. I have wrenched off the wires and things, and I hold it so.” He extended it over the hypnotist’s shoulders. “With that I can quite easily smash your skull. I *will*—unless you do as I tell you.”

===Chinese===
对后果的恐惧，潜入了他这颗自幼锦衣玉养的心。他转身朝门口走去。"不，"他出声说道，又走回屋子当中。他克服了一个平生从未见过暴力之举的人天生的厌恶，在对手身旁跪下，摸了摸他的心口。然后他仔细看了看那伤口。他静静地站起身，环顾四周。他渐渐看清了局势的更多端倪。

过了片刻，催眠师苏醒了过来；他头疼欲裂，背靠在登顿的膝上，登顿正为他擦着脸。

催眠师没有说话。但过了一会儿，他做了个手势，意思是依他看擦得够了。"让我起来，"他说。

"还不行，"登顿说。

"你动手打人，你这恶棍！"

"这里只有我们两个，"登顿说，"门是闩好的。"

有一阵思索的间隔。

"要是不擦，"登顿说，"您额头上要起一个老大的青包。"

"那你尽管擦下去吧，"催眠师没好气地说。

又是一阵沉默。

"我们简直像回到了石器时代，"催眠师说，"暴力！厮打！"

"在石器时代，可没有人敢插到一对男女之间，"登顿说。

催眠师又想了想。

"你打算怎么办？"他问。

"趁你昏迷的时候，我在你的记事板上找到了那位姑娘的住址。我原本不知道。我打了电话。她很快就到。那时——"

"她会带着她的女伴。"

"那正好。"

"可——？我不明白。你打算干什么？"

"我还找过一件家伙。如今这世上家伙之少，可真叫人惊奇。要知道在石器时代，人们所有的，几乎没有别的——便只是家伙。我末了找到了这盏灯。我把那些电线之类都拧掉了，是这样拿在手里的。"他把灯伸到催眠师的肩膀上方。"用这盏灯，我要砸碎你的脑壳，轻而易举。我一定砸——除非你照我吩咐的做。"

===Original===
“Violence is no remedy,” said the hypnotist, quoting from the *Modern Man’s Book of Moral Maxims*.

“It’s an undesirable disease,” said Denton.

“Well?”

“You will tell that chaperone you are going to order the girl to marry that knobby little brute with the red hair and ferrety eyes. I believe that’s how things stand?”

“Yes—that’s how things stand.”

“And, pretending to do that, you will restore her memory of me.”

“It’s unprofessional.”

“Look here! If I cannot have that girl I would rather die than not. I don’t propose to respect your little fancies. If anything goes wrong you shall not live five minutes. This is a rude makeshift of a weapon, and it may quite conceivably be painful to kill you. But I will. It is unusual, I know, nowadays to do things like this—mainly because there is so little in life that is worth being violent about.”

“The chaperone will see you directly she comes—”

“I shall stand in that recess. Behind you.”

The hypnotist thought. “You are a determined young man,” he said, “and only half civilised. I have tried to do my duty to my client, but in this affair you seem likely to get your own way…”

“You mean to deal straightly.”

“I’m not going to risk having my brains scattered in a petty affair like this.”

“And afterwards?”

“There is nothing a hypnotist or doctor hates so much as a scandal. I at least am no savage. I am annoyed… But in a day or so I shall bear no malice…”

“Thank you. And now that we understand each other, there is no necessity to keep you sitting any longer on the floor.”

===Chinese===
"暴力绝非良方，"催眠师说，引用《现代人格言录》（*Modern Man’s Book of Moral Maxims*）里的话。

"它是一种不可取的疾病，"登顿说。

"怎么样？"

"您要去告诉那位女伴，您打算吩咐那姑娘嫁给那个红头发、黄鼠狼眼、疙疙瘩瘩的小矮子。情形是这样吧？"

"是——情形是这样。"

"然后，您假装照此吩咐，却把关于我的记忆还给她。"

"这有违职业道德。"

"您听好！我若不能得到那位姑娘，宁可死。我不打算尊重您那些个小讲究。要是有半点差池，您活不过五分钟。这件家伙是粗糙的、临时的，拿它打死人说不定会很疼。可我一定打死您。我知道，如今做这种事是不合时宜的——主要是因为这世上没有什么东西值得为之动粗。"

"那女伴一来便会看见您——"

"我便站在那个凹槽里。在您身后。"

催眠师想了想。"您是个下定决心的人，"他说，"而且只有半开化。我对主顾已尽了本分，可这一回，看来您是要如愿以偿了……"

"您是说，打算照规矩办。"

"我可不愿为这样一桩小事，赔上自己这一脑袋。"

"那以后呢？"

"催眠师也好，大夫也罢，最恨的莫过于一桩丑闻。我至少不是蛮子。我恼火得很……可一两天后，我便记不得什么仇了……"

"多谢。既然我们彼此心照不宣，也就不必再让您坐地上了。"

## I Ugh-Lomi and Uya / 一、乌格-洛米与乌雅

===Original===
This story is of a time beyond the memory of man, before the beginning of history, a time when one might have walked dryshod from France (as we call it now) to England, and when a broad and sluggish Thames flowed through its marshes to meet its father Rhine, flowing through a wide and level country that is under water in these latter days, and which we know by the name of the North Sea. In that remote age the valley which runs along the foot of the Downs did not exist, and the south of Surrey was a range of hills, fir-clad on the middle slopes, and snow-capped for the better part of the year. The cores of its summits still remain as Leith Hill, and Pitch Hill, and Hindhead. On the lower slopes of the range, below the grassy spaces where the wild horses grazed, were forests of yew and sweet-chestnut and elm, and the thickets and dark places hid the grizzly bear and the hyena, and the grey apes clambered through the branches. And still lower amidst the woodland and marsh and open grass along the Wey did this little drama play itself out to the end that I have to tell. Fifty thousand years ago it was, fifty thousand years—if the reckoning of geologists is correct.

And in those days the springtime was as joyful as it is now, and sent the blood coursing in just the same fashion. The afternoon sky was blue with piled white clouds sailing through it, and the southwest wind came like a soft caress. The new-come swallows drove to and fro. The reaches of the river were spangled with white ranunculus, the marshy places were starred with lady’s-smock and lit with marshmallow wherever the regiments of the sedges lowered their swords, and the northward-moving hippopotami, shiny black monsters, sporting clumsily, came floundering and blundering through it all, rejoicing dimly and possessed with one clear idea, to splash the river muddy.

===Chinese===
本篇故事发生在一个远超出人类记忆、历史尚未开端的时代；那时人可以不湿脚地从法国（我们如今的叫法）一直走到英国；宽阔而迟缓的泰晤士河穿过沼泽，去与它的父亲莱茵河相会，流经的那片辽阔平展的原野，到了我们这些后世已被淹没水下，我们称之为北海。在那个遥远的年代，沿唐斯丘陵（the Downs）山脚伸展的那条河谷尚不存在，萨里（Surrey）的南部是一道山脉，山腰披满冷杉，一年中大半时间都顶着积雪。几座山顶的核心至今犹存，便是莱思山（Leith Hill）、皮奇山（Pitch Hill）和欣德黑德（Hindhead）。在山脉下方更低的坡地上，那野马啃食的草地下方，是紫杉、甜栗和榆树的森林，灌木丛和阴暗处藏着灰熊和鬣狗，灰猿在枝叶间攀爬。再往下，在韦河（the Wey）两岸的林地、沼泽与开阔草地上，这场我不得不讲述的小小戏剧，便演到了它的结局。那是五万年前的事了，五万年前——倘若地质学家的估算不差。

那时节，春天也如今日这般令人欢喜，使血液以同样的方式奔流。午后的天空碧蓝，堆叠的白云在其中航行，西南风像轻柔的抚摸般吹来。新到的燕子穿梭往返。河面铺满白色的毛茛（ranunculus），沼泽之地星布着碎米荠（lady’s-smock），凡莎草军团垂下它们剑刃的地方，都点亮了药用蜀葵（marshmallow）；向北迁徙的河马——油亮乌黑的庞然大物——笨拙地嬉戏着，一路踉踉跄跄、跌跌撞撞地闯过这一切，昏昏地欢喜着，心里只揣着一个清晰的念头：把河水搅个浑。

===Original===
Up the river and well in sight of the hippopotami, a number of little buff-coloured animals dabbled in the water. There was no fear, no rivalry, and no enmity between them and the hippopotami. As the great bulks came crashing through the reeds and smashed the mirror of the water into silvery splashes, these little creatures shouted and gesticulated with glee. It was the surest sign of high spring. “Boloo!” they cried. “Baayah. Boloo!” They were the children of the men folk, the smoke of whose encampment rose from the knoll at the river’s bend. Wild-eyed youngsters they were, with matted hair and little broad-nosed impish faces, covered (as some children are covered even nowadays) with a delicate down of hair. They were narrow in the loins and long in the arms. And their ears had no lobes, and had little pointed tips, a thing that still, in rare instances, survives. Stark-naked vivid little gipsies, as active as monkeys and as full of chatter, though a little wanting in words.

Their elders were hidden from the wallowing hippopotami by the crest of the knoll. The human squatting-place was a trampled area among the dead brown fronds of Royal Fern, through which the crosiers of this year’s growth were unrolling to the light and warmth. The fire was a smouldering heap of char, light grey and black, replenished by the old women from time to time with brown leaves. Most of the men were asleep—they slept sitting with their foreheads on their knees. They had killed that morning a good quarry, enough for all, a deer that had been wounded by hunting dogs; so that there had been no quarrelling among them, and some of the women were still gnawing the bones that lay scattered about. Others were making a heap of leaves and sticks to feed Brother Fire when the darkness came again, that he might grow strong and tall therewith, and guard them against the beasts. And two were piling flints that they brought, an armful at a time, from the bend of the river where the children were at play.

===Chinese===
在河的上游、离河马们视野不远的地方，有几只浅黄褐色的小兽在水里戏水。它们与河马之间既无恐惧，也无争竞，更无敌意。当那些硕大的身躯哗啦哗啦地撞穿芦苇、把水面的镜子击碎成银光闪闪的水花时，这些小生灵便欢叫着、比划着，雀跃不已。这是暮春时节最确凿的征兆。“波卢！”他们喊，“巴雅。波卢！”他们是男人族的孩子们，他们营地的炊烟从河弯处的小丘上升起。他们是些眼睛野野的小家伙，头发纠结，长着宽鼻子的小精怪似的脸，身上覆着一层细细的绒毛（如今有些孩子也是如此）。他们腰身窄、胳膊长。耳朵没有耳垂，尖端略尖——这种特征至今偶尔仍能见到。赤条条、活灵活现的小野人，像猴子一样好动，一样爱聒噪，只是词汇还少了些。

小丘的脊背把他们的长辈与那些打滚的河马隔开，彼此看不见。人类的栖息地是一片被踩平的空地，散落在王紫萁（Royal Fern）枯褐的旧叶之间，今春新生的卷头正舒展开来，迎向光与热。火是一堆闷烧的焦炭，浅灰色与黑色相间，老妇人们时时添些褐叶进去。多数男人在睡觉——他们坐着睡，额头抵着膝盖。那天早晨他们猎到了好猎物，够众人吃的——一头被猎狗咬伤的鹿；因此他们之间没有争吵，有些女人还在啃散落一地的骨头。另一些在堆叶子和树枝，等天再黑下来时喂给火兄弟（Brother Fire），好让它由此长得又高又旺，为他们驱赶野兽。还有两人在码燧石，他们一趟一趟抱着，从孩子们玩耍的河弯处运来。

===Original===
None of these buff-skinned savages were clothed, but some wore about their hips rude girdles of adder-skin or crackling undressed hide, from which depended little bags, not made, but torn from the paws of beasts, and carrying the rudely-dressed flints that were men’s chief weapons and tools. And one woman, the mate of Uya the Cunning Man, wore a wonderful necklace of perforated fossils—that others had worn before her. Beside some of the sleeping men lay the big antlers of the elk, with the tines chipped to sharp edges, and long sticks, hacked at the ends with flints into sharp points. There was little else save these things and the smouldering fire to mark these human beings off from the wild animals that ranged the country. But Uya the Cunning did not sleep, but sat with a bone in his hand and scraped busily thereon with a flint, a thing no animal would do. He was the oldest man in the tribe, beetle-browed, prognathous, lank-armed; he had a beard and his cheeks were hairy, and his chest and arms were black with thick hair. And by virtue both of his strength and cunning he was master of the tribe, and his share was always the most and the best.

Eudena had hidden herself among the alders, because she was afraid of Uya. She was still a girl, and her eyes were bright and her smile pleasant to see. He had given her a piece of the liver, a man’s piece, and a wonderful treat for a girl to get; but as she took it the other woman with the necklace had looked at her, an evil glance, and Ugh-lomi had made a noise in his throat. At that, Uya had looked at him long and steadfastly, and Ugh-lomi’s face had fallen. And then Uya had looked at her. She was frightened and she had stolen away, while the feeding was still going on, and Uya was busy with the marrow of a bone. Afterwards he had wandered about as if looking for her. And now she crouched among the alders, wondering mightily what Uya might be doing with the flint and the bone. And Ugh-lomi was not to be seen.

===Chinese===
这些浅黄皮肤的野人无一穿衣，但有些人腰间系着蝰蛇皮或嘎吱作响的生皮粗制腰带，腰带上挂着小袋子——并非缝制，而是从野兽脚爪上撕扯下来——里面装着粗加工的燧石，那是人类的主要武器和工具。还有一个女人，是巫师乌雅（Uya the Cunning Man）的伴侣，戴着一条穿孔化石串成的奇妙项链——在她之前已有别人戴过。一些熟睡的男人身旁放着麋鹿的大角，角尖被砍出锋利的边刃；还有长棍，末端用燧石削得尖锐。除了这些东西和那堆闷烧的火，再没什么能把这些人与乡间出没的野兽区分开来。但巫师乌雅没有睡，他手里拿着一根骨头，忙着用一块燧石刮它——这是动物绝不会做的事。他是部落里最年长的人，眉骨突出如甲虫，下颌前突，胳膊瘦长；他生着胡须，双颊多毛，胸膛和胳膊被浓密的黑毛盖满。凭力气与狡黠，他是部落之主，分到的一份向来最多也最好。

尤黛娜（Eudena）藏在桤木丛里，因为她怕乌雅。她还是个少女，眼睛明亮，笑容好看。他曾给她一块肝——男人的一份，对一个女孩来说是难得的恩赏；可她接过来时，那个戴项链的女人瞪了她一眼，目光凶狠；而乌格-洛米（Ugh-lomi）则从喉咙里发出了一声响动。乌雅闻声久久地、目不转睛地盯着他看，乌格-洛米的脸沉了下来。然后乌雅又看向她。她害怕了，乘着众人还在进食、乌雅正忙着啃一根骨头的髓时，悄悄溜走了。之后他曾四处游荡，像是在找她。此刻她蜷在桤木丛中，心里七上八下，不知乌雅拿那块燧石和那根骨头要做什么。乌格-洛米则不见踪影。

===Original===
Presently a squirrel came leaping through the alders, and she lay so quiet the little man was within six feet of her before he saw her. Whereupon he dashed up a stem in a hurry and began to chatter and scold her. “What are you doing here,” he asked, “away from the other men beasts?” “Peace,” said Eudena, but he only chattered more, and then she began to break off the little black cones to throw at him. He dodged and defied her, and she grew excited and rose up to throw better, and then she saw Uya coming down the knoll. He had seen the movement of her pale arm amidst the thicket—he was very keen-eyed.

At that she forgot the squirrel and set off through the alders and reeds as fast as she could go. She did not care where she went so long as she escaped Uya. She splashed nearly knee-deep through a swampy place, and saw in front of her a slope of ferns—growing more slender and green as they passed up out of the light into the shade of the young chestnuts. She was soon amidst the trees—she was very fleet of foot, and she ran on and on until the forest was old and the vales great, and the vines about their stems where the light came were thick as young trees, and the ropes of ivy stout and tight. On she went, and she doubled and doubled again, and then at last lay down amidst some ferns in a hollow place near a thicket, and listened with her heart beating in her ears.

===Chinese===
不一会儿，一只松鼠顺着桤木丛跳过来，她一动不动地伏着，这小东西直到离她六英尺远时才看见她。于是它慌忙蹿上一根树干，开始对她喋喋不休地数落。“你在这儿做什么，”它问，“离开其他人兽这么远？”“安静点，”尤黛娜说，可它只是叫得更欢，于是她开始折下黑色的小球果掷它。它左躲右闪，向她示威，她越发起劲，站起身来好投得更准——就在这时她看见乌雅从小丘上走下来。他看见了灌木丛中她那苍白胳膊的动静——他目光极为锐利。

她当下忘了松鼠，穿过桤木和芦苇拼命逃。只要能躲开乌雅，她不在乎逃往何处。她蹚过一片沼泽，水几乎没到膝盖，看见面前是一坡蕨类——越是往上长进幼龄栗树的阴影里，就越是细嫩青翠。她很快便钻进了树林——她脚程极快——跑啊跑啊，直跑到林木苍古、山谷开阔，光照之处缠在树干上的藤蔓粗如幼树，常春藤的绳索结实紧绷。她继续奔跑，绕了几个弯，又绕了几个弯，最后才在一片灌木旁的洼地里、藏进蕨丛躺下，倾听着，心跳声直撞耳鼓。

===Original===
She heard footsteps presently rustling among the dead leaves, far off, and they died away and everything was still again, except the scandalising of the midges—for the evening was drawing on—and the incessant whisper of the leaves. She laughed silently to think the cunning Uya should go by her. She was not frightened. Sometimes, playing with the other girls and lads, she had fled into the wood, though never so far as this. It was pleasant to be hidden and alone.

She lay a long time there, glad of her escape, and then she sat up listening.

===Chinese===
过了一阵，她听见远处有脚步声簌簌地踏过枯叶，又渐渐远去，一切重归寂静——只有蠓虫们恼人的嗡嗡声（因为天色向晚了）和树叶不停的低语。她暗暗好笑，那狡黠的乌雅竟从她身边走过。她并不害怕。从前和别的女孩少年玩耍时，她也逃进过树林，只是从未跑得这么远。藏起来独自一人，倒是惬意。

她在那儿躺了很久，为脱身而欣喜，然后坐起来倾听。

===Original===
It was a rapid pattering growing louder and coming towards her, and in a little while she could hear grunting noises and the snapping of twigs. It was a drove of lean grisly wild swine. She turned about her, for a boar is an ill fellow to pass too closely, on account of the sideway slash of his tusks, and she made off slantingly through the trees. But the patter came nearer, they were not feeding as they wandered, but going fast—or else they would not overtake her—and she caught the limb of a tree, swung on to it, and ran up the stem with something of the agility of a monkey.

Down below the sharp bristling backs of the swine were already passing when she looked. And she knew the short, sharp grunts they made meant fear. What were they afraid of? A man? They were in a great hurry for just a man.

And then, so suddenly it made her grip on the branch tighten involuntarily, a fawn started in the brake and rushed after the swine. Something else went by, low and grey, with a long body; she did not know what it was, indeed she saw it only momentarily through the interstices of the young leaves; and then there came a pause.

===Chinese===
那是一阵急促的吧嗒吧嗒声，越来越响，朝她逼近，不一会儿她便听见呼噜声和折断树枝的声响。是一群瘦骨嶙峋、毛色灰暗的野猪。她转过身——公猪可不是好惹的家伙，不能靠得太近，它的獠牙斜着一挑便能伤人——便斜穿过树林逃开。可那吧嗒声越来越近，它们并非边走边吃，而是飞快地赶路——否则也追不上她——她一把抓住一根树枝，荡上去，以几分猴子的矫健攀上了树干。

她往下看时，那些猪背锋刚鬃如刺，已从下面掠过。她知道它们发出那种又短又尖的呼噜声，是表示恐惧。它们怕什么？怕人？为了一个人，它们犯不着这么狼狈。

紧接着，一只小鹿从灌木丛中惊起，追着野猪的方向逃去——这突如其来的一幕让她不由自主地握紧了树枝。随后又有什么东西低低地、灰灰地掠过，身子长长的；她不知道那是什么，事实上她只是透过嫩叶的缝隙瞥了它一瞬；接着便是一阵静默。

===Original===
She remained stiff and expectant, as rigid almost as though she was a part of the tree she clung to, peering down.

Then, far away among the trees, clear for a moment, then hidden, then visible knee-deep in ferns, then gone again, ran a man. She knew it was young Ugh-lomi by the fair colour of his hair, and there was red upon his face. Somehow his frantic flight and that scarlet mark made her feel sick. And then nearer, running heavily and breathing hard, came another man. At first she could not see, and then she saw, foreshortened and clear to her, Uya, running with great strides and his eyes staring. He was not going after Ugh-lomi. His face was white. It was Uya—*afraid*! He passed, and was still loud hearing, when something else, something large and with grizzled fur, swinging along with soft swift strides, came rushing in pursuit of him.

Eudena suddenly became rigid, ceased to breathe, her clutch convulsive, and her eyes starting.

===Chinese===
她僵着身子，屏息以待，几乎像她紧抱的那棵树的一部分，向下张望。

随后，远处林木之间，一个人跑过——时清晰可见，时隐入树后，时又在齐膝的蕨丛中现身，随即又消失。她凭着那一头浅色的头发认出那是年轻的乌格-洛米，他脸上沾着血红色。不知怎的，他那亡命奔逃的样子和那一抹猩红让她心里发紧。接着又一个人跑近了，脚步沉重，气喘吁吁。起初她看不清，然后看清了——是乌雅，透视缩短的角度下格外分明，正大步流星地跑着，两眼直瞪。他追的不是乌格-洛米。他脸色惨白。是乌雅——在*害怕*！他跑过去了，喘息声仍清晰可闻；这时又有别的东西——一个毛色灰白、体型硕大的东西——迈着柔软而迅捷的步子荡过来，紧追在他身后。

尤黛娜猛地僵住，呼吸停止，手指痉挛般抠紧，双眼瞪出。

===Original===
She had never seen the thing before, she did not even see him clearly now, but she knew at once it was the Terror of the Woodshade. His name was a legend, the children would frighten one another, frighten even themselves with his name, and run screaming to the squatting-place. No man had ever killed any of his kind. Even the mighty mammoth feared his anger. It was the grizzly bear, the lord of the world as the world went then.

As he ran he made a continuous growling grumble. “Men in my very lair! Fighting and blood. At the very mouth of my lair. Men, men, men. Fighting and blood.” For he was the lord of the wood and of the caves.

Long after he had passed she remained, a girl of stone, staring down through the branches. All her power of action had gone from her. She gripped by instinct with hands and knees and feet. It was some time before she could think, and then only one thing was clear in her mind, that the Terror was between her and the tribe—that it would be impossible to descend.

===Chinese===
她从未见过这东西，此刻也看不真切，但她一下子便认出这是“林荫之恐怖”（the Terror of the Woodshade）。它的名字是个传说，孩子们常用它的名字相互吓唬，甚至把自己也吓住，尖叫着跑回栖息地。从没有人杀死过它的同类。连威猛的猛犸象也惧怕它的怒火。它就是灰熊——在那时的世间，它是世界之主。

它一边跑，一边不停地低吼嘟囔。“竟有人闯进我的兽穴！厮杀，血腥。就在我洞穴的门口。人，人，人。厮杀和血腥。”因为它是林木与洞穴之主。

它早已跑过去了很久，她仍在那儿——一座石雕般的少女，透过枝叶向下凝望。她身上一切行动的能力都已消失。她凭本能用手、用膝、用脚紧紧攀住。好一会儿她才能思考，而脑子里清晰的只有一件事：那恐怖之物就在她和部落之间——下树是不可能的了。

===Original===
Presently when her fear was a little abated she clambered into a more comfortable position, where a great branch forked. The trees rose about her, so that she could see nothing of Brother Fire, who is black by day. Birds began to stir, and things that had gone into hiding for fear of her movements crept out…

After a time the taller branches flamed out at the touch of the sunset. High overhead the rooks, who were wiser than men, went cawing home to their squatting-places among the elms. Looking down, things were clearer and darker. Eudena thought of going back to the squatting-place; she let herself down some way, and then the fear of the Terror of the Woodshade came again. While she hesitated a rabbit squealed dismally, and she dared not descend farther.

The shadows gathered, and the deeps of the forest began stirring. Eudena went up the tree again to be nearer the light. Down below the shadows came out of their hiding-places and walked abroad. Overhead the blue deepened. A dreadful stillness came, and then the leaves began whispering.

===Chinese===
过了一阵，恐惧稍减，她爬到一个更舒适的位置，落在一根粗枝的分杈处。树木环绕着她，使她看不见火兄弟——火兄弟在白天是黑色的。鸟儿开始骚动，因她的动静而躲起来的东西也悄悄爬了出来……

过了一阵，较高的树枝在落日的触碰下燃烧起来。头顶高处，比人更聪明的秃鼻鸦呱呱叫着，飞回榆树丛中的栖息之地。往下看，一切更为清晰，也更为幽暗。尤黛娜想回栖息地去；她往下爬了一段，然而对林荫之恐怖的惧意又涌上心头。她犹豫之际，一只野兔凄厉地尖叫了一声，她便不敢再往下去了。

阴影聚拢，森林深处开始骚动。尤黛娜又爬上树，好离光近些。下面，阴影从各自的藏身处走出，四处游荡。头顶的蓝色愈发深沉。一阵可怕的寂静降临，然后树叶开始低语。

===Original===
Eudena shivered and thought of Brother Fire.

The shadows now were gathering in the trees, they sat on the branches and watched her. Branches and leaves were turned to ominous, quiet black shapes that would spring on her if she stirred. Then the white owl, flitting silently, came ghostly through the shades. Darker grew the world and darker, until the leaves and twigs against the sky were black, and the ground was hidden.

She remained there all night, an agelong vigil, straining her ears for the things that went on below in the darkness, and keeping motionless lest some stealthy beast should discover her. Man in those days was never alone in the dark, save for such rare accidents as this. Age after age he had learnt the lesson of its terror—a lesson we poor children of his have nowadays painfully to unlearn. Eudena, though in age a woman, was in heart like a little child. She kept as still, poor little animal, as a hare before it is started.

===Chinese===
尤黛娜打了个寒颤，想起了火兄弟。

此刻阴影也聚到了树上，它们蹲在枝头，注视着她。枝叶都化作不祥、寂静的黑色形影，她只要一动，它们便会扑下来。接着白色猫头鹰无声地掠过，如幽灵般穿过暮色。世界愈来愈暗，愈来愈暗，直到映着天光的叶和枝都成了黑色，地面也隐没了。

她在那儿待了整整一夜，一场漫漫的守夜，竖起耳朵倾听下面黑暗中发生的事，一动不动，免得被哪只潜行的野兽发现。那个年代，人从不在黑暗中独处，除非碰上这样罕见的意外。一个时代又一个时代，他学会了惧怕黑暗这门功课——这门功课，我们这些可怜的他的孩子，如今却不得不艰难地忘掉。尤黛娜虽按年龄已是女人，心里却仍像个小孩子。这可怜的小动物，像未受惊的野兔一般，一动不动。

===Original===
The stars gathered and watched her—her one grain of comfort. In one bright one she fancied there was something like Ugh-lomi. Then she fancied it *was* Ugh-lomi. And near him, red and duller, was Uya, and as the night passed Ugh-lomi fled before him up the sky.

She tried to see Brother Fire, who guarded the squatting-place from beasts, but he was not in sight. And far away she heard the mammoths trumpeting as they went down to the drinking-place, and once some huge bulk with heavy paces hurried along, making a noise like a calf, but what it was she could not see. But she thought from the voice it was Yaaa the rhinoceros, who stabs with his nose, goes always alone, and rages without cause.

At last the little stars began to hide, and then the larger ones. It was like all the animals vanishing before the Terror. The Sun was coming, lord of the sky, as the grizzly was lord of the forest. Eudena wondered what would happen if one star stayed behind. And then the sky paled to the dawn.

===Chinese===
群星聚拢，注视着她——这是她仅有的一丝慰藉。在一颗明亮的星上，她恍惚觉得有点像乌格-洛米。然后她恍惚觉得那*便是*乌格-洛米。在他附近，红红的、黯淡些的，是乌雅；随着夜色流转，乌格-洛米在天上逃在他前面。

她想看看火兄弟——它替栖息地驱赶野兽——却看不见它。她远远听见猛犸象下到饮水处时发出的号角般的鸣叫；还有一次，一个步履沉重的庞然巨物匆匆走过，发出像小牛犊一样的声音，可她看不见那是什么。但从声音她猜那是亚阿（Yaaa），那头犀牛——它用鼻子戳人，永远独来独往，无端无故便会暴怒。

终于小星开始隐去，然后是更大的星。就像所有动物在恐怖之物面前纷纷消失。太阳要出来了——天空之主，一如灰熊是森林之主。尤黛娜想着，假如有一颗星留下来不走，会怎样呢？然后天空泛白，化为黎明。

===Original===
When the daylight came the fear of lurking things passed, and she could descend. She was stiff, but not so stiff as you would have been, dear young lady (by virtue of your upbringing), and as she had not been trained to eat at least once in three hours, but instead had often fasted three days, she did not feel uncomfortably hungry. She crept down the tree very cautiously, and went her way stealthily through the wood, and not a squirrel sprang or deer started but the terror of the grizzly bear froze her marrow.

Her desire was now to find her people again. Her dread of Uya the Cunning was consumed by a greater dread of loneliness. But she had lost her direction. She had run heedlessly overnight, and she could not tell whether the squatting-place was sunward or where it lay. Ever and again she stopped and listened, and at last, very far away, she heard a measured chinking. It was so faint even in the morning stillness that she could tell it must be far away. But she knew the sound was that of a man sharpening a flint.

Presently the trees began to thin out, and then came a regiment of nettles barring the way. She turned aside, and then she came to a fallen tree that she knew, with a noise of bees about it. And so presently she was in sight of the knoll, very far off, and the river under it, and the children and the hippopotami just as they had been yesterday, and the thin spire of smoke swaying in the morning breeze. Far away by the river was the cluster of alders where she had hidden. And at the sight of that the fear of Uya returned, and she crept into a thicket of bracken, out of which a rabbit scuttled, and lay awhile to watch the squatting-place.

===Chinese===
天亮了，对潜伏之物的那种恐惧过去了，她可以下树了。她身子僵硬，但不像您，亲爱的年轻小姐，会那样僵硬（您是娇生惯养的）；而且她不曾受过每三个小时至少进食一次的训练，反倒常常连饿三天，所以并不觉得怎么饿得难受。她小心翼翼地从树上爬下来，蹑手蹑脚地穿过树林——可无论是松鼠一蹦还是小鹿一惊，灰熊之恐都令她骨髓发凉。

此刻她只想重新找到自己的人。对巫师乌雅的畏惧，被一种更大的、对孤独的恐惧吞没了。可她迷失了方向。昨夜她慌不择路地奔逃，如今已分不清栖息地是在朝阳的那一侧还是何处。她不时停下倾听，终于，在极远的地方，她听见一阵有节奏的叮叮声。那声音即便在清晨的寂静中也十分微弱，她便知那一定离得很远。但她听得出，那是有人在磨利燧石。

渐渐地，树木稀疏起来，接着是一大片荨麻挡住去路。她绕开，又来到一棵她认识的倒木前，上面嗡嗡地绕着蜜蜂。就这样，她远远看见了那座小丘，丘下的河流，孩子们和河马还如昨日一般；一缕细细的炊烟在晨风中摇曳。再远处河边，便是她昨日藏身的那丛桤木。一看见那丛桤木，对乌雅的畏惧又回来了，她爬进一片欧洲蕨丛中——一只野兔从中窜了出来——她伏了一会儿，观察着栖息地。

===Original===
The men were mostly out of sight, saving Wau, the flint-chopper; and at that she felt safer. They were away hunting food, no doubt. Some of the women, too, were down in the stream, stooping intent, seeking mussels, crayfish, and water-snails, and at the sight of their occupation Eudena felt hungry. She rose, and ran through the fern, designing to join them. As she went she heard a voice among the bracken calling softly. She stopped. Then suddenly she heard a rustle behind her, and turning, saw Ugh-lomi rising out of the fern. There were streaks of brown blood and dirt on his face, and his eyes were fierce, and the white stone of Uya, the white Fire Stone, that none but Uya dared to touch, was in his hand. In a stride he was beside her, and gripped her arm. He swung her about, and thrust her before him towards the woods. “Uya,” he said, and waved his arms about. She heard a cry, looked back, and saw all the women standing up, and two wading out of the stream. Then came a nearer howling, and the old woman with the beard, who watched the fire on the knoll, was waving her arms, and Wau, the man who had been chipping the flint, was getting to his feet. The little children too were hurrying and shouting.

“Come!” said Ugh-lomi, and dragged her by the arm.

She still did not understand.

“Uya has called the death word,” said Ugh-lomi, and she glanced back at the screaming curve of figures, and understood.

===Chinese===
男人们大多看不见了，只有砍燧石的沃（Wau）还在；这让她安心了些。他们想必是外出打猎觅食去了。一些女人在河里弯腰专注地摸着河蚌、螯虾和水蜗牛，看见他们这营生，尤黛娜也觉饿了。她站起来，穿过蕨丛，打算加入他们。正走着，她听见蕨丛中有人轻声唤她。她停下。紧接着听见身后一阵窸窣，回头一看，是乌格-洛米从蕨丛中冒出来。他脸上沾着褐色的血污，目光凶狠；乌雅那块白石——那块白色的火石（Fire Stone），除了乌雅谁也不敢碰的——就在他手里。他一步跨到她身旁，抓住她的胳膊。他把她一转，推着她往树林那边走。“乌雅，”他说，挥动双臂比划着。她听见一声喊，回头一看，所有女人都站了起来，两个正从河里蹚出来。接着是更近处的嚎叫，看守丘顶火堆的长胡子老妇挥着胳膊；一直在削燧石的那个男人——沃——也站了起来。小孩子们也跑着喊着。

“快走！”乌格-洛米说，拽着她的胳膊。

她还是不明白。

“乌雅已经喊出了死亡判词（death word），”乌格-洛米说。她回头瞥了一眼那尖叫着的、弯弧般的人群，明白了。

===Original===
Wau and all the women and children were coming towards them, a scattered array of buff shock-headed figures, howling, leaping, and crying. Over the knoll two youths hurried. Down among the ferns to the right came a man, heading them off from the wood. Ugh-lomi left her arm, and the two began running side by side, leaping the bracken and stepping clear and wide. Eudena, knowing her fleetness and the fleetness of Ugh-lomi, laughed aloud at the unequal chase. They were an exceptionally straight-limbed couple for those days.

They soon cleared the open, and drew near the wood of chestnut-trees again—neither afraid now because neither was alone. They slackened their pace, already not excessive. And suddenly Eudena cried and swerved aside, pointing, and looking up through the tree-stems. Ugh-lomi saw the feet and legs of men running towards him. Eudena was already running off at a tangent. And as he too turned to follow her they heard the voice of Uya coming through the trees, and roaring out his rage at them.

Then terror came in their hearts, not the terror that numbs, but the terror that makes one silent and swift. They were cut off now on two sides. They were in a sort of corner of pursuit. On the right hand, and near by them, came the men swift and heavy, with bearded Uya, antler in hand, leading them; and on the left, scattered as one scatters corn, yellow dashes among the fern and grass, ran Wau and the women; and even the little children from the shallow had joined the chase. The two parties converged upon them. Off they went, with Eudena ahead.

===Chinese===
沃和所有女人孩子都朝他们涌来——一群散乱的浅黄皮肤、蓬头乱发的人影，嚎着，跳着，叫着。两个少年从小丘那边匆匆赶来。右边蕨丛中下来一个男人，截断了他们往树林的去路。乌格-洛米松开她的胳膊，两人并肩奔跑起来，跃过蕨丛，步子又大又稳。尤黛娜深知自己的脚程和乌格-洛米的脚程，对这场力量悬殊的追逐放声大笑。在那年代，他们俩算是四肢格外挺直的一对。

他们很快穿过开阔地，又一次接近了那片栗树林——如今两人都不怕了，因为谁也不是孤身一人。他们放慢了脚步——本就跑得不快。忽然尤黛娜叫了一声，斜斜地闪开，伸手指着，抬头透过树干望去。乌格-洛米看见有人的脚和腿正朝他跑来。尤黛娜已斜着切了出去。他转身要追她时，听见乌雅的声音穿过树林传来，朝他们咆哮着怒火。

接着恐惧钻进了他们的心——不是那种令人麻木的恐惧，而是叫人噤声、叫人迅捷的恐惧。他们此刻两面受堵。他们处在一种被三面合围的角落里。右边，离他们不远，男人们又快又重地扑来，为首的是手执鹿角的留胡子乌雅；左边，像撒谷子一般散开，蕨与草之间闪动着一道道黄色身影，是沃和女人们；连浅水处的小孩子们也加入了追逐。两拨人朝他们合拢。他们飞奔，尤黛娜在前。

===Original===
They knew there was no mercy for them. There was no hunting so sweet to these ancient men as the hunting of men. Once the fierce passion of the chase was lit, the feeble beginnings of humanity in them were thrown to the winds. And Uya in the night had marked Ugh-lomi with the death word. Ugh-lomi was the day’s quarry, the appointed feast.

They ran straight—it was their only chance—taking whatever ground came in the way—a spread of stinging nettles, an open glade, a clump of grass out of which a hyena fled snarling. Then woods again, long stretches of shady leaf-mould and moss under the green trunks. Then a stiff slope, tree-clad, and long vistas of trees, a glade, a succulent green area of black mud, a wide open space again, and then a clump of lacerating brambles, with beast tracks through it. Behind them the chase trailed out and scattered, with Uya ever at their heels. Eudena kept the first place, running light and with her breath easy, for Ugh-lomi carried the Fire Stone in his hand.

It told on his pace—not at first, but after a time. His footsteps behind her suddenly grew remote. Glancing over her shoulder as they crossed another open space, Eudena saw that Ugh-lomi was many yards behind her, and Uya close upon him, with antler already raised in the air to strike him down. Wau and the others were but just emerging from the shadow of the woods.

===Chinese===
他们知道不会有什么怜悯。对这些远古之人而言，再没有哪种狩猎比猎杀同类更让他们快意。一旦追逐的狂暴激情被点燃，他们身上那点薄弱的人性开端便被抛到九霄云外。而乌雅在夜里已经给乌格-洛米下了死亡判词。乌格-洛米便是今日的猎物，是预定的盛宴。

他们一路直奔——这是他们唯一的生机——遇到什么地势便踏过去：一片刺人的荨麻、一片开阔林地、一丛草——一只鬣狗咆哮着从中窜出。然后又是树林，绿树干下大片阴凉的腐叶土和苔藓。接着是一道陡坡，林木覆盖，长长的林间纵深；一片林中空地；一片多汁翠绿的黑泥湿地；又是一片开阔地；然后是一丛割人的荆棘，其中有野兽踩出的小径。身后，追逐拖长、散开，而乌雅始终紧追不舍。尤黛娜跑在头里，脚步轻盈，呼吸从容，因为火石在乌格-洛米手里。

这影响了他的速度——起初不觉，过一会儿便显现了。他在她身后的脚步声突然变得遥远。穿过又一片开阔地时她回头一瞥，看见乌格-洛米已落后许多码，而乌雅已逼近他，鹿角已高高举起要将他打翻。沃和其余的人则刚刚从林荫中现身。

===Original===
Seeing Ugh-lomi in peril, Eudena ran sideways, looking back, threw up her arms and cried aloud, just as the antler flew. And young Ugh-lomi, expecting this and understanding her cry, ducked his head, so that the missile merely struck his scalp lightly, making but a trivial wound, and flew over him. He turned forthwith, the quartzite Fire Stone in both hands, and hurled it straight at Uya’s body as he ran loose from the throw. Uya shouted, but could not dodge it. It took him under the ribs, heavy and flat, and he reeled and went down without a cry. Ugh-lomi caught up the antler—one tine of it was tipped with his own blood—and came running on again with a red trickle just coming out of his hair.

Uya rolled over twice, and lay a moment before he got up, and then he did not run fast. The colour of his face was changed. Wau overtook him, and then others, and he coughed and laboured in his breath. But he kept on.

At last the two fugitives gained the bank of the river, where the stream ran deep and narrow, and they still had fifty yards in hand of Wau, the foremost pursuer, the man who made the smiting-stones. He carried one, a large flint, the shape of an oyster and double the size, chipped to a chisel edge, in either hand.

===Chinese===
见乌格-洛米处境危急，尤黛娜侧身跑去，回头，双臂一挥，大声喊叫——就在鹿角飞出的一瞬。年轻的乌格-洛米早料到这一着，听得懂她的呼喊，便把头一低，那飞来之物只轻轻擦过他的头皮，划出一道微不足道的伤口，从头顶飞了过去。他当即转身，双手举起那块石英岩火石，在乌雅那一掷之后脚步松懈之时，直直朝他身上砸去。乌雅喊了一声，却躲不开。那石沉重而平钝地击中他的肋下，他一个趔趄，一声不吭地倒了下去。乌格-洛米抄起鹿角——其中一个尖叉上沾着他自己的血——又向前跑去，一缕殷红正从发间渗出。

乌雅连翻了两个身，躺了一阵才爬起来，爬起来之后也跑不快。他脸色变了。沃追上了他，然后是别的人；他咳着，喘得艰难。可他仍不停步。

终于两个逃亡者到了河岸，那儿河水又深又窄，他们仍领先追在最前的沃——那个造击石（smiting-stones）的人——五十码。沃一手一块燧石，形状像牡蛎、却比牡蛎大一倍，被砍出凿子般的锋刃。

===Original===
They sprang down the steep bank into the stream, rushed through the water, swam the deep current in two or three strokes, and came out wading again, dripping and refreshed, to clamber up the farther bank. It was undermined, and with willows growing thickly therefrom, so that it needed clambering. And while Eudena was still among the silvery branches and Ugh-lomi still in the water—for the antler had encumbered him—Wau came up against the sky on the opposite bank, and the smiting-stone, thrown cunningly, took the side of Eudena’s knee. She struggled to the top and fell.

They heard the pursuers shout to one another, and Ugh-lomi climbing to her and moving jerkily to mar Wau’s aim, felt the second smiting-stone graze his ear, and heard the water splash below him.

Then it was Ugh-lomi, the stripling, proved himself to have come to man’s estate. For running on, he found Eudena fell behind, limping, and at that he turned, and crying savagely and with a face terrible with sudden wrath and trickling blood, ran swiftly past her back to the bank, whirling the antler round his head. And Eudena kept on, running stoutly still, though she must needs limp at every step, and the pain was already sharp.

===Chinese===
他们跳下陡岸冲进溪流，蹚过浅水，两三下便游过深流，又蹚着水出来，浑身滴着水，神清气爽，去爬对岸。对岸被水掏空了根，上面密密地长着柳树，得手脚并用地爬。尤黛娜还在银色的枝条间，乌格-洛米仍在水中——鹿角碍着他——沃已在对岸映着天光现身，那块击石投得刁钻，正中尤黛娜膝盖外侧。她挣扎到岸顶，倒了下去。

他们听见追兵彼此呼喊，乌格-洛米爬到她身边，急促地移动以扰乱沃的准头——他觉得第二块击石擦过他的耳朵，听见下面水花溅起的声音。

就在此刻，少年乌格-洛米证明了自己已是一个真正的男人。因为再往前跑，他发现尤黛娜落在了后面，一瘸一拐；他便转过身，发出野蛮的呼号，脸上骤然的狂怒与淋漓的血使它狰狞可怖——他飞快地从她身旁掠过，退回岸边，鹿角在头顶呼呼生风地抡着。而尤黛娜仍向前行，跑得仍算稳当，尽管每一步都不得不一瘸一拐，疼痛已然尖锐。

===Original===
So that Wau, rising over the edge and clutching the straight willow branches, saw Ugh-lomi towering over him, gigantic against the blue; saw his whole body swing round, and the grip of his hands upon the antler. The edge of the antler came sweeping through the air, and he saw no more. The water under the osiers whirled and eddied and went crimson six feet down the stream. Uya following stopped knee-high across the stream, and the man who was swimming turned about.

The other men who trailed after—they were none of them very mighty men (for Uya was more cunning than strong, brooking no sturdy rivals)—slackened momentarily at the sight of Ugh-lomi standing there above the willows, bloody and terrible, between them and the halting girl, with the huge antler waving in his hand. It seemed as though he had gone into the water a youth, and come out of it a man full grown.

He knew what there was behind him. A broad stretch of grass, and then a thicket, and in that Eudena could hide. That was clear in his mind, though his thinking powers were too feeble to see what should happen thereafter. Uya stood knee-deep, undecided and unarmed. His heavy mouth hung open, showing his canine teeth, and he panted heavily. His side was flushed and bruised under the hair. The other man beside him carried a sharpened stick. The rest of the hunters came up one by one to the top of the bank, hairy, long-armed men clutching flints and sticks. Two ran off along the bank down stream, and then clambered to the water, where Wau had come to the surface struggling weakly. Before they could reach him he went under again. Two others threatened Ugh-lomi from the bank.

===Chinese===
于是沃攀上沿、抓住笔直的柳枝时，看见乌格-洛米高耸在他头顶，衬着蓝天显得巨大；他看见他整个身子转了过来，看见他双手握住鹿角。鹿角的锋刃横扫过空中——他便什么也看不见了。柳树下的河水打着旋儿，泛起涡流，朝下游六英尺都被染成了殷红。跟在后面的乌雅在齐膝的河水中停下，那个正在泅水的人也转过身来。

其余跟在后头的人——他们没有一个是多么强悍的汉子（因为乌雅智胜于力，容不得健壮的对手）——见乌格-洛米立在柳树之上，浑身血污、可怖可畏，挡在他们和那个跛行的少女之间，手里挥着那巨大的鹿角，都不由得迟疑了一瞬。仿佛他下水时还是个少年，出水时已是个成年的汉子。

他清楚身后有什么。一片宽阔的草地，然后是一片灌木丛，尤黛娜可以藏身其中。这一点他脑中清晰，尽管他的思维能力太弱，看不见此后会发生什么。乌雅站在齐膝的水中，举棋不定，手无寸铁。他那厚重的嘴半张着，露出犬齿，喘得厉害。肋下那一片皮毛下又红又青。他旁边的另一个男人拿着一根削尖的棍子。其余猎手一个接一个登上岸顶，都是些多毛、长臂的人，手里攥着燧石和木棍。两人沿岸向下游跑去，然后下到水里——沃刚浮出水面，虚弱地挣扎着。他们还没够着他，他又沉了下去。另有两人从岸上威胁着乌格-洛米。

===Original===
He answered back, shouts, vague insults, gestures. Then Uya, who had been hesitating, roared with rage, and whirling his fists plunged into the water. His followers splashed after him.

Ugh-lomi glanced over his shoulder and found Eudena already vanished into the thicket. He would perhaps have waited for Uya, but Uya preferred to spar in the water below him until the others were beside him. Human tactics in those days, in all serious fighting, were the tactics of the pack. Prey that turned at bay they gathered around and rushed. Ugh-lomi felt the rush coming, and hurling the antler at Uya, turned about and fled.

When he halted to look back from the shadow of the thicket, he found only three of his pursuers had followed him across the river, and they were going back again. Uya, with a bleeding mouth, was on the farther side of the stream again, but lower down, and holding his hand to his side. The others were in the river dragging something to shore. For a time at least the chase was intermitted.

===Chinese===
他回敬过去——喊声、含糊的辱骂、手势。然后乌雅不再犹豫，狂怒地咆哮一声，抡着双拳冲进水里。他的追随者们哗啦啦跟着下水。

乌格-洛米回头一瞥，见尤黛娜已消失在灌木丛中。他本可以等乌雅，但乌雅宁愿在他下方的水里周旋，等其他人聚到他身边。那个年代，人类在一切正经搏斗中所用的战术，便是狼群之术。被围困回身的猎物，他们便围而攻之。乌格-洛米感到那一拥而上的一刻逼近，便将鹿角朝乌雅掷去，转身逃了。

他从灌木丛的阴影里停步回头望，发现追他过河的只有三人，而他们正在折返。乌雅嘴角淌血，又回到了河对岸，但更靠下游，一手按着肋下。其余的人正在河里把什么东西往岸上拖。至少眼下，追逐暂告一段落。

===Original===
Ugh-lomi stood watching for a space, and snarled at the sight of Uya. Then he turned and plunged into the thicket.

In a minute, Eudena came hastening to join him, and they went on hand in hand. He dimly perceived the pain she suffered from the cut and bruised knee, and chose the easier ways. But they went on all that day, mile after mile, through wood and thicket, until at last they came to the chalkland, open grass with rare woods of beech, and the birch growing near water, and they saw the Wealden mountains nearer, and groups of horses grazing together. They went circumspectly, keeping always near thicket and cover, for this was a strange region—even its ways were strange. Steadily the ground rose, until the chestnut forests spread wide and blue below them, and the Thames marshes shone silvery, high and far. They saw no men, for in those days men were still only just come into this part of the world, and were moving but slowly along the river-ways. Towards evening they came on the river again, but now it ran in a gorge, between high cliffs of white chalk that sometimes overhung it. Down the cliffs was a scrub of birches and there were many birds there. And high up the cliff was a little shelf by a tree, whereon they clambered to pass the night.

They had had scarcely any food; it was not the time of year for berries, and they had no time to go aside to snare or waylay. They tramped in a hungry weary silence, gnawing at twigs and leaves. But over the surface of the cliffs were a multitude of snails, and in a bush were the freshly laid eggs of a little bird, and then Ugh-lomi threw at and killed a squirrel in a beech-tree, so that at last they fed well. Ugh-lomi watched during the night, his chin on his knees; and he heard young foxes crying hard by, and the noise of mammoths down the gorge, and the hyenas yelling and laughing far away. It was chilly, but they dared not light a fire. Whenever he dozed, his spirit went abroad, and straightway met with the spirit of Uya, and they fought. And always Ugh-lomi was paralysed so that he could not smite nor run, and then he would awake suddenly. Eudena, too, dreamt evil things of Uya, so that they both awoke with the fear of him in their hearts, and by the light of the dawn they saw a woolly rhinoceros go blundering down the valley.

===Chinese===
乌格-洛米站住看了一阵，看见乌雅便龇牙低吼。然后他转身钻进了灌木丛。

不一会儿，尤黛娜匆匆赶来与他会合，两人手拉手继续走。他隐隐察觉她那又割又磕的膝盖所受的苦，便拣好走的路。可他们整整走了一天，一里又一里，穿过树林与灌木丛，直到最后来到白垩地带——开阔的草地，偶尔一片山毛榉林，近水处长着桦树——他们望见韦尔德山脉（the Wealden mountains）更近了，还有成群结队吃草的马。他们处处小心，始终贴近灌木和掩蔽处，因为这是一片陌生的土地——连路都是陌生的。地势持续上升，直到栗树林在他们脚下铺展成一片淡蓝，泰晤士河的沼泽银光闪闪，高远地在天边。他们看不见一个人影，因为在那些日子里，人类才刚刚进入世间的这一带，只是沿着河道缓缓迁移。傍晚时分，他们又走到了那条河边，但此刻河水在峡谷中奔流，两岸是高耸的白色白垩崖壁，有时崖壁悬于河上。崖下是一片桦树丛，那里有许多鸟。崖壁高处有一棵树旁的小平台，他们爬上去过夜。

他们几乎没有吃过什么；这个时节浆果还未结，他们也没有工夫绕道去下套或设伏。他们在又饿又累的沉默中跋涉，嚼着细枝和树叶。可崖壁表面有许许多多蜗牛，一丛灌木里有只小鸟新下的蛋，后来乌格-洛米又用石子打死了一只山毛榉树上的松鼠——这样他们总算吃得不错。夜里乌格-洛米守夜，下巴抵着膝盖；他听见附近小狐狸的叫声，峡谷下方猛犸象的响动，远处鬣狗的嚎笑。夜里冷，可他们不敢生火。他一打盹，灵魂便出窍，立刻与乌雅的灵魂相遇，两人厮打。而乌格-洛米每次都被定住身，既不能打也不能逃，然后便猛然惊醒。尤黛娜也梦见乌雅作祟，于是两人都怀着对乌雅的恐惧醒来，而借着晨光，他们看见一头披毛犀踉踉跄跄地走下山谷。

===Original===
During the day they caressed one another and were glad of the sunshine, and Eudena’s leg was so stiff she sat on the ledge all day. Ugh-lomi found great flints sticking out of the cliff face, greater than any he had seen, and he dragged some to the ledge and began chipping, so as to be armed against Uya when he came again. And at one he laughed heartily, and Eudena laughed, and they threw it about in derision. It had a hole in it. They stuck their fingers through it, it was very funny indeed. Then they peeped at one another through it. Afterwards, Ugh-lomi got himself a stick, and thrusting by chance at this foolish flint, the stick went in and stuck there. He had rammed it in too tightly to withdraw it. That was still stranger—scarcely funny, terrible almost, and for a time Ugh-lomi did not greatly care to touch the thing. It was as if the flint had bit and held with its teeth. But then he got familiar with the odd combination. He swung it about, and perceived that the stick with the heavy stone on the end struck a better blow than anything he knew. He went to and fro swinging it, and striking with it; but later he tired of it and threw it aside. In the afternoon he went up over the brow of the white cliff, and lay watching by a rabbit-warren until the rabbits came out to play. There were no men thereabouts, and the rabbits were heedless. He threw a smiting-stone he had made and got a kill.

That night they made a fire from flint sparks and bracken fronds, and talked and caressed by it. And in their sleep Uya’s spirit came again, and suddenly, while Ugh-lomi was trying to fight vainly, the foolish flint on the stick came into his hand, and he struck Uya with it, and behold! it killed him. But afterwards came other dreams of Uya—for spirits take a lot of killing, and he had to be killed again. Then after that the stone would not keep on the stick. He awoke tired and rather gloomy, and was sulky all the forenoon, in spite of Eudena’s kindliness, and instead of hunting he sat chipping a sharp edge to the singular flint, and looking strangely at her. Then he bound the perforated flint on to the stick with strips of rabbit skin. And afterwards he walked up and down the ledge, striking with it, and muttering to himself, and thinking of Uya. It felt very fine and heavy in the hand.

===Chinese===
白天他们相互爱抚，欢喜着阳光，尤黛娜那条腿僵得厉害，便整天坐在岩台上。乌格-洛米发现崖壁上嵌着巨大的燧石——比他见过的任何一块都大——便拖了几块回岩台，开始敲打加工，以备乌雅再来时有所凭仗。其中有一块他看了放声大笑，尤黛娜也笑了，他们把它抛来抛去，嘲弄它。那石头上有一个洞。他们把手指穿过洞去，真是有趣极了。然后他们隔着洞互相窥望。后来，乌格-洛米找了一根棍子，朝这块蠢燧石随手一戳，棍子竟戳了进去，卡住了。他塞得太紧，抽不出来了。这就更怪了——简直不好笑，几乎有点可怕，乌格-洛米有一阵子不大愿意碰这东西。仿佛那燧石用牙齿咬住了，不肯松。可后来他对这古怪的组合熟络起来。他抡着它转圈，发觉棍头上顶着一块重石，打出去比他所知的任何武器都更有力。他走来走去地抡着、敲着；可后来他厌了，把它扔到一边。下午他爬上白垩崖的崖顶，伏在一个野兔窝旁守着，等兔子出来嬉戏。附近一带没有人，兔子们毫无戒心。他用一块自制的击石掷出去，猎到了一只。

那夜他们用燧石的火花和欧洲蕨叶生了火，在火边说话、亲热。睡梦中乌雅的灵魂又来了，忽然，正当乌格-洛米徒劳地试图搏斗时，那块蠢燧石和棍子到了他手中，他用它击中乌雅——你瞧！它杀死了他。可后来又有别的关于乌雅的梦——因为灵魂是不易被杀死的，他得再被杀一次。再后来，那石头又无法固定在棍子上了。他醒来时疲惫而郁郁，整个上午都闷闷不乐，任凭尤黛娜温存相待也无济于事；他不去打猎，却坐着给那块奇特的燧石削出锋刃，怪模怪样地望着她。然后他用兔皮条把穿孔的燧石绑到棍子上。之后他在岩台上走来走去，挥着它敲打，自言自语，想着乌雅。握在手里，沉甸甸的，颇为称手。

===Original===
Several days, more than there was any counting in those days, five days, it may be, or six, did Ugh-lomi and Eudena stay on that shelf in the gorge of the river, and they lost all fear of men, and their fire burnt redly of a night. And they were very merry together; there was food every day, sweet water, and no enemies. Eudena’s knee was well in a couple of days, for those ancient savages had quick-healing flesh. Indeed, they were very happy.

On one of those days Ugh-lomi dropped a chunk of flint over the cliff. He saw it fall, and go bounding across the river bank into the river, and after laughing and thinking it over a little he tried another. This smashed a bush of hazel in the most interesting way. They spent all the morning dropping stones from the ledge, and in the afternoon they discovered this new and interesting pastime was also possible from the cliffbrow. The next day they had forgotten this delight. Or at least, it seemed they had forgotten.

But Uya came in dreams to spoil the paradise. Three nights he came fighting Ugh-lomi. In the morning after these dreams Ugh-lomi would walk up and down, threatening him and swinging the axe, and at last came the night after Ugh-lomi brained the otter, and they had feasted. Uya went too far. Ugh-lomi awoke, scowling under his heavy brows, and he took his axe, and extending his hand towards Eudena he bade her wait for him upon the ledge. Then he clambered down the white declivity, glanced up once from the foot of it and flourished his axe, and without looking back again went striding along the river bank until the overhanging cliff at the bend hid him.

===Chinese===
在那河峡的岩台上，乌格-洛米和尤黛娜住了好些日子——那年代是无从计数的，也许是五天，也许是六天——他们完全忘了对人的恐惧，夜里火堆烧得红红的。他们在一起非常快活：每天有食物，有清甜的水，没有敌人。尤黛娜的膝盖两三天便好了，因为那些远古的野人皮肉愈合极快。他们确乎非常幸福。

有一天，乌格-洛米把一块燧石从崖上推下去。他看着它落下，从河岸一路弹跳进河里；他笑了一阵，又想了想，便再试了一块。这块把一丛榛树砸得稀烂，有趣极了。他们一上午都在从岩台上往下扔石头，下午他们又发现这新鲜有趣的消遣从崖顶也能进行。第二天他们就把这份乐子忘了。至少，看起来是忘了。

可乌雅在梦里来搅扰这乐园。一连三夜他都来与乌格-洛米搏斗。做了这些梦的清晨，乌格-洛米便会走来走去，威胁着他，挥舞那把斧子；终于到了那一夜——白天乌格-洛米砸碎了一只水獭的头，他们饱餐了一顿。乌雅做得太过分了。乌格-洛米醒来，浓眉下目光阴沉；他拿起斧子，向尤黛娜伸出手，要她在岩台上等他。然后他爬下那面白色的斜坡，在坡底抬头望了一次，挥了挥斧子，便头也不回地沿岸大步走去，直到河弯处悬伸的崖壁遮住了他。

===Original===
Two days and nights did Eudena sit alone by the fire on the ledge waiting, and in the night the beasts howled over the cliffs and down the valley, and on the cliff over against her the hunched hyenas prowled black against the sky. But no evil thing came near her save fear. Once, far away, she heard the roaring of a lion, following the horses as they came northward over the grass lands with the spring. All that time she waited—the waiting that is pain.

And the third day Ugh-lomi came back, up the river. The plumes of a raven were in his hair. The first axe was red-stained, and had long dark hairs upon it, and he carried the necklace that had marked the favourite of Uya in his hand. He walked in the soft places, giving no heed to his trail. Save a raw cut below his jaw there was not a wound upon him. “Uya!” cried Ugh-lomi exultant, and Eudena saw it was well. He put the necklace on Eudena, and they ate and drank together. And after eating he began to rehearse the whole story from the beginning, when Uya had cast his eyes on Eudena, and Uya and Ugh-lomi, fighting in the forest, had been chased by the bear, eking out his scanty words with abundant pantomime, springing to his feet and whirling the stone axe round when it came to the fighting. The last fight was a mighty one, stamping and shouting, and once a blow at the fire that sent a torrent of sparks up into the night. And Eudena sat red in the light of the fire, gloating on him, her face flushed and her eyes shining, and the necklace Uya had made about her neck. It was a splendid time, and the stars that look down on us looked down on her, our ancestor—who has been dead now these fifty thousand years.

===Chinese===
两天两夜，尤黛娜独自坐在岩台的火旁等候；夜里，野兽在崖上、在谷下嚎叫；对面崖壁上，蜷缩的鬣狗映着天光，黑影般地潜行。可除了恐惧，没有任何恶物靠近她。有一次，她远远听见一头狮子的吼声，它跟着随春天北迁过草地的马群而来。那整个时段她都在等——那种便是痛苦的等待。

第三天，乌格-洛米回来了，沿河而来。他发间插着渡鸦的羽毛。那第一把斧子上染着红色，上面还有长长的深色毛发；他手里拎着那条项链——那条曾标示乌雅宠妾身份的项链。他专走软地，不留心自己的足迹。除下颌下方一道生割的伤口外，他毫发无伤。“乌雅！”乌格-洛米扬眉吐气地喊，尤黛娜一看便知事情已了。他把项链戴到尤黛娜脖子上，他们一同吃喝。吃完之后，他从头讲起整件事的来龙去脉——从乌雅如何看上尤黛娜讲起，到乌雅和乌格-洛米在森林里厮打、被熊追逐——他词汇贫乏，便用大量的比划来补充，讲到打斗处便一跃而起，抡起石斧。最后那场搏斗是一场大战，他跺脚呼喝，有一次一斧朝火堆砍去，激起一片火星飞溅入夜。尤黛娜坐在火光中，脸被映得通红，痴痴地望着他，双颊绯红，目光灼灼，脖子上戴着乌雅所造的项链。那是一段辉煌的时光，如今俯瞰我们的群星，那时也俯瞰着她——我们的祖先——她已死去五万年了。

### I / 一

===Original===
Bru-a-a-a.
I listened, not understanding.
Wa-ra-ra-ra.
"Good Lord!" said I, still only half awake. "What an infernal shindy!"
Ra-ra-ra-ra-ra-ra-ra-ra-ra Ta-ra-rra-ra.
"It's enough," said I, "to wake—" and stopped short. Where was I?
Ta-rra-rara—louder and louder.
"It's either some new invention—"
Toora-toora-toora! Deafening!
"No," said I, speaking loud in order to hear myself. "That's the Last Trump."
Tooo-rraa!

===Chinese===
呜——啊——啊——啊。
我倾听着，不明所以。
哇——啦——啦——啦。
「老天爷！」我说，仍只是半睡半醒。「好一阵要命的喧闹！」
啦——啦——啦——啦——啦——啦——啦——啦——啦，哒——啦——啦啦——啦。
「这一阵，」我说，「足以把——」便戛然而止。我在哪儿？
哒——啦啦——啦——越来越响。
「这要么是哪样新发明——」
嘟——啦——嘟——啦——嘟——啦！震耳欲聋！
「不，」我说，为了听见自己的声音而提高了嗓门。「这是最后的号角。」
嘟——啦——啊！

## Aepyornis Island / 象鸟岛

===Original===
The man with the scarred face leant over the table and looked at my bundle.

“Orchids?” he asked.

“A few,” I said.

“Cypripediums,” he said.

“Chiefly,” said I.

“Anything new? I thought not. *I* did these islands twenty-five—twenty-seven years ago. If you find anything new here—well, it’s brand new. I didn’t leave much.”

“I’m not a collector,” said I.

“I was young then,” he went on. “Lord! how I used to fly round.” He seemed to take my measure. “I was in the East Indies two years, and in Brazil seven. Then I went to Madagascar.”

“I know a few explorers by name,” I said, anticipating a yarn. “Whom did you collect for?”

“Dawson’s. I wonder if you’ve heard the name of Butcher ever?”

“Butcher—Butcher?” The name seemed vaguely present in my memory; then I recalled *Butcher v. Dawson*. “Why!” said I, “you are the man who sued them for four years’ salary—got cast away on a desert island—”

===Chinese===
脸上有疤的那人探身凑近桌子，端详着我那一捆东西。

“兰花？”他问。

“有几株。”我说。

“杓兰（Cypripedium）。”他说。

“主要是。”我说。

“有什么新货色吗？我看没有。这些岛子，是*我*在二十五——二十七年前跑过的。你要是在这儿还能找到什么新东西——那可真是全新的了。我没留下多少。”

“我不是采集客。”我说。

“我那时年轻，”他接着说，“老天！我那阵子真叫满世界飞。”他像是把我从头到脚打量了一番。“我在东印度群岛待了两年，在巴西待了七年。后来我去了马达加斯加（Madagascar）。”

“几位探险家的大名我还算略有耳闻，”我说，料想他要讲一段故事了。“你是替哪家采集的？”

“道森公司（Dawson’s）。你有没有听过布彻（Butcher）这个名字？”

“布彻——布彻？”这名字在我记忆里仿佛有点影子；接着我想起了那桩*布彻诉道森案*。“哎呀！”我说，“你就是那个人——告他们讨要四年薪水——流落到了一个荒岛上——”

===Original===
“Your servant,” said the man with the scar, bowing. “Funny case, wasn’t it? Here was me, making a little fortune on that island, doing nothing for it neither, and them quite unable to give me notice. It often used to amuse me thinking over it while I was there. I did calculations of it—big—all over the blessed atoll in ornamental figuring.”

“How did it happen?” said I. “I don’t rightly remember the case.”

“Well… You’ve heard of the Aepyornis?”

“Rather. Andrews was telling me of a new species he was working on only a month or so ago. Just before I sailed. They’ve got a thigh bone, it seems, nearly a yard long. Monster the thing must have been!”

“I believe you,” said the man with the scar. “It *was* a monster. Sindbad’s roc was just a legend of ’em. But when did they find these bones?”

“Three or four years ago—’91, I fancy. Why?”

“Why? Because *I* found them—Lord!—it’s nearly twenty years ago. If Dawson’s hadn’t been silly about that salary they might have made a perfect ring in ’em… *I* couldn’t help the infernal boat going adrift.”

He paused. “I suppose it’s the same place. A kind of swamp about ninety miles north of Antananarivo. Do you happen to know? You have to go to it along the coast by boats. You don’t happen to remember, perhaps?”

“I don’t. I fancy Andrews said something about a swamp.”

===Chinese===
“正是小的，听您差遣，”脸上有疤的人说着，鞠了一躬。“那案子挺逗的，不是吗？我在那岛上，什么也不用干，倒是积下了一笔小小的家业，而他们那边呢，压根儿没法子解雇我。我在岛上那会儿，回想起来常常觉得可乐。我还把这事算计过——算得可大啦——满那个该死的环礁上，全是我用花体字写的一笔笔账。”

“那是怎么发生的？”我说，“这案子我记不太真切了。”

“这个嘛……你听说过象鸟（Aepyornis）吗？”

“那当然。安德鲁斯（Andrews）还跟我说起他正在研究的一个新种呢，也就一个月前的事。就在我起航之前。他们弄到了一根大腿骨，看样子将近一码长。那东西生前准是个庞然大物！”

“我信你的话，”脸上有疤的人说，“它*确是*庞然大物。辛巴达（Sindbad）的大鹏（roc），不过是它们的传说罢了。可这些骨头，他们是什么时候发现的？”

“三四年以前吧——我想是’91年。怎么啦？”

“怎么啦？因为是*我*找见的——老天！——都快二十年前的事了。要是道森公司没在薪水那事上犯傻，他们本可以借此做成一桩十全十美的大买卖……*我*有什么办法呢，那条该死的船自己漂走了。”

他停了一下。“我想是同一个地方。塔那那利佛（Antananarivo）以北约九十英里的一片沼泽。你碰巧知道吗？得沿着海岸划船才能进去。你也许不记得了吧？”

“我不知道。我仿佛记得安德鲁斯说过什么沼泽的话。”

===Original===
“It must be the same. It’s on the east coast. And somehow there’s something in the water that keeps things from decaying. Like creosote it smells. It reminded me of Trinidad. Did they get any more eggs? Some of the eggs I found were a foot-and-a-half long. The swamp goes circling round, you know, and cuts off this bit. It’s mostly salt, too. Well… What a time I had of it! I found the things quite by accident. We went for eggs, me and two native chaps, in one of those rum canoes all tied together, and found the bones at the same time. We had a tent and provisions for four days, and we pitched on one of the firmer places. To think of it brings that odd tarry smell back even now. It’s funny work. You go probing into the mud with iron rods, you know. Usually the egg gets smashed. I wonder how long it is since these Aepyornises really lived. The missionaries say the natives have legends about when they were alive, but I never heard any such stories myself.1 But certainly those eggs we got were as fresh as if they had been new laid. Fresh! Carrying them down to the boat one of my nigger chaps dropped one on a rock and it smashed. How I lammed into the beggar! But sweet it was, as if it was new laid, not even smelly, and its mother dead these four hundred years, perhaps. Said a centipede had bit him. However, I’m getting off the straight with the story. It had taken us all day to dig into the slush and get these eggs out unbroken, and we were all covered with beastly black mud, and naturally I was cross. So far as I knew they were the only eggs that have ever been got out not even cracked. I went afterwards to see the ones they have at the Natural History Museum in London; all of them were cracked and just stuck together like a mosaic, and bits missing. Mine were perfect, and I meant to blow them when I got back. Naturally I was annoyed at the silly duffer dropping three hours’ work just on account of a centipede. I hit him about rather.”

===Chinese===
“必是同一个地方。那是在东海岸。不知怎的，水里有点什么，能叫东西不腐烂。闻起来像杂酚油的味儿。那让我想起特立尼达（Trinidad）。他们又弄到别的蛋没有？我找见的一些蛋，有一尺半长呢。那片沼泽打了个弯，你知道，把这一块地方给圈了出去。那里头大多是咸水。哎……我在那上头过的什么日子啊！我找见这些东西，完全是凑巧。我和两个土人，坐一条那种古怪的独木舟——全是用绳子捆拢来的那种——去捡蛋，同时也找见了那些骨头。我们带了一顶帐篷和四天的口粮，在一块硬实点的地方扎了营。如今一回想，那股子柏油似的怪味儿还直冲鼻子。那活儿挺有意思。你知道，就是拿铁钎子往泥里戳。蛋多半都给戳碎了。我真纳闷，这些象鸟到底是从多久以前才绝了迹的。传教士们说，土人里头有关于它们还活着那时候的传说，可我自己从没听过这种故事。1 不过有一件事是千真万确的：我们弄到的那些蛋，新鲜得就跟刚下出来的一样。新鲜！我扛着它们往船边走，我的一个黑鬼伙计把一只掉在石头上，摔碎了。我狠狠抽了那家伙一顿！可那蛋新鲜得很，跟刚下出来的一样，连点异味都没有，而它的娘怕是已经死了四百年了。那家伙说被蜈蚣咬了一口。算了，我把话扯远了。我们花了一整天功夫，才从烂泥里把这几枚蛋完整地挖出来，浑身上下糊满了那臭黑的泥，我心里头自然窝火。据我所知，那是世上仅有的一些连条裂纹都没有的象鸟蛋。后来我专门去伦敦的自然历史博物馆（Natural History Museum）看过他们收藏的那些；全都是裂了缝、再像马赛克似的拼黏起来的，还缺东少西。我这几个却完美无缺，我本打算回去以后把它们抽空制成标本。那个蠢货害我白干了三个钟头——就因为一只蜈蚣——我自然来气。我把他着实揍了一顿。”

===Original===
The man with the scar took out a clay pipe. I placed my pouch before him. He filled up absentmindedly.

“How about the others? Did you get those home? I don’t remember—”

“That’s the queer part of the story. I had three others. Perfectly fresh eggs. Well, we put ’em in the boat, and then I went up to the tent to make some coffee, leaving my two heathens down by the beach—the one fooling about with his sting and the other helping him. It never occurred to me that the beggars would take advantage of the peculiar position I was in to pick a quarrel. But I suppose the centipede poison and the kicking I had given him had upset the one—he was always a cantankerous sort—and he persuaded the other.

===Chinese===
脸上有疤的人掏出一支陶土烟斗。我把我的烟叶袋推到他面前。他心不在焉地装了一斗。

“别的蛋呢？你把它们带回家了吗？我不记得——”

“这一段才是故事里最离奇的地方。我还有三只别的蛋。都是新鲜得不能再新鲜的蛋。我们把蛋放进船里，然后我上帐篷那边去煮点咖啡，把我那两个异教徒丢在底下海滩上——一个还在那儿折腾他那个伤口，另一个在一旁伺候他。我怎么也没想到，这两个家伙会趁我这般处境特殊，存心来跟我寻衅。可我想，是蜈蚣的毒加上我那一顿拳脚，把那一个惹恼了——他平日就是个爱抬杠的脾气——于是他又撺掇了另一个。

===Original===
“I remember I was sitting and smoking and boiling up the water over a spirit-lamp business I used to take on these expeditions. Incidentally I was admiring the swamp under the sunset.
