All black and bloodred it was, in streaks—a beautiful sight. And up beyond the land rose grey and hazy to the hills, and the sky behind them red, like a furnace mouth. And fifty yards behind the back of me was these blessed heathen—quite regardless of the tranquil air of things—plotting to cut off with the boat and leave me all alone with three days’ provisions and a canvas tent, and nothing to drink whatsoever beyond a little keg of water. I heard a kind of yelp behind me, and there they were in this canoe affair—it wasn’t properly a boat—and, perhaps, twenty yards from land. I realised what was up in a moment. My gun was in the tent, and, besides, I had no bullets—only duck shot. They knew that. But I had a little revolver in my pocket, and I pulled that out as I ran down to the beach.

“‘Come back!’ says I, flourishing it.

“They jabbered something at me, and the man that broke the egg jeered. I aimed at the other—because he was unwounded and had the paddle, and I missed. They laughed. However, I wasn’t beat. I knew I had to keep cool, and I tried him again and made him jump with the whang of it. He didn’t laugh that time. The third time I got his head, and over he went, and the paddle with him. It was a precious lucky shot for a revolver. I reckon it was fifty yards. He went right under. I don’t know if he was shot, or simply stunned and drowned. Then I began to shout to the other chap to come back, but he huddled up in the canoe and refused to answer. So I fired out my revolver at him and never got near him.

===Chinese===
“我记得我当时正坐着抽烟，用一盏我这种出门考察常带的小酒精灯烧水。顺便我还欣赏着夕阳下的沼泽。一片黑、一片血红，一道一道的——美极了。再往上，陆地灰蒙蒙、雾腾腾地向着山峦升起，山峦背后的天空一片通红，像炉口一般。而在我身后五十码开外，就是那两个该死的异教徒——满不管眼前一派宁静气氛——正暗中谋划着要把船划走，丢下我一个人，只有三天的口粮、一顶帆布帐篷，外加一丁点水，旁的什么喝的也没有。我听见身后一声吆喝似的怪叫，回头一看，他们已经上了那条独木舟——那玩意儿也算不得正经船——离岸怕有二十码了。我立时就明白怎么回事了。我的枪在帐篷里，再说我也没带子弹——只有打鸭子的散弹。他们都知道。可我口袋里有把小左轮，我一边往海滩上跑，一边把它掏了出来。

“‘回来！’我挥着枪喊。

“他们冲我叽里咕噜了一通，那个打破蛋的家伙还嘲笑我。我瞄准了另一个——因为他身上没伤，又拿着桨——却打偏了。他们大笑。可我还不死心。我知道自己得稳住，于是又朝他开了一枪，子弹嗖地一声从他耳边过，吓了他一跳。那一回他没笑。第三枪我打中了他的脑袋，他一个倒栽葱翻进水里，桨也跟着掉了。左轮能打出这一手，真是侥幸得很。我估算有五十码远。他整个沉下去了。我不知道他是中了枪，还是只被打晕了过去淹死的。接着我就开始喊另一个回来，可他缩在独木舟里，怎么也不肯答应。我把剩下的子弹全朝他打过去，一发也没挨着他。

===Original===
“I felt a precious fool, I can tell you. There I was on this rotten, black beach, flat swamp all behind me, and the flat sea, cold after the sun set, and just this black canoe drifting steadily out to sea. I tell you I damned Dawson’s and Jamrach’s and Museums and all the rest of it just to rights. I bawled to this nigger to come back, until my voice went up into a scream.

“There was nothing for it but to swim after him and take my luck with the sharks. So I opened my clasp-knife and put it in my mouth, and took off my clothes and waded in. As soon as I was in the water I lost sight of the canoe, but I aimed, as I judged, to head it off. I hoped the man in it was too bad to navigate it, and that it would keep on drifting in the same direction. Presently it came up over the horizon again to the southwestward about. The afterglow of sunset was well over now and the dim of night creeping up. The stars were coming through the blue. I swum like a champion, though my legs and arms were soon aching.

===Chinese===
“我跟你说，我当时真觉得自己蠢得要命。我就那么站在那片烂糟糟的黑海滩上，身后是一望平川的沼泽，眼前是一望平川的大海——太阳一下山，海水凉飕飕的——只有那一条黑独木舟，稳稳地往外海漂去。我告诉你，我把道森公司、贾姆拉赫（Jamrach’s）、博物馆，还有这一整套该死的行当，挨个儿骂了个狗血淋头。我冲着那个黑鬼喊他回来，直喊得嗓子发尖，变成了尖叫。

“毫无办法，只好游过去追他，把命交给鲨鱼去碰运气了。于是我打开折刀，衔在嘴里，脱了衣服，蹚进水里。一下水，我就看不见那独木舟了，但我凭判断，朝能截住它的方向游去。我指望船里那家伙伤得太重，没法驾船，它会顺着同一个方向继续漂。果然，过了一阵，它又在西南方浮上了海平面。日落的余晖这时已经过去了，夜色正悄悄爬上来。星星一颗颗地从蓝天里钻出来。我游得像个冠军似的，尽管胳膊和腿没多久就开始发酸。

===Original===
“However, I came up to him by the time the stars were fairly out. As it got darker I began to see all manner of glowing things in the water—phosphorescence, you know. At times it made me giddy. I hardly knew which was stars and which was phosphorescence, and whether I was swimming on my head or my heels. The canoe was as black as sin, and the ripple under the bows like liquid fire. I was naturally chary of clambering up into it. I was anxious to see what he was up to first. He seemed to be lying cuddled up in a lump in the bows, and the stern was all out of water. The thing kept turning round slowly as it drifted—kind of waltzing, don’t you know. I went to the stern and pulled it down, expecting him to wake up. Then I began to clamber in with my knife in my hand, and ready for a rush. But he never stirred. So there I sat in the stern of the little canoe, drifting away over the calm phosphorescent sea, and with all the host of the stars above me, waiting for something to happen.

“After a long time I called him by name, but he never answered. I was too tired to take any risks by going along to him. So we sat there. I fancy I dozed once or twice. When the dawn came I saw he was as dead as a doornail and all puffed up and purple. My three eggs and the bones were lying in the middle of the canoe, and the keg of water and some coffee and biscuits wrapped in a Cape *Argus* by his feet, and a tin of methylated spirit underneath him. There was no paddle, nor, in fact, anything except the spirit-tin that I could use as one, so I settled to drift until I was picked up. I held an inquest on him, brought in a verdict against some snake, scorpion, or centipede unknown, and sent him overboard.

===Chinese===
“不过，等星星全出来的时候，我总算追上了它。天色越发暗下来，我开始看见水里种种发光的东西——就是那种磷光，你知道的。有时候真叫我头昏眼花。我简直分不清哪是星星哪是磷光，也分不清自己是在仰游还是在俯游。那独木舟黑得像罪孽一般，船头下泛起的涟漪像液态的火。我自然不敢贸然爬上去。我急着想先看看他在搞什么名堂。他好像蜷成一团窝在船头，船尾则整个翘出了水面。那玩意儿一边漂一边慢慢地打着转——就跟跳华尔兹似的，你懂吧。我绕到船尾，把它往下按了按，指望着他会醒。然后我一手握着刀，一手攀着船帮爬上去，做好了被人猛扑一下的准备。可他一动也不动。我就这么坐在那条小独木舟的船尾，在那平静的、泛着磷光的海面上漂流，头顶上是漫天的繁星，等着瞧会发生什么事。

“过了好半天，我喊他的名字，他也不答应。我累得要命，不敢冒险爬过去。我们俩就这么待着。我想我中途还打了一两个盹。天亮的时候，我看清他早已死得透透的，浑身浮肿发紫。我的三只蛋和那些骨头都搁在独木舟正中，一桶水、一点咖啡和饼干用一张《开普阿尔戈斯报》（Cape *Argus*）裹着搁在他脚边，他身下还压着一罐变性酒精。船上没有桨——说实在的，除了那酒精罐子，我再也找不到什么能当桨使的东西了——于是我索性由它漂，等着哪天被人救起。我在他身上开了个验尸会，把死因定为某条蛇、某只蝎子或蜈蚣所为，款目不详，然后便把他推下了海。

===Original===
“I drifted ten days,” said the man with the scar. “It’s a little thing in the telling, isn’t it? Every day was like the last. Except in the morning and the evening I never kept a lookout even—the blaze was so infernal. I didn’t see a sail after the first three days, and those I saw took no notice of me. About the sixth night a ship went by scarcely half a mile away from me, with all its lights ablaze and its ports open, looking like a big firefly. There was music aboard. I stood up and shouted and screamed at it. The second day I broached one of the Aepyornis eggs, scraped the shell away at the end bit by bit, and tried it, and I was glad to find it was good enough to eat. A bit flavoury—not bad, I mean—but with something of the taste of a duck’s egg. There was a kind of circular patch, about six inches across, on one side of the yoke, and with streaks of blood and a white mark like a ladder in it that I thought queer, but I did not understand what this meant at the time, and I wasn’t inclined to be particular. The egg lasted me three days, with biscuits and a drink of water. I chewed coffee berries too—invigorating stuff. The second egg I opened about the eighth day, and it scared me.”

===Chinese===
“我就这么漂了十天，”脸上有疤的人说，“说起来也就轻描淡写一句话，不是吗？每一天都跟前一天一模一样。除了早晚，我连望都不望一眼——日头毒得要命。头三天以后我再没见过一条船，先前见着的那几条也没一条理我。大约第六天夜里，有一条船从我身边不到半英里的地方经过，灯火通明，舷窗大开，像一只大萤火虫似的。船上还有音乐。我站起来，冲它又喊又叫。第二天，我敲开了一只象鸟蛋，一点一点把蛋壳头那一端刮掉，尝了尝，发现还能吃，心里很高兴。味道有点冲——我的意思是，倒也不坏——不过带点鸭蛋味儿。蛋黄的一边有一块圆斑，约莫六英寸宽，里头有一丝一丝的血丝，还有一道像梯子似的白印子，我觉得有点古怪，可当时也搞不懂这是什么意思，何况我也没心思细究。那只蛋我吃了三天，配着饼干和一口水。我还嚼咖啡豆——提神得很。第八天前后，我开了第二只蛋，可把我吓了一跳。”

===Original===
The man with the scar paused. “Yes,” he said, “developing.”

“I daresay you find it hard to believe. *I* did, with the thing before me. There the egg had been, sunk in that cold black mud, perhaps three hundred years. But there was no mistaking it. There was the—what is it?—embryo, with its big head and curved back, and its heart beating under its throat, and the yolk shrivelled up and great membranes spreading inside of the shell and all over the yolk. Here was I hatching out the eggs of the biggest of all extinct birds, in a little canoe in the midst of the Indian Ocean. If old Dawson had known that! It was worth four years’ salary. What do *you* think?

“However, I had to eat that precious thing up, every bit of it, before I sighted the reef, and some of the mouthfuls were beastly unpleasant. I left the third one alone. I held it up to the light, but the shell was too thick for me to get any notion of what might be happening inside; and though I fancied I heard blood pulsing, it might have been the rustle in my own ears, like what you listen to in a seashell.

===Chinese===
脸上有疤的人顿了顿。“不错，”他说，“在发育呢。”

“我看你是不大容易相信的。*我*自己亲眼对着那玩意儿，都难以相信呢。那蛋，原本在那冰冷漆黑的烂泥里埋着，怕有三百年了。可这一点也错不了。里头那个——叫什么来着？——胚胎，大脑袋，弓着背，喉咙底下心在怦怦跳，蛋黄瘪下去了，壳里头和蛋黄外头铺展着好大几层薄膜。我竟然在这条荡在印度洋当中的小独木舟里，孵出了所有绝种鸟类里头最大的一种的蛋。要是老道森知道了这个！那可值四年的薪水呢。*你*说是不是？

“不管怎么说，在望见那片珊瑚礁以前，我只好把这宝贝一口一口吃得光光的，有几口咽下去真叫人难受极了。第三只我没动它。我把它举到光里照，可壳太厚，看不清里头到底怎么样了；虽说我觉得自己听见了血在跳，可也许不过是我自己耳朵里的嗡嗡声，就像你拿个海螺贴在耳边听到的那种响动。

===Original===
“Then came the atoll. Came out of the sunrise, as it were, suddenly, close up to me. I drifted straight towards it until I was about half a mile from shore, not more, and then the current took a turn, and I had to paddle as hard as I could with my hands and bits of the Aepyornis shell to make the place. However, I got there. It was just a common atoll about four miles round, with a few trees growing and a spring in one place, and the lagoon full of parrotfish. I took the egg ashore and put it in a good place, well above the tide lines and in the sun, to give it all the chance I could, and pulled the canoe up safe, and loafed about prospecting. It’s rum how dull an atoll is. As soon as I had found a spring all the interest seemed to vanish. When I was a kid I thought nothing could be finer or more adventurous than the Robinson Crusoe business, but that place was as monotonous as a book of sermons. I went round finding eatable things and generally thinking; but I tell you I was bored to death before the first day was out. It shows my luck—the very day I landed the weather changed. A thunderstorm went by to the north and flicked its wing over the island, and in the night there came a drencher and a howling wind slap over us. It wouldn’t have taken much, you know, to upset that canoe.

===Chinese===
“接着，那座环礁就出现了。仿佛是从日出里头一下子冒出来似的，离我很近。我径直朝它漂过去，直到离岸大约半英里——不到——然后洋流一转，我只得拼了命用手和几块象蛋壳当桨划水，好歹挨到地方。不管怎样，我是到了。那不过是一座寻常的环礁，周长四英里上下，长着几棵树，某处有一眼泉，潟湖里全是鹦嘴鱼。我把蛋搬上岸，搁在一个好地方——潮水线之上，太阳底下——好让它有最大的机会，又把独木舟安全地拉上岸，然后东逛西看地探查了一番。说起来你都不信，一座环礁能有多乏味。我刚找到那眼泉水，兴致好像就全没了。我小时候觉得，再没什么能比鲁滨逊漂流记那一套更了不起、更带劲的了，可那地方单调得像一本说教的书。我到处转悠，找些能吃的东西，一边胡思乱想；可我告诉你，头一天还没过完，我就无聊得要死。这也可见我的运气——我登岸的当天，天就变了。一场雷雨从北边过去，翅膀尖扫了一下这岛，到了夜里，一场瓢泼大雨和一阵鬼哭狼嚎的风就劈头盖脸砸了下来。你是知道的，要掀翻那条独木舟，原也用不着费多大的劲。

===Original===
“I was sleeping under the canoe, and the egg was luckily among the sand higher up the beach, and the first thing I remember was a sound like a hundred pebbles hitting the boat at once, and a rush of water over my body. I’d been dreaming of Antananarivo, and I sat up and holloaed to Intoshi to ask her what the devil was up, and clawed out at the chair where the matches used to be. Then I remembered where I was. There were phosphorescent waves rolling up as if they meant to eat me, and all the rest of the night as black as pitch. The air was simply yelling. The clouds seemed down on your head almost, and the rain fell as if heaven was sinking and they were baling out the waters above the firmament. One great roller came writhing at me, like a fiery serpent, and I bolted. Then I thought of the canoe, and ran down to it as the water went hissing back again; but the thing had gone. I wondered about the egg then, and felt my way to it. It was all right and well out of reach of the maddest waves, so I sat down beside it and cuddled it for company. Lord! what a night that was!

“The storm was over before the morning. There wasn’t a rag of cloud left in the sky when the dawn came, and all along the beach there were bits of plank scattered—which was the disarticulated skeleton, so to speak, of my canoe. However, that gave me something to do, for, taking advantage of two of the trees being together, I rigged up a kind of storm-shelter with these vestiges. And that day the egg hatched.

===Chinese===
“我那时正睡在独木舟底下，那蛋幸好搁在沙滩更高处的沙子里头，我记得头一件事，就是听见一声像一百颗石子同时砸在船上的响声，紧接着一股水从我身上冲过去。我刚才正梦见塔那那利佛，便一骨碌坐起来，冲着因托希（Intoshi）喊，问她到底出了什么事，一面伸手去摸原先放椅子那儿——火柴就放在那儿的。这时我才记起自己是在什么地方。磷光闪闪的浪头翻卷着扑上来，像要把我吞了似的，四下里一片漆黑，伸手不见五指。风声简直是在尖啸。云层低得几乎压到头上，那雨下得像天塌下来了，他们正把天穹之上的水往外舀似的。一个大浪像条火蛇似的扭动着朝我扑来，我撒腿就跑。接着我想起那条独木舟，等水嘶嘶地退回去时，我跑下去看——那玩意儿已经没了。我这才惦记起那蛋，摸黑过去找它。还好，它没事，搁在那些再疯的浪也够不着的地方，我便挨着它坐下，把它抱在怀里作个伴。老天！那一夜可真够受的！

“天亮以前，风暴就过去了。破晓时天上连一丝云彩也不剩，海滩一路散着些木板——可以说，那就是我那条独木舟被拆散了的骸骨。不过这倒也有事可干了，我便借着两棵长在一起的小树，用这些残骸搭了个临时的避风棚。就在那一天，蛋孵出来了。

===Original===
“Hatched, sir, when my head was pillowed on it and I was asleep. I heard a whack and felt a jar and sat up, and there was the end of the egg pecked out and a rum little brown head looking out at me. ‘Lord!’ I said, ‘you’re welcome’; and with a little difficulty he came out.

“He was a nice friendly little chap at first, about the size of a small hen—very much like most other young birds, only bigger. His plumage was a dirty brown to begin with, with a sort of grey scab that fell off it very soon, and scarcely feathers—a kind of downy hair. I can hardly express how pleased I was to see him. I tell you, Robinson Crusoe don’t make near enough of his loneliness. But here was interesting company. He looked at me and winked his eye from the front backwards, like a hen, and gave a chirp and began to peck about at once, as though being hatched three hundred years too late was just nothing. ‘Glad to see you, Man Friday!’ says I, for I had naturally settled he was to be called Man Friday if ever he was hatched, as soon as ever I found the egg in the canoe had developed. I was a bit anxious about his feed, so I gave him a lump of raw parrotfish at once. He took it, and opened his beak for more. I was glad of that for, under the circumstances, if he’d been at all fanciful, I should have had to eat him after all.

===Chinese===
“孵出来了，先生，那时我的头正枕在它上头，我睡着了。我听见“啪”的一声，觉得震了一下，一骨碌坐起来，只见蛋的一头已经被啄开了，一个古怪的小棕脑袋正从里头朝我张望着。‘老天！’我说，‘欢迎你’；它略略费了点劲，便钻了出来。

“它起初是个挺和气、挺亲人的小家伙，约莫一只小母鸡那么大——跟别的小鸟儿大体上差不多，只是更大些。它的毛一开始是脏兮兮的棕色，上头还带着一层灰灰的痂，没多久就脱落了，那几乎算不得羽毛——更像是一种绒毛。我见了它，心里那份高兴，简直没法说。我告诉你，鲁滨逊写他那本寂寞可还远不够味儿呢。这可是有趣的伴儿。它瞧着我，像母鸡那样把眼睛从前向后眨了一下，唧的一声，便立刻到处啄起来，仿佛迟了三百年才出世压根不算回事。‘见到你真高兴，星期五（Man Friday）！’我说，因为自从我发现在独木舟里的那蛋有了变化，我自然早就给它定好了：只要孵得出来，就叫它“星期五”。我有点发愁它的吃食，便赶紧塞给它一块生鹦嘴鱼。它接了，又张开嘴还要。这倒让我放了心，因为照当时的情形，它要是挑嘴，我也只好把它给吃了。

===Original===
“You’d be surprised what an interesting bird that Aepyornis chick was. He followed me about from the very beginning. He used to stand by me and watch while I fished in the lagoon, and go shares in anything I caught. And he was sensible, too. There were nasty green warty things, like pickled gherkins, used to lie about on the beach, and he tried one of these and it upset him. He never even looked at any of them again.

“And he grew. You could almost see him grow. And as I was never much of a society man, his quiet, friendly ways suited me to a T. For nearly two years we were as happy as we could be on that island. I had no business worries, for I knew my salary was mounting up at Dawsons’. We would see a sail now and then, but nothing ever came near us. I amused myself, too, by decorating the island with designs worked in sea-urchins and fancy shells of various kinds. I put **Aepyornis Island** all round the place very nearly, in big letters, like what you see done with coloured stones at railway stations in the old country, and mathematical calculations and drawings of various sorts. And I used to lie watching the blessed bird stalking round and growing, growing; and think how I could make a living out of him by showing him about if I ever got taken off. After his first moult he began to get handsome, with a crest and a blue wattle, and a lot of green feathers at the behind of him. And then I used to puzzle whether Dawsons’ had any right to claim him or not. Stormy weather and in the rainy season we lay snug under the shelter I had made out of the old canoe, and I used to tell him lies about my friends at home. And after a storm we would go round the island together to see if there was any drift. It was a kind of idyll, you might say. If only I had had some tobacco it would have been simply just like heaven.

===Chinese===
“你想象不出那只小象鸟有多有趣。它打从一开始就寸步不离地跟着我。我在潟湖钓鱼时，它就站在一旁看，我钓着什么，它都要分一份。它还挺懂道理。海滩上老有些叫人恶心的绿疙瘩玩意儿，像腌黄瓜似的，它尝了一个，就闹了肚子。从此它连看都不再朝那些东西看一眼。

“它一个劲儿地长。你几乎看得见它在长。我这人向来不大爱交际，它那安静、和气的脾气，正合我的意，再投契也没有了。将近两年，我们俩在那岛上过得要多自在有多自在。生意上的烦心事我一概没有，因为我知道我在道森公司的薪水一直在那儿往上累着。偶尔也能望见一条船，可从没有一条靠近过我们。我还自得其乐地用海胆和各种好看的贝壳，在岛上摆出种种花样来装饰。我几乎围着全岛，用大字摆出了**象鸟岛（Aepyornis Island）**几个字，就像老家火车站上用彩色石子摆出的那种，此外还有种种数学演算和图画。我就这么躺着，瞧着这只福鸟大摇大摆地踱来踱去，越长越大，越长越大；一边盘算着，万一哪天我能离开这儿，牵着它到处展览，怎么才能靠它谋生。它头一次换毛以后，便开始出落得漂亮起来，长出了冠子、蓝色的肉垂，屁股后头还生出一大簇绿色的羽毛。于是我就犯起愁来：道森公司到底有没有权利来认领它呢？遇到坏天，到了雨季，我们就舒舒服服地躺在我用那条旧独木舟搭起的棚子底下，我便给它讲些关于我那些老友的瞎话。每回暴风雨过后，我们就一块儿绕岛走一圈，看看有没有漂上来的什么东西。可以说，那是一种田园诗般的日子。要是再有烟叶抽，那简直就是天堂了。

===Original===
“It was about the end of the second year our little paradise went wrong. Friday was then about fourteen feet high to the bill of him, with a big, broad head like the end of a pickaxe, and two huge brown eyes with yellow rims, set together like a man’s—not out of sight of each other like a hen’s. His plumage was fine—none of the half-mourning style of your ostrich—more like a cassowary as far as colour and texture go. And then it was he began to cock his comb at me and give himself airs, and show signs of a nasty temper…

“At last came a time when my fishing had been rather unlucky, and he began to hang about me in a queer, meditative way. I thought he might have been eating sea-cucumbers or something, but it was really just discontent on his part. I was hungry too, and when at last I landed a fish I wanted it for myself. Tempers were short that morning on both sides. He pecked at it and grabbed it, and I gave him a whack on the head to make him leave go. And at that he went for me. Lord!…

===Chinese===
“大约到了第二年年底，我们这座小天堂出了岔子。那时候，星期五从喙算起大约有十四英尺高，脑袋又大又宽，像一把鹤嘴锄的头，两只棕色的大眼睛带着黄圈，长得像人一样挨在一起——不像母鸡那样分在头的两边谁也瞧不见谁。它那一身毛漂亮得很——全不似你那鸵鸟那副半丧服似的灰溜溜——无论颜色还是质地，倒更像鹤鸵。也就在这时候，它开始对我竖起冠子摆起架子，露出了一副坏脾气的端倪……

“后来终于有那么一回，我钓鱼的手气很不好，它便开始以一种古怪的、沉思的模样围着我打转。我还当它是吃了海参之类的什么东西，其实不过是它自己心里不痛快罢了。我也饿，等我好不容易钓上一条鱼来，我想留给自己吃。那天早上我们俩的火气都不小。它上来啄那条鱼，一把抢过去，我便在它脑袋上敲了一下，叫它松口。这下它就朝我扑过来了。老天！……

===Original===
“He gave me this in the face.” The man indicated his scar. “Then he kicked me. It was like a carthorse. I got up, and seeing he hadn’t finished, I started off full tilt with my arms doubled up over my face. But he ran on those gawky legs of his faster than a racehorse, and kept landing out at me with sledgehammer kicks, and bringing his pickaxe down on the back of my head. I made for the lagoon, and went in up to my neck. He stopped at the water, for he hated getting his feet wet, and began to make a shindy, something like a peacock’s, only hoarser. He started strutting up and down the beach. I’ll admit I felt small to see this blessed fossil lording it there. And my head and face were all bleeding, and—well, my body just one jelly of bruises.

“I decided to swim across the lagoon and leave him alone for a bit, until the affair blew over. I shinned up the tallest palm-tree, and sat there thinking of it all. I don’t suppose I ever felt so hurt by anything before or since. It was the brutal ingratitude of the creature. I’d been more than a brother to him. I’d hatched him, educated him. A great gawky, out-of-date bird! And me a human being—heir of the ages and all that.

===Chinese===
“它就给了我这脸一下。”那人指了指自己脸上的疤。“接着它踢了我一脚。那力道，跟一匹拉车的辕马差不多。我爬起来，一看它还没收手，便把两臂护在脸上，撒腿就跑。可它靠那两条笨拙的长腿跑起来比赛马还快，一边追，一边像抡大锤似的连踢带踹，还把那把“鹤嘴锄”一下一下砸在我后脑勺上。我朝潟湖奔过去，一直蹚到水没了脖子。它在水边站住了——它最怕弄湿了脚——便开始大呼小叫起来，有点像孔雀叫，只是更沙哑。它沿着海滩耀武扬威地踱来踱去。我承认，眼见这只该死的化石在那儿作威作福，我心里着实有点发怵。何况我头上脸上都是血，还有——唉，我那一身简直成了一摊青一块紫一块的烂肉。

“我决定游过潟湖，先让它独自待上一阵，等这桩公案平息下去。我爬上最高的那棵棕榈树，坐在上头把事情前前后后想了一遍。我想我这辈子，从前也好，往后也罢，再没叫什么事伤得这么重过。这纯粹是这畜生蛮不讲理的忘恩负义。我待它胜似亲兄弟。我把它孵出来，教导它成人。这么大一只笨手笨脚、过了时的怪鸟！而我是个堂堂的人——是万古文明的继承人云云。

===Original===
“I thought after a time he’d begin to see things in that light himself, and feel a little sorry for his behaviour. I thought if I was to catch some nice little bits of fish, perhaps, and go to him presently in a casual kind of way, and offer them to him, he might do the sensible thing. It took me some time to learn how unforgiving and cantankerous an extinct bird can be. Malice!

“I won’t tell you all the little devices I tried to get that bird round again, I simply can’t. It makes my cheek burn with shame even now to think of the snubs and buffets I had from this infernal curiosity. I tried violence. I chucked lumps of coral at him from a safe distance, but he only swallowed them. I shied my open knife at him and almost lost it, though it was too big for him to swallow. I tried starving him out and struck fishing, but he took to picking along the beach at low water after worms, and rubbed along on that. Half my time I spent up to my neck in the lagoon, and the rest up the palm-trees. One of them was scarcely high enough, and when he caught me up it he had a regular Bank Holiday with the calves of my legs. It got unbearable. I don’t know if you have ever tried sleeping up a palm-tree. It gave me the most horrible nightmares. Think of the shame of it, too! Here was this extinct animal mooning about my island like a sulky duke, and me not allowed to rest the sole of my foot on the place. I used to cry with weariness and vexation. I told him straight that I didn’t mean to be chased about a desert island by any damned anachronisms. I told him to go and peck a navigator of his own age. But he only snapped his beak at me. Great ugly bird, all legs and neck!

===Chinese===
“我原想，过一阵它自己也会把事情往这上头想，对自己的行径多少生出点悔意来。我想，倘若我钓几块不错的小鱼肉，过会儿若无其事地走到它跟前，奉上给它，它也许会识趣。我费了好些时候才明白，一只绝了种的鸟，能多么记仇、多么爱抬杠。它那是狠毒！

“我试过的种种法子，想叫这鸟回心转意，就不一一告诉你了，我也实在说不出口。如今一想想起从这该死的稀罕玩意儿那儿受的种种呵斥和窝囊气，我还觉得脸上烧得慌，羞愧难当。我动过硬的。我隔得远远地朝它扔珊瑚块，它倒好，把它们全吞了下去。我把折刀敞开着朝它掷过去，差点儿丢了那把刀——虽说那刀大得它吞不下去。我试着饿它，干脆不钓鱼了，可它便趁退潮时在海滩上捡蚯蚓吃，靠这个凑合着过。我一半时间泡在潟湖里，水没到脖子，另一半时间则爬在棕榈树上。其中有一棵还嫌不够高，有一回它把我堵在树上，把我的小腿肚当作银行假日一样，好好庆祝了一番。这日子实在没法过了。我不知道你有没有试过在棕榈树上睡觉。那叫我做了许许多多极其可怕的噩梦。再者，这也丢人呐！这只绝种的畜生像个闹别扭的公爵似的，在我这座岛上四处闲荡，倒不许我把脚底板往这地方搁一搁。我常常累得、气得直哭。我正正经经地告诉它，我可没打算在一座荒岛上，被任何该死的时代错乱之物追得团团转。我叫它去啄一个跟它同个年纪的航海家。它只朝我咔嚓咔嚓地咬咬嘴。好一只丑大鸟，除了腿就是脖子！

===Original===
“I shouldn’t like to say how long that went on altogether. I’d have killed him sooner if I’d known how. However, I hit on a way of settling him at last. It is a South American dodge. I joined all my fishing-lines together with stems of seaweed and things, and made a stoutish string, perhaps twelve yards in length or more, and I fastened two lumps of coral rock to the ends of this. It took me some time to do, because every now and then I had to go into the lagoon or up a tree as the fancy took me. This I whirled rapidly round my head, and then let it go at him. The first time I missed, but the next time the string caught his legs beautifully, and wrapped round them again and again. Over he went. I threw it standing waist-deep in the lagoon, and as soon as he went down I was out of the water and sawing at his neck with my knife…

“I don’t like to think of that even now. I felt like a murderer while I did it, though my anger was hot against him. When I stood over him and saw him bleeding on the white sand, and his beautiful great legs and neck writhing in his last agony… Pah!

===Chinese===
“这一拖就是多久，我不大敢说。早知道怎么下手，我早就把它弄死了。不过，我总算想出了一个法子来解决它。这是南美洲人的一个窍门。我把所有的钓鱼线都用海草茎之类的东西接起来，做成一根相当结实的绳子，大约十二码长，或者更长些，两头各拴上一块珊瑚石。这活儿我做了好些时候，因为时不时地，看情形，我就得跳进潟湖或者爬上树去。我把这根绳子在头顶上飞快地抡起来，然后对准它甩过去。头一回我甩偏了，可第二回，那绳子一下子就漂亮地缠住了它的两条腿，一圈又一圈地绕了上去。它扑通一声栽倒在地。我是站在齐腰深的潟湖水里把它甩倒的，它一倒下，我便从水里蹿出来，拿刀去锯它的脖子……

“这事至今我都不愿去想。我一边干，一边觉得自己像个杀人凶手，尽管我心里的火气正冲着它烧得旺着呢。等我站在它身上，看见它在白沙上流着血，看见它那两条漂亮的、又长又粗的腿和脖子在最后作痛中扭动……呸！

===Original===
“With that tragedy loneliness came upon me like a curse. Good Lord! you can’t imagine how I missed that bird. I sat by his corpse and sorrowed over him, and shivered as I looked round the desolate, silent reef. I thought of what a jolly little bird he had been when he was hatched, and of a thousand pleasant tricks he had played before he went wrong. I thought if I’d only wounded him I might have nursed him round into a better understanding. If I’d had any means of digging into the coral rock I’d have buried him. I felt exactly as if he was human. As it was, I couldn’t think of eating him, so I put him in the lagoon, and the little fishes picked him clean. I didn’t even save the feathers. Then one day a chap cruising about in a yacht had a fancy to see if my atoll still existed.

“He didn’t come a moment too soon, for I was about sick enough of the desolation of it, and only hesitating whether I should walk out into the sea and finish up the business that way, or fall back on the green things…

===Chinese===
“这一悲剧发生之后，寂寞便像诅咒一样降临到我头上。老天爷！你没法想象我有多想那只鸟。我坐在它的尸体旁，为它哀伤，打量着四下里那片荒凉寂静的珊瑚礁，不禁簌簌发抖。我想起它刚孵出来时是多么一只逗人喜爱的小鸟，想起它变坏以前跟我玩过的千百种有趣的小把戏。我想，倘若我只是伤了它，我也许还能把它调理过来，让它懂事一点。要是我有法子在珊瑚礁上刨坑，我一定会把它埋了。我觉得它就跟人一模一样。事已至此，我又不忍心吃它，便把它放进潟湖，让那些小鱼把它啃得干干净净。我连一根羽毛都没留下。后来有一天，一个驾游艇到处逛的人，忽然心血来潮，想看看我这座环礁还在不在。

“他来得再及时不过了，因为那荒凉劲儿已经叫我受得够呛，我正犹豫着，是该走进海里一了百了，还是退而求其次，靠那些绿色的玩意儿了此一生……

===Original===
“I sold the bones to a man named Winslow—a dealer near the British Museum, and he says he sold them to old Havers. It seems Havers didn’t understand they were extra large, and it was only after his death they attracted attention. They called ’em Aepyornis—what was it?”

“*Aepyornis vastus*,” said I. “It’s funny, the very thing was mentioned to me by a friend of mine. When they found an Aepyornis, with a thigh a yard long, they thought they had reached the top of the scale, and called him *Aepyornis maximus*. Then someone turned up another thighbone four feet six or more, and that they called *Aepyornis Titan*. Then your *vastus* was found after old Havers died, in his collection, and then a *vastissimus* turned up.”

“Winslow was telling me as much,” said the man with the scar. “If they get any more Aepyornises, he reckons some scientific swell will go and burst a blood-vessel. But it was a queer thing to happen to a man; wasn’t it—altogether?”

===Chinese===
“我把那些骨头卖给了一个叫温斯洛（Winslow）的人——大英博物馆（British Museum）附近的一个骨董商，他说他把它们又转手卖给了老哈弗斯（Havers）。看来哈弗斯当年没弄明白这些骨头大得异乎寻常，直到他死后，这些骨头才引起了注意。他们把它们叫作象鸟——什么来着？”

“*Aepyornis vastus*，”我说，“真巧，前些日子正好有个朋友跟我谈起这回事。他们最初发现一只象鸟，大腿骨有一码长，自以为已经登峰造极，便把它命名为*Aepyornis maximus*。后来又有人找出一根四英尺六英寸、甚至更长的大腿骨，于是把它叫作*Aepyornis Titan*。再后来，老哈弗斯死后，人们在他的收藏里发现了你的这个*vastus*，再后来又冒出一个*vastissimus*。”

“温斯洛也是这么跟我说的，”脸上有疤的人说，“他说，要是再找出几只象鸟，怕是哪位学界大老要激动得当场脑血管爆裂。不过，这么一桩事落在我这种人头上，倒也真是稀奇；是不是——你说，整个儿说来？”

## In the Modern Vein: An Unsympathetic Love Story / 摩登风格：一个不令人同情的爱情故事

===Original===
Of course the cultivated reader has heard of Aubrey Vair. He has published on three several occasions volumes of delicate verses—some, indeed, border on indelicacy—and his column "Of Things Literary" in the *Climax* is well known. His Byronic visage and an interview have appeared in the *Perfect Lady*. It was Aubrey Vair, I believe, who demonstrated that the humour of Dickens was worse than his sentiment, and who detected "a subtle bourgeois flavour" in Shakespeare. However, it is not generally known that Aubrey Vair has had erotic experiences as well as erotic inspirations. He adopted Goethe some little time since as his literary prototype, and that may have had something to do with his temporary lapse from sexual integrity.

For it is one of the commonest things that undermine literary men, giving us landslips and picturesque effects along the otherwise even cliff of their respectable life, ranking next to avarice, and certainly above drink, this instability called genius, or, more fully, the consciousness of genius, such as Aubrey Vair possessed. Since Shelley set the fashion, your man of gifts has been assured that his duty to himself and his duty to his wife are incompatible, and his renunciation of the Philistine has been marked by such infidelity as his means and courage warranted. Most virtue is lack of imagination. At anyrate, a minor genius without his affections twisted into an inextricable muddle, and who did not occasionally shed sonnets over his troubles, I have never met.

===Chinese===
那位有教养的读者，当然听过奥布里·韦尔（Aubrey Vair）其人。他曾先后三次付梓，出版了若干部精致的短诗集——其中有些甚至近乎失之于艳——而他在《高潮》（*Climax*）杂志上开设的"文坛杂话"专栏也广为人知。他那张拜伦式的面容，外加一篇访谈，还曾在《完美淑女》（*Perfect Lady*）上亮相。我相信，正是奥布里·韦尔论证了狄更斯的幽默比其感伤情调更为糟糕，也正是他品出了莎士比亚身上"一种微妙的市井气"。然而，世人大多并不知晓，奥布里·韦尔除了有艳情的灵感，也确曾有过艳情的经历。不久之前，他把歌德（Goethe）奉为自己文学上的楷模，这或许和他那一时的有负操守，多少有些干系。

因为，正是那种被称作天才、说得详尽些便是"天才的自我意识"的不稳定性——恰如奥布里·韦尔所拥有的那一种——才是最常见地侵蚀文人的东西之一；它在那些文人原本齐整体面的生活悬崖上，造成一处处的滑坡与如画的景致，其危害之深仅次于贪婪，固然又排在饮酒之上。自雪莱（Shelley）开了风气之先，但凡有些才情的男子便都被告知：他对自己的本分与对妻子的本分，两者水火不容；而他之所以弃绝庸众，便以那份他的财力与胆量所许可的不忠为印记。多数的美德，不过是因为缺乏想象力罢了。至少，一个感情不曾绞成一团解不开的乱麻、不曾偶尔为自己的烦扰洒下几首十四行诗的小小天才，我还从未遇见过。

===Original===
Even Aubrey Vair did this, weeping the sonnets overnight into his blotting-book, and pretending to write literary *causerie* when his wife came down in her bath slippers to see what kept him up. She did not understand him, of course. He did this even before the other woman appeared, so ingrained is conjugal treachery in the talented mind. Indeed, he wrote more sonnets before the other woman came than after that event, because thereafter he spent much of his leisure in cutting down the old productions, retrimming them, and generally altering this ready-made clothing of his passion to suit her particular height and complexion.

Aubrey Vair lived in a little red villa with a lawn at the back and a view of the Downs behind Reigate. He lived upon discreet investment eked out by literary work. His wife was handsome, sweet, and gentle, and—such is the tender humility of good married women—she found her life's happiness in seeing that little Aubrey Vair had well-cooked variety for dinner, and that their house was the neatest and brightest of all the houses they entered. Aubrey Vair enjoyed the dinners, and was proud of the house, yet nevertheless he mourned because his genius dwindled. Moreover, he grew plump, and corpulence threatened him.

We learn in suffering what we teach in song, and Aubrey Vair knew certainly that his soul could give no creditable crops unless his affections were harrowed. And how to harrow them was the trouble, for Reigate is a moral neighbourhood.

===Chinese===
就连奥布里·韦尔也未能免俗，他通宵把那些十四行诗泣写进吸墨纸簿里，待妻子穿着拖鞋下楼来看究竟是什么事让他迟迟不睡，他便装作在写一篇文学闲谈（*causerie*）。她自然是不理解他的。这事在那个女子尚未出现之前他便已如此做了——可见婚姻里的背弃在才子心中是何等根深蒂固。事实上，在那个女子到来之前，他写的十四行诗比那件事发生之后还多，因为自那以后，他便把大把的闲暇花在删削旧作、重新修饰之上，总而言之，是要把这一身现成的激情成衣，改裁得合乎她具体的身高与肤色。

奥布里·韦尔住在一栋带草坪的小红楼里，房后能望见雷盖特（Reigate）那一边的丘陵（the Downs）。他靠一份稳妥的投资、再辅以文字工作勉力维持生计。他的妻子容貌端丽、性情甜美而温婉——贤妻的温顺谦卑向来如此——她把毕生的快意，都放在这样两件事上：一是好让小奥布里·韦尔每顿晚饭都有花样翻新、烹调得宜的菜式；二是好让她那户人家，在所有他们出入的人家里头最整洁、最明亮。奥布里·韦尔享用那些晚饭，也为这所宅子感到自豪，可尽管如此，他仍因为自己天才的日渐凋零而黯然神伤。况且，他日渐发福，发胖之患已经逼近。

我们在苦痛中习得的事，正是我们在歌吟中传道的事；奥布里·韦尔深知，他的心灵除非经受感情的耙犁，否则断然结不出像样的庄稼来。而愁人的是：怎样去耙犁它呢——雷盖特这一带，毕竟是个风气端正的地方。

===Original===
So Aubrey Vair's romantic longings blew loose for a time, much as a seedling creeper might, planted in the midst of a flowerbed. But at last, in the fullness of time, the other woman came to the embrace of Aubrey Vair's yearning heart-tendrils, and his romantic episode proceeded as is here faithfully written down.

The other woman was really a girl, and Aubrey Vair met her first at a tennis party at Redhill. Aubrey Vair did not play tennis after the accident to Miss Morton's eye, and because latterly it made him pant and get warmer and moister than even a poet should be; and this young lady had only recently arrived in England, and could not play. So they gravitated into the two vacant basket chairs beside Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt, in front of the hollyhocks, and were presently talking at their ease together.

The other woman's name was unpropitious—Miss Smith—but you would never have suspected it from her face and costume. Her parentage was promising, she was an orphan, her mother was a Hindu, and her father an Indian civil servant; and Aubrey Vair—himself a happy mixture of Celt and Teuton, as, indeed, all literary men have to be nowadays—naturally believed in the literary consequences of a mixture of races. She was dressed in white. She had finely moulded pale features, great depth of expression, and a cloud of delicately *frisé* black hair over her dark eyes, and she looked at Aubrey Vair with a look half curious and half shy, that contrasted admirably with the stereotyped frankness of your common Reigate girl.

===Chinese===
于是，奥布里·韦尔那一片浪漫的情怀，有一阵子便只好无所依傍地飘荡着，颇像一株栽在花圃正中的藤苗。然而，时机一至，那另一个女子终于投入了奥布里·韦尔那渴慕着的心的卷须之中，他的这一段浪漫际遇，便循着此处忠实记下的样子，就此展开。

那另一个女子，其实还是个姑娘，奥布里·韦尔与她初次相逢，是在红山（Redhill）的一场网球茶会上。自从莫顿小姐（Miss Morton）出了那次眼睛的意外之后，奥布里·韦尔便不再打网球了，再说近来这项运动也让他气喘吁吁，身子比一个诗人所该有的还要更热、更冒汗；而这位年轻的女士刚到英国不久，也不善此道。于是，两人自然而然地凑到了贝恩太太（Mrs. Bayne）那位耳聋的姑母身旁、蜀葵花丛前面的两把空藤椅里，不一会儿便谈得十分投机。

那另一个女子的名字并不吉利——史密斯小姐（Miss Smith）——可你单看她的容貌和装束，是怎么也猜不出的。她的出身倒是大有前景：她是个孤儿，母亲是印度教徒（Hindu），父亲是印度文官（Indian civil servant）；而奥布里·韦尔——他自己便是凯尔特人与条顿人（Teuton）相融合的成功范例，时下凡搞文字的，又非如此不可——自然深信混血在文学上必有相应的好处。她一身素白。五官生得清秀白皙，神情的蕴藉极深，一头乌黑的卷发如云地覆在那一双黑眼睛之上，看奥布里·韦尔时，神色里一半是好奇、一半是羞涩，与寻常雷盖特姑娘那种千篇一律的爽朗，恰成令人赞叹的对照。

===Original===
"This is a splendid lawn—the best in Redhill," said Aubrey Vair in the course of the conversation; "and I like it all the better because the daisies are spared." He indicated the daisies with a graceful sweep of his rather elegant hand.

"They are sweet little flowers," said the lady in white, "and I have always associated them with England, chiefly, perhaps, through a picture I saw 'over there' when I was very little, of children making daisy chains. I promised myself that pleasure when I came home. But, alas! I feel now rather too large for such delights."

"I do not see why we should not be able to enjoy these simple pleasures as we grow older—why our growth should have in it so much forgetting. For my own part—"

"Has your wife got Jane's recipe for stuffing trout?" asked Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt abruptly.

"I really don't know," said Aubrey Vair.

"That's all right," said Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt. "It ought to please even you."

"Anything will please me," said Aubrey Vair; "I care very little—"

"Oh, it's a lovely dish," said Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt, and relapsed into contemplation.

===Chinese===
"这片草坪可真漂亮——在红山要数第一了，"谈话之间，奥布里·韦尔开口道，"我尤其喜欢它，还因为这些雏菊都给保留下来了。"他用那只颇为雅致的手，优雅地一挥，指了指那些雏菊。

"这些小花真可爱，"那位白衣女士说，"我向来把它们和英格兰联想在一起，或许主要是因为我很小的时候，'在那边'看过一幅画，画的是孩子们在编雏菊花环。我那时便许下心愿，回家之后一定要尝尝这个乐趣。可叹哪！如今我觉着自己个儿太大，这样的玩意儿是不相宜了。"

"我不明白，为什么人长大了，就不能再享受这些简单的乐趣——为什么我们的成长里，竟要这般地遗忘。就我自己而论——"

"你妻子拿到过简做填鳟鱼的那个方子吗？"贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母忽然插嘴道。

"我实在不清楚。"奥布里·韦尔说。

"那就好，"贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母说，"这事该叫你也满意的。"

"什么事我都会满意，"奥布里·韦尔说，"我倒是不大在乎——"

"哦，那可是一道顶好吃的菜，"贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母说罢，又陷入了沉思。

===Original===
"I was saying," said Aubrey Vair, "that I think I still find my keenest pleasures in childish pastimes. I have a little nephew that I see a great deal of, and when we fly kites together, I am sure it would be hard to tell which of us is the happier. By the by, you should get at your daisy chains in that way. Beguile some little girl."

"But I did. I took that Morton mite for a walk in the meadows, and timidly broached the subject. And she reproached me for suggesting 'frivolous pursuits.' It was a horrible disappointment."

"The governess here," said Aubrey Vair, "is robbing that child of its youth in a terrible way. What will a life be that has no childhood at the beginning?"

"Some human beings are never young," he continued, "and they never grow up. They lead absolutely colourless lives. They are—they are etiolated. They never love, and never feel the loss of it. They are—for the moment I can think of no better image—they are human flowerpots, in which no soul has been planted. But a human soul properly growing must begin in a fresh childishness."

"Yes," said the dark lady thoughtfully, "a careless childhood, running wild almost. That should be the beginning."

"Then we pass through the wonder and diffidence of youth."

"To strength and action," said the dark lady. Her dreamy eyes were fixed on the Downs, and her fingers tightened on her knees as she spoke. "Ah, it is a grand thing to live—as a man does—self-reliant and free."

===Chinese===
"我方才是想说，"奥布里·韦尔道，"我觉得自己最浓烈的乐趣，仍旧得自那些孩提时代的消遣。我有个小侄子，我常和他一处玩耍，我们一道放风筝的时候，保准谁也分不清我俩究竟哪个更乐。顺便说一句，你的雏菊花环，也该这样着手才好。去哄一个小女孩儿。"

"可我确曾这样做了呀。我领着莫顿家那个小不点儿到草地上散步，怯生生地把这事提了出来。结果倒被她数落了一顿，说我提议的是'轻佻的玩意儿'。那可真叫人大失所望。"

"这里头的家庭教师，"奥布里·韦尔说，"正在用一种可怕的方式剥夺那孩子的童年。开端没有童年的一生，将会是怎样的呢？"

"有些人从来就不曾年幼过，"他接着说道，"也永远长不大。他们过的日子绝对毫无色彩可言。他们是——他们是黄化了的（etiolated）。他们从不曾爱，也不觉得缺了爱。他们是——眼下我想不出更好的比方——他们是些空空如也的活花盆，里头不曾栽下过灵魂。可是一个人的灵魂若要好好地生长，便非得从一份崭新的童真开端不可。"

"是啊，"那位肤色黝黑的女士若有所思地说，"一个无忧无虑的童年，几乎是在野地里撒欢儿般长大的。那该是开端。"

"接下来，我们便穿过青春的惊奇与羞怯。"

"走向力量与行动。"那位黝黑的女士说。她那双梦一般的眼睛凝望着丘陵，说话时，手指在膝头上攥得更紧了。"啊，活着真是一件了不起的事——像男人那样——自食其力、自由自在。"

===Original===
"And so at last," said Aubrey Vair, "come to the culmination and crown of life." He paused and glanced hastily at her. Then he dropped his voice almost to a whisper—"And the culmination of life is love."

Their eyes met for a moment, but she looked away at once. Aubrey Vair felt a peculiar thrill and a catching in his breath, but his emotions were too complex for analysis. He had a certain sense of surprise, also, at the way his conversation had developed.

Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt suddenly dug him in the chest with her ear-trumpet, and someone at tennis bawled, "Love all!"

"Did I tell you Jane's girls have had scarlet fever?" asked Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt.

"No," said Aubrey Vair.

"Yes; and they are peeling now," said Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt, shutting her lips tightly, and nodding in a slow, significant manner at both of them.

There was a pause. All three seemed lost in thought, too deep for words.

===Chinese===
"于是到头来，"奥布里·韦尔说，"便走到了一生的极顶与冠冕。"他顿了一顿，匆匆地瞟了她一眼。然后他压低了声音，几乎成了耳语——"而一生的极顶，便是爱。"

两人的目光相交了一瞬，但她立刻便把视线移开了。奥布里·韦尔感到一阵奇异的战栗，喉间也随之一紧，可他的情绪太过复杂，难以细细剖析。对于这番谈话竟能如此发展，他也着实有些惊讶。

贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母忽然用助听器在他胸口戳了一下，球场上不知谁扯着嗓子喊了一声："零比零！"（Love all！）

"我可曾告诉过你，简家的几个女儿害了猩红热？"贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母问道。

"没有。"奥布里·韦尔说。

"是害了；眼下她们正在蜕皮呢。"贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母说，紧紧地抿着嘴，冲着他俩缓缓地、意味深长地点了点头。

一阵停顿。三个人似乎都陷入了言语所不能及的深思之中。

===Original===
"Love," began Aubrey Vair presently, in a severely philosophical tone, leaning back in his chair, holding his hands like a praying saint's in front of him, and staring at the toe of his shoe—"love is, I believe, the one true and real thing in life. It rises above reason, interest, or explanation. Yet I never read of an age when it was so much forgotten as it is now. Never was love expected to run so much in appointed channels, never was it so despised, checked, ordered, and obstructed. Policemen say, 'This way, Eros!' As a result, we relieve our emotional possibilities in the hunt for gold and notoriety. And after all, with the best fortune in these, we only hold up the gilded images of our success, and are weary slaves, with unsatisfied hearts, in the pageant of life."

Aubrey Vair sighed, and there was a pause. The girl looked at him out of the mysterious darkness of her eyes. She had read many books, but Aubrey Vair was her first literary man, and she took this kind of thing for genius—as girls have done before.

"We are," continued Aubrey Vair, conscious of a favourable impression—"we are like fireworks, mere dead, inert things until the appointed spark comes; and then—if it is not damp—the dormant soul blazes forth in all its warmth and beauty. That is living. I sometimes think, do you know, that we should be happier if we could die soon after that golden time, like the Ephemerides. There is a decay sets in."

"Eigh?" said Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt startlingly. "I didn't hear you."

"I was on the point of remarking," shouted Aubrey Vair, wheeling the array of his thoughts—"I was on the point of remarking that few people in Redhill could match Mrs. Morton's fine broad green."

"Others have noticed it," Mrs. Bayne's deaf aunt shouted back. "It is since she has had in her new false teeth."

This interruption dislocated the conversation a little. However—

"I must thank you, Mr. Vair," said the dark girl, when they parted that afternoon, "for having given me very much to think about."

And from her manner, Aubrey Vair perceived clearly he had not wasted his time.

===Chinese===
"爱，"过了片刻，奥布里·韦尔开了口，语调一本正经、煞有哲理，他往椅背上一靠，双手像祈祷的圣徒那样合在身前，眼睛盯着自己的鞋尖——"我相信，爱是这一生里唯一真实而确切的东西。它超乎理性、利害与解释之上。然而我从未读到过有哪一个时代，像如今这般把爱遗忘得这样彻底。爱从未被指望这样循着指定的渠道奔流，它也从未如此被人轻贱、阻遏、规训、窒碍。警察们会冲着它吆喝：'厄洛斯（Eros），打这边走！'其结果，我们便把感情上种种的可能，都发泄到对金钱与虚名的追逐里去。可到头来，纵然在这些上头运气再好，我们也不过是高高举起几个镀了金的、象征成功的偶像，依旧是些心力交瘁的奴隶，在这人生的大游行里空着那颗心。"

奥布里·韦尔叹了一声，又静默下来。那姑娘从她那双神秘的黑眼睛里望着他。她读过的书不少，可奥布里·韦尔是她遇见的头一个文人，于是便把这类话头当成了天才——在她之前，已有不少姑娘是这样了。

"我们，"奥布里·韦尔继续说道，觉察到自己已留下了不错的印象——"我们就像烟花，在没有等到那命定的火星之前，不过是些死的、呆的死物；可一旦那火星到来——倘若没有受潮——那蛰伏的灵魂便会在它的全部光热与华美之中迸发出来。那才叫活着。你们知道吗，我有时不禁想，要是我们能在那段黄金岁月过后不久便死去，像蜉蝣（Ephemerides）那样，或许反倒更幸福些。因为一种衰败会就此生了上来。"

"啊？"贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母猝然出声，把他吓了一跳。"我没听清。"

"我方才正要说，"奥布里·韦尔高声嚷道，一面掉转他那阵列般齐整的思绪——"我方才正要说，红山这一带，怕是没几家的草坪比得上莫顿太太那片又宽又漂亮的绿草坪。"

"旁人也注意到了，"贝恩太太那位耳聋的姑母也高声答道，"那是自打她换上新假牙以来才有的事。"

这一打岔，让谈话略略岔了开去。然而——

"我得谢谢您，韦尔先生，"那天下午两人作别时，那位黝黑的姑娘说，"您给了我许许多多可思索的东西。"

而从她的神气里，奥布里·韦尔分明看出，他这一趟功夫并未白费。

===Original===
It would require a subtler pen than mine to tell how from that day a passion for Miss Smith grew like Jonah's gourd in the heart of Aubrey Vair. He became pensive, and in the prolonged absence of Miss Smith, irritable. Mrs. Aubrey Vair felt the change in him, and put it down to a vitriolic Saturday Reviewer. Indisputably the *Saturday* does at times go a little far. He reread *Elective Affinities*; and lent it to Miss Smith. Incredible as it may appear to members of the Areopagus Club, where we know Aubrey Vair, he did also beyond all question inspire a sort of passion in that sombre-eyed, rather clever, and really very beautiful girl.

He talked to her a lot about love and destiny, and all that bric-a-brac of the minor poet. And they talked together about his genius. He elaborately, though discreetly, sought her society, and presented and read to her the milder of his unpublished sonnets. We consider his Byronic features pasty, but the feminine mind has its own laws. I suppose, also, where a girl is not a fool, a literary man has an enormous advantage over anyone but a preacher, in the show he can make of his heart's wares.

At last a day in that summer came when he met her alone, possibly by chance, in a quiet lane towards Horley. There were ample hedges on either side, rich with honeysuckle, vetch, and mullein.

===Chinese===
要从那一天起，对史密斯小姐的炽情是如何像约拿的藤蔓（Jonah's gourd）一般，在奥布里·韦尔心头蓬勃生长起来的，要把这事讲述清楚，需要一支比我更精微的笔。他变得郁郁沉思起来；史密斯小姐若是长久不在跟前，他便烦躁不安。韦尔太太觉出了他身上的变化，便归咎于《星期六评论》（*Saturday Review*）上一个出言刻毒的评论家。无可否认，《星期六》这份刊物有时确实也做得太过分了些。他把《亲和力》（*Elective Affinities*）重新读了一遍，又借给史密斯小姐看。叫阿雷奥帕古斯俱乐部（Areopagus Club）的会员们——我们便是在那里认识奥布里·韦尔的——听来或许难以置信，可他确确实实也激起了那黑眼睛、颇为聪颖、着实非常美貌的姑娘的一种炽情。

他对她谈了许多关于爱与命运的话，以及三流诗人那一整套的零碎家什。他们也一道谈起了他的天才。他煞费苦心、却又很有分寸地寻觅与她相处的机缘，把自己那些尚未刊行的、口味较淡的十四行诗念给她听、呈给她看。我们觉得他那张拜伦式的脸有些苍白浮肿，可女人的心思自有其法则。我又想，一个姑娘只要还不是个傻瓜，那么一个文人在摆弄他那颗心的存货上，所能做出来的排场，除了传教士之外，比任何人都占着莫大的便宜。

那个夏天里，终于有这么一天，他也许纯属偶然地、在一个通往霍利（Horley）的僻静小径上与她单独相遇了。小径两旁的树篱又高又密，里头缀满了忍冬、野豌豆和毛蕊花。

===Original===
They conversed intimately of his poetic ambitions, and then he read her those verses of his subsequently published in *Hobson's Magazine*: "Tenderly ever, since I have met thee." He had written these the day before; and though I think the sentiment is uncommonly trite, there is a redeeming note of sincerity about the lines not conspicuous in all Aubrey Vair's poetry.

He read rather well, and a swell of genuine emotion crept into his voice as he read, with one white hand thrown out to point the rhythm of the lines. "Ever, my sweet, for thee," he concluded, looking up into her face.

Before he looked up, he had been thinking chiefly of his poem and its effect. Straightway he forgot it. Her arms hung limply before her, and her hands were clasped together. Her eyes were very tender.

"Your verses go to the heart," she said softly.

Her mobile features were capable of wonderful shades of expression. He suddenly forgot his wife and his position as a minor poet as he looked at her. It is possible that his classical features may themselves have undergone a certain transfiguration. For one brief moment—and it was always to linger in his memory—destiny lifted him out of his vain little self to a nobler level of simplicity. The copy of "Tenderly ever" fluttered from his hand. Considerations vanished. Only one thing seemed of importance.

"I love you," he said abruptly.

An expression of fear came into her eyes. The grip of her hands upon one another tightened convulsively. She became very pale.

===Chinese===
两人亲密地谈着他的诗志，随后，他便把后来刊于《霍布森杂志》（*Hobson's Magazine*）上的那几行诗念给她听："温柔地永远，自打遇见了你。"这几行是他头一天写就的；虽说我觉得其中的情意俗套得不能再俗套，可字里行间却有一种真诚的调子为之补救，而这调子，在奥布里·韦尔所有的诗作里并不显眼。

他朗诵的功夫相当不错，随着诵读，他的嗓音里不知不觉涌上了一阵真切的感动，他伸出一只白净的手，替那些诗行打着节拍。"永远地，我的甜蜜，为你。"他收了尾，抬眼望着她的脸。

在他抬眼之前，他心里盘算的主要还是自己的诗、以及它将产生的效果。可一抬眼，他便把诗忘了个干净。她两条手臂软软地垂在身前，双手紧紧地扣在一起。她的眼神十分温柔。

"您这几行诗，直叫人动心。"她轻声道。

她那富于变化的面庞，能显出种种精妙的神情。他望着她，忽然便忘了自己的妻子，也忘了自己区区一个小诗人的身份。或许，他那张端正古典的脸本身，在这一刻也起了某种变化。在短短的一刹那间——这一刹那日后将永远萦绕在他的记忆里——命运把他从那虚荣渺小的自我之中提了起来，托到一个更为高贵的、单纯的境界。"温柔地永远"那份诗稿从他手中飘落在地。种种盘算都消散了。似乎只剩下一件事是要紧的。

"我爱你。"他突兀地说道。

一种惊惧的神色掠进她的眼底。她那只手在另一只手上，痉挛般地攥得更紧。她的脸登时煞白。

===Original===
Then she moved her lips as if to speak, bringing her face slightly nearer to his. There was nothing in the world at that moment for either of them but one another. They were both trembling exceedingly. In a whisper she said, "You love me?"

Aubrey Vair stood quivering and speechless, looking into her eyes. He had never seen such a light as he saw there before. He was in a wild tumult of emotion. He was dreadfully scared at what he had done. He could not say another word. He nodded.

"And this has come to me?" she said presently, in the same awestricken whisper, and then, "Oh, my love, my love!"

And thereupon Aubrey Vair had her clasped to himself, her cheek upon his shoulder and his lips to hers.

Thus it was that Aubrey Vair came by the cardinal memory of his life. To this day it recurs in his works.

A little boy clambering in the hedge some way down the lane saw this group with surprise, and then with scorn and contempt. Recking nothing of his destiny, he turned away, feeling that he at least could never come to the unspeakable unmanliness of hugging girls. Unhappily for Reigate scandal, his shame for his sex was altogether too deep for words.

===Chinese===
随后她动了动嘴唇，像是要说话的样子，把脸微微凑近了他一些。这一刻，这世上于他俩而言，除了彼此之外再无别物。两人都抖得厉害。她低声耳语般地问："你爱我？"

奥布里·韦尔颤栗着站在那里，一言不发，直望着她的眼睛。他从未见过像她眼底那样的光。他心中情绪翻腾，乱作一团。他对自己所做的事怕得要命。他一个字也说不出来。他点了点头。

"这样的事，竟落到了我头上？"过了片刻，她用同样敬畏般的低声说，接着又道，"哦，我的爱人，我的爱人！"

于是奥布里·韦尔便把她紧紧搂在了怀里，她的脸贴在他的肩头，他的唇贴在她的唇上。

奥布里·韦尔一生中那一桩至为要紧的记忆，便是这样得来的。直到今日，它仍时时在他的作品里重现。

稍远些的树篱里，有个小男孩正攀爬着玩耍，他先是惊愕地瞧见了这一幕，随即满眼是不屑和鄙夷。他把自己的命运全不放在心上，扭头便走，只觉得至少自己这辈子，绝计堕不到那种搂抱姑娘的、说不出口的没出息地步。只是于雷盖特的丑闻界而言，不幸的是，他这一份替本性别所感到的耻辱，实在深得无以言表。

===Original===
An hour after, Aubrey Vair returned home in a hushed mood. There were muffins after his own heart for his tea—Mrs. Aubrey Vair had had hers. And there were chrysanthemums, chiefly white ones—flowers he loved—set out in the china bowl he was wont to praise. And his wife came behind him to kiss him as he sat eating.

"De lill Jummuns," she remarked, kissing him under the ear.

Then it came into the mind of Aubrey Vair with startling clearness, while his ear was being kissed, and with his mouth full of muffin, that life is a singularly complex thing.

===Chinese===
一个钟头之后，奥布里·韦尔怀着一种怔忡的心情回到了家。他的茶点上有正合他意的松饼——韦尔太太的那一份她已经用过了。还有菊花，多半是白的——这是他心爱的花——插在一只他素来爱夸的瓷碗里。他坐着吃东西的时候，妻子便走到他身后，俯身吻他。

"亲爱的小东西（De lill Jummuns）。"她吻他耳朵下方的时候，说道。

就在自己的耳朵正被吻着、嘴里又塞满了松饼的当儿，一个念头异常清晰地涌上了奥布里·韦尔的心头：人生，实在是件复杂得出奇的东西。

===Original===
The summer passed at last into the harvest-time, and the leaves began falling. It was evening, the warm sunset light still touched the Downs, but up the valley a blue haze was creeping. One or two lamps in Reigate were already alight.

About halfway up the slanting road that scales the Downs, there is a wooden seat where one may obtain a fine view of the red villas scattered below, and of the succession of blue hills beyond. Here the girl with the shadowy face was sitting.

She had a book on her knees, but it lay neglected. She was leaning forward, her chin resting upon her hand. She was looking across the valley into the darkening sky, with troubled eyes.

Aubrey Vair appeared through the hazel-bushes, and sat down beside her. He held half a dozen dead leaves in his hand.

She did not alter her attitude. "Well?" she said.

"Is it to be flight?" he asked.

===Chinese===
夏天终于过去了，时令转入秋收，叶子也开始落了。正是黄昏时分，夕阳那暖融融的余光犹自映在丘陵之上，可沿着山谷上来，一抹蓝色的薄霭正悄悄漫了过来。雷盖特已有一两盏灯亮了起来。

在那条攀越丘陵的斜坡路上，约莫半山腰的地方，有一张木椅，坐在那里可以把下方星罗棋布的红色别墅、以及更远处那连绵的青色山峦尽收眼底。那个面庞带着阴影的姑娘，此刻便坐在这里。

她膝上搁着一本书，却搁着没去理会。她身子前倾，下巴支在手上。她正向着山谷那边、向那渐渐暗下去的天空望去，眼神里满是愁绪。

奥布里·韦尔从榛树丛后现了身，在她身旁坐下。他手里捏着半打枯叶。

她并没有改换姿势。"怎么样？"她说。

"是不是——要私奔？"他问。

===Original===
Aubrey Vair was rather pale. He had been having bad nights latterly, with dreams of the Continental Express, Mrs. Aubrey Vair possibly even in pursuit—he always fancied her making the tragedy ridiculous by tearfully bringing additional pairs of socks, and any such trifles he had forgotten, with her—all Reigate and Redhill in commotion. He had never eloped before, and he had visions of difficulties with hotel proprietors. Mrs. Aubrey Vair might telegraph ahead. Even he had had a prophetic vision of a headline in a halfpenny evening newspaper: "Young Lady abducts a Minor Poet." So there was a quaver in his voice as he asked, "Is it to be flight?"

"As you will," she answered, still not looking at him.

"I want you to consider particularly how this will affect you. A man," said Aubrey Vair, slowly, and staring hard at the leaves in his hand, "even gains a certain éclat in these affairs. But to a woman it is ruin—social, moral."

"This is not love," said the girl in white.

"Ah, my dearest! Think of yourself."

"Stupid!" she said, under her breath.

"You spoke?"

"Nothing."

"But cannot we go on, meeting one another, loving one another, without any great scandal or misery? Could we not—"

"That," interrupted Miss Smith, "would be unspeakably horrible."

===Chinese===
奥布里·韦尔的脸色颇为苍白。近来他一连几夜都睡不安稳，梦里尽是开往欧洲大陆的快车、韦尔太太说不定还在后面追——他总想象她哭哭啼啼地，把几双补加的袜子、以及凡是忘带的零碎物件都替他送了来，反倒把这场悲剧弄得滑稽可笑——整个雷盖特和红山都闹翻了天。他从没私奔过，便又想象出种种与旅馆老板打交道时遇到的麻烦。韦尔太太说不定会打电报到前面截他。他甚至有过一个预言般的幻象，是某家半便士晚报上的大字标题："妙龄女拐走三流诗人。"是以他问出"是不是要私奔？"时，嗓音里带着颤。

"随你。"她答道，仍旧不看他。

"我要你格外地想一想，这事会怎样地影响你。一个男人，"奥布里·韦尔一字一句地说，眼睛死死地盯着手里那几片叶子，"在这种事上甚至还能博得几分风光。可对一个女人来说，这就是身败名裂——社交上的，道德上的。"

"这不是爱。"那位白衣姑娘说。

"啊，我最亲爱的！想想你自己吧。"

"蠢货！"她压低了声音说。

"你说什么？"

"没什么。"

"可我们难道不能就这样下去，彼此相会，彼此相爱，而不招致什么大的风波与苦痛吗？我们难道不能——"

"那样，"史密斯小姐打断了他，"将是说不出口地可怕。"

===Original===
"This is a dreadful conversation to me. Life is so intricate, such a web of subtle strands binds us this way and that. I cannot tell what is right. You must consider—"

"A man would break such strands."

"There is no manliness," said Aubrey Vair, with a sudden glow of moral exaltation, "in doing wrong. My love"—

"We could at least die together, dearest," she said.

"Good Lord!" said Aubrey Vair. "I mean—consider my wife."

"You have not considered her hitherto."

"There is a flavour—of cowardice, of desertion, about suicide," said Aubrey Vair. "Frankly, I have the English prejudice, and do not like any kind of running away."

Miss Smith smiled very faintly. "I see clearly now what I did not see. My love and yours are very different things."

"Possibly it is a sexual difference," said Aubrey Vair; and then, feeling the remark inadequate, he relapsed into silence.

They sat for some time without a word. The two lights in Reigate below multiplied to a score of bright points, and, above, one star had become visible. She began laughing, an almost noiseless, hysterical laugh that jarred unaccountably upon Aubrey Vair.

Presently she stood up. "They will wonder where I am," she said. "I think I must be going."

He followed her to the road. "Then this is the end?" he said, with a curious mixture of relief and poignant regret.

"Yes, this is the end," she answered, and turned away.

===Chinese===
"这番话对我说来实在可怕。人生是如此错综复杂，这样一张由精微丝线织成的网，把我们这边那边地牵绊住。我实在分不清什么是对。你得想一想——"

"一个男人便会扯断这些丝线。"

"做错事，"奥布里·韦尔忽然涌起一阵道德上的激昂，说道，"是谈不上什么男子气概的。我的爱人——"

"至少，我们可以一道去死，亲爱的。"她说。

"老天爷！"奥布里·韦尔说，"我是说——想想我的妻子吧。"

"你至今可还没替她着想过。"

"自杀——总带着一股怯懦、临阵脱逃的味道。"奥布里·韦尔说，"坦白讲，我有英国人的成见，任何形式的逃跑我都不喜欢。"

史密斯小姐极淡地笑了一笑。"如今我看清了原先所没看清的。你我的爱，竟是截然不同的两回事。"

"或许这是男女之间的分别吧。"奥布里·韦尔说；继而觉得这话未尽其意，便又沉默下来。

两人默默地坐了一阵。下方雷盖特那两盏灯增多到了二十来个亮点，而在上空，已有一颗星星显现出来。她开始笑，一种几近无声的、歇斯底里的笑，奥布里·韦尔听了，莫名其妙地觉得刺耳难当。

过了片刻，她站起身来。"他们要奇怪我上哪儿去了。"她说，"我想我该走了。"

他跟着她走到路上。"那么，这就是结局了？"他说，一种古怪的心情里，既有如释重负，又有锥心的怅惘。

"是的，这就是结局了。"她答道，转身离去。

===Original===
There straightway dropped into the soul of Aubrey Vair a sense of infinite loss. It was an altogether new sensation. She was perhaps twenty yards away, when he groaned aloud with the weight of it, and suddenly began running after her with his arms extended.

"Annie," he cried—"Annie! I have been talking *rot*. Annie, now I know I love you! I cannot spare you. This must not be. I did not understand."

The weight was horrible.

"Oh, stop, Annie!" he cried, with a breaking voice, and there were tears on his face.

She turned upon him suddenly, and his arms fell by his side. His expression changed at the sight of her pale face.

"You do not understand," she said. "I have said goodbye."

She looked at him; he was evidently greatly distressed, a little out of breath, and he had just stopped blubbering. His contemptible quality reached the pathetic. She came up close to him, and, taking his damp Byronic visage between her hands, she kissed him again and again. "Goodbye, little man that I loved," she said; "and goodbye to this folly of love."

Then, with something that may have been a laugh or a sob—she herself, when she came to write it all in her novel, did not know which—she turned and hurried away again, and went out of the path that Aubrey Vair must pursue, at the crossroads.

Aubrey Vair stood, where she had kissed him, with a mind as inactive as his body, until her white dress had disappeared. Then he gave an involuntary sigh, a large exhaustive expiration, and so awoke himself, and began walking, pensively dragging his feet through the dead leaves, home. Emotions are terrible things.

===Chinese===
顷刻之间，一种无穷的失落之感便落进了奥布里·韦尔的灵魂。这是一种他全然没有尝过的滋味。她走开约莫二十码远时，他因这份重量而高声呻吟起来，忽然伸开双臂，拔腿便去追她。

"安妮（Annie），"他喊道——"安妮！我方才尽在胡说八道。安妮，我现在才知道我爱你！我不能没有你。这事不该这样。我先前是不明白。"

那重量实在可怕。

"哦，停一停，安妮！"他喊道，嗓音都破了，脸上已满是泪水。

她猛地回过身来，于是他那双手便垂回了身侧。一看见她那张苍白的脸，他的神情便变了。

"你并不明白，"她说，"我已经道过别了。"

她看着他；他显然大为痛苦，气喘吁吁，方才还止住了哭。他这一副可鄙的模样，竟有了几分叫人怜惜的意味。她走到他跟前，双手捧住他那张湿漉漉的拜伦式的脸，一遍又一遍地吻他。"再见，我曾爱过的这个小男人，"她说，"也再见了，这场爱情的荒唐。"

随后，她发出一种说不准是笑还是哽咽的声音——后来她把这一切写进自己的小说里时，连她自己也分不清究竟是哪一种——便又转过身，匆匆地走开了，到了十字路口处，便从奥布里·韦尔不得不走的那条道上岔了出去。

奥布里·韦尔站在她吻过他的地方，心神一如他的身子一般毫无动作，直到她那一身白裙消失不见。然后他不由自主地叹了一口气，一口长长的、仿佛要把一切呼尽的叹息，这才如梦初醒，开始拖着脚步、若有所思地蹚着落叶，往家走去。感情，实在是可怕的东西。

===Original===
"Do you like the potatoes, dear?" asked Mrs. Aubrey Vair at dinner. "I cooked them myself."

Aubrey Vair descended slowly from cloudy, impalpable meditations to the level of fried potatoes. "These potatoes"—he remarked, after a pause during which he was struggling with recollection. "Yes. These potatoes have exactly the tints of the dead leaves of the hazel."

"What a fanciful poet it is!" said Mrs. Aubrey Vair. "Taste them. They are very nice potatoes indeed."

===Chinese===
"土豆合你的口味吗，亲爱的？"吃饭时，韦尔太太问道。"是我亲手做的。"

奥布里·韦尔从云端那缥缈难名的玄想里，缓缓地降落到了炸土豆的高度。"这土豆——"他顿了一顿，在那一顿之间，正苦苦地与回忆相搏。"是的。这土豆的颜色，正和榛树枯叶的颜色一模一样。"

"真是个爱幻想的诗人！"韦尔太太说，"尝尝吧。这土豆可真好吃呢。"

## Filmer / 菲尔默

===Original===
In truth the mastery of flying was the work of thousands of men—this man a suggestion and that an experiment, until at last only one vigorous intellectual effort was needed to finish the work. But the inexorable injustice of the popular mind has decided that of all these thousands, one man, and that a man who never flew, should be chosen as the discoverer, just as it has chosen to honour Watt as the discoverer of steam and Stephenson of the steam-engine. And surely of all honoured names none is so grotesquely and tragically honoured as poor Filmer’s, the timid, intellectual creature who solved the problem over which the world had hung perplexed and a little fearful for so many generations, the man who pressed the button that has changed peace and warfare and well-nigh every condition of human life and happiness. Never has that recurring wonder of the littleness of the scientific man in the face of the greatness of his science found such an amazing exemplification. Much concerning Filmer is, and must remain, profoundly obscure—Filmers attract no Boswells—but the essential facts and the concluding scene are clear enough, and there are letters, and notes, and casual allusions to piece the whole together. And this is the story one makes, putting this thing with that, of Filmer’s life and death.

The first authentic trace of Filmer on the page of history is a document in which he applies for admission as a paid student in physics to the Government laboratories at South Kensington, and therein he describes himself as the son of a “military bootmaker” (“cobbler” in the vulgar tongue) of Dover, and lists his various examination proofs of a high proficiency in chemistry and mathematics. With a certain want of dignity he seeks to enhance these attainments by a profession of poverty and disadvantages, and he writes of the laboratory as the “gaol” of his ambitions, a slip which reinforces his claim to have devoted himself exclusively to the exact sciences. The document is endorsed in a manner that shows Filmer was admitted to this coveted opportunity; but until quite recently no traces of his success in the Government institution could be found.

===Chinese===
说到底，征服飞行是千千万万人共同的事业——这个人提出一个设想，那个人做了一次实验，直到最后，只需一次强有力的智慧努力，便可大功告成。然而公众那种不讲情面的偏颇判断，却要从这千千万万人中独独挑出一个人、而且是一个从未飞上过天的人，奉为发现者，正如他们曾把瓦特（Watt）奉为蒸汽的发现者，把史蒂文森（Stephenson）奉为蒸汽机的发明者一样。诚然，在所有被尊崇的名字里，没有一个像可怜的菲尔默（Filmer）那样，所受的尊崇如此荒诞、又如此悲惨——这个怯懦而富有智识的生灵，解开了世世代代以来令世人困惑、乃至略带恐惧的那个难题；这个按下了那枚按钮的人，从此改变了和平与战争，几乎改变了人类生活与幸福的一切境况。科学家的渺小与其科学的伟大之间的反差，这一再令人惊叹的现象，从未有过如此惊人的例证。关于菲尔默的许多事情，如今是、将来也必定依然是晦暗不明的——菲尔默这样的人引不来鲍斯韦尔（Boswell）为之立传——但基本事实和结局却是足够清楚的，还有书信、笔记和零星的提及，可以把全貌拼凑起来。把这一件与那一件拼合在一起，所能复原的关于菲尔默生死的故事，便是如下这一篇。

菲尔默在历史篇章上留下的第一道确凿痕迹，是一份申请书——他以此请求获准成为南肯辛顿（South Kensington）政府实验室物理学科的付费生。他在文中自称是多佛（Dover）一位"军用靴匠"（用俗话来说就是"修鞋匠"）的儿子，并开列了各项考试证明，表明自己在化学和数学方面造诣颇高。他带着几分有失体面的口气，力图以自陈贫寒、境遇不利来为自己的这些才学增色，又把实验室写作他雄心的"牢狱"（gaol）——这一笔误，倒恰好印证了他自称一心潜心于精密科学的说法。这份文件上有批注，表明菲尔默获准得到了这个令人垂青的机会；但直到不久以前，他在这一政府机构里究竟有何成就，却找不到任何痕迹。

===Original===
It has now, however, been shown that in spite of his professed zeal for research, Filmer, before he had held this scholarship a year, was tempted, by the possibility of a small increase in his immediate income, to abandon it in order to become one of the ninepence-an-hour computers employed by a well-known Professor in his vicarious conduct of those extensive researches of his in solar physics—researches which are still a matter of perplexity to astronomers. Afterwards, for the space of seven years, save for the pass lists of the London University, in which he is seen to climb slowly to a double first class B. Sc., in mathematics and chemistry, there is no evidence of how Filmer passed his life. No one knows how or where he lived, though it seems highly probable that he continued to support himself by teaching while he prosecuted the studies necessary for this distinction. And then, oddly enough, one finds him mentioned in the correspondence of Arthur Hicks, the poet.

===Chinese===
然而如今已经查明，菲尔默尽管口口声声热衷于研究，但享受这项奖学金不足一年，便因眼前收入可稍有增加的诱因，弃之而去，受雇于一位名教授，做了他那每小时九便士的计算员（computer）之一，替这位教授代为从事他那规模宏大的太阳物理学研究——那些研究至今仍是令天文学家困惑的难题。此后整整七年，除了伦敦大学的及格名单上可见他缓缓攀升，终于取得数学与化学的双重一等理学学士（B.Sc.）学位之外，再无任何迹象可考菲尔默是如何度过他的日子的。没有人知道他怎样谋生、住在哪里，不过他极可能是一边教书糊口，一边继续攻读取得这一学位所必需的功课。而后，颇为奇特的是，人们竟在诗人阿瑟·希克斯（Arthur Hicks）的书信里见到了他的名字。

===Original===
“You remember Filmer,” Hicks writes to his friend Vance; “well, *he* hasn’t altered a bit, the same hostile mumble and the nasty chin—how *can* a man contrive to be always three days from shaving?—and a sort of furtive air of being engaged in sneaking in front of one; even his coat and that frayed collar of his show no further signs of the passing years. He was writing in the library and I sat down beside him in the name of God’s charity, whereupon he deliberately insulted me by covering up his memoranda. It seems he has some brilliant research on hand that he suspects me of all people—with a Bodley Booklet a-printing!—of stealing. He has taken remarkable honours at the University—he went through them with a sort of hasty slobber, as though he feared I might interrupt him before he had told me all—and he spoke of taking his D. Sc. as one might speak of taking a cab. And he asked what I was doing—with a sort of comparative accent, and his arm was spread nervously, positively a protecting arm, over the paper that hid the precious idea—his one hopeful idea.

“ ‘Poetry,’ he said, ‘Poetry. And what do you profess to teach in it, Hicks?’

“The thing’s a Provincial professorling in the very act of budding, and I thank the Lord devoutly that but for the precious gift of indolence I also might have gone this way to D. Sc. and destruction … ”

===Chinese===
"你还记得菲尔默吧，"希克斯在写给朋友万斯（Vance）的信中说，"嘿，他可一点没变，还是那副带敌意的咕哝腔，那叫人讨厌的下巴——一个男人怎么能想方设法让自己永远处于该刮脸已三天的状态？——还有那种鬼鬼祟祟、像是在人前偷摸行事的神气；就连他那身外套和磨了边的领子，也看不出岁月又添了几分痕迹。当时他在图书馆里写东西，我以上帝慈悲的名义在他身旁坐下，他便存心侮辱我，把他的手稿一一盖了起来。看来他手头正做着什么了不起的研究，竟怀疑我——在所有人里偏偏怀疑我——其时我还有一本博德利小册子（Bodley Booklet）正在排印呢！——要偷他的成果。他在大学里得了令人瞩目的优等荣誉——他匆匆忙忙、口沫四溅地一口气说完，仿佛生怕我会在他还没讲完时打断他——他谈起要拿理学博士（D.Sc.）学位，口气就像别人说起要打一辆马车那样。他又问我最近在做什么——带着一种与人较量高下的意味，他那条胳膊却紧张地摊开，简直就是一条护卫的臂膀，护住那张遮着他宝贵想法——他那唯一一线希望所系的想法——的纸。"

"'诗歌，'他说，'诗歌。你在这上头到底自称能教些什么呢，希克斯？'"

"这家伙是个正在破苞而出的外省小教授胚子，我衷心感谢上苍，多亏了懒惰这份宝贵的恩赐，否则我也可能走上这条通往理学博士与毁灭的道路……"

===Original===
A curious little vignette that I am inclined to think caught Filmer in or near the very birth of his discovery. Hicks was wrong in anticipating a provincial professorship for Filmer. Our next glimpse of him is lecturing on “rubber and rubber substitutes,” to the Society of Arts—he had become manager to a great plastic-substance manufactory—and at that time, it is now known, he was a member of the Aeronautical Society, albeit he contributed nothing to the discussions of that body, preferring no doubt to mature his great conception without external assistance. And within two years of that paper before the Society of Arts he was hastily taking out a number of patents and proclaiming in various undignified ways the completion of the divergent inquiries which made his flying machine possible. The first definite statement to that effect appeared in a halfpenny evening paper through the agency of a man who lodged in the same house with Filmer. His final haste after his long laborious secret patience seems to have been due to a needless panic, Bootle, the notorious American scientific quack, having made an announcement that Filmer interpreted wrongly as an anticipation of his idea.

===Chinese===
这是一幅奇特的小品，我倾向于认为，它恰好捕捉到了菲尔默做出那项发现、或将近做出那项发现的时刻。希克斯预言菲尔默将做一个外省教授，这回可猜错了。我们下一次瞥见他，是在艺术协会（Society of Arts）作一场关于"橡胶及其代用品"的讲演——他已当上一家大型塑性材料制造厂的经理——如今我们知道，那时他已是航空协会（Aeronautical Society）的会员，尽管他从不在这个团体的讨论中发言，无疑宁可独自孕育他那伟大的构想，不假外力。在艺术协会那篇论文之后不出两年，他便匆匆申请了好几项专利，并以种种有失体面的方式宣扬，那些分头进行的研究已告完成，使他的飞行机器成为可能。最早一条对此明确的报道，登在一份半便士的晚报上，是一个与菲尔默同租一屋的人捅出去的。他在漫长、艰辛、暗中忍耐之后，最后这一阵仓皇行事，似乎是源于一场不必要的恐慌——臭名昭著的美国科学江湖骗子布特尔（Bootle）发表了一项声明，菲尔默误解为对方已抢在了自己前面。

===Original===
Now what precisely was Filmer’s idea? Really a very simple one. Before his time the pursuit of aeronautics had taken two divergent lines, and had developed on the one hand balloons—large apparatus lighter than air, easy in ascent, and comparatively safe in descent, but floating helplessly before any breeze that took them; and on the other, flying machines that flew only in theory—vast flat structures heavier than air, propelled and kept up by heavy engines and for the most part smashing at the first descent. But, neglecting the fact that the inevitable final collapse rendered them impossible, the weight of the flying machines gave them this theoretical advantage, that they could go through the air against a wind, a necessary condition if aerial navigation was to have any practical value. It is Filmer’s particular merit that he perceived the way in which the contrasted and hitherto incompatible merits of balloon and heavy flying machine might be combined in one apparatus, which should be at choice either heavier or lighter than air. He took hints from the contractile bladders of fish and the pneumatic cavities of birds. He devised an arrangement of contractile and absolutely closed balloons which when expanded could lift the actual flying apparatus with ease, and when retracted by the complicated “musculature” he wove about them, were withdrawn almost completely into the frame; and he built the large framework which these balloons sustained, of hollow, rigid tubes, the air in which, by an ingenious contrivance, was automatically pumped out as the apparatus fell, and which then remained exhausted so long as the aeronaut desired. There were no wings or propellers to his machine, such as there had been to all previous aeroplanes, and the only engine required was the compact and powerful little appliance needed to contract the balloons. He perceived that such an apparatus as he had devised might rise with frame exhausted and balloons expanded to a considerable height, might then contract its balloons and let the air into its frame, and by an adjustment of its weights slide down the air in any desired direction. As it fell it would accumulate velocity and at the same time lose weight, and the momentum accumulated by its down-rush could be utilised by means of a shifting of its weights to drive it up in the air again as the balloons expanded. This conception, which is still the structural conception of all successful flying machines, needed, however, a vast amount of toil upon its details before it could actually be realised, and such toil Filmer—as he was accustomed to tell the numerous interviewers who crowded upon him in the heyday of his fame—“ungrudgingly and unsparingly gave.” His particular difficulty was the elastic lining of the contractile balloon. He found he needed a new substance, and in the discovery and manufacture of that new substance he had, as he never failed to impress upon the interviewers, “performed a far more arduous work than even in the actual achievement of my seemingly greater discovery.”

===Chinese===
那么菲尔默的构想究竟是什么？说起来很简单。在他之前，航空学的探索沿着两条分道扬镳的路线发展：一方面是气球——比空气轻的大型装置，升空容易，降落也相对安全，但任何一阵风都能把它无可奈何地吹着乱飘；另一方面是只存在于理论中的飞行机器——比空气重的庞大扁平结构，靠沉重的发动机推动和维持升空，而一下降多半就摔得粉碎。可是，暂且不论那不可避免的最终坠毁使之根本不可行，飞行机器因其自重倒有这样一个理论上的优势：它能逆风穿行于空中——这是空中航行若要具有任何实用价值所必备的条件。气球与重型飞行机器，二者各有长短、互不相容，如何能将这两面合为一体、造出一具既能比空气重又能比空气轻的装置——这正是菲尔默独具的功劳，他看出了门道。他从鱼类可收缩的鳔和鸟类的气腔得到启发。他设计了一组可收缩的、绝对密闭的气球，膨胀时能轻松地把整个飞行装置吊起；被他在其周围编织的复杂"肌肉组织"收缩之后，又几乎完全收进骨架里；他又建造了由这些气球支撑的大型骨架，用空心而坚固的管子做成，凭借一种巧妙的机关，装置下落时管内的空气会被自动抽出，此后只要飞行者愿意，便一直保持真空。他的机器没有翅膀，也没有螺旋桨——此前所有的飞机都备有这些东西——唯一需要的发动机，只是一具紧凑而有力的小装置，用以收缩气球。他看出，他所设计的这种装置，可以在骨架抽空、气球胀起的状态下升到相当的高度，继而收缩气球、让空气回到骨架里，再通过调整重心，沿任何想要的方向从空中滑降。下落时它会不断积累速度，同时又不断减轻重量，而它俯冲所积蓄的动量，则可以借调整重心、趁气球重新膨胀之机，把它再次送上半空。这一构想，至今仍是所有成功飞行机器的结构原理，但在它真正实现之前，其各个细节仍需付出浩繁的辛劳；而这辛劳，菲尔默——正如他在名声鼎盛时蜂拥而至的众多采访者面前常说的那样——"毫不吝惜、毫不保留地奉献了出来。"他格外棘手的是可收缩气球的弹性衬里。他发现自己需要一种新物质；而在这种新物质的发现与制造上，他——这一点他从不忘了让记者们铭记——"完成了一项比我那看似更伟大的发现之真正实现还要艰巨得多的工作。"

===Original===
But it must not be imagined that these interviews followed hard upon Filmer’s proclamation of his invention. An interval of nearly five years elapsed during which he timidly remained at his rubber factory—he seems to have been entirely dependent on his small income from this source—making misdirected attempts to assure a quite indifferent public that he really *had* invented what he had invented. He occupied the greater part of his leisure in the composition of letters to the scientific and daily press, and so forth, stating precisely the net result of his contrivances, and demanding financial aid. That alone would have sufficed for the suppression of his letters. He spent such holidays as he could arrange in unsatisfactory interviews with the doorkeepers of leading London papers—he was singularly not adapted for inspiring hall-porters with confidence—and he positively attempted to induce the War Office to take up his work with him. There remains a confidential letter from Major-General Volleyfire to the Earl of Frogs. “The man’s a crank and a bounder to boot,” says the Major-General in his bluff, sensible, army way, and so left it open for the Japanese to secure, as they subsequently did, the priority in this side of warfare—a priority they still to our great discomfort retain.

===Chinese===
但不要以为这些采访是紧跟着菲尔默宣告其发明而来的。中间隔了将近五年，他怯怯地待在那家橡胶厂——他似乎全靠这处微薄收入维持生计——一再徒劳地想向一个完全漠不关心的公众保证，他确实*已经*发明了他所发明的东西。他闲暇的大半光阴，都用来给科学期刊和日报等撰文，准确陈述其装置的净成果，并索取资助。光凭这一点，就足以让他的信件石沉大海。他能安排出的假期，都耗费在与伦敦各大报的门房进行毫无成效的会面上了——他这个人，实在不擅长让看门人对他的来历产生信任——他甚至还一本正经地设法游说陆军部与他合作开展这项工作。如今还留存着一封沃尔利法耶少将（Major-General Volleyfire）写给弗罗格斯伯爵（the Earl of Frogs）的机密信函。"此人是个疯子，还是个无赖，"少将以他那种直率、务实的军人做派写道。于是他便把这一块战争的优先权拱手让给了日本人，而日本人后来果真把它拿了过去——这一优先权至今仍令我们十分难受地为他们所把持。

===Original===
And then by a stroke of luck the membrane Filmer had invented for his contractile balloon was discovered to be useful for the valves of a new oil-engine, and he obtained the means for making a trial model of his invention. He threw up his rubber factory appointment, desisted from all further writing, and, with a certain secrecy that seems to have been an inseparable characteristic of all his proceedings, set to work upon the apparatus. He seems to have directed the making of its parts and collected most of it in a room in Shoreditch, but its final putting together was done at Dymchurch, in Kent. He did not make the affair large enough to carry a man, but he made an extremely ingenious use of what were then called the Marconi rays to control its flight. The first flight of this first practicable flying machine took place over some fields near Burford Bridge, near Hythe, in Kent, and Filmer followed and controlled its flight upon a specially constructed motor tricycle.

The flight was, considering all things, an amazing success. The apparatus was brought in a cart from Dymchurch to Burford Bridge, ascended there to a height of nearly three hundred feet, swooped thence very nearly back to Dymchurch, came about in its sweep, rose again, circled, and finally sank uninjured in a field behind the Burford Bridge Inn. At its descent a curious thing happened. Filmer got off his tricycle, scrambled over the intervening dyke, advanced perhaps twenty yards towards his triumph, threw out his arms in a strange gesticulation, and fell down in a dead faint. Everyone could then recall the ghastliness of his features and all the evidences of extreme excitement they had observed throughout the trial, things they might otherwise have forgotten. Afterwards in the inn he had an unaccountable gust of hysterical weeping.

===Chinese===
后来机缘巧合，菲尔默为他的可收缩气球所发明的薄膜被发现可用于一种新式燃油机的阀门，他由此得到了制造试验模型的本钱。他辞去橡胶厂的职务，不再撰写任何文字，带着一种似乎与他一切行事都形影不离的诡秘，着手制造这具装置。他似乎是在肖迪奇（Shoreditch）的一间屋子里指挥制造它的零部件，并把大半都装配在那里，但最后的总装是在肯特（Kent）的迪姆彻奇（Dymchurch）完成的。他没有把东西做得大到能载人，却极巧妙地利用了当时所谓的马可尼射线（Marconi rays）来操纵它的飞行。这第一架实用的飞行机器的首次飞行，是在肯特海斯（Hythe）附近、伯福德桥（Burford Bridge）附近的几块田野上空进行的，菲尔默则骑在一辆特制的机动三轮车上追随并操纵它的飞行。

通盘来看，这次飞行是一次惊人的成功。装置由大车从迪姆彻奇运到伯福德桥，在那里升到将近三百英尺的高空，从那里俯冲而下，几乎一路飞回迪姆彻奇，在盘旋中调头，再升起，绕圈，最后毫发无损地落在伯福德桥客栈后面的一块田里。降落时发生了一件怪事。菲尔默从三轮车上下来，翻过中间的一道沟渠，朝他的胜利品前进了约莫二十码，伸开双臂做出一种奇异的比划，便一头栽倒，不省人事。这时众人才回想起，在整个试验过程中，他脸上那死人般的神情和种种极度亢奋的迹象——那些否则他们早忘了的细节。随后在客栈里，他又莫名其妙地一阵歇斯底里地大哭起来。

===Original===
Altogether there were not twenty witnesses of this affair, and those for the most part uneducated men. The New Romney doctor saw the ascent but not the descent, his horse being frightened by the electrical apparatus on Filmer’s tricycle and giving him a nasty spill. Two members of the Kent constabulary watched the affair from a cart in an unofficial spirit, and a grocer calling round the Marsh for orders and two lady cyclists seem almost to complete the list of educated people. There were two reporters present, one representing a Folkestone paper and the other being a fourth-class interviewer and “symposium” journalist, whose expenses down, Filmer, anxious as ever for adequate advertisement—and now quite realising the way in which adequate advertisement may be obtained—had paid. The latter was one of those writers who can throw a convincing air of unreality over the most credible events, and his half-facetious account of the affair appeared in the magazine page of a popular journal. But, happily for Filmer, this person’s colloquial methods were more convincing. He went to offer some further screed upon the subject to Banghurst, the proprietor of the *New Paper*, and one of the ablest and most unscrupulous men in London journalism, and Banghurst instantly seized upon the situation. The interviewer vanishes from the narrative, no doubt very doubtfully remunerated, and Banghurst, Banghurst himself, double chin, grey twill suit, abdomen, voice, gestures and all, appears at Dymchurch, following his large, unrivalled journalistic nose. He had seen the whole thing at a glance, just what it was and what it might be.

===Chinese===
目击此事的总共不足二十人，且多半是没有受过教育的人。新罗姆尼（New Romney）的一位医生看见了起飞，却没看见降落——他的马被菲尔默三轮车上的电气装置惊了，把他狠狠摔了一跤。肯特郡警察队的两名警员以非官方身份坐在一辆大车里观看了全程，一位到沼泽地带各处招揽生意的杂货商和两位骑自行车的女士，似乎就差不多构成了在场受过教育者的全部名单。在场有两名记者，一名代表福克斯通（Folkestone）的一家报纸，另一名是个四流采访记者、专写"圆桌讨论"的报人——此人南下的路费，是一向渴求足够宣传、如今又颇懂得如何得到足够宣传的菲尔默掏的。这后一位，正属于那种能给最可信的事件蒙上一层令人信服的不真实感的撰稿人，他那半带戏谑的报道登在一家通俗期刊的杂志版上。然而，对菲尔默而言幸运的是，此人当面闲谈起来却更有说服力。他跑去向《新报》（the *New Paper*）老板、伦敦新闻界最能干也最不择手段的人之一班赫斯特（Banghurst）兜售关于此事的又一篇稿子，班赫斯特当即看中了这件事。这位采访记者就此从我们的叙述中消失了，所得酬劳无疑少得令他满腹狐疑；而班赫斯特——班赫斯特本人，带着他的双下巴、灰色斜纹呢西装、便便大腹、嗓门、手势以及一切——凭着他那硕大无双的新闻鼻子，出现在了迪姆彻奇。他一眼就看穿了整件事——它是什么，又可能成为什么。

===Original===
At his touch, as it were, Filmer’s long-pent investigations exploded into fame. He instantly and most magnificently was a boom. One turns over the files of the journals of the year 1907 with a quite incredulous recognition of how swift and flaming the boom of those days could be. The July papers know nothing of flying, see nothing in flying, state by a most effective silence that men never would, could or should fly. In August flying and Filmer and flying and parachutes and aerial tactics and the Japanese Government and Filmer and again flying, shouldered the war in Yunnan and the gold mines of Upper Greenland off the leading page. And Banghurst had given ten thousand pounds, and, further, Banghurst was giving five thousand pounds, and Banghurst had devoted his well-known, magnificent (but hitherto sterile) private laboratories and several acres of land near his private residence on the Surrey hills to the strenuous and violent completion—Banghurst fashion—of the life-size practicable flying machine. Meanwhile, in the sight of privileged multitudes in the walled-garden of the Banghurst town residence in Fulham, Filmer was exhibited at weekly garden parties putting the working model through its paces. At enormous initial cost, but with a final profit, the *New Paper* presented its readers with a beautiful photographic souvenir of the first of these occasions.

===Chinese===
经他这么一碰，菲尔默长久压抑、深藏不露的研究便轰轰烈烈地炸成了盛名。他顷刻之间、极其壮阔地成了一股热潮。翻阅 1907 年各报的合订本，人会带着一种近乎难以置信的心情认识到，当年的那种炒作风潮能有多么迅猛、多么炽烈。七月份的报纸对飞行一无所知，看不出飞行有什么名堂，以一种极有效的沉默表示：人类永远不会、也不可能、更不应当飞上天。到了八月，飞行与菲尔默，飞行与降落伞，空中战术与日本政府，菲尔默，又是飞行，硬是把云南的战事和上格陵兰（Upper Greenland）的金矿从头条版面挤了下去。班赫斯特已经捐出了一万镑，而且，班赫斯特正在捐出五千镑，班赫斯特还把他那远近闻名的、气派（却至今未出成果）的私人实验室，以及他在萨里丘陵（Surrey hills）私人宅邸附近的好几英亩地，全部用于以班赫斯特式的大干快上、雷厉风行的劲头，去完成一架与实物同大的实用飞行机器。与此同时，在富勒姆（Fulham）班赫斯特城里宅邸那座有围墙的花园里，菲尔默每逢每周一次的花园招待会便被展示在众多特权宾客面前，让工作模型当众演练它的本领。《新报》以极高的初始成本、却最终有赚头地，向读者赠送了一份首次盛会上的精美摄影纪念品。

===Original===
Here again the correspondence of Arthur Hicks and his friend Vance comes to our aid.

“I saw Filmer in his glory,” he writes, with just the touch of envy natural to his position as a poet passe. “The man is brushed and shaved, dressed in the fashion of a Royal-Institution-Afternoon Lecturer, the very newest shape in frock-coats and long patent shoes, and altogether in a state of extraordinary streakiness between an owlish great man and a scared abashed self-conscious bounder cruelly exposed. He hasn’t a touch of colour in the skin of his face, his head juts forward, and those queer little dark amber eyes of his watch furtively round him for his fame. His clothes fit perfectly and yet sit upon him as though he had bought them ready-made. He speaks in a mumble still, but he says, you perceive indistinctly, enormous self-assertive things, he backs into the rear of groups by instinct if Banghurst drops the line for a minute, and when he walks across Banghurst’s lawn one perceives him a little out of breath and going jerky, and that his weak white hands are clenched. His is a state of tension—horrible tension. And he is the Greatest Discoverer of This or Any Age﻿—the Greatest Discoverer of This or Any Age! What strikes one so forcibly about him is that he didn’t somehow quite expect it ever, at any rate, not at all like this. Banghurst is about everywhere, the energetic M.C. of his great little catch, and I swear he will have everyone down on his lawn there before he has finished with the engine; he had bagged the prime minister yesterday, and he, bless his heart! didn’t look particularly outsize, on the very first occasion. Conceive it! Filmer! Our obscure unwashed Filmer, the Glory of British Science! Duchesses crowd upon him, beautiful, bold peeresses say in their beautiful, clear loud voices﻿—have you noticed how penetrating the great lady is becoming nowadays?﻿—‘Oh, Mr. Filmer, how *did* you do it?’

“Common men on the edge of things are too remote for the answer. One imagines something in the way of that interview, ‘toil ungrudgingly and unsparingly given, Madam, and, perhaps﻿—I don’t know﻿—but perhaps a little special aptitude.’ ”

===Chinese===
在这里，阿瑟·希克斯与友人万斯的通信又一次帮了我们的忙。

"我见过菲尔默风头最劲的样子，"他写道，语气中带着一位过气诗人那种自然的几分醋意。"这人梳洗剃刮干净，穿得像皇家研究院下午场讲演人那样入时——最新款式的礼服大衣，长长的漆皮鞋——可整个人处于一种奇异的斑驳状态，介于一位像猫头鹰般呆气的大人物与一个被当众曝光、惊惶失措、自惭形秽的粗鄙之徒之间。他脸上没有一点血色，脑袋向前探着，那双古怪的深琥珀色小眼睛鬼鬼祟祟地向四周张望，寻觅着自己的盛名。他的衣服合身极了，穿在他身上却好像是从成衣铺买来的。他说话仍旧含混不清，但你隐隐约约能听出，他说的尽是一些极其自大的话；只要班赫斯特有一会儿没牵着他这根线，他便本能地往人群后面缩；当他穿过班赫斯特的草坪时，你会看出他有点气喘，动作发僵，那双苍白无力的手紧紧攥着。他处于一种紧张状态——可怕的紧张。而他就是当代乃至亘古以来最伟大的发现者——当代乃至亘古以来最伟大的发现者！他给人最强烈的印象是，不知怎的，他从没真正指望过这种事，至少绝没有指望会是这样。班赫斯特满场飞，是这位了不起的小猎获物精力充沛的司仪，我敢发誓，等他对付完了这台发动机，定要把所有人物都弄到他草坪上来不可；昨天他已经把首相也猎到了手，而首相呢，上帝保佑他！在最隆重的首演上看着也并不怎么出格。你想象一下！菲尔默！我们那位默默无闻、连澡都不常洗的菲尔默，竟成了英国科学之光！公爵夫人们簇拥着他，美丽大胆的贵族夫人用她们那美丽、清亮而响亮的嗓音——你可曾注意到，如今大人物家的夫人说起话来多么穿透？——说道：'哦，菲尔默先生，您是*怎么*做到的？'

"圈子外头的普通人隔得太远，听不见他的回答。人们不妨想象那次交谈会是这般光景：'夫人，那是毫不吝惜、毫不保留地奉献的辛劳，外加，或许——我也说不好——或许还有一点点特殊的天赋。'"

===Original===
So far Hicks, and the photographic supplement to the *New Paper* is in sufficient harmony with the description. In one picture the machine swings down towards the river, and the tower of Fulham church appears below it through a gap in the elms, and in another, Filmer sits at his guiding batteries, and the great and beautiful of the Earth stand around him, with Banghurst massed modestly but resolutely in the rear. The grouping is oddly apposite. Occluding much of Banghurst, and looking with a pensive, speculative expression at Filmer, stands the Lady Mary Elkinghorn, still beautiful, in spite of the breath of scandal and her eight-and-thirty years, the only person whose face does not admit a perception of the camera that was in the act of snapping them all.

===Chinese===
希克斯就说到这里，而《新报》的摄影副刊与这番描述也大体吻合。其中一张照片上，机器正朝着河面俯冲而下，透过榆树的一处空隙，富勒姆教堂的塔楼出现在它下方；另一张上，菲尔默坐在他操纵的电池组前，世上的显贵与佳丽簇拥在侧，班赫斯特则谦逊而坚定地挤在后方。这构图莫名地贴切。遮住了班赫斯特大半个身子、正以若有所思、打量的神色望着菲尔默的，是玛丽·埃尔金霍恩小姐（the Lady Mary Elkinghorn）——尽管有流言蜚语沾身、年已三十有八，她依旧美丽，是画面中唯一一个没意识到此刻正有架相机在给众人偷拍的人。

===Original===
