可是鸟从离巢那一刻起就在练习这门技艺。它不仅有完美的器官，更有使用这器官的完美本能。人一旦双脚离地，在保持平衡方面就笨拙到了极点。哪怕只是骑自行车这样一个简单把戏，也得花上他几个钟头的工夫。机翼那种瞬息之间的调整、对一阵过路微风所作的敏捷回应、对平衡的迅速恢复、那些需要绝对精确的令人眼花缭乱的旋转动作——这一切，他都非得学会不可，要付出无穷的辛劳、冒无穷的危险去学，才有望征服飞行。那种有朝一日靠着灵巧的"小拉杆"开动起来、有着一艘邮轮般漂亮的开敞甲板、满载着炸弹和大炮的飞行器，只不过是文人们轻飘飘的梦呓罢了。要征服空中这个帝国，在性命和钱财上所花的代价，甚至可能超过人类为征服海洋那桩伟业所花费的一切。它肯定比有史以来蹂躏过世界的任何一场战争都要昂贵。

这两点，没有人比这两位实干家更清楚。他们也知道自己是即将到来的那支大军中的前锋。然而，即便是敢死队一般的九死一生之中，也还是有希望的。有时候，留在后方的人会当场阵亡；而被丢在最激烈的角落里、以为必死的人，倒爬了出来，活了下来。

"万一我们错过了这片草地——"伍德豪斯用他那慢吞吞的腔调过了一会儿才说。

"老兄，"蒙森说——这几天他的情绪一阵阵地高扬起来，"我们绝不能错过这片草地。足有四分之一平方英里的地方供我们落，篱笆都拆了，沟也填平了。我们会稳稳当当地下来的——你放心。万一我们落不中——"

"啊！"伍德豪斯说，"万一落不中！"

===Original===
Before the day of the start, the newspaper people got wind of the alterations at the northward end of the framework, and Monson was cheered by a decided change in the comments Romeike forwarded him. “He will be off some day,” said the papers. “He will be off some day,” said the Southwestern season-ticket holders one to another; the seaside excursionists, the Saturday-to-Monday trippers from Sussex and Hampshire and Dorset and Devon, the eminent literary people from Hazlemere, all remarked eagerly one to another, “He will be off some day,” as the familiar scaffolding came in sight. And actually, one bright morning, in full view of the ten-past-ten train from Basingstoke, Monson’s flying-machine started on its journey.

They saw the carrier running swiftly along its rail, and the white and gold screw spinning in the air. They heard the rapid rumble of wheels, and a thud as the carrier reached the buffers at the end of its run. Then a whirr as the Flying-Machine was shot forward into the networks. All that the majority of them had seen and heard before. The thing went with a drooping flight through the framework and rose again, and then every beholder shouted, or screamed, or yelled, or shrieked after his kind. For instead of the customary concussion and stoppage, the Flying Machine flew out of its five years’ cage like a bolt from a crossbow, and drove slantingly upward into the air, curved round a little, so as to cross the line, and soared in the direction of Wimbledon Common.

It seemed to hang momentarily in the air and grow smaller, then it ducked and vanished over the clustering blue treetops to the east of Coombe Hill, and no one stopped staring and gasping until long after it had disappeared.

That was what the people in the train from Basingstoke saw. If you had drawn a line down the middle of that train, from engine to guard’s van, you would not have found a living soul on the opposite side to the flying-machine. It was a mad rush from window to window as the thing crossed the line. And the engine-driver and stoker never took their eyes off the low hills about Wimbledon, and never noticed that they had run clean through Coombe and Maiden and Raynes Park, until, with returning animation, they found themselves pelting, at the most indecent pace, into Wimbledon station.

===Chinese===
起飞那天的前夕，报界的人嗅到了脚手架北端所做改动的风声，罗迈克转给蒙森的评论里有了明显的变化，这让他为之一振。"他哪天就要飞起来了，"各家报纸说。"他哪天就要飞起来了，"西南线上持季票的乘客们彼此相传；海边度假的游客，从萨塞克斯（Sussex）、汉普郡（Hampshire）、多塞特（Dorset）、德文（Devon）来的"周六到周一"的短途客，以及从黑兹尔米尔（Hazlemere）来的鼎鼎大名的文人们，一见那熟悉的脚手架映入眼帘，便都急切地彼此相告："他哪天就要飞起来了。"果然，在一个晴朗的早晨，当着十点十分那班从贝辛斯托克（Basingstoke）开来的列车全体乘客的面，蒙森的飞行器踏上了它的旅程。

他们看见运载滑车沿着铁轨飞快地滑行，那白金两色的螺旋桨在空中旋转。他们听见车轮急促的轰隆声，以及滑车冲到跑道尽头撞上缓冲器时发出的一声闷响。接着是一声嗖响——飞行器被弹射进了绳网之中。这些，大多数人以前都见过、听过。这东西以一种低垂的飞行姿态穿过脚手架，又重新升起——紧接着，每一个旁观者都按照各自的性子，或者欢呼，或者尖叫，或者大喊，或者嘶吼起来。因为这一回，它没有像往常那样撞一下便停下来——飞行器像一支离弦的弩箭，从它那五年的囚笼里飞射而出，斜斜地冲上天空，又略微转了个弯，好横跨过铁路线，朝温布尔登公地（Wimbledon Common）的方向飞去。

它似乎在空中悬停了一瞬，越缩越小，随即一侧身，消失在库姆山（Coombe Hill）以东那一簇簇蓝茸茸的树梢后面。人们目瞪口呆地凝视着，直到它消失之后许久，还没有人肯把目光收回来。

这就是从贝辛斯托克开来的那趟列车上的人所看到的情景。倘若你从车头到守车，在这趟列车正中画一道线，你会发现，在飞行器所在的那一面，对面已经没有一个活人。那东西越过铁路线的当儿，人们疯了一样从一扇窗奔到另一扇窗。司机和司炉一直目不转睛地盯着温布尔登一带的低矮山丘，压根儿没察觉自己已经一口气驶过了库姆、莫尔登（Maiden）和雷恩斯公园（Raynes Park），直到他们回过神来，才发现自己正以一种极不雅观的速度冲进了温布尔登车站。

===Original===
From the moment when Monson had started the carrier with a “*Now!*” neither he nor Woodhouse said a word. Both men sat with clenched teeth. Monson had crossed the line with a curve that was too sharp, and Woodhouse had opened and shut his white lips; but neither spoke. Woodhouse simply gripped his seat, and breathed sharply through his teeth, watching the blue country to the west rushing past, and down, and away from him. Monson knelt at his post forward, and his hands trembled on the spoked wheel that moved the wings. He could see nothing before him but a mass of white clouds in the sky.

The machine went slanting upward, travelling with an enormous speed still, but losing momentum every moment. The land ran away underneath with diminishing speed.

“*Now!*” said Woodhouse at last, and with a violent effort Monson wrenched over the wheel and altered the angle of the wings. The machine seemed to hang for half a minute motionless in midair, and then he saw the hazy blue house-covered hills of Kilburn and Hampstead jump up before his eyes and rise steadily, until the little sunlit dome of the Albert Hall appeared through his windows. For a moment he scarcely understood the meaning of this upward rush of the horizon, but as the nearer and nearer houses came into view, he realised what he had done. He had turned the wings over too far, and they were swooping steeply downward towards the Thames.

The thought, the question, the realisation were all the business of a second of time. “Too much!” gasped Woodhouse. Monson brought the wheel halfway back with a jerk, and forthwith the Kilburn and Hampstead ridge dropped again to the lower edge of his windows. They had been a thousand feet above Coombe and Maiden station; fifty seconds after they whizzed, at a frightful pace, not eighty feet above the East Putney station, on the Metropolitan District line, to the screaming astonishment of a platformful of people. Monson flung up the vans against the air, and over Fulham they rushed up their atmospheric switchback again, steeply—too steeply. The ’buses went floundering across the Fulham Road, the people yelled.

===Chinese===
自从蒙森一声"走！"把滑车放出去那一刻起，他和伍德豪斯便再没说过一句话。两个人都咬紧了牙关。越过铁路线时蒙森把弯拐得太急了，伍德豪斯那一张毫无血色的嘴唇一张一合，却也没出声。伍德豪斯只是死死抓着自己的座位，从牙缝里急促地吸着气，眼看着西边那片蓝茸茸的乡野向后、向下、离他越来越远地掠去。蒙森在前面的岗位上跪着，两只手在那只带动翼面的带辐方向盘上颤抖。他眼前除了天上一团白云之外什么也看不见。

机器斜斜地向上升，速度仍然惊人，可动量却在一点一点地衰减。脚下的土地以越来越慢的速度向后退去。

"现在！"伍德豪斯终于说。蒙森用一把蛮力把方向盘猛地扳过去，改变了机翼的角度。机器似乎在半空中悬停了半分钟一动不动，随即他就看见基尔伯恩（Kilburn）和汉普斯特德（Hampstead）那一片蓝蒙蒙、布满房屋的山丘，从眼前跃起，并稳稳地抬升，直到阿尔伯特音乐厅（Albert Hall）那只浴在阳光下的小小圆顶从他的窗子里显现出来。有一瞬间他几乎没明白这条地平线猛地往上窜是什么意思，可随着越来越近的房屋一栋栋映入眼帘，他意识到自己干了什么。他把机翼扳过头了，他们正朝着泰晤士河（the Thames）的方向陡然俯冲下去。

这个念头、这个问题、这番领悟，前前后后不过是一秒钟的事。"过头了！"伍德豪斯喘着气说。蒙森猛地把方向盘往回扳了一半，基尔伯恩和汉普斯特德的山脊立刻又坠回到他窗子的下沿。方才在库姆和莫尔登车站上空他们还在一千英尺的高空；五十秒钟后，他们便以骇人的速度，呼啸着掠过大都会区线（Metropolitan District line）上的东帕特尼站（East Putney station），离地还不足八十英尺，惊得月台上一群人尖声大叫。蒙森把翼板迎空一扬，飞越富勒姆（Fulham）时，他们又沿着那条空中的过山车道重新冲了上去，陡——太陡了。富勒姆大道（Fulham Road）上的公共汽车七颠八倒地乱成一团，人们大呼小叫。

===Original===
Then down again, too steeply still, and the distant trees and houses about Primrose Hill leapt up across Monson’s window, and then suddenly he saw straight before him the greenery of Kensington Gardens and the towers of the Imperial Institute. They were driving straight down upon South Kensington. The pinnacles of the Natural History Museum rushed up into view. There came one fatal second of swift thought, a moment of hesitation. Should he try and clear the towers, or swerve eastward?

He made a hesitating attempt to release the right wing, left the catch half released, and gave a frantic clutch at the wheel.

The nose of the machine seemed to leap up before him. The wheel pressed his hand with irresistible force, and jerked itself out of his control.

Woodhouse, sitting crouched together, gave a hoarse cry, and sprang up towards Monson. “Too far!” he cried, and then he was clinging to the gunwale for dear life, and Monson had been jerked clean overhead, and was falling backwards upon him.

So swiftly had the thing happened that barely a quarter of the people going to and fro in Hyde Park, and Brompton Road, and the Exhibition Road saw anything of the aerial catastrophe. A distant winged shape had appeared above the clustering houses to the south, had fallen and risen, growing larger as it did so; had swooped swiftly down towards the Imperial Institute, a broad spread of flying wings, had swept round in a quarter circle, dashed eastward, and then suddenly sprang vertically into the air. A black object shot out of it, and came spinning downward. A man! Two men clutching each other! They came whirling down, separated as they struck the roof of the Students’ Club, and bounded off into the green bushes on its southward side.

===Chinese===
然后又是一下俯冲，仍然太陡。樱草山（Primrose Hill）一带远处的树木与房屋从蒙森的窗前跃起；紧接着，他猛然看见正前方是肯辛顿花园（Kensington Gardens）那一片葱茏的绿意，以及帝国研究院（Imperial Institute）的塔楼。他们正笔直地朝南肯辛顿（South Kensington）俯冲下去。自然历史博物馆（Natural History Museum）的一座座尖塔迎面扑入眼帘。接着是一秒钟决定生死的迅疾思量，一刹那的犹豫：是设法越过那些塔楼呢，还是向东拐？

他犹犹豫豫地想松开右翼，销子只松开了一半，他便发了疯似地去抓方向盘。

机器的机头仿佛在他眼前猛然翘起。方向盘以一种不可抗拒的力量反压到他的手上，猛地一挣，脱出了他的掌控。

蜷缩着坐着的伍德豪斯嘶哑地喊了一声，朝蒙森这边一跃而起。"过头了！"他喊道，随即便死命地攀住船舷般的座舱边沿；而蒙森已被整个儿抛过头顶，朝他仰面砸了下来。

这一切发生得如此之快，以至于在海德公园（Hyde Park）、布朗普顿路（Brompton Road）和展览路（Exhibition Road）上来来往往的人里，亲眼看见这场空中惨剧的，还不到四分之一。一个带翅膀的远影先是出现在南边鳞次栉比的房屋上空，下落又升起，随之越来越大；接着，展开着宽阔双翼，朝帝国研究院迅速俯冲下去，兜了四分之一个圈，猛地向东一冲，然后忽然间垂直地弹射向空中。一个黑色的物体从它身上射了出来，旋转着坠落。一个人！两个人，彼此紧紧抱在一起！他们旋转着坠落下来，撞上学生俱乐部（Students' Club）的屋顶时被甩开，又弹进了它南面的绿色灌木丛里。

===Original===
For perhaps half a minute, the pointed stem of the big machine still pierced vertically upward, the screw spinning desperately. For one brief instant, that yet seemed an age to all who watched, it had hung motionless in midair. Then a spout of yellow flame licked up its length from the stern engine, and swift, swifter, swifter, and flaring like a rocket, it rushed down upon the solid mass of masonry which was formerly the Royal College of Science. The big screw of white and gold touched the parapet, and crumpled up like wet linen. Then the blazing spindle-shaped body smashed and splintered, smashing and splintering in its fall, upon the northwestward angle of the building.

But the crash, the flame of blazing paraffin that shot heavenward from the shattered engines of the machine, the crushed horrors that were found in the garden beyond the Students’ Club, the masses of yellow parapet and red brick that fell headlong into the roadway, the running to and fro of people like ants in a broken anthill, the galloping of fire-engines, the gathering of crowds—all these things do not belong to this story, which was written only to tell how the first of all successful flying-machines was launched and flew. Though he failed, and failed disastrously, the record of Monson’s work remains—a sufficient monument—to guide the next of that band of gallant experimentalists who will sooner or later master this great problem of flying. And between Worcester Park and Malden there still stands that portentous avenue of ironwork, rusting now, and dangerous here and there, to witness to the first desperate struggle for man’s right of way through the air.

===Chinese===
足足有半分钟，那架大机器尖尖的机头仍笔直地刺向天空，螺旋桨拼死地旋转着。在所有目击者看来恍如隔世的那短短一刹那，它在半空中一动不动地悬停了一下。随即，一柱黄色的火焰从尾部的发动机处舔遍了它的全身，越来越快、越来越快、越来越快地，像一枚烟花似的，它朝着那一整块坚不可摧的石砌建筑——昔日的皇家理学院（Royal College of Science）——直冲下去。那只白金两色的大螺旋桨碰上胸墙，像湿布一样皱巴巴地瘪了下去。接着，那燃烧着的纺锤形机身轰然撞碎、迸裂开来，一边坠落、一边继续撞碎、迸裂，砸在了那座建筑朝西北的转角上。

然而，那一声巨响、从机器破碎的发动机里冲天而起的熊熊石蜡油火焰、在学生俱乐部那一边花园里发现的那些被砸得血肉模糊的可怖景象、大块大块的黄色胸墙和红砖一股脑儿栽进马路里、人们像被捣毁的蚁穴里的蚂蚁一样四下奔窜、消防车疾驰而来、人群越聚越多——这一切，都不属于本篇故事。这篇故事，只不过是要讲述世上第一架真正飞起来的飞行器是如何升空、如何飞翔的。蒙森虽然失败了，而且败得惨烈，但他那番事业的记录却留存了下来——这便是一座足够的丰碑——足以指引那一群英勇的实验家中后来的人，他们迟早会攻克飞行这一伟大难题。而在伍斯特公园与莫尔登之间，那条骇人的钢铁廊道至今仍然矗立着，业已锈迹斑斑，到处都是险处，它见证着人类为争取在空中通行的权利，所进行的第一次殊死的搏斗。

## The Beautiful Suit / 美丽的衣裳

===Original===
There was once a little man whose mother made him a beautiful suit of clothes. It was green and gold, and woven so that I cannot describe how delicate and fine it was, and there was a tie of orange fluffiness that tied up under his chin. And the buttons in their newness shone like stars. He was proud and pleased by his suit beyond measure, and stood before the long looking-glass when first he put it on, so astonished and delighted with it that he could hardly turn himself away. He wanted to wear it everywhere, and show it to all sorts of people. He thought over all the places he had ever visited, and all the scenes he had ever heard described, and tried to imagine what the feel of it would be if he were to go now to those scenes and places wearing his shining suit, and he wanted to go out forthwith into the long grass and the hot sunshine of the meadow wearing it. Just to wear it! But his mother told him “No.” She told him he must take great care of his suit, for never would he have another nearly so fine; he must save it and save it, and only wear it on rare and great occasions. It was his wedding-suit, she said. And she took the buttons and twisted them up with tissue paper for fear their bright newness should be tarnished, and she tacked little guards over the cuffs and elbows, and wherever the suit was most likely to come to harm. He hated and resisted these things, but what could he do? And at last her warnings and persuasions had effect, and he consented to take off his beautiful suit and fold it into its proper creases, and put it away. It was almost as though he gave it up again. But he was always thinking of wearing it, and of the supreme occasions when some day it might be worn without the guards, without the tissue paper on the buttons, utterly and delightfully, never caring, beautiful beyond measure.

===Chinese===
从前有一个矮小的男子，他母亲给他做了一身美丽的衣裳。那衣裳是金绿两色织就的，织得之精巧细致，我简直无法用言语形容；还有一条橘黄色的蓬松领带，系在下巴底下。那些崭新的纽扣，闪闪发亮犹如星星。他对这身衣裳得意极了，欢喜得无法衡量，头一回穿上它的时候，便站在那面长长的穿衣镜前，惊奇赞叹得几乎舍不得把目光移开。他想穿着它到一切地方去，把它给各种各样的人看。他把所有自己曾去过的地方，所有曾听人描绘过的场景，一一在心头过了一遍，想象着倘若此刻就穿着他这身闪亮的衣裳到那些场景、那些地方去，那感觉该是如何，恨不得立刻就穿着它奔进那长长的草丛、奔进牧场上滚烫的阳光里。只是想穿一穿它！可他母亲对他说：“不行。”她对他说，他务必格外爱惜这身衣裳，因为他再也得不到一身几乎同样讲究的了；他必须省着穿、省着穿，只在难得而又隆重的场合才能上身。这是他的结婚礼服，她说。于是她把那些纽扣取下来，用薄棉纸一一包缠起来，生怕那崭新的光亮被蒙上暗影；她又在那衣裳的袖口和肘部，以及任何最易受损的地方，缝上小小的护布。他痛恨这些东西，也反抗过，可他又有什么法子呢？终于，在她的一再告诫和劝说之下，他答应脱下他这身美丽的衣裳，把它按原样叠出该有的折痕，收了起来。这几乎就等于把它再一次交了出去。可他心里无时不在想着穿它，想着将来某一天那至高无上的时刻——那时它可以不必套着护布，不必裹着薄棉纸，彻彻底底、欢欢喜喜地被穿上身，什么都不顾忌，美丽得无以复加。

===Original===
One night, when he was dreaming of it after his habit, he dreamt he took the tissue paper from one of the buttons, and found its brightness a little faded, and that distressed him mightily in his dream. He polished the poor faded button and polished it, and, if anything, it grew duller. He woke up and lay awake, thinking of the brightness a little dulled, and wondering how he would feel if perhaps when the great occasion (whatever it might be) should arrive, one button should chance to be ever so little short of its first glittering freshness, and for days and days that thought remained with him distressingly. And when next his mother let him wear his suit, he was tempted and nearly gave way to the temptation just to fumble off one little bit of tissue paper and see if indeed the buttons were keeping as bright as ever.

===Chinese===
有一天夜里，他像往常一样在梦里想着这身衣裳，梦见自己把一颗纽扣上的薄棉纸取了下来，却发现它的光亮已褪了少许，这让他梦里好不难受。他把那颗可怜的、褪了光的纽扣擦了又擦，可它若有变化，反倒变得更暗淡了。他醒了过来，躺在床上睡不着，想着那一点变得暗淡的光亮，心想倘若等那重大的时刻（管它是什么时刻）到来之时，偏偏有一颗纽扣的色泽比起最初那闪闪发亮的簇新样子稍有逊色，他心里该是什么滋味——这个念头苦恼了他一天又一天。等到下一次他母亲让他穿那身衣裳的时候，他受了诱惑，几乎就要屈服于这诱惑了——想偷偷揭下那么一小片薄棉纸，看看那些纽扣到底是不是还像从前一样明亮。

===Original===
He went trimly along on his way to church, full of this wild desire. For you must know his mother did, with repeated and careful warnings, let him wear his suit at times, on Sundays, for example, to and fro from church, when there was no threatening of rain, no dust blowing, nor anything to injure it, with its buttons covered and its protections tacked upon it, and a sunshade in his hand to shadow it if there seemed too strong a sunlight for its colours. And always, after such occasions, he brushed it over and folded it exquisitely as she had taught him, and put it away again.

===Chinese===
他衣冠楚楚地走在去教堂的路上，满心都是这个狂野的念头。须知他母亲确实会一再地、仔仔细细地告诫一番之后，才偶尔让他穿一穿这身衣裳，比如礼拜天上教堂做礼拜来回的路上，那时节天上没有下雨的苗头，没有扬尘，也没有任何可能伤着它的东西，纽扣罩着、护布缝着，手里还要撑一把阳伞，一旦日头太烈、怕伤了它的颜色，便好遮一遮。而每一次这样穿过之后，他总照她教的法子，把它细细刷过，精致地叠好，再重新收起来。

===Original===
Now all these restrictions his mother set to the wearing of his suit he obeyed, always he obeyed them, until one strange night he woke up and saw the moonlight shining outside his window. It seemed to him the moonlight was not common moonlight, nor the night a common night, and for awhile he lay quite drowsily, with this odd persuasion in his mind. Thought joined on to thought like things that whisper warmly in the shadows. Then he sat up in his little bed suddenly very alert, with his heart beating very fast, and a quiver in his body from top to toe. He had made up his mind. He knew that now he was going to wear his suit as it should be worn. He had no doubt in the matter. He was afraid, terribly afraid, but glad, glad.

===Chinese===
母亲定下的关于穿这身衣裳的种种限制，他都一一遵从了，向来都遵从着，直到一个奇异的夜晚，他忽然醒来，看见窗外月华如水。在他看来，那月光似乎不是寻常的月光，那夜也不是寻常的夜，有一阵子他昏昏沉沉地躺着，心头盘桓着这么一个奇特的念头。一个念头接着一个念头，就像那些在阴影里暖声低语的事物一样连了上来。接着他猛地在那张小床上坐起身来，神志分外清醒，心跳得飞快，浑身从头到脚都在轻轻颤动。他已下了决心。他知道，此刻他要把这身衣裳照它该被穿着的样子穿出去了。此事他再无半点犹疑。他怕，怕得要命，可又欢喜，欢喜。

===Original===
He got out of his bed and stood for a moment by the window looking at the moonshine-flooded garden, and trembling at the thing he meant to do. The air was full of a minute clamour of crickets and murmurings, of the infinitesimal shoutings of little living things. He went very gently across the creaking boards, for fear that he might wake the sleeping house, to the big dark clothespress wherein his beautiful suit lay folded, and he took it out garment by garment, and softly and very eagerly tore off its tissue-paper covering and its tacked protections until there it was, perfect and delightful as he had seen it when first his mother had given it to him—a long time it seemed ago. Not a button had tarnished, not a thread had faded on this dear suit of his; he was glad enough for weeping as in a noiseless hurry he put it on. And then back he went, soft and quick, to the window that looked out upon the garden, and stood there for a minute, shining in the moonlight, with his buttons twinkling like stars, before he got out on the sill, and, making as little of a rustling as he could, clambered down to the garden path below. He stood before his mother’s house, and it was white and nearly as plain as by day, with every window-blind but his own shut like an eye that sleeps. The trees cast still shadows like intricate black lace upon the wall.

===Chinese===
他下了床，在窗边站了片刻，望着那片被月光浸透的花园，为他将要去做的事而微微发抖。空气里满是蟋蟀细碎的喧闹和窃窃私语，满是那些极微小的生灵发出的极微小的呼喊。他蹑手蹑脚地走过那些会吱呀作响的木地板，生怕惊醒沉睡的一屋子人，走到那只又大又黑的衣橱前——他美丽的衣裳便叠放在里面——一件一件把它取出来，轻轻地、急切地撕下那层薄棉纸包缠和缝着的护布，直到它完整而令人欢悦地呈现在眼前，正如他母亲头一回把它交给他时所见到的那般——那仿佛已是很久很久以前的事了。这身他心爱的衣裳上，没有一颗纽扣失了光泽，没有一丝线褪了颜色；他欢喜得几乎要落泪，悄无声息地、匆匆忙忙地把它穿到了身上。然后他又轻又快地回到那扇面向花园的窗前，在月光下站了一分钟，闪闪发亮，纽扣如星星般熠熠闪烁，接着他跨上窗台，尽可能弄出最小的窸窣声，攀爬下去，落到下面的花园小径上。他站在母亲的房子前，那房子一片煞白，几乎和白天一样清晰可辨，每一扇百叶窗——除了他自己那一扇——都闭着，像一只只睡着的眼。树木投下静定的阴影，如同繁复的黑色蕾丝，铺在墙上。

===Original===
The garden in the moonlight was very different from the garden by day; moonshine was tangled in the hedges and stretched in phantom cobwebs from spray to spray. Every flower was gleaming white or crimson black, and the air was a-quiver with the thridding of small crickets and nightingales singing unseen in the depths of the trees.

===Chinese===
月色中的花园与白日里的花园已大不相同；月光缠结在篱笆上，又像虚幻的蛛网一般，从这一簇枝叶伸到那一簇枝叶之间。每一朵花都闪着洁白或深绯近黑的光，空气则因小蟋蟀的穿行、因躲在树林深处看不见的夜莺的歌唱而微微颤动。

===Original===
There was no darkness in the world, but only warm, mysterious shadows, and all the leaves and spikes were edged and lined with iridescent jewels of dew. The night was warmer than any night had ever been, the heavens by some miracle at once vaster and nearer, and, spite of the great ivory-tinted moon that ruled the world, the sky was full of stars.

===Chinese===
世上再没有黑暗，只有温暖而神秘的阴影，所有的叶子和花穗，都镶着、衬着彩虹般闪烁的露珠宝石。这一夜比任何一个夜晚都要温暖，苍穹因着某种奇迹，一下子变得既更辽阔，又更迫近；而且，尽管一轮乳白色的大月高悬天际、主宰着这个世界，天上依然满天星斗。

===Original===
The little man did not shout nor sing for all his infinite gladness. He stood for a time like one awestricken, and then, with a queer small cry and holding out his arms, he ran out as if he would embrace at once the whole round immensity of the world. He did not follow the neat set paths that cut the garden squarely, but thrust across the beds and through the wet, tall, scented herbs, through the night-stock and the nicotine and the clusters of phantom white mallow flowers and through the thickets of southernwood and lavender, and knee-deep across a wide space of mignonette. He came to the great hedge, and he thrust his way through it; and though the thorns of the brambles scored him deeply and tore threads from his wonderful suit, and though burrs and goose-grass and havers caught and clung to him, he did not care. He did not care, for he knew it was all part of the wearing for which he had longed. “I am glad I put on my suit,” he said; “I am glad I wore my suit.”

===Chinese===
那矮小的男子虽有无限的欢喜，却既没有呼喊，也没有歌唱。他像被震慑住了一般，站了一阵，然后发出一声古怪而细小的喊叫，伸开双臂，跑了出去，仿佛要一下子拥抱整个圆滚滚、无边无际的世界。他并没有沿着那把花园整整齐齐切成方块的、修剪得规规矩矩的小径走，而是横穿过花圃，穿过那些湿漉漉、高高的、芬芳的药草，穿过紫罗兰和烟草，穿过那一簇簇如幻影般的白色锦葵花，穿过青蒿和薰衣草的灌丛，又膝盖深地蹚过一大片木樨草。他来到那道大篱笆前，便从当中硬挤了过去；虽然野莓的刺在他身上划出一道道深痕，又从他奇妙的衣裳上扯下一缕缕线头，虽然苍耳、茜草和刺果挂住他、粘住他，他却全不在意。他全不在意，因为他知道这正是他一直渴望的那番穿着的一部分。“我真高兴穿上了我的衣裳，”他说，“我真高兴穿过我的衣裳。”

===Original===
Beyond the hedge he came to the duck-pond, or at least to what was the duck-pond by day. But by night it was a great bowl of silver moonshine all noisy with singing frogs, of wonderful silver moonshine twisted and clotted with strange patternings, and the little man ran down into its waters between the thin black rushes, knee-deep and waist-deep and to his shoulders, smiting the water to black and shining wavelets with either hand, swaying and shivering wavelets, amidst which the stars were netted in the tangled reflections of the brooding trees upon the bank. He waded until he swam, and so he crossed the pond and came out upon the other side, trailing, as it seemed to him, not duckweed, but very silver in long, clinging, dripping masses. And up he went through the transfigured tangles of the willow-herb and the uncut seeding grasses of the farther bank. He came glad and breathless into the high road. “I am glad,” he said, “beyond measure, that I had clothes that fitted this occasion.”

===Chinese===
过了篱笆，他来到了鸭子池塘边，至少是白天那个鸭子池塘的所在。可到了夜里，它却成了一大碗银色的月光，满是青蛙的歌唱之声，一片热闹；那奇妙的银色月华，被扭结、凝结成种种怪异的图案。矮小的男子顺着那些纤细漆黑的芦苇之间奔下水面，由膝而腰，一直没到肩膀，用两只手把水击成一簇簇黑亮黑亮的小浪花——摇摇晃晃、颤颤巍巍的小浪花，浪花之间，星星被网进了岸上那些若有所思的树木倒影交织而成的乱影里。他蹚着蹚着便游了起来，就这样横渡了池塘，从对岸爬上来，身后拖着——在他看来——拖着的不是浮萍，而是一缕缕长长的、湿淋淋的、紧贴着身子的纯银。接着他穿上了岸，穿过柳兰那些仿佛变了一副模样、纷乱交缠的茎丛，穿过对岸那些未曾割过、已经结籽的野草。他气喘吁吁、满心欢喜地来到了大路上。“我真是高兴极了，”他说，“竟有这样一身衣裳，配得上这个场合。”

===Original===
The high road ran straight as an arrow flies, straight into the deep-blue pit of sky beneath the moon, a white and shining road between the singing nightingales, and along it he went, running now and leaping, and now walking and rejoicing, in the clothes his mother had made for him with tireless, loving hands. The road was deep in dust, but that for him was only soft whiteness; and as he went a great dim moth came fluttering round his wet and shimmering and hastening figure. At first he did not heed the moth, and then he waved his hands at it, and made a sort of dance with it as it circled round his head. “Soft moth!” he cried, “dear moth! And wonderful night, wonderful night of the world! Do you think my clothes are beautiful, dear moth? As beautiful as your scales and all this silver vesture of the Earth and sky?”

===Chinese===
那条大路像箭一样笔直地伸展，笔直地伸进月亮底下那一片深蓝色的天空深渊里，是一条白色的、闪闪发亮的路，夹在歌唱的夜莺之间。他便沿着这条路走去，时而奔跑、时而跳跃，时而又步行、又欢喜，身上穿的是他母亲用不知疲倦的、慈爱的双手为他做成的衣裳。路上积着厚厚的尘土，可对他来说，那不过是柔软的洁白罢了；他正走着，一只硕大的、颜色幽暗的飞蛾翩翩飞来，围着他那湿漉漉、闪闪发亮、急急前行的身影打转。起初他没有理会这只蛾子，后来便朝它挥起手来，随着它绕着他头顶盘旋，他竟像与它一同跳起舞来。“温柔的蛾子！”他喊道，“亲爱的蛾子！还有奇妙的夜啊，奇妙的世界的夜啊！你觉得我的衣裳美吗，亲爱的蛾子？像你的鳞粉一样美吗？像大地和天空这一袭银色的盛装一样美吗？”

===Original===
And the moth circled closer and closer until at last its velvet wings just brushed his lips…
---
And next morning they found him dead, with his neck broken, in the bottom of the stone pit, with his beautiful clothes a little bloody, and foul and stained with the duckweed from the pond. But his face was a face of such happiness that, had you seen it, you would have understood indeed how that he had died happy, never knowing that cool and streaming silver for the duckweed in the pond.

===Chinese===
那只飞蛾便越飞越近，越飞越近，直到最后，它那天鹅绒般的翅膀，恰好轻轻拂过了他的双唇……
---
第二天早上，人们在那个石坑底下发现了他，脖子已经摔断了，断了气，他美丽的衣裳上沾着一点血迹，又脏又污，沾满了从池塘带出来的浮萍。可他脸上是一种如此幸福的神情，要是你看见，你当真会明白——他是怀着幸福死去的，至死都不知道，那清凉的、流淌着的银，其实不过是池塘里的浮萍。

## The Cone / 锥形盖

===Original===
The night was hot and overcast, the sky red-rimmed with the lingering sunset of midsummer. They sat at the open window, trying to fancy the air was fresher there. The trees and shrubs of the garden stood stiff and dark; beyond in the roadway a gas-lamp burnt, bright orange against the hazy blue of the evening. Farther were the three lights of the railway signal against the lowering sky. The man and woman spoke to one another in low tones.

"He does not suspect?" said the man, a little nervously.

"Not he," she said peevishly, as though that too irritated her. "He thinks of nothing but the works and the prices of fuel. He has no imagination, no poetry."

"None of these men of iron have," he said sententiously. "They have no hearts."

"*He* has not," she said. She turned her discontented face towards the window. The distant sound of a roaring and rushing drew nearer and grew in volume; the house quivered; one heard the metallic rattle of the tender. As the train passed, there was a glare of light above the cutting and a driving tumult of smoke; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight black oblongs—eight trucks—passed across the dim grey of the embankment, and were suddenly extinguished one by one in the throat of the tunnel, which, with the last, seemed to swallow down train, smoke, and sound in one abrupt gulp.

===Chinese===
夜闷热而阴沉，天边镶着一圈仲夏残阳的暗红。他们坐在敞开的窗前，竭力想象那里的空气要清爽些。园子里的树木灌丛都僵直地黑立着；外头路上，一盏煤气灯亮着，鲜亮的橙色衬在暮色朦胧的蓝里。更远处，是铁路信号灯的三盏灯火，映着低垂的天空。一男一女低声交谈着。

"他没有起疑吧？"男人说，神情有些紧张。

"他才不会，"她恼恼地说，仿佛这件事也惹她烦。"他什么都不想，只惦着那工厂、那燃料的价。他没有想象力，没有诗意。"

"这些铁汉子个个都这样，"他煞有介事地说，"他们没有心。"

"他确实没有，"她说。她把那张不满的脸转向窗外。远处一阵轰鸣呼啸之声越来越近，越响越烈；屋子都跟着颤了一下；听得见煤水车那金属的哐啷声。火车驶过时，路堑上方猛地亮起一片光，随之是翻涌逼人的烟尘；一节、两节、三节、四节、五节、六节、七节、八节——八节车皮——黑色的长方块从路堤暗灰的底色前掠过，又逐一骤然熄灭在隧道的喉口里，而那隧道，仿佛随最后一节车厢一同，把整列火车、那片烟、那片声，一口吞了个干净。

===Original===
"This country was all fresh and beautiful once," he said; "and now—it is Gehenna. Down that way—nothing but pot-banks and chimneys belching fire and dust into the face of heaven… But what does it matter? An end comes, an end to all this cruelty… *Tomorrow.*" He spoke the last word in a whisper.

"*Tomorrow*," she said, speaking in a whisper too, and still staring out of the window.

"Dear!" he said, putting his hand on hers.

She turned with a start, and their eyes searched one another's. Hers softened to his gaze. "My dear one!" she said, and then: "It seems so strange—that you should have come into my life like this—to open—" She paused.

"To open?" he said.

"All this wonderful world"—she hesitated, and spoke still more softly—"this world of *love* to me."

===Chinese===
"这片地方从前可是清新秀美的，"他说，"如今——却成了欣嫩子谷（Gehenna）。往那边去——净是些陶窑、烟囱，直往老天爷脸上喷火喷灰……可那又有什么要紧？终有个了的，这一切的酷虐终有个了断……就在*明天*。"最后那个词他几乎是耳语着说出口的。

"*明天*，"她也低语着应道，眼睛仍望着窗外出神。

"亲爱的！"他说着，把手覆在她的手上。

她猛地一惊转过脸来，两人的目光彼此探询着。她的眼神在他的注视下柔和下来。"我亲爱的人儿！"她说，接着又道："真是奇怪——你竟这样走进我的生命里——来打开——"她顿住了。

"打开什么？"他问。

"这整个奇妙的世界"——她迟疑了一下，声音压得更轻了——"这个*爱*的世界，为我打开了。"

===Original===
Then suddenly the door clicked and closed. They turned their heads, and he started violently back. In the shadow of the room stood a great shadowy figure-silent. They saw the face dimly in the half-light, with unexpressive dark patches under the penthouse brows. Every muscle in Raut's body suddenly became tense. When could the door have opened? What had he heard? Had he heard all? What had he seen? A tumult of questions.

The newcomer's voice came at last, after a pause that seemed interminable. "Well?" he said.

"I was afraid I had missed you, Horrocks," said the man at the window, gripping the window-ledge with his hand. His voice was unsteady.

The clumsy figure of Horrocks came forward out of the shadow. He made no answer to Raut's remark. For a moment he stood above them.

The woman's heart was cold within her. "I told Mr. Raut it was just possible you might come back," she said in a voice that never quivered.

Horrocks, still silent, sat down abruptly in the chair by her little worktable. His big hands were clenched; one saw now the fire of his eyes under the shadow of his brows. He was trying to get his breath. His eyes went from the woman he had trusted to the friend he had trusted, and then back to the woman.

By this time and for the moment all three half understood one another. Yet none dared say a word to ease the pent-up things that choked them.

It was the husband's voice that broke the silence at last.

"You wanted to see me?" he said to Raut.

===Chinese===
就在这时，门咔哒一响，关上了。两人回过头，他猛地一下朝后退去。屋里的阴影中，立着一个硕大的、模糊的身影——默不作声。借着半明半暗的光，他们依稀看见那张脸，突出的眉脊下是两团毫无表情的黑影。劳特（Raut）浑身的肌肉骤然绷紧。门是什么时候开的？他听见了什么？他全听见了吗？他看见了什么？一连串问题在心头翻涌。

来人沉默了许久，久得仿佛没有尽头，终于开了口："怎么啦？"

"我还当错过你了呢，霍洛克斯（Horrocks），"窗前的男人说，一只手紧紧攥着窗台。他的声音不稳。

霍洛克斯那笨重的身形从阴影里走了出来。他对劳特的话不置一词。有一阵子，他居高临下地立在两人面前。

女人的心里冷透了。"我刚跟劳特先生讲，你兴许会回来的，"她说，嗓音竟没有一丝颤抖。

霍洛克斯依旧不吭声，猛地在妻子那只小活计桌旁的椅子上坐了下来。他那双大手攥成了拳；此刻人们才看清他眉骨阴影下眼里的火。他正竭力喘过气来。他的目光，从那个他曾信任的女人，移到那个他曾信任的朋友身上，又移回那个女人。

到这时候，一时间，三个人心里都彼此明白了几分。然而谁也不敢开口，去松一松堵在喉咙里的那些话。

终究是丈夫的声音打破了沉默。

"你要见我？"他对劳特说。

===Original===
Raut started as he spoke. "I came to see you," he said, resolved to lie to the last.

"Yes," said Horrocks.

"You promised," said Raut, "to show me some fine effects of moonlight and smoke."

"I promised to show you some fine effects of moonlight and smoke," repeated Horrocks in a colourless voice.

"And I thought I might catch you tonight before you went down to the works," proceeded Raut, "and come with you."

There was another pause. Did the man mean to take the thing coolly? Did he, after all, know? How long had he been in the room? Yet even at the moment when they heard the door, their attitudes… Horrocks glanced at the profile of the woman, shadowy pallid in the half-light. Then he glanced at Raut, and seemed to recover himself suddenly. "Of course," he said, "I promised to show you the works under their proper dramatic conditions. It's odd how I could have forgotten."

"If I am troubling you—" began Raut.

Horrocks started again. A new light had suddenly come into the sultry gloom of his eyes. "Not in the least," he said.

===Chinese===
劳特一听，吓了一跳。"我是来看你的，"他说，横下心要撒谎撒到底。

"嗯。"霍洛克斯说。

"你答应过，"劳特说，"要让我看看月光和烟雾搭配出的几种妙景。"

"我答应过，要让你看看月光和烟雾搭配出的几种妙景。"霍洛克斯毫无色彩地重复了一遍。

"我想着，今儿夜里趁你还没下厂，兴许能堵着你，"劳特接着说，"好跟你一道去。"

又是一阵沉默。这人莫非是想装作若无其事？他到底知不知道？他在屋里待了多久了？可即便在他们听见门响的那一刻，他们的姿态……霍洛克斯瞥了一眼妻子的侧脸，在半明半暗中苍白而模糊。随后他看了看劳特，像是一下子回了神。"当然，"他说，"我答应过，要在恰到好处的戏剧性条件下让你看看那工厂。真是怪了，我怎么竟会忘了。"

"要是我打扰了你——"劳特开口道。

霍洛克斯又陡地一震。他那双闷热阴沉的眼里，忽然掠过一道新的光亮。"哪儿的话，"他说。

===Original===
"Have you been telling Mr. Raut of all these contrasts of flame and shadow you think so splendid?" said the woman, turning now to her husband for the first time, her confidence creeping back again, her voice just one half-note too high—"that dreadful theory of yours that machinery is beautiful, and everything else in the world ugly. I thought he would not spare you, Mr. Raut. It's his great theory, his one discovery in art."

"I am slow to make discoveries," said Horrocks grimly, damping her suddenly. "But what I discover—" He stopped.

"Well?" she said.

"Nothing;" and suddenly he rose to his feet.

"I promised to show you the works," he said to Raut, and put his big, clumsy hand on his friend's shoulder. "And you are ready to go?"

"Quite," said Raut, and stood up also.

There was another pause. Each of them peered through the indistinctness of the dusk at the other two.

Horrocks' hand still rested on Raut's shoulder. Raut half fancied still that the incident was trivial after all. But Mrs. Horrocks knew her husband better, knew that grim quiet in his voice, and the confusion in her mind took a vague shape of physical evil. "Very well," said Horrocks, and, dropping his hand, turned towards the door.

"My hat?" Raut looked round in the half-light.

"That's my workbasket," said Mrs. Horrocks with a gust of hysterical laughter. Their hands came together on the back of the chair. "Here it is!" he said. She had an impulse to warn him in an undertone, but she could not frame a word. "Don't go!" and "Beware of him!" struggled in her mind, and the swift moment passed.

"Got it?" said Horrocks, standing with the door half open.

Raut stepped towards him. "Better say goodbye to Mrs. Horrocks," said the ironmaster, even more grimly quiet in his tone than before.

Raut started and turned. "Good evening, Mrs. Horrocks," he said, and their hands touched.

===Chinese===
"您有没有跟劳特先生讲过，您自个儿觉得多么了不起的那些火焰与阴影的对照？"女人说，这是她头一回转向丈夫，那点底气又悄悄回到了身上，嗓音却高了半个调子——"您那套可怕的说法，说机器是美的，世上别的一切都是丑的。我原以为他会饶不了您呢，劳特先生。那是他的大理论，他在艺术上唯一的一项发现。"

"我这人发现得慢，"霍洛克斯阴沉地说，一下子把她噎住了。"可我一经发现——"他收住了口。

"怎么？"她问。

"没什么。"说着，他陡然站起身来。

"我答应过带你看看工厂，"他对劳特说，把他那只又大又笨的手搁在朋友肩头。"你这就可以走了？"

"完全可以。"劳特说着，也站了起来。

又是一阵沉默。三个人在暮色的朦胧中，彼此打量着另外两个。

霍洛克斯那只手仍搁在劳特肩上。劳特还有一半心思以为，这事到底不过是桩小事。可霍洛克斯太太更了解自己的丈夫，识得他嗓音里那阴沉的静，于是她心头的慌乱，模模糊糊地凝成了一种肉体上的不祥之感。"很好，"霍洛克斯说，放下手，转身朝门口走去。

"我的帽子呢？"劳特在半明半暗里四下张望。

"那是我的针线篮，"霍洛克斯太太说，迸出一阵歇斯底里的笑。两人的手在椅背上碰到了一块儿。"在这儿呢！"他说。她有一股冲动，想低声提他一句，可就是吐不出一个字。"别去！"和"当心他！"在她心里扭打，可这转瞬即逝的工夫已经过去了。

"找到了？"霍洛克斯站在半开的门边问。

劳特朝他走过去。"最好跟霍洛克斯太太道个别，"这位铁厂老板说，嗓音比刚才更阴沉地平静。

劳特一惊，回过身来。"晚安，霍洛克斯太太，"他说，两人的手碰了碰。

===Original===
Horrocks held the door open with a ceremonial politeness unusual in him towards men. Raut went out, and then, after a wordless look at her, her husband followed. She stood motionless while Raut's light footfall and her husband's heavy tread, like bass and treble, passed down the passage together. The front door slammed heavily. She went to the window, moving slowly, and stood watching, leaning forward. The two men appeared for a moment at the gateway in the road, passed under the street lamp, and were hidden by the black masses of the shrubbery. The lamplight fell for a moment on their faces, showing only unmeaning pale patches, telling nothing of what she still feared, and doubted, and craved vainly to know. Then she sank down into a crouching attitude in the big armchair, her eyes-wide open and staring out at the red lights from the furnaces that flickered in the sky. An hour after she was still there, her attitude scarcely changed.

The oppressive stillness of the evening weighed heavily upon Raut. They went side by side down the road in silence, and in silence turned into the cinder-made byway that presently opened out the prospect of the valley.

A blue haze, half dust, half mist, touched the long valley with mystery. Beyond were Hanley and Etruria, grey and dark masses, outlined thinly by the rare golden dots of the street lamps, and here and there a gas-lit window, or the yellow glare of some late-working factory or crowded public-house. Out of the masses, clear and slender against the evening sky, rose a multitude of tall chimneys, many of them reeking, a few smokeless during a season of "play." Here and there a pallid patch and ghostly stunted beehive shapes showed the position of a pot-bank or a wheel, black and sharp against the hot lower sky, marked some colliery where they raise the iridescent coal of the place. Nearer at hand was the broad stretch of railway, and half-invisible trains shunted—a steady puffing and rumbling, with every run a ringing concussion and a rhymthic series of impacts, and a passage of intermittent puffs of white steam across the further view. And to the left, between the railway and the dark mass of the low hill beyond, dominating the whole view, colossal, inky-black, and crowned with smoke and fitful flames, stood the great cylinders of the Jeddah Company Blast Furnaces, the central edifices of the big ironworks of which Horrocks was the manager. They stood heavy and threatening, full of an incessant turmoil of flames and seething molten iron, and about the feet of them rattled the rolling-mills, and the steam-hammer beat heavily and splashed the white iron sparks hither and thither. Even as they looked, a truckful of fuel was shot into one of the giants, and the red flames gleamed out, and a confusion of smoke and black dust came boiling upwards towards the sky.

===Chinese===
霍洛克斯替他扶着门，礼数周全得异乎寻常——他对男人向来不如此。劳特走了出去，随后，她丈夫无言地望了她一眼，也跟了出去。她一动不动地站着，劳特那轻巧的脚步声和丈夫那沉重的脚步声，仿佛低音与高音，一同顺着过道渐远。前门沉沉地砰一声关上。她慢慢走到窗前，身子前倾，伫立着张望。两个人影在路上的院门口出现了一瞬，从街灯下走过，随即被灌木丛黑压压的一团吞没。灯光有一刻落在他们脸上，却只照出两片了无意义的苍白，对她仍在恐惧、犹疑、徒然渴望得知的一切，没有透露半分。随后她跌坐进那张大扶手椅，蜷成一团，两眼圆睁，直勾勾地望着炉火映在天际、明明灭灭的红光。一小时后她仍在那儿，姿态几乎没变。

傍晚那沉闷的寂静，重重地压在劳特心头。两人并肩沿路走着，一言不发，又默然拐进一条炉渣铺成的小路，不一会儿，山谷的景象便在眼前铺展开来。

一层蓝色的薄霭，半是尘、半是雾，给这道长长的山谷笼上一层神秘。再远处是汉利（Hanley）和伊特鲁里亚（Etruria），灰黑的一团团，被零零落落的金色街灯点细细勾出轮廓，间或一扇亮着煤气灯的窗，或是某家开到很晚的工厂、某间挤满人的酒馆那昏黄的强光。从那一片灰黑之间，一根根高耸的烟囱拔地而起，清晰而修长地映着暮色——其中许多根还在冒着烟，少数几根在这个"停火"的当口则无烟。这里那里，一片惨白的色块、几只形如鬼影、矮小如蜂巢似的东西，标示着某座陶窑或某个辘轳的位置；而一座座黑黢黢、棱角分明、衬在低处滚烫天空下的建筑，则是某处矿井——他们在那儿开采当地那种泛着虹彩的煤。再近些，是一大片铁路，半隐半现的列车在调车——一阵阵不息的喷气与轰隆，每跑一趟便是一声清脆的撞击、一连串有节奏的磕碰，间或一蓬一蓬的白蒸汽掠过更远处的视野。而左边，在铁路和远处那座低矮山丘的黝黑一团之间，高踞在整个景象之上，赫然矗立着杰达公司（Jeddah Company）高炉那几根巨大的圆柱——那是霍洛克斯所管辖的这座大型铁厂的核心建筑，墨黑，庞大，顶上笼罩着浓烟与明灭不定的火苗。它们沉沉地立着，带着一股威压，腹中是不息的烈焰和翻腾沸腾的铁水；在它们的脚下，轧钢机哐啷作响，蒸汽锤沉沉地砸下，把白热的铁花溅得四下都是。就在他们望去的同时，一整车燃料被倒进了那几个巨人中的一个，红色的火光骤然一亮，一团乱纷纷的烟和黑灰便朝着天空沸腾升腾。

===Original===
"Certainly you get some colour with your furnaces," said Raut, breaking a silence that had become apprehensive.

Horrocks grunted. He stood with his hands in his pockets, frowning down at the dim steaming railway and the busy ironworks beyond, frowning as if he were thinking out some knotty problem.

Raut glanced at him and away again. "At present your moonlight effect is hardly ripe," he continued, looking upward; "the moon is still smothered by the vestiges of daylight."

Horrocks stared at him with the expression of a man who has suddenly awakened. "Vestiges of daylight?… Of course, of course." He too looked up at the moon, pale still in the midsummer sky. "Come along," he said suddenly, and gripping Raut's arm in his hand, made a move towards the path that dropped from them to the railway.

Raut hung back. Their eyes met and saw a thousand things in a moment that their lips came near to say. Horrocks's hand tightened and then relaxed. He let go, and before Raut was aware of it, they were arm in arm, and walking, one unwillingly enough, down the path.

"You see the fine effect of the railway signals towards Burslem," said Horrocks, suddenly breaking into loquacity, striding fast and tightening the grip of his elbow the while—"little green lights and red and white lights, all against the haze. You have an eye for effect, Raut. It's fine. And look at those furnaces of mine, how they rise upon us as we come down the hill. That to the right is my pet—seventy feet of him. I packed him myself, and he's boiled away cheerfully with iron in his guts for five long years. I've a particular fancy for *him*. That line of red there—a lovely bit of warm orange you'd call it, Raut—that's the puddlers' furnaces, and there, in the hot light, three black figures—did you see the white splash of the steam-hammer then?—that's the rolling mills. Come along! Clang, clatter, how it goes rattling across the floor! Sheet tin, Raut—amazing stuff. Glass mirrors are not in it when that stuff comes from the mill. And, squelch! there goes the hammer again. Come along!"

He had to stop talking to catch at his breath. His arm twisted into Raut's with benumbing tightness. He had come striding down the black path towards the railway as though he was possessed. Raut had not spoken a word, had simply hung back against Horrocks's pull with all his strength.

===Chinese===
"你们的炉子倒是真有些颜色可看，"劳特说，打破了一段已渐渐变得叫人心慌的沉默。

霍洛克斯哼了一声。他双手插在口袋里，皱着眉，俯瞰着下方雾气蒸腾的铁路和远处忙碌的铁厂，那皱眉的样子像是在苦想什么难解的题。

劳特瞥了他一眼，又移开了目光。"眼下你这月光的效果还欠火候，"他接着说，仰头看去，"月亮还让那点残余的天光闷着呢。"

霍洛克斯瞪着他，神情像一个猛地惊醒的人。"残余的天光？……对，对，对。"他也抬头去看月亮，在仲夏的夜空里仍是苍白的。"走，"他忽然说道，一把抓住劳特的胳膊，迈步朝那条从他们脚下直落到铁路的小路走去。

劳特往后缩了缩。两人的目光相遇，一刹那间都看见了千般万种几乎就要脱口而出的话。霍洛克斯的手紧了紧，又松开。他放开了手，等劳特回过神来，两人已经挽着胳膊，一前一后——其中一个实在不大情愿——顺着小路走下去。

"你瞧朝伯斯勒姆（Burslem）那边的铁路信号灯，效果多好，"霍洛克斯说，忽然打开了话匣子，一边大步流星地走，一边把挽着劳特那只胳膊的肘弯扣得更紧——"一盏盏小小的绿灯、红灯、白灯，全都衬在那层薄霭上。你是个懂效果的人，劳特。真不赖。再瞧瞧我那些炉子，咱们一下山，它们就一节节地在眼前升起来。靠右边那个是我的心头好——足有七十英尺高。是我亲手把它填起来的，整整五年了，它肚子里烧着铁，咕嘟咕嘟地欢快翻腾。我对他格外有种偏爱。那边一道红——你会管它叫一截可爱的暖橙色，劳特——那是搅拌炉，就在那片炽热的光里，三个黑影——你刚才看见蒸汽锤溅出的那道白火花了吗？——那就是轧钢厂。来！哐啷、哐啷，听它在地皮上滚得多带劲！白铁皮啊，劳特——妙不可言的东西。等这东西从轧钢机里出来，连玻璃镜子都给它比下去了。嘿，扑哧！锤子又落下来了。走！"

他不得不停下来喘口气。他的胳膊死死地挽住劳特的，紧得叫人发麻。他是一路大步流星地顺着那条漆黑的小径奔向铁路的，活像着了魔。劳特一个字也没说，只是使尽全身力气，往后坠着，抵挡霍洛克斯的拖拽。

===Original===
"I say," he said now, laughing nervously, but with an undertone of snarl in his voice, "why on earth are you nipping my arm off, Horrocks, and dragging me along like this?"

At length Horrocks released him. His manner changed again. "Nipping your arm off?" he said. "Sorry. But it's you taught me the trick of walking in that friendly way."

"You haven't learnt the refinements of it yet then," said Raut, laughing artificially again. "By Jove! I'm black and blue." Horrocks offered no apology. They stood now near the bottom of the hill, close to the fence that bordered the railway. The ironworks had grown larger and spread out with their approach. They looked up to the blast furnaces now instead of down; the further view of Etruria and Hanley had dropped out of sight with their descent. Before them, by the stile, rose a notice-board, bearing, still dimly visible, the words, "**Beware of the Trains**," half hidden by splashes of coaly mud.

"Fine effects," said Horrocks, waving his arm. "Here comes a train. The puffs of smoke, the orange glare, the round eye of light in front of it, the melodious rattle. Fine effects! But these furnaces of mine used to be finer, before we shoved cones in their throats, and saved the gas."

"How?" said Raut. "Cones?"

"Cones, my man, cones. I'll show you one nearer. The flames used to flare out of the open throats, great—what is it?—pillars of cloud by day, red and black smoke, and pillars of fire by night. Now we run it off—in pipes, and burn it to heat the blast, and the top is shut by a cone. You'll be interested in that cone."

"But every now and then," said Raut, "you get a burst of fire and smoke up there."

"The cone's not fixed, it's hung by a chain from a lever, and balanced by an equipoise. You shall see it nearer. Else, of course, there'd be no way of getting fuel into the thing. Every now and then the cone dips, and out comes the flare."

"I see," said Raut. He looked over his shoulder. "The moon gets brighter," he said.

"Come along," said Horrocks abruptly, gripping his shoulder again, and moving him suddenly towards the railway crossing. And then came one of those swift incidents, vivid, but so rapid that they leave one doubtful and reeling. Halfway across, Horrocks's hand suddenly clenched upon him like a vice, and swung him backward and through a half-turn, so that he looked up the line. And there a chain of lamp-lit carriage windows telescoped swiftly as it came towards them, and the red and yellow lights of an engine grew larger and larger, rushing down upon them. As he grasped what this meant, he turned his face to Horrocks, and pushed with all his strength against the arm that held him back between the rails. The struggle did not last a moment. Just as certain as it was that Horrocks held him there, so certain was it that he had been violently lugged out of danger.

"Out of the way," said Horrocks with a gasp, as the train came rattling by, and they stood panting by the gate into the ironworks.

"I did not see it coming," said Raut, still, even in spite of his own apprehensions, trying to keep up an appearance of ordinary intercourse.

===Chinese===
"我说，"这会儿他开口了，神经质地干笑了一声，嗓音底下却暗藏一丝咆哮的味道，"你到底发的什么疯，要把我的胳膊拧下来哟，霍洛克斯，这么拽着我走？"

霍洛克斯终于松开了他。他的神色又变了。"把你的胳膊拧下来？"他说，"对不住。还是你教我这套勾肩搭背一块儿走的本事呢。"

"那这本事里的讲究你还没学到家，"劳特说着，又干笑了两声。"我的老天！我都被你掐得青一块紫一块了。"霍洛克斯并未道歉。这会儿两人已站在山脚附近，紧挨着铁路边的那道栅栏。随着他们的走近，铁厂在眼前愈发高大、铺展开来。他们现在是仰望着那些高炉，而不是俯瞰了；伊特鲁里亚和汉利那片更远的景致，已随着他们的下行而退出了视野。在他们前面，那道跨栏梯旁立着一块告示牌，依稀可辨地写着"**当心火车**"几个字，半截被溅上的煤泥糊住了。

"效果真好，"霍洛克斯挥了挥手臂，"火车来了。那一蓬蓬的烟，那橙色的强光，车头前那只圆圆的光眼，那悦耳的哐啷声。多好的效果！可我这炉子，从前还要更好，在我们往它们喉口里塞进锥形盖、把煤气省下来之前。"

"什么？"劳特说，"锥形盖？"

"锥形盖，老兄，锥形盖。我带你近处去看一个。从前那火焰是从敞开的炉口直往外窜的，喷得老高——怎么说来着？——白天是一根根云柱似的红黑浓烟，夜里则是一道道火柱。如今我们把它接走——顺着管子引出来，烧了去给鼓风加热，而炉顶就用一个锥形盖封住。你会对那个锥形盖感兴趣的。"

"可时不时地，"劳特说，"你们那儿还是会冒出一股火和烟来。"

"那锥形盖不是固定的，它由一根杠杆上垂下的链子吊着，再用一个配重把它稳住。等会儿让你近处看。要不，当然就没法子往那家伙肚子里添燃料了。每隔一会儿，锥形盖往下一沉，火光就窜了出来。"

"我明白了，"劳特说着，回头看了一眼。"月亮亮起来了，"他说。

"走，"霍洛克斯猝然说道，又抓住他的肩膀，猛地把他朝铁路道口推过去。接着便发生了那样一桩转瞬即逝的事——鲜明，却快得叫人满心狐疑、站立不稳。走到一半，霍洛克斯的手忽然像虎钳一样攥住他，把他往后一甩、半转个身，使他面朝铁路的前方望去。只见一串灯光明亮的车窗，像望远镜一节套进一节那样，朝着他们迅速缩近，一节火车的红黄灯火越来越大，朝他们直冲过来。他猛地明白这意味着什么，便把脸转向霍洛克斯，拼尽全身力气，去推那只把他卡在两条铁轨之间的胳膊。这场挣扎连一瞬间都没持续到。正如霍洛克斯确确实实把他按在了那儿一样，他也确确实实是被狠狠一把拽出了险境。

"靠边，"火车哐啷而过时，霍洛克斯喘着粗气说；两人站在铁厂大门边，大口喘着气。

"我没看见它过来，"劳特说——尽管自己心里也满是不安，却仍竭力装出一副寻常寒暄的模样。

===Original===
Horrocks answered with a grunt. "The cone," he said, and then, as one who recovers himself, "I thought you did not hear."

"I didn't," said Raut.

"I wouldn't have had you run over then for the world," said Horrocks.

"For a moment I lost my nerve," said Raut.

Horrocks stood for half a minute, then turned abruptly towards the ironworks again. "See how fine these great mounds of mine, these clinker-heaps, look in the night! That truck yonder, up above there! Up it goes, and out-tilts the slag. See the palpitating red stuff go sliding down the slope. As we get nearer, the heap rises up and cuts the blast furnaces. See the quiver up above the big one. Not that way! This way, between the heaps. That goes to the puddling furnaces, but I want to show you the canal first." He came and took Raut by the elbow, and so they went along side by side. Raut answered Horrocks vaguely. What, he asked himself, had really happened on the line? Was he deluding himself with his own fancies, or had Horrocks actually held him back in the way of the train? Had he just been within an ace of being murdered?

Suppose this slouching, scowling monster *did* know anything? For a minute or two then Raut was really afraid for his life, but the mood passed as he reasoned with himself. After all, Horrocks might have heard nothing. At any rate, he had pulled him out of the way in time. His odd manner might be due to the mere vague jealousy he had shown once before. He was talking now of the ash-heaps and the canal. "Eigh?" said Horrocks.

"What?" said Raut. "Rather! The haze in the moonlight. Fine!"

"Our canal," said Horrocks, stopping suddenly. "Our canal by moonlight and firelight is immense. You've never seen it? Fancy that! You've spent too many of your evenings philandering up in Newcastle there. I tell you, for real florid quality—But you shall see. Boiling water…"

As they came out of the labyrinth of clinker-heaps and mounds of coal and ore, the noises of the rolling-mill sprang upon them suddenly, loud, near, and distinct. Three shadowy workmen went by and touched their caps to Horrocks. Their faces were vague in the darkness. Raut felt a futile impulse to address them, and before he could frame his words they passed into the shadows. Horrocks pointed to the canal close before them now: a weird-looking place it seemed, in the bloodred reflections of the furnaces. The hot water that cooled the *tuyères* came into it, some fifty yards up—a tumultuous, almost boiling affluent, and the steam rose up from the water in silent white wisps and streaks, wrapping damply about them, an incessant succession of ghosts coming up from the black and red eddies, a white uprising that made the head swim. The shining black tower of the larger blast-furnace rose overhead out of the mist, and its tumultuous riot filled their ears. Raut kept away from the edge of the water, and watched Horrocks.

===Chinese===
霍洛克斯哼了一声算是回答。"锥形盖，"他说，又像回过神来似的补一句，"我以为你没听见。"

"我确实没听见，"劳特说。

"那我可断断不能让你给碾过去。"霍洛克斯说。

"有那么一瞬，我慌了神，"劳特说。

霍洛克斯站了半分钟，又陡然转身朝铁厂走去。"你瞧，我这一座座大堆、这些炉渣堆，夜里看着多带劲！那边那辆车上头那辆！升上去了，炉渣就倒了出来。瞧那通红的东西，一颤一颤地顺着坡滑下去。咱们一走近，这堆就越升越高，把高炉都遮住了。瞧那大炉子上头那一阵阵的颤动。别走那边！这边，从堆中间走。那条是去搅拌炉的，可我想先让你看看那条运河。"他过来挽住劳特的胳膊肘，于是两人并肩往前走。劳特含含糊糊地应着霍洛克斯。他心里问自己：刚才在线路上，到底出了什么事？是自己一厢情愿的胡思乱想把自己骗了，还是霍洛克斯当真把他按在了火车经过的路上？他刚才是不是险些就被人谋害了？

倘若这个佝偻着身、横眉竖眼的怪物*当真*知道些什么呢？有那么一两分钟，劳特当真是为自己的性命捏了一把汗，但他在心里把自己劝服后，这股劲也就过去了。毕竟，霍洛克斯也许什么都没听见。无论如何，他是及时把他拽开了的。他那古怪的做派，也许只是出于从前流露过的那种含含糊糊的嫉妒。这会儿他谈的，是炉灰堆和运河。"嗯？"霍洛克斯说。

"什么？"劳特说，"可不是嘛！月光里的那层雾。妙极了！"

"咱们的运河，"霍洛克斯猝然站住，"咱们这条运河，在月光和火光底下，那叫一个壮观。你没见过？真难得！你那些晚上都耗在北边纽卡斯尔（Newcastle）跟人调情去了。我告诉你，那种真正艳丽的效果——罢了，你等会儿自己看。滚烫的水……"

他们从那片炉渣堆、煤堆和矿石堆堆成的迷宫里钻出来时，轧钢厂的嘈杂声猛地向他们扑来——响亮、切近、分明。三个模糊的身影走过，朝霍洛克斯举帽致意。他们的脸在黑暗里看不真切。劳特涌起一股徒然的冲动，想开口招呼他们，可还没等他凑出话来，他们已经没人了黑影里。霍洛克斯指着就在眼前的那条运河：在炉子那血红的倒影里，那地方看上去透着一股诡异。冷却*风口*（tuyères）的热水，从上游五十来码的地方流进来——一股汹涌、几乎沸腾的支流，水汽从水面无声地升起，化作一缕缕、一道道白色的烟，潮湿地缠裹在他们周身，像一群接连不断、从黑红漩涡里冒出来的幽灵，那一片白腾腾的升腾，直搅得人头晕目眩。那座较大的高炉，闪着黑亮的塔身，从雾气中拔起，矗立在他们头顶，它那一片沸腾的喧嚣灌满了两人的耳朵。劳特离着水边远远的，眼睛盯着霍洛克斯。

===Original===
"Here it is red," said Horrocks, "bloodred vapour as red and hot as sin; but yonder there, where the moonlight falls on it, and it drives across the clinker-heaps, it is as white as death."

Raut turned his head for a moment, and then came back hastily to his watch on Horrocks. "Come along to the rolling-mills," said Horrocks. The threatening hold was not so evident that time, and Raut felt a little reassured. But all the same, what on earth did Horrocks mean about "white as death" and "red as sin"? Coincidence, perhaps?

They went and stood behind the puddlers for a little while, and then through the rolling-mills, where amidst an incessant din the deliberate steam-hammer beat the juice out of the succulent iron, and black, half-naked Titans rushed the plastic bars, like hot sealing-wax, between the wheels, "Come on," said Horrocks in Raut's ear; and they went and peeped through the little glass hole behind the *tuyères*, and saw the tumbled fire writhing in the pit of the blast-furnace. It left one eye blinded for a while. Then, with green and blue patches dancing across the dark, they went to the lift by which the trucks of ore and fuel and lime were raised to the top of the big cylinder.

And out upon the narrow rail that overhung the furnace Raut's doubts came upon him again. Was it wise to be here? If Horrocks did know—everything! Do what he would, he could not resist a violent trembling. Right under foot was a sheer depth of seventy feet. It was a dangerous place. They pushed by a truck of fuel to get to the railing that crowned the thing. The reek of the furnace, a sulphurous vapour streaked with pungent bitterness, seemed to make the distant hillside of Hanley quiver. The moon was riding out now from among a drift of clouds, halfway up the sky above the undulating wooded outlines of Newcastle. The steaming canal ran away from below them under an indistinct bridge, and vanished into the dim haze of the flat fields towards Burslem.

"That's the cone I've been telling you of," shouted Horrocks; "and, below that, sixty feet of fire and molten metal, with the air of the blast frothing through it like gas in soda-water."

===Chinese===
"这里是红的，"霍洛克斯说，"血红的水汽，红得、烫得像罪孽；可那边，月光落在上面、把它赶过那一堆堆炉渣的地方，它白得像死亡。"

劳特回头望了一瞬，便又急急把目光收回，盯着霍洛克斯。"上轧钢厂去吧，"霍洛克斯说。这一回，那种威吓似的钳制不那么明显了，劳特心里稍稍安定了些。可话说回来，霍洛克斯那句"白得像死亡"、"红得像罪孽"到底是什么意思？也许只是巧合？

两人去搅拌工身后站了一小会儿，又穿过轧钢厂——在那一片不息的喧响中，那柄不慌不忙的蒸汽锤，正把饱含汁水的熟铁一下下挤出浆来；一个个黝黑、半裸的巨人，把那些像滚烫火漆一样柔软的铁条，在轧轮之间推来搡去。"走，"霍洛克斯凑在劳特耳边说；两人便走到*风口*后头那个小小的玻璃窥孔前往里瞧，只见高炉炉膛里一团翻滚的火在扭动。那火光刺得人眼睛好一阵发花。随后，他们眼前一片漆黑里跳动着蓝一块绿一块的光斑，两人来到那部升降机前——一车车的矿石、燃料和石灰，就是由它送上那根巨大圆柱的顶端的。

走上那条悬在炉子上方的窄窄铁道，劳特心头的疑虑又涌了上来。到这里来，明智吗？倘若霍洛克斯当真知道——知道一切！他怎么也禁不住一阵剧烈的发抖。脚底下，是一落七十英尺的垂直深渊。这地方凶险。他们从一辆燃料车旁挤过去，走到高踞炉顶的那道栏杆前。炉子那股呛人的烟气，一股夹着刺鼻辛辣的硫磺味，似乎把远处汉利那边的山坡都熏得颤动起来。这会儿月亮正从一堆乱云里钻出来，挂在纽卡斯尔那起伏林木剪影之上半空的位置。蒸腾着水汽的运河从他们脚下延伸出去，钻过一座影影绰绰的桥，没入朝伯斯勒姆那片平野的朦胧薄霭之中。

"那就是我跟你说起的锥形盖，"霍洛克斯喊道，"它下面，是六十英尺的火焰和熔化的金属，鼓风的空气在里面起泡翻腾，就像苏打水里冒的气。"

===Original===
Raut gripped the handrail tightly, and stared down at the cone. The heat was intense. The boiling of the iron and the tumult of the blast made a thunderous accompaniment to Horrocks's voice. But the thing had to be gone through now. Perhaps, after all…

"In the middle," bawled Horrocks, "temperature near a thousand degrees. If *you* were dropped into it… flash into flame like a pinch of gunpowder in a candle. Put your hand out and feel the heat of his breath. Why, even up here I've seen the rainwater boiling off the trucks. And that cone there. It's a damned sight too hot for roasting cakes. The top side of it's three hundred degrees."

"Three hundred degrees!" said Raut.

"Three hundred centigrade, mind!" said Horrocks. "It will boil the blood out of you in no time."

"Eigh?" said Raut, and turned.

"Boil the blood out of you in… No, you don't!"

"Let me go!" screamed Raut. "Let go my arm!"

With one hand he clutched at the handrail, then with both. For a moment the two men stood swaying. Then suddenly, with a violent jerk, Horrocks had twisted him from his hold. He clutched at Horrocks and missed, his foot went back into empty air; in midair he twisted himself, and then cheek and shoulder and knee struck the hot cone together.

He clutched the chain by which the cone hung, and the thing sank an infinitesimal amount as he struck it. A circle of glowing red appeared about him, and a tongue of flame, released from the chaos within, flickered up towards him. An intense pain assailed him at the knees, and he could smell the singeing of his hands. He raised himself to his feet, and tried to climb up the chain, and then something struck his head. Black and shining with the moonlight, the throat of the furnace rose about him.

Horrocks, he saw, stood above him by one of the trucks of fuel on the rail. The gesticulating figure was bright and white in the moonlight, and shouting, "Fizzle, you fool! Fizzle, you hunter of women! You hot-blooded hound! Boil! boil! boil!"

Suddenly he caught up a handful of coal out of the truck, and flung it deliberately, lump after lump, at Raut.

"Horrocks!" cried Raut. "Horrocks!"

He clung, crying, to the chain, pulling himself up from the burning of the cone. Each missile Horrocks flung hit him. His clothes charred and glowed, and as he struggled the cone dropped, and a rush of hot, suffocating gas whooped out and burned round him in a swift breath of flame.

His human likeness departed from him. When the momentary red had passed, Horrocks saw a charred, blackened figure, its head streaked with blood, still clutching and fumbling with the chain, and writhing in agony—a cindery animal, an inhuman, monstrous creature that began a sobbing, intermittent shriek.

Abruptly at the sight the ironmaster's anger passed. A deadly sickness came upon him. The heavy odour of burning flesh came drifting up to his nostrils. His sanity returned to him.

"God have mercy upon me!" he cried. "O God! what have I done?"

He knew the thing below him, save that it still moved and felt, was already a dead man—that the blood of the poor wretch must be boiling in his veins. An intense realisation of that agony came to his mind, and overcame every other feeling. For a moment he stood irresolute, and then, turning to the truck, he hastily tilted its contents upon the struggling thing that had once been a man. The mass fell with a thud, and went radiating over the cone. With the thud the shriek ended, and a boiling confusion of smoke, dust, and flame came rushing up towards him. As it passed, he saw the cone clear again.

Then he staggered back, and stood trembling, clinging to the rail with both hands. His lips moved, but no words came to them.

Down below was the sound of voices and running steps. The clangour of rolling in the shed ceased abruptly.

===Chinese===
劳特紧紧攥住栏杆，俯瞰着那只锥形盖。热气逼人。铁水的沸腾和鼓风的轰响，为霍洛克斯的嗓音配上一阵雷霆般的伴奏。可事到如今，这一关是非过不可了。也许，到底……

"在当中，"霍洛克斯大吼，"温度将近一千度。要是把*你*扔进去……就会像一撮火药凑近烛火那样，噗地一下烧成一团火。伸出手去，感受一下它呼出来的热气。嘿，就在这儿这么高的地方，我都见过雨水从那些车上往下滚开呢。再说那个锥形盖。烤饼干什么的话，那温度可高得离谱了。它朝上那一面，就有三百度。"

"三百度！"劳特说。

"是摄氏三百度，记住！"霍洛克斯说，"它一转眼就能把你身上的血煮干。"

"什么？"劳特说着，转过身来。

"把你身上的血煮干，一转眼……哼，休想！"

"放开我！"劳特尖叫起来，"松开我的胳膊！"

他先是一只手去抓栏杆，接着两只手都抓了上去。两个男人摇晃着对峙了一瞬。随即，霍洛克斯猛地一拽，把他从栏杆上扭脱了手。他伸手去抓霍洛克斯，抓了个空，一脚踩进了虚空的空气里；半空中他扭动身躯，紧接着脸颊、肩膀和膝盖一齐撞上了滚烫的锥形盖。

他一把抓住了吊着锥形盖的那根链子，那一撞，锥形盖微微往下沉了一丝。他四周绽开一圈炽红，一缕从内里混沌中挣脱出来的火舌，朝着他舔了上来。一阵剧痛从双膝袭来，他闻得到自己手上烤焦的糊味。他挣扎着站起身，想顺着链子往上爬，接着有什么东西砸在了他头上。炉口那道喉壁，黑亮亮地反射着月光，在他四周拔起。

他看见，霍洛克斯正立在他头顶，铁道旁一辆燃料车边。那个手舞足蹈的身影在月光下白得发亮，正嘶声叫着："烧吧，你这蠢货！烧吧，你这猎艳的色鬼！你这条发情的公狗！煮吧！煮吧！煮吧！"

他猛地捧起一捧车里的煤，一块接一块，蓄意地朝劳特砸下去。

"霍洛克斯！"劳特叫道，"霍洛克斯！"

他哭喊着，死死攀住链子，把自己从滚烫的锥形盖上拽起来。霍洛克斯掷出的每一块煤都砸中了他。他的衣服烧焦了、发着红光；他挣扎间，锥形盖往下一沉，一股滚烫、令人窒息的煤气呼地涌出，化作一道迅猛的火舌，在他周身灼烧起来。

他那一点人形就此离他而去。待那一时的红光过去，霍洛克斯看见的是一个焦黑的人形，头上淌着一道道血，仍死死抓着链子摸索，痛苦地扭动着——一团焦炭般的畜生，一个不成样子、非人的怪物，开始发出一阵抽泣般的、断断续续的尖叫。

一见这光景，铁厂老板的怒火骤然消了。一阵要命的恶心袭上他心头。烧焦的人肉那股浓重的气味，飘进了他的鼻孔。他恢复了神志。

"上帝饶恕我吧！"他喊道，"哦，上帝！我都干了些什么？"

他明白，脚底下这个东西，除了还在动、还在感觉之外，已经是一具死尸了——那可怜虫血管里的血，必已在沸腾。对那份痛苦的一种强烈的体认涌上他心头，盖过了一切别的感受。他迟疑了一阵，随即转身朝着那辆小车，急急忙忙地把车里的东西，一股脑儿倒向那一团还在挣扎、曾经是个人的东西。那堆东西砰的一声砸了下去，朝着锥形盖四下辐射开去。随着那声闷响，尖叫声戛然而止，一团沸腾的烟、灰、火，朝他扑面涌上来。待这一阵过去，他看见锥形盖又清清爽爽地露了出来。

他这才踉跄着倒退几步，浑身发抖地站着，双手死死攥住栏杆。他的嘴唇翕动着，却吐不出半个字。

下边传来人声和奔跑的脚步声。工棚里轧钢的哐啷声陡然停了下来。

## The Country of the Blind / 盲人国

===Original===
Three hundred miles and more from Chimborazo, one hundred from the snows of Cotopaxi, in the wildest wastes of Ecuador’s Andes, there lies that mysterious mountain valley, cut off from the world of men, the Country of the Blind. Long years ago that valley lay so far open to the world that men might come at last through frightful gorges and over an icy pass into its equable meadows; and thither indeed men came, a family or so of Peruvian half-breeds fleeing from the lust and tyranny of an evil Spanish ruler. Then came the stupendous outbreak of Mindobamba, when it was night in Quito for seventeen days, and the water was boiling at Yaguachi and all the fish floating dying even as far as Guayaquil; everywhere along the Pacific slopes there were landslips and swift thawings and sudden floods, and one whole side of the old Arauca crest slipped and came down in thunder, and cut off the Country of the Blind forever from the exploring feet of men. But one of these early settlers had chanced to be on the hither side of the gorges when the world had so terribly shaken itself, and he perforce had to forget his wife and his child and all the friends and possessions he had left up there, and start life over again in the lower world. He started it again but ill, blindness overtook him, and he died of punishment in the mines; but the story he told begot a legend that lingers along the length of the Cordilleras of the Andes to this day.

===Chinese===
在钦博拉索山（Chimborazo）三百多英里之外，距科托帕希山（Cotopaxi）的雪峰一百英里开外，在厄瓜多尔安第斯山脉（Ecuador’s Andes）最荒凉的旷野之中，卧着那个与世人隔绝的神秘山谷——盲人国（the Country of the Blind）。许多许多年以前，那山谷尚向世人敞开一条通路，人们最终可以穿过险恶的峡谷、翻过一道冰雪的隘口，进入它气候温和的草甸；果然也有人来了——一两户秘鲁混血人家，为躲避一个恶毒的西班牙统治者的贪淫暴虐而逃到此地。后来，明多班巴（Mindobamba）那场惊天动地的大爆发来了：基多（Quito）一连十七天黑夜如漆，雅瓜奇（Yaguachi）的水滚沸，死鱼漂浮直连到瓜亚基尔（Guayaquil）；沿太平洋一侧的山坡处处山崩、雪线骤融、洪水猝发，古老的阿劳卡（Arauca）山峰整整一面山坡轰然崩塌，从此把盲人国与踏勘者的脚步永远隔绝开来。然而，在这些最早的移民之中，有一人恰巧在天地那样可怕地摇晃时，身处峡谷的这一边；他不得不抛下留在那边的妻儿、亲友和全部家产，到下界去重新开创生活。他重新开创，却十分不顺，双目失明缠上了他，他终于在矿坑的苦役中死去；可他讲过的那段经历，却孕育出一个传说，沿着安第斯山脉（the Cordilleras of the Andes）全境流传，至今不绝。

===Original===
He told of his reason for venturing back from that fastness, into which he had first been carried lashed to a llama, beside a vast bale of gear, when he was a child. The valley, he said, had in it all that the heart of man could desire—sweet water, pasture, and even climate, slopes of rich brown soil with tangles of a shrub that bore an excellent fruit, and on one side great hanging forests of pine that held the avalanches high. Far overhead, on three sides, vast cliffs of grey-green rock were capped by cliffs of ice; but the glacier stream came not to them but flowed away by the farther slopes, and only now and then huge ice masses fell on the valley side. In this valley it neither rained nor snowed, but the abundant springs gave a rich green pasture, that irrigation would spread over all the valley space. The settlers did well indeed there. Their beasts did well and multiplied, and but one thing marred their happiness. Yet it was enough to mar it greatly. A strange disease had come upon them, and had made all the children born to them there—and indeed, several older children also—blind. It was to seek some charm or antidote against this plague of blindness that he had with fatigue and danger and difficulty returned down the gorge. In those days, in such cases, men did not think of germs and infections but of sins; and it seemed to him that the reason of this affliction must lie in the negligence of these priestless immigrants to set up a shrine so soon as they entered the valley. He wanted a shrine—a handsome, cheap, effectual shrine—to be erected in the valley; he wanted relics and suchlike potent things of faith, blessed objects and mysterious medals and prayers. In his wallet he had a bar of native silver for which he would not account; he insisted there was none in the valley with something of the insistence of an inexpert liar. They had all clubbed their money and ornaments together, having little need for such treasure up there, he said, to buy them holy help against their ill. I figure this dim-eyed young mountaineer, sunburnt, gaunt, and anxious, hat-brim clutched feverishly, a man all unused to the ways of the lower world, telling this story to some keen-eyed, attentive priest before the great convulsion; I can picture him presently seeking to return with pious and infallible remedies against that trouble, and the infinite dismay with which he must have faced the tumbled vastness where the gorge had once come out. But the rest of his story of mischances is lost to me, save that I know of his evil death after several years. Poor stray from that remoteness! The stream that had once made the gorge now bursts from the mouth of a rocky cave, and the legend his poor, ill-told story set going developed into the legend of a race of blind men somewhere “over there” one may still hear today.

===Chinese===
他讲到自己为何要从那座险阻的避地冒险折返——他起初被送进去时还是个孩子，被绑在一头美洲驼（llama）背上，旁边驮着一捆巨大的行囊。他说，那山谷里凡人心所愿的一切应有尽有——甘甜的水、丰美的牧草、四季如春的气候；棕色沃土的山坡上缠满了灌木丛，结着上好的果子；一侧还悬挂着大片苍翠的松林，把雪崩高高地挡在上方。头顶极远之处，三面都是灰绿色的巨岩峭壁，峭壁之上又覆着冰崖；可冰川融水并不流到他们这边，而是顺着另一面的山坡淌走了，只有偶尔巨大的冰块会砸到谷里这一侧。这山谷里既不下雨也不落雪，但丰沛的泉水滋养出一片油绿的牧草，靠灌溉便可铺满整个谷地。移民们在那儿日子过得确实不错。他们的牲畜也长得好，繁殖兴旺，唯有一桩事败坏了他们的幸福。可这一桩事，已足以把幸福败坏得够呛。一种怪病悄然袭来，使他们此后在那儿生下的孩子——其实还有好几个较大的孩子也都——双目失明。正是为了寻一道能够抵挡这场失明瘟疫的符咒或解药，他才疲劳已极、历尽艰险、九死一生地从峡谷里折了回来。在那个年代，遇着这种事，人们想到的不是细菌和传染，而是罪过；在他看来，这场灾祸的根由，必是这些没有神父的移民进了山谷之后，迟迟不曾立起一座神龛。他要在山谷里立一座神龛——一座体面、便宜、灵验的神龛——他想要圣物之类大有灵验的信物，想要祝圣过的物件、神秘的圣牌和祷词。他钱袋里带着一锭原生银，却不肯交代它的来历；他一口咬定山谷里没有这种东西，那语气颇像一个拙劣的撒谎者。他说，他们已把所有的钱和首饰凑在一起——在那上头谁也用不着这些财宝——好为他们这场病患买些神圣的助力。我可以想见，这个目光朦胧的年轻山民，晒得黝黑，瘦削，满脸焦急，紧紧攥着帽檐，一个完全不谙下界规矩的人，在大动乱之前，向某位目光锐利、凝神谛听的神父讲着这个故事；我可以想见他随后揣着种种虔诚而万无一失的药方，想要回去救治那场病患，以及他面对曾经通向峡谷的那片、如今已乱石崩云的茫茫山野时，心头那无边的绝望。至于他此后种种不幸的遭遇，我已无从得知，只知道几年之后他悲惨地死去了。可怜的、从那片迢迢绝域里流落出来的人啊！曾经冲开那道峡谷的溪流，如今从一处岩洞口涌出；他那讲得拙劣的故事所引发的传说，渐渐演变成“在某个‘那边’，住着一族盲人”的传闻——这个传闻，今日犹可闻诸人口。

===Original===
And amidst the little population of that now isolated and forgotten valley the disease ran its course. The old became groping and purblind, the young saw but dimly, and the children that were born to them saw never at all. But life was very easy in that snow-rimmed basin, lost to all the world, with neither thorns nor briars, with no evil insects nor any beasts save the gentle breed of llamas they had lugged and thrust and followed up the beds of the shrunken rivers in the gorges up which they had come. The seeing had become purblind so gradually that they scarcely noted their loss. They guided the sightless youngsters hither and thither until they knew the whole valley marvellously, and when at last sight died out among them the race lived on. They had even time to adapt themselves to the blind control of fire, which they made carefully in stoves of stone. They were a simple strain of people at the first, unlettered, only slightly touched with the Spanish civilisation, but with something of a tradition of the arts of old Peru and of its lost philosophy. Generation followed generation. They forgot many things; they devised many things. Their tradition of the greater world they came from became mythical in colour and uncertain. In all things save sight they were strong and able, and presently the chance of birth and heredity sent one who had an original mind and who could talk and persuade among them, and then afterwards another. These two passed, leaving their effects, and the little community grew in numbers and in understanding, and met and settled social and economic problems that arose. Generation followed generation. Generation followed generation. There came a time when a child was born who was fifteen generations from that ancestor who went out of the valley with a bar of silver to seek God’s aid, and who never returned. Thereabouts it chanced that a man came into this community from the outer world. And this is the story of that man.

===Chinese===
在这个如今已与世隔绝、被人遗忘的山谷里，那小小的一群人中间，疾病走完了它的全程。老人变得摸索、半盲，年轻人只能模模糊糊地看见，而他们所生的孩子则什么也看不见。然而，在这片被雪峰环绕、为世人所不知的盆地里，生活非常安逸：既无荆棘蒺藜，也无恶虫猛兽，除了他们牵拽着、推搡着、顺着来时峡谷里干涸的河床一路赶上来的那温驯的美洲驼之外。视力健全的人变成半盲是那样地渐进，他们几乎不曾觉察自己的损失。他们引领着失明的孩子四处走动，直到孩子们把整座山谷熟得不能再熟；而当视力终于在他们中间彻底消亡之后，这个种族依旧延续了下去。他们甚至有时间慢慢适应，在失明的状态下驾驭火——他们在石砌的炉灶里小心翼翼地生火。他们最初是一支淳朴的人种，没有文字，只受过西班牙文明些许影响，却多少保留着古秘鲁的工艺传统和它那失传的哲学。一代过去，一代又来。他们忘却了许多事物；也发明了许多事物。他们对自己所由来的那个更大世界的记忆，染上了神话的色彩，变得模糊不定。除视力之外，他们在各方面都强壮而能干；不久，出生与遗传的机缘，在他们中间送来了一个具有独创之才、能言善辩的人；之后又来了一个。这两人都已去世，却留下了他们的影响；这个小小的共同体在人数和见识上都有了长进，遇到社会和经济上出现的难题，便开会商议，加以解决。一代过去，一代又来。一代过去，一代又来。终于有一天，一个孩子出生了，他距离当年那个带着一锭银子出谷去寻求神助、却一去不返的先祖，已有十五代之远。大约就在这个时候，有一个人从外面的世界走进了这群人之中。下面要讲的，就是这个人的故事。

===Original===
He was a mountaineer from the country near Quito, a man who had been down to the sea and had seen the world, a reader of books in an original way, an acute and enterprising man, and he was taken on by a party of Englishmen who had come out to Ecuador to climb mountains, to replace one of their three Swiss guides who had fallen ill. He climbed here and he climbed there, and then came the attempt on Parascotopetl, the Matterhorn of the Andes, in which he was lost to the outer world. The story of the accident has been written a dozen times. Pointer’s narrative is the best. He tells how the little party worked their difficult and almost vertical way up to the very foot of the last and greatest precipice, and how they built a night shelter amidst the snow upon a little shelf of rock, and, with a touch of real dramatic power, how presently they found Nunez had gone from them. They shouted, and there was no reply; shouted and whistled, and for the rest of that night they slept no more.

As the morning broke they saw the traces of his fall. It seems impossible he could have uttered a sound. He had slipped eastward towards the unknown side of the mountain; far below he had struck a steep slope of snow, and ploughed his way down it in the midst of a snow avalanche. His track went straight to the edge of a frightful precipice, and beyond that everything was hidden. Far, far below, and hazy with distance, they could see trees rising out of a narrow, shut-in valley—the lost Country of the Blind. But they did not know it was the lost Country of the Blind, nor distinguish it in any way from any other narrow streak of upland valley. Unnerved by this disaster, they abandoned their attempt in the afternoon, and Pointer was called away to the war before he could make another attack. To this day Parascotopetl lifts an unconquered crest, and Pointer’s shelter crumbles unvisited amidst the snows.

===Chinese===
他是基多附近山区的山民，曾下到海边、见过世面，读书别有会心，为人机敏而富有进取之心。一队英国人到厄瓜多尔来登山，他们三个瑞士向导中有一个病倒了，便雇了他来补缺。他这儿攀攀，那儿登登，接着就到了进攻帕拉斯科托佩特尔山（Parascotopetl）——安第斯山的马特洪峰（Matterhorn）——的那一役，从此他便在外面的世界里失踪了。这桩事故的前后经过，已被写过了十来遍。其中以波因特（Pointer）的叙述为最佳。他讲到那一小队人如何艰难地、几乎是垂直地，攀到了最后一道也是最高的那道峭壁脚下；讲到他们如何在雪地里一块小小的岩架上搭起过夜的庇护棚；又以一缕真正的戏剧笔触，讲到他们不久就发现努涅斯（Nunez）已经不见了。他们高声呼喊，没有回音；又喊又吹口哨，那一夜余下的时光，他们再没能合一合眼。

天一亮，他们便看见了他坠落下去的痕迹。看样子他不可能发出过一点声响。他朝东滑向了山那不为人知的一面；远远的下方，他撞上一道陡峭的雪坡，在一场雪崩之中一路犁着冲了下去。他的足迹笔直地通到一道骇人的悬崖边缘，再过去的一切都被遮蔽了。远远的、远远的下方，在朦胧的远方里，他们可以看见树木从一道狭长、幽闭的山谷中升起——那就是失落的盲人国。可他们并不知道那就是失落的盲人国，也分不出它与其余任何一条狭长高地山谷有什么不同。这场灾祸令他们心神俱丧，下午便放弃了攀登；波因特还没来得及再度进攻此山，就被召去打仗了。直到今日，帕拉斯科托佩特尔山依旧高擎着一座未被征服的峰巅，而波因特留下的那间庇护棚，则在积雪之间无人问津地日渐坍圮。

===Original===
And the man who fell survived.

At the end of the slope he fell a thousand feet, and came down in the midst of a cloud of snow upon a snow slope even steeper than the one above. Down this he was whirled, stunned and insensible, but without a bone broken in his body; and then at last came to gentler slopes, and at last rolled out and lay still, buried amidst a softening heap of the white masses that had accompanied and saved him. He came to himself with a dim fancy that he was ill in bed; then realised his position with a mountaineer’s intelligence, and worked himself loose and, after a rest or so, out until he saw the stars. He rested flat upon his chest for a space, wondering where he was and what had happened to him. He explored his limbs, and discovered that several of his buttons were gone and his coat turned over his head. His knife had gone from his pocket and his hat was lost, though he had tied it under his chin. He recalled that he had been looking for loose stones to raise his piece of the shelter wall. His ice-axe had disappeared.

He decided he must have fallen, and looked up to see, exaggerated by the ghastly light of the rising moon, the tremendous flight he had taken. For a while he lay, gazing blankly at that vast pale cliff towering above, rising moment by moment out of a subsiding tide of darkness. Its phantasmal, mysterious beauty held him for a space, and then he was seized with a paroxysm of sobbing laughter…

After a great interval of time he became aware that he was near the lower edge of the snow. Below, down what was now a moonlit and practicable slope, he saw the dark and broken appearance of rock-strewn turf. He struggled to his feet, aching in every joint and limb, got down painfully from the heaped loose snow about him, went downward until he was on the turf, and there dropped rather than lay beside a boulder, drank deep from the flask in his inner pocket, and instantly fell asleep…

===Chinese===
坠落的那个人，却活了下来。

在那道雪坡尽头，他又坠落了一千英尺，在一团雪雾之中，落到了一道比上面那道更陡的雪坡上。他神志昏迷、人事不省地被卷着往下滚，身上却没断一根骨头；随后终于到了较缓的坡面，最后滚了出来，一动不动地躺着，被一堆随之滚下、也救了他一命的白色雪团半埋半盖着。他醒过来时，模模糊糊地以为自己正病在床上；随后以一个登山者的清醒，认清了自己的处境，挣扎着从雪堆里挣脱出来，歇一阵、挣一阵，直到望见满天星斗。他趴在地上歇了一会儿，纳罕自己身在何处，又遭遇了什么。他逐一活动四肢，发现身上好几颗扣子不见了，外衣翻起来蒙在头上。口袋里的折刀没了，帽子也丢了——虽然他原把它在下巴底下系了结。他记起自己当时正在找些松动的石块，好把他那一截棚墙加高。他的冰镐也不知去向。

他断定自己一定是摔了下来，抬头望去，在初升之月那惨淡的光辉里，那段骇人的飞行路程被映照得分外夸张。他躺了一会儿，茫然地凝望着头顶那巍然耸立的巨大苍白的峭壁，它正一点一点地从渐渐退去的黑暗潮水里浮现出来。它那幽灵般的、神秘的美丽，使他怔住了一会儿；随后，一阵哽咽的狂笑攫住了他……

过了好长一段时间，他才察觉自己已临近积雪的下缘。再往下，沿着如今被月光照得可以通行的坡面，他看见满是乱石的草地呈现一片幽暗破碎的样子。他挣扎着站起身来，周身的骨节和四肢无不酸痛，从堆积在身边的松雪里艰难地走下去，一直下到草地上，在一块大石头旁与其说是躺下，不如说是瘫倒了；他从内袋里掏出酒壶，痛饮了一气，随即沉沉睡去……

===Original===
He was awakened by the singing of birds in the trees far below.

He sat up and perceived he was on a little alp at the foot of a vast precipice, that was grooved by the gully down which he and his snow had come. Over against him another wall of rock reared itself against the sky. The gorge between these precipices ran east and west and was full of the morning sunlight, which lit to the westward the mass of fallen mountain that closed the descending gorge. Below him it seemed there was a precipice equally steep, but behind the snow in the gully he found a sort of chimney-cleft dripping with snow-water down which a desperate man might venture. He found it easier than it seemed, and came at last to another desolate alp, and then after a rock climb of no particular difficulty to a steep slope of trees. He took his bearings and turned his face up the gorge, for he saw it opened out above upon green meadows, among which he now glimpsed quite distinctly a cluster of stone huts of unfamiliar fashion. At times his progress was like clambering along the face of a wall, and after a time the rising sun ceased to strike along the gorge, the voices of the singing birds died away, and the air grew cold and dark about him. But the distant valley with its houses was all the brighter for that. He came presently to talus, and among the rocks he noted—for he was an observant man—an unfamiliar fern that seemed to clutch out of the crevices with intense green hands. He picked a frond or so and gnawed its stalk and found it helpful.

About midday he came at last out of the throat of the gorge into the plain and the sunlight. He was stiff and weary; he sat down in the shadow of a rock, filled up his flask with water from a spring and drank it down, and remained for a time resting before he went on to the houses.

===Chinese===
他被下方远处树丛里的鸟鸣声吵醒了。

他坐起身来，发觉自己置身于一片小高地草坪上，脚下是一道巨大峭壁，峭壁上有一道槽沟，正是他和他的雪团滚下来的路径。对面，另一堵岩壁拔地而起，直插青天。两道峭壁之间的峡谷东西走向，里头满是晨光，把西边那座封闭了下倾峡谷的崩塌山体照得通明。脚下看来似乎有一道同样陡峭的悬崖，但在沟里的积雪背后，他找到了一道仿佛烟囱般的裂隙，融雪水滴滴答答地淌下来，一个不惜冒险的人，或可勉力一试。他下来时发现这路比看上去好走，最后到了另一片荒凉的小草坪，接着又经过一段并不怎么难的岩壁攀登，到了一片陡峭的林坡。他辨认了一下方向，把脸朝着峡谷的上游走去，因为他看见峡谷上方豁然开朗，展向一片青绿的草甸，其间他如今已相当分明地瞥见了一簇样式陌生的石屋。有几段路他简直像是在贴着峭壁的立面攀行；过了一阵，升起的太阳不再照进峡谷，鸟鸣声也渐渐消失，他身边的空气变得又冷又暗。可那座有房屋的远处的谷地，反倒因此显得越发亮了。不久他走到了碎石坡，在乱石之间——因为他是个留意细节的人——他注意到一种陌生的蕨类，仿佛用一只只浓绿的手，从岩缝里紧紧地伸出来。他采了一两片叶子，嚼了嚼它的茎，觉得颇有提神之效。

将近正午，他终于从峡谷的咽喉里走了出来，到了平原上、阳光里。他浑身僵硬，疲惫不堪；他在一块岩石的阴影里坐下，用泉水灌满酒壶，一口饮尽，又歇息了一阵，才朝那些房屋走去。

===Original===
They were very strange to his eyes, and indeed the whole aspect of that valley became, as he regarded it, queerer and more unfamiliar. The greater part of its surface was lush green meadow, starred with many beautiful flowers, irrigated with extraordinary care, and bearing evidence of systematic cropping piece by piece. High up and ringing the valley about was a wall, and what appeared to be a circumferential water-channel, from which the little trickles of water that fed the meadow plants came, and on the higher slopes above this flocks of llamas cropped the scanty herbage. Sheds, apparently shelters or feeding-places for the llamas, stood against the boundary wall here and there. The irrigation streams ran together into a main channel down the centre of the valley, and this was enclosed on either side by a wall breast high. This gave a singularly urban quality to this secluded place, a quality that was greatly enhanced by the fact that a number of paths paved with black and white stones, and each with a curious little kerb at the side, ran hither and thither in an orderly manner. The houses of the central village were quite unlike the casual and higgledy-piggledy agglomeration of the mountain villages he knew; they stood in a continuous row on either side of a central street of astonishing cleanness; here and there their parti-coloured façade was pierced by a door, and not a solitary window broke their even frontage. They were parti-coloured with extraordinary irregularity, smeared with a sort of plaster that was sometimes grey, sometimes drab, sometimes slate-coloured or dark brown; and it was the sight of this wild plastering first brought the word “blind” into the thoughts of the explorer. “The good man who did that,” he thought, “must have been as blind as a bat.”

===Chinese===
那些房屋在他眼中十分古怪；事实上，整座山谷的景象，越看越觉离奇、陌生。谷地的大部分表面是葱绿的草甸，点缀着许多美丽的花朵，灌溉得极其用心，并留有一块块系统轮作的痕迹。高处环绕山谷的是一道围墙，以及一条看样子是环山的供水渠，灌溉牧草的涓涓细水便从这条渠里分出来；在这条渠上方的更高坡上，成群的美洲驼啃着稀疏的牧草。围墙边这儿那儿立着些棚子，看样子是给美洲驼遮风挡雨或喂食用的。灌溉的小水流汇入一条贯穿谷底中央的主渠，主渠两岸各有一道齐胸高的墙。这给这片幽僻之地平添了一种少见的城镇气息；而这一点，又因下列事实而被大大强化：许多用黑白两色石子铺成的小路，每一条旁边都带着一道古怪的小路缘，井然有序地向四面八方延伸开去。中央村落的房屋，与他所熟知的山地村落那种杂乱无章、横七竖八的聚落截然不同；它们在一条干净得惊人的中央街道两旁排成连续的一长行；它们那五颜六色的立面，这里那里被一扇门洞穿，却没有一扇窗户打破它们平整的临街面。它们上色的花样乱得离奇，抹着一种灰泥，有时灰，有时黄褐，有时石板色，有时深褐；正是这乱抹一气的灰泥，头一个把“盲”字送进了这位探险者的脑海。“干这活儿的好汉，”他想，“必瞎得跟蝙蝠一般。”

===Original===
He descended a steep place, and so came to the wall and channel that ran about the valley, near where the latter spouted out its surplus contents into the deeps of the gorge in a thin and wavering thread of cascade. He could now see a number of men and women resting on piled heaps of grass, as if taking a siesta, in the remoter part of the meadow, and nearer the village a number of recumbent children, and then nearer at hand three men carrying pails on yokes along a little path that ran from the encircling wall towards the houses. These latter were clad in garments of llama cloth and boots and belts of leather, and they wore caps of cloth with back and ear flaps. They followed one another in single file, walking slowly and yawning as they walked, like men who have been up all night. There was something so reassuringly prosperous and respectable in their bearing that after a moment’s hesitation Nunez stood forward as conspicuously as possible upon his rock, and gave vent to a mighty shout that echoed round the valley.

The three men stopped, and moved their heads as though they were looking about them. They turned their faces this way and that, and Nunez gesticulated with freedom. But they did not appear to see him for all his gestures, and after a time, directing themselves towards the mountains far away to the right, they shouted as if in answer. Nunez bawled again, and then once more, and as he gestured ineffectually the word “blind” came up to the top of his thoughts. “The fools must be blind,” he said.

===Chinese===
他攀下一段陡坡，便到了环抱山谷的那道墙和那条水渠近旁，渠水在此把多余的水，化作一缕飘摇如线的细小瀑布，喷洒进峡谷深处。此时他已能看见，在草地更远的那一头，有若干男女正卧在一堆堆垛好的草上歇晌；离村子近些的地方，有一些躺着的孩童；再近一些，则有三个男子挑着水桶，沿着一条从围墙通向房屋的小路走来。这三人穿着驼绒织成的衣裳，皮作的靴子和腰带，头上戴着有后襟和护耳的布帽。他们一个跟一个鱼贯而行，走得很慢，一边走一边打呵欠，活像熬了一整夜的人。他们的举止间，有一种令人心安的富足和体面，努涅斯略一踌躇，便尽量惹眼地站到他所立的那块岩石前面，发出一声洪亮的喊叫，回声在谷中四处回荡。

那三个人停下脚步，把头转来转去，仿佛在四下张望。他们的脸一会儿朝这边，一会儿朝那边，努涅斯尽情地向他们打着手势。可任凭他怎样比画，他们似乎都看不见他；过了一阵，他们朝着右方遥远的群山，像是回答似地喊了起来。努涅斯又喊了一声，再喊了一声，眼见自己的手势全无用处，“盲”字便浮上了他心头最高的位置。“这帮蠢货，必是瞎子，”他说。

===Original===
When at last, after much shouting and wrath, Nunez crossed the stream by a little bridge, came through a gate in the wall, and approached them, he was sure that they were blind. He was sure that this was the Country of the Blind of which the legends told. Conviction had sprung upon him, and a sense of great and rather enviable adventure. The three stood side by side, not looking at him, but with their ears directed towards him, judging him by his unfamiliar steps. They stood close together like men a little afraid, and he could see their eyelids closed and sunken, as though the very balls beneath had shrunk away. There was an expression near awe on their faces.

“A man,” one said, in hardly recognisable Spanish—“a man it is—a man or a spirit—coming down from the rocks.”

But Nunez advanced with the confident steps of a youth who enters upon life. All the old stories of the lost valley and the Country of the Blind had come back to his mind, and through his thoughts ran this old proverb, as if it were a refrain—

“In the Country of the Blind the One-eyed Man is King.”

“In the Country of the Blind the One-eyed Man is King.”

And very civilly he gave them greeting. He talked to them and used his eyes.

===Chinese===
经过一番大呼小叫和恼怒之后，努涅斯终于从一座小桥上越过溪流，穿过围墙的一道门，朝他们走过去——他这时已确信他们是瞎子了。他确信，这便是传说中所讲的那座盲人国。一份确凿的把握在他心头跃然而生，随之而来的，是一种堪称伟大、颇令人艳羡的冒险之感。那三个人并肩站着，并不朝他看，却把耳朵朝向他，凭他那陌生的脚步声来判断他。他们紧紧地挨在一起，像有些害怕的人那样；他可以看见他们的眼睑紧闭着、深深凹陷下去，仿佛底下的眼球已经萎缩了。他们脸上有一种近乎敬畏的神情。

“一个人，”其中一人用一种几乎听不出是西班牙语的话说道——“是一个人——是一个人呢，还是一个精灵——从岩石上下来。”

可努涅斯却以一个青年踏入人生时的那种自信步伐向前走去。关于那失落山谷和盲人国的种种古老传说，一齐涌回了他的脑际，而下面这句古老的谚语，像副歌似的，在他的思绪里反复回荡——

“在盲人国里，独眼者为王。”

“在盲人国里，独眼者为王。”

他彬彬有礼地向他们致了问候。他一边同他们说话，一边运用着自己的双眼。

===Original===
“Where does he come from, brother Pedro?” asked one.

“Down out of the rocks.”

“Over the mountains I come,” said Nunez, “out of the country beyond there—where men can see. From near Bogota, where there are a hundred thousands of people, and where the city passes out of sight.”

“Sight?” muttered Pedro. “Sight?”

“He comes,” said the second blind man, “out of the rocks.”

The cloth of their coats Nunez saw was curiously fashioned, each with a different sort of stitching.

They startled him by a simultaneous movement towards him, each with a hand outstretched. He stepped back from the advance of these spread fingers.
