“Come hither,” said the third blind man, following his motion and clutching him neatly.

And they held Nunez and felt him over, saying no word further until they had done so.

“Carefully,” he cried, with a finger in his eye, and found they thought that organ, with its fluttering lids, a queer thing in him. They went over it again.

“A strange creature, Correa,” said the one called Pedro. “Feel the coarseness of his hair. Like a llama’s hair.”

“Rough he is as the rocks that begot him,” said Correa, investigating Nunez’s unshaven chin with a soft and slightly moist hand. “Perhaps he will grow finer.” Nunez struggled a little under their examination, but they gripped him firm.

===Chinese===
“他是从哪儿来的，佩德罗（Pedro）兄弟？”其中一人问。

“从石头堆里下来的。”

“我是翻山过来的，”努涅斯说，“从那边的国度来——那里的人能看。从波哥大（Bogota）附近来，那里有十万人口，那城长得一眼望不到头。”

“看？”佩德罗嘟哝着，“看？”

“他是从石头里出来的，”第二个盲人说。

努涅斯注意到他们外衣的料子裁剪得古怪，每一件都用了一种不同的针法。

他们同时朝他这边一动，把他吓了一跳，各自伸出一只手来。面对这伸过来的、张开的手指，他后退了一步。

“过来，”第三个盲人一边说着，一边循着他的动作利落地抓住了他。

于是他们按住努涅斯，把他从头到脚摸了一遍，没再开口，直到摸完。

“轻点，”他叫起来，一根手指戳进了眼睛里；他发现他们竟把那只带着扑闪眼皮的东西，看作他身上一件古怪的物事。他们又把那只眼睛摸了一遍。

“一个古怪的造物，科雷亚（Correa），”那个叫佩德罗的说。“摸摸他那头发的粗硬。跟美洲驼的毛一样。”

“他糙得跟生他的石头似的，”科雷亚说，用一只柔软、略带潮气的手摸着努涅斯那没刮的下巴。“也许他将来会长细嫩些。”努涅斯在他们的体检下略略挣扎，但他们把他攥得紧紧的。

===Original===
“Carefully,” he said again.

“He speaks,” said the third man. “Certainly he is a man.”

“Ugh!” said Pedro, at the roughness of his coat.

“And you have come into the world?” asked Pedro.

“*Out* of the world. Over mountains and glaciers; right over above there, halfway to the sun. Out of the great big world that goes down, twelve days’ journey to the sea.”

They scarcely seemed to heed him. “Our fathers have told us men may be made by the forces of Nature,” said Correa. “It is the warmth of things and moisture, and rottenness—rottenness.”

“Let us lead him to the elders,” said Pedro.

“Shout first,” said Correa, “lest the children be afraid… This is a marvellous occasion.”

So they shouted, and Pedro went first and took Nunez by the hand to lead him to the houses.

He drew his hand away. “I can see,” he said.

“See?” said Correa.

“Yes, see,” said Nunez, turning towards him, and stumbled against Pedro’s pail.

“His senses are still imperfect,” said the third blind man. “He stumbles, and talks unmeaning words. Lead him by the hand.”

“As you will,” said Nunez, and was led along, laughing.

It seemed they knew nothing of sight.

Well, all in good time he would teach them.

He heard people shouting, and saw a number of figures gathering together in the middle roadway of the village.

===Chinese===
“轻点。”他又说。

“他会说话，”第三个人说。“那他确是一个人了。”

“哼！”佩德罗摸着他外衣的粗砺说。

“你是来到了这世上？”佩德罗问。

“是从这世外来的。翻过雪山和冰川；就打那上头，那上头到太阳只一半路。从那个往下走、要走十二天才能到海边的、广袤无垠的大千世界来的。”

他们几乎像是没听他的话。“我们的先人告诉过我们，人是自然之力造出来的，”科雷亚说。“是万物的暖和潮气，加上腐烂——腐烂。”

“带他去见长老们吧，”佩德罗说。

“先喊一声，”科雷亚说，“免得孩子们害怕……这可是桩了不得的大事。”

于是他们喊了起来，佩德罗走在前头，拉着努涅斯的手，把他往那些房屋带。

他把手抽了回去。“我能看。”他说。

“看？”科雷亚说。

“是的，看，”努涅斯朝他转过身去，却被佩德罗的水桶绊了一跤。

“他的感官还没有长全，”第三个盲人说。“他东倒西歪，嘴里说着莫名其妙的话。牵着他的手走吧。”

“随你们的便，”努涅斯说着，被牵着走，笑了起来。

他们似乎对“看”这件事一无所知。

好吧，时辰一到，他自会教他们。

他听见有人喊叫，看见一群人影正在村中央那条大路上聚拢过来。

===Original===
He found it tax his nerve and patience more than he had anticipated, that first encounter with the population of the Country of the Blind. The place seemed larger as he drew near to it, and the smeared plasterings queerer, and a crowd of children and men and women (the women and girls, he was pleased to note, had some of them quite sweet faces, for all that their eyes were shut and sunken) came about him, holding on to him, touching him with soft, sensitive hands, smelling at him, and listening at every word he spoke. Some of the maidens and children, however, kept aloof as if afraid, and indeed his voice seemed coarse and rude beside their softer notes. They mobbed him. His three guides kept close to him with an effect of proprietorship, and said again and again, “A wild man out of the rock.”

“Bogota,” he said. “Bogota. Over the mountain crests.”

“A wild man—using wild words,” said Pedro. “Did you hear that—*Bogota?* His mind is hardly formed yet. He has only the beginnings of speech.”

A little boy nipped his hand. “Bogota!” he said mockingly.

“Ay! A city to your village. I come from the great world—where men have eyes and see.”

“His name’s Bogota,” they said.

“He stumbled,” said Correa, “stumbled twice as we came hither.”

“Bring him to the elders.”

And they thrust him suddenly through a doorway into a room as black as pitch, save at the end there faintly glowed a fire. The crowd closed in behind him and shut out all but the faintest glimmer of day, and before he could arrest himself he had fallen headlong over the feet of a seated man. His arm, outflung, struck the face of someone else as he went down; he felt the soft impact of features and heard a cry of anger, and for a moment he struggled against a number of hands that clutched him. It was a one-sided fight. An inkling of the situation came to him, and he lay quiet.

“I fell down,” he said; “I couldn’t see in this pitchy darkness.”

There was a pause as if the unseen persons about him tried to understand his words. Then the voice of Correa said: “He is but newly formed. He stumbles as he walks and mingles words that mean nothing with his speech.”

Others also said things about him that he heard or understood imperfectly.

“May I sit up?” he asked, in a pause. “I will not struggle against you again.”

They consulted and let him rise.

===Chinese===
这头一回与盲人国百姓的遭遇，比他所预料的更考验他的神经和耐性。走近了看，这地方似乎更大了，那些乱抹的灰泥也更古怪了；一大群孩子和男女老少（他欣然注意到，其中有些妇女和姑娘，虽然双目紧闭、眼窝深陷，脸蛋儿却颇为清秀）围拢过来，拽住他，用柔软而敏锐的手摸他，闻他，专心谛听他说的每一个字。不过也有些少女和孩子躲得远远的，像是害怕，而事实上，比起他们那些柔和的声音来，他的嗓音的确显得粗砺、唐突。人们簇拥着他。他那三个引路人寸步不离地守着他，一副对他拥有主权似的神情，一遍又一遍地说：“从石头里出来的一个野人。”

“波哥大，”他说，“波哥大。在山脊的那一边。”

“一个野人——说着野话，”佩德罗说。“你们听见没有——波哥大？他的脑子还没长成呢。他才刚学说话。”

一个小男孩捏了捏他的手。“波哥大！”他学着嘲弄道。

“嗬！一座城对你们这个村子。我是从大千世界来的——那里的人有眼睛，能看。”

“他叫波哥大。”他们说。

“他绊了一跤，”科雷亚说，“我们来的路上绊了两跤。”

“带他去见长老们。”

他们冷不丁把他推进一道门里，推进一间漆黑如墨的屋子，只有尽头处隐隐地亮着一堆火。人群在他身后合拢，几乎把外头天光全挡了去；他还来不及收住脚步，便一头栽倒在一个坐着的人脚边。他伸出的胳膊，倒下去时打在另一个人的脸上；他觉出拳头撞在一张脸上的那种柔软的反冲，听见一声怒喝，有一阵子，他与好些抓住他的手扭作一团。这是一场实力悬殊的较量。他隐约明白了处境，便乖乖躺着不动了。

“我摔倒了，”他说，“这漆黑里我什么也看不见。”

停了一阵，仿佛周围那些看不见的人正在琢磨他的话。然后科雷亚的声音说：“他才刚造出来不久。他走路跌跌撞撞，话里夹着些莫名其妙的词儿。”

旁人也在议论他，他听不太清，也听不大懂。

“我可以坐起来吗？”趁着一个间隙他问。“我不再跟你们扭打了。”

他们商量了一下，允许他起来。

===Original===
The voice of an older man began to question him, and Nunez found himself trying to explain the great world out of which he had fallen, and the sky and mountains and sight and suchlike marvels, to these elders who sat in darkness in the Country of the Blind. And they would believe and understand nothing whatever he told them, a thing quite outside his expectation. They would not even understand many of his words. For fourteen generations these people had been blind and cut off from all the seeing world; the names for all the things of sight had faded and changed; the story of the outer world was faded and changed to a child’s story; and they had ceased to concern themselves with anything beyond the rocky slopes above their circling wall. Blind men of genius had arisen among them and questioned the shreds of belief and tradition they had brought with them from their seeing days, and had dismissed all these things as idle fancies, and replaced them with new and saner explanations. Much of their imagination had shrivelled with their eyes, and they had made for themselves new imaginations with their ever more sensitive ears and fingertips. Slowly Nunez realised this; that his expectation of wonder and reverence at his origin and his gifts was not to be borne out; and after his poor attempt to explain sight to them had been set aside as the confused version of a new-made being describing the marvels of his incoherent sensations, he subsided, a little dashed, into listening to their instruction. And the eldest of the blind men explained to him life and philosophy and religion, how that the world (meaning their valley) had been first an empty hollow in the rocks, and then had come, first, inanimate things without the gift of touch, and llamas and a few other creatures that had little sense, and then men, and at last angels, whom one could hear singing and making fluttering sounds, but whom no one could touch at all, which puzzled Nunez greatly until he thought of the birds.

He went on to tell Nunez how this time had been divided into the warm and the cold, which are the blind equivalents of day and night, and how it was good to sleep in the warm and work during the cold, so that now, but for his advent, the whole town of the blind would have been asleep. He said Nunez must have been specially created to learn and serve the wisdom, they had acquired, and that for all his mental incoherency and stumbling behaviour he must have courage, and do his best to learn, and at that all the people in the doorway murmured encouragingly. He said the night—for the blind call their day night—was now far gone, and it behoved everyone to go back to sleep. He asked Nunez if he knew how to sleep, and Nunez said he did, but that before sleep he wanted food.

They brought him food—llama’s milk in a bowl, and rough salted bread—and led him into a lonely place, to eat out of their hearing, and afterwards to slumber until the chill of the mountain evening roused them to begin their day again. But Nunez slumbered not at all.

Instead, he sat up in the place where they had left him, resting his limbs and turning the unanticipated circumstances of his arrival over and over in his mind.

Every now and then he laughed, sometimes with amusement, and sometimes with indignation.

“Unformed mind!” he said. “Got no senses yet! They little know they’ve been insulting their heaven-sent king and master. I see I must bring them to reason. Let me think—let me think.”

He was still thinking when the sun set.

===Chinese===
一位老者的声音开始盘问他，努涅斯便发现自己正竭力向这些端坐在盲人国黑暗中的长老们，解释他所坠落出来的那个大千世界，解释天空、山峦、视觉以及诸般奇观。可无论他说什么，他们都不肯相信、也毫不理解，这完全出乎他的意料。他们甚至连他的许多词儿都听不懂。这些人在十四代人之前便已失明，与一切能看的世界隔绝；一切与视觉有关的事物之名，都已磨灭、变样；关于外面世界的传闻，也已磨灭、变样，成了一个哄孩子的故事；除了那道围墙之上、那片岩石坡以外的事物，他们早已不再关心。他们中间也出过几位盲人中的天才，对他们由明眼时世带过来的那些残破的信仰和传说提出质疑，把它们一概斥为无稽之谈，而代之以新的、更合情理的解释。他们的想象力随着眼睛一道萎缩了，却又凭借日益敏锐的耳朵和指尖，为自己造出了一套新的想象力。努涅斯这才慢慢明白了：他原以为自己那一身来历和天赋，会换来他们的惊叹和敬畏，看来是无望了；他那番要给他们讲解视觉的拙劣努力，被当作一个新造出来的人在絮絮叨叨地描绘自己那些语无伦次的感官奇遇，而被搁到一边之后，他便有些泄气地住口，转而恭听他们的教诲。盲人中最年长的一位向他讲解了生活、哲学和宗教，说世界（指的是他们的山谷）起初是岩石中的一个空洞，后来先出现了那些没有触觉的无生物，以及美洲驼和其他几种感觉迟钝的生物，然后是人，最后是天使——这些天使人们能听见他们歌唱、听见他们扑棱翅膀的声音，却谁也摸不着他们——这一点让努涅斯大惑不解，直到他想起了鸟。

老者接着告诉努涅斯，时间是如何被分作暖和凉两个部分——这便是盲人用以对应昼夜的说法——又说要趁暖睡觉、趁凉干活才好；所以此时要不是他来了，整座盲人城本都该在睡梦之中。他说，努涅斯想必是上天特地造出来，好让他来学习并侍奉他们已得的那份智慧的；尽管他神志不清、行动莽撞，他也须拿出勇气来，竭力学习才是。门口那些人听了，都低声附和着鼓励他。他说夜——盲人把他们的白昼叫作夜——此刻已经过了大半，众人理当回去续眠。他问努涅斯会不会睡觉，努涅斯说会，只是睡前得先吃东西。

他们给他端来吃的——一碗驼奶，几块粗咸面包——把他领到一个僻静之处去吃，免得他打扰别人；之后再让他打盹，一直睡到山地傍晚的寒意把他们唤醒，重新开始他们的一天。可努涅斯一点也没睡着。

他只是在他们安置他的地方坐着，歇着四肢，把降临到自己头上这桩出乎意料的事，在脑子里翻来覆去地想。

他不时笑出声来，有时是觉得好笑，有时是愤愤不平。

“脑子没长成！”他说，“感官还没全！他们做梦也想不到，自己一直在冒犯上天赐给他们的国王和主子。看来我得让他们开开窍。让我想想——让我想想。”

太阳落下去了，他还在想。

===Original===
Nunez had an eye for all beautiful things, and it seemed to him that the glow upon the snowfields and glaciers that rose about the valley on every side was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen. His eyes went from that inaccessible glory to the village and irrigated fields, fast sinking into the twilight, and suddenly a wave of emotion took him, and he thanked God from the bottom of his heart that the power of sight had been given him.

He heard a voice calling to him from out of the village. “Ya ho there, Bogota! Come hither!”

At that he stood up smiling. He would show these people once and for all what sight would do for a man. They would seek him, but not find him.

“You move not, Bogota,” said the voice.

He laughed noiselessly, and made two stealthy steps aside from the path.

“Trample not on the grass, Bogota; that is not allowed.”

Nunez had scarcely heard the sound he made himself. He stopped amazed.

The owner of the voice came running up the piebald path towards him.

He stepped back into the pathway. “Here I am,” he said.

“Why did you not come when I called you?” said the blind man. “Must you be led like a child? Cannot you hear the path as you walk?”

Nunez laughed. “I can see it,” he said.

“There is no such word as *see*,” said the blind man, after a pause. “Cease this folly, and follow the sound of my feet.”

Nunez followed, a little annoyed.

“My time will come,” he said.

“You’ll learn,” the blind man answered. “There is much to learn in the world.”

“Has no one told you, ‘In the Country of the Blind the One-eyed Man is King’?”

“What is blind?” asked the blind man carelessly over his shoulder.

===Chinese===
凡是美的东西，努涅斯都爱看；在他看来，环抱着山谷、四面升起的雪原和冰川上那一派霞光，是他平生所见最美的景象。他的目光从那份高不可攀的荣耀，转向正在迅速沉入暮色的村落和灌溉着的田地，一阵感情的浪潮忽然涌上心头，他从心底里感谢上苍，赐给了他视觉这一份天赋。

他听见一个声音从村子里朝他喊。“喂——波哥大！过来！”

他笑眯眯地站了起来。他要把视觉对一个人意味着什么，向这些人彻彻底底地演示一回。他们要找他，却找他不着。

“你别动啊，波哥大，”那声音说。

他无声地笑了，悄悄地离了小路，往旁边挪了两步。

“别踩草地，波哥大；那是不许可的。”

努涅斯几乎听不见自己走路的声响。他惊讶地站住了。

那声音的主人沿着那条花斑小路跑过来。

他回到小路上。“我在这儿，”他说。

“我叫你，你为什么不过来？”那盲人说。“还要人像牵小孩一样牵着你吗？你走路时就听不见路在哪儿吗？”

努涅斯笑了。“我能看见它。”他说。

“世上没有‘*看*’这个词儿，”那盲人停了停说。“别再胡说了，跟着我的脚步声走吧。”

努涅斯跟着他，有些恼。

“我的时辰会来的。”他说。

“你会学到的，”那盲人答道。“这世上要学的东西多着呢。”

“没有人跟你说过，‘盲人国里，独眼者为王’吗？”

“什么叫盲？”那盲人头也不回地随口问。

===Original===
Four days passed, and the fifth found the King of the Blind still incognito, as a clumsy and useless stranger among his subjects.

It was, he found, much more difficult to proclaim himself than he had supposed, and in the meantime, while he meditated his *coup d’etat*, he did what he was told and learnt the manners and customs of the Country of the Blind. He found working and going about at night a particularly irksome thing, and he decided that that should be the first thing he would change.

They led a simple, laborious life, these people, with all the elements of virtue and happiness, as these things can be understood by men. They toiled, but not oppressively; they had food and clothing sufficient for their needs; they had days and seasons of rest; they made much of music and singing, and there was love among them, and little children.

It was marvellous with what confidence and precision they went about their ordered world. Everything, you see, had been made to fit their needs; each of the radiating paths of the valley area had a constant angle to the others, and was distinguished by a special notch upon its kerbing; all obstacles and irregularities of path or meadow had long since been cleared away; all their methods and procedure arose naturally from their special needs. Their senses had become marvellously acute; they could hear and judge the slightest gesture of a man a dozen paces away—could hear the very beating of his heart. Intonation had long replaced expression with them, and touches gesture, and their work with hoe and spade and fork was as free and confident as garden work can be. Their sense of smell was extraordinarily fine; they could distinguish individual differences as readily as a dog can, and they went about the tending of the llamas, who lived among the rocks above and came to the wall for food and shelter, with ease and confidence. It was only when at last Nunez sought to assert himself that he found how easy and confident their movements could be.

He rebelled only after he had tried persuasion.

He tried at first on several occasions to tell them of sight. “Look you here, you people,” he said. “There are things you do not understand in me.”

Once or twice one or two of them attended to him; they sat with faces downcast and ears turned intelligently towards him, and he did his best to tell them what it was to see. Among his hearers was a girl, with eyelids less red and sunken than the others, so that one could almost fancy she was hiding eyes, whom especially he hoped to persuade. He spoke of the beauties of sight, of watching the mountains, of the sky and the sunrise, and they heard him with amused incredulity that presently became condemnatory. They told him there were indeed no mountains at all, but that the end of the rocks where the llamas grazed was indeed the end of the world; thence sprang a cavernous roof of the universe, from which the dew and the avalanches fell; and when he maintained stoutly the world had neither end nor roof such as they supposed, they said his thoughts were wicked. So far as he could describe sky and clouds and stars to them it seemed to them a hideous void, a terrible blankness in the place of the smooth roof to things in which they believed—it was an article of faith with them that the cavern roof was exquisitely smooth to the touch. He saw that in some manner he shocked them, and gave up that aspect of the matter altogether, and tried to show them the practical value of sight. One morning he saw Pedro in the path called Seventeen and coming towards the central houses, but still too far off for hearing or scent, and he told them as much. “In a little while,” he prophesied, “Pedro will be here.” An old man remarked that Pedro had no business on path Seventeen, and then, as if in confirmation, that individual as he drew near turned and went transversely into path Ten, and so back with nimble paces towards the outer wall. They mocked Nunez when Pedro did not arrive, and afterwards, when he asked Pedro questions to clear his character, Pedro denied and outfaced him, and was afterwards hostile to him.

Then he induced them to let him go a long way up the sloping meadows towards the wall with one complacent individual, and to him he promised to describe all that happened among the houses. He noted certain goings and comings, but the things that really seemed to signify to these people happened inside of or behind the windowless houses—the only things they took note of to test him by—and of these he could see or tell nothing; and it was after the failure of this attempt, and the ridicule they could not repress, that he resorted to force. He thought of seizing a spade and suddenly smiting one or two of them to earth, and so in fair combat showing the advantage of eyes. He went so far with that resolution as to seize his spade, and then he discovered a new thing about himself, and that was that it was impossible for him to hit a blind man in cold blood.

===Chinese===
四天过去了，到了第五天，这位盲人之国的国王，仍然隐姓埋名地混在他的子民之间，被当作一个笨手笨脚、一无用处的陌路人。

原来，要自立为王，比他所想的要难得多；他在那边盘算着他的政变（coup d’état）的同时，便一边听话照做，一边学着盲人国的礼俗。他发觉在夜间做事和行动格外累人，便决意先拿这一条来开刀。

这些人过着一种俭朴、勤劳的生活，照人们所能理解的标准，凡是美德和幸福的要素，他们一应俱全。他们劳作，但不被压榨；衣食足以自给；他们有定期的休息日和休息的时令；他们极重音乐和歌唱；他们中间有爱，也有小孩子。

他们在这井然有序的小天地里行动起来，那份从容和精确，实在令人赞叹。你看，一切都已安排得与他们的需要丝丝入扣：山谷里每一条放射状的小路，与其他各路之间都保持着一个固定的角度，并以其路缘上一种特有的缺口相区别；小路上和草地上的所有障碍和不平整之处，早就清除干净了；他们一切做事的方法和步骤，都是从他们那特殊的需要里自然生发出来的。他们的感官已敏锐到了极点——十二步开外一个人的最细微的动作，他们都能听见、都能据此判断；连那人心脏的跳动，他们都听得见。语调早已取代了表情，触摸早已取代了手势；他们用锄、用铲、用叉干活，那种从容自如，是侍弄花圃的活儿所能做到的最高境界。他们的嗅觉精细异常，分辨人与人之间的不同，跟一只猎犬一样在行；他们照管起那些住在上方岩石间、到围墙边来觅食和避风的美洲驼，也十分得心应手。直到最后努涅斯想要立威的时候，他才发现，他们的行动可以多么地从容、多么地自如。

他是先试过说服，而后才造反的。

头几回，他试着把“视觉”这件事告诉他们。“你们这些人听着，”他说，“我身上有些事，你们是不懂的。”

有一两次，有那么一两个人听他了；他们低着脸，把耳朵机警地朝向他，他便尽其所能地告诉他们，所谓能看见，是怎么一回事。听他说话的人里头，有一个姑娘，她的眼睑不像别人那样又红又陷，倒让人几乎以为她是藏着两只眼睛的；他尤其希望能说服的，就是她。他讲到视觉之美，讲到眺望群山，讲到天空和日出，他们起初是以一种带几分好笑的不信来听着，不久便转为责难。他们告诉他，根本没有什么山，美洲驼吃草处那片岩石的尽头，便是世界的尽头；从此处升起一道穹隆状的宇宙之顶，露水和雪崩便是从那上面落下来的；等他一口咬定世界既无他们所说的尽头、也无他们所说的顶盖时，他们便说他的念头是邪恶的。他尽力把天空、云彩和星辰描述给他们听，可在他们听来，那简直是可怖的虚空，是他们所信的那道平滑穹顶之上的一处可怖的空白——他们信的一条是：那道穹窿之顶，摸起来细腻光滑到了极点。他看出来自己不知怎地触怒了他们，便索性丢开这一层，转而想要向他们显示视觉在实用上的价值。一天早上，他看见佩德罗走上了第十七条小路，朝中央的几座房子走来，但还远远地听不见、闻不着；他便把这事告诉了他们。“过一会儿，”他预言道，“佩德罗就到。”一个老头子说佩德罗不该上第十七条小路；果然，像是为了印证这话似的，那人走近时一拐弯，斜插进了第十条小路，又迈着轻快的步子，回到外圈墙那边去了。佩德罗既然没到，众人便嘲笑起努涅斯来；后来他质问佩德罗几个问题，要为自己澄清，佩德罗却一口否认，还当面抢白他，从此便对他怀恨在心。

后来，他又设法让他们准许自己，跟一个自满的家伙一道，沿着倾斜的草甸朝着围墙远远地走了一程，他向那人许诺，要把房子那边发生的一切都讲给他听。他记下了若干来来往往，但这些人眼里看来真正要紧的事，都发生在那些没有窗户的屋子里面或背后——而这正是他们拿来考他的唯一一类事——这种事他却一件也看不见、说不出；正是这一回努力失败、他们又憋不住冷嘲热讽之后，他才动起了武。他想要抄起一把铲子，猝不及防地把他们中的一两个打翻在地，借一场光明正大的较量，来显示一双眼睛的好处。他这份决心已经下到了抓起铲子的地步，可就在这时，他对自己又有了一个新的发现——他发现自己断不可能冷血地动手打一个瞎子。

===Original===
He hesitated, and found them all aware that he had snatched up the spade. They stood alert, with their heads on one side, and bent ears towards him for what he would do next.

“Put that spade down,” said one, and he felt a sort of helpless horror. He came near obedience.

Then he thrust one backwards against a house wall, and fled past him and out of the village.

He went athwart one of their meadows, leaving a track of trampled grass behind his feet, and presently sat down by the side of one of their ways. He felt something of the buoyancy that comes to all men in the beginning of a fight, but more perplexity. He began to realise that you cannot even fight happily with creatures who stand upon a different mental basis to yourself. Far away he saw a number of men carrying spades and sticks come out of the street of houses, and advance in a spreading line along the several paths towards him. They advanced slowly, speaking frequently to one another, and ever and again the whole cordon would halt and sniff the air and listen.

The first time they did this Nunez laughed. But afterwards he did not laugh.

One struck his trail in the meadow grass, and came stooping and feeling his way along it.

For five minutes he watched the slow extension of the cordon, and then his vague disposition to do something forthwith became frantic. He stood up, went a pace or so towards the circumferential wall, turned, and went back a little way. There they all stood in a crescent, still and listening.

He also stood still, gripping his spade very tightly in both hands. Should he charge them?

The pulse in his ears ran into the rhythm of “In the Country of the Blind the One-eyed Man is King!”

Should he charge them?

He looked back at the high and unclimbable wall behind—unclimbable because of its smooth plastering, but withal pierced with many little doors, and at the approaching line of seekers. Behind these others were now coming out of the street of houses.

Should he charge them?

“Bogota!” called one. “Bogota! where are you?”

He gripped his spade still tighter, and advanced down the meadows towards the place of habitations, and directly he moved they converged upon him. “I’ll hit them if they touch me,” he swore; “by Heaven, I will. I’ll hit.” He called aloud, “Look here, I’m going to do what I like in this valley. Do you hear? I’m going to do what I like and go where I like!”

They were moving in upon him quickly, groping, yet moving rapidly. It was like playing blind man’s buff, with everyone blindfolded except one. “Get hold of him!” cried one. He found himself in the arc of a loose curve of pursuers. He felt suddenly he must be active and resolute.

“You don’t understand,” he cried in a voice that was meant to be great and resolute, and which broke. “You are blind, and I can see. Leave me alone!”

“Bogota! Put down that spade, and come off the grass!”

The last order, grotesque in its urban familiarity, produced a gust of anger.

“I’ll hurt you,” he said, sobbing with emotion. “By Heaven, I’ll hurt you. Leave me alone!”

He began to run, not knowing clearly where to run. He ran from the nearest blind man, because it was a horror to hit him. He stopped, and then made a dash to escape from their closing ranks. He made for where a gap was wide, and the men on either side, with a quick perception of the approach of his paces, rushed in on one another. He sprang forward, and then saw he must be caught, and *swish*! the spade had struck. He felt the soft thud of hand and arm, and the man was down with a yell of pain, and he was through.

Through! And then he was close to the street of houses again, and blind men, whirling spades and stakes, were running with a sort of reasoned swiftness hither and thither.

He heard steps behind him just in time, and found a tall man rushing forward and swiping at the sound of him. He lost his nerve, hurled his spade a yard wide at his antagonist, and whirled about and fled, fairly yelling as he dodged another.

He was panic-stricken. He ran furiously to and fro, dodging when there was no need to dodge, and in his anxiety to see on every side of him at once, stumbling. For a moment he was down and they heard his fall. Far away in the circumferential wall a little doorway looked like heaven, and he set off in a wild rush for it. He did not even look round at his pursuers until it was gained, and he had stumbled across the bridge, clambered a little way among the rocks, to the surprise and dismay of a young llama, who went leaping out of sight, and lay down sobbing for breath.

And so his *coup d’etat* came to an end.

===Chinese===
他犹豫了，却发现他们全都察觉他抄起了铲子。他们警觉地站着，头偏向一边，把耳朵朝向他，等着瞧他下一步要做什么。

“把铲子放下，”其中一人说，他心里生出一种无能为力的恐惧。他险些就照办了。

接着他把一个人往后一推，按在一堵屋墙上，从他身边飞奔而过，逃出了村子。

他横穿过他们的一片草地，身后留下一道被踩倒的草痕，不久便在他们的一条小路旁坐了下来。开打之初人人心里都有的一股子兴奋，他觉出了一些，可更多的是迷惘。他开始意识到：与那些跟你心思根本不在一个基础上的人，你连打一场痛快的架也办不到。远处，他看见一群手持铲子和棍棒的人从那排房子的街上走出来，分作几路小径，呈扇形朝他逼过来。他们走得很慢，彼此不断地搭话，每隔一会儿，整道包围圈便一齐停下，嗅一嗅空气，听一听动静。

头一回他们这么干，努涅斯笑了。可后来他就笑不出来了。

有一个人在草地里循着他留下的踪迹，弯着腰，一路摸索着追过来。

他望着那道包围圈慢慢地拉大，看了五分钟，那种想要立刻干点什么的模糊念头，便急成了发疯似的冲动。他站起来，朝那道环形的墙走了几步，又回转身，往回走了几步。他们就都站在那儿，排成一道新月形的弧线，一动不动地听着。

他也站着不动，两手紧紧攥着铲子。他要不要冲过去？

他耳畔的脉搏，应和着“在盲人国里，独眼者为王！”的节奏。

他要不要冲过去？

他回头望了望身后那道高高的、爬不上去的墙——之所以爬不上去，是因为它抹得光滑；不过墙上还是开了许多扇小门——又看了看逼近过来的搜寻人马。在这些人的背后，还有更多的人正从那条房屋街上走出来。

他要不要冲过去？

“波哥大！”有人喊，“波哥大！你在哪儿？”

他把铲子攥得更紧，沿着草甸朝房屋那边走去，他一动，他们便朝他一齐围拢过来。“他们敢碰我，我就打，”他起誓道，“皇天在上，我一定打。我要打。”他放声喊道：“你们听着，在这山谷里，我爱做什么就做什么。听见没有？我爱做什么就做什么，爱去哪儿就去哪儿！”

他们一边摸索，一边迅速地朝他逼拢。这就像在玩一场捉迷藏，除了一个人之外，其余的都被蒙了眼。“抓住他！”有人喊。他发觉自己正处在一道松松散散的弧形追兵的包围之中。他忽然觉得，自己得利落果决才行。

“你们不懂，”他高声喊道，那嗓音本想威武果决，却一下子破了音。“你们是瞎子，我能看见。别碰我！”

“波哥大！放下铲子，从草地上出来！”

这最后一道命令，因带着一股街坊邻里似的俗常口吻而显得荒诞，反倒激得他一阵怒火上冲。

“我要伤你们了，”他说，激动得哽咽起来。“皇天在上，我要伤你们了。别碰我！”

他开始奔跑，却不大清楚该往哪儿跑。他从离他最近的那个盲人身边跑开，因为打那个盲人是一件令他害怕的事。他停了下来，接着又猛冲一下，要从他们合拢的人墙里突围。他朝着一处较宽的空隙冲去，两边的汉子凭着他脚步声逼近的方向迅速一判断，便朝中间一挤。他一个箭步向前，随即明白自己非被逮住不可了——嗖！铲子已挥了出去。他觉出铲子砍在手和胳膊上那种闷闷的一记，那人痛得一声大叫倒了下去，而他已经冲了出去。

冲出来了！可随即便又靠近了那条房屋街，那些挥舞着铲子和木桩的盲人，正以一种胸有成竹的迅捷，东奔西跑。

他及时听见身后有脚步声，回头一瞧，是个高个子正冲上来，循着他的声音劈头一棍扫来。他没了胆气，把铲子朝对手偏开一码远掷了出去，回身就跑，一边闪过另一个盲人，一边嘴里鬼哭狼嚎。

他吓破了胆。他疯狂地来回乱跑，无须躲闪时也躲闪，因为急于一眼看顾四面，反倒绊起跤来。有一阵子他跌倒在地，他们听见了他的跌倒。远处环形墙上一扇小门，看起来像天堂一样，他便发疯似的朝它奔去。他甚至都没有回头看一眼追兵，直到奔到了那里，跌跌撞撞地过了小桥，在乱石间爬了一段，惊得一头小美洲驼狼狈地一跳一跳逃出视野，他自己便趴了下来，喘得上气不接下气。

他的这场政变，就此收场。

===Original===
He stayed outside the wall of the valley of the Blind for two nights and days without food or shelter, and meditated upon the unexpected. During these meditations he repeated very frequently and always with a profounder note of derision the exploded proverb: “In the Country of the Blind the One-Eyed Man is King.” He thought chiefly of ways of fighting and conquering these people, and it grew clear that for him no practicable way was possible. He had no weapons, and now it would be hard to get one.

The canker of civilisation had got to him even in Bogota, and he could not find it in himself to go down and assassinate a blind man. Of course, if he did that, he might then dictate terms on the threat of assassinating them all. But—sooner or later he must sleep!…

He tried also to find food among the pine trees, to be comfortable under pine boughs while the frost fell at night, and—with less confidence—to catch a llama by artifice in order to try to kill it—perhaps by hammering it with a stone—and so finally, perhaps, to eat some of it. But the llamas had a doubt of him and regarded him with distrustful brown eyes, and spat when he drew near. Fear came on him the second day and fits of shivering. Finally he crawled down to the wall of the Country of the Blind and tried to make terms. He crawled along by the stream, shouting, until two blind men came out to the gate and talked to him.

“I was mad,” he said. “But I was only newly made.”

They said that was better.

He told them he was wiser now, and repented of all he had done.

Then he wept without intention, for he was very weak and ill now, and they took that as a favourable sign.

They asked him if he still thought he could “*see*.”

“No,” he said. “That was folly. The word means nothing—less than nothing!”

They asked him what was overhead.

“About ten times ten the height of a man there is a roof above the world—of rock—and very, very smooth.”… He burst again into hysterical tears. “Before you ask me any more, give me some food or I shall die.”

He expected dire punishments, but these blind people were capable of toleration. They regarded his rebellion as but one more proof of his general idiocy and inferiority; and after they had whipped him they appointed him to do the simplest and heaviest work they had for anyone to do, and he, seeing no other way of living, did submissively what he was told.

He was ill for some days, and they nursed him kindly. That refined his submission. But they insisted on his lying in the dark, and that was a great misery. And blind philosophers came and talked to him of the wicked levity of his mind, and reproved him so impressively for his doubts about the lid of rock that covered their cosmic casserole that he almost doubted whether indeed he was not the victim of hallucination in not seeing it overhead.

===Chinese===
他在盲人国围墙外头，无食无掩地待了两天两夜，思忖着这桩意料之外的事。在反复的思索中，他一遍又一遍地——而且一次比一次带着更深的自嘲口吻——重复着那句已被戳穿的谚语：“盲人国里，独眼者为王。”他主要琢磨的是如何与这些人作战并战而胜之，可事情越来越清楚：对他而言，并无一条行得通的法子。他没有武器，如今要弄到一件也难了。

文明的积习即便在波哥大也已渗进了他骨头里，他到底狠不下心，下去暗杀一个瞎子。当然，他若真这么干了，倒可以以杀尽他们相威胁，从此发号施令。但是——他迟早总得睡觉啊！……

他也试过在松林里找吃的，在霜降的夜里靠在松枝底下将就，也试过——信心不大——用计捉一头美洲驼来试着杀掉——也许拿石头砸死它——这样最后也许还能吃上几口它的肉。可那些美洲驼对他心存戒备，用棕色的眼睛不信任地打量他，他一凑近就朝他吐口水。第二天恐惧缠上了他，他一阵阵地发抖。最后他爬到盲人国的围墙下，设法讲和。他沿着溪流一路爬着、喊着，终于出来两个盲人，到门口来跟他说话。

“我那是疯了，”他说。“不过我才刚造出来不久。”

他们说，这样还好些。

他告诉他们，自己如今明白事理了，对所做的一切追悔莫及。

接着他不由自主地哭了起来——他此刻又虚弱又病——他们把这一点当作一个好兆头。

他们问他，是否还以为自己能“*看*”。

“不，”他说。“那是胡话。这词毫无意义——比无更无！”

他们问他头顶之上是什么。

“约莫十乘以十……一个人那么高，世界的上头有一道顶——岩石做的——非常非常光滑。”……他又歇斯底里地哭了起来。“你们再问下去之前，先给我点吃的吧，不然我要死了。”

他原以为会遭重罚，但这些盲人倒有几分宽容。他们把他的造反，看作他那一贯的愚笨和低能的又一证据；他们抽了他一顿鞭子之后，便派他去做他们这儿谁都能做、最简单也最重的活，而他，眼见无以为生，便乖乖地叫干什么干什么。

他病了几天，他们尽心照料他。这使他更加服帖了。但他们坚持让他躺在黑暗里，这是一桩大苦事。盲人哲学家们还来对他讲他心术之轻浮可恶，对他疑心那盖在他们“宇宙砂锅”之上的岩石盖子一事，训斥得极有声色，以至于他几乎都要怀疑：自己头顶上明明什么也看不见，莫非真是自己生了幻觉不成。

===Original===
So Nunez became a citizen of the Country of the Blind, and these people ceased to be a generalised people and became individualities and familiar to him, while the world beyond the mountains became more and more remote and unreal. There was Yacob, his master, a kindly man when not annoyed; there was Pedro, Yacob’s nephew; and there was Medina-saroti, who was the youngest daughter of Yacob. She was little esteemed in the world of the blind, because she had a clear-cut face, and lacked that satisfying, glossy smoothness that is the blind man’s ideal of feminine beauty; but Nunez thought her beautiful at first, and presently the most beautiful thing in the whole creation. Her closed eyelids were not sunken and red after the common way of the valley, but lay as though they might open again at any moment; and she had long eyelashes, which were considered a grave disfigurement. And her voice was strong, and did not satisfy the acute hearing of the valley swains. So that she had no lover.

There came a time when Nunez thought that, could he win her, he would be resigned to live in the valley for all the rest of his days.

He watched her; he sought opportunities of doing her little services, and presently he found that she observed him. Once at a rest-day gathering they sat side by side in the dim starlight, and the music was sweet. His hand came upon hers and he dared to clasp it. Then very tenderly she returned his pressure. And one day, as they were at their meal in the darkness, he felt her hand very softly seeking him, and as it chanced the fire leapt then and he saw the tenderness of her face.

He sought to speak to her.

He went to her one day when she was sitting in the summer moonlight spinning. The light made her a thing of silver and mystery. He sat down at her feet and told her he loved her, and told her how beautiful she seemed to him. He had a lover’s voice, he spoke with a tender reverence that came near to awe, and she had never before been touched by adoration. She made him no definite answer, but it was clear his words pleased her.

After that he talked to her whenever he could take an opportunity. The valley became the world for him, and the world beyond the mountains where men lived in sunlight seemed no more than a fairy tale he would some day pour into her ears. Very tentatively and timidly he spoke to her of sight.

Sight seemed to her the most poetical of fancies, and she listened to his description of the stars and the mountains and her own sweet white-lit beauty as though it was a guilty indulgence. She did not believe, she could only half understand, but she was mysteriously delighted, and it seemed to him that she completely understood.

His love lost its awe and took courage. Presently he was for demanding her of Yacob and the elders in marriage, but she became fearful and delayed. And it was one of her elder sisters who first told Yacob that Medina-saroti and Nunez were in love.

===Chinese===
于是努涅斯成了盲人国的一位公民，这里的人也不再是一个面目模糊的群体，而成了各有各的性情、与他朝夕相熟的人；山外那个世界则越来越远，越来越不真实。这里有雅各布（Yacob），他的主人，不恼的时候是个和善的人；有佩德罗，雅各布的侄子；还有梅迪娜-萨罗蒂（Medina-saroti），是雅各布最小的女儿。她在盲人的世界里不怎么受敬重，因为她那张轮廓分明的脸，欠缺那种令盲人满意的、光溜溜的平滑——而那才是盲人眼里女性美的理想；可努涅斯起初只觉得她漂亮，不久便以为她是天地间最美的物事。她那合着的眼睑，不像谷中一般人那样又红又陷，却平平地覆着，仿佛随时都可能重新睁开似的；她又生着长长的睫毛，这在谷中被认为是一种严重的缺陷。她的嗓音也过于响亮，不合谷中那些后生们敏锐的耳朵。因此她没有情人。

有一阵子，努涅斯心想：倘若能赢得她，他便甘心在这山谷里度过自己余生所有的日子。

他留意着她；他寻机为她做些小服务，不久便发觉她也注意到了他。有一回在一个休息日的集会上，他们在朦胧的星光下并肩坐着，乐声悠扬。他的手落到了她的手上，他大着胆子把它握住了。她十分温柔地回握了他。又有一天，他们在黑暗里用饭，他感到她的手极轻地朝他摸索过来，恰好那时火光一跳，他看见了她脸上的柔情。

他想要对她诉说。

一天，她坐在夏夜的月光下纺线，他走到她跟前。那月光把她化成了一件银色的、神秘的事物。他在她脚边坐下，告诉她他爱她，告诉她在他眼里她是何等的美丽。他有一副恋人的嗓音，他说话带着一种近乎敬畏的温柔的虔敬，而她此前从未受过这样的崇拜。她没有给他一个明确的答复，但显然他的话使她高兴。

从此，但凡能寻到机会，他便同她说话。山谷成了他的天地，山外那个世人活在阳光之下的世界，在他看来，不过是他有朝一日要倾注到她耳中的一个童话。他试探着、怯怯地向她讲起视觉。

视觉在她听来，是所有奇想里最具诗意的一种；她听他描述星星、群山，以及她自己在洁白光线下的甜美之美，那神情仿佛在听一桩有罪的放纵。她并不相信，也只能半懂，但她有一种说不清的喜悦，而他则以为她完全听懂了。

他的爱褪去了敬畏，鼓起了勇气。不久他便要去向雅各布和长老们求亲，要娶她为妻，可她却害怕起来，一拖再拖。倒是最先告诉雅各布、说梅迪娜-萨罗蒂和努涅斯相好的，是她的一位姐姐。

===Original===
There was from the first very great opposition to the marriage of Nunez and Medina-saroti; not so much because they valued her as because they held him as a being apart, an idiot, incompetent thing below the permissible level of a man. Her sisters opposed it bitterly as bringing discredit on them all; and old Yacob, though he had formed a sort of liking for his clumsy, obedient serf, shook his head and said the thing could not be. The young men were all angry at the idea of corrupting the race, and one went so far as to revile and strike Nunez. He struck back. Then for the first time he found an advantage in seeing, even by twilight, and after that fight was over no one was disposed to raise a hand against him. But they still found his marriage impossible.

Old Yacob had a tenderness for his last little daughter, and was grieved to have her weep upon his shoulder.

“You see, my dear, he’s an idiot. He has delusions; he can’t do anything right.”

“I know,” wept Medina-saroti. “But he’s better than he was. He’s getting better. And he’s strong, dear father, and kind—stronger and kinder than any I other man in the world. And he loves me—and, father, I love him.”

Old Yacob was greatly distressed to find her inconsolable, and, besides—what made it more distressing—he liked Nunez for many things. So he went and sat in the windowless council-chamber with the other elders and watched the trend of the talk, and said, at the proper time, “He’s better than he was. Very likely, some day, we shall find him as sane as ourselves.”

Then afterwards one of the elders, who thought deeply, had an idea. He was the great doctor among these people, their medicine-man, and he had a very philosophical and inventive mind, and the idea of curing Nunez of his peculiarities appealed to him. One day when Yacob was present he returned to the topic of Nunez.

“I have examined Bogota,” he said, “and the case is clearer to me. I think very probably he might be cured.”

“That is what I have always hoped,” said old Yacob.

“His brain is affected,” said the blind doctor.

The elders murmured assent.

“Now, *what* affects it?”

“Ah!” said old Yacob.

“*This*,” said the doctor, answering his own question. “Those queer things that are called the eyes, and which exist to make an agreeable soft depression in the face, are diseased, in the case of Bogota, in such a way as to affect his brain. They are greatly distended, he has eyelashes, and his eyelids move, and consequently his brain is in a state of constant irritation and distraction.”

“Yes?” said old Yacob. “Yes?”

“And I think I may say with reasonable certainty that, in order to cure him completely, all that we need do is a simple and easy surgical operation—namely, to remove these irritant bodies.”

“And then he will be sane?”

“Then he will be perfectly sane, and a quite admirable citizen.”

“Thank Heaven for science!” said old Yacob, and went forth at once to tell Nunez of his happy hopes.

But Nunez’s manner of receiving the good news struck him as being cold and disappointing.

“One might think,” he said, “from the tone you take, that you did not care for my daughter.”

===Chinese===
从一开始，努涅斯和梅迪娜-萨罗蒂的婚事便遭到了极大的反对；这倒不全是因他们看重她，而更是因他们视他为异类，一个白痴、无能之辈，够不上人的最低标准。她的姐姐们激烈地反对，说这会连累她们全体蒙羞；老雅各布虽然已对这笨拙、听话的奴仆生出几分好感，也只是摇头，说这事断断不可。年轻后生们一想到要玷污种族，无不义愤填膺；有一个竟破口辱骂努涅斯，还动手打他。他还了手。这头一遭，他发现即便在昏暗中，能看见也是一桩便宜；那一架打完，再没人敢对他动手。但他们仍觉得他的婚事不可行。

老雅各布心疼他这个最小的女儿，见她伏在自己肩头哭泣，心里很难过。

“你瞧，亲爱的，他是个白痴。他满脑子妄想；他什么事也做不对。”

“我知道，”梅迪娜-萨罗蒂哭着说，“可他比以前好些了。他一天天在好起来。他又强壮、又和气，好爹爹——比世上别的任何男人都更强壮、更和气。而他爱我——爹，我也爱他。”

老雅各布见她劝也劝不住，心里十分难过；何况——更叫他为难的——他也因许多事喜欢努涅斯。于是他去那间没有窗的议事厅里，与其他长老一同坐着，听他们谈锋的趋向，到了时机成熟的时候，便插嘴道：“他比以前好些了。说不定哪一天，我们会发现他跟我们一样神志清明呢。”

后来，长老中有一位惯于深思的，有了一个主意。他是这些人里的名医，是他们的萨满，心思极富哲学与创造的意味；把努涅斯那些怪癖治一治这个念头，颇引起了他的兴致。一天，雅各布在场的时候，他又提起了努涅斯这个话题。

“我诊过波哥大，”他说，“这病况我看得更清楚了。我想，他是很有可能治好的。”

“这正是我素来盼望的，”老雅各布说。

“他的脑子受了损，”那盲人医生说。

众长老低声附和。

“那么，是*什么*损了他的脑子呢？”

“啊！”老雅各布说。

“是*这个*，”医生自问自答道。“就是那些被叫作眼睛的古怪玩意儿——它们存在于脸上，本是为了在脸上做出一个讨人喜欢的、柔和的凹陷——在波哥大身上，这些器官却病了，而且病得损及了他的脑子。它们胀得大大的，他长着睫毛，眼皮还会动个不停，因此他的脑子就处在一种持续的烦躁和分心之中。”

“是吗？”老雅各布说，“是吗？”

“我想我可以相当有把握地说：要彻底治好他，我们只需做一个简单易行的小手术——就是把这几个惹事的玩意儿摘掉。”

“那他就会神志清明了？”

“那他便会完全神志清明，成为一名极可称道的公民。”

“感谢上苍，赐给我们科学！”老雅各布说，随即出去把这一份好消息告诉了努涅斯。

可努涅斯听了这好消息的态度，却让他觉得冷淡得令人失望。

“听你这口气，”他说，“倒像是不大把我女儿放在心上。”

===Original===
It was Medina-saroti who persuaded Nunez to face the blind surgeons.

“*You* do not want me,” he said, “to lose my gift of sight?”

She shook her head.

“My world is sight.”

Her head drooped lower.

“There are the beautiful things, the beautiful little things—the flowers, the lichens among the rocks, the lightness and softness on a piece of fur, the far sky with its drifting down of clouds, the sunsets and the stars. And there is you. For you alone it is good to have sight, to see your sweet, serene face, your kindly lips, your dear, beautiful hands folded together… It is these eyes of mine you won, these eyes that hold me to you, that these idiots seek. Instead, I must touch you, hear you, and never see you again. I must come under that roof of rock and stone and darkness, that horrible roof under which your imagination stoops… No; you would not have me do that?”

A disagreeable doubt had arisen in him. He stopped, and left the thing a question.

“I wish,” she said, “sometimes—” She paused.

“Yes,” said he, a little apprehensively.

“I wish sometimes—you would not talk like that.”

“Like what?”

“I know it’s pretty—it’s your imagination. I love it, but *now*—”

He felt cold. “*Now?*” he said faintly.

She sat quite still.

“You mean—you think—I should be better, better perhaps—”

He was realising things very swiftly. He felt anger, indeed, anger at the dull course of fate, but also sympathy for her lack of understanding—a sympathy near akin to pity.

“*Dear*,” he said, and he could see by her whiteness how intensely her spirit pressed against the things she could not say. He put his arms about her, he kissed her ear, and they sat for a time in silence.

“If I were to consent to this?” he said at last, in a voice that was very gentle.

She flung her arms about him, weeping wildly. “Oh, if you would,” she sobbed, “if only you would!”

---

===Chinese===
是梅迪娜-萨罗蒂劝服了努涅斯，让他去面对那些盲人外科医生。

“*你*并不想让我失去我的视觉天赋吧？”他说。

她摇了摇头。

“我的天地，就是视觉。”

她的头垂得更低了。

“有那么些美的东西，那些美的小东西——花朵，岩石间的地衣，一袭皮毛上的轻盈与柔软，远处那飘着朵朵云絮的天空，那些日落和星星。还有你。为了你一个人，有视觉才是好的：要看见你那张甜美的、宁静的脸，看见你慈和的嘴唇，看见你那亲爱的、美丽的手交叠在一起……你赢来的，正是我这一双眼睛；把我系在你身上的，也正是这一双眼睛，可这些蠢货要的，就是这双眼睛。从此以后，我只能触摸你，只能听见你，却再也见不到你了。我只能钻进那岩石、石头和黑暗盖成的穹顶之下，那可怕的穹顶之下，你的想象力也只能在它底下俯首……不；你不会叫我去做那种事的吧？”

他心里生起了一股不快的疑虑。他住了口，把这事搁成了一个问号。

“我但愿，”她说，“有时候——”她顿住了。

“什么？”他略带不安地说。

“我但愿有时候——你别那样说话。”

“哪样？”

“我知道那很美——那是你的想象。我是喜欢它的，可是*如今*——”

他打了个寒战。“*如今*？”他虚弱地说。

她一动不动地坐着。

“你的意思是——你是觉得——我会好些，也许好些，假如——”

他明白得极快。他感到愤怒，是的，对命运这种沉闷的安排的愤怒；可也感到对她这份不懂的同情——一种近于怜悯的同情。

“*亲爱的*，”他说，从她脸上的苍白，他能看出她的心是多么用力地在那些她说不出口的事上挣扎。他用胳膊搂住她，吻了吻她的耳朵，他们默默地坐了一阵。

“要是我答应了这事呢？”他终于开口，声音极尽温柔。

她伸出双臂抱住他，放声痛哭。“啊，要是你肯，”她抽泣着，“只要、只要你肯！”

---

===Original===
For a week before the operation that was to raise him from his servitude and inferiority to the level of a blind citizen, Nunez knew nothing of sleep, and all through the warm sunlit hours, while the others slumbered happily, he sat brooding or wandered aimlessly, trying to bring his mind to bear on his dilemma. He had given his answer, he had given his consent, and still he was not sure. And at last work-time was over, the sun rose in splendour over the golden crests, and his last day of vision began for him. He had a few minutes with Medina-saroti before she went apart to sleep.

“Tomorrow,” he said, “I shall see no more.”

“Dear heart!” she answered, and pressed his hands with all her strength.

“They will hurt you but little,” she said; “and you are going through this pain—you are going through it, dear lover, for *me*… Dear, if a woman’s heart and life can do it, I will repay you. My dearest one, my dearest with the tender voice, I will repay.”

He was drenched in pity for himself and her.

He held her in his arms, and pressed his lips to hers, and looked on her sweet face for the last time. “Goodbye!” he whispered at that dear sight, “goodbye!”

And then in silence he turned away from her.

She could hear his slow retreating footsteps, and something in the rhythm of them threw her into a passion of weeping.

He had fully meant to go to a lonely place where the meadows were beautiful with white narcissus, and there remain until the hour of his sacrifice should come, but as he went he lifted up his eyes and saw the morning, the morning like an angel in golden armour, marching down the steeps…

It seemed to him that before this splendour he, and this blind world in the valley, and his love, and all, were no more than a pit of sin.

He did not turn aside as he had meant to do, but went on, and passed through the wall of the circumference and out upon the rocks, and his eyes were always upon the sunlit ice and snow.

===Chinese===
手术前的一周里——这场手术将把他从奴仆和低人一等的身份，提升到一个盲人公民的地位——努涅斯彻夜难眠；在那些温暖的、阳光普照的时辰里，当旁人幸福地酣睡，他却坐着沉思，或漫无目的地游荡，想让自己的心面对这个两难。他已经给了答复，已经点了头，可他心里仍不踏实。终于，劳作的时辰过完了，太阳以万丈光芒升上金色的群峰，他一生中最后一个能看见的日子，开始了。在梅迪娜-萨罗蒂到一边去睡觉之前，他和她独处了几分钟。

“明天，”他说，“我就再也看不见了。”

“我的心肝！”她答着，使出全身的力气握紧他的手。

“他们只会让你疼上一点点，”她说，“而你这番苦——你这番苦，亲爱的，你是为*我*受的……亲爱的，只要一个女人的一颗心和一条命能做到，我一定报答你。我最亲爱的人，我那嗓音温柔的最亲爱的人，我一定报答。”

他心里为自己、也为她，浸透了一片怜惜。

他把她拥在怀里，把嘴唇贴上她的嘴唇，最后看了她那张甜美的脸一眼。“再见！”他面对那亲爱的景象悄声道，“再见！”

然后他默默地转过身，离开了她。

她听得见他越走越远的、缓慢的脚步声，那脚步声里的某种节拍，叫她痛哭失声。

他本来一心要去一个僻静的地方，那里的草甸开满了雪白的水仙，他要在那儿一直待到献祭的时辰到来；可他走着走着，抬起眼来，望见了早晨——那早晨，如一位身披金甲的天使，正从一层层阶地之上踏步而下……

他觉得，在这份辉煌面前，他自己，以及谷里这个盲人的世界，以及他的爱情，以及一切，都不过是罪孽的深渊。

他没有像原来打算的那样拐到一旁去，而是继续前行，穿过那道环形的墙，走到了岩石之上，他的双眼始终不离那片阳光下的冰雪。

===Original===
He saw their infinite beauty, and his imagination soared over them to the things beyond he was now to resign forever.

He thought of that great free world he was parted from, the world that was his own, and he had a vision of those further slopes, distance beyond distance, with Bogota, a place of multitudinous stirring beauty, a glory by day, a luminous mystery by night, a place of palaces and fountains and statues and white houses, lying beautifully in the middle distance. He thought how for a day or so one might come down through passes, drawing ever nearer and nearer to its busy streets and ways. He thought of the river journey, day by day, from great Bogota to the still vaster world beyond, through towns and villages, forest and desert places, the rushing river day by day, until its banks receded and the big steamers came splashing by, and one had reached the sea—the limitless sea, with its thousand islands, its thousands of islands, and its ships seen dimly far away in their incessant journeyings round and about that greater world. And there, unpent by mountains, one saw the sky—the sky, not such a disc as one saw it here, but an arch of immeasurable blue, a deep of deeps in which the circling stars were floating…

His eyes scrutinised the great curtain of the mountains with a keener inquiry.

For example, if one went so, up that gully and to that chimney there, then one might come out high among those stunted pines that ran round in a sort of shelf and rose still higher and higher as it passed above the gorge. And then? That talus might be managed. Thence perhaps a climb might be found to take him up to the precipice that came below the snow; and if that chimney failed, then another farther to the east might serve his purpose better. And then? Then one would be out upon the amber-lit snow there, and halfway up to the crest of those beautiful desolations.

He glanced back at the village, then turned right round and regarded it steadfastly.

He thought of Medina-saroti, and she had become small and remote.

He turned again towards the mountain wall, down which the day had come to him.

Then very circumspectly he began to climb.

When sunset came he was no longer climbing, but he was far and high. He had been higher, but he was still very high. His clothes were torn, his limbs were bloodstained, he was bruised in many places, but he lay as if he were at his ease, and there was a smile on his face.

From where he rested the valley seemed as if it were in a pit and nearly a mile below. Already it was dim with haze and shadow, though the mountain summits around him were things of light and fire. The mountain summits around him were things of light and fire, and the little details of the rocks near at hand were drenched with subtle beauty—a vein of green mineral piercing the grey, the flash of crystal faces here and there, a minute, minutely-beautiful orange lichen close beside his face. There were deep mysterious shadows in the gorge, blue deepening into purple, and purple into a luminous darkness, and overhead was the illimitable vastness of the sky. But he heeded these things no longer, but lay quite inactive there, smiling as if he were satisfied merely to have escaped from the valley of the Blind in which he had thought to be King.

The glow of the sunset passed, and the night came, and still he lay peacefully contented under the cold clear stars.

===Chinese===
他望见它们那无穷的美，他的想象力越过它们，飞向他从此要永远舍弃的、那边的事物。

他想到了那个与他隔绝了的、广袤而自由的世界，那个原属于他的世界；他仿佛看见了那些更远的山坡，一程又一程地远去，那远处是波哥大——一处万般动人之美的所在，白日里是一团光辉，夜晚是一种发光的神秘，一个有宫殿、有喷泉、有雕像、有白色房屋的地方，优美地坐落在不远不近的中景之中。他想到，人可以花上一两天，从一道道山口下来，离它那繁忙的街道和路途越来越近，越来越近。他想到从大波哥大沿着水路，日复一日，通往更广大的世界，穿过城镇和村庄、森林和荒漠，那条急流日复一日地奔泻，直到两岸退远，大轮船哗哗地驶过，人便到了海——那无边无际的海，海上有一千座岛屿，有几千座岛屿，还有那些船，在围绕那个更广大的世界不停地航行的途中，远远地、影影绰绰地看得见……而在那里，不受群山囚禁，可以望见天空——那天空，不是在这里所看见的这种圆盘，而是一道不可测量的蓝色拱顶，一个深渊之渊，旋转的星辰便漂浮在它之中……

他的眼睛，以一种更急切的探询，细细察看那道巨大的山峦之幕。

比方说，要是这么走，顺那条沟上去，到那道烟囱似的裂隙，那么人便可能从那些矮松之间高高地钻出来——那些矮松沿着一片阶地似的地方绕过去，越过峡谷上方，越走越高。再然后呢？那片碎石坡也许可以对付。从那儿也许可以找到一段攀路，把他带上雪线之下的那道峭壁；要是那道烟囱走不通，那么更东边的一道，也许更合他的用。再然后？再然后，人便会站到那片琥珀色光照的雪地上，到了那片美丽荒凉的中途，离峰巅只剩一半的路。

他回头瞥了一眼村子，然后转过身，定定地端详着它。

他想到了梅迪娜-萨罗蒂，她已经变得渺小而遥远了。

他又转向那道山壁——白昼便是从那道山壁上下到他这里的。

然后，他审慎地、一步一步地，开始向上攀登。

日落时分，他已经不再攀登了，但他已又高又远。他曾经爬得更高，可如今他仍旧很高。他的衣裳破碎，四肢染血，身上多处瘀伤，可他躺着，仿佛怡然自得，脸上还挂着一丝微笑。

从他所歇之处望去，山谷仿佛位于一个深坑之中，在他之下将近一英里。它已笼罩在一片烟霭和阴影里，可他身边的山巅，还是光与火的物事。他身边的山巅，还是光与火的物事，而近处岩石上那些细微之处，都浸透着一种幽微的美——一条绿色的矿脉穿过灰色岩石，到处闪着晶体的面，紧贴他脸旁，是一片极其细小、极其美丽的橙色地衣。峡谷深处有幽秘的阴影，蓝色深成紫色，紫色深成一种发光的黑暗，而头顶，是无边无际的苍穹。可这些，他已不再理会；他只是一动不动地躺在那里，微笑着，仿佛心满意足，只因为逃出了那座他原以为自己会做国王的盲人之谷。

落日的余晖散去，夜来了，他依旧平静而满足地躺在那寒冷而清澈的群星之下。

## The Crystal Egg / 水晶蛋

===Original===
There was, until a year ago, a little and very grimy-looking shop near Seven Dials, over which, in weatherworn yellow lettering, the name of "C. Cave, Naturalist and Dealer in Antiquities," was inscribed. The contents of its window were curiously variegated. They comprised some elephant tusks and an imperfect set of chessmen, beads and weapons, a box of eyes, two skulls of tigers and one human, several moth-eaten stuffed monkeys (one holding a lamp), an old-fashioned cabinet, a flyblown ostrich egg or so, some fishing-tackle, and an extraordinarily dirty, empty glass fish-tank. There was also, at the moment the story begins, a mass of crystal, worked into the shape of an egg and brilliantly polished. And at that two people, who stood outside the window, were looking, one of them a tall, thin clergyman, the other a black-bearded young man of dusky complexion and unobtrusive costume. The dusky young man spoke with eager gesticulation, and seemed anxious for his companion to purchase the article.

While they were there, Mr. Cave came into his shop, his beard still wagging with the bread and butter of his tea. When he saw these men and the object of their regard, his countenance fell. He glanced guiltily over his shoulder, and softly shut the door. He was a little old man, with a pale face and peculiar watery blue eyes; his hair was a dirty grey, and he wore a shabby blue frock coat, an ancient silk hat, and carpet slippers very much down at heel. He remained watching the two men as they talked. The clergyman went deep into his trouser pocket, examined a handful of money, and showed his teeth in an agreeable smile. Mr. Cave seemed still more depressed when they came into the shop.

The clergyman, without any ceremony, asked the price of the crystal egg. Mr. Cave glanced nervously towards the door leading into the parlour, and said five pounds. The clergyman protested that the price was high, to his companion as well as to Mr. Cave—it was, indeed, very much more than Mr. Cave had intended to ask, when he had stocked the article—and an attempt at bargaining ensued. Mr. Cave stepped to the shop-door, and held it open. "Five pounds is my price," he said, as though he wished to save himself the trouble of unprofitable discussion. As he did so, the upper portion of a woman's face appeared above the blind in the glass upper panel of the door leading into the parlour, and stared curiously at the two customers. "Five pounds is my price," said Mr. Cave, with a quiver in his voice.

===Chinese===
一年前，七晷区（Seven Dials）附近还有一家又小又脏的铺子，门上方用褪色的黄漆写着"C·凯夫（C. Cave），博物学家暨古董商"几个字。橱窗里陈列的东西五花八门，颇为古怪：几根象牙，一副残缺的象棋，若干珠子和武器，一盒眼珠子，两颗老虎头骨和一颗人的头骨，几只被虫蛀了的猴子标本（其中一只还捧着一盏灯），一个老式橱柜，一两个生了蝇卵的鸵鸟蛋，一些钓具，还有一只脏得非同寻常的、空着的玻璃鱼缸。故事开始时，橱窗里还有一块水晶，被雕琢成蛋形，打磨得晶亮。窗外站着两个人，正盯着这件东西瞧：一个是高瘦的牧师，另一个是个黑胡须、肤色黝黑的年轻人，衣着并不起眼。那黝黑的年轻人一边说着，一边热切地打着手势，似乎急切地希望他的同伴把这件东西买下来。

他们正站在那里的时候，凯夫先生（Mr. Cave）走进了铺子，胡子上还沾着茶点吃的黄油面包屑。他一看见这两个人，又看见他们盯着的东西，脸色顿时一沉。他心虚地回头看了一眼，轻轻把门带上。他是个矮小的老头，脸色苍白，生着一双奇特的、水汪汪的蓝眼睛；头发是脏兮兮的灰色，身上穿一件寒酸的蓝色礼服大衣，戴一顶古旧的丝质礼帽，脚上是一双后跟磨塌了的绒毯拖鞋。他站在那里，看着那两人交谈。那牧师把一只手深深伸进裤袋里，掏出一把零钱数了数，龇着牙，露出一个讨人喜欢的微笑。待两人走进铺子，凯夫先生的神色愈发沮丧了。

那牧师也不寒暄，开口便问这枚水晶蛋要多少钱。凯夫先生紧张地朝通往起居室的那扇门瞥了一眼，说要五英镑。牧师连声嫌贵，既对他的同伴说，也对凯夫先生说——事实上，这价钱比凯夫先生当初进货时本打算开的价高得多——于是双方开始讨价还价。凯夫先生走到店门口，把门拉开，撑在那儿。"五英镑，一分不少。"他说，仿佛想省去这种白费口舌的争论。就在这时，通往起居室那扇门上半截玻璃窗的帘子上方，露出了一张女人的上半张脸，好奇地盯着这两位顾客。"五英镑，一分不少。"凯夫先生又说了一遍，声音里带着一丝颤抖。

===Original===
The swarthy young man had so far remained a spectator, watching Cave keenly. Now he spoke. "Give him five pounds," he said. The clergyman glanced at him to see if he were in earnest, and, when he looked at Mr. Cave again, he saw that the latter's face was white. "It's a lot of money," said the clergyman, and, diving into his pocket, began counting his resources. He had little more than thirty shillings, and he appealed to his companion, with whom he seemed to be on terms of considerable intimacy. This gave Mr. Cave an opportunity of collecting his thoughts, and he began to explain in an agitated manner that the crystal was not, as a matter of fact, entirely free for sale. His two customers were naturally surprised at this, and inquired why he had not thought of that before he began to bargain. Mr. Cave became confused, but he stuck to his story, that the crystal was not in the market that afternoon, that a probable purchaser of it had already appeared. The two, treating this as an attempt to raise the price still further, made as if they would leave the shop. But at this point the parlour door opened, and the owner of the dark fringe and the little eyes appeared.

She was a coarse-featured, corpulent woman, younger and very much larger than Mr. Cave; she walked heavily, and her face was flushed. "That crystal *is* for sale," she said. "And five pounds is a good enough price for it. I can't think what you're about, Cave, not to take the gentleman's offer!"

Mr. Cave, greatly perturbed by the irruption, looked angrily at her over the rims of his spectacles, and, without excessive assurance, asserted his right to manage his business in his own way. An altercation began. The two customers watched the scene with interest and some amusement, occasionally assisting Mrs. Cave with suggestions. Mr. Cave, hard driven, persisted in a confused and impossible story of an enquiry for the crystal that morning, and his agitation became painful. But he stuck to his point with extraordinary persistence. It was the young Oriental who ended this curious controversy. He proposed that they should call again in the course of two days—so as to give the alleged enquirer a fair chance. "And then we must insist," said the clergyman, "Five pounds." Mrs. Cave took it on herself to apologise for her husband, explaining that he was sometimes "a little odd," and as the two customers left, the couple prepared for a free discussion of the incident in all its bearings.

===Chinese===
那黝黑的年轻人此前一直袖手旁观，目光锐利地打量着凯夫。这时他开口了："给他五英镑。"他说。牧师瞥了他一眼，看他是否当真，待再看凯夫先生时，只见对方脸色惨白。"这可不少钱啊。"牧师说着，又把手伸进口袋，数起自己所有的钱来。他身上拢共不过三十先令出头，便向同伴求助——看样子他与这位同伴关系颇为亲密。这一下倒给了凯夫先生一个缓神的机会，他激动地解释说，这枚水晶眼下其实并不完全出售。两位顾客自然感到诧异，问他既然如此，为什么不在开价之前就想清楚。凯夫先生越说越乱，但一口咬定那水晶今天下午不卖，说可能已经有买家看上了。两人把这当作变相抬价，便作势要走。可就在这时，起居室的门开了，那个留着黑色刘海、长着一双小眼睛的女人走了出来。

她是个五官粗大、体态臃肿的女人，比凯夫先生年轻，块头也比他大得多；她脚步沉重，满脸通红。"那水晶是卖的。"她说，"五英镑这个价够好的了。我真不懂你搞什么名堂，凯夫，人家出这个价你都不接！"

凯夫先生被她这番闯出来搅局弄得大为慌乱，隔着镜框上方怒气冲冲地瞪了她一眼，并不十分理直气壮地声言，自己的买卖该由自己做主。争吵由此而起。两位顾客饶有兴致地看着这场戏，还带着几分好笑，偶尔插上一两句，给凯夫太太（Mrs. Cave）帮腔。凯夫先生被逼得紧，却仍旧含混不清地咬定说，那天上午曾有人来问过这枚水晶，他的激动越发难以掩饰。可他固执得异乎寻常，死咬着这一点不放。最终了结这场奇怪争执的，是那位年轻的东方人（Oriental）。他提议：他们过两天再来——也好让那位所谓的问价者有个公平的机会。"那到时候，我们可就不能让了。"牧师说，"五英镑。"凯夫太太主动替丈夫赔了不是，解释说他这人有时候"有点儿古怪"。待两位顾客离去，这对夫妻便开始就这件事的方方面面畅所欲言地讨论起来。

===Original===
Mrs. Cave talked to her husband with singular directness. The poor little man, quivering with emotion, muddled himself between his stories, maintaining on the one hand that he had another customer in view, and on the other asserting that the crystal was honestly worth ten guineas. "Why did you ask five pounds?" said his wife. "*Do* let me manage my business my own way!" said Mr. Cave.

Mr. Cave had living with him a stepdaughter and a stepson, and at supper that night the transaction was re-discussed. None of them had a high opinion of Mr. Cave's business methods, and this action seemed a culminating folly.

===Chinese===
凯夫太太跟丈夫说话，直截了当得少见。这可怜的小个子男人浑身颤抖，一会儿说另有一位顾客在看，一会儿又说这枚水晶实实在在值十几尼，自己把自己说乱了。"那你为什么要五英镑？"他妻子问。"就让我用自己的法子做我这买卖吧！"凯夫先生说。

凯夫先生身边还带着一个继女和一个继子，那天晚饭时，这笔买卖又被重新议论了一番。家里没有一个人看得起凯夫先生做买卖的法子，而这次的行为更像是蠢到了头。

===Original===
"It's my opinion he's refused that crystal before," said the stepson, a loose-limbed lout of eighteen.

"But *five pounds*!" said the stepdaughter, an argumentative young woman of six-and-twenty.

Mr. Cave's answers were wretched; he could only mumble weak assertions that he knew his own business best. They drove him from his half-eaten supper into the shop, to close it for the night, his ears aflame and tears of vexation behind his spectacles. "Why had he left the crystal in the window so long? The folly of it!" That was the trouble closest in his mind. For a time he could see no way of evading sale.

===Chinese===
"依我看，他之前就拒过这枚水晶的生意。"那个继子说——一个十八岁、手脚松垮的愣小子。

"可那是五英镑啊！"那个继女说——一个二十六岁、爱抬杠的年轻女子。

凯夫先生回答得可怜巴巴；只能含含糊糊地、有气无力地声言，自己的买卖自己最清楚。他们把他从吃了一半的晚饭前赶到铺子里去关门过夜，他两耳烧得通红，眼镜后面憋着懊恼的泪水。"自己怎么把那水晶留在橱窗里那么久呢？这不是蠢吗！"这才是他心头最切近的烦恼。一时间，他实在想不出法子怎样躲过这笔买卖。

===Original===
After supper his stepdaughter and stepson smartened themselves up and went out and his wife retired upstairs to reflect upon the business aspects of the crystal, over a little sugar and lemon and so forth in hot water. Mr. Cave went into the shop, and stayed there until late, ostensibly to make ornamental rockeries for goldfish cases but really for a private purpose that will be better explained later. The next day Mrs. Cave found that the crystal had been removed from the window, and was lying behind some secondhand books on angling. She replaced it in a conspicuous position. But she did not argue further about it, as a nervous headache disinclined her from debate. Mr. Cave was always disinclined. The day passed disagreeably. Mr. Cave was, if anything, more absentminded than usual, and uncommonly irritable withal. In the afternoon, when his wife was taking her customary sleep, he removed the crystal from the window again.

===Chinese===
晚饭后，继女和继子梳洗打扮出门去了，他妻子则上了楼，就着一杯加了点儿糖、柠檬之类的热水，反复盘算这枚水晶生意上的种种好处。凯夫先生走进铺子，一直待到很晚，表面上是在为金鱼缸做装饰用的假山，实则另有私衷，这点后文再说。第二天，凯夫太太发现那枚水晶已经从橱窗里挪走了，藏在几本关于垂钓的旧书后面。她把它重新摆到一个显眼的位置。但她没有再为这件事多说，因为一阵神经性头痛让她懒得再争执。凯夫先生倒一向都是懒得争的。这一天过得十分不痛快。凯夫先生比平时更加心不在焉，若说有什么不同的话，便是格外暴躁。下午，趁他妻子照例午睡，他又把那枚水晶从橱窗里挪走了。

===Original===
The next day Mr. Cave had to deliver a consignment of dogfish at one of the hospital schools, where they were needed for dissection. In his absence Mrs. Cave's mind reverted to the topic of the crystal, and the methods of expenditure suitable to a windfall of five pounds. She had already devised some very agreeable expedients, among others a dress of green silk for herself and a trip to Richmond, when a jangling of the front door bell summoned her into the shop. The customer was an examination coach who came to complain of the non-delivery of certain frogs asked for the previous day. Mrs. Cave did not approve of this particular branch of Mr. Cave's business, and the gentleman, who had called in a somewhat aggressive mood, retired after a brief exchange of words—entirely civil so far as he was concerned. Mrs. Cave's eye then naturally turned to the window; for the sight of the crystal was an assurance of the five pounds and of her dreams. What was her surprise to find it gone!

She went to the place behind the locker on the counter, where she had discovered it the day before. It was not there; and she immediately began an eager search about the shop.

When Mr. Cave returned from his business with the dogfish, about a quarter to two in the afternoon, he found the shop in some confusion, and his wife, extremely exasperated and on her knees behind the counter, routing among his taxidermic material. Her face came up hot and angry over the counter, as the jangling bell announced his return, and she forthwith accused him of "hiding it."

===Chinese===
第二天，凯夫先生得往一所医学院送一批角鲨，那里解剖课要用。他不在家时，凯夫太太的心思又转回了那枚水晶上，盘算起这笔五英镑意外之财该怎么花。她已经琢磨出几条十分称心的妙计——其中包括给自己置办一件绿绸衣裙、去里士满（Richmond）游玩一趟——正在这时，店门前一阵叮叮当当的门铃声把她唤进了铺子。来客是一位应试辅导老师，前来抱怨昨天要的几只青蛙没有送到。凯夫太太本就看不上凯夫先生这门生意里的这一项，那位先生来时本来带着点儿兴师问罪的意思，三言两语之后便走了——就他这方面而言，言辞完全是客客气气的。于是凯夫太太的目光自然而然地转向了橱窗——只要看见那枚水晶，那五英镑和她的一番美梦便算落了实。谁知她竟发现那枚水晶不见了！

她走到柜台后面那个柜格背后——前一天她正是在那儿发现它的。它不在那里；她立刻在铺子里急切地翻找起来。

下午差一刻两点，凯夫先生送完角鲨回来，只见铺子里乱糟糟的，他妻子正恼怒万分地跪在柜台后面，在他那些做动物标本的材料堆里翻来找去。门铃叮当地通报他回来了，她那张滚烫、怒气冲冲的脸从柜台上沿冒了出来，劈头就指责他"把它藏起来了"。

===Original===
"Hid *what*?" asked Mr. Cave.

"The crystal!"

At that Mr. Cave, apparently much surprised, rushed to the window. "Isn't it here?" he said. "Great Heavens! what has become of it?"

Just then, Mr. Cave's stepson reentered the shop from the inner room—he had come home a minute or so before Mr. Cave—and he was blaspheming freely. He was apprenticed to a secondhand furniture dealer down the road, but he had his meals at home, and he was naturally annoyed to find no dinner ready.

===Chinese===
"藏什么？"凯夫先生问。

"那枚水晶！"

闻言，凯夫先生一脸吃惊地冲到橱窗前。"不在这儿吗？"他说，"老天爷！它会到哪儿去呢？"

就在这时，凯夫先生的继子从里屋走进铺子——他比凯夫先生早回家大约一分钟——嘴里不干不净地骂着。他在马路那头一家旧家具店当学徒，但饭是在家里吃的，回来一看午饭还没做好，自然是一肚子火。

===Original===
But, when he heard of the loss of the crystal, he forgot his meal, and his anger was diverted from his mother to his stepfather. Their first idea, of course, was that he had hidden it. But Mr. Cave stoutly denied all knowledge of its fate—freely offering his bedabbled affidavit in the matter—and at last was worked up to the point of accusing, first, his wife and then his stepson of having taken it with a view to a private sale. So began an exceedingly acrimonious and emotional discussion, which ended for Mrs. Cave in a peculiar nervous condition midway between hysterics and amuck, and caused the stepson to be half-an-hour late at the furniture establishment in the afternoon. Mr. Cave took refuge from his wife's emotions in the shop.

In the evening the matter was resumed, with less passion and in a judicial spirit, under the presidency of the stepdaughter. The supper passed unhappily and culminated in a painful scene. Mr. Cave gave way at last to extreme exasperation, and went out banging the front door violently. The rest of the family, having discussed him with the freedom his absence warranted, hunted the house from garret to cellar, hoping to light upon the crystal.

===Chinese===
可一听说了水晶丢失的事，他便把午饭抛在了脑后，怒火也从母亲身上转到了继父身上。他们首先想到的，当然是凯夫先生把它藏起来了。可凯夫先生一口咬定自己丝毫不知它的去向——满口赌咒发誓——末了竟激动到反咬一口，先是指妻子、继而指继子拿了它，想私下卖掉。于是一场唇枪舌剑、你死我活的争吵就此开始，凯夫太太落得个介于歇斯底里和发狂之间的古怪神经症状，继子下午去家具店也迟到了半个钟头。凯夫先生躲进铺子，才算逃开了他妻子的那番情绪。

到了晚上，这件事又被重新提起，火气小了些，多了几分秉公而断的味道，由继女主审。晚饭吃得不痛快，最后以一场难堪的闹剧收场。凯夫先生终于忍无可忍，冲了出去，把大门砰地一声重重摔上。剩下的一家人趁他不在，肆无忌惮地把他数落了一番，然后从阁楼到地窖把整栋房子搜了个遍，巴望能翻出那枚水晶来。

===Original===
The next day the two customers called again. They were received by Mrs. Cave almost in tears. It transpired that no one *could* imagine all that she had stood from Cave at various times in her married pilgrimage… She also gave a garbled account of the disappearance. The clergyman and the Oriental laughed silently at one another, and said it was very extraordinary. As Mrs. Cave seemed disposed to give them the complete history of her life they made to leave the shop. Thereupon Mrs. Cave, still clinging to hope, asked for the clergyman's address, so that, if she could get anything out of Cave, she might communicate it. The address was duly given, but apparently was afterwards mislaid. Mrs. Cave can remember nothing about it.

In the evening of that day, the Caves seem to have exhausted their emotions, and Mr. Cave, who had been out in the afternoon, supped in a gloomy isolation that contrasted pleasantly with the impassioned controversy of the previous days. For some time matters were very badly strained in the Cave household, but neither crystal nor customer reappeared.

===Chinese===
第二天，那两位顾客又来了。出来招待他们的凯夫太太简直泪眼汪汪。原来，在嫁给他这些年里，她从凯夫那儿受了多少委屈，谁也想象不出……她颠三倒四地把水晶失踪的事又说了一遍。那牧师和那位东方人对视一眼，无声地笑了，都说这事真是蹊跷。眼见凯夫太太大有要把她一生的完整经历都讲给他们听的势头，两人便作势要走。于是凯夫太太仍不肯死心，要了牧师的地址，以便万一能从凯夫嘴里问出点儿什么，可以通知他。地址是留下了，可事后显然又弄丢了。凯夫太太一点儿都记不起来了。

那天傍晚，凯夫夫妇的情绪似乎都已耗尽，下午出去了一趟的凯夫先生阴郁地独自吃着晚饭——与前几日那番剑拔弩张的争执相比，倒也清静自在。此后一段时间，凯夫家里的气氛紧张到了极点，但那枚水晶和那两位顾客都没有再出现。

===Original===
Now, without mincing the matter, we must admit that Mr. Cave was a liar. He knew perfectly well where the crystal was. It was in the rooms of Mr. Jacoby Wace, Assistant Demonstrator at St. Catherine's Hospital, Westbourne Street. It stood on the sideboard partially covered by a black velvet cloth, and beside a decanter of American whisky. It is from Mr. Wace, indeed, that the particulars upon which this narrative is based were derived. Cave had taken off the thing to the hospital hidden in the dogfish sack, and there had pressed the young investigator to keep it for him. Mr. Wace was a little dubious at first. His relationship to Cave was peculiar. He had a taste for singular characters, and he had more than once invited the old man to smoke and drink in his rooms, and to unfold his rather amusing views of life in general and of his wife in particular. Mr. Wace had encountered Mrs. Cave, too, on occasions when Mr. Cave was not at home to attend to him. He knew the constant interference to which Cave was subjected, and having weighed the story judicially, he decided to give the crystal a refuge. Mr. Cave promised to explain the reasons for his remarkable affection for the crystal more fully on a later occasion, but he spoke distinctly of seeing visions therein. He called on Mr. Wace the same evening.

===Chinese===
说到底，不绕弯子地讲，我们得承认凯夫先生是个说谎的人。他心里清楚得很，那枚水晶在哪里。它在韦斯特本街（Westbourne Street）圣凯瑟琳医院（St. Catherine's Hospital）的助理示教员雅各比·韦斯先生（Mr. Jacoby Wace）的房间里。它立在餐具柜上，半遮着一块黑天鹅绒布，旁边放着一细颈瓶美国威士忌。事实上，本篇故事所依据的种种细节，正是从韦斯先生那里得来的。凯夫把这件东西藏在装角鲨的袋子里带到了医院，在那里恳请这位年轻的调查者替他保管。韦斯先生起初还有些犹豫。他与凯夫的关系颇为特别。他素来喜欢结交奇人，不止一次请这位老人到他房里抽烟喝酒，听他畅谈自己那些颇为有趣的人生见解——尤其是关于他妻子的那一套。凯夫先生不在家、未能亲自接待时，韦斯先生也曾与凯夫太太打过照面。他深知凯夫所遭受的那种没完没了的干涉；将事情前前后后斟酌了一番后，他决定给这枚水晶一个避难所。凯夫先生答应改日再把他对这枚水晶异乎寻常的眷恋之情详加解释，但他明确提到了能在其中看见种种幻象。当天傍晚他就来拜访韦斯先生了。

===Original===
He told a complicated story. The crystal he said had come into his possession with other oddments at the forced sale of another curiosity dealer's effects, and not knowing what its value might be, he had ticketed it at ten shillings. It had hung upon his hands at that price for some months, and he was thinking of "reducing the figure," when he made a singular discovery.

At that time his health was very bad—and it must be borne in mind that, throughout all this experience, his physical condition was one of ebb—and he was in considerable distress by reason of the negligence, the positive ill-treatment even, he received from his wife and stepchildren. His wife was vain, extravagant, unfeeling, and had a growing taste for private drinking; his stepdaughter was mean and overreaching; and his stepson had conceived a violent dislike for him, and lost no chance of showing it. The requirements of his business pressed heavily upon him, and Mr. Wace does not think that he was altogether free from occasional intemperance. He had begun life in a comfortable position, he was a man of fair education, and he suffered, for weeks at a stretch, from melancholia and insomnia. Afraid to disturb his family, he would slip quietly from his wife's side, when his thoughts became intolerable, and wander about the house. And about three o'clock one morning, late in August, chance directed him into the shop.

===Chinese===
他讲了一个颇为曲折的故事。他说，这枚水晶是他在另一位古玩商破产清货的拍卖会上，连同一些杂七杂八的东西一道到手的；他不知道它值多少，就标价十先令。这个价钱在他手里压了几个月也没卖出，他正盘算着"把价钱往下压一压"——就在这时，他有了一个奇特的发现。

那时他身体很不好——必须记住，在整个这段经历里，他的身体状况一直处于日渐衰弱的状态——再加上妻子和继子女对他的疏忽，甚至是公然的苛待，他更是苦不堪言。他妻子虚荣、奢侈、冷酷，而且越来越爱背着人偷酒喝；继女刻薄贪小；继子则对他怀有一种强烈的厌恶，只要有机会就要表露一番。生意的种种负担压得他喘不过气来，韦斯先生也认为他并非完全没有偶尔酗酒的情形。他早年境况殷实，受过相当的教育，却一连几个星期地为忧郁症和失眠所苦。他怕惊扰家人，每当脑子里乱得难以忍受时，便悄悄从妻子身边起身，在屋里到处徘徊。八月下旬的一天清晨三点钟左右，他鬼使神差地走进了铺子。

===Original===
The dirty little place was impenetrably black except in one spot, where he perceived an unusual glow of light. Approaching this, he discovered it to be the crystal egg, which was standing on the corner of the counter towards the window. A thin ray smote through a crack in the shutters, impinged upon the object, and seemed as it were to fill its entire interior.

It occurred to Mr. Cave that this was not in accordance with the laws of optics as he had known them in his younger days. He could understand the rays being refracted by the crystal and coming to a focus in its interior, but this diffusion jarred with his physical conceptions. He approached the crystal nearly, peering into it and round it, with a transient revival of the scientific curiosity that in his youth had determined his choice of a calling. He was surprised to find the light not steady, but writhing within the substance of the egg, as though that object was a hollow sphere of some luminous vapour. In moving about to get different points of view, he suddenly found that he had come between it and the ray, and that the crystal none the less remained luminous. Greatly astonished, he lifted it out of the light ray and carried it to the darkest part of the shop. It remained bright for some four or five minutes, when it slowly faded and went out. He placed it in the thin streak of daylight, and its luminousness was almost immediately restored.

===Chinese===
这间肮脏的小铺子黑得伸手不见五指，只有一处地方透出异样的光亮。走近一看，原来是那枚水晶蛋，立在靠橱窗那一头的柜台角上。一线细细的光从百叶窗的一道缝里射进来，正照在这件东西上，仿佛把它整个内部都照亮了。

凯夫先生想起，这与他年轻时所知的光学定律并不相符。他能理解光线被水晶折射后汇聚到内部某一点上，可这种漫射却与他的物理学常识相悖。他凑近水晶，绕着它、对着它里面细细端详，青年时代那种决定了他择业方向的科研好奇心，一度又在他身上苏醒过来。他惊讶地发现，那光并不稳定，而是在这枚蛋的实体里蠕动着，仿佛这件东西是一个由某种发光蒸气构成的空心球体。为了从不同角度观察，他来回移动，忽而发现自己已经站在了它和那束光之间，可那枚水晶依旧亮着。他大吃一惊，把它从光束里拿出来，端到铺子里最暗的角落。它持续亮了大约四五分钟，然后慢慢暗了下去，熄灭了。他把它重新放进那一丝日光里，它的光亮几乎立刻又恢复了。

===Original===
So far, at least, Mr. Wace was able to verify the remarkable story of Mr. Cave. He has himself repeatedly held this crystal in a ray of light (which had to be of a less diameter than one millimetre). And in a perfect darkness, such as could be produced by velvet wrapping, the crystal did undoubtedly appear very faintly phosphorescent. It would seem, however, that the luminousness was of some exceptional sort, and not equally visible to all eyes; for Mr. Harbinger—whose name will be familiar to the scientific reader in connection with the Pasteur Institute—was quite unable to see any light whatever. And Mr. Wace's own capacity for its appreciation was out of comparison inferior to that of Mr. Cave's. Even with Mr. Cave the power varied very considerably: his vision was most vivid during states of extreme weakness and fatigue.

===Chinese===
至少到此为止，韦斯先生还能一一验证凯夫先生这番离奇的讲述。他自己也曾多次将这枚水晶置于光束中观察（光束的直径须小于一毫米）。而在用天鹅绒包裹所造成的完全黑暗中，这枚水晶确实隐隐约约地呈现出发磷光的样子。然而，这种发光似乎属于某种特殊的性质，并非所有人的眼睛都能同样看得见——因为哈宾杰先生（Mr. Harbinger）——其名字因与巴斯德研究所（Pasteur Institute）的渊源而为科学界读者所熟知——根本就看不见任何光。而韦斯先生自己感受这种光的能力，与凯夫先生相比更是差得远，不可同日而语。即便对凯夫先生本人而言，这种能力也时有起伏：在他极度虚弱、疲惫之时，所见最为鲜明。

===Original===
Now, from the outset this light in the crystal exercised a curious fascination upon Mr. Cave. And it says more for his loneliness of soul than a volume of pathetic writing could do, that he told no human being of his curious observations. He seems to have been living in such an atmosphere of petty spite that to admit the existence of a pleasure would have been to risk the loss of it. He found that as the dawn advanced, and the amount of diffused light increased, the crystal became to all appearance non-luminous. And for some time he was unable to see anything in it, except at nighttime, in dark corners of the shop.

But the use of an old velvet cloth, which he used as a background for a collection of minerals, occurred to him, and by doubling this, and putting it over his head and hands, he was able to get a sight of the luminous movement within the crystal even in the daytime. He was very cautious lest he should be thus discovered by his wife, and he practised this occupation only in the afternoons, while she was asleep upstairs, and then circumspectly in a hollow under the counter. And one day, turning the crystal about in his hands, he saw something. It came and went like a flash, but it gave him the impression that the object had for a moment opened to him the view of a wide and spacious and strange country; and, turning it about, he did, just as the light faded, see the same vision again.

===Chinese===
打从一开始，水晶里的这道光便对凯夫先生施展出一种奇异的吸引力。而他把这番奇特的观察对任何人都只字不提——这件事所道出的他灵魂深处的孤独，胜过一整部缠绵悱恻的著作。他似乎长久生活在这样一种琐碎恶意的氛围里，以致只要承认自己有一份乐趣，就等于冒着失去它的风险。他发现，随着天色渐明、漫射光增强，那枚水晶表面上看便不再发光了。此后有一段时间，除了夜里在铺子的黑暗角落，他在水晶里什么也看不见。

后来他想起一块旧天鹅绒布——平日里他把它用作收藏矿石的衬底——把这块布折叠起来蒙在头上和手上，他便连白天也能窥见水晶内部那种发光的律动了。他格外小心，生怕这样被妻子撞见，只在下午趁她楼上熟睡时才敢一试，而且还要审慎地缩在柜台下面的一处凹槽里。一日，他把水晶在手里翻转着，忽然看见了什么。那东西像闪电般一闪而过，却给他留下这样的印象：这件东西曾有一刹那向他展露出一片辽阔、空旷而奇异的乡野的景象；他把水晶再转了转，就在那道光行将熄灭之际，他确实又看见了同样的景象。

===Original===
Now, it would be tedious and unnecessary to state all the phases of Mr. Cave's discovery from this point. Suffice that the effect was this: the crystal, being peered into at an angle of about 137 degrees from the direction of the illuminating ray, gave a clear and consistent picture of a wide and peculiar countryside. It was not dreamlike at all: it produced a definite impression of reality, and the better the light the more real and solid it seemed. It was a moving picture: that is to say, certain objects moved in it, but slowly in an orderly manner like real things, and, according as the direction of the lighting and vision changed, the picture changed also. It must, indeed, have been like looking through an oval glass at a view, and turning the glass about to get at different aspects.

Mr. Cave's statements, Mr. Wace assures me, were extremely circumstantial, and entirely free from any of that emotional quality that taints hallucinatory impressions. But it must be remembered that all the efforts of Mr. Wace to see any similar clarity in the faint opalescence of the crystal were wholly unsuccessful, try as he would. The difference in intensity of the impressions received by the two men was very great, and it is quite conceivable that what was a view to Mr. Cave was a mere blurred nebulosity to Mr. Wace.

===Chinese===
在此，要把凯夫先生此后的发现一一经历的各个阶段都罗列出来，既冗长又无必要。只需说明效果是这样：从与入射光线大约成 137 度角的方向往水晶里窥视，就能看到一幅清晰、连贯的画面，是一片辽阔而奇特的乡野。这画面毫无梦境之感：它给人一种明确的真实感，光线越好，它便越显得真实、实在。它是一幅会动的画面：也就是说，画面里有些东西在动，但动作缓慢、井然有序，一如真实之物；而随着光线与视线方向的改变，画面也随之改变。这感觉，想必就像透过一块椭圆形的玻璃观看一处风景，并转动这块玻璃以查看不同的角度一样。

韦斯先生向我保证，凯夫先生的讲述极为详尽具体，完全不像幻觉那般带着情绪化的色彩。但必须记住，韦斯先生无论怎样努力，想在那枚水晶微弱的乳白色光泽里看到同样清晰的画面，都是全然不成功。两人所接收到的印象在强烈程度上相差悬殊，完全可以想见：在凯夫先生看来是一幅景象的东西，在韦斯先生眼里不过是一团模糊的云雾。

===Original===
The view, as Mr. Cave described it, was invariably of an extensive plain, and he seemed always to be looking at it from a considerable height, as if from a tower or a mast. To the east and to the west the plain was bounded at a remote distance by vast reddish cliffs, which reminded him of those he had seen in some picture; but what the picture was Mr. Wace was unable to ascertain. These cliffs passed north and south—he could tell the points of the compass by the stars that were visible of a night—receding in an almost illimitable perspective and fading into the mists of the distance before they met. He was nearer the eastern set of cliffs, on the occasion of his first vision the sun was rising over them, and black against the sunlight and pale against their shadow appeared a multitude of soaring forms that Mr. Cave regarded as birds. A vast range of buildings spread below him; he seemed to be looking down upon them; and, as they approached the blurred and refracted edge of the picture, they became indistinct. There were also trees curious in shape, and in colouring, a deep mossy green and an exquisite grey, beside a wide and shining canal. And something great and brilliantly coloured flew across the picture. But the first time Mr. Cave saw these pictures he saw only in flashes, his hands shook, his head moved, the vision came and went, and grew foggy and indistinct. And at first he had the greatest difficulty in finding the picture again once the direction of it was lost.

===Chinese===
凯夫先生所描述的那幅景象，始终是一片辽阔的平原，而他似乎总是从相当高的地方——仿佛从一座塔或一根桅杆上——俯瞰着它。东西两面，极远处以巨大的赭红色悬崖为界，使他想起在某幅画里见过的类似景象；只是那是哪一幅画，韦斯先生无从查明。这些悬崖南北绵延——夜间凭肉眼可见的星辰，他可以判断出方位——向远处延伸，几乎望不到头，在相接之前便消融在远方的雾气里。他离东边那一列悬崖较近，第一次看见景象时，太阳正从悬崖上方升起；逆着阳光显出黑色、衬着悬崖的阴影显出苍白的，是无数盘旋飞翔的形体，凯夫先生把它们看作鸟。一大片建筑在脚下铺展开来，他似乎正从高处俯瞰它们；待它们接近那幅画面因折射而模糊的边缘时，便渐渐看不真切了。还有一些形状奇特的树，颜色是深苔绿和一种精致的灰色，旁边是一条宽阔、波光粼粼的运河。还有某个硕大、色彩绚烂的东西掠过画面。不过凯夫先生头一次看见这些景象时，只是惊鸿一瞥地看得断断续续：他的手在抖，头在动，那景象时隐时现，越来越模糊不清。起初，一旦弄丢了看景象的角度，要想再把它找回来，他便要费上九牛二虎之力。

===Original===
His next clear vision, which came about a week after the first, the interval having yielded nothing but tantalising glimpses and some useful experience, showed him the view down the length of the valley. The view was different, but he had a curious persuasion, which his subsequent observations abundantly confirmed, that he was regarding this strange world from exactly the same spot, although he was looking in a different direction. The long façade of the great building, whose roof he had looked down upon before, was now receding in perspective. He recognised the roof. In the front of the façade was a terrace of massive proportions and extraordinary length, and down the middle of the terrace, at certain intervals, stood huge but very graceful masts, bearing small shiny objects which reflected the setting sun. The import of these small objects did not occur to Mr. Cave until some time after, as he was describing the scene to Mr. Wace. The terrace overhung a thicket of the most luxuriant and graceful vegetation, and beyond this was a wide grassy lawn on which certain broad creatures, in form like beetles but enormously larger, reposed. Beyond this again was a richly decorated causeway of pinkish stone; and beyond that, and lined with dense *red* weeds, and passing up the valley exactly parallel with the distant cliffs, was a broad and mirror-like expanse of water. The air seemed full of squadrons of great birds, manoeuvring in stately curves; and across the river was a multitude of splendid buildings, richly coloured and glittering with metallic tracery and facets, among a forest of moss-like and lichenous trees. And suddenly something flapped repeatedly across the vision, like the fluttering of a jewelled fan or the beating of a wing, and a face, or rather the upper part of a face with very large eyes, came as it were close to his own and as if on the other side of the crystal. Mr. Cave was so startled and so impressed by the absolute reality of these eyes, that he drew his head back from the crystal to look behind it. He had become so absorbed in watching that he was quite surprised to find himself in the cool darkness of his little shop, with its familiar odour of methyl, mustiness, and decay. And, as he blinked about him, the glowing crystal faded, and went out.

===Chinese===
他第二次看得真切，是在头一次之后大约一个星期——这中间的日子除了几个叫人心痒的惊鸿一瞥和一点儿有用的经验之外，一无所获——这一次，向他展现了沿山谷纵深望去的那片景象。景象不同了，但他有一种奇特的感觉——而这种感觉后来被他的多次观察充分证实——觉得自己是从同一处地方看这个陌生世界的，只不过朝向不同罢了。那座大建筑长长的正面——他先前曾从上往下俯瞰过它的屋顶——此刻正以透视的方式向远处退去。他认出了那屋顶。那座正面的前方，是一条体量厚重、长得惊人的露台；露台中央，按一定间隔立着一根根粗大却极为优雅的桅杆，上面挂着些小小的、闪亮的东西，反射着落日余晖。这些小玩意儿的含义，凯夫先生是许久之后、在向韦斯先生描述这一情景时才恍然意识到的。露台下方是一片葱茏而姿态曼妙的密林；密林之外，是一片宽阔的草地，上面伏着几种宽体的生物，形状像甲虫，却比甲虫大得不可计量。再往外，是一条粉红色石头砌成的、装饰华丽的石板路；那条路之外，则是一片宽阔如镜的水面，两岸长满了密密的红色水草，沿着山谷一路向上，与远处的悬崖完全平行。空中似乎满是成群结队的大鸟，盘旋翱翔，划出庄严的弧线。河对岸，是一片鳞次栉比的壮丽建筑，色彩斑斓，闪耀着金属构件和棱面的光泽，掩映在一片苔藓状、地衣状的林木之中。蓦地，有样东西一次次地扑闪着掠过画面，像一把缀满珠宝的扇子在扇动，又像一只翅膀在拍击；接着，一张脸——准确地说，是一张脸的上半部，生着一双极大的眼睛——仿佛凑到了他眼前，像是隔着一层水晶在另一边看着他。这两只眼睛的真实感是如此之强，凯夫先生又是如此震撼，以至于他猛地把头从水晶前挪开，朝它后面看了一眼。他看得太过出神，待回过神来，发现自己竟还在那间阴凉幽暗的小铺子里，四周是熟悉的甲醇、霉味和朽腐的气息，不禁大为诧异。他眨巴着眼睛四下张望，发光的水晶便暗了下去，熄灭了。

===Original===
Such were the first general impressions of Mr. Cave. The story is curiously direct and circumstantial. From the outset, when the valley first flashed momentarily on his senses, his imagination was strangely affected, and, as he began to appreciate the details of the scene he saw, his wonder rose to the point of a passion. He went about his business listless and distraught, thinking only of the time when he should be able to return to his watching. And then a few weeks after his first sight of the valley came the two customers, the stress and excitement of their offer, and the narrow escape of the crystal from sale, as I have already told.

===Chinese===
这些便是凯夫先生最初的总体印象。他的讲述出奇地直接、详尽。从那山谷头一次在他感官上一闪而过的那一刻起，他的想象力便受到了一种奇异的触动，而随着他开始留意所见图景的种种细节，他的惊异也一路升腾，直至化为一种近乎狂热的激情。他料理生意时无精打采、神不守舍，心里只想着能再回去守着那枚水晶观看的时刻。就在他初次得见那山谷的几个星期之后，便来了那两位顾客，有了他们那番报价的紧张与激动，以及那枚水晶险些被卖出去的惊险一幕——这些我已经讲过了。

===Original===
Now, while the thing was Mr. Cave's secret, it remained a mere wonder, a thing to creep to covertly and peep at, as a child might peep upon a forbidden garden. But Mr. Wace has, for a young scientific investigator, a particularly lucid and consecutive habit of mind.
