Directly the crystal and its story came to him, and he had satisfied himself, by seeing the phosphorescence with his own eyes, that there really was a certain evidence for Mr. Cave's statements, he proceeded to develop the matter systematically. Mr. Cave was only too eager to come and feast his eyes on this wonderland he saw, and he came every night from half-past eight until half-past ten, and sometimes, in Mr. Wace's absence, during the day. On Sunday afternoons, also, he came. From the outset Mr. Wace made copious notes, and it was due to his scientific method that the relation between the direction from which the initiating ray entered the crystal and the orientation of the picture were proved. And, by covering the crystal in a box perforated only with a small aperture to admit the exciting ray, and by substituting black holland for his buff blinds, he greatly improved the conditions of the observations; so that in a little while they were able to survey the valley in any direction they desired.

So having cleared the way, we may give a brief account of this visionary world within the crystal. The things were in all cases seen by Mr. Cave, and the method of working was invariably for him to watch the crystal and report what he saw, while Mr. Wace (who as a science student had learnt the trick of writing in the dark) wrote a brief note of his report. When the crystal faded, it was put into its box in the proper position and the electric light turned on. Mr. Wace asked questions, and suggested observations to clear up difficult points. Nothing, indeed, could have been less visionary and more matter-of-fact.

===Chinese===
这件秘密还只属于凯夫先生一人时，它不过是一桩奇事，一件要偷偷摸摸凑过去窥探的东西，正如一个孩子会偷偷窥视一座不许他进去的花园。但韦斯先生作为一名年轻的科研工作者，思路格外清晰而条理分明。那枚水晶及其故事一到了他手里，他便亲眼看过了那磷光（phosphorescence），确信凯夫先生的讲述确实有一定证据，于是开始系统地展开这件事的探究。凯夫先生巴不得能来看他这个奇境，让自己大饱眼福，于是每晚八点半到十点半都来，有时趁韦斯先生不在，白天也来。星期天下午他也来。韦斯先生从一开始便做了大量笔记，也多亏了他的科学方法，入射光线进入水晶的方向与画面朝向之间的关系才得以证实。进而，他把水晶罩在一个只开了小孔以引进入射光的盒子里，又用黑色荷兰亚麻布换下了原来的浅黄色窗帘，大大改善了观测条件；不久，他们便能随心所欲地从任何方向俯瞰那片山谷了。

铺平了路之后，我们便可以简略地讲一讲这枚水晶里那个幻象世界了。这些景象一概是凯夫先生看见的，他们的工作方式始终如一：由他盯着水晶报告所见，韦斯先生——身为理科学生，他学过摸黑写字的窍门——则把他的报告简要记下来。水晶变暗时，便按正确的角度放回盒子里，然后打开电灯。韦斯先生提出问题，并建议他做一些观察以澄清疑难之处。事实上，整个过程一点都不玄乎，简直再实在不过了。

===Original===
The attention of Mr. Cave had been speedily directed to the birdlike creatures he had seen so abundantly present in each of his earlier visions. His first impression was soon corrected, and he considered for a time that they might represent a diurnal species of bat. Then he thought, grotesquely enough, that they might be cherubs. Their heads were round, and curiously human, and it was the eyes of one of them that had so startled him on his second observation. They had broad, silvery wings, not feathered, but glistening almost as brilliantly as new-killed fish and with the same subtle play of colour, and these wings were not built on the plan of bird-wing or bat, Mr. Wace learned, but supported by curved ribs radiating from the body. (A sort of butterfly wing with curved ribs seems best to express their appearance.) The body was small, but fitted with two bunches of prehensile organs, like long tentacles, immediately under the mouth. Incredible as it appeared to Mr. Wace, the persuasion at last became irresistible, that it was these creatures which owned the great quasi-human buildings and the magnificent garden that made the broad valley so splendid. And Mr. Cave perceived that the buildings, with other peculiarities, had no doors, but that the great circular windows, which opened freely, gave the creatures egress and entrance. They would alight upon their tentacles, fold their wings to a smallness almost rod-like, and hop into the interior. But among them was a multitude of smaller-winged creatures, like great dragonflies and moths and flying beetles, and across the greensward brilliantly-coloured gigantic ground-beetles crawled lazily to and fro. Moreover, on the causeways and terraces, large-headed creatures similar to the greater winged flies, but wingless, were visible, hopping busily upon their hand-like tangle of tentacles.

===Chinese===
凯夫先生的注意力很快便被他先前在每次幻象中都大量见到的那些似鸟生物吸引了过去。他最初的印象很快就被纠正了，曾一度以为它们也许是某种昼行性的蝙蝠。后来他竟然古怪地想到，它们也许是某种小天使。它们的脑袋圆圆的，出奇地像人，第二次观察时令他大吃一惊的，正是其中一只的眼睛。它们长着宽阔的银色翅膀，没有羽毛，却像刚死的鱼一样闪着近乎耀眼的光泽，带着同样微妙的色彩变幻；韦斯先生得知，这种翅膀并非按照鸟翼或蝙蝠翼的构造，而是由从身体辐射而出的弯曲翼肋所支撑。（一种带弯曲翼肋的蝴蝶式翅膀，似乎最能描摹它们的样子。）它们的身体很小，但嘴的正下方长着两束能抓握的器官，像长长的触手。尽管在韦斯先生看来难以置信，但最终有一种信念变得无法抗拒：正是这些生物拥有那些庞大的、近似人类的建筑和那片使整片宽阔山谷熠熠生辉的瑰丽花园。凯夫先生还察觉到，这些建筑有一个奇特之处：它们没有门，但那些可以自由开合的巨大圆形窗户，便是这些生物出入的通道。它们会先用触手着陆，把翅膀收得几乎像一根棍子那么细，然后跳进去。但它们之间，还有许多翅膀较小的生物，像巨大的蜻蜓、飞蛾和会飞的甲虫；而碧绿的草地上，色彩艳丽的巨型步行虫懒洋洋地爬来爬去。此外，在石板路和露台上，还能看见一些脑袋硕大的生物，样子像那些较大的有翅飞虫，却没有翅膀，正用它们那像手一样缠成一团的触手忙碌地跳来跳去。

===Original===
Allusion has already been made to the glittering objects upon masts that stood upon the terrace of the nearer building. It dawned upon Mr. Cave, after regarding one of these masts very fixedly on one particularly vivid day, that the glittering object there was a crystal exactly like that into which he peered. And a still more careful scrutiny convinced him that each one in a vista of nearly twenty carried a similar object.

Occasionally one of the large flying creatures would flutter up to one, and, folding its wings and coiling a number of its tentacles about the mast, would regard the crystal fixedly for a space—sometimes for as long as fifteen minutes. And a series of observations, made at the suggestion of Mr. Wace, convinced both watchers that, so far as this visionary world was concerned, the crystal into which they peered actually stood at the summit of the endmost mast on the terrace, and that on one occasion at least one of these inhabitants of this other world had looked into Mr. Cave's face while he was making these observations.

===Chinese===
前面已经提到过，那座较近建筑物的露台上，桅杆顶端挂着一些闪闪发亮的东西。某一日景象格外清晰，凯夫先生久久凝视其中一根桅杆，忽然领悟到：那上面闪闪发亮的东西，竟是一枚水晶，与他正往里窥视的这枚一模一样。进而更仔细地审视一番后，他确信，在他望过去所见的近二十根桅杆上，每一根都挂着同样的东西。

偶尔，那些会飞的大生物中会有一只扑棱着翅膀飞到一根桅杆前，收拢翅膀，用几根触手攀住桅杆，一动不动地盯着那枚水晶看上去——有时一看就是十五分钟之久。而在韦斯先生建议下进行的一系列观察，使两位观看者都确信：就这个幻象世界而言，他们正往里窥视的这枚水晶，实际上就立在那条露台最末端一根桅杆的顶端；而且至少有那么一次，这个另一世界的居民之一，在凯夫先生进行这些观察时，也正看着凯夫先生的脸。

===Original===
So much for the essential facts of this very singular story. Unless we dismiss it all as the ingenious fabrication of Mr. Wace, we have to believe one of two things: either that Mr. Cave's crystal was in two worlds at once, and that, while it was carried about in one, it remained stationary in the other, which seems altogether absurd; or else that it had some peculiar relation of sympathy with another and exactly similar crystal in this other world, so that what was seen in the interior of the one in this world was, under suitable conditions, visible to an observer in the corresponding crystal in the other world; and vice versa. At present, indeed, we do not know of any way in which two crystals could so come *en rapport*, but nowadays we know enough to understand that the thing is not altogether impossible. This view of the crystals as *en rapport* was the supposition that occurred to Mr. Wace, and to me at least it seems extremely plausible.

And where was this other world? On this, also, the alert intelligence of Mr. Wace speedily threw light. After sunset, the sky darkened rapidly—there was a very brief twilight interval indeed—and the stars shone out. They were recognisably the same as those we see, arranged in the same constellations. Mr. Cave recognised the Bear, the Pleiades, Aldebaran, and Sirius: so that the other world must be somewhere in the solar system, and, at the utmost, only a few hundreds of millions of miles from our own. Following up this clue, Mr. Wace learned that the midnight sky was a darker blue even than our midwinter sky, and that the sun seemed a little smaller. *And there were two small moons!* "like our moon but smaller, and quite differently marked" one of which moved so rapidly that its motion was clearly visible as one regarded it. These moons were never high in the sky, but vanished as they rose: that is, every time they revolved they were eclipsed because they were so near their primary planet. And all this answers quite completely, although Mr. Cave did not know it, to what must be the condition of things on Mars.

===Chinese===
这桩离奇故事的基本事实，便到此为止。除非我们把这一切统统当作韦斯先生精心编造的谎话，否则我们就得相信二者之一：要么是凯夫先生那枚水晶同时存在于两个世界，在一个世界里被搬来搬去，而在另一个世界里却纹丝不动——这看起来简直荒谬；要么是它与另一个世界里的另一枚完全相同的水晶之间，存在着某种奇特的心灵感应般的关系，于是在这个世界里这枚水晶内部所看见的景象，在适当条件下，便能被另一个世界里那枚相应水晶前的观察者所看见，反之亦然。诚然，眼下我们并不知道两枚水晶如何才能达成这种心灵相通（en rapport），但如今我们已懂得不少，足以理解这件事并非完全不可能。把两枚水晶看作心灵相通，正是韦斯先生所想到的假设，而在我看来——至少——它似乎是极有道理的。

那么，这个另一个世界又在哪里呢？对于这一点，韦斯先生敏锐的头脑也很快就给出了线索。日落之后，天色迅速暗下来——暮色时分的确非常短暂——繁星便开始闪耀。这些星子可以辨认出来，与我们平日所见并无二致，排列成同样的星座。凯夫先生认出了大熊座（the Bear）、昴宿星团（the Pleiades）、毕宿五（Aldebaran）和天狼星（Sirius）：可见那个另一个世界必在某处太阳系内，至多离我们这个世界不过几亿英里。顺此线索追查下去，韦斯先生得知，那里的子夜天空是比我们隆冬的天空还要深的蓝色，而太阳似乎也比我们的要小一些。而且，那里还有两颗小月亮！"像我们的月亮，但更小，表面的斑纹也全然不同"——其中一颗运行得极快，凝视之下能明显看出它在移动。这两颗月亮从不会升得很高，而是一升起来便消失：也就是说，它们每转一圈就会被所围绕的主星遮蔽，因为它们离主星太近了。而这一切，尽管凯夫先生并不知情，却与火星（Mars）上的状况完全吻合。

===Original===
Indeed, it seems an exceedingly plausible conclusion that peering into this crystal Mr. Cave did actually see the planet Mars and its inhabitants. And, if that be the case, then the evening star that shone so brilliantly in the sky of that distant vision, was neither more nor less than our own familiar Earth.

For a time the Martians—if they were Martians—do not seem to have known of Mr. Cave's inspection. Once or twice one would come to peer, and go away very shortly to some other mast, as though the vision was unsatisfactory. During this time Mr. Cave was able to watch the proceedings of these winged people without being disturbed by their attentions, and, although his report is necessarily vague and fragmentary, it is nevertheless very suggestive. Imagine the impression of humanity a Martian observer would get who, after a difficult process of preparation and with considerable fatigue to the eyes, was able to peer at London from the steeple of St. Martin's Church for stretches, at longest, of four minutes at a time. Mr. Cave was unable to ascertain if the winged Martians were the same as the Martians who hopped about the causeways and terraces, and if the latter could put on wings at will. He several times saw certain clumsy bipeds, dimly suggestive of apes, white and partially translucent, feeding among certain of the lichenous trees, and once some of these fled before one of the hopping, round-headed Martians. The latter caught one in its tentacles, and then the picture faded suddenly and left Mr. Cave most tantalisingly in the dark. On another occasion a vast thing, that Mr. Cave thought at first was some gigantic insect, appeared advancing along the causeway beside the canal with extraordinary rapidity. As this drew nearer Mr. Cave perceived that it was a mechanism of shining metals and of extraordinary complexity. And then, when he looked again, it had passed out of sight.

===Chinese===
的确，凯夫先生往这枚水晶里窥视时所看见的，实际上就是火星和它的居民——这个结论看来极其可信。倘若果真如此，那么那幅遥远景象的天空中闪耀得如此明亮的昏星，不是别的，正是我们所熟悉的地球。

有一段时间，那些火星人（Martians）——如果他们确是火星人的话——似乎并不知道凯夫先生在对他们窥探。他们偶尔会有一两个过来察看，但很快又飞到别的桅杆上去，仿佛所见的景象并不令人满意。在这段时间里，凯夫先生得以观察这些有翅族类的种种活动而不被他们的注意所打扰，尽管他的讲述不免零碎、片段，却仍极富启发性。不妨设想一下：一位火星观察者，经过一番繁复的准备、并为此弄得两眼酸痛之后，方能从圣马丁教堂（St. Martin's Church）的尖塔上，一次至多连续四分钟地窥视伦敦——他对人类会留下怎样的印象。凯夫先生无法查明，那些有翅的火星人与那些在石板路和露台上蹦来蹦去的火星人是否同一种，后者是否能随意安上翅膀。他曾数次看见一些笨拙的两足生物，隐约像猿猴，浑身白色、半透明，在某些地衣状的树木间觅食；有一次，其中几只正被一只蹦跳着、圆脑袋的火星人吓得四散奔逃。后者用触手逮住了其中一只——就在这时，画面骤然消失，让凯夫先生落到了最令人心痒难耐的一片漆黑里。另一次，凯夫先生看到一个庞然大物，起初以为是什么巨型昆虫，正沿着运河旁的石板路以惊人的速度驶来。待它再近一些，凯夫先生看出那是一件由闪闪发光的金属构成的机械，结构异常复杂。然后，待他再看时，它已驶出了视野。

===Original===
After a time Mr. Wace aspired to attract the attention of the Martians, and the next time that the strange eyes of one of them appeared close to the crystal Mr. Cave cried out and sprang away, and they immediately turned on the light and began to gesticulate in a manner suggestive of signalling. But when at last Mr. Cave examined the crystal again the Martian had departed.

Thus far these observations had progressed in early November, and then Mr. Cave, feeling that the suspicions of his family about the crystal were allayed, began to take it to and fro with him in order that, as occasion arose in the daytime or night, he might comfort himself with what was fast becoming the most real thing in his existence.

===Chinese===
过了一阵，韦斯先生动了吸引火星人注意的念头。下一次，当其中一双奇怪的眼睛凑近水晶时，凯夫先生大喊一声，跳开了；他们随即打开了灯，并打起手势，那样子像是在发信号。可等凯夫先生再去看水晶时，那位火星人已经走了。

到十一月初，他们的观察已推进到此。这时，凯夫先生感到家人对那枚水晶的疑心已经平息，便开始随身带着它来来去去，好让自己无论白天黑夜，只要一有空，便能沉浸于这件正迅速成为他生命中最真实的东西之中，聊以自慰。

===Original===
In December Mr. Wace's work in connection with a forthcoming examination became heavy, the sittings were reluctantly suspended for a week, and for ten or eleven days—he is not quite sure which—he saw nothing of Cave. He then grew anxious to resume these investigations, and, the stress of his seasonal labours being abated, he went down to Seven Dials. At the corner he noticed a shutter before a bird fancier's window, and then another at a cobbler's. Mr. Cave's shop was closed.

He rapped and the door was opened by the stepson in black. He at once called Mrs. Cave, who was, Mr. Wace could not but observe, in cheap but ample widow's weeds of the most imposing pattern. Without any very great surprise Mr. Wace learnt that Cave was dead and already buried. She was in tears, and her voice was a little thick. She had just returned from Highgate. Her mind seemed occupied with her own prospects and the honourable details of the obsequies, but Mr. Wace was at last able to learn the particulars of Cave's death. He had been found dead in his shop in the early morning, the day after his last visit to Mr. Wace, and the crystal had been clasped in his stone-cold hands. His face was smiling, said Mrs. Cave, and the velvet cloth from the minerals lay on the floor at his feet. He must have been dead five or six hours when he was found.

===Chinese===
十二月，韦斯先生因一场即将到来的考试所牵连的事务变得繁重起来，他们很不情愿地把观察停了一个星期；足足有十到十一天——他记不太清究竟几天——他都没见到凯夫。随后他急着想恢复这番探究，待到这阵季节性工作的紧张稍稍缓解，他便动身去了七晷区。他在街角注意到一家鸟贩的橱窗前已装上了窗板，接着又看见一家鞋匠铺也是这样。凯夫先生的铺子关着门。

他叩了叩门，开门的是那个继子，一身黑衣。继子立刻叫来了凯夫太太——韦斯先生不能不注意到，她身上那套孝服虽说不贵，却十分宽大、式样颇为惹眼。韦斯先生得知凯夫已经去世、并且已经下葬，倒也没有太大的惊讶。她眼泪汪汪的，声音有些含混。她刚从海格特（Highgate）回来。她的心思似乎都放在了自己今后的前程和葬礼上那些体面的细节上，不过韦斯先生最终还是问清了凯夫去世的始末。那是他最后一次到韦斯先生处之后的第二天清晨，他被发现死在了自己的铺子里，那枚水晶就攥在他冰冷僵硬的双手里。凯夫太太说，他脸上带着微笑，那块原本垫矿石用的天鹅绒布就落在他脚边的地上。被发现时，他大约已死了五六个钟头。

===Original===
This came as a great shock to Wace, and he began to reproach himself bitterly for having neglected the plain symptoms of the old man's ill-health. But his chief thought was of the crystal. He approached that topic in a gingerly manner, because he knew Mrs. Cave's peculiarities. He was dumbfounded to learn that it was sold.

Mrs. Cave's first impulse, directly Cave's body had been taken upstairs, had been to write to the mad clergyman who had offered five pounds for the crystal, informing him of its recovery; but after a violent hunt in which her daughter joined her, they were convinced of the loss of his address. As they were without the means required to mourn and bury Cave in the elaborate style the dignity of an old Seven Dials inhabitant demands, they had appealed to a friendly fellow-tradesman in Great Portland Street. He had very kindly taken over a portion of the stock at a valuation. The valuation was his own and the crystal egg was included in one of the lots. Mr. Wace, after a few suitable consolatory observations, a little offhandedly proffered perhaps, hurried at once to Great Portland Street. But there he learned that the crystal egg had already been sold to a tall, dark man in grey. And there the material facts in this curious, and to me at least very suggestive, story come abruptly to an end. The Great Portland Street dealer did not know who the tall dark man in grey was, nor had he observed him with sufficient attention to describe him minutely. He did not even know which way this person had gone after leaving the shop. For a time Mr. Wace remained in the shop, trying the dealer's patience with hopeless questions, venting his own exasperation. And at last, realising abruptly that the whole thing had passed out of his hands, had vanished like a vision of the night, he returned to his own rooms, a little astonished to find the notes he had made still tangible and visible upon his untidy table.

===Chinese===
这个消息对韦斯先生犹如晴天霹雳，他开始痛悔自己忽视了老人健康状况明显不妙的种种征兆。但他最主要的念头，还在那枚水晶上。他小心翼翼地触及这个话题，因为他深知凯夫太太的脾性。得知它已被卖掉，他目瞪口呆。

凯夫的尸体一被抬上楼，凯夫太太头一个念头便是写信给那位愿出五英镑买水晶的"疯牧师"，告诉他水晶失而复得；可她和女儿翻箱倒柜大找一通之后，才确信地址已不知去向。她们手头拮据，无法按一位七晷区老住户的体面所要求的那种铺张来举哀、安葬凯夫，便求助于大波特兰街（Great Portland Street）一位同行的情谊。那位同行很爽快地作价盘下了一部分存货。作价由他说了算，而那枚水晶蛋也被归在其中一批货里了。韦斯先生说了几句得体的安慰话——也许稍显敷衍——便急忙赶往大波特兰街。可到了那里，他才得知那枚水晶蛋已经卖给了一个高个子、肤色黝黑的灰衣男子。这桩离奇——至少在我看来意味深长——的故事，其物质层面的事实便到此戛然而止。大波特兰街那位商人不知道那个高个子、肤色黝黑的灰衣男子是谁，也未曾把人家看得仔细到足以描摹其细貌的地步。他甚至不知道此人离开铺子后朝哪个方向走了。韦斯先生在铺子里耽了一阵子，用一连串无望的问题磨着那位商人的耐心，也借机宣泄自己的懊恼。最后，他猛然意识到，整件事已从自己手中溜走，像夜里的幻影一样无影无踪了，便返回了自己的住处——看到自己记下的那些笔记仍凌乱地摊在桌上、看得见摸得着，倒不免有些诧异。

===Original===
His annoyance and disappointment were naturally very great. He made a second call (equally ineffectual) upon the Great Portland Street dealer, and he resorted to advertisements in such periodicals as were likely to come into the hands of a bric-a-brac collector. He also wrote letters to *The Daily Chronicle* and *Nature*, but both those periodicals, suspecting a hoax, asked him to reconsider his action before they printed, and he was advised that such a strange story, unfortunately so bare of supporting evidence, might imperil his reputation as an investigator. Moreover, the calls of his proper work were urgent. So that after a month or so, save for an occasional reminder to certain dealers, he had reluctantly to abandon the quest for the crystal egg, and from that day to this it remains undiscovered. Occasionally, however, he tells me, and I can quite believe him, he has bursts of zeal, in which he abandons his more urgent occupation and resumes the search.

Whether or not it will remain lost forever, with the material and origin of it, are things equally speculative at the present time. If the present purchaser is a collector, one would have expected the enquiries of Mr. Wace to have reached him through the dealers. He has been able to discover Mr. Cave's clergyman and "Oriental"—no other than the Rev. James Parker and the young Prince of Bosso-Kuni in Java. I am obliged to them for certain particulars. The object of the Prince was simply curiosity—and extravagance. He was so eager to buy, because Cave was so oddly reluctant to sell. It is just as possible that the buyer in the second instance was simply a casual purchaser and not a collector at all, and the crystal egg, for all I know, may at the present moment be within a mile of me, decorating a drawing-room or serving as a paperweight—its remarkable functions all unknown. Indeed, it is partly with the idea of such a possibility that I have thrown this narrative into a form that will give it a chance of being read by the ordinary consumer of fiction.

===Chinese===
他的懊恼与失望自然极大。他又去了大波特兰街那位商人那里一趟（同样无济于事），并在一些有可能到古玩收藏者手中的刊物上刊登了广告。他还给《每日纪事报》（The Daily Chronicle）和《自然》（Nature）写了信，但两家刊物都怀疑这是一场恶作剧，请他在刊发之前三思；并且有人劝他，这样一则离奇的故事又不幸缺乏佐证，恐会危及他身为研究者的名声。况且他本职工作的催迫也很紧要。于是，大约一个月之后，除了偶尔向几位商人提个醒之外，他不得不无可奈何地放弃了对这枚水晶蛋的追寻；从那时至今，它依旧下落不明。不过他告诉我——我也完全相信他——他偶尔还会一阵心血来潮，撂下手中更要紧的事务，重新展开寻找。

它是否会永远遗失，连同它的来历与材质如何，眼下都同样是悬案。倘若现在这位买主是一位收藏家，那么韦斯先生的打听想必早已通过商人们传到他那里了。韦斯先生倒是已经查出了凯夫先生那位牧师和"东方人"的身份——不是别人，正是詹姆斯·帕克牧师（the Rev. James Parker）和爪哇博索-库尼族年轻的王子（the young Prince of Bosso-Kuni in Java）。我从前二位那里得到了一些具体情况，在此谨致谢意。这位王子的动机无非是好奇——外加挥霍。凯夫越是古怪地不肯卖，他便越是要买。同样有可能的是，第二位买主不过是一位随手的顾客，压根儿就不是什么收藏家；这枚水晶蛋，据我所知，眼下说不定就在离我一英里之内，正装饰着某家的客厅，或者干脆被当作镇纸——它那些非同寻常的功能，全无人知晓。事实上，我之所以把这段故事整理成这样一种形式，让它有机会被读小说的寻常读者读到，某种程度上也正是出于对这种可能性的考虑。

===Original===
My own ideas in the matter are practically identical with those of Mr. Wace. I believe the crystal on the mast in Mars and the crystal egg of Mr. Cave's to be in some physical, but at present quite inexplicable, way *en rapport*, and we both believe further that the terrestrial crystal must have been—possibly at some remote date—sent hither from that planet, in order to give the Martians a near view of our affairs. Possibly the fellows to the crystals in the other masts are also on our globe. No theory of hallucination suffices for the facts.

===Chinese===
对此事，我自己的想法与韦斯先生几乎一致。我相信火星上那根桅杆上的水晶，与凯夫先生那枚水晶蛋，正以某种物理的、眼下完全无法解释的方式相通着；我们俩还进一步相信，地球上的这枚水晶必是——也许在某个遥远的年代——由那颗行星送到此处来的，好让火星人近距离地察看我们这边的事务。其他那些桅杆上水晶的同伴，说不定也都在我们这颗星球上。任何幻觉之说都解释不了这些事实。

## The Diamond Maker / 钻石制造者

===Original===
Some business had detained me in Chancery Lane nine in the evening, and thereafter, having some inkling of a headache, I was disinclined either for entertainment or further work. So much of the sky as the high cliffs of that narrow canon of traffic left visible spoke of a serene night, and I determined to make my way down to the Embankment, and rest my eyes and cool my head by watching the variegated lights upon the river. Beyond comparison the night is the best time for this place; a merciful darkness hides the dirt of the waters, and the lights of this transitional age, red glaring orange, gas-yellow, and electric white, are set in shadowy outlines of every possible shade between grey and deep purple. Through the arches of Waterloo Bridge a hundred points of light mark the sweep of the Embankment, and above its parapet rise the towers of Westminster, warm grey against the starlight. The black river goes by with only a rare ripple breaking its silence, and disturbing the reflections of the lights that swim upon its surface.

===Chinese===
晚上九点，有些事务把我在大法官巷（Chancery Lane）耽搁了下来，之后我又微微觉得有些头痛，便既无心消遣，也无心再做事。那一条狭窄如峡谷的车道两侧高楼林立，只在楼顶之间漏出一线天空，预示着一个宁静的夜晚，我便决定一路走到河滨大道（the Embankment），凭栏看河面上那五彩缤纷的灯火，让眼睛歇一歇，让头脑清凉清凉。毫无疑问，夜晚才是赏玩此地最好的时辰：仁慈的夜色将河水里的肮脏藏了起来；这个过渡时代的种种灯火——红得刺目的橙色、煤气灯的黄、电灯的白——嵌在由浅灰到深紫之间各种色调的朦胧轮廓里。透过滑铁卢桥（Waterloo Bridge）的桥洞，可以看见一百点亮光标出河滨大道蜿蜒的走向；在桥的栏墙之上，则耸起威斯敏斯特（Westminster）的诸多塔楼，在星光映衬下呈现出温暖的灰色。黑色的河水静静流过，偶尔一两道涟漪打破它的沉寂，搅动了浮在水面上的那些灯火的倒影。

===Original===
“A warm night,” said a voice at my side.

I turned my head, and saw the profile of a man who was leaning over the parapet beside me. It was a refined face, not unhandsome, though pinched and pale enough, and the coat collar turned up and pinned round the throat marked his status in life as sharply as a uniform. I felt I was committed to the price of a bed and breakfast if I answered him.

I looked at him curiously. Would he have anything to tell me worth the money, or was he the common incapable—incapable even of telling his own story? There was a quality of intelligence in his forehead and eyes, and a certain tremulousness in his nether lip that decided me.

“Very warm,” said I; “but not too warm for us here.”

“No,” he said, still looking across the water, “it is pleasant enough here… just now.”

===Chinese===
“今晚真暖和，”身旁一个声音说。

我转过头，看见一个男子正俯身在旁边的栏墙上。他的侧面轮廓相当清秀，说不上难看，只是清瘦苍白得很；他把外衣领子竖起来，用别针别在脖颈周围，这一身装束就像制服一样，把他在世上的身份标得清清楚楚。我明白，只要我一搭腔，便等于许诺了供他一夜宿食的那点花销。

我好奇地打量着他。他能讲出什么值得一听、对得起这笔开销的事来吗？还是说，他不过是个寻常的无能之辈——连自己的来历都说不周全？然而他的额头和眼睛里透着几分聪慧，下唇微微颤动，倒叫我下了决心。

“是挺暖和的，”我说，“不过咱们待在这儿倒还不至于太热。”

“是啊，”他说，眼睛仍望着对岸，“这儿确实挺惬意……眼下这一刻。”

===Original===
“It is good,” he continued after a pause, “to find anything so restful as this in London. After one has been fretting about business all day, about getting on, meeting obligations, and parrying dangers, I do not know what one would do if it were not for such pacific corners.” He spoke with long pauses between the sentences. “You must know a little of the irksome labour of the world, or you would not be here. But I doubt if you can be so brain-weary and footsore as I am… Bah! Sometimes I doubt if the game is worth the candle. I feel inclined to throw the whole thing over—name, wealth and position—and take to some modest trade. But I know if I abandoned my ambition—hardly as she uses me—I should have nothing but remorse left for the rest of my days.”

He became silent. I looked at him in astonishment. If ever I saw a man hopelessly hard-up it was the man in front of me. He was ragged and he was dirty, unshaven and unkempt; he looked as though he had been left in a dustbin for a week. And he was talking to *me* of the irksome worries of a large business. I almost laughed outright. Either he was mad or playing a sorry jest on his own poverty.

“If high aims and high positions,” said I, “have their drawbacks of hard work and anxiety, they have their compensations. Influence, the power of doing good, of assisting those weaker and poorer than ourselves; and there is even a certain gratification in display…”

My banter under the circumstances was in very vile taste. I spoke on the spur of the contrast of his appearance and speech. I was sorry even while I was speaking.

He turned a haggard but very composed face upon me. Said he: “I forgot myself. Of course you would not understand.”

===Chinese===
“在伦敦，”停了一会儿他又接着说，“竟能找到这样一处可以歇息的地方，实在难得。一个人整天为生意操劳，为出人头地奔走，为履行种种义务、应付种种风险而殚精竭虑，要是没有这样一些宁静的角落，我真不知该怎样活下去才好。”他说话时，每两句之间都有长长的停顿。“您想必也尝过一点这世上令人厌倦的劳碌吧，否则就不会到这儿来了。不过，您怕是不至于像我这样头脑疲惫、双脚酸软吧……呸！有时候我甚至怀疑这事到底值不值得这样操劳。我真想把这副担子全抛了——名声也好，财富也好，地位也好——转而去干一门稳稳当当的小营生。可我又明白，若是我抛弃了我的抱负——尽管她对我何其苛刻——我后半生便只剩下悔恨了。”

他住了口。我惊讶地望着他。要说我见过谁穷得走投无路，那便是眼前这位了。他衣衫褴褛，浑身肮脏，胡子拉碴，蓬头垢面；看上去仿佛被人扔进垃圾箱里搁了一个礼拜。可他居然跟我谈什么大买卖的种种烦忧。我差点儿笑出声来。他要么是个疯子，要么是在拿自己的穷困开一个可悲的玩笑。

“要是高远的目标和显赫的地位，”我说，“也有辛苦操劳和忧虑焦心的一面，那它们自然也有补偿。权势，做好事的能耐，扶助那些比我们弱小、比我们贫穷的人的能力；甚至炫耀本身也有几分满足感……”

这种场合下我那番调侃实在俗不可耐。我不过是见他的外表与谈吐反差太大，一时脱口而出。话一出口我便懊悔了。

他把一张憔悴却异常镇定的脸转向我。他说：“我失态了。您当然不会理解。”

===Original===
He measured me for a moment. “No doubt it is very absurd. You will not believe me even when I tell you, so that it is fairly safe to tell you. And it will be a comfort to tell someone. I really have a big business in hand, a very big business. But there are troubles just now. The fact is… I make diamonds.”

“I suppose,” said I, “you are out of work just at present?”

“I am sick of being disbelieved,” he said impatiently, and suddenly unbuttoning his wretched coat he pulled out a little canvas bag that was hanging by a cord round his neck. From this he produced a brown pebble. “I wonder if you know enough to know what that is?” He handed it to me.

Now, a year or so ago, I had occupied my leisure in taking a London science degree, so that I have a smattering of physics and mineralogy. The thing was not unlike an uncut diamond of the darker sort, though far too large, being almost as big as the top of my thumb. I took it, and saw it had the form of a regular octahedron, with the curved faces peculiar to the most precious of minerals. I took out my penknife and tried to scratch it—vainly. Leaning forward towards the gas-lamp, I tried the thing on my watch-glass, and scored a white line across that with the greatest ease.

===Chinese===
他打量了我片刻。“毫无疑问，这事听起来荒唐之极。我说出来您也不会相信，所以告诉您倒也颇为安全。能把这事告诉一个人，于我也算一种宽慰。我手里确实在做一桩大买卖，一桩极大的买卖。只是眼下有些麻烦。事情是这样的……我是造钻石的。”

“我想，”我说，“您眼下大概是失业了吧？”

“我受够了别人不信我那一套，”他不耐烦地说，一边突然解开那件破旧的外衣，从脖子上用细绳挂着的一只小帆布袋里掏出一样东西。他从中取出一颗褐色的小石子。“不知道您识不识货，认不认得出这是什么东西？”他把它递给了我。

说来凑巧，一年多前我曾利用空闲攻读了一个伦敦大学的理学学位，所以对物理学和矿物学也略知一二。这东西倒是颇像一颗深色的、未经琢磨的钻石，只是个头大得离谱，差不多有我拇指顶那么大。我接过来细看，见它呈规整的八面体，面上略带弧度，正是最珍贵的矿物所特有的那种晶面。我掏出铅笔刀想刻划它——刻不动。我又凑近煤气灯，把它在我的表玻璃上一试，竟轻而易举地在上面划出了一道白痕。

===Original===
I looked at my interlocutor with rising curiosity. “It certainly is rather like a diamond. But, if so, it is a Behemoth of diamonds. Where did you get it?”

“I tell you I made it,” he said. “Give it back to me.”

He replaced it hastily and buttoned his jacket. “I will sell it you for one hundred pounds,” he suddenly whispered eagerly. With that my suspicions returned. The thing might, after all, be merely a lump of that almost equally hard substance, corundum, with an accidental resemblance in shape to the diamond. Or if it was a diamond, how came he by it, and why should he offer it at a hundred pounds?

We looked into one another’s eyes. He seemed eager, but honestly eager. At that moment I believed it was a diamond he was trying to sell. Yet I am a poor man, a hundred pounds would leave a visible gap in my fortunes and no sane man would buy a diamond by gaslight from a ragged tramp on his personal warranty only. Still, a diamond that size conjured up a vision of many thousands of pounds. Then, thought I, such a stone could scarcely exist without being mentioned in every book on gems, and again I called to mind the stories of contraband and light-fingered Kaffirs at the Cape. I put the question of purchase on one side.

“How did you get it?” said I.

“I made it.”

I had heard something of Moissan, but I knew his artificial diamonds were very small. I shook my head.

===Chinese===
我望着我的对话者，好奇心愈发浓重。“它的确很像一颗钻石。可要是真的，那它就是钻石里的庞然大物（Behemoth）了。您是从哪儿弄来的？”

“我告诉您，是我造的，”他说，“还给我吧。”

他急忙把它收好，扣上外套。“我把它卖给您，一百镑，”他突然急切地低声说。这一来，我心中的疑窦又生。这东西说不定不过是一块硬度与之几乎相当的别的物质——刚玉（corundum）——只是形状偶然与钻石相似罢了。又或者它真是钻石，那他又是怎么弄到手的？为什么要以一百镑出手？

我们彼此对视。他神情急切，但那急切看上去却是真诚的。那一刻我也相信他想卖的确实是一颗钻石。可我是个穷汉，一百镑会在我那份家产里留下一道看得见的窟窿，再讲道理的人也不会凭对方一句话作担保，就在煤气灯下从衣衫褴褛的流浪汉手里买下一颗钻石。然而，一颗那种尺寸的钻石意味着几千镑的财富。我又想，这样一颗石头要是真存在，没有一本谈宝石的书会不提到它的；我又想起了好望角（the Cape）那些走私的故事和手脚不干净的卡菲尔人（Kaffirs）。我把买不买的问题暂且搁在一边。

“您怎么得到它的？”我问。

“我造的。”

我曾听过一些关于莫瓦桑（Moissan）的事，但我知道他造的人造钻石极小。我摇了摇头。

===Original===
“You seem to know something of this kind of thing. I will tell you a little about myself. Perhaps then you may think better of the purchase.” He turned round with his back to the river, and put his hands in his pockets. He sighed. “I know you will not believe me.”

“Diamonds,” he began—and as he spoke his voice lost its faint flavour of the tramp and assumed something of the easy tone of an educated man—“are to be made by throwing carbon out of combination in a suitable flux and under a suitable pressure; the carbon crystallises out, not as black-lead or charcoal-powder, but as small diamonds. So much has been known to chemists for years, but no one yet had hit upon exactly the right flux in which to melt up the carbon, or exactly the right pressure for the best results. Consequently the diamonds made by chemists are small and dark, and worthless as jewels. Now I, you know, have given up my life to this problem—given my life to it.

“I began to work at the conditions of diamond making when I was seventeen, and now I am thirty-two. It seemed to me that it might take all the thought and energies of a man for ten years, or twenty years, but, even if it did, the game was still worth the candle. Suppose one to have at last just hit the right trick before the secret got out and diamonds became as common as coal, one might realize millions. Millions!”

===Chinese===
“看来您对这类事情也略知一二。我就把我的事略略跟您说一说吧。说不定听完之后，您对这桩买卖会重新考虑。”他转过身，背对着河，双手插进口袋。他叹了口气。“我知道您不会相信我的。”

“钻石，”他开口道——说话间，他声音里那一丝流浪汉的腔调消褪了下去，换上了一副受过教育的人那种从容的口吻——“是可以这样制造出来的：把碳从它的化合物中分离出来，让它在一合适的熔剂里、在合适的压力下析出；这时碳便结晶析出，不是形成黑铅或木炭粉，而是细小的钻石。这些道理化学家们早已知道多年了，可是至今还没有人恰好找到合适的熔剂来熔化碳，也无人找到恰好合适的压力以取得最佳效果。因此化学家造出的钻石既小又暗，作为宝石一文不值。至于我，您知道，已经把我这一生都搭在这道难题上了——把一辈子都搭上了。

“我十七岁开始研究制造钻石的条件，如今已经三十二岁了。我原想这事或许要耗尽一个人整整十年、甚至二十年的心血与精力，可即便如此，这买卖也还是值得的。设想一个人赶在这秘密泄露出去、钻石变得像煤炭一样司空见惯之前，恰好摸到了那关键的门道，他便能赚到几百万。几百万啊！”

===Original===
He paused and looked for my sympathy. His eyes shone hungrily. “To think,” said he, “that I am on the verge of it all, and here!

“I had,” he proceeded, “about a thousand pounds when I was twenty-one, and this, I thought, eked out by a little teaching, would keep my researches going. A year or two was spent in study, at Berlin chiefly, and then I continued on my own account. The trouble was the secrecy. You see, if once I had let out what I was doing, other men might have been spurred on by my belief in the practicability of the idea; and I do not pretend to be such a genius as to have been sure of coming in first, in the case of a race for the discovery. And you see it was important that if I really meant to make a pile, people should not know it was an artificial process and capable of turning out diamonds by the ton. So I had to work all alone. At first I had a little laboratory, but as my resources began to run out I had to conduct my experiments in a wretched unfurnished room in Kentish Town, where I slept at last on a straw mattress on the floor among all my apparatus. The money simply flowed away. I grudged myself everything except scientific appliances. I tried to keep things going by a little teaching, but I am not a very good teacher, and I have no university degree, nor very much education except in chemistry, and I found I had to give a lot of time and labour for precious little money. But I got nearer and nearer the thing. Three years ago I settled the problem of the composition of the flux, and got near the pressure by putting this flux of mine and a certain carbon composition into a closed-up gun-barrel, filling up with water, sealing tightly, and heating.”

===Chinese===
他顿了顿，似乎在期待我的同情。他的眼睛里闪烁着一种饥渴的光芒。“想一想吧，”他说，“我已经站在这一切的边缘，却落得这般田地！

“我二十一岁的时候，”他接着说，“手里大约有一千镑。我想，这点钱再凑合着教一点书，应能维持我的研究。我先花了一两年工夫学习，主要在柏林（Berlin），之后便独自干了起来。难就难在要保密。您想，一旦我走漏风声，让别人知道我在干什么，别的人就会因我相信这事切实可行而受到鼓舞，争相追赶；我可不敢自命为那样的天才，敢打包票在这场发现的赛跑里头一名冲线。再说，要是我真打算发一笔大财，就不能让人知道这是一种人工方法，能成吨成吨地造出钻石——这一点也很要紧。所以我只能独自苦干。起初我还有一个小小的工作室，可后来钱越来越少，我便只好搬到肯蒂什镇（Kentish Town）一间破旧的无家具的房间里做实验，到末了，我就睡在地板上一张草垫子上，身边堆满了我那些器具。钱简直像流水一样淌了出去。除了科学仪器，我对自己什么都吝啬。我想靠教一点书来勉强维持，可我又不是个好老师，我没有大学学位，除了化学之外也没什么学问，于是我发现得花上大量的时间和劳力，换来的钱却少得可怜。但我却离那门道越来越近了。三年前我解决了熔剂配方的问题；至于压力，我把我的这种熔剂和某种含碳的混合物装进一根封死的枪管里，灌满水，紧紧封住，再加热——靠这个办法，我大致也摸到了所需的压力。”

===Original===
He paused.

“Rather risky,” said I.

“Yes. It burst, and smashed all my windows and a lot of my apparatus; but I got a kind of diamond powder nevertheless. Following out the problem of getting a big pressure upon the molten mixture from which the things were to crystallise, I hit upon some researches of Daubrée’s at the Paris *Laboratorie des Poudres et Salpetres*. He exploded dynamite in a tightly screwed steel cylinder, too strong to burst, and I found he could crush rocks into a muck not unlike the South African bed in which diamonds are found. It was a tremendous strain on my resources, but I got a steel cylinder made for my purpose after his pattern. I put in all my stuff and my explosives, built up a fire in my furnace, put the whole concern in, and—went out for a walk.”

I could not help laughing at his matter-of-fact manner. “Did you not think it would blow up the house? Were there other people in the place?”

“It was in the interest of science,” he said, ultimately. “There was a costermonger family on the floor below, a begging-letter writer in the room behind mine, and two flower-women were upstairs. Perhaps it was a bit thoughtless. But possibly some of them were out.

===Chinese===
他顿了一下。

“相当冒险哪，”我说。

“是啊。它炸了，把我的窗户和我一大堆器具都炸得粉碎；可我还是得到了一种钻石粉末。为了解决从那要析出晶体的熔融混合物身上取得巨大压力的问题，我又钻研起多布雷（Daubrée）在巴黎*火药与硝石实验室*（Laboratorie des Poudres et Salpetres）所做的几项研究。他在一只拧得很紧、坚固得炸不开的钢筒里引爆了达纳炸药，我发现他由此能把岩石研成一种烂泥般的东西，与南非产钻石的那层矿床颇为相像。这对我那点家底来说，是一笔极大的开支，可我还是照着他的路子，请人按我的用途打了一只钢筒。我把所有的材料和炸药都装进去，在炉子里生了火，把这一整套家伙放进去——然后便出门散步去了。”

他这副不动声色的口吻叫我忍不住笑了起来。“您就没想过它会炸掉整座房子？那房子里还住着别人吧？”

“那是为了科学，”他末了说道。“我楼下住着一户卖菜小贩人家，我房间后面那一间住着一个专写乞讨信的，楼上还住着两个卖花女。也许这事是有点欠考虑。不过他们里头说不定有些人正好出门了。”

===Original===
“When I came back the thing was just where I left it, among the white-hot coals. The explosive hadn’t burst the case. And then I had a problem to face. You know time is an important element in crystallisation. If you hurry the process the crystals are small—it is only by prolonged standing that they grow to any size. I resolved to let this apparatus cool for two years, letting the temperature go down slowly during the time. And I was now quite out of money; and with a big fire and the rent of my room, as well as my hunger to satisfy, I had scarcely a penny in the world.

“I can hardly tell you all the shifts I was put to while I was making the diamonds. I have sold newspapers, held horses, opened cab-doors. For many weeks I addressed envelopes. I had a place as assistant to a man who owned a barrow, and used to call down one side of the road while he called down the other.

“Once for a week I had absolutely nothing to do, and I begged. What a week that was! One day the fire was going out and I had eaten nothing all day, and a little chap taking his girl out, gave me sixpence—to show off. Thank heaven for vanity! How the fish-shops smelt! But I went and spent it all on coals, and had the furnace bright red again, and then—Well, hunger makes a fool of a man.

===Chinese===
“等我回来的时候，那东西还在我原来的位置上，夹在白热的煤炭之间。炸药并没有把外壳炸开。于是我便面临一个难题。您知道时间在结晶过程中是个重要的因素。要是操之过急，长出的晶体便小——只有长久静置，晶体才能长到一定的大小。我决心让这套装置慢慢冷却两年，让温度在这段时间里缓缓降下来。可我这时已经身无分文；既要烧那么大一炉火，又要付房租，还要填饱肚子，我在世上简直连一个便士都没有了。

“我造钻石那阵子，受了种种周折，难以一一向您细述。我卖过报纸，替人牵过马，给人开过马车的门。有好几个星期，我专门替人写信封地址。我还给一个推手推车摆摊的人做过伙计，沿着马路这一边吆喝，他则在另一边吆喝。

“有一次我整整一个礼拜实在没事可做，便上街乞讨。那是怎样一个礼拜啊！有一天炉火就要灭了，我整天粒米未进，有个带姑娘出门的小伙子给了我一枚六便士——为了在姑娘面前摆阔。谢天谢地有虚荣心这回事！鱼铺子那股香味儿哟！可我还是把钱全花在买煤上了，把炉子烧得通红，然后——唉，饥饿真叫人犯傻。”

===Original===
“At last, three weeks ago, I let the fire out. I took my cylinder and unscrewed it while it was still so hot that it punished my hands, and I scraped out the crumbling lava-like mass with a chisel, and hammered it into a powder upon an iron plate. And I found three big diamonds and five small ones. As I sat on the floor hammering, my door opened, and my neighbour, the begging-letter writer came in. He was drunk—as he usually is. ‘ ’‘Nerchist,’ said he. ‘You’re drunk,’ said I. ‘ ’Structive scoundrel,’ said he. ‘Go to your father,’ said I, meaning the Father of Lies. ‘Never you mind,’ said he, and gave me a cunning wink, and hiccuped, and leaning up against the door, with his other eye against the doorpost, began to babble of how he had been prying in my room, and how he had gone to the police that morning, and how they had taken down everything he had to say—‘ ’siffiwas a ge’m,’ said he. Then I suddenly realised I was in a hole. Either I should have to tell these police my little secret, and get the whole thing blown upon, or be lagged as an Anarchist. So I went up to my neighbour and took him by the collar, and rolled him about a bit, and then I gathered up my diamonds and cleared out. The evening newspapers called my den the Kentish Town Bomb Factory. And now I cannot part with the things for love or money.

“If I go in to respectable jewellers they ask me to wait, and go and whisper to a clerk to fetch a policeman, and then I say I cannot wait. And I found out a receiver of stolen goods, and he simply stuck to the one I gave him and told me to prosecute if I wanted it back. I am going about now with several hundred thousand pounds-worth of diamonds round my neck, and without either food or shelter. You are the first person I have taken into my confidence. But I like your face and I am hard-driven.”

===Chinese===
“终于，三个礼拜以前，我把炉火熄了。我把钢筒拧开，它还烫得灼手；我用凿子把里头那种酥松、状如熔岩的东西一点点凿出来，放在铁板上砸成粉末。结果我找到了三颗大钻石和五颗小钻石。我正坐在地板上敲着，门开了，我那位邻居——那个写乞讨信的——走了进来。他喝得酩酊大醉——他平日就这副模样。‘无……政府党徒，’他说。‘你喝醉了，’我说。‘破……坏性的恶棍，’他说。‘回你老子那儿去吧，’我说——我指的是谎言之父（the Father of Lies）。‘少来管我，’他说着，狡黠地眨眨眼，打了个酒嗝，一手撑在门上，另一只眼睛抵着门柱，开始絮絮叨叨地说起他怎么偷看我屋子里的动静，又怎么那天早上跑到警察局去告发我，警方又怎么把他说的每一句话都记了下来——‘就……就像我是个正经绅士似的，’他说。我这才猛然意识到自己惹上了麻烦。要么我得向警察交代我那点小秘密，让整个事情大白于天下；要么就被当作无政府主义者（Anarchist）抓进去。于是我走到邻居跟前，一把揪住他的领子，把他来回推搡了一通，然后收拾起我的钻石，溜之大吉。晚报把我那间小屋称作‘肯蒂什镇炸弹工厂’。如今我就是想把这东西脱手，求也求不掉，卖也卖不出。

“我走进一家体面的珠宝店，他们让我稍候，便悄悄去叫一个伙计报警，于是我便说自己不能等了。我又找了一个收赃的，可他干脆把我给他的那一颗据为己有，反过来叫我去起诉，想要回东西再去告他。我现在脖子上挂着价值几十万镑的钻石到处走，却既无饭吃，又无屋住。您是我头一个推心置腹的人。我看您面善，我也是被逼得走投无路了。”

===Original===
He looked into my eyes.

“It would be madness,” said I, “for me to buy a diamond under the circumstances. Besides, I do not carry hundreds of pounds about in my pocket. Yet I more than half believe your story. I will, if you like, do this: come to my office tomorrow—”

“You think I am a thief!” said he keenly. “You will tell the police. I am not coming into a trap.”

“Somehow I am assured you are no thief. Here is my card. Take that, anyhow. You need not come to any appointment. Come when you will.”

He took the card, and an earnest of my goodwill.

“Think better of it and come,” said I.

He shook his head doubtfully. “I will pay back your half-crown with interest some day—such interest as will amaze you,” said he. “Anyhow, you will keep the secret?… Don’t follow me.”

He crossed the road and went into the darkness towards the little steps under the archway leading into Essex Street, and I let him go. And that was the last I ever saw of him.

===Chinese===
他凝视着我的眼睛。

“眼下这情形，”我说，“我若买下这颗钻石，未免太不理智。再说，我口袋里也不常揣着几百镑。不过，您说的故事我倒有大半相信。要是您愿意，我可以这样做：明天到我的事务所来——”

“您以为我是小偷！”他尖锐地说，“您要报警。我可不会自投罗网。”

“不知怎的，我就确信您绝非小偷。这是我的名片。无论如何先收下。您不必赴什么约会，随时来都行。”

他接过名片，也接受了我表示善意的一点小钱。

“再想想，还是来吧，”我说。

他迟疑地摇了摇头。“总有一天，我会把您这半克朗（half-crown）连本带利还给您——那利息定叫您吃惊，”他说，“不过无论如何，您会替我保守这个秘密吧？……别跟着我。”

他穿过马路，朝着通往埃塞克斯街（Essex Street）那座拱门下的一小段台阶走去，没入了黑暗里，我便由他去了。那是我最后一次见到他。

===Original===
Afterwards I had two letters from him asking me to send banknotes—not cheques—to certain addresses. I weighed the matter over and took what I conceived to be the wisest course. Once he called upon me when I was out. My urchin described him as a very thin, dirty, and ragged man, with a dreadful cough. He left no message. That was the finish of him so far as my story goes. I wonder sometimes what has become of him. Was he an ingenious monomaniac, or a fraudulent dealer in pebbles, or has he really made diamonds as he asserted? The latter is just sufficiently credible to make me think at times that I have missed the most brilliant opportunity of my life. He may of course be dead, and his diamonds carelessly thrown aside—one, I repeat, was almost as big as my thumb. Or he may be still wandering about trying to sell the things. It is just possible he may yet emerge upon society, and, passing athwart my heavens in the serene altitude sacred to the wealthy and the well-advertised, reproach me silently for my want of enterprise. I sometimes think I might at least have risked five pounds.

===Chinese===
后来我又收到他两封信，求我把钞票——不是支票——按某些地址寄去。我把事情再三权衡，采取了在我看来最稳妥的做法。有一次我不在的时候，他来过我那儿。我那个跑腿的小厮形容他说，是个瘦骨嶙峋、肮脏不堪、衣衫褴褛的人，咳得厉害。他没留下话。就我这篇故事而言，那便是他的结局了。我有时也会想，他后来究竟怎样了。他到底是个别出心裁的偏执狂，是个卖鹅卵石的骗子，还是真如他所说，造出了钻石？这后一种可能，听上去恰恰又有几分可信，以至于我有时会想：我错过了这一生中最辉煌的一次机会。他当然也可能已经死了，那些钻石被人随手丢弃——我再说一遍，其中有一颗几乎有我的拇指那么大。又或许，他至今仍在四处流浪，想方设法把那些东西脱手。说不定将来某一天，他还会在社交界冒出头来，掠过我头顶那片专属于富人和大名鼎鼎之人的宁静高空，无声地责备我缺乏魄力。我有时想，我至少本该冒险押上五镑试试的。

### I / 一

===Original===
One confidential evening, not three months ago, Lionel Wallace told me this story of the Door in the Wall. And at the time I thought that so far as he was concerned it was a true story.

He told it me with such a direct simplicity of conviction that I could not do otherwise than believe in him. But in the morning, in my own flat, I woke to a different atmosphere, and as I lay in bed and recalled the things he had told me, stripped of the glamour of his earnest slow voice, denuded of the focused, shaded table light, the shadowy atmosphere that wrapped about him and me, and the pleasant bright things, the dessert and glasses and napery of the dinner we had shared, making them for the time a bright little world quite cut off from everyday realities, I saw it all as frankly incredible. “He was mystifying!” I said, and then: “How well he did it!﻿ ﻿… It isn’t quite the thing I should have expected him, of all people, to do well.”

Afterwards as I sat up in bed and sipped my morning tea, I found myself trying to account for the flavour of reality that perplexed me in his impossible reminiscences, by supposing they did in some way suggest, present, convey﻿—I hardly know which word to use﻿—experiences it was otherwise impossible to tell.

===Chinese===
就在三个月前的一个推心置腹的夜晚，莱昂内尔·华莱士（Lionel Wallace）把这道“墙上的门”（the Door in the Wall）的故事讲给我听。当时在我看来，就他而言，这是一个真实的故事。

他讲述时那种直截了当、毫不做作的笃定，让我由不得他不信。可到了第二天早晨，在我自己的寓所里，我却在另一种气氛中醒来。我躺在床上回想他告诉我的一切，那些话一旦剥去了他那恳切迟缓嗓音的魅力，剥去了那一盏聚光、带罩的台灯，剥去了裹住他和我的幽暗氛围，以及那些悦目的明亮事物——我们共享的那顿晚餐的甜点、酒杯和台布，这些当时让我们仿佛置身一个与日常现实完全隔绝的明亮小天地——我便觉得这一切坦率地说简直难以置信。“他在故弄玄虚！”我说，接着又道，“他演得真像啊！……这倒不大像是我会指望他能做好的事，在他所有能做的事里。”

后来我坐起来喝茶时，又试着为我为何在他那些不可能的回忆中感到一种真实的味道而寻找解释：我猜想，它们或许是用了某种方式暗示、呈现、传达——我几乎不知道该用哪个词——那些除此之外就无法言说的经历。

===Original===
Well, I don’t resort to that explanation now. I have got over my intervening doubts. I believe now, as I believed at the moment of telling, that Wallace did to the very best of his ability strip the truth of his secret for me. But whether he himself saw, or only thought he saw, whether he himself was the possessor of an inestimable privilege or the victim of a fantastic dream, I cannot pretend to guess. Even the facts of his death, which ended my doubts forever, throw no light on that.

That much the reader must judge for himself.

===Chinese===
如今我已不再求助于那种解释了。我度过了其间那些疑虑。此刻我相信，正如他在讲述的那一刻我相信的那样——华莱士是竭尽所能地向我剖白了他那桩秘密的真相。但他自己是真看见了，还是仅仅以为看见了；他自己是一项无可估量的恩宠的拥有者，还是一场荒诞梦境的受害者，我就装不出能猜测一二了。即便是他那场永远终结了我疑虑的死亡，也未能对此投下丝毫光亮。

这一点，须由读者自行判断。

===Original===
I forget now what chance comment or criticism of mine moved so reticent a man to confide in me. He was, I think, defending himself against an imputation of slackness and unreliability I had made in relation to a great public movement, in which he had disappointed me. But he plunged suddenly. “I have,” he said, “a preoccupation﻿—

“I know,” he went on, after a pause, “I have been negligent. The fact is﻿—it isn’t a case of ghosts or apparitions﻿—but﻿—it’s an odd thing to tell of, Redmond﻿—I am haunted. I am haunted by something﻿—that rather takes the light out of things, that fills me with longings﻿ ﻿…”

He paused, checked by that English shyness that so often overcomes us when we would speak of moving or grave or beautiful things. “You were at Saint Aethelstan’s all through,” he said, and for a moment that seemed to me quite irrelevant. “Well﻿—” and he paused. Then very haltingly at first, but afterwards more easily, he began to tell of the thing that was hidden in his life, the haunting memory of a beauty and a happiness that filled his heart with insatiable longings, that made all the interests and spectacle of worldly life seem dull and tedious and vain to him.

===Chinese===
我现在已记不清，是我哪一句偶然的议论或批评，叫这样一个沉默寡言的人对我吐露了心事。我想，他当时是在为自己辩护，反驳我就一项重大公共运动对他所作的懒散、不可靠的指摘——在那件事上他让我失望了。可他突然就一头扎了进去。“我有，”他说，“一桩心事——”

“我知道，”他停了停，又接着说，“我是疏忽了。实情是——这不是什么鬼魂作祟——而是——说出来挺怪的，雷德蒙（Redmond）——我是被缠住了。我被某种东西缠住了——它把事物的光彩夺去不少，又让我心里充满渴望……”

他停了下来，被那种英国人的羞怯绊住了——每当我们想谈论动情的、沉重的或美丽的事物时，这种羞怯常常会压倒我们。“你是一直在圣阿塞尔斯坦（Saint Aethelstan’s）读书的，”他说，那一瞬间我觉得这话与我们的话题毫不相干。“嗯——”他又停了一下。然后，起初十分结巴，渐渐地便顺畅了些，他开始讲起藏在他生命中的那件事——一段对一种美、一种幸福的缠人的记忆，它使他的心充满无法餍足的渴望，又使尘世生活所有的趣味与排场在他眼里显得乏味、无聊、空虚。

===Original===
Now that I have the clue to it, the thing seems written visibly in his face. I have a photograph in which that look of detachment has been caught and intensified. It reminds me of what a woman once said of him﻿—a woman who had loved him greatly. “Suddenly,” she said, “the interest goes out of him. He forgets you. He doesn’t care a rap for you﻿—under his very nose﻿ ﻿…”

Yet the interest was not always out of him, and when he was holding his attention to a thing Wallace could contrive to be an extremely successful man. His career, indeed, is set with successes. He left me behind him long ago: he soared up over my head, and cut a figure in the world that I couldn’t cut﻿—anyhow. He was still a year short of forty, and they say now that he would have been in office and very probably in the new Cabinet if he had lived. At school he always beat me without effort﻿—as it were by nature. We were at school together at Saint Aethelstan’s College in West Kensington for almost all our school-time. He came into the school as my coequal, but he left far above me, in a blaze of scholarships and brilliant performance. Yet I think I made a fair average running. And it was at school I heard first of the “Door in the Wall”﻿—that I was to hear of a second time only a month before his death.

To him at least the Door in the Wall was a real door, leading through a real wall to immortal realities. Of that I am now quite assured.

===Chinese===
如今我有了线索，便觉得那件事明明白白地写在他脸上。我有一张照片，恰巧把那种超然出神的神情捕捉下来并强化了。这让我想起一位女子曾经说过的一句话——一位深爱过他的女子。“忽然之间，”她说，“他对你的兴趣就没了。他把你忘了。他对你毫不在乎——就在他眼皮底下……”

然而他也并非总是兴味索然，只要把心思定在一件事上，华莱士便能成为一个极其成功的人。事实上，他这一路走来处处皆是成功。他早就把我远远甩在身后：他从我头顶上一飞冲天，在世上露了那般头角，那是我怎样也露不出的。他离世时离四十还差一年，如今人们都说，他若是活着，必已入阁，而且极可能进新内阁（the new Cabinet）。上学时他总是不费吹灰之力便胜过我——仿佛出于天性。我们几乎整个求学时代都一同在西肯辛顿（West Kensington）的圣阿塞尔斯坦学院（Saint Aethelstan’s College）度过。他进校时与我是同级，离校时却已远远凌驾于我之上，带着一身奖学金和出众的成绩。不过我想，我也算跑出了中游水平。而正是在学校里，我第一次听说了“墙上的门”——直到他死前一个月，我才再次听到它。

至少对他而言，墙上的门是一道真实的门，穿过一道真实的墙，通往不朽的真实。这一点，我如今深信不疑。

===Original===
And it came into his life quite early, when he was a little fellow between five and six. I remember how, as he sat making his confession to me with a slow gravity, he reasoned and reckoned the date of it. “There was,” he said, “a crimson Virginia creeper in it﻿—all one bright uniform crimson, in a clear amber sunshine against a white wall. That came into the impression somehow, though I don’t clearly remember how, and there were horse-chestnut leaves upon the clean pavement outside the green door. They were blotched yellow and green, you know, not brown nor dirty, so that they must have been new fallen. I take it that means October. I look out for horse-chestnut leaves every year and I ought to know.

“If I’m right in that, I was about five years and four months old.”

He was, he said, rather a precocious little boy﻿—he learnt to talk at an abnormally early age, and he was so sane and “old-fashioned,” as people say, that he was permitted an amount of initiative that most children scarcely attain by seven or eight. His mother died when he was two, and he was under the less vigilant and authoritative care of a nursery governess. His father was a stern, preoccupied lawyer, who gave him little attention, and expected great things of him. For all his brightness he found life a little grey and dull, I think. And one day he wandered.

===Chinese===
这事走进他的生命很早，那时他还是个五六岁的小家伙。我记得他坐着，以缓慢而郑重的口吻向我忏悔时，是如何推断和盘算这件事的日期的。“那里，”他说，“有一株绯红的五叶地锦（Virginia creeper）——一色明艳匀净的猩红，映在清亮的琥珀色阳光里，衬着一面白墙。这一点不知怎的就留在了印象里，尽管我记不清是怎样留的；还有，绿门外那干净的人行石板上，落着七叶树（horse-chestnut）的叶子。你要知道，那些叶子斑驳地黄绿相间，不是棕色，也不脏，所以一定是新落的。我想这意思是十月。我每年都留意七叶树的叶子，应当不会弄错。

“如果我这点没记错，那时我大概是五岁零四个月。”

他说自己当年算是个颇早慧的小男孩——他学说话早得出奇，又那么懂事、“老成”——人们都这么讲——所以被允许有相当的自主，那种自主大多数孩子七八岁也未必能有。他母亲在他两岁时就去世了，他便由一位照看不那么严、也不那么有威信的育儿室家庭教师（nursery governess）管带。父亲是个严厉、心思沉重的律师，对他几乎不闻不问，却对他寄予厚望。我想，尽管他聪慧，他还是觉得生活有点灰暗、有点乏味。于是有一天，他溜达了出去。

===Original===
He could not recall the particular neglect that enabled him to get away, nor the course he took among the West Kensington roads. All that had faded among the incurable blurs of memory. But the white wall and the green door stood out quite distinctly.

As his memory of that childish experience ran, he did at the very first sight of that door experience a peculiar emotion, an attraction, a desire to get to the door and open it and walk in. And at the same time he had the clearest conviction that either it was unwise or it was wrong of him﻿—he could not tell which﻿—to yield to this attraction. He insisted upon it as a curious thing that he knew from the very beginning﻿—unless memory has played him the queerest trick﻿—that the door was unfastened, and that he could go in as he chose.

I seem to see the figure of that little boy, drawn and repelled. And it was very clear in his mind, too, though why it should be so was never explained, that his father would be very angry if he went in through that door.

===Chinese===
他想不起来是哪一次具体的疏忽让他得以脱身，也想不起来自己在西肯辛顿的那些街道上是怎么走的。这一切早已模糊在记忆里那些无法治愈的模糊之中。唯有那道白墙和那扇绿门，依然清晰可辨。

照他对那段孩提经历的回忆，他第一眼看见那扇门时，便生出一种奇特的情感，一种吸引，一种想走到门前、推开它、走进去的渴望。与此同时，他又最清楚地意识到：屈从于这种吸引，要么是不明智，要么是不对——他分不清是哪一种。他坚持说有一件事很奇怪：他从一开始——除非记忆给他开了最离奇的玩笑——就知道那门没闩，他随时可以进去。

我仿佛看得见那小男孩的身影，被吸引又带着排斥。他心里也十分清楚——尽管从来无人解释为什么会这样——一旦他从那扇门进去，父亲一定会非常生气。

===Original===
Wallace described all these moments of hesitation to me with the utmost particularity. He went right past the door, and then, with his hands in his pockets and making an infantile attempt to whistle, strolled right along beyond the end of the wall. There he recalls a number of mean dirty shops, and particularly that of a plumber and decorator with a dusty disorder of earthenware pipes, sheet lead, ball taps, pattern books of wall paper, and tins of enamel. He stood pretending to examine these things, and *coveting*, passionately desiring, the green door.

Then, he said, he had a gust of emotion. He made a run for it, lest hesitation should grip him again; he went plump with outstretched hand through the green door and let it slam behind him. And so, in a trice, he came into the garden that has haunted all his life.

It was very difficult for Wallace to give me his full sense of that garden into which he came.

===Chinese===
华莱士把所有这些犹豫的瞬间都向我描述得细致入微。他径直从门前走过，然后，双手插在口袋里，嘴里学着吹口哨——一副小小孩童的笨拙模样——顺着墙一路溜达到了墙的尽头。他还记得那里有一排又破又脏的小铺子，尤其记得一家管子工兼装修工的店，里头凌乱蒙尘地堆着陶土管、铅皮、球阀、墙纸样本簿，还有几听瓷漆。他站在那儿假装打量这些东西，心里却*觊觎*着——热切地渴望着——那扇绿门。

然后，他说，他心里忽地涌起一阵冲动。他撒腿就跑，生怕又被犹豫攫住；他伸出手，一头冲进了那扇绿门，任它在身后砰地关上。就这样，转眼之间，他走进了那座缠了他一辈子的花园。

华莱士很难向我完整地说清他走进的那座花园给他的全部感受。

===Original===
There was something in the very air of it that exhilarated, that gave one a sense of lightness and good happening and well-being; there was something in the sight of it that made all its colour clean and perfect and subtly luminous. In the instant of coming into it one was exquisitely glad﻿—as only in rare moments, and when one is young and joyful one can be glad in this world. And everything was beautiful there﻿ ﻿…

Wallace mused before he went on telling me. “You see,” he said, with the doubtful inflection of a man who pauses at incredible things, “there were two great panthers there﻿ ﻿… Yes, spotted panthers. And I was not afraid. There was a long wide path with marble-edged flower borders on either side, and these two huge velvety beasts were playing there with a ball. One looked up and came towards me, a little curious as it seemed. It came right up to me, rubbed its soft round ear very gently against the small hand I held out, and purred. It was, I tell you, an enchanted garden. I know. And the size? Oh! it stretched far and wide, this way and that. I believe there were hills far away. Heaven knows where West Kensington had suddenly got to. And somehow it was just like coming home.

“You know, in the very moment the door swung to behind me, I forgot the road with its fallen chestnut leaves, its cabs and tradesmen’s carts, I forgot the sort of gravitational pull back to the discipline and obedience of home, I forgot all hesitations and fear, forgot discretion, forgot all the intimate realities of this life. I became in a moment a very glad and wonder-happy little boy﻿—in another world. It was a world with a different quality, a warmer, more penetrating and mellower light, with a faint clear gladness in its air, and wisps of sun-touched cloud in the blueness of its sky. And before me ran this long wide path, invitingly, with weedless beds on either side, rich with untended flowers, and these two great panthers. I put my little hands fearlessly on their soft fur, and caressed their round ears and the sensitive corners under their ears, and played with them, and it was as though they welcomed me home. There was a keen sense of homecoming in my mind, and when presently a tall, fair girl appeared in the pathway and came to meet me, smiling, and said ‘Well?’ to me, and lifted me, and kissed me, and put me down, and led me by the hand, there was no amazement, but only an impression of delightful rightness, of being reminded of happy things that had in some strange way been overlooked. There were broad red steps, I remember, that came into view between spikes of delphinium, and up these we went to a great avenue between very old and shady dark trees. All down this avenue, you know, between the red chapped stems, were marble seats of honour and statuary, and very tame and friendly white doves﻿ ﻿…”

===Chinese===
那园中的空气本身就有一种令人振奋的东西，叫人感到轻盈，感到好事将至，感到安康；它的景象又使一切色彩显得洁净、完美，泛着一层隐隐的光。踏入其中的刹那，人会感到一种至极的欢喜——这世上只有在难得的瞬间，在人年轻而快乐的时候，才能有的那种欢喜。那里的一切都是美的……

华莱士沉吟了一阵，才又往下讲。“你要知道，”他说，带着一个人讲到难以置信之事时那种迟疑的语调，“那里有两头大豹子……对，是有斑点的豹子。可我并不害怕。有一条又长又宽的小径，两边的花坛镶着大理石边，那两头毛茸茸、丝绒般的大兽就在那儿玩一只球。有一只抬头看了看我，朝我走来，似乎带着点好奇。它一直走到我跟前，把它柔软浑圆的耳朵轻轻地蹭了蹭我伸出的小手，呜呜地叫着。我跟你说，那是一座被施了魔法的花园。我知道的。至于它有多大？噢！它向四面八方远远地铺展开去。我相信远处还有山。天知道西肯辛顿一下子跑到哪儿去了。而且不知怎的，那感觉就像是回了家。

“你要知道，门在身后一摆而合的那一瞬间，我就忘了那条落满七叶树叶的路，忘了路上的马车和送货的车子，忘了那种把我往家里的规矩与服从中拽的引力，忘了所有的犹豫和恐惧，忘了谨慎，忘了这一生里所有切身的现实。转眼之间，我变成了一个无比欢喜、惊奇幸福的小男孩——在另一个世界里。那是一个质地不同的世界，光线更暖、更透、更柔和，空气里有一缕清淡的喜悦，湛蓝的天空里飘着一缕缕被阳光点亮的云。在我面前，这条又长又宽的小径诱人地伸展着，两边是不生杂草的花坛，开满了无人看管却丰茂的花，还有那两头大豹子。我毫无惧色地把小手放在它们柔软的毛上，抚摸它们圆圆的耳朵、它们耳根敏感的角落，和它们玩耍，仿佛它们是在欢迎我回家。我心里有一种强烈的归家之感；过了一会儿，一位高挑、金发的姑娘在小径上出现，朝我走来，含笑对我说了声‘怎么啦？’，便把我抱起来，亲了亲我，又把我放下，牵着我的手往前走——这一切我毫不惊讶，只觉得恰如其分，令人愉悦，仿佛有人提醒了我一些以某种奇异方式被忽略了的快乐往事。我还记得，有几级宽阔的红台阶，从一簇簇飞燕草（delphinium）间显出来，我们拾级而上，走进一条林荫大道，夹道是些年代久远、浓荫蔽日的暗色大树。你要知道，这条大道两旁，在那些皲裂的红色树干之间，是一尊尊大理石的宝座和雕像，还有非常温驯友善的白鸽……”

===Original===
“Along this cool avenue my girl friend led me, looking down﻿—I recall the pleasant lines, the finely-modelled chin of her sweet kind face﻿—asking me questions in a soft, agreeable voice, and telling me things, pleasant things I know, though what they were I was never able to recall﻿ ﻿… Presently a little Capuchin monkey, very clean, with a fur of ruddy brown and kindly hazel eyes, came down a tree to us and ran beside me, looking up at me and grinning, and presently leapt to my shoulder. So we two went on our way in great happiness.”

He paused.

“Go on,” I said.

===Chinese===
“我那位女朋友伴着我沿这条凉爽的大道往前走，她低头看着我——我还记得她那张甜美慈爱的脸上好看的轮廓，那轮廓精致的下巴——她用柔和悦耳的声音问我话，也讲些事给我听，我知道她讲的尽是叫人高兴的事，可那些话到底是什么，我再也想不起来了……过了一会儿，一只小卷尾猴（Capuchin monkey），干干净净的，一身红棕色的毛，一双温和的淡褐色眼睛，从一棵树上下来，跑到我们身边，挨着我跑，一边仰头望着我，咧嘴笑，再过一会儿便跳上了我的肩头。我们俩就这样一路欢欢喜喜地往前走。”

他停了一下。

“讲下去，”我说。

===Original===
“I remember little things. We passed an old man musing among laurels, I remember, and a place gay with parakeets, and came through a broad shaded colonnade to a spacious cool palace, full of pleasant fountains, full of beautiful things, full of the quality and promise of heart’s desire. And there were many things and many people, some that still seem to stand out clearly and some that are a little vague; but all these people were beautiful and kind. In some way﻿—I don’t know how﻿—it was conveyed to me that they all were kind to me, glad to have me there, and filling me with gladness by their gestures, by the touch of their hands, by the welcome and love in their eyes. Yes﻿—”

He mused for a while. “Playmates I found there. That was very much to me, because I was a lonely little boy. They played delightful games in a grass-covered court where there was a sundial set about with flowers. And as one played one loved﻿ ﻿…

“But﻿—it’s odd﻿—there’s a gap in my memory. I don’t remember the games we played. I never remembered. Afterwards, as a child, I spent long hours trying, even with tears, to recall the form of that happiness. I wanted to play it all over again﻿—in my nursery﻿—by myself. No! All I remember is the happiness and two dear playfellows who were most with me﻿ ﻿… Then presently came a sombre dark woman, with a grave, pale face and dreamy eyes, a sombre woman, wearing a soft long robe of pale purple, who carried a book, and beckoned and took me aside with her into a gallery above a hall﻿—though my playmates were loth to have me go, and ceased their game and stood watching as I was carried away. ‘Come back to us!’ they cried. ‘Come back to us soon!’ I looked up at her face, but she heeded them not at all. Her face was very gentle and grave. She took me to a seat in the gallery, and I stood beside her, ready to look at her book as she opened it upon her knee. The pages fell open. She pointed, and I looked, marvelling, for in the living pages of that book I saw myself; it was a story about myself, and in it were all the things that had happened to me since ever I was born﻿ ﻿…”

===Chinese===
“我记得一些零碎的小事。我们走过一位在月桂树间沉思的老人身边，我记得；还经过一处鹦鹉喧闹、色彩绚丽的地方；我们穿过一条宽阔、阴凉的柱廊，来到一座宽敞凉爽的宫殿，里面满是悦人的喷泉，满是美丽的事物，满是那种能成全心之所愿的气息与许诺。那里有许多东西，也有许多人，有些至今仍清晰地浮现在我眼前，有些则有些模糊；但这些人全都美丽而和善。我不知道是怎么传达给我的——他们都对我好，都因我在那儿而高兴，都借他们的举止、借他们手的触碰、借他们眼中的欢迎与喜爱，把喜悦灌进我心里。是的——”

他沉思了一会儿。“在那儿我找到了玩伴。这对我来说非同小可，因为我本是个孤零零的小男孩。我们在一个铺着青草、中央立着一座四周绕满鲜花的日晷的院子里，玩那些叫人开心的游戏。人玩着，便也爱着……

“可是——说来奇怪——我的记忆里有一段空白。我不记得我们玩的是什么游戏。我一直都没能记起来。后来还是孩子的时候，我曾花上好几个钟头，甚至流着泪去努力回想那种幸福的样子。我想把它重新玩一遍——在我的育儿室里——一个人玩。不！我记得的，只有那种幸福，还有两位最常陪我玩的亲爱的玩伴……过了一会儿，走来一位神情阴郁的妇人，一张严肃苍白的脸，一双如梦的眼睛，她身着一件淡紫色的柔软长袍，手里拿着一本书，她朝我招手，把我带到一边，领我走进一条凌驾于一座大厅之上的画廊——我的玩伴们舍不得我走，停下了游戏，站着看我被带走。‘回来呀！’他们喊，‘快点回来呀！’我抬头看她的脸，可她对他们毫不在意。她的脸十分温柔，也十分严肃。她把我带到画廊里的一张座椅前，我站在她身旁，准备看她把书在膝上翻开。书页自行摊开。她伸指一指，我看了过去，惊奇不已，因为在那本书活生生的书页里，我看见了我自己；那是关于我自己的一个故事，里面写着从我出生以来发生在我身上的所有事……”

===Original===
“It was wonderful to me, because the pages of that book were not pictures, you understand, but realities.”

Wallace paused gravely﻿—looked at me doubtfully.

“Go on,” I said. “I understand.”

===Chinese===
“这对我而言奇妙极了，因为你要明白，那本书的书页不是图画，而是真实。”

华莱士郑重地停了一下——又迟疑地望着我。

“讲下去，”我说，“我懂。”

===Original===
“They were realities﻿—yes, they must have been; people moved and things came and went in them; my dear mother, whom I had near forgotten; then my father, stern and upright, the servants, the nursery, all the familiar things of home. Then the front door and the busy streets, with traffic to and fro. I looked and marvelled, and looked half doubtfully again into the woman’s face and turned the pages over, skipping this and that, to see more of this book and more, and so at last I came to myself hovering and hesitating outside the green door in the long white wall, and felt again the conflict and the fear.

“ ‘And next?’ I cried, and would have turned on, but the cool hand of the grave woman delayed me.

“ ‘Next?’ I insisted, and struggled gently with her hand, pulling up her fingers with all my childish strength, and as she yielded and the page came over she bent down upon me like a shadow and kissed my brow.

===Chinese===
“它们是真的——是的，它们一定是真的；人在里面动，事物在里面来去；我那几乎已被我忘掉的亲爱的母亲；接着是我的父亲，严厉而正直至极；仆人、育儿室、家里所有熟悉的事物。然后是前门，是熙来攘往的繁忙街道。我看着，惊奇不已，又带着半信半疑看了看那位妇人的脸，再把书页一页页翻过去，跳过这一段、那一段，想多看一些、再多看一些这本书，就这样，翻到最后，我看见我自己在那道长长的白墙外、在那扇绿门外徘徊迟疑，又感到了那种冲突与恐惧。

“‘后来呢？’我叫道，正要往下翻，可那位严肃妇人的凉凉的手按住了我。

“‘后来呢？’我坚持着，轻轻地与她那只手较量，用我孩童全部的力气去掰开她的手指；她让步了，书页翻了过去，她便如一道阴影似的俯身下来，吻了吻我的额头。

===Original===
“But the page did not show the enchanted garden, nor the panthers, nor the girl who had led me by the hand, nor the playfellows who had been so loth to let me go. It showed a long grey street in West Kensington, in that chill hour of afternoon before the lamps are lit, and I was there, a wretched little figure, weeping aloud, for all that I could do to restrain myself, and I was weeping because I could not return to my dear playfellows who had called after me, ‘Come back to us! Come back to us soon!’ I was there. This was no page in a book, but harsh reality; that enchanted place and the restraining hand of the grave mother at whose knee I stood had gone﻿—whither had they gone?”

He halted again, and remained for a time staring into the fire.

“Oh! the woefulness of that return!” he murmured.

===Chinese===
“可那一页并没有显出那座被施了魔法的花园，没有那两头豹子，没有那位牵着我手走的姑娘，也没有那些舍不得让我走的玩伴。它显示的是西肯辛顿一条灰蒙蒙的长街，正值下午路灯点亮之前那段清冷的时辰，我就在那儿，一个可怜巴巴的小小身影，放声大哭，怎么也忍不住——我哭，是因为我再也不能回到那些亲爱的玩伴身边去了，他们在我身后喊：‘回来呀！快点回来呀！’我就在那里。这不是书中的一页，而是严酷的现实；那个施了魔法的地方，那只按住我的、那位我所倚膝而立的严肃母亲的手——都不见了——它们到哪里去了？”

他又停了下来，有一阵子只盯着炉火出神。

“噢！那一趟回去，真是凄惨啊！”他喃喃地说。

===Original===
“Well?” I said, after a minute or so.

“Poor little wretch I was!﻿—brought back to this grey world again! As I realised the fullness of what had happened to me, I gave way to quite ungovernable grief. And the shame and humiliation of that public weeping and my disgraceful homecoming remain with me still. I see again the benevolent-looking old gentleman in gold spectacles who stopped and spoke to me﻿—prodding me first with his umbrella. ‘Poor little chap,’ said he; ‘and are you lost then?’﻿—and me a London boy of five and more! And he must needs bring in a kindly young policeman and make a crowd of me, and so march me home. Sobbing, conspicuous, and frightened, I came back from the enchanted garden to the steps of my father’s house.

“That is as well as I can remember my vision of that garden﻿—the garden that haunts me still. Of course, I can convey nothing of that indescribable quality of translucent unreality, that *difference* from the common things of experience that hung about it all; but that﻿—that is what happened. If it was a dream, I am sure it was a daytime and altogether extraordinary dream﻿ ﻿… H’m!﻿—naturally there followed a terrible questioning, by my aunt, my father, the nurse, the governess﻿—everyone﻿ ﻿…”

===Chinese===
“后来呢？”约莫过了一分钟，我问。

“我这个可怜的小东西！——又被带回了这个灰色的世界！待我明白发生在我身上的究竟是什么，我便放声痛哭，怎么也止不住。当众哭泣的羞耻与丢脸，以及那场不光彩的回家，至今仍留在我心里。我又看见那位面相和善、戴着金丝眼镜的老绅士停下来对我说话——说话前还先用伞尖戳了戳我。‘可怜的小家伙，’他说，‘那么说你是迷路了？’——我可是一个五岁多的伦敦孩子呢！他偏偏还要请来一位和气的年轻警察，把我弄得围了一大圈人看，就那样押送我回家。我一路抽噎，引人注目，又惊又怕，就这样从那座魔法花园，回到了我父亲宅邸门前的台阶上。

“这就是我所能记得的关于那座花园的景象了——那座至今仍缠着我的花园。当然，那种半透明的不真实之感，那种与寻常经验之物迥然有异的*不同*，笼罩着它的一切，我是无法向你传达分毫的；可是——事情就是那样发生的。如果那是一个梦，我敢肯定，那是一个白日里做的、彻头彻尾不同寻常的梦……哼！——接下来自然是一顿可怕的盘问，姑母问、父亲问、保姆问、家庭教师问——所有人都问……”

===Original===
“I tried to tell them, and my father gave me my first thrashing for telling lies. When afterwards I tried to tell my aunt, she punished me again for my wicked persistence. Then, as I said, everyone was forbidden to listen to me, to hear a word about it. Even my fairytale books were taken away from me for a time﻿—because I was too ‘imaginative.’ Eh? Yes, they did that! My father belonged to the old school﻿ ﻿… And my story was driven back upon myself. I whispered it to my pillow﻿—my pillow that was often damp and salt to my whispering lips with childish tears. And I added always to my official and less fervent prayers this one heartfelt request: ‘Please God I may dream of the garden. Oh! take me back to my garden!’ Take me back to my garden! I dreamt often of the garden. I may have added to it, I may have changed it; I do not know﻿ ﻿… All this, you understand, is an attempt to reconstruct from fragmentary memories a very early experience. Between that and the other consecutive memories of my boyhood there is a gulf. A time came when it seemed impossible I should ever speak of that wonder glimpse again.”

===Chinese===
“我试着讲给他们听，父亲却因为我撒谎而给了我平生第一顿打。后来我再试着讲给姑母听，她又因为我顽固不化而惩罚了我一次。再后来，就像我说的，所有人都不许再听我讲，不许再听关于这件事的一个字。连我的童话书都被收走了一阵——因为我太‘富于想象’。嗯？是的，他们就这么干了！我父亲是老派做派……于是这个故事就被逼回了我自己心里。我对着枕头低声讲它——那只枕头常常被孩童的泪水浸得又湿又咸，沾在我低声诉说的嘴唇上。我还在那些例行公事、不算热切的祷告之外，加上这一句发自心底的祈求：‘上帝啊，求你让我梦见那座花园吧。噢！把我带回我的花园吧！’把我带回我的花园吧！我常常梦见那座花园。我也许给它添过些什么，也许改动过些什么；我不知道……这一切，你要明白，都是我试图从记忆的碎片里，重建一段极其久远的经历。在这段经历与我能连贯记得的别的童年记忆之间，隔着一条鸿沟。曾有一段日子，我仿佛再也不可能向人说起那一瞥奇景了。”

===Original===
I asked an obvious question.

“No,” he said. “I don’t remember that I ever attempted to find my way back to the garden in those early years. This seems odd to me now, but I think that very probably a closer watch was kept on my movements after this misadventure to prevent my going astray. No, it wasn’t till you knew me that I tried for the garden again. And I believe there was a period﻿—incredible as it seems now﻿—when I forgot the garden altogether﻿—when I was about eight or nine it may have been. Do you remember me as a kid at Saint Aethelstan’s?”

“Rather!”

“I didn’t show any signs, did I, in those days of having a secret dream?”

===Chinese===
我问了一个显而易见的问题。

“没有，”他说，“我不记得在那几年幼小的日子里，我曾试图找回那条通往花园的路。如今想来也觉得奇怪，不过我想，那次闯祸之后，大人们很可能把我看得更紧了，免得我再走丢。不，直到你认识我之后，我才又一次去找那座花园。而且我相信，曾有过一段日子——如今说来虽然难以置信——我把那座花园彻底忘了——大概是八九岁的时候。你还记得我在圣阿塞尔斯坦做小孩时的样子吗？”

“当然记得！”

“在那些日子里，我可曾露出过什么心怀一个秘密的梦的迹象吗？”

### I / 一

===Original===
When Captain Gerilleau received instructions to take his new gunboat, the *Benjamin Constant*, to Badama on the Batemo arm of the Guaramadema and there assist the inhabitants against a plague of ants, he suspected the authorities of mockery. His promotion had been romantic and irregular, the affections of a prominent Brazilian lady and the captain’s liquid eyes had played a part in the process, and the *Diario* and *O Futuro* had been lamentably disrespectful in their comments. He felt he was to give further occasion for disrespect.

===Chinese===
当杰里约舰长接到命令，要他率新炮舰“本杰明·康斯坦特号”开赴瓜拉马德马河的支流巴特莫河上游的巴达马，去协助当地居民对付一场蚁患时，他疑心上头是在拿他开涮。他的晋升本就既浪漫又不合常规，一位显赫的巴西贵妇人的垂青以及舰长那一双水汪汪的眼睛在其中都起了一份作用，而《日报》（Diario）与《未来报》（O Futuro）在评说此事时那一副可悲的不敬口吻更叫他难堪。他觉得自己这回怕是又要给人添上新的笑柄了。

===Original===
He was a Creole, his conceptions of etiquette and discipline were pure-blooded Portuguese, and it was only to Holroyd, the Lancashire engineer who had come over with the boat, and as an exercise in the use of English—his “th” sounds were very uncertain—that he opened his heart.

“It is in effect,” he said, “to make me absurd! What can a man do against ants? Dey come, dey go.”

“They say,” said Holroyd, “that these don’t go. That chap you said was a Sambo—”

“Zambo;—it is a sort of mixture of blood.”

“Sambo. He said the people are going!”

The captain smoked fretfully for a time. “Dese tings ’ave to happen,” he said at last. “What is it? Plagues of ants and suchlike as God wills. Dere was a plague in Trinidad—the little ants that carry leaves. Orl der orange-trees, all der mangoes! What does it matter? Sometimes ant armies come into your houses—fighting ants; a different sort. You go and they clean the house. Then you come back again;—the house is clean, like new! No cockroaches, no fleas, no jiggers in the floor.”

“That Sambo chap,” said Holroyd, “says these are a different sort of ant.”

The captain shrugged his shoulders, fumed, and gave his attention to a cigarette.

Afterwards he reopened the subject. “My dear ’Olroyd, what am I to do about dese infernal ants?”

===Chinese===
他是克里奥尔人，对礼仪和军纪的观念却是纯而又纯的葡萄牙血统。也只有在霍尔罗伊德面前——这位兰开夏的工程师是随这条船一起过来的——他才肯吐露心声，顺便也算是练一练英语——他那两个“th”音发得实在含糊得很。

“这其实是，”他说，“存心叫我出洋相！人对蚂蚁能有什么办法？它们来，它们走。”

“人家都说，”霍尔罗伊德道，“这一回的蚂蚁不走。你说的那个萨姆博（Sambo）家伙——”

“赞博——是一种混血。”

“萨姆博。他说当地的人都走光了！”

舰长烦躁地抽了一阵烟。“这种事总是免不了的，”他终于开口道，“算什么呢？蚁灾这一类的事，乃是出于上帝的旨意。特立尼达（Trinidad）就闹过一回——就是那种会衔着叶子走的小蚂蚁。所有的橘树，所有的芒果树，全完了！这又有什么要紧？有时候蚂蚁大军会闯进你家——那是打仗的蚂蚁，另一种。你出去，它们就把屋子打扫干净。你再回来；——屋子便干净了，像新的一样！没有蟑螂，没有跳蚤，地板缝里也没有沙蚤。”

“那个萨姆博家伙，”霍尔罗伊德说，“说这一回的又是另一种蚂蚁。”

舰长耸耸肩，气鼓鼓地转而专心对付一支香烟去了。

过了一阵，他又把话头拾了起来。“我亲爱的奥尔罗伊德啊，这些该死的蚂蚁，我到底该怎么办？”

===Original===
The captain reflected. “It is ridiculous,” he said. But in the afternoon he put on his full uniform and went ashore, and jars and boxes came back to the ship and subsequently he did. And Holroyd sat on deck in the evening coolness and smoked profoundly and marvelled at Brazil. They were six days up the Amazon, some hundreds of miles from the ocean, and east and west of him there was a horizon like the sea, and to the south nothing but a sandbank island with some tufts of scrub. The water was always running like a sluice, thick with dirt, animated with crocodiles and hovering birds, and fed by some inexhaustible source of tree trunks; and the waste of it, the headlong waste of it, filled his soul. The town of Alemquer, with its meagre church, its thatched sheds for houses, its discoloured ruins of ampler days, seemed a little thing lost in this wilderness of Nature, a sixpence dropped on Sahara. He was a young man, this was his first sight of the tropics, he came straight from England, where Nature is hedged, ditched, and drained, into the perfection of submission, and he had suddenly discovered the insignificance of man. For six days they had been steaming up from the sea by unfrequented channels; and man had been as rare as a rare butterfly. One saw one day a canoe, another day a distant station, the next no men at all. He began to perceive that man is indeed a rare animal, having but a precarious hold upon this land.

===Chinese===
舰长寻思了一会儿。“荒唐，”他说。可到了下午，他还是换上全套军服上了岸，随后一罐罐一盒盒的东西便被运回船上，再后来，他果真动了手。傍晚凉爽时分，霍尔罗伊德坐在甲板上，深深吸着烟，对巴西啧啧称奇。他们已在亚马逊河上溯行了六日，离海已有好几百英里，东西两面是一片海一般的地平线，南边则只有一座沙洲小岛，上头稀稀落落地长着几丛灌木。河水像泄洪闸的水一般奔流不息，浑浊不堪，里面有鳄鱼游动，有群鸟盘旋，更有一根根漂来的树干，仿佛出自某个永不枯竭的源头；而那水这般奔流，这般不管不顾地奔流浪费，直叫他的灵魂也为之发堵。阿伦克尔镇上那座寒酸的教堂，那几间茅草棚屋，那几处昔日繁华留下来的褪色废墟，在这大自然的莽莽荒野之中，就像落在撒哈拉大沙漠上的一枚六便士硬币，渺小得寻也寻不见。他是个年轻人，这是他头一回见识热带，他是直接从英国过来的——在英国，大自然早被树篱、沟渠和下水道收拾得服服帖帖、百依百顺——可眼下，他骤然间发现了人的渺小。这六天来，他们顺着人迹罕至的水道从海口一路上行，人像罕见的蝴蝶一样难得一见。这一天能瞧见一只独木舟，又一天能远远望见一座哨所，再下一天便一个人影也无。他开始隐约感到，人果然是一种稀罕的动物，在这片土地上立足得岌岌可危。

===Original===
He perceived it more clearly as the days passed, and he made his devious way to the Batemo, in the company of this remarkable commander, who ruled over one big gun, and was forbidden to waste his ammunition. Holroyd was learning Spanish industriously, but he was still in the present tense and substantive stage of speech, and the only other person who had any words of English was a negro stoker, who had them all wrong. The second in command was a Portuguese, da Cunha, who spoke French, but it was a different sort of French from the French Holroyd had learnt in Southport, and their intercourse was confined to politenesses and simple propositions about the weather. And the weather, like everything else in this amazing new world, the weather had no human aspect, and was hot by night and hot by day, and the air steam, even the wind was hot steam, smelling of vegetation in decay: and the alligators and the strange birds, the flies of many sorts and sizes, the beetles, the ants, the snakes and monkeys seemed to wonder what man was doing in an atmosphere that had no gladness in its sunshine and no coolness in its night. To wear clothing was intolerable, but to cast it aside was to scorch by day, and expose an ampler area to the mosquitoes by night; to go on deck by day was to be blinded by glare and to stay below was to suffocate. And in the daytime came certain flies, extremely clever and noxious about one’s wrist and ankle. Captain Gerilleau, who was Holroyd’s sole distraction from these physical distresses, developed into a formidable bore, telling the simple story of his heart’s affections day by day, a string of anonymous women, as if he was telling beads. Sometimes he suggested sport, and they shot at alligators, and at rare intervals they came to human aggregations in the waste of trees, and stayed for a day or so, and drank and sat about, and, one night, danced with Creole girls, who found Holroyd’s poor elements of Spanish, without either past tense or future, amply sufficient for their purposes. But these were mere luminous chinks in the long grey passage of the streaming river, up which the throbbing engines beat. A certain liberal heathen deity, in the shape of a demijohn, held seductive court aft, and, it is probable, forward.

===Chinese===
随着日子一天天过去，他跟着这位不同寻常的指挥官，七弯八绕地朝巴特莫河前行——这位长官手下只管着一门大炮，又被严令不得浪费弹药——他对这一点的认识也就越发清晰了。霍尔罗伊德正起劲地学着西班牙语，可他说出口的话仍停留在“现在时”加“名词”的阶段，船上另一个会几句英语的，是一个黑人司炉，偏偏那几句还全都是错的。副舰长是个葡萄牙人，叫达库尼亚（da Cunha），会说法语，可他这种法语与霍尔罗伊德当年在索斯波特所学的那一套法语并不太对得上号，他俩之间的交谈，也就仅限于一些客套话和关于天气的简单陈述。而这天气，也同这个令人惊异的新世界里的万事万物一样，毫无半点人情味，夜里是热的，白天也是热的，空气是蒸汽，连风也是滚烫的蒸汽，一股草木腐烂的气味；那些短吻鳄、那些奇异的鸟，那些大大小小形形色色的苍蝇、甲虫、蚂蚁、蛇和猴子，似乎都在纳闷：人跑到这种阳光里没有一丝欢悦、夜晚里没有一丝凉意的空气中来，究竟所为何来？穿衣服叫人难以忍受，可脱了衣服，白天要被晒焦，夜里又得把更大一片皮肉暴露给蚊子；白天上甲板，会被强光刺得睁不开眼，待在下层舱里，又闷得透不过气。白天还会飞来几种苍蝇，极其刁钻毒辣，专在你手腕脚踝一带作祟。杰里约舰长本是霍尔罗伊德摆脱这些肉体苦楚的唯一消遣，如今却渐渐成了一个叫人吃不消的唠叨鬼，日复一日地讲述着他那颗心的一桩桩风流韵事，一连串连名字也说不清的女人，仿佛他是在拨着念珠数念经。有时候他提议玩点什么，他们就射击鳄鱼；偶尔难得地，他们在这林木的荒海中遇见一处人烟聚集之地，便停下来歇上一两天，喝喝酒，到处坐坐；有一个夜晚，他们还同几个克里奥尔姑娘跳了舞——这些姑娘发现，霍尔罗伊德那一星半点既无过去时、又无将来时的西班牙语，已足以满足她们的目的。然而这些都不过是那条奔腾不息的大河那段长长的灰色甬道里偶尔漏进来的几缕亮光，那条甬道之上，只有砰砰跳动的引擎在一下又一下地捶打着。船尾有一位慷慨的异教神祇，化作一个大肚酒坛的形貌，在那儿妖娆地坐殿，船头想必也同样供奉着一位。

===Original===
But Gerilleau learnt things about the ants, more things and more, at this stopping-place and that, and became interested in his mission.

“Dey are a new sort of ant,” he said. “We have got to be—what do you call it?—entomologie? Big. Five centimetres! Some bigger! It is ridiculous. We are like the monkeys—sent to pick insects… But dey are eating up the country.”

He burst out indignantly. “Suppose—suddenly, there are complications with Europe. Here am I—soon we shall be above the Rio Negro—and my gun, useless!”

He nursed his knee and mused.

===Chinese===
可杰里约在这一站那一站地听来了关于这些蚂蚁的事，越听越多，竟对自己这趟差使生出了兴趣。

“这是一种新种蚂蚁，”他说。“我们得——你们怎么说的来着？——昆虫学？大。有五厘米！有的更大！荒唐。我们倒像那些猴子——给派来捉虫子……可它们简直要把这一国的土地都吃光了。”

他愤愤不平地发作起来。“假如——忽然之间，跟欧洲起了什么纠葛。我倒好——眼瞅着就要过内格罗河（Rio Negro）了——我那门炮，没用！”

他抱着膝盖，陷入了沉思。

===Original===
“Dose people who were dere at de dancing place, dey ’ave come down. Dey ’ave lost all they got. De ants come to deir house one afternoon. Everyone run out. You know when de ants come one must—everyone runs out and they go over the house. If you stayed they’d eat you. See? Well, presently dey go back; dey say, ‘The ants ’ave gone.’… De ants *’aven’t* gone. Dey try to go in—de son, ’e goes in. De ants fight.”

“Swarm over him?”

“Bite ’im. Presently he comes out again—screaming and running. He runs past them to the river. See? He gets into de water and drowns de ants—yes.” Gerilleau paused, brought his liquid eyes close to Holroyd’s face, tapped Holroyd’s knee with his knuckle. “That night he dies, just as if he was stung by a snake.”

“Poisoned—by the ants?”

“Who knows?” Gerilleau shrugged his shoulders. “Perhaps they bit him badly… When I joined dis service I joined to fight men. Dese things, dese ants, dey come and go. It is no business for men.”

===Chinese===
“跳舞那地方见过的那些人，他们下来了。他们把家底全丢了。一天下午，蚂蚁进了他们的屋。一家老小统统跑出去。你知道，蚂蚁来的时候，一个人必须——大家都跑出去，让它们从屋上爬过。你要是留下，它们就把你吃了。明白？哎，过了一阵他们回去；他们说：‘蚂蚁走了。’……蚂蚁没走。他们想进屋——那儿子，他进去了。蚂蚁反击。”

“成群扑到他身上？”

“咬他。过了一会儿他又跑出来——又喊又叫地跑。他打他们身边奔过，直奔河边。明白？他跳进水里，把身上的蚂蚁淹死——对。”杰里约顿了顿，把他那双水汪汪的眼睛凑到霍尔罗伊德的脸跟前，用指节敲了敲霍尔罗伊德的膝盖。“那天夜里他就死了，就像被蛇咬了似的。”

“中了毒——叫蚂蚁毒的？”

“谁知道呢？”杰里约耸了耸肩。“也许是它们咬得太凶……我入这一行，本是来打人的。这些东西，这些蚂蚁，它们来，它们走。这哪是男人该干的营生。”

===Original===
After that he talked frequently of the ants to Holroyd, and whenever they chanced to drift against any speck of humanity in that waste of water and sunshine and distant trees, Holroyd’s improving knowledge of the language enabled him to recognise the ascendant word *Saüba*, more and more completely dominating the whole.

He perceived the ants were becoming interesting, and the nearer he drew to them the more interesting they became. Gerilleau abandoned his old themes almost suddenly, and the Portuguese lieutenant became a conversational figure; he knew something about the leaf-cutting ant, and expanded his knowledge. Gerilleau sometimes rendered what he had to tell to Holroyd. He told of the little workers that swarm and fight, and the big workers that command and rule, and how these latter always crawled to the neck and how their bites drew blood. He told how they cut leaves and made fungus beds, and how their nests in Caracas are sometimes a hundred yards across. Two days the three men spent disputing whether ants have eyes. The discussion grew dangerously heated on the second afternoon, and Holroyd saved the situation by going ashore in a boat to catch ants and see. He captured various specimens and returned, and some had eyes and some hadn’t. Also, they argued, do ants bite or sting?

“Dese ants,” said Gerilleau, after collecting information at a rancho, “have big eyes. They don’t run about blind—not as most ants do. No! Dey get in corners and watch what you do.”

“And they sting?” asked Holroyd.

“Yes. Dey sting. Dere is poison in the sting.” He meditated. “I do not see what men can do against ants. Dey come and go.”

“But these don’t go.”

“They will,” said Gerilleau.

===Chinese===
打那以后他便常常对霍尔罗伊德谈起蚂蚁，而每当他们在这片水光、骄阳与远方林木的荒原之中碰巧撞见一星半点人迹时，霍尔罗伊德日渐长进的语言功底便使他能够辨出那个压倒一切的字眼——萨乌巴（Saüba），它正越来越彻底地主宰着一切。

他觉得这些蚂蚁渐渐变得有趣起来，而且越靠近它们，它们便越发有趣。杰里约几乎是突然间抛弃了那些旧话题，那位葡萄牙副舰长也成了一位谈兴颇健的人物——他对切叶蚁略知一二，便借机大加发挥。杰里约有时把他讲的话转述给霍尔罗伊德。他讲那些成群结队冲锋陷阵的小工蚁，讲那些发号施令、统治全群的大工蚁，讲这些大工蚁如何总爱爬到人的颈项上，如何一口下去便见血。他讲它们怎样切叶、怎样造菌圃，讲它们在加拉加斯（Caracas）的巢穴有的竟有一百码宽。一连两天，三个人都在争一个蚂蚁到底有没有眼睛的问题。第二天下午，那场争论已热得有几分危险，霍尔罗伊德靠划船上岸去捉几只蚂蚁看看，才算救了场。他捉回了各式各样的标本，有的有眼睛，有的没有。他们还争论：蚂蚁到底是咬人，还是蜇人？

“这些蚂蚁，”杰里约在一处农庄打听到一些消息后说，“眼睛很大。它们不像大多数蚂蚁那样瞎闯瞎跑。不！它们躲在角落里，瞧着你的一举一动。”

“那它们蜇人？”霍尔罗伊德问。

“对。它们蜇人。那蜇刺里有毒。”他沉吟了一下。“我看不出人能拿蚂蚁怎么样。它们来，它们走。”

“可这一回的不走啊。”

“它们会走的，”杰里约说。

===Original===
Past Tamandu there is a long low coast of eighty miles without any population, and then one comes to the confluence of the main river and the Batemo arm like a great lake, and then the forest came nearer, came at last intimately near. The character of the channel changes, snags abound, and the *Benjamin Constant* moored by a cable that night, under the very shadow of dark trees.
