那是简的幸福到了顶的时候。她回来时说：“梅纳德先生跟威廉谈过了，太太，说下次大减价的时候，他要让他像那些年轻的店员先生一样接待顾客。要是干得好，一有机会就升他做店员，太太。他得尽量把自己弄得像个绅士，太太；要是弄不像，太太，他说那绝不是因为没有尽力。梅纳德先生可真是看上他了。”

他*是*在出人头地了，简。”我妻子说。

“是的，太太，”简若有所思地说，“他*是*在出人头地。”

说着她叹了一口气。

第二个礼拜天，我正喝着茶，便盘问起我妻子来。“这个礼拜天跟别的时候有什么不一样呢，小女人？出什么事了？你换窗帘了，还是挪过家具了，要不那种说不清道不明的不同到底在哪儿？你没打招呼就换了新发式吗？我明明看出有变化，可怎么也说不清是哪儿变了。”

于是我妻子用她那最沉痛的声调答道：“乔治，”她说，“那个威廉今天压根儿就没上咱们家的门！简在楼上正哭得心都要碎了。”

===Original===
There followed a period of silence. Jane, as I have said, stopped singing about the house, and began to care for our brittle possessions, which struck my wife as being a very sad sign indeed. The next Sunday, and the next, Jane asked to go out, “to walk with William,” and my wife, who never attempts to extort confidences, gave her permission, and asked no questions. On each occasion Jane came back looking flushed and very determined. At last one day she became communicative.

“William is being led away,” she remarked abruptly, with a catching of the breath, apropos of tablecloths. “Yes, m’m. She is a milliner, and she can play on the piano.”

“I thought,” said my wife, “that you went out with him on Sunday.”

“Not out with him, m’m﻿—after him. I walked along by the side of them, and told her he was engaged to me.”

“Dear me, Jane, did you? What did they do?”

“Took no more notice of me than if I was dirt. So I told her she should suffer for it.”

“It could not have been a very agreeable walk, Jane.”

“Not for no parties, ma’am.”

“I wish,” said Jane, “I could play the piano, ma’am. But anyhow, I don’t mean to let *her* get him away from me. She’s older than him, and her hair ain’t gold to the roots, ma’am.”

===Chinese===
此后便是一段沉默的日子。正如我所说，简不再满屋子唱歌，开始爱惜起我们家那些易碎的东西来，这在我妻子看来，是一个很不妙的征兆。第二个礼拜天，再下一个礼拜天，简都请求出门，“跟威廉散步去”，我妻子从不肯逼问别人的心事，便准了她，一字未问。每次回来，简都涨红着脸，神色十分坚决。终于有一天，她肯开口了。

“威廉正被人拐跑呢，”她猝然冒出一句，喘了一口粗气，说的当儿正在收拾桌布。“是的，太太。她是个做女帽的，还会弹钢琴。”

“我还以为，”我妻子说，“礼拜天你跟他一起出去呢。”

“不是一起出去，太太——是追出去。我沿着他们俩旁边走，告诉她他已经跟我订了婚。”

“天哪，简，你真这么做了？他们怎么着？”

“理都不理我，当我是地上一摊泥。我就告诉她，她要为此付出代价。”

“这一趟散步怕是没什么意思吧，简。”

“对谁都没意思，太太。”

“我倒真希望，”简说，“我会弹钢琴，太太。可不管怎样，我不打算让*她*把他从我手里抢走。她比他年纪大，她的头发根子也不是金色的呢，太太。”

===Original===
It was on the August Bank Holiday that the crisis came. We do not clearly know the details of the fray, but only such fragments as poor Jane let fall. She came home dusty, excited, and with her heart hot within her.

The milliner’s mother, the milliner, and William had made a party to the Art Museum at South Kensington, I think. Anyhow, Jane had calmly but firmly accosted them somewhere in the streets, and asserted her right to what, in spite of the consensus of literature, she held to be her inalienable property. She did, I think, go so far as to lay hands on him. They dealt with her in a crushingly superior way. They “called a cab.” There was a “scene,” William being pulled away into the four-wheeler by his future wife and mother-in-law from the reluctant hands of our discarded Jane. There were threats of giving her “in charge.”

“My poor Jane!” said my wife, mincing veal as though she was mincing William. “It’s a shame of them. I would think no more of him. He is not worthy of you.”

“No, m’m,” said Jane. “He *is* weak.

“But it’s that woman has done it,” said Jane. She was never known to bring herself to pronounce “that woman’s” name or to admit her girlishness. “I can’t think what minds some women must have﻿—to try and get a girl’s young man away from her. But there, it only hurts to talk about it,” said Jane.

===Chinese===
正是八月银行假日那天，事情闹到了极点。这场风波的详情我们不大清楚，只零碎地从可怜的简嘴里听见一些。她回家时一身尘土，激动不已，心里烧着一团火。

那做女帽的之母、那做女帽的，还有威廉，三人结伴要去南肯辛顿（South Kensington）的艺术博物馆，大概是。反正简在街上某个地方冷静而坚决地把他们拦了下来，主张她对——尽管文学作品的众口一词另有所云——她所认为不可剥夺的属于自己的财物之权。我想，她甚至动手抓住了他。对方以一种居高临下、压得人喘不过气来的态度来对付她。他们“叫了一辆马车”。上演了一出“好戏”，威廉被他未来的妻子和岳母从我们那位已被弃的简不肯松开的手里硬拽开，塞进了那辆四轮马车。还威胁说要“把她交给警察”。

“我可怜的简！”我妻子说，剁着小牛肉，仿佛剁的就是威廉。“他们太不要脸了。你别再想他了。他不配你。”

“是不配，太太，”简说，“他*是*软弱。

“可这是那个女人干的好事，”简说。她从不肯——别人也见她不肯——把“那个女人”的名字说出口，也不肯承认对方年轻漂亮。“我真想不通有些女人是长着什么样的心肝——竟想把一个姑娘的小伙子从她身边拐走。可说出来也只是徒增伤痛罢了，”简说。

===Original===
Thereafter our house rested from William. But there was something in the manner of Jane’s scrubbing the front doorstep or sweeping out the rooms, a certain viciousness, that persuaded me that the story had not yet ended.

“Please, m’m, may I go and see a wedding tomorrow?” said Jane one day.

My wife knew by instinct whose wedding. “Do you think it is wise, Jane?” she said.

“I would like to see the last of him,” said Jane.

“My dear,” said my wife, fluttering into my room about twenty minutes after Jane had started, “Jane has been to the boot-hole and taken all the left-off boots and shoes, and gone off to the wedding with them in a bag. Surely she cannot mean﻿—”

“Jane,” I said, “is developing character. Let us hope for the best.”

Jane came back with a pale, hard face. All the boots seemed to be still in her bag, at which my wife heaved a premature sigh of relief. We heard her go upstairs and replace the boots with considerable emphasis.

===Chinese===
此后我们这所房子总算歇下了威廉这个名字。可简擦门前台阶、扫屋子时那股劲儿里，带着一种说不出的狠劲，让我心里认定：这事还没完。

“请问，太太，明天我能去看一场婚礼吗？”有一天简说。

我妻子凭本能就知道是谁的婚礼。“你觉得这样妥当吗，简？”她说。

“我想看着他最后一眼。”简说。

“亲爱的，”简出门后约莫二十分钟，我妻子慌慌张张地跑进我房间，“简到放鞋的杂物间，把所有不穿的旧鞋旧靴都收走了，装在一个袋子里带去婚礼。她总不至于要——”

“简嘛，”我说，“是在养成她的性子。咱们还是往好处想吧。”

简回来了，脸色苍白，神情冷峻。那些靴子好像还都在她袋子里，我妻子不由得过早地松了一口气。我们听见她上楼，把那些靴子砰砰地一一放回原处。

===Original===
“Quite a crowd at the wedding, ma’am,” she said presently, in a purely conversational style, sitting in our little kitchen, and scrubbing the potatoes; “and such a lovely day for them.” She proceeded to numerous other details, clearly avoiding some cardinal incident.

“It was all extremely respectable and nice, ma’am; but *her* father didn’t wear a black coat, and looked quite out of place, ma’am. Mr. Piddingquirk﻿—”

“*Who?*”

“Mr. Piddingquirk﻿—William that was, ma’am﻿—had white gloves, and a coat like a clergyman, and a lovely chrysanthemum. He looked so nice, ma’am. And there was red carpet down, just like for gentlefolks. And they say he gave the clerk four shillings, ma’am. It was a real kerridge they had﻿—not a fly. When they came out of church there was rice-throwing, and her two little sisters dropping dead flowers. And someone threw a slipper, and then I threw a boot﻿—”

“Threw a *boot*, Jane!”

“Yes, ma’am. Aimed at her. But it hit *him*. Yes, ma’am, hard. Gev him a black eye, I should think. I only threw that one. I hadn’t the heart to try again. All the little boys cheered when it hit him.”

After an interval﻿—“I am sorry the boot hit *him*.”

Another pause. The potatoes were being scrubbed violently. “He always *was* a bit above me, you know, ma’am. And he was led away.”

===Chinese===
“婚礼上人可真不少，太太，”过了一阵她以一种纯属闲谈的口吻说道，坐在我们家小厨房里刷着土豆，“天气也好得很，正配他们。”她又往下讲了一连串细节，显然有意避开某个要紧的关节。

“全场都体面极了，也舒服极了，太太；只是*她*父亲没穿黑外套，看着格格不入，太太。皮丁柯克先生（Mr. Piddingquirk）——”

“谁？”

“皮丁柯克先生——就是从前的威廉，太太——戴着白手套，穿着像牧师一样的袍子，胸前别着一朵漂亮的菊花。他那模样可真俊，太太。还铺了红地毯呢，跟给正经阔人家的一样。听说他给了教堂执事四先令，太太。他们坐的可是真马车——不是那种出租小马车。他们从教堂出来时有人撒米，她那两个小妹妹撒着枯花。还有人扔了一只拖鞋，于是我就扔了一只靴子——”

“扔了一只*靴子*，简！”

“是的，太太。我瞄的是她。可砸到的是*他*。是的，太太，砸得结结实实。给他砸出一只乌青眼，我估摸着。我就扔了那一只。我没那心思再扔第二回。砸中他的时候，一帮小男孩全欢呼起来。”

隔了一会儿——“靴子砸的是*他*，我心里过意不去。”

又顿了顿。土豆被刷得哗哗作响。“他本来就比我*高*那么一截，您是知道的，太太。他是被人带坏的。”

===Original===
The potatoes were more than finished. Jane rose sharply with a sigh, and rapped the basin down on the table.

“I don’t care,” she said. “I don’t care a rap. He will find out his mistake yet. It serves me right. I was stuck up about him. I ought not to have looked so high. And I am glad things are as things are.”

My wife was in the kitchen, seeing to the higher cookery. After the confession of the boot-throwing, she must have watched poor Jane fuming with a certain dismay in those brown eyes of hers. But I imagine they softened again very quickly, and then Jane’s must have met them.

“Oh, ma’am,” said Jane, with an astonishing change of note, “think of all that *might* have been! Oh, ma’am, I *could* have been so happy! I ought to have known, but I didn’t know﻿ ﻿… You’re very kind to let me talk to you, ma’am﻿ ﻿… for it’s hard on me, ma’am﻿ ﻿… it’s har-r-r-r-d﻿—”

And I gather that Euphemia so far forgot herself as to let Jane sob out some of the fullness of her heart on a sympathetic shoulder. My Euphemia, thank Heaven, has never properly grasped the importance of “keeping up her position.” And since that fit of weeping, much of the accent of bitterness has gone out of Jane’s scrubbing and brush work.

Indeed, something passed the other day with the butcher-boy﻿—but that scarcely belongs to this story. However, Jane is young still, and time and change are at work with her. We all have our sorrows, but I do not believe very much in the existence of sorrows that never heal.

===Chinese===
土豆早就刷得不能再刷了。简叹了一声，猛地站起身，把盆子砰一声搁到桌上。

“我不在乎，”她说，“我一点都不在乎。他早晚有后悔的那一天。我也是活该。我当初把他看得太高，眼高手低。如今这样，我反倒高兴。”

我妻子正在厨房里料理那较高深的烹饪。听完了扔靴子的自白之后，她那双棕色的眼睛望着可怜的简在那儿愤愤不平，一定是带着几分心疼的。可我想，那目光很快又柔和了下来，那时简的眼睛便迎上了她的眼睛。

“噢，太太，”简说，腔调一下子变得令人吃惊，“您想想，那一切*原本*可以多么美好！噢，太太，我*本可以*那么幸福的！我早该知道的，可我那时不懂……您真是太好了，肯让我对您说这些，太太……因为我心里苦啊，太太……苦——苦——苦啊——”

我揣想，欧菲米娅竟一时忘了身份，由着简在她那感同身受的肩头把一腔心事抽抽搭搭哭了出来。我这位欧菲米娅，谢天谢地，从来没真正懂得“端着自家身份”有多么要紧。自打那一通痛哭之后，简刷锅扫地那股狠劲儿里的怨毒，去了大半。

说起来，前些日子送肉的伙计那儿又有点事儿——可那已不太属于本篇的故事了。不过简年纪还轻，光阴与变故都在她身上悄悄做工。人人都有自己的伤心事，但我并不怎么相信世上有那种永无愈期的伤痛。

### I / 一

===Original===
The young lieutenant lay beside the war correspondent and admired the idyllic calm of the enemy’s lines through his field-glass.
“So far as I can see,” he said, at last, “one man.”
“What’s he doing?” asked the war correspondent.
“Field-glass at us,” said the young lieutenant.
“And this is war!”
“No,” said the young lieutenant; “it’s Bloch.”
“The game’s a draw.”
“No! They’ve got to win or else they lose. A draw’s a win for our side.”
They had discussed the political situation fifty times or so, and the war correspondent was weary of it. He stretched out his limbs. “Aaai s’pose it *is*!” he yawned.
“*Flut!*”
“What was that?”
“Shot at us.”
The war correspondent shifted to a slightly lower position. “No one shot at him,” he complained.
“I wonder if they think we shall get so bored we shall go home?”
The war correspondent made no reply.
“There’s the harvest, of course…”

===Chinese===
年轻的陆军中尉躺在战地记者身旁，透过望远镜端详着敌方阵线上那田园诗般的宁静。
“就我所见，”他终于开口道，“只有一个人。”
“他在干什么？”战地记者问。
“在拿望远镜看我们，”年轻的中尉说。
“这就是战争！”
“不，”年轻的中尉说，“这是布洛赫（Bloch）。”
“这局棋算和了。”
“不！他们要么赢，要么就是输。和局便是我们这边赢。”
政治局势这一套他们已讨论过五十来遍，战地记者早就腻了。他伸展了一下四肢。“我——想也是吧！”他打了个哈欠。
“*嗖！*”
“那是什么？”
“朝我们开的枪。”
战地记者挪了挪身子，换到稍低一点的位置。“没人朝他开枪，”他抱怨道。
“你说他们是不是想着，把我们熬得无聊透顶，自个儿就卷铺盖回家了？”
战地记者没有作声。
“当然啦，还有庄稼要收……”

===Original===
They had been there a month. Since the first brisk movements after the declaration of war things had gone slower and slower, until it seemed as though the whole machine of events must have run down. To begin with, they had had almost a scampering time; the invader had come across the frontier on the very dawn of the war in half a dozen parallel columns behind a cloud of cyclists and cavalry, with a general air of coming straight on the capital, and the defender horsemen had held him up, and peppered him and forced him to open out to outflank, and had then bolted to the next position in the most approved style, for a couple of days, until in the afternoon, bump! they had the invader against their prepared lines of defense. He did not suffer so much as had been hoped and expected: he was coming on, it seemed with his eyes open, his scouts winded the guns, and down he sat at once without the shadow of an attack and began grubbing trenches for himself, as though he meant to sit down there to the very end of time. He was slow, but much more wary than the world had been led to expect, and he kept convoys tucked in and shielded his slow marching infantry sufficiently well to prevent any heavy adverse scoring.

===Chinese===
他们驻扎在这里已经一个月了。开战之初那阵利落的调动之后，战事便越来越迟缓，到最后简直让人觉得，整部时事的机器仿佛已经发条走尽。起初，他们几乎过了一段马不停蹄的日子；侵略者在大战揭幕的那个黎明便越过边境，兵分六路，齐头并进，前面是一大片自行车兵和骑兵作前导，一副直扑首都的架势；防守一方的骑兵将他阻挡住，向他连连射击，迫使他展开队列迂回包抄，随后又以最标准的姿态，一溜烟撤往下一道阵地，如此折腾了两日，直到某天下午，砰！他们便将侵略者顶在了预先构筑好的防线前。可敌军所受的损失并不如人们所希望、所预料的那样惨重：它一路压上来，似乎是睁着眼睛、心里有数的，它的侦察兵嗅到了大炮的气味，便毫不迟疑地坐定下来，连一次像样的进攻的影子都没有，就地挖起堑壕来，仿佛打算就这么一直蹲到天荒地老。它行动迟缓，却远比世人被引导着去预期的要谨慎得多，它把辎重车队藏得严严实实，又把那慢吞吞推进的步兵掩护得相当周到，足以避免任何重大的折损。

===Original===
“But he ought to attack,” the young lieutenant had insisted.
“He’ll attack us at dawn, somewhere along the lines. You’ll get the bayonets coming into the trenches just about when you can see,” the war correspondent had held until a week ago.
The young lieutenant winked when he said that.
When one early morning the men the defenders sent to lie out five hundred yards before the trenches, with a view to the unexpected emptying of magazines into any night attack, gave way to causeless panic and blazed away at nothing for ten minutes, the war correspondent understood the meaning of that wink.

===Chinese===
“可他总该进攻吧，”年轻的中尉曾一口咬定。
“他会在拂晓时分沿防线某处进攻我们。等到天色刚能看清的时候，你就会看见刺刀插进堑壕里来了，”直到一周以前，战地记者都还这样断言。
中尉当时听他这么说，眨了眨眼。
直到有一天清晨，防守方派到堑壕前方五百码处匍匐潜伏、准备给任何夜袭来个出其不意的弹匣扫射的士兵们，莫名其妙地一阵惊慌，对着空气胡乱猛射了十分钟，战地记者才明白那一眨眼是什么意思。

===Original===
“What would you do if you were the enemy?” said the war correspondent, suddenly.
“If I had men like I’ve got now?”
“Yes.”
“Take those trenches.”
“How?”
“Oh—dodges! Crawl out halfway at night before moonrise and get into touch with the chaps we send out. Blaze at ’em if they tried to shift, and so bag some of ’em in the daylight. Learn that patch of ground by heart, lie all day in squatty holes, and come on nearer next night. There’s a bit over there, lumpy ground, where they could get across to rushing distance—easy. In a night or so. It would be a mere game for our fellows; it’s what they’re made for… Guns? Shrapnel and stuff wouldn’t stop good men who meant business.”

===Chinese===
“你要是敌人，你会怎么办？”战地记者忽然问。
“要是我的兵跟我手底下这些一样？”
“对。”
“拿下那些堑壕。”
“怎么拿下？”
“哦——使花招！月升之前半夜里匍匐爬出一半路，跟我们派出去的人接上火。他们一动就朝他们猛扫，这样天亮以后就能撂倒几个。把那片地段背得烂熟，白天蹲在浅坑里躺着，第二天夜里再凑近一些。那边有一小块地方，地面疙疙瘩瘩的，他们可以从那儿一直摸到冲锋的距离——轻而易举。一两个夜晚的工夫。这对咱们弟兄不过是小孩子的游戏；他们天生就是干这个的……大炮？榴霰弹那一套，挡不住真心要上的人。”

===Original===
“Why don’t *they* do that?”
“Their men aren’t brutes enough: that’s the trouble. They’re a crowd of devitalized townsmen, and that’s the truth of the matter. They’re clerks, they’re factory hands, they’re students, they’re civilized men. They can write, they can talk, they can make and do all sorts of things, but they’re poor amateurs at war. They’ve got no physical staying power, and that’s the whole thing. They’ve never slept in the open one night in their lives; they’ve never drunk anything but the purest water-company water; they’ve never gone short of three meals a day since they left their feeding-bottles. Half their cavalry never cocked leg over horse till it enlisted six months ago. They ride their horses as though they were bicycles—you watch ’em! They’re fools at the game, and they know it. Our boys of fourteen can give their grown men points… Very well—”

===Chinese===
“那*他们*怎么不这么干？”
“他们的人不够凶悍：毛病就在这儿。他们是一群没精打采的城里人，事情的真相处就在于此。他们是店员，是工厂工人，是学生，是文明人。他们会写会算，能说会道，会造会做各式各样的东西，可一打仗就是一群蹩脚的门外汉。他们身上没有一点体力上的韧劲，而这一点才是全部的要害。他们一辈子没有在露天里睡过一夜；他们喝的，除了自来水公司最最纯净的水，再没旁的；自打离开奶瓶之后，他们就没少过一日三餐。他们的骑兵有一半，直到六个月前入伍，才头一回跨上马背。他们骑马就跟骑自行车似的——你瞧着吧！这行当里他们是蠢货，他们自己也心知肚明。咱们十四岁的小子，能让他们那些成年汉子几步棋都不在话下……好极了——”

===Original===
The war correspondent mused on his face with his nose between his knuckles.
“If a decent civilization,” he said, “cannot produce better men for war than—”
He stopped with belated politeness.
“I mean—”
“Than our open-air life,” said the young lieutenant, politely.
“Exactly,” said the war correspondent. “Then civilization has to stop.”
“It looks like it,” the young lieutenant admitted.
“Civilization has science, you know,” said the war correspondent. “It invented and it makes the rifles and guns and things you use.”
“Which our nice healthy hunters and stockmen and so on, rowdy-dowdy cowpunchers and negro-whackers, can use ten times better than—*What’s that?*”

===Chinese===
战地记者把鼻子抵在两根指节之间，沉思着。
“如果一种像样的文明，”他说，“培养不出更好的士兵，胜过——”
他戛然而止，带了几分迟来的客气。
“我的意思是——”
“胜过我们这种户外生活，”年轻的中尉客气地接话。
“一点不错，”战地记者说，“那么文明就得停下脚步了。”
“看起来是这么回事，”年轻的中尉承认道。
“要知道，文明有科学，”战地记者说，“是它发明、制造了你手上所用的步枪、大炮那些东西。”
“而我们这些体魄强健的猎人、牧人什么的，吵吵嚷嚷的赶牛汉、拿鞭子抽黑人的家伙，用起这些东西来，可比——*那是什么？*”

===Original===
“What?” said the war correspondent, and then seeing his companion busy with his field-glass he produced his own: “Where?” said the war correspondent, sweeping the enemy’s lines.
“It’s nothing” said the young lieutenant, still looking.
“What’s nothing?”
The young lieutenant put down his glass and pointed. “I thought I saw something there, behind the stems of those trees. Something black. What it was I don’t know.”
The war correspondent tried to get even by intense scrutiny.
“It wasn’t anything” said the young lieutenant, rolling over to regard the darkling evening sky, and generalized: “There never will be anything any more forever. Unless—”
The war correspondent looked inquiry.
“They may get their stomachs wrong, or something—living without proper drains.”

===Chinese===
“什么？”战地记者问，接着见同伴正举着望远镜端详，便也掏出自己的：“在哪儿？”战地记者一边问，一边扫视着敌方阵线。
“没什么，”年轻的中尉说着，仍在望着。
“没什么是什么？”
年轻的中尉放下望远镜，伸手一指。“我刚才好像看见那边有什么东西，在那些树的树干后面。黑乎乎的。到底是什么，我说不上来。”
战地记者想扳回一城，便使劲细看。
“什么也不是，”年轻的中尉说着，翻过身去凝视渐暗的暮色苍穹，并泛泛地断言道，“往后永远再也不会有什么了。除非——”
战地记者投去一道探询的目光。
“他们也许会把肠胃搞坏，诸如此类——住的地方连像样的下水道都没有。”

===Original===
A sound of bugles came from the tents behind. The war correspondent slid backward down the sand and stood up. “Boom!” came from somewhere far away to the left. “Halloa!” he said, hesitated, and crawled back to peer again. “Firing at this time is jolly bad manners.”
The young lieutenant was incommunicive again for a space.
Then he pointed to the distant clump of trees again. “One of our big guns. They were firing at that,” he said.
“The thing that wasn’t anything?”
“Something over there, anyhow.”
Both men were silent, peering through their glasses for a space. “Just when it’s twilight,” the lieutenant complained. He stood up.
“I might stay here a bit,” said the war correspondent.
The lieutenant shook his head. “There is nothing to see,” he apologized, and then went down to where his little squad of sun-brown, loose-limbed men had been yarning in the trench. The war correspondent stood up also, glanced for a moment at the businesslike bustle below him, gave perhaps twenty seconds to those enigmatical trees again, then turned his face toward the camp.

===Chinese===
帐后人声之外，传来一阵军号。战地记者从沙地上溜了下来，站起身。“轰！”一声从左边远处某处传来。“哎哟！”他喊了一声，迟疑片刻，又爬回去再望。“这会儿开火，真是大大地不讲规矩。”
年轻的中尉又沉默了一阵。
然后他又一次指向远处那一丛树木。“是我们的一门大炮。在朝那个开火，”他说。
“朝那个什么也不是的东西？”
“不管怎么说，那边是有点什么。”
两人都默不作声，举着望远镜望了一阵。“偏偏赶上天色擦黑的当口，”中尉抱怨道。他站起身。
“我倒可以在这儿多待会儿，”战地记者说。
中尉摇摇头。“没什么可看的，”他带着歉意说，随即走下去，到了他那小小一队晒得黝黑、手脚利落的人马跟前——他们一直在堑壕里闲扯着。战地记者也站起身，朝下面那副干练的忙碌扫了一眼，又给了那片叫人捉摸不透的树林大约二十秒的工夫，便转身朝营地走去。

===Original===
He found himself wondering whether his editor would consider the story of how somebody thought he saw something black behind a clump of trees, and how a gun was fired at this illusion by somebody else, too trivial for public consultation.
“It’s the only gleam of a shadow of interest,” said the war correspondent, “for ten whole days.”
“No,” he said, presently; “I’ll write that other article, ‘Is War Played Out?’”
He surveyed the darkling lines in perspective, the tangle of trenches one behind another, one commanding another, which the defender had made ready. The shadows and mists swallowed up their receding contours, and here and there a lantern gleamed, and here and there knots of men were busy about small fires.
“No troops on earth could do it,” he said…

===Chinese===
他心里琢磨着：有人觉得他看见一丛树后面有团黑乎乎的东西，又有人朝这幻影开了一炮——这样的故事，他那位主编会不会嫌它鸡毛蒜皮，不值得刊登出来呢。
“这已经是整整十天里，唯一一丝一线的看点了，”战地记者说。
“不，”过了一会儿他说，“我还是写那另一篇吧——《战争是不是玩儿完了？》”
他放眼望去，打量着渐暗的防线纵深——防守方所构筑的那一道套一道、一道俯瞰着另一道的纵横堑壕。阴影与薄雾吞没了堑壕层层退去的轮廓，这里那里，有灯笼闪着光，这里那里，三五成群的士兵在小小的火堆旁忙碌着。
“天底下没有哪支军队能攻得下来，”他说……

===Original===
He was depressed. He believed that there were other things in life better worth having than proficiency in war; he believed that in the heart of civilization, for all its stresses, its crushing concentrations of forces, its injustice and suffering, there lay something that might be the hope of the world, and the idea that any people by living in the open air, hunting perpetually, losing touch with books and art and all the things that intensify life, might hope to resist and break that great development to the end of time, jarred on his civilized soul.
Apt to his thought came a file of defender soldiers and passed him in the gleam of a swinging lamp that marked the way.
He glanced at their red-lit faces, and one shone out for a moment, a common type of face in the defender’s ranks: ill-shaped nose, sensuous lips, bright clear eyes full of alert cunning, slouch hat cocked on one side and adorned with the peacock’s plume of the rustic Don Juan turned soldier, a hard brown skin, a sinewy frame, an open, tireless stride, and a master’s grip on the rifle.
The war correspondent returned their salutations and went on his way.
“Louts,” he whispered. “Cunning, elementary louts. And they are going to beat the townsmen at the game of war!”
From the red glow among the nearer tents came first one and then half a dozen hearty voices, bawling in a drawling unison the words of a particularly slab and sentimental patriotic song.
“Oh, *go* it!” muttered the war correspondent, bitterly.

## The Lord of the Dynamos / 发电机之主

===Original===
The chief attendant of the three dynamos that buzzed and rattled at Camberwell, and kept the electric railway going, came out of Yorkshire, and his name was James Holroyd. He was a practical electrician, but fond of whisky, a heavy, red-haired brute with irregular teeth. He doubted the existence of the Deity, but accepted Carnot’s cycle, and he had read Shakespeare and found him weak in chemistry. His helper came out of the mysterious East, and his name was Azuma-zi. But Holroyd called him Pooh-bah. Holroyd liked a nigger help because he would stand kicking—a habit with Holroyd—and did not pry into the machinery and try to learn the ways of it. Certain odd possibilities of the negro mind brought into abrupt contact with the crown of our civilisation Holroyd never fully realised, though just at the end he got some inkling of them.

To define Azuma-zi was beyond ethnology. He was, perhaps, more negroid than anything else, though his hair was curly rather than frizzy, and his nose had a bridge. Moreover, his skin was brown rather than black, and the whites of his eyes were yellow. His broad cheekbones and narrow chin gave his face something of the viperine V. His head, too, was broad behind, and low and narrow at the forehead, as if his brain had been twisted round in the reverse way to a European’s. He was short of stature and still shorter of English. In conversation he made numerous odd noises of no known marketable value, and his infrequent words were carved and wrought into heraldic grotesqueness. Holroyd tried to elucidate his religious beliefs, and—especially after whisky—lectured to him against superstition and missionaries. Azuma-zi, however, shirked the discussion of his gods, even though he was kicked for it.

Azuma-zi had come, clad in white but insufficient raiment, out of the stokehole of the *Lord Clive*, from the Straits Settlements and beyond, into London. He had heard even in his youth of the greatness and riches of London, where all the women are white and fair, and even the beggars in the streets are white, and he had arrived, with newly-earned gold coins in his pocket, to worship at the shrine of civilisation. The day of his landing was a dismal one; the sky was dun, and a wind-worried drizzle filtered down to the greasy streets, but he plunged boldly into the delights of Shadwell, and was presently cast up, shattered in health, civilised in costume, penniless, and, except in matters of the direst necessity, practically a dumb animal, to toil for James Holroyd, and to be bullied by him in the dynamo shed at Camberwell. And to James Holroyd bullying was a labour of love.

===Chinese===
坎伯韦尔（Camberwell）那三台嗡嗡作响、哐啷作响、维持着电气铁路运转的发电机，其主管是约克郡（Yorkshire）来的人，名叫詹姆斯·霍尔罗伊德（James Holroyd）。他是个务实的电工，却嗜饮威士忌，是个红头发、身形粗壮、牙齿参差不齐的莽汉。他怀疑神明的存在，却信奉卡诺循环（Carnot’s cycle）；他读过莎士比亚，觉得此人在化学方面颇为薄弱。他的助手来自神秘的东方，名叫阿祖玛齐（Azuma-zi）。可霍尔罗伊德管他叫“扑哈”（Pooh-bah）。霍尔罗伊德喜欢使唤黑鬼帮工，因为这种人挨得住踢——踢人是霍尔罗伊德的老习惯——也不会窥探机器、想弄清其中的门道。黑人那颗心灵与我国文明的冠冕骤然相触，其中潜藏的某些古怪可能性，霍尔罗伊德始终未能充分领悟，虽然到了最后，他总算隐约察觉到了一丝。

要给阿祖玛齐下个准确定义，超出了民族学的范畴。他也许更偏向黑种人血统，虽说他的头发是卷曲的而非纠结成团的，鼻梁也还算高。况且他的皮肤是棕色而非黑色，眼白则泛黄。宽阔的颧骨与尖窄的下巴，使他的脸呈现出几分蝰蛇似的V形。他的脑袋也是后脑宽阔、前额低窄，仿佛他的脑浆与欧洲人相反地拧了个个儿。他身材矮小，英语则更加蹩脚。说话时他会发出许多古怪的、毫无市场价值的声响，偶尔吐出的几个词，则被雕琢锻造成纹章式的怪诞模样。霍尔罗伊德曾试图理清他的宗教信仰，并且——尤其是灌下威士忌之后——向他训诫，反对迷信与传教士。然而阿祖玛齐总是回避谈论他的那些神，哪怕为此挨踢也不肯改口。

阿祖玛齐是从“克莱夫勋爵号”（*Lord Clive*）的锅炉舱里出来的，身上穿着白色却嫌单薄的衣裳，从海峡殖民地（Straits Settlements）乃至更远的地方，来到了伦敦。他自幼便听说过伦敦的伟大与富庶——那里的女人都是白皮肤、美貌的，连街上的乞丐也是白人——他揣着新挣来的金币，前来文明的神殿朝拜。他登岸那天是个阴郁的日子；天空灰沉沉的，被风吹得零乱的毛毛雨渗落到油腻腻的街上。他却一头扎进沙德威尔（Shadwell）的种种“乐事”之中，不久便被抛上了岸——身体垮了、装束倒是“文明”了、身无分文，而且除却最紧迫的需要之外，简直就是一头哑巴牲口——只为詹姆斯·霍尔罗伊德卖命，在坎伯韦尔的发电机棚里任他欺凌。而对詹姆斯·霍尔罗伊德而言，欺凌人正是一桩赏心乐事。

===Original===
There were three dynamos with their engines at Camberwell. The two that have been there since the beginning are small machines; the larger one was new. The smaller machines made a reasonable noise; their straps hummed over the drums, every now and then the brushes buzzed and fizzled, and the air churned steadily, whoo! whoo! whoo! between their poles. One was loose in its foundations and kept the shed vibrating. But the big dynamo drowned these little noises altogether with the sustained drone of its iron core, which somehow set part of the ironwork humming. The place made the visitor’s head reel with the throb, throb, throb of the engines, the rotation of the big wheels, the spinning ball-valves, the occasional spittings of the steam, and over all the deep, unceasing, surging note of the big dynamo. This last noise was from an engineering point of view a defect, but Azuma-zi accounted it unto the monster for mightiness and pride.

If it were possible we would have the noises of that shed always about the reader as he reads, we would tell all our story to such an accompaniment. It was a steady stream of din, from which the ear picked out first one thread and then another; there was the intermittent snorting, panting, and seething of the steam engines, the suck and thud of their pistons, the dull beat on the air as the spokes of the great driving wheels came round, a note the leather straps made as they ran tighter and looser, and a fretful tumult from the dynamos; and, over all, sometimes inaudible, as the ear tired of it, and then creeping back upon the senses again, was this trombone note of the big machine. The floor never felt steady and quiet beneath one’s feet, but quivered and jarred. It was a confusing, unsteady place, and enough to send anyone’s thoughts jerking into odd zigzags. And for three months, while the big strike of the engineers was in progress, Holroyd, who was a blackleg, and Azuma-zi, who was a mere black, were never out of the stir and eddy of it, but slept and fed in the little wooden shanty between the shed and the gates.

Holroyd delivered a theological lecture on the text of his big machine soon after Azuma-zi came. He had to shout to be heard in the din. “Look at that,” said Holroyd; “where’s your ’eathen idol to match ’im?” And Azuma-zi looked. For a moment Holroyd was inaudible, and then Azuma-zi heard: “Kill a hundred men. Twelve percent, on the ordinary shares,” said Holroyd, “and that’s something like a Gord.”

===Chinese===
坎伯韦尔有三台发电机，各配一台引擎。最初就在那里的两台是小机器；那台大些的是新装的。小机器发出的噪音还算合理：传动带在鼓轮上嗡嗡作响，电刷时不时发出嗡嗡和噼啪声，空气在两极之间稳定地搅动，呼！呼！呼！有一台的地脚松了，震得整座棚子直颤。可大发电机以其铁芯持续不断的嗡鸣，把这些细碎的声响一概淹没了，那嗡鸣 somehow 又引得一部分铁件也跟着共鸣。这地方叫来访者头晕目眩——引擎的突、突、突，大轮子的旋转，飞旋的球阀，蒸汽偶尔的噗噗作响，还有压过一切的那大发电机深沉、不息、汹涌的鸣响。最后这一种噪声，从工程的角度看是个缺陷，可阿祖玛齐却把它算作这怪物之所以为怪物的威风与骄傲。

倘若可能，我们真愿让读者读这篇故事时，那棚里的声响始终萦绕在他耳畔，我们愿以这样的伴奏来讲述整个故事。那是一片绵延不绝的喧嚣之流，耳朵从中先撷出这一股、又撷出那一股；有蒸汽机断断续续的喷气、喘息和沸腾，活塞的吸气和砰击，大驱动轮的轮辐转过来时对空气沉闷的拍打，皮带给紧一阵松一阵时奏出的某个调子，还有发电机们发出的烦躁的喧闹；而压过一切的，便是这大机器长号似的鸣响，有时耳朵听倦了便听不见它，可它接着又悄悄爬回到感官上来。脚底下的地面从来不曾稳当安静过，而是颤动着、震晃着。这是个叫人迷糊、失稳的地方，足以把任何人的思绪都颠得歪歪扭扭、七拐八折。在那场工程师大罢工进行的三个月里，身为工贼的霍尔罗伊德，和不过是个黑人的阿祖玛齐，从未离开过这番喧嚣扰攘，吃住都在棚子与大门之间那座小木棚里。

阿祖玛齐刚来不久，霍尔罗伊德便以他那台大机器为题，发表了一通神学讲演。在这么嘈杂的环境里，他得扯着嗓子才让人听得见。“瞧这个，”霍尔罗伊德说，“你们那些异教偶像哪个比得上‘他’？”阿祖玛齐便瞧了过去。有一阵子霍尔罗伊德被淹没了听不见，随后阿祖玛齐听见：“能杀一百个人。普通股分红百分之十二，”霍尔罗伊德说，“这才叫名副其实的上帝。”

===Original===
Holroyd was proud of his big dynamo, and expatiated upon its size and power to Azuma-zi until heaven knows what odd currents of thought that and the incessant whirling and shindy set up within the curly black cranium. He would explain in the most graphic manner the dozen or so ways in which a man might be killed by it, and once he gave Azuma-zi a shock as a sample of its quality. After that, in the breathing-times of his labour—it was heavy labour, being not only his own, but most of Holroyd’s—Azuma-zi would sit and watch the big machine. Now and then the brushes would sparkle and spit blue flashes, at which Holroyd would swear, but all the rest was as smooth and rhythmic as breathing. The band ran shouting over the shaft, and ever behind one as one watched was the complacent thud of the piston. So it lived all day in this big airy shed, with him and Holroyd to wait upon it; not prisoned up and slaving to drive a ship as the other engines he knew—mere captive devils of the British Solomon—had been, but a machine enthroned. Those two smaller dynamos Azuma-zi by force of contrast despised; the large one he privately christened the Lord of the Dynamos. They were fretful and irregular, but the big dynamo was steady. How great it was! How serene and easy in its working! Greater and calmer even than the Buddhas he had seen at Rangoon, and yet not motionless, but living! The great black coils spun, spun, spun, the rings ran round under the brushes, and the deep note of its coil steadied the whole. It affected Azuma-zi queerly.

Azuma-zi was not fond of labour. He would sit about and watch the Lord of the Dynamos while Holroyd went away to persuade the yard porter to get whisky, although his proper place was not in the dynamo shed but behind the engines, and, moreover, if Holroyd caught him skulking he got hit for it with a rod of stout copper wire. He would go and stand close to the colossus, and look up at the great leather band running overhead. There was a black patch on the band that came round, and it pleased him somehow among all the clatter to watch this return again and again. Odd thoughts spun with the whirl of it. Scientific people tell us that savages give souls to rocks and trees—and a machine is a thousand times more alive than a rock or a tree. And Azuma-zi was practically a savage still; the veneer of civilisation lay no deeper than his slop suit, his bruises, and the coal grime on his face and hands. His father before him had worshipped a meteoric stone, kindred blood, it may be, had splashed the broad wheels of Juggernaut.

He took every opportunity Holroyd gave him of touching and handling the great dynamo that was fascinating him. He polished and cleaned it until the metal parts were blinding in the sun. He felt a mysterious sense of service in doing this. He would go up to it and touch its spinning coils gently. The gods he had worshipped were all far away. The people in London hid their gods.

===Chinese===
霍尔罗伊德为他那台大发电机感到自豪，对阿祖玛齐大谈其体积与力量，天知道这一切连同那不息的旋转和喧嚣，在那颗卷发的黑脑壳里激起了怎样古怪的思绪。他会用最活灵活现的方式，讲解一个人被它弄死的十来种法子，有一次还让阿祖玛齐触了一下电，作为它威力的样品。自此之后，每逢劳作的间隙——这劳作沉重得很，不但是他分内的活，大半还是霍尔罗伊德分内的——阿祖玛齐便坐下来，盯着那台大机器。电刷时不时迸出火星、噼啪吐出蓝色的闪光，每逢这时霍尔罗伊德便破口大骂，可其余一切都像呼吸一样平稳而有节奏。传动带在轴上呼啸着跑过，而当人注视着它时，身后始终是活塞那怡然自得的砰砰声。它就这样整日栖息在这宽敞的大棚里，由他和霍尔罗伊德侍奉着；并不像它所熟知的那些引擎——那些不过是英伦所罗门手下区区的囚奴恶魔——被囚禁着做牛做马地推动一艘船，它是登上了宝座的机器。那两台较小的发电机，阿祖玛齐因对比之下而心生鄙视；大的那台，他私下里给它施了洗礼，称作“发电机之主”。那两台小的是浮躁的、不规律的，可这台大发电机却稳如磐石。它是何等伟大啊！运转起来何等从容自如！比他在仰光（Rangoon）所见过的佛像还要高大、还要宁静，可它又并非纹丝不动，而是活生生的！巨大的黑色线圈转啊、转啊、转啊，集电环在电刷下旋转，它那线圈深沉的鸣响稳住了整个世界。它对阿祖玛齐产生了一种古怪的影响。

阿祖玛齐并不爱劳作。每当霍尔罗伊德走开，去哄院子里的搬运工替他打威士忌时，他便坐在一旁守着“发电机之主”——虽然他该待的地方不是发电机棚，而是在引擎背后；况且要是霍尔罗伊德撞见他偷懒，免不了要用一根粗铜丝抽他。他会走到那巨物跟前，仰头望着头顶上方奔行的大皮带。皮带上有一块黑斑，转着转着就转了回来，在一片哐啷声中一遍又一遍地看着它归来，不知怎地叫他心中欢喜。古怪的念头随着它一同旋转。懂科学的人告诉我们，野蛮人会给岩石和树木赋予灵魂——而一台机器，比一块岩石或一棵树要鲜活一千倍。阿祖玛齐实际上仍是个野蛮人；文明的那层虚饰，不过深及他那身成衣、他身上的青肿，以及脸和手上的煤灰罢了。他的父亲在他之前曾崇拜过一块陨石，同宗同脉的血，说不定也曾溅洒在加甘纳特（Juggernaut）宽阔的车轮上。

霍尔罗伊德每给他一次机会，他便去触摸、去摆弄那台令他着迷的大发电机。他把机器擦了又擦，直擦得金属部件在日光下晃得人睁不开眼。做这事时，他心里有一种神秘的侍奉之感。他会走上前去，轻轻抚摸它旋转着的线圈。他从前所崇拜的神祇都已远在天边。伦敦的人们则把他们的神藏了起来。

===Original===
At last his dim feelings grew more distinct, and took shape in thoughts, and at last in acts. When he came into the roaring shed one morning he salaamed to the Lord of the Dynamos, and then, when Holroyd was away, he went and whispered to the thundering machine that he was its servant, and prayed it to have pity on him and save him from Holroyd. As he did so a rare gleam of light came in through the open archway of the throbbing machine-shed, and the Lord of the Dynamos, as he whirled and roared, was radiant with pale gold. Then Azuma-zi knew that his service was acceptable to his Lord. After that he did not feel so lonely as he had done, and he had indeed been very much alone in London. And even when his work-time was over, which was rare, he loitered about the shed.

Then, the next time Holroyd maltreated him, Azuma-zi went presently to the Lord of the Dynamos and whispered, “Thou seest, O my Lord!” and the angry whirr of the machinery seemed to answer him. Thereafter it appeared to him that whenever Holroyd came into the shed a different note came into the sounds of the dynamo. “My Lord bides his time,” said Azuma-zi to himself. “The iniquity of the fool is not yet ripe.” And he waited and watched for the day of reckoning. One day there was evidence of short circuiting, and Holroyd, making an unwary examination—it was in the afternoon—got a rather severe shock. Azuma-zi from behind the engine saw him jump off and curse at the peccant coil.

“He is warned,” said Azuma-zi to himself. “Surely my Lord is very patient.”

===Chinese===
终于，他那模糊的情感渐渐清晰起来，先凝成了念头，继而又化作了行动。一天早晨他走进轰鸣的棚子，朝发电机之主行了一个额手礼，待霍尔罗伊德走开，他便走上前去，对那雷鸣般的机器悄声说，自己是它的仆人，祈求它怜悯他、把他从霍尔罗伊德手里救出来。就在这时，一束难得的光线透过那颤动着的机器棚敞开的拱门射了进来，发电机之主一边旋转轰鸣，一边泛出淡金色的光辉。于是阿祖玛齐明白，他的侍奉已被他的主所悦纳。自那以后，他不再像从前那样觉得孤单了——而他在伦敦，实在是形单影只已极。哪怕收了工——这样的时候本就稀罕——他也在棚子四周流连不去。

后来，霍尔罗伊德又一次虐待了他，阿祖玛齐随即走到发电机之主跟前，悄声说道：“主啊，您看见了！”机器那愤怒的嗡鸣似乎在回答他。此后在他看来，霍尔罗伊德每回走进棚子，发电机的声响里便多出一种不同的调子。“我的主在等候时机，”阿祖玛齐自言自语，“那蠢货的罪孽尚未成熟。”他便等待着、窥伺着那个清算之日。有一天出现了短路的迹象，霍尔罗伊德不当心地前去检查——那是在下午——挨了一记颇重的电击。阿祖玛齐从引擎背后看见他跳开，冲那作怪的线圈破口大骂。

“他受到了警告，”阿祖玛齐对自己说，“我的主真是耐心极了。”

===Original===
Holroyd had at first initiated his “nigger” into such elementary conceptions of the dynamo’s working as would enable him to take temporary charge of the shed in his absence. But when he noticed the manner in which Azuma-zi hung about the monster he became suspicious. He dimly perceived his assistant was “up to something,” and connecting him with the anointing of the coils with oil that had rotted the varnish in one place, he issued an edict, shouted above the confusion of the machinery, “Don’t ’ee go nigh that big dynamo any more, Pooh-bah, or a’ll take thy skin off!” Besides, if it pleased Azuma-zi to be near the big machine, it was plain sense and decency to keep him away from it.

Azuma-zi obeyed at the time, but later he was caught bowing before the Lord of the Dynamos. At which Holroyd twisted his arm and kicked him as he turned to go away. As Azuma-zi presently stood behind the engine and glared at the back of the hated Holroyd, the noises of the machinery took a new rhythm, and sounded like four words in his native tongue.

It is hard to say exactly what madness is. I fancy Azuma-zi was mad. The incessant din and whirl of the dynamo shed may have churned up his little store of knowledge and big store of superstitious fancy, at last, into something akin to frenzy. At any rate, when the idea of making Holroyd a sacrifice to the Dynamo Fetish was thus suggested to him, it filled him with a strange tumult of exultant emotion.

===Chinese===
起初，霍尔罗伊德曾向他那个“黑鬼”传授过一些发电机工作原理的基本概念，好让他在自己外出时临时照看一下棚子。可当他留意到阿祖玛齐在那怪物跟前盘桓的样子，便起了疑心。他隐隐约约地察觉到这个助手“不怀好意”，又把这事同线圈被人涂了油、以致一处清漆被腐蚀了联系起来，于是颁布了一道谕旨，盖过机器的嘈杂声吼道：“你往后不许再挨近那台大发电机了，扑哈，不然我扒了你的皮！”况且，既然阿祖玛齐乐意向那台大机器靠近，那么从情理和体面上讲，自该把他支得远远的。

阿祖玛齐当时应承了下来，可后来又被撞见在发电机之主面前鞠躬行礼。霍尔罗伊德当即拧住他的胳膊，又趁他转身走开时踢了他一脚。待阿祖玛齐回到引擎背后，怒目注视着那个可恨的霍尔罗伊德的后背时，机器的声响换上了一种新的节奏，听上去像是用他的母语说出的四个字。

究竟什么是癫狂，很难说得准。我揣想阿祖玛齐是疯了。发电机棚里不息的喧嚣与旋转，到末了也许真把他那点可怜的知识和满脑子的迷信想象，搅成了一种近于狂乱的东西。无论如何，当把霍尔罗伊德献祭给发电机神物（Dynamo Fetish）这个念头这样被引逗起来之后，他便满心涌起一阵奇异的、狂喜的激荡。

===Original===
That night the two men and their black shadows were alone in the shed together. The shed was lit with one big arc light that winked and flickered purple. The shadows lay black behind the dynamos, the ball governors of the engines whirled from light to darkness, and their pistons beat loud and steady. The world outside seen through the open end of the shed seemed incredibly dim and remote. It seemed absolutely silent, too, since the riot of the machinery drowned every external sound. Far away was the black fence of the yard with grey shadowy houses behind, and above was the deep blue sky and the pale little stars. Azuma-zi suddenly walked across the centre of the shed above which the leather bands were running, and went into the shadow by the big dynamo. Holroyd heard a click, and the spin of the armature changed.

“What are you dewin’ with that switch?” he bawled in surprise. “Han’t I told you—”

Then he saw the set expression of Azuma-zi’s eyes as the Asiatic came out of the shadow towards him.

In another moment the two men were grappling fiercely in front of the great dynamo.

“You coffee-headed fool!” gasped Holroyd, with a brown hand at his throat. “Keep off those contact rings.” In another moment he was tripped and reeling back upon the Lord of the Dynamos. He instinctively loosened his grip upon his antagonist to save himself from the machine.

---

===Chinese===
那天夜里，棚里只有他们两人和他们的黑色影子。棚子由一盏大弧光灯照亮，那灯眨着眼，闪烁着紫色的光。阴影黑沉沉地躺在发电机背后，引擎的离心调速球从光里旋到暗里，活塞则搏动得又响又稳。透过棚子敞开的那一头望出去，外面的世界显得难以置信地朦胧而遥远。它似乎也死寂无声，因为机器的咆哮淹没了外界的一切声响。远处是院子黑色的栅栏，栅栏后面是一排灰蒙蒙的影子似的房屋；头顶上方则是深蓝的天空和几点惨淡的小星星。阿祖玛齐忽然穿过棚子中央——头顶上正有传动带奔行——走进了那台大发电机旁的阴影里。霍尔罗伊德听见咔哒一响，电枢的旋转变了调。

“你捣鼓那个电闸干什么？”他惊诧地大吼。“我不是跟你说过——”

紧接着他看见了阿祖玛齐的眼睛——那双眼睛神情凝固——这个亚洲人正从阴影里朝他走来。

下一个瞬间，两人已在巨大的发电机前猛烈地扭打起来。

“你这咖啡色脑壳的蠢货！”霍尔罗伊德喘着气，一只棕色的手掐住了他的喉咙。“离那些集电环远点。”再一转眼，他已被绊了一跤，踉跄着向后跌向发电机之主。他本能地松开了对手，好让自己不被机器卷进去。

---

===Original===
The messenger, sent in furious haste from the station to find out what had happened in the dynamo shed, met Azuma-zi at the porter’s lodge by the gate. Azuma-zi tried to explain something, but the messenger could make nothing of the black’s incoherent English, and hurried on to the shed. The machines were all noisily at work, and nothing seemed to be disarranged. There was, however, a queer smell of singed hair. Then he saw an odd-looking crumpled mass clinging to the front of the big dynamo, and, approaching, recognised the distorted remains of Holroyd.

The man stared and hesitated a moment. Then he saw the face, and shut his eyes convulsively. He turned on his heel before he opened them, so that he should not see Holroyd again, and went out of the shed to get advice and help.

When Azuma-zi saw Holroyd die in the grip of the Great Dynamo he had been a little scared about the consequences of his act. Yet he felt strangely elated, and knew that the favour of the Lord Dynamo was upon him. His plan was already settled when he met the man coming from the station, and the scientific manager who speedily arrived on the scene jumped at the obvious conclusion of suicide. This expert scarcely noticed Azuma-zi, except to ask a few questions. Did he see Holroyd kill himself? Azuma-zi explained he had been out of sight at the engine furnace until he heard a difference in the noise from the dynamo. It was not a difficult examination, being untinctured by suspicion.

===Chinese===
从车站急如星火地派来、查探发电机棚里究竟出了什么事的人，在大门口的门房处遇见了阿祖玛齐。阿祖玛齐想向他解释点什么，可这信使根本听不懂这黑人语无伦次的英语，便径直赶往棚子。几台机器都在吵吵嚷嚷地运转，似乎什么也没有乱套。不过，有一股烧焦毛发的古怪气味。随即他看见一团圆鼓鼓的、怪模怪样的东西贴在大发电机正面，走近一看，才认出那是霍尔罗伊德变了形的残骸。

那人盯着看，迟疑了片刻。接着他看清了那张脸，便猛地闭上了眼睛。他在睁眼之前先转过身去，免得再看见霍尔罗伊德，然后走出棚子去讨主意、搬救兵。

阿祖玛齐亲眼看见霍尔罗伊德在大发电机的钳制下死去时，对自己的行为会有什么后果，心里多少有些发怵。可他又奇怪地感到振奋，知道发电机之主的恩宠已临到他身上。他在遇见那个从车站来的人之前，计划便已拿定了；而不久便赶到现场的技术主管，一口便认定了那个再明显不过的结论——自杀。这位专家几乎没怎么留意阿祖玛齐，只问了他几个问题。他有没有看见霍尔罗伊德自杀？阿祖玛齐解释说，他一直待在引擎的炉子那边、看不见这边，直到听见发电机的声响有异才过来。这场问询并不难对付，因为它丝毫不带怀疑的色彩。

===Original===
The distorted remains of Holroyd, which the electrician removed from the machine, were hastily covered by the porter with a coffee-stained tablecloth. Somebody, by a happy inspiration, fetched a medical man. The expert was chiefly anxious to get the machine at work again, for seven or eight trains had stopped midway in the stuffy tunnels of the electric railway. Azuma-zi, answering or misunderstanding the questions of the people who had by authority or impudence come into the shed, was presently sent back to the stokehole by the scientific manager. Of course a crowd collected outside the gates of the yard—a crowd, for no known reason, always hovers for a day or two near the scene of a sudden death in London—two or three reporters percolated somehow into the engine-shed, and one even got to Azuma-zi; but the scientific expert cleared them out again, being himself an amateur journalist.

Presently the body was carried away, and public interest departed with it. Azuma-zi remained very quietly at his furnace, seeing over and over again in the coals a figure that wriggled violently and became still. An hour after the murder, to anyone coming into the shed it would have looked exactly as if nothing remarkable had ever happened there. Peeping presently from his engine-room the black saw the Lord Dynamo spin and whirl beside his little brothers, and the driving wheels were beating round, and the steam in the pistons went thud, thud, exactly as it had been earlier in the evening. After all, from the mechanical point of view, it had been a most insignificant incident—the mere temporary deflection of a current. But now the slender form and slender shadow of the scientific manager replaced the sturdy outline of Holroyd travelling up and down the lane of light upon the vibrating floor under the straps between the engines and the dynamos.

“Have I not served my Lord?” said Azuma-zi inaudibly, from his shadow, and the note of the great dynamo rang out full and clear. As he looked at the big whirling mechanism the strange fascination of it that had been a little in abeyance since Holroyd’s death resumed its sway.

===Chinese===
电工从机器上取下的那具霍尔罗伊德扭曲的残骸，被搬运工用一块沾着咖啡渍的桌布匆匆盖上了。有人灵机一动，去请了一位医生来。那位专家最挂念的是赶紧让机器重新运转起来，因为已有七八列车停在了电气铁路那些闷罐似的隧道半途。阿祖玛齐回答着、或者说误解着那些凭职权或厚脸皮闯进棚子来的人所提的问题，不久便被技术主管打发回了锅炉舱。自然，院子大门外聚起了一群人——在伦敦，不知为什么，总有一群人在猝死事件的现场附近盘桓上一两天——两三个记者不知怎地渗进了引擎棚，其中一个甚至还摸到了阿祖玛齐跟前；可那位技术专家又把他们统统撵了出去，因为本人就是个业余的新闻记者。

不久尸体便被抬走了，公众的兴趣也随之一并散去。阿祖玛齐安安静静地守在他的炉子旁，一遍又一遍地看见煤炭里有一个剧烈挣扎、随后归于不动的身影。命案发生一小时之后，任谁走进这棚子，都会觉得这里仿佛从未发生过什么了不得的事。那黑人从引擎间里探出头来看，只见发电机之主在它的小兄弟们身旁旋转飞舞，驱动轮照旧转着，活塞里的蒸汽照旧突、突、突，和前半夜里一模一样。归根到底，从机械的角度看，这不过是一桩微不足道的小事——一道电流短暂的偏转罢了。只是如今，在那颤动着的地板上、在引擎与发电机之间那条传动带底下的光道里来回走动的，已是技术主管那瘦削的身形和瘦削的影子，替换了霍尔罗伊德那粗壮的轮廓。

“我难道没有侍奉我的主吗？”阿祖玛齐从他的阴影里无声地说道，大发电机那深沉的鸣响洪亮而清越地应和出来。他望着那旋转着的巨大机构，自霍尔罗伊德死后稍有收敛的那股古怪的痴迷，重新又攫住了他。

===Original===
Never had Azuma-zi seen a man killed so swiftly and pitilessly. The big humming machine had slain its victim without wavering for a second from its steady beating. It was indeed a mighty god.

The unconscious scientific manager stood with his back to him, scribbling on a piece of paper. His shadow lay at the foot of the monster.

Was the Lord Dynamo still hungry? His servant was ready.

Azuma-zi made a stealthy step forward; then stopped. The scientific manager suddenly ceased his writing, walked down the shed to the endmost of the dynamos, and began to examine the brushes.

===Chinese===
阿祖玛齐从未见过一个人被如此迅捷、如此无情地结果掉。那台嗡嗡作响的大机器结果了它的猎物，稳健的搏动不曾有一秒迟疑。它确实是位大能的神。

那位毫无察觉的技术主管背对着他站着，在一张纸上潦草地写着什么。他的影子落在那怪物的脚下。

发电机之主仍然饥饿吗？他的仆人已经准备就绪。

阿祖玛齐悄悄向前迈了一步；随即停住。技术主管忽然停了笔，沿着棚子走到最末端的那台发电机前，开始检查起电刷来。

===Original===
Azuma-zi hesitated, and then slipped across noiselessly into the shadow by the switch. There he waited. Presently the manager’s footsteps could be heard returning. He stopped in his old position, unconscious of the stoker crouching ten feet away from him. Then the big dynamo suddenly fizzled, and in another moment Azuma-zi had sprung out of the darkness upon him.

First, the scientific manager was gripped round the body and swung towards the big dynamo, then, kicking with his knee and forcing his antagonist’s head down with his hands, he loosened the grip on his waist and swung round away from the machine. Then the black grasped him again, putting a curly head against his chest, and they swayed and panted as it seemed for an age or so. Then the scientific manager was impelled to catch a black ear in his teeth and bite furiously. The black yelled hideously.

They rolled over on the floor, and the black, who had apparently slipped from the vice of the teeth or parted with some ear—the scientific manager wondered which at the time—tried to throttle him. The scientific manager was making some ineffectual efforts to claw something with his hands and to kick, when the welcome sound of quick footsteps sounded on the floor. The next moment Azuma-zi had left him and darted towards the big dynamo. There was a splutter amid the roar.

The officer of the company who had entered stood staring as Azuma-zi caught the naked terminals in his hands, gave one horrible convulsion, and then hung motionless from the machine, his face violently distorted.

===Chinese===
阿祖玛齐迟疑了一下，便悄无声息地溜到了电闸旁的阴影里。他在那里等着。不久便听见主管的脚步声回来了。他在老位置站定，全然不知那个司炉正蹲在十英尺开外。这时大发电机突然噼啪一响，下一瞬间阿祖玛齐已从黑暗中扑到了他身上。

先是技术主管被拦腰抱住，朝大发电机甩了过去；接着他用膝盖猛蹬、双手把对手的头按下去，挣开了腰间的钳制，转身闪离了机器。那黑人又抓住了他，把一颗卷发的头抵在他胸口，两人摇晃着、喘息着，仿佛僵持了一个世纪之久。于是技术主管情急之下用牙咬住了一只黑耳朵，狠狠地咬了下去。那黑人惨叫一声，叫得骇人。

两人在地上翻滚，那黑人显然是从牙齿的钳制中滑脱了，又或者是丢掉了半只耳朵——技术主管当时也拿不准究竟是哪样——便试图掐死他。技术主管正徒劳地用手乱抓乱蹬，忽听得地板上传来一阵急促的脚步声，如闻天籁。说时迟那时快，阿祖玛齐已撇下他，朝大发电机冲了过去。轰鸣声中响起一阵噼啪。

进来的那位公司职员目瞪口呆地站着，只见阿祖玛齐双手抓住裸露的接线端，浑身一阵可怕的痉挛，随即一动不动地挂在了机器上，脸扭曲得不成人形。

===Original===
“I’m jolly glad you came in when you did,” said the scientific manager, still sitting on the floor.

He looked at the still quivering figure. “It is not a nice death to die, apparently—but it is quick.”

The official was still staring at the body. He was a man of slow apprehension.

There was a pause.

===Chinese===
“你来得正好，真是谢天谢地，”技术主管说，仍旧坐在地上。

他望着那还在微微抽搐的身影。“这种死法看来不大好受——不过倒干脆。”

那位职员仍盯着尸体。他是个反应迟钝的人。

一阵沉默。

===Original===
The scientific manager got up on his feet rather awkwardly. He ran his fingers along his collar thoughtfully, and moved his head to and fro several times.

“Poor Holroyd! I see now.” Then almost mechanically he went towards the switch in the shadow and turned the current into the railway circuit again. As he did so the singed body loosened its grip upon the machine and fell forward on its face. The core of the dynamo roared out loud and clear, and the armature beat the air.

So ended prematurely the worship of the Dynamo Deity, perhaps the most short-lived of all religions. Yet withal it could at least boast a Martyrdom and a Human Sacrifice.

===Chinese===
技术主管颇为笨拙地站起身来。他用手指沿着衣领摸了一圈，若有所思地把头来回摇了几摇。

“可怜的霍尔罗伊德！我现在明白了。”接着他几乎是机械地走向阴影中的电闸，把电流重新接回了铁路的电路上。他这一动，那具烧焦的尸体便松开了对机器的钳抓，脸朝下扑倒在地。发电机的铁芯轰鸣得响亮而清越，电枢拍击着空气。

发电机之神（Dynamo Deity）的崇拜就这样过早地收场了，它也许是所有宗教中最短命的一种。然而它至少还能以此自夸：它曾有过一场殉道，也曾有过一场人祭。

## The Lost Inheritance / 失落的遗产

===Original===
“My uncle,” said the man with the glass eye, “was what you might call a hemi-semi-demi millionaire. He was worth about a hundred and twenty thousand. Quite. And he left me all his money.”

I glanced at the shiny sleeve of his coat, and my eye travelled up to the frayed collar.

“Every penny,” said the man with the glass eye, and I caught the active pupil looking at me with a touch of offence.

“I’ve never had any windfalls like that,” I said, trying to speak enviously and propitiate him.

“Even a legacy isn’t always a blessing,” he remarked with a sigh, and with an air of philosophical resignation he put the red nose and the wiry moustache into his tankard for a space.

“Perhaps not,” I said.

“He was an author, you see, and he wrote a lot of books.”

“Indeed!”

“That was the trouble of it all.” He stared at me with the available eye to see if I grasped his statement, then averted his face a little and produced a toothpick.

===Chinese===
"我舅舅，"那只玻璃眼的人说，"算得上是个八分之一个百万富翁吧。他名下大约有十二万镑的身家。足足的。他把钱全留给了我。"

我瞥了一眼他那发亮的外套袖子，目光又上移到磨破了边的领口。

"一个子儿都没落下，"那只玻璃眼的人说，我察觉那只活的眼珠带着几分被冒犯的神情直瞪着我。

"我可从没碰上过这种天上掉馅饼的好事，"我说，竭力把话说得透着几分眼红，好平一平他的气。

"遗产这种东西，也未必就是福气。"他叹了口气，带着一副达观认命的架势，把那只红鼻头和硬扎扎的八字胡浸进啤酒杯里，泡了一阵。

"也许是吧，"我说。

"他是位作家，您要知道，写了一大堆书。"

"是么！"

"麻烦正出在这上头。"他用那只管用的眼珠死死盯住我，看我领会了他的意思没有，接着稍稍侧过脸，摸出一根牙签。

===Original===
“You see,” he said, smacking his lips after a pause, “it was like this. He was my uncle—my maternal uncle. And he had—what shall I call it?—a weakness for writing edifying literature. Weakness is hardly the word—downright mania is nearer the mark. He’d been librarian in a Polytechnic, and as soon as the money came to him he began to indulge his ambition. It’s a simply extraordinary and incomprehensible thing to me. Here was a man of thirty-seven suddenly dropped into a perfect pile of gold, and he didn’t go—not a day’s bust on it. One would think a chap would go and get himself dressed a bit decent—say a couple of dozen pairs of trousers at a West End tailor’s; but he never did. You’d hardly believe it, but when he died he hadn’t even a gold watch. It seems wrong for people like that to have money. All he did was just to take a house, and order in pretty nearly five tons of books and ink and paper, and set to writing edifying literature as hard as ever he could write. I *can’t* understand it! But he did. The money came to him, curiously enough, through a maternal uncle of *his*, unexpected like, when he was seven-and-thirty. My mother, it happened, was his only relation in the wide, wide world, except some second cousins of his. And I was her only son. You follow all that? The second cousins had one only son, too, but they brought him to see the old man too soon. He was rather a spoilt youngster, was this son of theirs, and directly he set eyes on my uncle, he began bawling out as hard as he could. ‘Take ’im away—er,’ he says, ‘take ’im away,’ and so did for himself entirely. It was pretty straight sailing, you’d think, for me, eh? And my mother, being a sensible, careful woman, settled the business in her own mind long before he did.”

===Chinese===
"您听我说，"他停了停，咂了咂嘴，"事情是这样的。他是我舅舅——我母亲的兄弟。他有——该怎么说呢——一种写劝善文学的癖好。说癖好还嫌轻了——说是痴狂倒更贴切些。他原在一所工艺学校（Polytechnic）的图书馆当馆员，那笔钱一到手，他就开始放手去圆他的抱负了。这事在我看来简直离奇到了不可理喻的地步。一个三十七岁的人，忽然间天上掉下整整一堆金子，他居然不去挥霍——连一天的痛快都不肯花。换了谁都会想，好歹该去打扮打扮、体面一点——比如到西区（West End）的裁缝铺做上那么两打裤子；可他偏不。说了您怕都不信，他死的时候，连一块金表都没有。这种人手里有钱，简直是没天理。他所做的，不过是租下一幢房子，差不多订进五吨重的书、墨水和纸张，然后就埋头写他的劝善文学，能写多快写多快。我就是想不通！可他偏偏就这么干了。说来也怪，那笔钱是他从一个舅舅——他母亲那边的兄弟——手里得来的，事先毫无征兆，就在他三十七岁那年。我母亲，碰巧是他在这广阔天地间唯一的亲人，除开他那几个隔代的表兄弟。而我，是她唯一的儿子。这些您都听明白了吧？那几位表兄弟家也有一个独生子，可他们把那孩子领去见老头子，领得太早了点。那孩子给他们惯坏了，一瞧见我舅舅，就扯开嗓子拼命哭喊。'把他抱走——呃，'他说，'把他抱走，'这一下可就把自己彻底断送了。这么一来，您瞧，对我来说岂不一帆风顺了吗？我母亲是个明白人，做事又仔细，早在这老头子拿定主意之前，她心里已经把这桩事安排得妥妥帖帖了。"

===Original===
“He was a curious little chap, was my uncle, as I remember him. I don’t wonder at the kid being scared. Hair, just like these Japanese dolls they sell, black and straight and stiff all round the brim and none in the middle, and below, a whitish kind of face and rather large dark grey eyes moving about behind his spectacles. He used to attach a great deal of importance to dress, and always wore a flapping overcoat and a big-brimmed felt hat of a most extraordinary size. He looked a rummy little beggar, I can tell you. Indoors it was, as a rule, a dirty red flannel dressing-gown and a black skullcap he had. That black skullcap made him look like the portraits of all kinds of celebrated people. He was always moving about from house to house, was my uncle, with his chair which had belonged to Savage Landor, and his two writing-tables, one of Carlyle’s and the other of Shelley’s, so the dealer told him, and the completest portable reference library in England, he said he had—and he lugged the whole caravan, now to a house at Down, near Darwin’s old place, then to Reigate, near Meredith, then off to Haslemere, then back to Chelsea for a bit, and then up to Hampstead. He knew there was something wrong with his stuff, but he never knew there was anything wrong with his brains. It was always the air, or the water, or the altitude, or some tommyrot like that. ‘So much depends on environment,’ he used to say, and stare at you hard, as if he half suspected you were hiding a grin at him somewhere under your face. ‘So much depends on environment to a sensitive mind like mine.’”

===Chinese===
"我那舅舅啊，是个古怪的小矮个儿——至少我记忆里他是那副模样。也难怪那孩子会害怕。他的头发，就跟他们卖的日本娃娃似的，又黑又直又硬，围着头一圈，当中却是秃的；下面是一张泛白的脸，鼻梁上架着眼镜，一双挺大的深灰色眼珠在镜片后面滴溜溜地乱转。他极讲究穿着，总披一件晃荡的大衣，戴一顶大得离了谱的宽边毡帽。我跟您说，他瞧着就是个古里古怪的小矮人。在屋里呢，照例是一袭脏兮兮的红色法兰绒晨衣，加上一顶黑色小圆便帽。那顶黑便帽让他看起来像是各种名人画像里走出来的人物。他老是搬家，搬来搬去，带着他那把据说曾是萨维奇·兰多（Savage Landor）坐过的椅子，还有两张写字台——一张据说是卡莱尔（Carlyle）的，另一张是雪莱（Shelley）的，那旧货商是这么告诉他的——再加上全英国最齐全的一部便携参考书库，他自称——他就拖着这整支大篷车队，一会儿搬到唐恩（Down）的一所房子，就在达尔文（Darwin）故居附近；一会儿搬到雷盖特（Reigate），挨着梅瑞狄斯（Meredith）住过的地方；再一会儿又挪到黑斯尔米尔（Haslemere）；再又折回切尔西（Chelsea）住上一阵；末了又搬上汉普斯特德（Hampstead）。他心里明白自己写的东西有毛病，却从不晓得自己的脑子也有毛病。他总怪空气不好，要不就怪水、怪海拔、怪诸如此类的胡说八道。'环境的影响可大着呢，'他常这么说，一双眼睛死死瞪着您，仿佛有点疑心您脸上哪个角落正憋着一个没忍住的笑。'像我这样一颗敏感的心灵，环境的影响可太大了。'"

===Original===
“What was his name? You wouldn’t know it if I told you. He wrote nothing that anyone has ever read—nothing. No one *could* read it. He wanted to be a great teacher, he said, and he didn’t know what he wanted to teach any more than a child. So he just blethered at large about Truth and Righteousness, and the Spirit of History, and all that. Book after book he wrote and published at his own expense. He wasn’t quite right in his head, you know, really; and to hear him go on at the critics—not because they slated him, mind you—he liked that—but because they didn’t take any notice of him at all. ‘What do the nations want?’ he would ask, holding out his brown old claw. ‘Why, teaching—guidance! They are scattered upon the hills like sheep without a shepherd. There is War and Rumours of War, the unlaid Spirit of Discord abroad in the land, Nihilism, Vivisection, Vaccination, Drunkenness, Penury, Want, Socialistic Error, Selfish Capital! Do you see the clouds, Ted?’—My name, you know—‘Do you see the clouds lowering over the land? and behind it all—the Mongol waits!’ He was always very great on Mongols and the Spectre of Socialism, and suchlike things.”

===Chinese===
"他叫什么名字？我告诉您，您也不会知道。他写的东西，从来没有人读过——一本也没有。谁也读不下去。他自诩要做一位伟大的导师，可他到底想教导什么，他自己比个孩子还不明白。于是他就信口开河，大谈什么真理与正义、历史的精神之类的玩意儿。他一本接一本地写书，全是他自掏腰包出版的。您要知道，他这脑子实在不大对劲，真的；您要是听他数落那些评论家——您留神，倒不是因为他们挖苦他——他巴不得人家挖苦——而是因为他们压根儿不搭理他。'万国所渴求的是什么呢？'他会这么问，伸出他那只枯黄的老爪子。'是教导啊——是指引！他们如同没有牧人的羊，散落在群山之上。到处是战争与战争的风声，是不和之灵在这片土地上四处游荡，是无政府主义、活体解剖、种痘、酗酒、贫乏、匮乏、社会主义谬误、自私的资本！您可看见那重重阴云，泰德（Ted）？'——这是我的名字，您知道——'您可看见那阴云压境么？而在这一切背后——蒙古人正虎视眈眈呢！'他向来最爱谈蒙古人，还有社会主义的幽灵，诸如此类的东西。"

===Original===
“Then out would come his finger at me, and with his eyes all afire and his skullcap askew, he would whisper: ‘And here am I. What do I want? Nations to teach. Nations! I say it with all modesty, Ted, I *could*. I would guide them; nay! but I *will* guide them to a safe haven, to the land of Righteousness, flowing with milk and honey.’

“That’s how he used to go on. Ramble, rave about the nations, and righteousness, and that kind of thing. Kind of mincemeat of Bible and blethers. From fourteen up to three-and-twenty, when I might have been improving my mind, my mother used to wash me and brush my hair (at least in the earlier years of it), with a nice parting down the middle, and take me, once or twice a week, to hear this old lunatic jabber about things he had read of in the morning papers, trying to do it as much like Carlyle as he could, and I used to sit according to instructions, and look intelligent and nice, and pretend to be taking it all in. Afterwards I used to go of my own free will, out of a regard for the legacy. I was the only person that used to go and see him. He wrote, I believe, to every man who made the slightest stir in the world, sending him a copy or so of his books, and inviting him to come and talk about the nations to him; but half of them didn’t answer, and none ever came. And when the girl let you in—she was an artful bit of goods, that girl—there were heaps of letters on the hall-seat waiting to go off, addressed to Prince Bismark, the President of the United States, and suchlike people. And one went up the staircase and along the cobwebby passage—the housekeeper drank like fury, and his passages were always cobwebby—and found him at last, with books turned down all over the room, and heaps of torn paper on the floor, and telegrams and newspapers littered about, and empty coffee-cups and half-eaten bits of toast on the desk and the mantel. You’d see his back humped up, and his hair would be sticking out quite straight between the collar of that dressing-gown thing and the edge of the skullcap.”

===Chinese===
"接着那根手指就朝我一指，两眼烧得通亮，那顶便帽也歪到了一边，他便压低嗓子耳语：'而我就在此。我渴求的是什么呢？是万国可教。万民啊！我说这话毫无自夸之意，泰德，我办得到的。我要指引他们；不！我定要指引他们驶入安全的港湾，进入那流着奶与蜜的正义之国。'

"他往常就是这么个调子。东拉西扯，大发议论，说的尽是国家民族、正义公道那一套。半是圣经，半是胡话，搅成一锅粥。从十四岁到二十三岁，本是我长见识的年纪，我母亲却要给我洗脸、梳头（至少那头几年是这样），给我梳一条齐齐整整的中分，一周带我去一两回，听这个老疯子瞎扯——净是些他从晨报上看来的东西，还拼命想学卡莱尔那副腔调。我呢，照吩咐规规矩矩坐着，装出一副聪明乖巧、讨人喜欢的样子，假装句句都听进了心里。后来我是自己乐意去的——为的是那份遗产。只有我一个人去看他。我相信，但凡世上哪个人稍稍闹出过一点动静，他就给人家写信，奉上他几本书，请人家来跟他谈谈'万国'的事；可半数人根本不回信，一个也没来过。每当那女仆开门放您进去——那丫头是个精明伶俐的小滑头——门厅的衣帽凳上总堆着一摞摞等着寄出的信件，收信人有俾斯麦亲王（Prince Bismark）、美利坚合众国总统，以及诸如此类的大人物。然后您顺着楼梯上去，沿着那条结满蜘蛛网的走廊往前走——那管家婆喝酒喝得凶，他家的走廊便常年挂着蛛网——末了总算找到他：满屋子摊着翻开倒扣的书，地板上堆着一沓沓碎纸，电报和报纸丢得到处都是，书桌上、壁炉台上搁着空的咖啡杯和啃了一半的吐司。您会瞧见他的背弓着，那头发从晨衣的领子和便帽帽檐之间笔直地戳出来。"

===Original===
“‘A moment!’ he would say. ‘A moment!’ over his shoulder. ‘The *mot juste*, you know, Ted, *le mot juste*. Righteous thought righteously expressed—Aah!—concatenation. And now, Ted,’ he’d say, spinning round in his study chair, ‘how’s Young England?’ That was his silly name for me.

“Well, that was my uncle, and that was how he talked—to me, at any rate. With others about he seemed a bit shy. And he not only talked to me, but he gave me his books, books of six hundred pages or so, with cockeyed headings, ‘The Shrieking Sisterhood,’ ‘The Behemoth of Bigotry,’ ‘Crucibles and Cullenders,’ and so on. All very strong, and none of them original. The very last time but one that I saw him he gave me a book. He was feeling ill even then, and his hand shook and he was despondent. I noticed it because I was naturally on the lookout for those little symptoms. ‘My last book, Ted,’ he said. ‘My last book, my boy; my last word to the deaf and hardened nations;’ and I’m hanged if a tear didn’t go rolling down his yellow old cheek. He was regular crying because it was so nearly over, and he hadn’t only written about fifty-three books of rubbish. ‘I’ve sometimes thought, Ted’—he said, and stopped.”

===Chinese===
"'等一会儿！'他会隔着肩膀喊。'等一会儿！《恰切的字眼》啊，您知道的，泰德，le mot juste（恰切的字眼）。正义之思以正义之言出之——啊哈！——环环相扣。好了，泰德，'他说着，在那张书桌转椅里一旋过身子，'少年英格兰（Young England）近来可好？'——这是他给我起的蠢绰号。

"这便是我那舅舅，他说话就是这个腔调——至少跟我说话是这样。有外人在场，他倒显得腼腆几分。他不但跟我唠叨，还把他的书塞给我——一本本六百来页的大厚书，书名古怪得离谱：《尖叫的姐妹会》（The Shrieking Sisterhood）、《偏执的巨兽》（The Behemoth of Bigotry）、《坩埚与漏勺》（Crucibles and Cullenders），等等。火气都挺足，却没一句是新鲜的。我见他的倒数第二回，他给了我一本书。那时他身子已经不爽快了，手直打颤，神情颓丧。这些我都留意到了，因为这种种小征候，我自然是要上心盯着的。'我最后一本书了，泰德，'他说，'最后一本啦，孩子；这是我对那些又聋又硬心肠的万国所说的最后一番话了。'——岂有此理，一颗泪珠竟当真顺着他那又黄又皱的老脸滚了下来。他是真的哭了——因为这一切眼看就要收场，而他写过的，满打满算也不过是五十三本废话而已。'我有时候想，泰德——'他说着，停住了。"

===Original===
“‘Perhaps I’ve been a bit hasty and angry with this stiff-necked generation. A little more sweetness, perhaps, and a little less blinding light. I’ve sometimes thought—I might have swayed them. But I’ve done my best, Ted.’

“And then, with a burst, for the first and last time in his life he owned himself a failure. It showed he was really ill. He seemed to think for a minute, and then he spoke quietly and low, as sane and sober as I am now. ‘I’ve been a fool, Ted,’ he said. ‘I’ve been flapping nonsense all my life. Only He who readeth the heart knows whether this is anything more than vanity. Ted, I don’t. But He knows, He knows, and if I have done foolishly and vainly, in my heart—in my heart’—”

===Chinese===
"'也许我对这一代硬着颈项的人，是急躁了些、动怒了些。或许该多一点温存，少一点那晃眼的强光。我有时候想——我原本是可以感化他们的。可我已经尽了力，泰德。'

"紧接着，他猛地一阵，平生头一回也是最后一回，承认了自己是个失败者。这说明他是真的病了。他似乎想了一会儿，然后压低了声音，又轻又缓地说起话来，神志清醒得就像我现在这样。'我是个傻瓜，泰德，'他说。'我这一辈子，尽在鼓捣些不知所云的东西。只有洞察人心的主才知道，这一切究竟是不是虚荣。泰德，我不知道。可他知道，他知道，如果我行事愚蠢虚妄，在我心里——在我心里——'"

===Original===
“Just like that he spoke, repeating himself, and he stopped quite short and handed the book to me, trembling. Then the old shine came back into his eye. I remember it all fairly well, because I repeated it and acted it to my old mother when I got home, to cheer her up a bit. ‘Take this book and read it,’ he said. ‘It’s my last word, my very last word. I’ve left all my property to you, Ted, and may you use it better than I have done.’ And then he fell a-coughing.

“I remember that quite well even now, and how I went home cock-a-hoop, and how he was in bed the next time I called. The housekeeper was downstairs drunk, and I fooled about—as a young man will—with the girl in the passage before I went to him. He was sinking fast. But even then his vanity clung to him.

“‘Have you read it?’ he whispered.

“‘Sat up all night reading it,’ I said in his ear to cheer him. ‘It’s the last,’ said I, and then, with a memory of some poetry or other in my head, ‘but it’s the bravest and best.’

“He smiled a little and tried to squeeze my hand as a woman might do, and left off squeezing in the middle, and lay still. ‘The bravest and the best,’ said I again, seeing it pleased him. But he didn’t answer. I heard the girl giggle outside the door, for occasionally we’d had just a bit of innocent laughter, you know, at his ways. I looked at his face, and his eyes were closed, and it was just as if somebody had punched in his nose on either side. But he was still smiling. It’s queer to think of—he lay dead, lay dead there, an utter failure, with the smile of success on his face.”

===Chinese===
"他就是这样说的，颠来倒去地重复，戛然而止，颤巍巍地把那本书递到了我手里。随后，往日那点光芒又回到了他眼中。这一切我记得相当清楚，因为回家之后，我还把这番情景学说了一遍、演给老母亲看，好让她也宽宽心。'拿着这本书，去读吧，'他说。'这是我的遗言，最后的遗言了。我把全部家产都留给了您，泰德，但愿您用它用得比我好些。'说完，他便咳嗽起来。

"这件事我至今记得清清楚楚——记得我怎样得意洋洋地回了家，记得下次登门时他已卧床不起。那管家婆在楼下醉得不省人事，我去见他之前，还在走廊里跟那女仆厮混了一阵——年轻人嘛，难免的。他眼看是不行了。可即便到了那时，他的虚荣心还紧紧缠着他不放。

"'您读过了吗？'他低声问。

"'熬了个通宵读完的，'我在他耳边大声说，好让他高兴。'这是最后一本了，'我说，随即脑子里掠起不知哪首诗里的句子，又补了一句：'可也是最勇敢、最好的一本。'

"他微微一笑，想捏捏我的手，像个女人似的；捏到一半就不捏了，静静地躺着。'最勇敢、最好的一本。'我又说了一遍，见他听了高兴。可他没有回话。我听见门外那女仆咯咯地笑——说起来，他那些做派，我俩偶尔也忍不住要笑话他几句，您知道，全是没什么恶意的笑。我看了看他的脸，他的眼睛已经闭上了，鼻梁两边像是被人往里捶进去似的塌了下去。可他脸上还挂着笑。想起来真是稀奇——他躺在那儿，死了，彻彻底底地死了，一个十足的失败者，脸上却带着成功的微笑。"

===Original===
“That was the end of my uncle. You can imagine me and my mother saw that he had a decent funeral. Then, of course, came the hunt for the will. We began decent and respectful at first, and before the day was out we were ripping chairs, and smashing bureau panels, and sounding walls. Every hour we expected those others to come in. We asked the housekeeper, and found she’d actually witnessed a will—on an ordinary half-sheet of notepaper it was written, and very short, she said—not a month ago. The other witness was the gardener, and he bore her out word for word. But I’m hanged if there was that or any other will to be found. The way my mother talked must have made him turn in his grave. At last a lawyer at Reigate sprang one on us that had been made years ago during some temporary quarrel with my mother. I’m blest if that wasn’t the only will to be discovered anywhere, and it left every penny he possessed to that ‘Take ’im away’ youngster of his second cousin’s—a chap who’d never had to stand his talking not for one afternoon of his life.”

===Chinese===
"这便是我舅舅的结局。您想也想得到，我和我母亲总归是让他风风光光地下了葬。接下来，自然便是搜寻遗嘱了。起初我们还斯文体面、客客气气；没到天黑，就已经是在掀椅子、砸写字台的面板、敲墙壁了。我们无时无刻不在防着那一拨人上门。我们去问那管家婆，才知道她竟真的在一纸遗嘱上签过名、做过见证——就写在一张普通的半张信纸上，她说，简短得很——还不到一个月以前的事。另一位见证人是那个花匠，他所说的与她一字不差。可岂有此理，偏偏这份也好，别的什么也好，哪儿也找不到半张遗嘱。我母亲说的那些话，怕是能让他在棺材里都翻来覆去。后来到底还是雷盖特（Reigate）的一位律师拿出一份来——那是多年前他跟我母亲闹过一场什么别扭时立的。您说气人不气人，满世界能找着的，就这一份遗嘱，却把他名下每一分钱都留给了他那个二表哥家的、当初喊'把他抱走'的小崽子——一个这辈子连一个下午都不曾耐着性子听过他唠叨的小子。"

===Original===
The man with the glass eye stopped.

“I thought you said”—I began.

“Half a minute,” said the man with the glass eye. “*I* had to wait for the end of the story till this very morning, and I was a blessed sight more interested than you are. You just wait a bit too. They executed the will, and the other chap inherited, and directly he was one-and-twenty he began to blew it. How he did blew it, to be sure! He bet, he drank, he got in the papers for this and that. I tell you, it makes me wriggle to think of the times he had. He blewed every ha’penny of it before he was thirty, and the last I heard of him was—Holloway! Three years ago.”

===Chinese===
那只玻璃眼的人住了口。

"我记得您方才说——"我开口道。

"您等半分钟，"那只玻璃眼的人说，"这故事的后半段，我自己也是直到今天早上才等到结果的，您想想，我可比您急得多呢。您也请稍稍等一等。遗嘱照章执行了，那一位继承了遗产，一满二十一岁，他就开始挥霍起来。您瞧他挥霍得那叫一个痛快！他赌，他喝，今天为这桩事、明天为那桩事，名字隔三差五就上报。我告诉您，一想到他过的那些好日子，我就浑身不是滋味。不到三十岁，他把钱花得一个子儿不剩；我最后听到他的消息是——霍洛威（Holloway）监狱！三年前的事了。"

===Original===
“Well, I naturally fell on hard times, because, as you see, the only trade I knew was legacy-cadging. All my plans were waiting over to begin, so to speak, when the old chap died. I’ve had my ups and downs since then. Just now it’s a period of depression. I tell you frankly, I’m on the lookout for help. I was hunting round my room to find something to raise a bit on for immediate necessities, and the sight of all those presentation volumes—no one will buy them, not to wrap butter in, even—well, they annoyed me. I’d promised him not to part with them, and I never kept a promise easier. I let out at them with my boot, and sent them shooting across the room. One lifted at the kick, and spun through the air. And out of it flapped—You guess?

“It was the will. He’d given it me himself in that very last volume of all.”

He folded his arms on the table, and looked sadly with the active eye at his empty tankard. He shook his head slowly, and said softly, “I’d never *opened* the book, much more cut a page!” Then he looked up, with a bitter laugh, for my sympathy. “Fancy hiding it there! Eigh? Of all places.”

===Chinese===
"这一来，我自然就走了下坡路，因为您也看得出来，我唯一会的营生，就是变着法儿去讨那笔遗产。老头子一死，我那些盘算——可以说——正等着开张呢。这以后我是起起落落，没个定准。眼下正走霉运。我跟您掏心窝子说吧，我正四下里找门路求帮衬呢。我在屋里翻箱倒柜，想寻点东西当当、对付眼前的急用，可瞧着那满屋子的赠阅本——没人肯要，连包黄油都没人肯拿去用——唉，真把我给气着了。我答应过他不撒手的，可这诺言我还从没这么容易守过。我一脚踹过去，把那些书踢得满屋乱飞。其中一本被这一脚带了起来，在半空中滴溜溜打着转。从书页里飘出一样东西——您猜是什么？

"是那份遗嘱。是他亲手把它夹进那最后一本书里、亲手交给我的。"

他把双臂交叠在桌上，用那只活的眼珠忧伤地望着空空的啤酒杯。他缓缓摇了摇头，轻轻说道："我从来没有翻开过那本书，更别提裁页了！"随后他抬起头来，苦笑一声，向我讨一份同情。"想想看，竟把它藏在那儿！嗐？天底下那么多地方，偏偏那个地方。"

===Original===
He began to fish absently for a dead fly with his finger. “It just shows you the vanity of authors,” he said, looking up at me. “It wasn’t no trick of his. He’d meant perfectly fair. He’d really thought I was really going home to read that blessed book of his through. But it shows you, don’t it?”—his eye went down to the tankard again—“It shows you, too, how we poor human beings fail to understand one another.”

But there was no misunderstanding the eloquent thirst of his eye. He accepted with ill-feigned surprise. He said, in the usual subtle formula, that he didn’t mind if he did.

===Chinese===
他心不在焉地用手指去捞一只死苍蝇。"这恰恰让您看到了作家的虚荣，"他抬眼望着我。"他那可不是耍什么花招。他是真心实意的。他真以为我会回家把他那本宝贝书从头到尾读一遍呢。可这事儿不就说明问题了吗？"——他的目光又落回到那只啤酒杯上——"这不也同样说明，我们这些可怜的人类，彼此之间是多么不能相互理解么。"

可他眼里那份滔滔不绝的干渴，却再清楚不过了，绝不会让人误会。他装出一副难以置信的样子，接受了我请的那杯酒。他照例用那句微妙的老套话说，他不介意也来上一杯。

## The Magic Shop / 魔术店

===Original===
I had seen the Magic Shop from afar several times; I had passed it once or twice, a shop window of alluring little objects, magic balls, magic hens, wonderful cones, ventriloquist dolls, the material of the basket trick, packs of cards that *looked* all right, and all that sort of thing, but never had I thought of going in until one day, almost without warning, Gip hauled me by my finger right up to the window, and so conducted himself that there was nothing for it but to take him in. I had not thought the place was there, to tell the truth﻿—a modest-sized frontage in Regent Street, between the picture shop and the place where the chicks run about just out of patent incubators﻿—but there it was sure enough. I had fancied it was down nearer the Circus, or round the corner in Oxford Street, or even in Holborn; always over the way and a little inaccessible it had been, with something of the mirage in its position; but here it was now quite indisputably, and the fat end of Gip’s pointing finger made a noise upon the glass.

“If I was rich,” said Gip, dabbing a finger at the Disappearing Egg, “I’d buy myself that. And that”﻿—which was The Crying Baby, Very Human﻿—“and that,” which was a mystery, and called, so a neat card asserted, “Buy One and Astonish Your Friends.”

“Anything,” said Gip, “will disappear under one of those cones. I have read about it in a book.

“And there, dadda, is the Vanishing Halfpenny﻿—only they’ve put it this way up so’s we can’t see how it’s done.”

===Chinese===
那家魔术店（the Magic Shop）我远远地瞧见过好几回；也曾打它跟前走过一两次，橱窗里摆满了诱人的小玩意儿：魔术球、魔术母鸡、奇妙的圆锥筒、腹语娃娃、变空篮魔术用的家什，还有看着*没毛病*的扑克牌，诸如此类，可我从未动过进去瞧瞧的念头。直到有一天，几乎毫无预兆地，吉普（Gip）拽着我的手指头径直把他拉到橱窗前，又使出那么一套作派，弄得我毫无办法，只好带他进去。说实话，我原没想到那地方就在那儿——摄政街（Regent Street）上一爿门面不大不小的店铺，夹在一家画店和一家让小鸡雏儿刚出专利孵化器就满地乱跑的铺子之间——可它确确实实在那儿。我向来以为它该在靠近杂技场的地方，要么在牛津街（Oxford Street）拐角一带，甚至可能在霍尔本（Holborn）；它总好像在马路对面，又有点儿够不着，位置上带着几分海市蜃楼的味道；可这一回它明明白白就在这儿，吉普那根胖指头指着的一头在玻璃上笃笃地敲着响。

“我要是有钱，”吉普说着，伸指头戳了戳那枚“会消失的蛋”（Disappearing Egg），“我就给自己买那个。还有那个”——那是“会哭的娃娃，栩栩如生”（The Crying Baby, Very Human）——“还有那个，”那是一件神秘物事，据一张精致的小卡片声称，叫做“买一个，让朋友们大吃一惊”（Buy One and Astonish Your Friends）。

“随便什么东西，”吉普说，“扣在那样的圆锥筒底下都会不见。我在一本书里读到过。

“还有那儿，爸爸，是‘会消失的半便士’（Vanishing Halfpenny）——只是他们把它这样扣着摆，我们就看不见它是怎么变没的。”

===Original===
Gip, dear boy, inherits his mother’s breeding, and he did not propose to enter the shop or worry in any way; only, you know, quite unconsciously, he lugged my finger doorward, and he made his interest clear.

“That,” he said, and pointed to the Magic Bottle.

“If you had that?” I said; at which promising inquiry he looked up with a sudden radiance.

“I could show it to Jessie,” he said, thoughtful as ever of others.

“It’s less than a hundred days to your birthday, Gibbles,” I said, and laid my hand on the door-handle.

Gip made no answer, but his grip tightened on my finger, and so we came into the shop.

It was no common shop this; it was a magic shop, and all the prancing precedence Gip would have taken in the matter of mere toys was wanting. He left the burden of the conversation to me.

===Chinese===
这孩子真乖，继承了他母亲的教养，他并不打算进店，也没有任何纠缠的意思；只是，您也知道，全然无意识地，他把我的手指头往门口那个方向拽，他的心思是明摆着的。

“那个，”他说，指着那只“魔术瓶”（Magic Bottle）。

“要是你有了那个呢？”我说；这一句颇有指望的问话让他抬起头来，忽地满脸放光。

“我可以拿给杰西（Jessie）看，”他说，一如既往地惦记着别人。

“离你生日不到一百天了，吉宝宝（Gibbles），”我说着，把手按在了门把上。

吉普没作声，可他攥着我手指头的劲儿更紧了，我们就这样走进了店里。

这不是寻常的铺子；这是一家魔术店，至于吉普在普通玩具面前本会摆出的那种神气活现、抢先逞能的架势，此刻全不见了。他把说话的重担一股脑儿丢给了我。

===Original===
It was a little, narrow shop, not very well lit, and the doorbell pinged again with a plaintive note as we closed it behind us. For a moment or so we were alone and could glance about us. There was a tiger in *papier-mâché* on the glass case that covered the low counter﻿—a grave, kind-eyed tiger that waggled his head in a methodical manner; there were several crystal spheres, a china hand holding magic cards, a stock of magic fishbowls in various sizes, and an immodest magic hat that shamelessly displayed its springs. On the floor were magic mirrors; one to draw you out long and thin, one to swell your head and vanish your legs, and one to make you short and fat like a draught; and while, we were laughing at these the shopman, as I suppose, came in.

At any rate, there he was behind the counter﻿—a curious, sallow, dark man, with one ear larger than the other and a chin like the toecap of a boot.

“What can we have the pleasure?” he said, spreading his long magic fingers on the glass case; and so with a start we were aware of him.

“I want,” I said, “to buy my little boy a few simple tricks.”

“Legerdemain?” he asked. “Mechanical? Domestic?”

“Anything amusing?” said I.

“Um!” said the shopman, and scratched his head for a moment as if thinking. Then, quite distinctly, he drew from his head a glass ball. “Something in this way?” he said, and held it out.

===Chinese===
那是一间又小又窄的铺子，光线不大好，我们随手关上门，门铃又叮地响了一声，带着些幽怨的调子。有那么片刻工夫，店里只有我们俩，可以四下打量。低矮的柜台外罩着玻璃匣，匣上趴着一只纸浆塑的老虎（papier-mâché）——一只神情庄重、目光和善的老虎，正一下一下、有板有眼地摇晃着脑袋；还有几只水晶球，一只瓷手握着魔术扑克牌，一摞大大小小的魔术金鱼缸，还有一顶毫不矜持的魔术帽，恬不知耻地把里头的弹簧露给人看。地上摆着几面魔术镜；一面能把你照得又长又瘦，一面能让你的脑袋鼓起来、腿不见了，还有一面能让你又矮又胖像个棋子；我们正对着这些镜子笑呢，那店伙计——我猜是伙计——便走了进来。

无论如何，他就在柜台后面了——一个古怪的、肤色蜡黄的黝黑男人，一只耳朵比另一只大，下巴像皮靴的鞋头。

“您二位有何贵干？”他说着，把他那双长长的、有魔术味儿的手指摊在玻璃匣上；我们这才猛地发觉了他。

“我想，”我说，“给我这小家伙买几样简单的小戏法。”

“手彩？”他问，“机械的？家用型的？”

“好玩的就行？”我说。

“唔！”伙计应了一声，挠了挠头，像是在想。然后，清清楚楚地，他从脑袋里掏出了一只玻璃球。“这一路的，怎么样？”他说着，把它递了过来。

===Original===
The action was unexpected. I had seen the trick done at entertainments endless times before﻿—it’s part of the common stock of conjurers﻿—but I had not expected it here. “That’s good,” I said, with a laugh.

“Isn’t it?” said the shopman.

Gip stretched out his disengaged hand to take this object and found merely a blank palm.

“It’s in your pocket,” said the shopman, and there it was!

“How much will that be?” I asked.

“We make no charge for glass balls,” said the shopman politely. “We get them”﻿—he picked one out of his elbow as he spoke﻿—“free.” He produced another from the back of his neck, and laid it beside its predecessor on the counter. Gip regarded his glass ball sagely, then directed a look of inquiry at the two on the counter, and finally brought his round-eyed scrutiny to the shopman, who smiled. “You may have those two,” said the shopman, “and, if you *don’t* mind one from my mouth. *So!*”

Gip counselled me mutely for a moment, and then in a profound silence put away the four balls, resumed my reassuring finger, and nerved himself for the next event.

“We get all our smaller tricks in that way,” the shopman remarked.

I laughed in the manner of one who subscribes to a jest. “Instead of going to the wholesale shop,” I said. “Of course, it’s cheaper.”

===Chinese===
这一手来得毫无预兆。这种戏法我在各种演出里看过无数次——本是魔术师们的寻常家当——可我没料到在这儿碰上。“真好，”我笑着说。

“可不是嘛？”伙计说。

吉普腾出那只空着的手去接这件物事，摊开手心，却什么也没有。

“在您口袋里呢，”伙计说，果然就在那儿！

“这个多少钱？”我问。

“玻璃球我们不收钱，”伙计客客气气地说，“我们这东西都是”——他一边说，一边从胳膊肘里摸出一只来——“白得的。”他又从后颈窝里变出一只，搁在柜台上先那只旁边。吉普老成地端详着自己手里那只玻璃球，又拿探询的目光瞧瞧柜台上的那两只，最后把他那双瞪得溜圆的眼睛对准了伙计，伙计笑了笑。“这两只您也拿着吧，”伙计说，“要是您不介意再从我嘴里来一只。*瞧！*”

吉普默默地跟我商量了一阵，然后在一派深沉的肃静中收好了那四只球，重新攥住我那根叫人安心的手指头，鼓起勇气来应付下一桩事。

“我们所有这些小玩意儿，都是这么弄来的，”伙计说。

我顺着话头笑了笑，像是一个肯凑趣捧场的人。“不用上批发行去进货了，”我说，“当然喽，便宜些。”

===Original===
“In a way,” the shopman said. “Though we pay in the end. But not so heavily﻿—as people suppose﻿ ﻿… Our larger tricks, and our daily provisions and all the other things we want, we get out of that hat﻿ ﻿… And you know, sir, if you’ll excuse my saying it, there *isn’t* a wholesale shop, not for Genuine Magic goods, sir. I don’t know if you noticed our inscription﻿—the Genuine Magic Shop.” He drew a business card from his cheek and handed it to me. “Genuine,” he said, with his finger on the word, and added, “There is absolutely no deception, sir.”

He seemed to be carrying out the joke pretty thoroughly, I thought.

He turned to Gip with a smile of remarkable affability. “You, you know, are the Right Sort of Boy.”

I was surprised at his knowing that, because, in the interests of discipline, we keep it rather a secret even at home; but Gip received it in unflinching silence, keeping a steadfast eye on him.

“It’s only the Right Sort of Boy gets through that doorway.”

And, as if by way of illustration, there came a rattling at the door, and a squeaking little voice could be faintly heard. “Nyar! I *warn* ’a go in there, dadda, I **warn** ’a go in there. Ny-a-a-ah!” and then the accents of a downtrodden parent, urging consolations and propitiations. “It’s locked, Edward,” he said.

“But it isn’t,” said I.

“It is, sir,” said the shopman, “always﻿—for that sort of child,” and as he spoke we had a glimpse of the other youngster, a little, white face, pallid from sweet-eating and over-sapid food, and distorted by evil passions, a ruthless little egotist, pawing at the enchanted pane. “It’s no good, sir,” said the shopman, as I moved, with my natural helpfulness, doorward, and presently the spoilt child was carried off howling.

===Chinese===
“可以这么说，”伙计说，“不过我们到底还是要付代价的。只是没有——像旁人想象的那么重……我们那些大些的戏法，还有我们日常的吃食，以及一切所需的东西，都是从那顶帽子里弄出来的……还有您知道吗，先生，恕我直言，这世上*没有*批发行，至少正经的魔术货色没有批发行，先生。不知您留意到我们的招牌没有——正经魔术店（Genuine Magic Shop）。”他从腮帮子里抽出一张名片，递到我手里。“正经，”他用手指点着那个词说，又补了一句，“货真价实，毫不掺假，先生。”

我看他这玩笑开得也算是到家了，我心里想。

他转向吉普，露出了一个格外和蔼的微笑。“您哪，您是知道，您就是那种‘合适的好孩子’（Right Sort of Boy）。”

我倒诧异他怎么知道这事儿，因为为了管教起见，我们在家里都把这一点当作一桩秘密保守着；可吉普却毫不退缩地默默受下，目不转睛地盯着他。

“只有‘合适的好孩子’才进得了那扇门。”

仿佛是为了现身说法似的，门外忽地传来一阵擂门声，还能隐约听见一个又尖又细的小嗓门。“咿呀！我要*进*去，爸爸，我要**进去**。咿——呀——啊！”接着便是一个被孩子压制惯了的父亲那苦口婆心的劝哄声，又是安慰又是讨好的。“锁上了，爱德华（Edward），”他说。

“可门没锁呀，”我说。

“锁上了，先生，”伙计说，“对那种孩子——永远是锁上的。”他说着，我们瞥见那另一个小家伙——一张小小的、煞白的脸，吃糖和过咸的食物吃得没了血色，被种种邪门的情绪扭歪了，一个毫不讲理的小自私鬼，正用爪子抓挠那扇着了魔的玻璃门。“没用的，先生，”伙计说，我凭着天生的热心肠正要往门那边去，转眼间那被惯坏了的孩子就被抱着嚎叫着抱走了。

===Original===
“How do you manage that?” I said, breathing a little more freely.

“Magic!” said the shopman, with a careless wave of the hand, and behold! sparks of coloured fire flew out of his fingers and vanished into the shadows of the shop.

“You were saying,” he said, addressing himself to Gip, “before you came in, that you would like one of our ‘Buy One and Astonish your Friends’ boxes?”

Gip, after a gallant effort, said “Yes.”

“It’s in your pocket.”

And leaning over the counter﻿—he really had an extraordinary long body﻿—this amazing person produced the article in the customary conjurer’s manner. “Paper,” he said, and took a sheet out of the empty hat with the springs; “string,” and behold his mouth was a string box, from which he drew an unending thread, which when he had tied his parcel he bit off﻿—and, it seemed to me, swallowed the ball of string. And then he lit a candle at the nose of one of the ventriloquist’s dummies, stuck one of his fingers (which had become sealing-wax red) into the flame, and so sealed the parcel. “Then there was the Disappearing Egg,” he remarked, and produced one from within my coat-breast and packed it, and also The Crying Baby, Very Human. I handed each parcel to Gip as it was ready, and he clasped them to his chest.

He said very little, but his eyes were eloquent; the clutch of his arms was eloquent. He was the playground of unspeakable emotions. These, you know, were *real* magics.

===Chinese===
“这是怎么做到的？”我说，呼吸稍微松快了些。

“魔术！”伙计说，随手一挥，您瞧！指缝间便飞出几点彩色的火星，没入店里的阴影中不见了。

“您方才在——”他对吉普说，“您进门前说，想要一盒我们的‘买一个，让朋友们大吃一惊’？”

吉普鼓了鼓劲儿，才说出一个“是”字。

“就在您口袋里。”

这个了不起的人物探身越过柜台——他的身子可真是长得出奇——用魔术师惯用的那套手法把东西变了出来。“纸，”他说着，从那顶里头带弹簧的空帽子里抽出一张纸来；“绳子，”于是瞧吧，他的嘴就成了一个线团匣子，他从里头抽出一条抽之不竭的线绳，把包裹系好后，一口咬断——依我看，他把那团线绳吞进了肚里。接着，他又在一个腹语假人的鼻子上点着了一支蜡烛，把一根手指（那手指已变得像火漆一样通红）伸进火苗里，就这样把包裹封好。“还有那枚‘会消失的蛋’呢，”他说着，从我的上衣怀里变出一枚来，一并包好，又把那只“会哭的娃娃，栩栩如生”也包了进去。每包好一个，我便递给吉普，他一一抱在胸前。

他话不多，可那双眼睛会说得很；他那两条胳膊紧紧搂着，也会说得很。他简直成了一块游乐场，各种说不清道不明的情绪在上面翻涌。要知道，这些可都是*真*魔术。

===Original===
Then, with a start, I discovered something moving about in my hat﻿—something soft and jumpy. I whipped it off, and a ruffled pigeon﻿—no doubt a confederate﻿—dropped out and ran on the counter, and went, I fancy, into a cardboard box behind the papier-mâché tiger.

“Tut, tut!” said the shopman, dexterously relieving, me of my headdress; “careless bird, and﻿—as I live﻿—nesting!”
