可我们没法足够快地离开这儿。也许倒是万幸！因为我们本可以拔腿就跑的，倘若跑了，我相信我们一定会浑身起火。几乎可以肯定我们会浑身起火！要知道，这一点我们俩谁也没想到……可不等我们甚至开始迈步，那药的作用便已停止。前前后后不过是一秒的极其微小的几分之一。"新加速剂"的作用过去了，仿佛拉开了帘子，在一挥手之间便消失了。我听见吉伯恩无比惊惶的声音。"坐下。"他说——扑通，我在利斯边的草地上坐了下来——坐着的时候烫得厉害。那儿至今还有一块焦了边的草地，便是我坐下去的地方。我这一坐，整片的停滞仿佛随之醒来：乐队那支离破碎的振动骤然汇成一阵乐声，散步的人们把脚踩下去，各走各的路；报纸和旗子开始猎猎翻飞，笑容化作话语，那个眨眼的人眨完了这一眨，得意洋洋地继续上路，坐着的人也都动起来、说起话来。

===Original===
The whole world had come alive again, was going as fast as we were, or rather we were going no faster than the rest of the world. It was like slowing down as one comes into a railway station. Everything seemed to spin round for a second or two, I had the most transient feeling of nausea, and that was all. And the little dog, which had seemed to hang for a moment when the force of Gibberne’s arm was expended, fell with a swift acceleration clean through a lady’s parasol!

That was the saving of us. Unless it was for one corpulent old gentleman in a bath-chair, who certainly did start at the sight of us, and afterwards regarded us at intervals with a darkly suspicious eye, and, finally, I believe, said something to his nurse about us, I doubt if a solitary person remarked our sudden appearance among them. Plop! We must have appeared abruptly. We ceased to smoulder almost at once, though the turf beneath me was uncomfortably hot. The attention of everyone﻿—including even the Amusements’ Association band, which on this occasion, for the only time in its history, got out of tune﻿—was arrested by the amazing fact, and the still more amazing yapping and uproar caused by the fact, that a respectable, overfed lapdog sleeping quietly to the east of the bandstand should suddenly fall through the parasol of a lady on the west﻿—in a slightly singed condition due to the extreme velocity of its movements through the air. In these absurd days, too, when we are all trying to be as psychic, and silly, and superstitious as possible! People got up and trod on other people, chairs were overturned, the Leas policeman ran. How the matter settled itself I do not know﻿—we were much too anxious to disentangle ourselves from the affair and get out of range of the eye of the old gentleman in the bath-chair to make minute inquiries. As soon as we were sufficiently cool and sufficiently recovered from our giddiness and nausea and confusion of mind to do so we stood up, and skirting the crowd, directed our steps back along the road below the Metropole towards Gibberne’s house. But amidst the din I heard very distinctly the gentleman who had been sitting beside the lady of the ruptured sunshade using quite unjustifiable threats and language to one of those chair-attendants who have “Inspector” written on their caps: “If you didn’t throw the dog,” he said, “who *did*?”

===Chinese===
整个世界又重新活了过来，跑得跟我们一样快——或者说，我们不再比世间其余的一切更快了。就像火车进站时减速那样。一切都好像打了一两秒的旋，我有一种一闪而过的恶心感，仅此而已。至于那只小狗——当吉伯恩手臂的力道耗尽，它似乎在空中悬了片刻，随即以飞快的加速度落下，正正穿过一位女士的阳伞！

正是这一下救了我们。除了一位坐在轮椅里的胖老先生——他瞧见我们确实吃了一惊，过后又不时用一种满腹狐疑的目光打量我们，最后，我相信他还就我们的事对他的看护嘟囔了些什么——除此之外，我怕没有第二个人留意到我们这一群人之间突然冒出来的我们俩。扑通！我们准是突然现身的。我们身上的烟气几乎立刻就停了，尽管我身下的草地还是烫得叫人难受。所有人的注意力——就连那个游乐协会乐队也包括在内，这一次，是有史以来唯一一次，它走了调——都被一桩奇事攫住了，还有这件事引出的更加匪夷所思的一片尖叫与骚动：一只受人宠爱、营养过剩、安安静静地睡在奏乐台东边的哈巴狗，竟忽然之间从天而降，穿过奏乐台西边一位女士的阳伞——还因为穿越空气的速度太快而略带焦糊。况且如今这等荒唐年月，人人都变着法儿要让自己尽量通灵、尽量犯傻、尽量迷信！人们站起来，你踩着我我踩着你，椅子被掀翻，利斯的警察撒腿就跑。这件事末了是怎么收场的，我不得而知——我们当时正急于脱身，又想躲开轮椅里那位老先生的目光，顾不上去细细打听。等到我们身上的热气退得差不多，从眩晕、恶心和神志的混乱中缓过劲来，我们便站起身，绕开人群，沿着大都会酒店（Metropole）下方的路，朝吉伯恩家方向折了回去。可在一片喧嚣之中，我十分清楚地听见那位原本坐在被砸穿阳伞的女士身旁的先生，正气急败坏地对一位帽子上写着"稽查"二字的看椅人发狠话："这狗不是你扔的，"他说，"那又是谁扔的？"

===Original===
The sudden return of movement and familiar noises, and our natural anxiety about ourselves (our clothes were still dreadfully hot, and the fronts of the thighs of Gibberne’s white trousers were scorched a drabbish brown), prevented the minute observations I should have liked to make on all these things. Indeed, I really made no observations of any scientific value on that return. The bee, of course, had gone. I looked for that cyclist, but he was already out of sight as we came into the Upper Sandgate Road or hidden from us by traffic; the charabanc, however, with its people now all alive and stirring, was clattering along at a spanking pace almost abreast of the nearer church.

We noted, however, that the windowsill on which we had stepped in getting out of the house was slightly singed, and that the impressions of our feet on the gravel of the path were unusually deep.

===Chinese===
运动的骤然归来、那些熟悉声响的归来，加之我们对自身的自然担忧（我们的衣裳仍烫得吓人，吉伯恩白裤子两条大腿前侧已烧成了灰褐色），都妨碍了我本想就这一切所作的细致观察。说真的，回程路上我并没作出任何有科学价值的观察。那只蜜蜂自然已经飞走了。我四下找那位骑车人，可等我们走进上桑盖特路时，他已不见踪影，或被别的车辆挡住了；不过那辆客车——里头的人此刻全都活过来、动起来——倒正以飞快的速度咔哒咔哒地驶着，几乎与较近的那座教堂并齐。

不过我们注意到，我们翻出屋子时踩过的那个窗台略略烤焦了一些，而我们在小径砾石上留下的脚印也深得异乎寻常。

===Original===
So it was I had my first experience of the New Accelerator. Practically we had been running about and saying and doing all sorts of things in the space of a second or so of time. We had lived half an hour while the band had played, perhaps, two bars. But the effect it had upon us was that the whole world had stopped for our convenient inspection. Considering all things, and particularly considering our rashness in venturing out of the house, the experience might certainly have been much more disagreeable than it was. It showed, no doubt, that Gibberne has still much to learn before his preparation is a manageable convenience, but its practicability it certainly demonstrated beyond all cavil.

Since that adventure he has been steadily bringing its use under control, and I have several times, and without the slightest bad result, taken measured doses under his direction; though I must confess I have not yet ventured abroad again while under its influence. I may mention, for example, that this story has been written at one sitting and without interruption, except for the nibbling of some chocolate, by its means. I began at 6:25, and my watch is now very nearly at the minute past the half-hour. The convenience of securing a long, uninterrupted spell of work in the midst of a day full of engagements cannot be exaggerated. Gibberne is now working at the quantitative handling of his preparation, with especial reference to its distinctive effects upon different types of constitution. He then hopes to find a Retarder, with which to dilute its present rather excessive potency. The Retarder will, of course, have the reverse effect to the Accelerator; used alone it should enable the patient to spread a few seconds over many hours of ordinary time, and so to maintain an apathetic inaction, a glacier-like absence of alacrity, amidst the most animated or irritating surroundings. The two things together must necessarily work an entire revolution in civilised existence. It is the beginning of our escape from that Time Garment of which Carlyle speaks. While this Accelerator will enable us to concentrate ourselves with tremendous impact upon any moment or occasion that demands our utmost sense and vigour, the Retarder will enable us to pass in passive tranquillity through infinite hardship and tedium. Perhaps I am a little optimistic about the Retarder, which has indeed still to be discovered, but about the Accelerator there is no possible sort of doubt whatever. Its appearance upon the market in a convenient, controllable, and assimilable form is a matter of the next few months. It will be obtainable of all chemists and druggists, in small green bottles, at a high but, considering its extraordinary qualities, by no means excessive price. Gibberne’s Nervous Accelerator it will be called, and he hopes to be able to supply it in three strengths: one in 200, one in 900, and one in 2000, distinguished by yellow, pink, and white labels respectively.

No doubt its use renders a great number of very extraordinary things possible; for, of course, the most remarkable and, possibly, even criminal proceedings may be effected with impunity by thus dodging, as it were, into the interstices of time. Like all potent preparations, it will be liable to abuse. We have, however, discussed this aspect of the question very thoroughly, and we have decided that this is purely a matter of medical jurisprudence and altogether outside our province. We shall manufacture and sell the Accelerator, and as for the consequences﻿—we shall see.

===Chinese===
这便是我的"新加速剂"初体验。实际上，在一秒上下的时间里，我们又跑又跳、又说话又做事，干了一大堆。乐队大约才奏了两小节，我们却已经过了半个钟头。可这药给我们的感受是：整个世界为了我们方便的视察而停了下来。把一切都算进去，再特别把我们贸然出门这一桩冒失事算进去，这一番经历本可以比实际情形难受得多。毫无疑问，它表明在把他的药剂变成一件好操控的便利之物之前，吉伯恩还有许多东西要学；然而它的可行性，是毋庸置疑地被证明了。

自那次冒险之后，他便一直在稳步地把它的使用纳入可控之列。我也曾数度在他指导下服过定量的药剂，毫无不良反应——不过我得承认，服药之后我还没再敢出门到外面去过。比方说，我可以提一句，这篇故事便是借了它的力，一气呵成、毫无间断地写就的，中间不过是啃了几口巧克力。我从6:25动笔，此刻我的表已差不多走到半点过一分。在一天诸事缠身之中，能挤出一大段不受打扰的时间来工作，这便利之大，再怎样夸张也不为过。吉伯恩眼下正在研究他的药剂的定量用法，尤其着眼于它对不同体质所产生的不同效果。他下一步希望能找出一种"减速剂"（Retarder），用来稀释它目前过于凶猛的药力。当然，减速剂的功效与加速剂正好相反；单独使用，它能让服药者把几秒钟的光景铺开，摊到寻常时间的好几个钟头里去，从而在最热闹或最恼人的环境里，保持一种冷漠无为、如冰川一般毫无动静的迟钝。这两样东西合起来，必将给文明人的生活带来一场彻底的革命。卡莱尔（Carlyle）曾谈到一件"时间之衣"（Time Garment），而我们正开始从中挣脱出来。这加速剂能叫我们以雷霆万钧之力，把全部身心倾注到每一个需要我们最敏锐的感官与最饱满的精力的时刻与场合之上；而那减速剂，则能叫我们以被动的恬静，穿过无尽的艰辛与沉闷。关于减速剂，也许我乐观得早了一些——它的确还有待发现——可关于加速剂，则再无可疑之处。用一种方便、可控、可被吸收的形式上市，只是今后几个月的事。届时所有药店药房均有售，装在绿色小瓶里，售价不菲，但念及其惊人的品质，倒也算不得太贵。它将被命名为"吉伯恩神经加速剂"（Gibberne’s Nervous Accelerator），他希望能提供三种浓度：1:200、1:900、1:2000，分别以黄色、粉色、白色标签加以区分。

毫无疑问，它的使用会让许许多多非常离奇的事情成为可能；因为，只要这样一头钻进时间的缝隙里——可以说是——那么世间最惊人、甚至有可能是犯罪的勾当，便都能干了而全身而退。与一切烈性药剂一样，它难免会被人滥用。不过，我们已经把问题的这一面反复讨论得十分透彻，并认定这纯粹是法医学上的事，完全不属于我们的职责范围。我们只管制造和销售加速剂，至于后果嘛——到时候再说。

## The Obliterated Man / 被抹去的人

===Original===
I was—you shall hear immediately why I am not now—Egbert Craddock Cummins. The name remains. I am still (Heaven help me!) Dramatic Critic to the *Fiery Cross*. What I shall be in a little while I do not know. I write in great trouble and confusion of mind. I will do what I can to make myself clear in the face of terrible difficulties. You must bear with me a little. When a man is rapidly losing his own identity, he naturally finds a difficulty in expressing himself. I will make it perfectly plain in a minute, when once I get my grip upon the story. Let me see—where *am* I? I wish I knew. Ah, I have it! Dead self! Egbert Craddock Cummins!

In the past I should have disliked writing anything quite so full of “I” as this story must be. It is full of “I’s” before and behind, like the beast in Revelation—the one with a head like a calf, I am afraid. But my tastes have changed since I became a Dramatic Critic and studied the masters—G.A.S., G.B.S., G.R.S., and the others. Everything has changed since then. At least the story is about myself—so that there is some excuse for me. And it is really not egotism, because, as I say, since those days my identity has undergone an entire alteration.

That past!… I was—in those days—rather a nice fellow, rather shy—taste for grey in my clothes, weedy little moustache, face “interesting,” slight stutter which I had caught in my early life from a schoolfellow. Engaged to a very nice girl, named Delia. Fairly new, she was—cigarettes—liked me because I was human and original. Considered I was like Lamb—on the strength of the stutter, I believe. Father, an eminent authority on postage stamps. She read a great deal in the British Museum. (A perfect pairing ground for literary people, that British Museum—you should read George Egerton and Justin Huntly M’Carthy and Gissing and the rest of them.) We loved in our intellectual way, and shared the brightest hopes. (All gone now.) And her father liked me because I seemed honestly eager to hear about stamps. She had no mother. Indeed, I had the happiest prospects a young man could have. I never went to theatres in those days. My Aunt Charlotte before she died had told me not to.

===Chinese===
我曾是——您马上就会听到，为什么我现在已经不是了——埃格伯特·克拉多克·卡明斯（Egbert Craddock Cummins）。这个名字还在。我依然是（老天帮帮我吧！）《烈火十字》（*Fiery Cross*）报的戏剧评论家。再过一会儿我会变成什么，我不知道。我提笔时心乱如麻，惶惑不已。在可怕的困难面前，我会尽力把自己说清楚。您得稍稍担待我一些。一个人正在迅速地失去自己的本来面目，自然就很难把意思表达出来。等我抓住了这桩故事的脉络，我立刻就能把它讲得一清二楚。让我想想——我现在是在哪儿？要是我知道就好了。啊，有了！逝去的自我！埃格伯特·克拉多克·卡明斯！

从前，要我写一篇像这个故事这般满纸都是"我"字的文章，我是不乐意的。前后到处都是"我"，活像《启示录》里那头兽——怕就是那头长着牛犊一般脑袋的家伙。可自从我当上戏剧评论家、研习了几位大师——G.A.S.、G.B.S.、G.R.S.，还有其他几位——之后，我的口味已经变了。从那以后，样样事情都变了。至少这故事讲的是我自己的事——所以我也算有个借口。再说这实在也算不得自大，因为，正如我所说，自那段日子以来，我的身份已经整个儿地变了样。

那段往事啊！……那时候的我——是个相当不错的小伙子，相当腼腆——衣服偏爱灰色，一撮稀稀拉拉的小胡子，长相"有趣"，略略有些口吃——这是早年从一个同学那里染上的。与一位很好的姑娘订了婚，名叫迪莉娅（Delia）。挺新派的姑娘，她会抽烟——喜欢我，是因为我有人情味儿，又与众不同。她觉得我像兰姆（Lamb）——我想多半是冲着那口吃下的判断。她父亲是邮票方面的一位显赫权威。她自己则在大英博物馆（British Museum）里读了许许多多的书。（那大英博物馆可真是文人雅士寻觅佳偶的绝佳之地——您该读读乔治·埃格顿（George Egerton）、贾斯汀·亨特利·麦卡锡（Justin Huntly M’Carthy）、吉辛（Gissing）他们那一帮子。）我们以我们那种知识分子的方式相爱，怀抱着最光明的前景。（如今一切都完了。）她父亲也喜欢我，因为我看上去是真心实意地爱听他讲邮票。她没有母亲。说真的，我有着一个年轻人所能拥有的最幸福的前景。那些日子我从不上剧院。我姑母夏洛特（Aunt Charlotte）在世时，曾嘱咐过我不要去。

===Original===
Then Barnaby, the editor of the *Fiery Cross*, made me—in spite of my spasmodic efforts to escape—Dramatic Critic. He is a fine, healthy man, Barnaby, with an enormous head of frizzy black hair and a convincing manner, and he caught me on the staircase going to see Wembly. He had been dining, and was more than usually buoyant. “Hullo, Cummins!” he said. “The very man I want!” He caught me by the shoulder or the collar or something, ran me up the little passage, and flung me over the wastepaper basket into the armchair in his office. “Pray be seated,” he said, as he did so. Then he ran across the room and came back with some pink and yellow tickets and pushed them into my hand. “Opera Comique,” he said, “Thursday; Friday, the Surrey; Saturday, the Frivolity. That’s all, I think.”

“But—” I began.

“Glad you’re free,” he said, snatching some proofs off the desk and beginning to read.

“I don’t quite understand,” I said.

“*Eigh?*” he said, at the top of his voice, as though he thought I had gone and was startled at my remark.

“Do you want me to criticise these plays?”

“Do something with ’em… Did you think it was a treat?”

“But I can’t.”

===Chinese===
后来，《烈火十字》的主编巴纳比（Barnaby）——尽管我一阵阵地拼命挣脱——还是让我做了戏剧评论家。巴纳比是个结实健壮的汉子，一头浓密卷曲的黑发，说起话来一套套的，让人服气。他在我去找温布利（Wembly）的楼梯上把我逮了个正着。他刚吃过饭，比平时更加兴高采烈。"嘿，卡明斯！"他说，"我要找的正是你！"他一把抓住我的肩膀——也可能是衣领，或者别的什么部位——把我沿着那条小走廊一路推上去，越过废纸篓，甩进了他办公室的扶手椅里。"请坐。"他一边这么干一边说。接着他又穿过房间跑了一趟，回来时手里多了几张粉色和黄色的票子，塞进我手里。"喜歌剧院（Opera Comique），"他说，"周四；周五，萨里剧院（the Surrey）；周六，弗里沃利蒂剧院（the Frivolity）。我想，就这些。"

"可是——"我开口道。

"真高兴你有空。"他说着，从桌上抓起几份校样，埋头读了起来。

"我不太明白。"我说。

"啊？"他扯着嗓子应了一声，仿佛以为我已经走了，又被我的话吓了一跳。

"您是要我去评这些戏吗？"

"做点儿什么……难不成你以为这是什么赏赐？"

"可我不会呀。"

===Original===
“Did you call me a fool?”

“Well, I’ve never been to a theatre in my life.”

“Virgin soil.”

“But I don’t know anything about it, you know.”

“That’s just it. New view. No habits. No clichés in stock. Ours is a live paper, not a bag of tricks. None of your clockwork professional journalism in this office. And I can rely on your integrity—”

“But I’ve conscientious scruples—”

He caught me up suddenly and put me outside his door. “Go and talk to Wembly about that,” he said. “He’ll explain.”

As I stood perplexed, he opened the door again, said, “I forgot this,” thrust a fourth ticket into my hand (it was for that night—in twenty minutes’ time) and slammed the door upon me. His expression was quite calm, but I caught his eye.

===Chinese===
"你是说我傻咯？"

"呃，我这辈子还从来没进过剧院。"

"处女地啊。"

"可您知道，我对这一行什么也不懂。"

"要的就是这个。全新的视角。没有积习。库存里没有陈词滥调。咱们是一张活的报纸，不是一袋子花招。咱们这间办公室里，可不兴那种发条式的职业记者套路。何况，你的正直我也信得过——"

"可我良心上有些过不去——"

他猛地把我提起来，扔出门外。"这事儿你去跟温布利说吧。"他说，"他会给你解释。"

我正手足无措地站着，他又把门打开了，说："差点把这个忘了。"把第四张票子塞进我手里（是当晚的——离开场只有二十分钟），砰地一声又把门摔上。他神情十分平静，可我撞上了他的眼神。

===Original===
I hate arguments. I decided that I would take his hint and become (to my own destruction) a Dramatic Critic. I walked slowly down the passage to Wembly. That Barnaby has a remarkable persuasive way. He has made few suggestions during our very pleasant intercourse of four years that he has not ultimately won me round to adopting. It may be, of course, that I am of a yielding disposition; certainly I am too apt to take my colour from my circumstances. It is, indeed, to my unfortunate susceptibility to vivid impressions that all my misfortunes are due. I have already alluded to the slight stammer I had acquired from a schoolfellow in my youth. However, this is a digression… I went home in a cab to dress.

I will not trouble the reader with my thoughts about the first-night audience, strange assembly as it is—those I reserve for my Memoirs—nor the humiliating story of how I got lost during the *entr’acte* in a lot of red plush passages, and saw the third act from the gallery. The only point upon which I wish to lay stress was the remarkable effect of the acting upon me. You must remember I had lived a quiet and retired life, and had never been to the theatre before, and that I am extremely sensitive to vivid impressions. At the risk of repetition I must insist upon these points.

The first effect was a profound amazement, not untinctured by alarm. The phenomenal unnaturalness of acting is a thing discounted in the minds of most people by early visits to the theatre. They get used to the fantastic gestures, the flamboyant emotions, the weird mouthings, melodious snortings, agonising yelps, lip-gnawings, glaring horrors, and other emotional symbolism of the stage. It becomes at last a mere deaf-and-dumb language to them, which they read intelligently *pari passu* with the hearing of the dialogue. But all this was new to me. The thing was called a modern comedy, the people were supposed to be English and were dressed like fashionable Americans of the current epoch, and I fell into the natural error of supposing that the actors were trying to represent human beings. I looked round on my first-night audience with a kind of wonder, discovered—as all new Dramatic Critics do—that it rested with me to reform the Drama, and, after a supper choked with emotion, went off to the office to write a column, piebald with “new paragraphs” (as all my stuff is—it fills out so) and purple with indignation. Barnaby was delighted.

===Chinese===
我讨厌争辩。我决定就照他的意思，去做一个（结果害了我自己的）戏剧评论家。我沿着走廊慢慢往温布利那边走。巴纳比这个人的劝人本事可谓一绝。在我们四年愉快的交往里，他出的主意，最终没有几个不被他说动我采纳的。当然，也可能是我这人天生耳根子软；至少我太容易让环境给我染上色。说真的，我所有的不幸，都要归咎于我这种对鲜明印象过分敏感的天性。前文已经提到过，我少年时从一个同学那里染上了那点轻微的口吃。不过这是题外话了……我坐马车回家换衣服去了。

首演夜的观众是一群什么样的人——这奇怪的集合——我就不拿我的看法来烦扰读者了，那些我留给我的《回忆录》再说；我也不必细述幕间休息时我在那些红丝绒走廊里迷了路、最后只好从顶层楼座看完第三幕的那段丢人经历。我唯一想强调的是，那些表演对我产生了非同小可的影响。您必须记得，我此前过的是一种安静退隐的生活，从来没有进过剧院，而且我对鲜明的印象极为敏感。哪怕冒着重复之嫌，我也必须把这一点再说一遍。

头一个影响，是深深的惊愕，其中还不无惊恐。演戏那种匪夷所思的不自然，在大多数人心里，早已被早年到剧院看戏的经历打了折扣而习以为常。他们看惯了那些奇奇怪怪的手势，那种花里胡哨的情感，那些怪里怪气的念白、带旋律的鼻息、撕心裂肺的尖叫、咬嘴唇、瞪眼睛的恐怖相，以及舞台上种种别的表情达意的程式。到后来，这一切对他们不过是另一种聋哑人手语，他们一边听着台词，一边同步自如地读懂这种语言。可这一切对我来说都是头一遭。这出戏叫作一出"现代喜剧"，剧中人本应是英国人，穿戴却像当今时髦的美国佬，我便顺理成章地犯了个错误——以为演员们正努力再现真正的人类。我以一种惊奇的心情环顾首演夜的观众，发现了——正如一切新晋戏剧评论家所发现的那样——改革戏剧的重任落在了我的肩上。于是在一顿噎得人喘不过气来的晚饭之后，我便赶到报社，写了一整栏文章，斑驳杂乱地塞满了"新起的段落"（我所有的稿子都这样——这样子好凑篇幅），又因义愤填膺而写得通篇紫红。巴纳比乐坏了。

===Original===
But I could not sleep that night. I dreamt of actors—actors glaring, actors smiting their chests, actors flinging out a handful of extended fingers, actors smiling bitterly, laughing despairingly, falling hopelessly, dying idiotically. I got up at eleven with a slight headache, read my notice in the *Fiery Cross*, breakfasted, and went back to my room to shave, (It’s my habit to do so.) Then an odd thing happened. I could not find my razor. Suddenly it occurred to me that I had not unpacked it the day before.

“Ah!” said I, in front of the looking-glass. Then “Hullo!”

Quite involuntarily, when I had thought of my portmanteau, I had flung up the left arm (fingers fully extended) and clutched at my diaphragm with my right hand. I am an acutely self-conscious man at all times. The gesture struck me as absolutely novel for me. I repeated it, for my own satisfaction. “Odd!” Then (rather puzzled) I turned to my portmanteau.

===Chinese===
可那天夜里我睡不着。我梦见了演员——演员瞪眼睛，演员捶胸顿足，演员甩出一把伸开的手指，演员苦笑，演员绝望地大笑，演员无可奈何地倒下，演员愚蠢透顶地死去。我十一点钟起床，头有点儿疼，读了我在《烈火十字》上那篇剧评，吃了早饭，回到自己房里准备刮脸。（这是我的习惯。）接着，一桩怪事发生了。我找不到我的剃须刀。我忽然想起，前一天我并没有把它从箱子里取出来。

"啊！"我在镜子前说。接着又"哟！"

完全是下意识的——我一想到旅行箱，便甩起左臂（五指尽量张开），右手一把捂住了自己的横膈膜。我这人是无时无刻不高度自省的。这个动作在我看来，对我而言是绝对新奇的。为了让自己满意，我又做了一遍。"怪了！"然后（颇感纳闷地）我转向我的旅行箱。

===Original===
After shaving, my mind reverted to the acting I had seen, and I entertained myself before the cheval glass with some imitations of Jafferay’s more exaggerated gestures. “Really, one might think it a disease,” I said—“Stage-Walkitis!” (There’s many a truth spoken in jest.) Then, if I remember rightly, I went off to see Wembly, and afterwards lunched at the British Museum with Delia. We actually spoke about our prospects, in the light of my new appointment.

But that appointment was the beginning of my downfall. From that day I necessarily became a persistent theatregoer, and almost insensibly I began to change. The next thing I noticed after the gesture about the razor was to catch myself bowing ineffably when I met Delia, and stooping in an old-fashioned, courtly way over her hand. Directly I caught myself, I straightened myself up and became very uncomfortable. I remember she looked at me curiously. Then, in the office, I found myself doing “nervous business,” fingers on teeth, when Barnaby asked me a question I could not very well answer. Then, in some trifling difference with Delia, I clasped my hand to my brow. And I pranced through my social transactions at times singularly like an actor! I tried not to—no one could be more keenly alive to the arrant absurdity of the histrionic bearing. And I did!

It began to dawn on me what it all meant. The acting, I saw, was too much for my delicately-strung nervous system. I have always, I know, been too amenable to the suggestions of my circumstances. Night after night of concentrated attention to the conventional attitudes and intonation of the English stage was gradually affecting my speech and carriage. I was giving way to the infection of sympathetic imitation. Night after night my plastic nervous system took the print of some new amazing gesture, some new emotional exaggeration—and retained it. A kind of theatrical veneer threatened to plate over and obliterate my private individuality altogether. I saw myself in a kind of vision. Sitting by myself one night, my new self seemed to me to glide, posing and gesticulating, across the room. He clutched his throat, he opened his fingers, he opened his legs in walking like a high-class marionette. He went from attitude to attitude. He might have been clockwork. Directly after this I made an ineffectual attempt to resign my theatrical work. But Barnaby persisted in talking about the Polywhiddle Divorce all the time I was with him, and I could get no opportunity of saying what I wished.

And then Delia’s manner began to change towards me. The ease of our intercourse vanished. I felt she was learning to dislike me. I grinned, and capered, and scowled, and posed at her in a thousand ways, and knew—with what a voiceless agony!—that I did it all the time. I tried to resign again, and Barnaby talked about “X” and “Z” and “Y” in the *New Review*, and gave me a strong cigar to smoke, and so routed me. And then I walked up the Assyrian Gallery in the manner of Irving to meet Delia, and so precipitated the crisis.

===Chinese===
刮完脸，我的心思又转回到我看过的那场戏上，便在穿衣镜前自娱自乐地模仿了几下贾弗雷（Jafferay）几个最为夸张的动作。"说真的，简直可以当成一种病，"我说，"舞台步态炎（Stage-Walkitis）！"（戏言之中往往藏着真理。）接下来，如果我没记错的话，我去看望了温布利，而后又和在大英博物馆里的迪莉娅一起吃了午饭。鉴于我这新任命，我们竟然还认真谈论了一番我们的前程。

可那任命，就是我败落的开端。从那一天起，我便不得不成了一个锲而不舍的看戏人，几乎在不知不觉中开始变了。剃须刀那事之后，我注意到的下一桩，是遇见迪莉娅时，竟发现自己正以一种难以言喻的风度鞠躬，又以一种旧式的、宫廷般的姿态俯身凑向她的手。我一察觉到自己这样做，便赶紧挺直身子，浑身不自在。我记得她好奇地打量着我。再后来，在办公室里，巴纳比问我一个不太好回答的问题时，我发现自己正在做"紧张的小动作"——手指放在牙齿上。又一次，因为与迪莉娅起了点儿小口角，我便一手捂住了额头。时不时地，我在各种社交往来中昂首阔步，活脱脱像个演员！我不想这样——没人比我更敏锐地意识到那种舞台做派的彻头彻尾的可笑。可我偏就做了出来！

渐渐地，我开始明白这是怎么回事。我看出来，那些表演对我这根弦绷得过紧的神经系统来说，实在是承受不住。我知道，我一向过于容易受环境暗示左右。一夜复一夜地，聚精会神地关注着英国舞台上那些约定俗成的姿态和声调，正一点一点地影响着我的言语和举止。我正向着那种共鸣式模仿的感染力屈服。一夜复一夜，我那可塑的神经系统又印上了某种新的、令人瞠目的姿态，某种新的情感夸张——并且留住了它。一层戏剧性的釉光，眼看就要把我私人的个性整个儿镀盖、抹杀。我在一种近乎幻象中看到了自己。某夜我独自坐着，我那个新的自我仿佛就这样摆着姿势、比划着手势，滑过房间。他掐住自己的喉咙，他张开五指，他走路时双腿分得开开的，像一个上等的提线木偶。他从一种姿态变换到另一种姿态。他活像一架上了发条的机器。这事过后不久，我试图辞去这份剧院的差事，但毫无结果。因为我和巴纳比在一起的全部时间里，他一直喋喋不休地谈论着波利怀德尔（Polywhiddle）离婚案，我根本插不上嘴说我想说的话。

接着，迪莉娅对我的态度也开始变了。我们之间往来时那份自在消失了。我感到她正学着讨厌我。我对着她咧嘴笑、蹦跳、皱眉，摆出千般姿态——心里明明知道——怀着一种说不出口的痛苦！——自己无时无刻不在这样做。我又一次试图辞职，可巴纳比又扯起了《新评论》（*New Review*）上署名"X""Z""Y"的文章，又塞给我一支烈性雪茄，就这么把我打发了。再后来，我模仿着欧文（Irving）的派头，穿过亚述展厅（Assyrian Gallery）去会迪莉娅，便这样加速引爆了那场危机。

===Original===
“Ah!—*Dear!*” I said, with more sprightliness and emotion in my voice than had ever been in all my life before I became (to my own undoing) a Dramatic Critic.

She held out her hand rather coldly, scrutinising my face as she did so. I prepared, with a new-won grace, to walk by her side. “Egbert,” she said, standing still, and thought. Then she looked at me.

I said nothing. I felt what was coming. I tried to be the old Egbert Craddock Cummins of shambling gait and stammering sincerity, whom she loved, but I felt even as I did so that I was a new thing, a thing of surging emotions and mysterious fixity—like no human being that ever lived, except upon the stage. “Egbert,” she said, “you are not yourself.”

“Ah!” Involuntarily I clutched my diaphragm and averted my head (as is the way with them).

“There!” she said.

“What do you mean?” I said, whispering in vocal italics—you know how they do it—turning on her, perplexity on face, right hand down, left on brow. I knew quite well what she meant. I knew quite well the dramatic unreality of my behaviour. But I struggled against it in vain. “What do you mean?” I said, and, in a kind of hoarse whisper, “I don’t understand!”

===Chinese===
"啊！——亲爱的！"我说，声音里的活泼与激动，是我成为（结果害了我自己的）戏剧评论家以前一辈子都不曾有过的。

她相当冷淡地伸出手来，一边端详着我的脸。我以新近赢得的风度，准备走在她身侧。"埃格伯特。"她站住了，思索着说。然后她看着我。

我什么也没说。我感到即将到来的是什么。我努力想做回那个拖着脚步、真诚得有些结巴的旧日埃格伯特·克拉多克·卡明斯——她所爱的那一个——可我边这么做边感到，我已是一个全新的东西，一个情感汹涌、姿态莫名定格的东西——除了舞台之上，世间从未有过这样的人。"埃格伯特，"她说，"你不是你自己了。"

"啊！"我不由自主地捂住横膈膜，把头偏到一边（这都是他们那一路的做法）。

"瞧！"她说。

"你什么意思？"我说，用舞台腔那种把字念成斜体一样的方式低语——您是知道他们怎么念的——猛地转向她，满脸的困惑，右手下垂，左手按在额上。我完全明白她是什么意思。我完全明白自己行为的那种戏剧性的不真实。可我徒劳地与之抗争。"你什么意思？"我又说一遍，然后以一种嘶哑的低语，"我不明白！"

===Original===
She really looked as though she disliked me. “What do you keep on posing for?” she said. “I don’t like it. You didn’t use to.”

“Didn’t use to!” I said slowly, repeating this twice. I glared up and down the gallery with short, sharp glances. “We are alone,” I said swiftly. “*Listen!*” I poked my forefinger towards her, and glared at her. “I am under a curse.”

I saw her hand tighten upon her sunshade. “You are under some bad influence or other,” said Delia. “You should give it up. I never knew anyone change as you have done.”

“Delia!” I said, lapsing into the pathetic. “Pity me, Augh! Delia! *Pit*—y me!”

She eyed me critically. “*Why* you keep playing the fool like this I don’t know,” she said. “Anyhow, I really cannot go about with a man who behaves as you do. You made us both ridiculous on Wednesday. Frankly, I dislike you, as you are now. I met you here to tell you so—as it’s about the only place where we can be sure of being alone together—”

“Delia!” said I, with intensity, knuckles of clenched hands white. “You don’t mean—”

“I do,” said Delia. “A woman’s lot is sad enough at the best of times. But with you—”

I clapped my hand on my brow.

===Chinese===
她看上去真的像是讨厌我了。"你干吗老是这么装腔作势？"她说，"我不喜欢。你从前不这样。"

"从前不这样！"我慢吞吞地说，把这话重复了两遍。我用短促犀利的目光，上下打量着展厅。"这儿就咱们俩，"我飞快地说，"听着！"我把食指戳向她，瞪着她。"我中了诅咒。"

我看见她的手在阳伞上捏紧了。"你是受了什么坏影响。"迪莉娅说，"你该把它戒掉。我从没见过谁像你变得这么厉害。"

"迪莉娅！"我说，滑入了悲情的腔调。"可怜可怜我吧，啊！迪莉娅！可——怜可怜我吧！"

她挑剔地打量着我。"我不知道你为什么老这样装疯卖傻，"她说，"无论如何，我实在没法再跟一个举止像你这般的人一同出入社交场合。星期三那天你让我们俩都成了笑柄。坦白说，如今这副模样，我不喜欢你。我约你在这里见面，就是要告诉你这件事——因为这儿差不多是咱们唯一能确保单独相处的地方——"

"迪莉娅！"我热烈地说，攥紧的双手指节发白。"你不是说——"

"我是说。"迪莉娅说，"女人的命运即使在最好的时候也已经够悲哀了。可要是跟你——"

我一掌按在额头上。

===Original===
“So, goodbye,” said Delia, without emotion.

“Oh, Delia!” I said. “Not *this*?”

“Goodbye, Mr. Cummins,” she said.

By a violent effort I controlled myself and touched her hand. I tried to say some word of explanation to her. She looked into my working face and winced. “I *must* do it,” she said hopelessly. Then she turned from me and began walking rapidly down the gallery.

Heavens! How the human agony cried within me! I loved Delia. But nothing found expression—I was already too deeply crusted with my acquired self.

“Good-baye!” I said at last, watching her retreating figure. How I hated myself for doing it! After she had vanished, I repeated in a dreamy way, “Good-baye!” looking hopelessly round me. Then, with a kind of heartbroken cry, I shook my clenched fists in the air, staggered to the pedestal of a winged figure, buried my face in my arms, and made my shoulders heave. Something within me said “Ass!” as I did so. (I had the greatest difficulty in persuading the Museum policeman, who was attracted by my cry of agony, that I was not intoxicated, but merely suffering from a transient indisposition.)

===Chinese===
"那么，再见。"迪莉娅毫无感情地说。

"哦，迪莉娅！"我说，"别——别这样？"

"再见，卡明斯先生。"她说。

我拼了极大的力气才克制住自己，碰了碰她的手。我努力想对她解释一两句。她望着我那张抽动的脸，向后瑟缩了一下。"我非这么做不可。"她绝望地说。然后她转过身，快步沿展厅走开了。

老天！我内里那人性的痛苦怎样地呼号着啊！我是爱迪莉娅的。可什么也表达不出来——我早已被我这后天习得的自我，包裹得太厚了。

"再——见咯！"我终于说出，望着她远去的身影。我多么恨自己会做出这种举动！她消失之后，我又恍恍惚惚地重复了一遍："再——见咯！"绝望地四下张望着。接着，我发出一种心碎的喊声，朝着空中挥舞紧握的双拳，踉跄地走到一座带翅膀的雕像底座前，把脸埋进双臂，让肩膀一抽一抽地起伏。我这么做的时候，心里有个声音说："蠢驴！"（博物馆的警察被我那声痛苦的喊叫引了过来，我费了好大劲才让他相信我并没有喝醉，不过是突发的一阵身体不适罢了。）

===Original===
But even this great sorrow has not availed to save me from my fate. I see it; everyone sees it: I grow more “theatrical” every day. And no one could be more painfully aware of the pungent silliness of theatrical ways. The quiet, nervous, but pleasing E. C. Cummins vanishes. I cannot save him. I am driven like a dead leaf before the winds of March. My tailor even enters into the spirit of my disorder. He has a peculiar sense of what is fitting. I tried to get a dull grey suit from him this spring, and he foisted a brilliant blue upon me, and I see he has put braid down the sides of my new dress trousers. My hairdresser insists upon giving me a “wave.”

I am beginning to associate with actors. I detest them, but it is only in their company that I can feel I am not glaringly conspicuous. Their talk infects me. I notice a growing tendency to dramatic brevity, to dashes and pauses in my style, to a punctuation of bows and attitudes. Barnaby has remarked it too. I offended Wembly by calling him “Dear Boy” yesterday. I dread the end, but I cannot escape from it.

The fact is, I am being obliterated. Living a grey, retired life all my youth, I came to the theatre a delicate sketch of a man, a thing of tints and faint lines. Their gorgeous colouring has effaced me altogether. People forget how much mode of expression, method of movement, are a matter of contagion. I have heard of stage-struck people before, and thought it a figure of speech. I spoke of it jestingly, as a disease. It is no jest. It is a disease. And I have got it badly! Deep down within me I protest against the wrong done to my personality—unavailingly. For three hours or more a week I have to go and concentrate my attention on some fresh play, and the suggestions of the drama strengthen their awful hold upon me. My manners grow so flamboyant, my passions so professional, that I doubt, as I said at the outset, whether it is really myself that behaves in such a manner. I feel merely the core to this dramatic casing, that grows thicker and presses upon me—me and mine. I feel like King John’s abbot in his cope of lead.

I doubt, indeed, whether I should not abandon the struggle altogether—leave this sad world of ordinary life for which I am so ill fitted, abandon the name of Cummins for some professional pseudonym, complete my self-effacement, and—a thing of tricks and tatters, of posing and pretence—go upon the stage. It seems my only resort—“to hold the mirror up to Nature.” For in the ordinary life, I will confess, no one now seems to regard me as both sane and sober. Only upon the stage, I feel convinced, will people take me seriously. That will be the end of it. I *know* that will be the end of it. And yet… I will frankly confess… all that marks off your actor from your common man… I *detest*. I am still largely of my Aunt Charlotte’s opinion, that playacting is unworthy of a pure-minded man’s attention, much more participation. Even now I would resign my dramatic criticism and try a rest. Only I can’t get hold of Barnaby. Letters of resignation he never notices. He says it is against the etiquette of journalism to write to your Editor. And when I go to see him, he gives me another big cigar and some strong whisky and soda, and then something always turns up to prevent my explanation.

===Chinese===
可即便是这样一场大悲恸，也没能把我从命运里救出来。我看出来了；人人都看出来了：我一天比一天更"舞台腔"。而论到对舞台做派那种刺鼻的愚蠢有多么痛切地自觉，再没人能比得过我。那个沉静、神经质却讨人喜欢的 E. C. 卡明斯正在消失。我救不了他。我像一片枯叶，被三月的风吹着到处飘荡。连我的裁缝也感染了我这毛病的精神。他对什么得体有一份独到的感觉。今年春天我本想在他那儿做一套暗灰色的西服，他却硬塞给我一套鲜蓝色的，而我还看见，他把我新做的礼服裤腿两旁都滚上了辫带。我的理发师则非要给我做一个"波浪卷"。

我开始和演员们来往。我讨厌他们，可只有在他们中间，我才能感觉自己不是那么显眼得刺目。他们的谈吐感染着我。我注意到自己的言谈越来越倾向于戏剧化的简洁，越来越爱用破折号和停顿，越来越多地用鞠躬和姿态来作标点。巴纳比也察觉到了。昨天我还冒犯了温布利，管他叫"亲爱的孩子"。我害怕那个结局，可我逃不开它。

事实上，我正在被抹去。年轻时过的是灰色、退隐的生活，来到剧院时，我还是一个人纤细的素描，一件由淡彩和细线构成的东西。他们那些浓墨重彩，已把我整个儿涂没了。人们忘记了，表达方式、行动方法，在很大程度上都是会传染的。我从前也听说过"中了舞台魔"的人，还以为那是一种修辞。我曾戏言这是一种病。这不是戏言。这就是一种病。而且我病得不轻！在我内心深处，我对自己的人格所遭受的不公提出抗议——可徒劳无功。每周我得花三个多小时去把注意力集中在某出新戏上，而戏剧的种种暗示也在不断加强对我的可怕控制。我的举止变得愈发浮夸，我的情感变得愈发职业化，以至于我——正如我一开头所说的那样——怀疑如此举止的究竟是不是真正的我自己。我只觉得自己成了这副戏剧性外壳的内核，外壳越长越厚，压迫着我——我和属于我的一切。我觉得自己就像约翰王那位院长，披着一件铅制的斗篷。

说真的，我倒怀疑自己是不是干脆放弃这场挣扎算了——离开这个我如此格格不入的、平凡的悲哀人世，抛弃卡明斯这个名字，换上一个职业的化名，完成我这场自我湮灭，然后——一具由花招与破布、做派与矫饰拼凑而成之物——登上舞台。这似乎是我唯一的出路——"把镜子举到自然面前"。因为不瞒您说，在平凡生活里，如今似乎再没有人把我当作一个神志清醒、脚步稳当的人看待了。我深信，只有登上了舞台，人们才会认真地对待我。那将是这一切的终局。我知道那将是终局。然而……我坦白地承认……凡是把你这种演员与凡夫俗子区分开来的那一套……我都憎恶。我在很大程度上仍持我姑母夏洛特的看法：演戏这种事，配不上一个心地纯洁者的关注，更别说亲身参与了。即使到现在，我也宁愿辞去这份剧评的差事，歇上一歇。只是我怎么也抓不住巴纳比。辞职信他从不理会。他说给主编写信是违背新闻礼节的。而每当我去看他，他就又塞给我一支大雪柯、一杯烈性的威士忌苏打，然后总有什么事情冒出来，让我没法把话说完。

## The Pearl of Love / 爱之珠

===Original===
The pearl is lovelier than the most brilliant of crystalline stones, the moralist declares, because it is made through the suffering of a living creature. About that I can say nothing because I feel none of the fascination of pearls. Their cloudy lustre moves me not at all. Nor can I decide for myself upon that agelong dispute whether the Pearl of Love is the cruellest of stories or only a gracious fable of the immortality of beauty.

Both the story and the controversy will be familiar to students of mediaeval Persian prose. The story is a short one, though the commentary upon it is a respectable part of the literature of that period. They have treated it as a poetic invention and they have treated it as an allegory meaning this, that, or the other thing. Theologians have had their copious way with it, dealing with it particularly as concerning the restoration of the body after death, and it has been greatly used as a parable by those who write about aesthetics. And many have held it to be the statement of a fact, simply and baldly true.

===Chinese===
道德家说，珍珠比最璀璨的结晶宝石还要可爱，因为它是用一个生灵的痛苦凝成的。对此我无话可说，因为我对珍珠体会不到丝毫的迷恋。它们那朦胧的光泽一点也打动不了我。而关于那场由来已久的争论——《爱之珠》（the Pearl of Love）究竟是世上最残酷的故事，还只是一个讲美之不朽的雅致寓言——我也无法为自己下一断语。

不论是这个故事，还是围绕它的那场论战，研究波斯（Persian）中古散文的人都不会陌生。故事本身不长，可对它的注疏，却堪称那个时代文学里可观的一部分。有人把它当作诗人的虚构，有人把它当作寓言，解释为这意思、那意思，或是别的什么意思。神学家们对它更是滔滔不绝地各抒己见，尤其喜欢把它和死后肉身的复元联系起来谈论；那些论述美学的作者也大把它当作一个譬喻来用。还有许多人认定，它所讲的乃是一件实事，简简单单、直截了当地真实。

===Original===
The story is laid in North India, which is the most fruitful soil for sublime love stories of all the lands in the world. It was in a country of sunshine and lakes and rich forests and hills and fertile valleys; and far away the great mountains hung in the sky, peaks, crests, and ridges of inaccessible and eternal snow. There was a young Prince, lord of all the land; and he found a maiden of indescribable beauty and delightfulness and he made her his Queen and laid his heart at her feet. Love was theirs, full of joys and sweetness, full of hope, exquisite, brave and marvellous love, beyond anything you have ever dreamt of love. It was theirs for a year and a part of a year; and then suddenly, because of some venomous sting that came to her in a thicket, she died.

She died and for a while the Prince was utterly prostrated. He was silent and motionless with grief. They feared he might kill himself, and he had neither sons nor brothers to succeed him. For two days and nights he lay upon his face, fasting, across the foot of the couch which bore her calm and lovely body. Then he arose and ate, and went about very quietly like one who has taken a great resolution. He caused her body to be put in a coffin of lead mixed with silver, and for that he had an outer coffin made of the most precious and scented woods wrought with gold, and about that there was to be a sarcophagus of alabaster, inlaid with precious stones. And while these things were being done he spent his time for the most part by the pools and in the garden-houses and pavilions and groves and in those chambers in the palace where they two had been most together, brooding upon her loveliness. He did not rend his garments nor defile himself with ashes and sackcloth as the custom was, for his love was too great for such extravagances. At last he came forth again among his councillors and before the people, and told them what he had a mind to do.

===Chinese===
故事的背景设在北印度（North India），在天下所有的国土之中，那里是最能孕育崇高爱情故事的沃土。那是一片充满阳光、湖泊、丰茂森林、山峦与肥沃谷地的国度；极目远眺，巍峨的大山悬于天际，那终古不化、人迹难至的积雪构成无数山尖、峰峦和山脊。那片土地属于一位年轻的王子（Prince），他是全境的主人；他寻得了一位美得无法形容、令人欢悦无穷的少女，立她为王后（Queen），将自己的心放在了她的脚下。爱，是属于他们的——满溢着欢愉与甜蜜，满溢着希望，那一份精致、勇敢、奇绝的爱，远胜过你曾梦见过的任何爱情。这份爱属于他们整整一年，又一年有余；随后，猝不及防地，因为她在丛林里被什么毒物所蛰，她死去了。

她死了，王子有一阵子完全垮了下来。他悲不自胜，不声不响，纹丝不动。旁人都怕他寻短见，而他既无子嗣，又无兄弟可以继位。两天两夜，他俯卧在她那安详而美丽的遗体所卧的榻足前，水米不进。然后他起身进食，行动极其沉静，像一个已经下了大决心的人。他命人将她的遗体盛入一具铅银合铸的棺中，又为它打造了一具外椁，用最名贵、最芬芳的木料制成，上嵌金饰；外椁之外，再套一具雪花石膏（alabaster）的石椁，镶满了宝石。在这些事进行之际，他大半的时光都消磨在池畔、园中亭阁、轩榭、林丛之间，以及宫里他们二人最常相伴的那几间内室里，沉浸地冥想她的可爱。他并不撕裂衣裳，也不按风俗用炉灰和麻衣来玷污自己，因为他的爱太过深重，容不得这些铺张做作。到了最后，他再次出现在群臣与百姓之间，把自己心里打算要做的事告诉了他们。

===Original===
He said he could never more touch woman, he could never more think of them, and so he would find a seemly youth to adopt for his heir and train him to his task, and that he would do his princely duties as became him; but that for the rest of it, he would give himself with all his power and all his strength and all his wealth, all that he could command, to make a monument worthy of his incomparable, dear, lost mistress. A building it should be of perfect grace and beauty, more marvellous than any other building had ever been or could ever be, so that to the end of time it should be a wonder, and men would treasure it and speak of it and desire to see it and come from all the lands of the earth to visit and recall the name and the memory of his Queen. And this building he said was to be called the Pearl of Love.

And this his councillors and people permitted him to do, and so he did.

===Chinese===
他说，他此生再不会去触碰女人，再不会去想她们；因此他将择一合适的少年收为嗣子，加以调教，好让他担当得起这份重任；至于他自己，身为王子该尽的职责，他仍会恰如其分地一一尽到；但除此之外的一切，他都要把自己的全部心力、全部精力、全部财富，凡是他所能支配的一切，统统献出去，只为造起一座配得上他那位无可比拟、心爱而永失的爱人的纪念之物。那要是一座尽善尽美、风姿与美俱备的建筑，胜过古往今来任何建筑所曾经是或所能是的模样，使它直到时间的尽头都是一桩奇迹，使世人珍之、重之、谈论它、渴望一睹它的真容，从天下四方前来瞻仰，并借此记起、唤起他王后的姓名与音容。他说，这座建筑，就叫做《爱之珠》。

他的群臣和百姓都应允了他这么做，他也就这么做了。

---

===Original===
Year followed year, and all the years he devoted himself to building and adorning the Pearl of Love. A great foundation was hewn out of the living rock in a place whence one seemed to be looking at the snowy wilderness of the great mountain across the valley of the world. Villages and hills there were, a winding river, and very far away three great cities. Here they put the sarcophagus of alabaster beneath a pavilion of cunning workmanship; and about it there were set pillars of strange and lovely stone and wrought and fretted walls, and a great casket of masonry bearing a dome and pinnacles and cupolas, as exquisite as a jewel. At first the design of the Pearl of Love was less bold and subtle than it became later. At first it was smaller and more wrought and encrusted; there were many pierced screens and delicate clusters of rosy-hued pillars, and the sarcophagus lay like a child that sleeps among flowers. The first dome was covered with green tiles, framed and held together by silver, but this was taken away again because it seemed close, because it did not soar grandly enough for the broadening imagination of the Prince.

For by this time he was no longer the graceful youth who had loved the girl Queen. He was now a man, grave and intent, wholly set upon the building of the Pearl of Love. With every year of effort he had learnt new possibilities in arch and wall and buttress; he had acquired greater power over the material he had to use and he had learnt of a hundred stones and hues and effects that he could never have thought of in the beginning. His sense of colour had grown finer and colder; he cared no more for the enamelled gold-lined brightness that had pleased him first, the brightness of an illuminated missal; he sought now for blue colourings like the sky and for the subtle hues of great distances, for recondite shadows and sudden broad floods of purple opalescence and for grandeur and space. He wearied altogether of carvings and pictures and inlaid ornamentation and all the little careful work of men. “Those were pretty things,” he said of his earlier decorations; and had them put aside into subordinate buildings where they would not hamper his main design. Greater and greater grew his artistry. With awe and amazement people saw the Pearl of Love sweeping up from its first beginnings to a superhuman breadth and height and magnificence. They did not know clearly what they had expected, but never had they expected so sublime a thing as this. “Wonderful are the miracles,” they whispered, “that love can do,” and all the women in the world, whatever other loves they had, loved the Prince for the splendour of his devotion.

===Chinese===
年复一年，岁复一岁，他把所有的年头都用来建造和装点《爱之珠》。从原生岩石里凿出了一处宏大的基址，所在之地，仿佛让人正遥遥望着那座大山上的雪之荒原，相隔着一个尘世之谷。四下里有村落、有丘陵，有一条蜿蜒的河，极远处还有三座大城。雪花石膏的石椁便安置在此处一座精工巧构的亭阁之下；环绕它的，是奇异而可爱的石柱、雕镂繁复的墙垣，还有一口巨大的砖石外椁，承着一座圆顶、若干尖塔与小圆顶，精致得有如一颗宝石。起初，《爱之珠》的设计还没有后来那样大胆而精微。起初它小些，也更雕琢满饰；有许多镂空的屏壁和一簇簇秀美的玫瑰色石柱，石椁躺在其间，像一个酣睡于花丛中的孩子。头一座穹顶覆着绿瓦，以银为框、为箍，把它拢在一起；可它不久便被拆去了，因为它显得逼仄，因为它还不够恢弘高远，配不上王子日益开阔的想象。

因为到这个时候，他早已不再是当年那个钟爱着少女王后的翩翩少年了。他如今是个庄重专注的男子，把整个心神都放在《爱之珠》的建造上。每多一年的努力，他都在拱门、墙壁和扶壁里习得新的可能；他对所用的材料有了更深的驾驭，他认识了上百种石材、色调与效果，都是他当初断然想不到的。他对色彩的趣味变得更精微，也更冷峻；他不再喜欢那一开始让他心动的、如彩绘弥撒书般亮堂堂的珐琅嵌金的光泽；他如今追寻的是天空一般的青蓝，是极远处那种幽微的色调，是幽深难明的阴影，是忽然大片大片倾泻而下的紫色珠光，追寻一种壮阔与空阔。他全然厌倦了雕刻、图画、镶嵌的纹饰，厌倦了一切由人力精雕细琢的小巧功夫。“那些玩意儿是挺漂亮，”他这样评说自己早年的装饰；便命人把它们挪到附属的建筑里去，免得妨碍他总体的设计。他的艺术造诣一日高过一日。人们怀着敬畏与惊叹，眼看着《爱之珠》从最初的雏形扶摇直上，长成一种超乎人世的广度、高度与辉煌。他们原本也说不清自己期待的是什么，但从未想过竟能见到这样崇高的一件物事。“爱所能行的奇迹，”他们低声议论着，“真是不可思议啊，”而天下的女子，无论各自还有着怎样的爱恋，都因王子这份挚爱的光辉而爱上了他。

===Original===
Through the middle of the building ran a great aisle, a vista, that the Prince came to care for more and more. From the inner entrance of the building he looked along the length of an immense pillared gallery and across the central area from which the rose-hued columns had long since vanished, over the top of the pavilion under which lay the sarcophagus, through a marvellously designed opening, to the snowy wildernesses of the great mountain, the Lord of all Mountains, two hundred miles away. The pillars and arches and buttresses and galleries soared and floated on either side, perfect yet unobtrusive, like great archangels waiting in the shadows about the presence of God. When men saw that austere beauty for the first time they were exalted, and then they shivered and their hearts bowed down.

Very often would the Prince come to stand there and look at that vista, deeply moved and not yet fully satisfied. The Pearl of Love had still something for him to do, he felt, before his task was done. Always he would order some little alteration to be made or some recent alterations to be put back again. And one day he said that the sarcophagus would be clearer and simpler without the pavilion; and after regarding it very steadfastly for a long time, he had the pavilion dismantled and removed.

The next day he came and said nothing, and the next day and the next. Then for two days he stayed away altogether. Then he returned, bringing with him an architect and two master craftsmen and a small retinue.

All looked, standing together silently in a little group, amidst the serene vastness of their achievement. No trace of toil remained in its perfection. It was as if the God of nature’s beauty had taken over their offspring to himself.

Only one thing there was to mar the absolute harmony. There was a certain disproportion about the sarcophagus. It had never been enlarged﻿—and indeed how could it have been enlarged?﻿—since the early days. It challenged the eye; it nicked the streaming lines. In that sarcophagus was the casket of lead and silver, and in the casket of lead and silver was the Queen, the dear immortal cause of all this beauty. But now that sarcophagus seemed no more than a little dark oblong that lay incongruously in the great vista of the Pearl of Love. It was as if someone had dropped a small valise upon the crystal sea of heaven.

Long the Prince mused, but no one knew the thoughts that passed through his mind.

At last he spoke. He pointed.

“Take that thing away,” he said.

===Chinese===
一条宏大的廊道，一道深远的景致，贯穿建筑的正中，王子对它越来越放在心上。从建筑的内门入口朝里望去，他的目光沿着一条列柱如林的长廊延伸，越过中央那片早已撤去玫瑰色石柱的空地，越过安放石椁的那座亭阁的顶，穿过一处设计得神乎其神的开口，一直投向那座大山——万山之主——的雪之荒原，远在两百英里之外。两侧的柱、拱、扶壁和回廊高高耸起、飘飘浮动，完美而不张扬，如同侍立在上帝左右阴影中的几位大天使。人初次见到那一份清峻之美，先是心神为之一扬，继而不禁一颤，心便低低地垂了下去。

王子常常来到那里伫立，望着那道景致，心潮翻涌，却仍不觉得全然满足。他感到《爱之珠》在他大功告成之前，似乎还有一件事要他去做。他总要下令这里做点小小的改动，或是把近来刚改过的地方再改回去。后来有一天，他说，没有那座亭阁，石椁会显得更加明净简洁；他定定地端详了很久，便命人把亭阁拆去、移走。

第二天他来了，一言不发；再一天，又一天，也都是如此。然后整整两天，他索性没有露面。之后他回来了，带回一位建筑师、两名工匠头领和一小队随从。

他们一齐站着，默默聚作一小群，置身于自己所成就的那一片宁静而恢弘之中。它的完美里已寻不见一丝劳作的痕迹。仿佛那位主掌自然之美的神，已亲手把他们这件造物收归己有了。

只有一处打破了这绝对的和谐。那石椁，多少有些不相称。自早年起，它便从未被放大过——其实又怎能把它放大呢？——它刺目；它截断了那道流畅的线条。那石椁里盛着铅银合铸的棺，那棺里盛着王后——这位可爱而不朽的、这一切美的缘起。可如今，那石椁却仿佛只是《爱之珠》那条宏大景致里，一个不调和地横陈着的小小的暗色长方块。就像是有人在水晶般的天海之上，遗落了一只小小的手提箱。

王子沉思良久，但没有人知道他心里掠过的是怎样的念头。

终于，他开口了。他伸手指去。

“把那东西搬走。”他说。

## The Plattner Story / 普拉特纳的故事

===Original===
Whether the story of Gottfried Plattner is to be credited or not is a pretty question in the value of evidence. On the one hand, we have seven witnesses﻿—to be perfectly exact, we have six and a half pairs of eyes, and one undeniable fact; and on the other we have﻿—what is it?﻿—prejudice, common sense, the inertia of opinion. Never were there seven more honest-seeming witnesses; never was there a more undeniable fact than the inversion of Gottfried Plattner’s anatomical structure, and﻿—never was there a more preposterous story than the one they have to tell! The most preposterous part of the story is the worthy Gottfried’s contribution (for I count him as one of the seven). Heaven forbid that I should be led into giving countenance to superstition by a passion for impartiality, and so come to share the fate of Eusapia’s patrons! Frankly, I believe there is something crooked about this business of Gottfried Plattner; but what that crooked factor is, I will admit as frankly, I do not know. I have been surprised at the credit accorded to the story in the most unexpected and authoritative quarters. The fairest way to the reader, however, will be for me to tell it without further comment.

===Chinese===
戈特弗里德·普拉特纳（Gottfried Plattner）的故事究竟可信不可信，这是关于证据价值的一个颇堪玩味的问题。一方面，我们有七位证人——精确地说，我们有六双半眼睛，还有一个不容否认的事实；而另一方面，我们有——怎么说呢？——偏见、常识，以及舆论的惰性。再没有比这七位更显得诚实的证人了；再没有比戈特弗里德·普拉特纳的解剖结构发生左右颠倒这一事实更无可争辩的了；然而——也再没有比他们不得不讲的这个故事更荒诞不经的了！整桩事情里最荒诞的部分，恰恰是这位可敬的戈特弗里德本人的说法（因为我也把他算作七人之一）。上天不容我因为一味追求公允而落入替迷信撑腰的境地，从而落得尤萨皮亚（Eusapia）那些庇护者那样的下场！坦白讲，我相信戈特弗里德·普拉特纳这件事里有些蹊跷；但那蹊跷究竟是什么，我同样坦白地承认——我不知道。这个故事竟得到一些最出人意料、最具权威的圈子的采信，这一点让我颇为惊讶。不过，对读者最公允的做法，还是让我不加任何评论地把这故事原原本本讲出来。

===Original===
Gottfried Plattner is, in spite of his name, a freeborn Englishman. His father was an Alsatian who came to England in the ’sixties, married a respectable English girl of unexceptionable antecedents, and died, after a wholesome and uneventful life (devoted, I understand, chiefly to the laying of parquet flooring), in 1887. Gottfried’s age is seven-and-twenty. He is, by virtue of his heritage of three languages, Modern Languages Master in a small private school in the south of England. To the casual observer he is singularly like any other Modern Languages Master in any other small private school. His costume is neither very costly nor very fashionable, but, on the other hand, it is not markedly cheap or shabby; his complexion, like his height and his bearing, is inconspicuous. You would notice, perhaps, that, like the majority of people, his face was not absolutely symmetrical, his right eye a little larger than the left, and his jaw a trifle heavier on the right side. If you, as an ordinary careless person, were to bare his chest and feel his heart beating, you would probably find it quite like the heart of anyone else. But here you and the trained observer would part company. If you found his heart quite ordinary, the trained observer would find it quite otherwise. And once the thing was pointed out to you, you too would perceive the peculiarity easily enough. It is that Gottfried’s heart beats on the right side of his body.

===Chinese===
戈特弗里德·普拉特纳虽是这么个名字，却是生而自由的英国人。他父亲是阿尔萨斯人（Alsatian），六十年代来到英国，娶了一位家世清白、无可挑剔的正派英国姑娘，度过规矩而平稳的一生（据我所知，主要从事镶嵌拼花地板的营生），于1887年去世。戈特弗里德今年二十七岁。他凭着继承下来的三种语言能力，在英格兰南部一所小型私立学校里担任现代语文教师。在随便一个旁观者眼里，他跟任何别的小型私立学校里任何别的现代语文教师都出奇地相像。他的衣着既不算很贵，也不算很时髦，但反过来也不算特别寒酸或邋遢；他的面色，也跟他那身高、他那气度一样，毫不惹眼。你或许会注意到，跟大多数人一样，他的脸并不是绝对对称的：他的右眼比左眼稍大一点，右边的下颌也比左边略宽一些。倘若你作为一个粗心大意的普通人去袒开他的胸膛，听他的心跳，你多半会觉得它跟任何别人的心没什么两样。但是在这儿，你跟受过训练的观察者就要分道扬镳了。你觉得他的心再寻常不过，而受过训练的观察者却会发现全然不是那么回事。一旦有人把这个特点指给你看，你也不难就能看出这个奇异之处——那就是，戈特弗里德的心，在他身体的右侧跳动。

===Original===
Now, that is not the only singularity of Gottfried’s structure, although it is the only one that would appeal to the untrained mind. Careful sounding of Gottfried’s internal arrangements by a well-known surgeon seems to point to the fact that all the other unsymmetrical parts of his body are similarly misplaced. The right lobe of his liver is on the left side, the left on his right; while his lungs, too, are similarly contraposed. What is still more singular, unless Gottfried is a consummate actor, we must believe that his right hand has recently become his left. Since the occurrences we are about to consider (as impartially as possible), he has found the utmost difficulty in writing, except from right to left across the paper with his left hand. He cannot throw with his right hand, he is perplexed at mealtimes between knife and fork, and his ideas of the rule of the road﻿—he is a cyclist﻿—are still a dangerous confusion. And there is not a scrap of evidence to show that before these occurrences Gottfried was at all left-handed.

===Chinese===
不过，这还不是戈特弗里德身体构造上唯一的奇特之处，虽说这是唯一一处能引起未受训练之人的注意的。据一位著名外科医生对戈特弗里德内脏的仔细叩诊，似乎可以得出这样一个结论：他身上其他不对称的器官也都同样地错位了。他肝脏的右叶在左边，左叶在右边；他的两肺也是同样地左右相反。更奇的是，除非戈特弗里德是个出神入化的演员，否则我们只能相信，他的右手最近变成了左手。自我们即将要考察（并尽可能公允地考察）的那桩变故发生以来，他发觉写字变得极其困难，除非用左手从右往左在纸上写。他用右手扔不出东西；吃饭时刀叉拿得颠三倒四；至于行路的规则——他是个骑自行车的人——他脑子里至今还是一团危险的糊涂账。而没有任何一丝证据能表明，在那桩变故之前，戈特弗里德有什么左撇子的迹象。

===Original===
There is yet another wonderful fact in this preposterous business. Gottfried produces three photographs of himself. You have him at the age of five or six, thrusting fat legs at you from under a plaid frock, and scowling. In that photograph his left eye is a little larger than his right, and his jaw is a trifle heavier on the left side. This is the reverse of his present living condition. The photograph of Gottfried at fourteen seems to contradict these facts, but that is because it is one of those cheap “Gem” photographs that were then in vogue, taken direct upon metal, and therefore reversing things just as a looking-glass would. The third photograph represents him at one-and-twenty, and confirms the record of the others. There seems here evidence of the strongest confirmatory character that Gottfried has exchanged his left side for his right. Yet how a human being can be so changed, short of a fantastic and pointless miracle, it is exceedingly hard to suggest.

===Chinese===
在这桩荒唐事里，还有一个令人称奇的事实。戈特弗里德拿出三张自己的照片。其中一张是他五六岁时的样子，从一件格子小袍子底下伸出胖乎乎的小腿朝着你，皱着眉头。在那张照片上，他的左眼比右眼稍大，左边的下颌也比右边略宽。这与他如今活生生的状态恰好相反。戈特弗里德十四岁的那张照片似乎与这些事实相抵触，但那是因为它是当时流行的那种廉价的“宝石（Gem）”照片之一，是直接拍在金属板上的，因此会像镜子一样把左右颠倒过来。第三张照片是他二十一岁时的，与前两张的记录相互印证。这里似乎有最强的佐证，证明戈特弗里德把他的左侧与右侧调换了。然而，一个人怎么会变成这样，除非借助某种离奇而又毫无意义的奇迹，否则实在难以解释。

===Original===
In one way, of course, these facts might be explicable on the supposition that Plattner has undertaken an elaborate mystification, on the strength of his heart’s displacement. Photographs may be faked, and left-handedness imitated. But the character of the man does not lend itself to any such theory. He is quiet, practical, unobtrusive, and thoroughly sane, from the Nordau standpoint. He likes beer, and smokes moderately, takes walking exercise daily, and has a healthily high estimate of the value of his teaching. He has a good but untrained tenor voice, and takes a pleasure in singing airs of a popular and cheerful character. He is fond, but not morbidly fond, of reading﻿—chiefly fiction pervaded with a vaguely pious optimism﻿—sleeps well, and rarely dreams. He is, in fact, the very last person to evolve a fantastic fable. Indeed, so far from forcing this story upon the world, he has been singularly reticent on the matter. He meets enquirers with a certain engaging﻿—bashfulness is almost the word, that disarms the most suspicious. He seems genuinely ashamed that anything so unusual has occurred to him.

===Chinese===
当然，从某个角度来看，这些事实或许可以这样解释：普拉特纳借自己心脏易位一事，刻意搞了一场精心策划的骗局。照片可以做假，左撇子也可以装出来。但这人的性格却不支持任何这种说法。他沉静、务实、不事张扬，而且——按诺尔道（Nordau）的标准——头脑完全健全。他喜欢喝啤酒，抽烟有节制，每天散步锻炼，对自己所从事的教学工作的价值有一种健康而略偏高的自我评价。他有一副不错但未经训练的男高音嗓子，喜欢唱一些通俗而欢快的曲调。他爱读书，但并不病态地爱读——主要读那种渗透着一种模糊的虔信式乐观主义之类的小说——他睡眠很好，极少做梦。事实上，他是天底下最不可能编造离奇神话的人。其实，非但他没有把这故事硬推给世人，他对这事反倒异常缄默。他面对询问者时，带着一种挺讨人喜欢的——几乎可用“羞怯”来形容——神态，足以解除最疑心的人的戒备。对于这么一桩异乎寻常的事竟落到了自己头上，他似乎真心觉得难为情。

===Original===
It is to be regretted that Plattner’s aversion to the idea of postmortem dissection may postpone, perhaps forever, the positive proof that his entire body has had its left and right sides transposed. Upon that fact mainly the credibility of his story hangs. There is no way of taking a man and moving him about in space as ordinary people understand space, that will result in our changing his sides. Whatever you do, his right is still his right, his left his left. You can do that with a perfectly thin and flat thing, of course. If you were to cut a figure out of paper, any figure with a right and left side, you could change its sides simply by lifting it up and turning it over. But with a solid it is different. Mathematical theorists tell us that the only way in which the right and left sides of a solid body can be changed is by taking that body clean out of space as we know it﻿—taking it out of ordinary existence, that is, and turning it somewhere outside space. This is a little abstruse, no doubt, but anyone with any knowledge of mathematical theory will assure the reader of its truth. To put the thing in technical language, the curious inversion of Plattner’s right and left sides is proof that he has moved out of our space into what is called the Fourth Dimension, and that he has returned again to our world. Unless we choose to consider ourselves the victims of an elaborate and motiveless fabrication, we are almost bound to believe that this has occurred.

===Chinese===
遗憾的是，普拉特纳对死后解剖一事颇为反感，这或许会把关于他全身左右两侧已经互换的最终证据无限期地搁置下去。而他那个故事之能否取信于人，主要就系于这一事实。按照常人所理解的空间，无论你怎样把一个人在空间里搬来搬去，都不可能把他的左右两侧调换过来。无论你怎么办，他的右侧仍是他的右侧，他的左侧仍是他的左侧。当然，如果那是一个绝对薄而平的东西，你倒是可以做到。倘若你从纸上剪下一个图形，任何一个有左右两侧的图形，你只要把它拿起来翻个面，就能把它的两侧调换。但对于一个立体来说就不同了。数学理论家告诉我们：要使一个立体的左右两侧互换，唯一的办法是把这个立体从我们所知的这个空间里整个地拿出去——也就是把它从寻常的存在中拿出去，到空间之外的某个地方翻转一下。这一点无疑有点儿深奥，但凡对数学理论有所了解的人，都会向读者保证它是对的。用专门的话来说，普拉特纳左右两侧这种奇异的颠倒，证明他曾一度离开了我们这个空间，进入了所谓的“第四维度（the Fourth Dimension）”，而后又返回了我们的世界。除非我们情愿把自己看作是一场精心策划而又毫无动机的骗局的受害者，否则我们几乎不能不相信事情确是如此。

===Original===
So much for the tangible facts. We come now to the account of the phenomena that attended his temporary disappearance from the world. It appears that in the Sussexville Proprietary School, Plattner not only discharged the duties of Modern Languages Master, but also taught chemistry, commercial geography, bookkeeping, shorthand, drawing, and any other additional subject to which the changing fancies of the boys’ parents might direct attention. He knew little or nothing of these various subjects, but in secondary as distinguished from Board or elementary schools, knowledge in the teacher is, very properly, by no means so necessary as high moral character and gentlemanly tone. In chemistry he was particularly deficient, knowing, he says, nothing beyond the Three Gases (whatever the three gases may be). As, however, his pupils began by knowing nothing, and derived all their information from him, this caused him (or anyone) but little inconvenience for several terms. Then a little boy named Whibble joined the school, who had been educated (it seems) by some mischievous relative into an inquiring habit of mind. This little boy followed Plattner’s lessons with marked and sustained interest, and in order to exhibit his zeal on the subject, brought, at various times, substances for Plattner to analyse. Plattner, flattered by this evidence of his power of awakening interest, and trusting to the boy’s ignorance, analysed these, and even, made general statements as to their composition. Indeed, he was so far stimulated by his pupil as to obtain a work upon analytical chemistry, and study it during his supervision of the evening’s preparation. He was surprised to find chemistry quite an interesting subject.

===Chinese===
关于摸得着的事实，便是这些。下面我们来讲伴随他短暂地从人世消失而发生的那一桩桩怪事。看来，在萨塞克斯维尔私立学校（Sussexville Proprietary School）里，普拉特纳不仅担任现代语文教师，还教化学、商业地理、簿记、速记、图画，以及学生家长一时兴起的念头所可能注目的任何别的附加科目。对这些五花八门的科目，他几乎一无所知，不过在中等学校——区别于公理会学校或初等学校——里，教师有没有学问，按理也远不如他品格高尚、举止斯文来得要紧。化学这一门他尤其不行，据他自己说，除了“三种气体”（这三种气体究竟是什么，不得而知）之外，他一概不懂。然而，由于他的学生起初也是一无所知，所知道的一切都从他这儿来，所以一连几个学期，这倒也并没给他（或任何人）带来什么不便。后来有一个名叫惠布尔（Whibble）的小男孩入了学，这孩子（据说是）被某个爱恶作剧的亲戚调教出了一种爱追根究底的脾性。这小男孩听普拉特纳的课，表现出一种明显而持久不衰的兴趣，为了显示自己在这门课上的热忱，还屡次三番地带了各种东西来让普拉特纳分析。普拉特纳见自己竟能引起学生这样的兴趣，颇为得意，加之信赖那孩子的无知，便一一作了分析，甚至对它们的成分还发表了一些泛泛之论。他甚至被这学生激发到这般地步：专门去弄了一本论分析化学的书，在监督晚自习的时候研读起来。他惊讶地发现，化学竟是一门颇有趣味的学科。

===Original===
So far the story is absolutely commonplace. But now the greenish powder comes upon the scene. The source of that greenish powder seems, unfortunately, lost. Master Whibble tells a tortuous story of finding it done up in a packet in a disused limekiln near the Downs. It would have been an excellent thing for Plattner, and possibly for Master Whibble’s family, if a match could have been applied to that powder there and then. The young gentleman certainly did not bring it to school in a packet, but in a common eight-ounce graduated medicine bottle, plugged with masticated newspaper. He gave it to Plattner at the end of the afternoon school. Four boys had been detained after school prayers in order to complete some neglected tasks, and Plattner was supervising these in the small classroom in which the chemical teaching was conducted. The appliances for the practical teaching of chemistry in the Sussexville Proprietary School, as in most small schools in this country, are characterised by a severe simplicity. They are kept in a small cupboard standing in a recess, and having about the same capacity as a common travelling trunk. Plattner, being bored with his passive superintendence, seems to have welcomed the intervention of Whibble with his green powder as an agreeable diversion, and, unlocking this cupboard, proceeded at once with his analytical experiments. Whibble sat, luckily for himself, at a safe distance, regarding him. The four malefactors, feigning a profound absorption in their work, watched him furtively with the keenest interest. For even within the limits of the Three Gases, Plattner’s practical chemistry was, I understand, temerarious.

===Chinese===
到此为止，这个故事平淡无奇。但此刻，那种绿色的粉末要登场了。不幸的是，那种绿色粉末的来历似乎已不可考。小惠布尔讲了一个绕来绕去的故事，说是他在丘陵地带（the Downs）附近一座废弃的石灰窑里找到一个纸包，里头包的就是它。倘若当时就在那儿用一根火柴把那粉末点着，对普拉特纳，或许也对小惠布尔一家，都会是一件大好事。这位小少爷当然不是用纸包把它带到学校来的，而是装在一只普通的八盎司有刻度的药瓶里，瓶口用嚼烂的报纸塞着。他在下午放学的时候把它交给了普拉特纳。学校晚祷之后，有四个男孩因为要补做拖欠的功课被留了下来，普拉特纳就在那间进行化学教学的小教室里监督他们。萨塞克斯维尔私立学校——也跟本国大多数小学校一样——里教化学实用课的器材，其特点是极其简陋。它们都被收在一个嵌在墙里的小橱里，那橱的容量大约跟一只普通的旅行箱差不多。普拉特纳厌倦了他那种消极的监督，似乎很乐意惠布尔带着他的绿色粉末插进来作为一种消遣，于是便打开橱门，立刻着手他的分析实验。惠布尔幸好坐得远远的，安全地观望着。那四个小罪犯则假装埋头用功，暗地里却以最热切的好奇心偷看着他。因为据我所知，即便是在“三种气体”的范围之内，普拉特纳的实用化学也是相当莽撞的。

===Original===
They are practically unanimous in their account of Plattner’s proceedings. He poured a little of the green powder into a test-tube, and tried the substance with water, hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, and sulphuric acid in succession. Getting no result, he emptied out a little heap﻿—nearly half the bottleful, in fact﻿—upon a slate and tried a match. He held the medicine bottle in his left hand. The stuff began to smoke and melt, and then exploded with deafening violence and a blinding flash.

The five boys, seeing the flash and being prepared for catastrophes, ducked below their desks, and were none of them seriously hurt. The window was blown out into the playground, and the blackboard on its easel was upset. The slate was smashed to atoms. Some plaster fell from the ceiling. No other damage was done to the school edifice or appliances, and the boys at first, seeing nothing of Plattner, fancied he was knocked down and lying out of their sight below the desks. They jumped out of their places to go to his assistance, and were amazed to find the space empty. Being still confused by the sudden violence of the report, they hurried to the open door, under the impression that he must have been hurt, and have rushed out of the room. But Carson, the foremost, nearly collided in the doorway with the principal, Mr. Lidgett.

===Chinese===
关于普拉特纳当时所作的种种举动，他们几个的讲述几乎是完全一致的。他把一点绿色粉末倒进试管，依次用水、盐酸、硝酸、硫酸去试验那东西。得不到任何结果，他便倒出一小堆——其实将近半瓶——到一块石板上，划了一根火柴去点。那药瓶他左手拿着。那东西开始冒烟、熔化，接着便爆炸了，震耳欲聋，并伴着一道令人目眩的闪光。

那五个男孩见闪光便有准备地躲到课桌底下，没有一个受重伤。窗户被炸飞到了操场上，架子上的黑板被掀翻。石板炸成了齑粉。天花板上掉下一些灰泥。校舍和设备除此以外并无别的损伤；那几个男孩起初没看见普拉特纳的踪影，还以为他被震倒，躺在他们视线之外的课桌底下。他们跳出座位要去救他，却惊讶地发现那地方空空如也。他们仍被那突如其来、猛烈异常的爆炸声弄得有些发懵，便急忙涌到敞开的门口，以为他准是受了伤，冲出教室去了。可跑在最前面的卡森（Carson），在门口险些跟校长利杰特先生（Mr. Lidgett）撞个满怀。

===Original===
Mr. Lidgett is a corpulent, excitable man with one eye. The boys describe him as stumbling into the room mouthing some of those tempered expletives irritable schoolmasters accustom themselves to use﻿—lest worse befall. “Wretched mumchancer!” he said. “Where’s Mr. Plattner?” The boys are agreed on the very words. (“Wobbler,” “snivelling puppy,” and “mumchancer” are, it seems, among the ordinary small change of Mr. Lidgett’s scholastic commerce.)

Where’s Mr. Plattner? That was a question that was to be repeated many times in the next few days. It really seemed as though that frantic hyperbole, “blown to atoms,” had for once realised itself. There was not a visible particle of Plattner to be seen; not a drop of blood nor a stitch of clothing to be found. Apparently he had been blown clean out of existence and left not a wrack behind. Not so much as would cover a sixpenny piece, to quote a proverbial expression! The evidence of his absolute disappearance as a consequence of that explosion is indubitable.

===Chinese===
利杰特先生是个身材肥胖、脾气急躁的独眼人。据那几个男孩描述，他踉踉跄跄地闯进屋里，嘴里咕哝着一些动辄发火的校长们所惯用的、有所节制的骂人话——免得脱口而出更难听的。“可恶的闷葫芦！”他说，“普拉特纳先生呢？”孩子们口径一致，连原话都一样。（“窝囊废”、“爱哭鼻子的狗崽子”、“闷葫芦”这几句，看来是利杰特先生学界交往中习用的零碎口头禅。）

普拉特纳先生呢？在接下来的几天里，这个问题要被重复许多遍。看起来，那句语无伦次的夸张话——“炸得粉碎”——这一次竟当真应验了。普拉特纳连一星半点可见的痕迹都没留下；一滴血、一片衣角也找不到。他显然被炸得干干净净地从世上抹去了，未留一丝残迹。套一句俗话——连盖住一枚六便士硬币的份儿都不剩！他因那场爆炸而彻底消失的证据是无可置疑的。

===Original===
It is not necessary to enlarge here upon the commotion excited in the Sussexville Proprietary School, and in Sussexville and elsewhere, by this event. It is quite possible, indeed, that some of the readers of these pages may recall the hearing of some remote and dying version of that excitement during the last summer holidays. Lidgett, it would seem, did everything in his power to suppress and minimise the story. He instituted a penalty of twenty-five lines for any mention of Plattner’s name among the boys, and stated in the schoolroom that he was clearly aware of his assistant’s whereabouts. He was afraid, he explains, that the possibility of an explosion happening, in spite of the elaborate precautions taken to minimise the practical teaching of chemistry, might injure the reputation of the school; and so might any mysterious quality in Plattner’s departure. Indeed, he did everything in his power to make the occurrence seem as ordinary as possible. In particular, he cross-examined the five eyewitnesses of the occurrence so searchingly that they began to doubt the plain evidence of their senses. But, in spite of these efforts, the tale, in a magnified and distorted state, made a nine days’ wonder in the district, and several parents withdrew their sons on colourable pretexts. Not the least remarkable point in the matter is the fact that a large number of people in the neighbourhood dreamed singularly vivid dreams of Plattner during the period of excitement before his return, and that these dreams had a curious uniformity. In almost all of them Plattner was seen, sometimes singly, sometimes in company, wandering about through a coruscating iridescence. In all cases his face was pale and distressed, and in some he gesticulated towards the dreamer. One or two of the boys, evidently under the influence of nightmare, fancied that Plattner approached them with remarkable swiftness, and seemed to look closely into their very eyes. Others fled with Plattner from the pursuit of vague and extraordinary creatures of a globular shape. But all these fancies were forgotten in inquiries and speculations when on the Wednesday next but one after the Monday of the explosion, Plattner returned.

===Chinese===
这件事在萨塞克斯维尔私立学校、在萨塞克斯维尔本地以及别处所引起的骚动，此处不必赘述。事实上，本文的一些读者很可能还记得，在去年暑假里曾隐约听见过这场风波某种遥远而残存的回响。看来利杰特先生已经尽其所能地把这件事压下去、化小。他立下规矩：学生中谁要提到普拉特纳的名字，就罚抄二十五行字；并在学校礼堂里声称，他清楚地知道他这位助教的去向。他解释说，他担心尽管已煞费苦心地使化学实用课的器材减到最少，爆炸仍有可能发生，这一事实会损害学校的声誉；普拉特纳这一走所带有的任何神秘色彩，也会同样损害学校的声誉。事实上，他已竭尽全力使这件事显得尽可能地平常。尤其是，他对五位目击证人盘问得如此严厉，以至于他们自己也开始怀疑起亲眼所见的一切。然而，尽管他做了这些努力，这件事在被夸大和扭曲的状态下，在当地轰动一时，好几个家长都借种种似是而非的借口把孩子领走了。这件事中，同样值得注意的是：在普拉特纳回来之前那段骚动不安的日子里，当地许许多多的人都做得异常清晰的关于普拉特纳的梦，而且这些梦有一种古怪的一致性。在几乎所有的梦里，都能看见普拉特纳，有时独自一人，有时与人相伴，在一片流光溢彩中徘徊。在所有的梦里，他脸色苍白、神色凄楚；有的梦里，他还朝做梦的人比划手势。有一两个孩子显然是在做噩梦，恍惚觉得普拉特纳以惊人的速度向他们逼近，似乎凑近了直视他们的眼睛。还有一些人则跟普拉特纳一起，逃避某种模糊而奇异的圆球状生物的追逐。然而，当爆炸那个星期一之后的第二个星期三，普拉特纳回来时，所有这些胡思乱想便都在各种盘问和猜测之中被遗忘了。

===Original===
The circumstances of his return were as singular as those of his departure. So far as Mr. Lidgett’s somewhat choleric outline can be filled in from Plattner’s hesitating statements, it would appear that on Wednesday evening, towards the hour of sunset, the former gentleman, having dismissed evening preparation, was engaged in his garden, picking and eating strawberries, a fruit of which he is inordinately fond. It is a large old-fashioned garden, secured from observation, fortunately, by a high and ivy-covered redbrick wall. Just as he was stooping over a particularly prolific plant, there was a flash in the air and a heavy thud, and before he could look round, some heavy body struck him violently from behind. He was pitched forward, crushing the strawberries he held in his hand, and that so roughly, that his silk hat﻿—Mr. Lidgett adheres to the older ideas of scholastic costume﻿—was driven violently down upon his forehead, and almost over one eye. This heavy missile, which slid over him sideways and collapsed into a sitting posture among the strawberry plants, proved to be our long-lost Mr. Gottfried Plattner, in an extremely dishevelled condition. He was collarless and hatless, his linen was dirty, and there was blood upon his hands. Mr. Lidgett was so indignant and surprised that he remained on all-fours, and with his hat jammed down on his eye, while he expostulated vehemently with Plattner for his disrespectful and unaccountable conduct.

===Chinese===
他回来的情形，跟他离去时一样离奇。把利杰特先生那幅略带怒气的轮廓，用普拉特纳吞吞吐吐的陈述加以充实，大约是这样的：星期三傍晚，日落时分，这位先生（指利杰特）刚刚结束晚自习的监督，正在自家花园里摘草莓吃——草莓是他格外贪爱的一种果子。那是一座旧式的大花园，幸好有高高的、爬满常春藤的红砖墙遮住外人视线。正当他俯身在一棵特别多产的草莓棵前，半空中忽地一道闪光，紧接着沉闷的一声重响，他还来不及回头，一个沉重的物体便从背后猛地撞在他身上。他一个跟头朝前栽去，把手里捏着的草莓都压烂了；撞得那样猛，以至于他那顶丝质礼帽——利杰特先生坚守着旧式的学界着装观念——被狠狠地砸到了额头上，几乎遮住了一只眼睛。这个从他身侧滑过去、又一屁股坐进草莓丛里的沉重抛射物，不是别人，正是我们那位失踪已久的戈特弗里德·普拉特纳先生，一副狼狈不堪的模样。他没戴领子，没戴帽子，内衣脏兮兮的，手上还沾着血。利杰特先生又惊又气，竟就那么四肢着地趴着，帽子卡在眼睛上，嘴里激烈地斥责着普拉特纳这种无礼而又无可解释的行为。

===Original===
This scarcely idyllic scene completes what I may call the exterior version of the Plattner story﻿—its exoteric aspect. It is quite unnecessary to enter here into all the details of his dismissal by Mr. Lidgett. Such details, with the full names and dates and references, will be found in the larger report of these occurrences that was laid before the Society for the Investigation of Abnormal Phenomena. The singular transposition of Plattner’s right and left sides was scarcely observed for the first day or so, and then first in connection with his disposition to write from right to left across the blackboard. He concealed rather than ostended this curious confirmatory circumstance, as he considered it would unfavourably affect his prospects in a new situation. The displacement of his heart was discovered some months after, when he was having a tooth extracted under anaesthetics. He then, very unwillingly, allowed a cursory surgical examination to be made of himself, with a view to a brief account in the *Journal of Anatomy*. That exhausts the statement of the material facts; and we may now go on to consider Plattner’s account of the matter.

===Chinese===
这一幕几乎算不上田园风光的场景，便构成了我所谓的普拉特纳故事的外在版本——它那公开的一面。利杰特先生如何辞退他的种种细节，此处不必赘述。这些细节，连同完整的人名、日期和出处，可见于提交给异常现象调查会（Society for the Investigation of Abnormal Phenomena）的那份较为详尽的报告。普拉特纳左右两侧这种奇异的颠倒，头一两天里几乎没人察觉；后来最先被注意到的，是他有一种在黑板上从右往左写字的倾向。他宁可把这个古怪的佐证藏起来，也不愿摆出来给人看，因为他觉得这会有损他谋新职的前程。他心脏位置的异常，是几个月之后他麻醉拔牙时才被发现的。后来他十分勉强地接受了一次粗略的外科检查，以便在《解剖学杂志》（*Journal of Anatomy*）上发表一篇简短的报告。摸得着的物质性事实，便到此说尽；下面我们可以转而考察普拉特纳本人对这件事的说法了。

===Original===
But first let us clearly differentiate between the preceding portion of this story and what is to follow. All I have told thus far is established by such evidence as even a criminal lawyer would approve. Every one of the witnesses is still alive; the reader, if he have the leisure, may hunt the lads out tomorrow, or even brave the terrors of the redoubtable Lidgett, and cross-examine and trap and test to his heart’s content; Gottfried Plattner himself, and his twisted heart and his three photographs, are producible. It may be taken as proved that he did disappear for nine days as the consequence of an explosion; that he returned almost as violently, under circumstances in their nature annoying to Mr. Lidgett, whatever the details of those circumstances may be; and that he returned inverted, just as a reflection returns from a mirror. From the last fact, as I have already stated, it follows almost inevitably that Plattner, during those nine days, must have been in some state of existence altogether out of space. The evidence to these statements is, indeed, far stronger than that upon which most murderers are hanged. But for his own particular account of where he had been, with its confused explanations and well-nigh self-contradictory details, we have only Mr. Gottfried Plattner’s word. I do not wish to discredit that, but I must point out﻿—what so many writers upon obscure psychic phenomena fail to do﻿—that we are passing here from the practically undeniable to that kind of matter which any reasonable man is entitled to believe or reject as he thinks proper. The previous statements render it plausible; its discordance with common experience tilts it towards the incredible. I would prefer not to sway the beam of the reader’s judgment either way, but simply to tell the story as Plattner told it me.

===Chinese===
不过，首先让我们把上文这一部分与下文将要讲的内容明确地区分开来。我至此所讲的一切，都有连刑法律师也会认可的证据作支撑。每一位证人都还健在；读者若有闲暇，明天便可以去把那几个小伙子找出来，甚至可以去冒犯那位令人望而生畏的利杰特先生，随心所欲地盘问、设套、考查他们；戈特弗里德·普拉特纳本人，连同他那颗挪了位的心脏和他那三张照片，都可随时候质。以下几点大可视为已被证明：他确因那次爆炸而失踪了九天；他回来时动静几乎同样猛烈，其情形无论细节如何，本身对利杰特先生而言都是恼人的；他回来时左右颠倒了，就像镜中的映像颠倒了一样。由最后这一事实——如我已经说过的——几乎不可避免地可以推出：那九天里，普拉特纳必定处于一种完全脱离空间的生存状态。支持这些说法的证据，事实上比绞死大多数杀人犯所凭的证据要有力得多。然而，至于他自己关于究竟去了哪里的那段叙述，连同其中混乱的解释和近乎自相矛盾的细节，我们便只有戈特弗里德·普拉特纳先生的一面之词。我并不想抹杀这一点，但我必须指出——许多写晦涩心灵现象的作者恰恰忽略了这一点——我们在此正从几乎无可否认的事实，过渡到任何有理智的人都有权凭自己的判断去相信或拒斥的那一类事情。前面的种种说法使它显得有几分道理；它与日常经验的相悖又把它推向了不可信的一端。我无意把读者判断的天平往哪一头拨动，只想把普拉特纳怎么讲给我听的，原原本本地讲出来。

===Original===
He gave me his narrative, I may state, at my house at Chislehurst, and so soon as he had left me that evening, I went into my study and wrote down everything as I remembered it. Subsequently he was good enough to read over a typewritten copy, so that its substantial correctness is undeniable.

He states that at the moment of the explosion he distinctly thought he was killed. He felt lifted off his feet and driven forcibly backward. It is a curious fact for psychologists that he thought clearly during his backward flight, and wondered whether he should hit the chemistry cupboard or the blackboard easel. His heels struck ground, and he staggered and fell heavily into a sitting position on something soft and firm. For a moment the concussion stunned him. He became aware at once of a vivid scent of singed hair, and he seemed to hear the voice of Lidgett asking for him. You will understand that for a time his mind was greatly confused.

===Chinese===
顺便说一句，他是在我奇斯尔赫斯特（Chislehurst）的家里给我讲这段经历的；那天傍晚他一走，我便进了书房，凭着记忆把一切都写了下来。后来他好心地审阅了一份打字稿，因此其内容大体无误这一点，是无可辩驳的。

他说，爆炸的那一刻，他清楚地以为自己被炸死了。他觉得自己被掀离地面，被一股力量猛烈地向后推去。对心理学家而言，这里有一个有趣的事实：他在向后飞去的那一瞬，神志依然清醒，还在琢磨自己究竟是会撞上化学橱，还是撞上黑板架。他的脚跟落了地，踉跄了一下，重重地一屁股坐在了某个又软又结实的东西上。那一震一时把他震懵了。他立刻闻到一股浓烈的烧焦毛发的气味，又似乎听见利杰特先生在喊他。读者自能理解，他一时神志极为混乱。

===Original===
At first he was under the impression that he was still standing in the classroom. He perceived quite distinctly the surprise of the boys and the entry of Mr. Lidgett. He is quite positive upon that score. He did not hear their remarks; but that he ascribed to the deafening effect of the experiment. Things about him seemed curiously dark and faint, but his mind explained that on the obvious but mistaken idea that the explosion had engendered a huge volume of dark smoke. Through the dimness the figures of Lidgett and the boys moved, as faint and silent as ghosts. Plattner’s face still tingled with the stinging heat of the flash. He, was, he says, “all muddled.” His first definite thoughts seem to have been of his personal safety. He thought he was perhaps blinded and deafened. He felt his limbs and face in a gingerly manner. Then his perceptions grew clearer, and he was astonished to miss the old familiar desks and other schoolroom furniture about him. Only dim, uncertain, grey shapes stood in the place of these. Then came a thing that made him shout aloud, and awoke his stunned faculties to instant activity. *Two of the boys, gesticulating, walked one after the other clean through him!* Neither manifested the slightest consciousness of his presence. It is difficult to imagine the sensation he felt. They came against him, he says, with no more force than a wisp of mist.

===Chinese===
起初，他还以为自己仍站在教室里。他清清楚楚地察觉到孩子们的惊讶和利杰特先生的进门。这一点他笃定无疑。他听不见他们说的话，但他把这归因于那实验震耳欲聋的声响。他周围的事物似乎出奇地昏暗、朦胧，但他的脑子用一个明显却错误的念头来解释这一点：爆炸腾起了一大团黑烟。在朦胧中，利杰特先生和孩子们的身影晃来晃去，像鬼魂一样无声无息、虚淡不实。普拉特纳脸上还火辣辣地刺痛着，那是闪光灼热留下的余威。据他自己说，他当时“全乱了套”。他最初比较明确的念头，似乎是关于自身的安危。他觉得自己或许已经被炸瞎、炸聋了。他小心翼翼地摸了摸自己的四肢和脸。接着，他的知觉渐渐清晰起来，他惊愕地发现，周围那些熟悉的旧课桌和别的教室家具都不见了。取而代之的，只是一些朦胧、模糊、灰色的形影。紧接着发生了一件事，使他失声大叫，并使他那被震懵了的神志立刻清醒过来。*两个男孩比划着，竟一个接一个径直从他身体里穿了过去！* 两人都丝毫没有意识到他的存在。他当时是什么感受，很难想象。他说，他们撞到他身上，力道还不如一缕薄雾。

===Original===
Plattner’s first thought after that was that he was dead. Having been brought up with thoroughly sound views in these matters, however, he was a little surprised to find his body still about him. His second conclusion was that he was not dead, but that the others were: that the explosion had destroyed the Sussexville Proprietary School and every soul in it except himself. But that, too, was scarcely satisfactory. He was thrown back upon astonished observation.

Everything about him was profoundly dark: at first it seemed to have an altogether ebony blackness. Overhead was a black firmament. The only touch of light in the scene was a faint greenish glow at the edge of the sky in one direction, which threw into prominence a horizon of undulating black hills. This, I say, was his impression at first. As his eye grew accustomed to the darkness, he began to distinguish a faint quality of differentiating greenish colour in the circumambient night. Against this background the furniture and occupants of the classroom, it seems, stood out like phosphorescent spectres, faint and impalpable. He extended his hand, and thrust it without an effort through the wall of the room by the fireplace.

===Chinese===
普拉特纳随后的第一个念头，便是自己已经死了。不过，他自幼受的是这方面最为正派的观念的教育，所以发现自己身上还裹着这副肉身，倒有些诧异。他的第二个结论是：死的不是他，而是别的人——那场爆炸把萨塞克斯维尔私立学校连同里面每一个人都炸死了，只除了他一个。但这同样难以令人满意。他只好又回过头来，惊奇地观察起来。

他四周一片死寂的黑：起初似乎是一种漆黑如乌木的黑。头顶是一片黑色的苍穹。整个景象中唯一的亮光，是某一方向天际处隐约的一抹淡绿色微光，这道光把一条起伏的黑色山峦的天际线衬得分外清晰。我再说一遍，这是他最初的印象。等他的眼睛渐渐习惯了黑暗，他开始在四周的夜里辨别出一种隐隐约约、带着绿色调的差别。据推测，教室里的家具和人在这一背景上，就像磷火一般的鬼影那样凸显出来，淡淡的，不可触摸。他伸出一只手，毫不费力地便把它穿过了壁炉旁那面墙。

===Original===
He describes himself as making a strenuous effort to attract attention. He shouted to Lidgett, and tried to seize the boys as they went to and fro. He only desisted from these attempts when Mrs. Lidgett, whom he (as an Assistant Master) naturally disliked, entered the room. He says the sensation of being in the world, and yet not a part of it, was an extraordinarily disagreeable one. He compared his feelings, not inaptly, to those of a cat watching a mouse through a window. Whenever he made a motion to communicate with the dim, familiar world about him, he found an invisible, incomprehensible barrier preventing intercourse.

He then turned his attention to his solid environment. He found the medicine bottle still unbroken in his hand, with the remainder of the green powder therein. He put this in his pocket, and began to feel about him. Apparently he was sitting on a boulder of rock covered with a velvety moss. The dark country about him he was unable to see, the faint, misty picture of the schoolroom blotting it out, but he had a feeling (due perhaps to a cold wind) that he was near the crest of a hill, and that a steep valley fell away beneath his feet. The green glow along the edge of the sky seemed to be growing in extent and intensity. He stood up, rubbing his eyes.

===Chinese===
据他自己描述，他使了很大的劲儿想引起别人注意。他朝利杰特大喊，又想去抓那几个跑来跑去的孩子。直到利杰特夫人——他作为一个助教，对她自然没什么好感——走进教室，他才放弃了这些尝试。他说，身在这世上，却又不是它的一部分，这种感觉真是别扭到了极点。他把自己的感受比作一只隔着窗户望着老鼠的猫——这个比方倒也恰当。每当他想做点什么动作，去跟周围那个朦胧而熟悉的世界沟通，便总有一道看不见、说不清的屏障横在中间，阻隔了一切往来。

于是他把注意力转向自己周围这个实实在在的环境。他发现那只药瓶仍完好无损地攥在他手里，瓶里还剩着一些绿色粉末。他把它揣进口袋，开始摸索四周。他似乎是坐在一块巨石上，石头上覆着一层天鹅绒般柔软的苔藓。他四下里那片黑暗的原野，他却看不见——教室那一幅朦胧的、雾似的影像把它遮住了——但他有一种感觉（也许是由于一阵寒风），觉得自己正靠近一座山岭的顶部，一道陡峭的山谷在他脚下深切下去。天际那一抹绿色的微光似乎在范围和强度上都在增长。他站起身来，揉了揉眼睛。

===Original===
It would seem that he made a few steps, going steeply downhill, and then stumbled, nearly fell, and sat down again upon a jagged mass of rock to watch the dawn. He became aware that the world about him was absolutely silent. It was as still as it was dark, and though there was a cold wind blowing up the hill-face, the rustle of grass, the soughing of the boughs that should have accompanied it, were absent. He could hear, therefore, if he could not see, that the hillside upon which he stood was rocky and desolate. The green grew brighter every moment, and as it did so a faint, transparent bloodred mingled with, but did not mitigate, the blackness of the sky overhead and the rocky desolations about him. Having regard to what follows, I am inclined to think that that redness may have been an optical effect due to contrast. Something black fluttered momentarily against the livid yellow-green of the lower sky, and then the thin and penetrating voice of a bell rose out of the black gulf below him. An oppressive expectation grew with the growing light.
