Mr. Bessel was the senior partner in the firm of Bessel, Hart, and Brown, of St. Paul’s Churchyard, and for many years he was well known among those interested in psychical research as a liberal-minded and conscientious investigator. He was an unmarried man, and instead of living in the suburbs, after the fashion of his class, he occupied rooms in the Albany, near Piccadilly. He was particularly interested in the questions of thought transference and of apparitions of the living, and in November, 1896, he commenced a series of experiments in conjunction with Mr. Vincey, of Staple Inn, in order to test the alleged possibility of projecting an apparition of one’s self by force of will through space.

Their experiments were conducted in the following manner: At a prearranged hour Mr. Bessel shut himself in one of his rooms in the Albany and Mr. Vincey in his sitting-room in Staple Inn, and each then fixed his mind as resolutely as possible on the other. Mr. Bessel had acquired the art of self-hypnotism, and, so far as he could, he attempted first to hypnotise himself and then to project himself as a “phantom of the living” across the intervening space of nearly two miles into Mr. Vincey’s apartment. On several evenings this was tried without any satisfactory result, but on the fifth or sixth occasion Mr. Vincey did actually see or imagine he saw an apparition of Mr. Bessel standing in his room. He states that the appearance, although brief, was very vivid and real. He noticed that Mr. Bessel’s face was white and his expression anxious, and, moreover, that his hair was disordered. For a moment Mr. Vincey, in spite of his state of expectation, was too surprised to speak or move, and in that moment it seemed to him as though the figure glanced over its shoulder and incontinently vanished.

===Chinese===
贝塞尔先生（Mr. Bessel）是圣保罗教堂墓地（St. Paul’s Churchyard）贝塞尔、哈特与布朗商行的资深合伙人。多年来，在那些对心灵研究（psychical research）感兴趣的人们中间，他素负盛名，是一位思想开明、办事认真细致的研究者。他是个未婚男子，没有像他那个阶层的人那样住在郊区，而是在靠近皮卡迪利（Piccadilly）的奥尔巴尼（the Albany）租了几间屋子。他尤其对思想传感（thought transference）与活人显形（apparitions of the living）这两个问题感兴趣。1896 年 11 月，他与斯特普尔律师学院（Staple Inn）的文西先生（Mr. Vincey）一道，开始了一系列实验，意在验证那种据说可以凭借意志之力将自己的身影投射穿越空间的可能。

他们的实验是这样进行的：事先约定好一个时间，贝塞尔先生把自己关在奥尔巴尼的一间屋里，文西先生则关在斯特普尔律师学院自己的起居室里，两人各自竭尽全力把心思凝注在对方身上。贝塞尔先生已掌握了自我催眠的法门，他尽可能先把自己催眠，然后将自己作为一具“活人幻影”（phantom of the living）投射出去，横越将近两英里的空间，进入文西先生的房间。接连好几个晚上他们都这样尝试，毫无令人满意的结果；但到第五次或第六次时，文西先生确实看见——或者自以为看见——贝塞尔先生的身影站在自己房里。据他所述，那幻影虽然短暂，却十分鲜明真切。他注意到贝塞尔先生脸色发白，神情焦虑，而且头发凌乱。一时间，文西先生尽管早有心理准备，却惊得说不出话、动弹不得；就在那一刹那，他觉得那身影似乎回头瞥了一眼，随即猝然消失。

===Original===
It had been arranged that an attempt should be made to photograph any phantasm seen, but Mr. Vincey had not the instant presence of mind to snap the camera that lay ready on the table beside him, and when he did so he was too late. Greatly elated, however, even by this partial success, he made a note of the exact time, and at once took a cab to the Albany to inform Mr. Bessel of this result.

He was surprised to find Mr. Bessel’s outer door standing open to the night, and the inner apartments lit and in an extraordinary disorder. An empty champagne magnum lay smashed upon the floor; its neck had been broken off against the inkpot on the bureau and lay beside it. An octagonal occasional table, which carried a bronze statuette and a number of choice books, had been rudely overturned, and down the primrose paper of the wall inky fingers had been drawn, as it seemed for the mere pleasure of defilement. One of the delicate chintz curtains had been violently torn from its rings and thrust upon the fire, so that the smell of its smouldering filled the room. Indeed the whole place was disarranged in the strangest fashion. For a few minutes Mr. Vincey, who had entered sure of finding Mr. Bessel in his easy chair awaiting him, could scarcely believe his eyes, and stood staring helplessly at these unanticipated things.

===Chinese===
两人事先约定，凡看见任何幻影都要设法拍下来；可文西先生一时来不及反应，没能按下就在他身旁桌上备好的相机快门，等他按下时已为时太晚。然而，即便是这一星半点的成功也令他大为振奋，他记下了准确的时间，随即叫了一辆马车赶到奥尔巴尼，要把这个结果告知贝塞尔先生。

他却惊讶地发现，贝塞尔先生外间的门朝夜色大敞着，里间的几间屋子灯火通明，却乱得一塌糊涂。一只空的大瓶香槟摔碎在地上；瓶颈是磕在写字台的墨水瓶上砸断的，就躺在那瓶子旁边。一张八边形的小桌，上面摆着一尊青铜小像和几本精心挑选的书，被人粗暴地掀翻在地；沿着墙上那樱花色的壁纸，有沾了墨水的手指一路划下来，看那样子，简直只为图弄脏的快意。一幅精巧的印花布窗帘被蛮横地从帘环上扯下，塞进了炉火里，那闷烧的焦糊味弥漫了整间屋子。的确，整处地方以一种最古怪的方式被搅得天翻地覆。文西先生进门时本以为会看见贝塞尔先生坐在安乐椅里等他，此时却几乎不敢相信自己的眼睛，呆立在那里，无助地瞪着这些出乎意料的东西。

===Original===
Then, full of a vague sense of calamity, he sought the porter at the entrance lodge. “Where is Mr. Bessel?” he asked. “Do you know that all the furniture is broken in Mr. Bessel’s room?” The porter said nothing, but, obeying his gestures, came at once to Mr. Bessel’s apartment to see the state of affairs. “This settles it,” he said, surveying the lunatic confusion. “I didn’t know of this. Mr. Bessel’s gone off. He’s mad!”

He then proceeded to tell Mr. Vincey that about half an hour previously, that is to say, at about the time of Mr. Bessel’s apparition in Mr. Vincey’s rooms, the missing gentleman had rushed out of the gates of the Albany into Vigo Street, hatless and with disordered hair, and had vanished into the direction of Bond Street. “And as he went past me,” said the porter, “he laughed—a sort of gasping laugh, with his mouth open and his eyes glaring—I tell you, sir, he fair scared me!—like this.”

===Chinese===
随后，怀着一种隐约的灾祸之感，他到大门口的门房去找看门人。“贝塞尔先生在哪里？”他问，“您知不知道贝塞尔先生屋里的家具全砸烂了？”看门人一言不发，可顺着他手势的招呼，立刻跟着来到贝塞尔先生的住所查看情形。“这下子事情就清楚了，”他打量着这疯子般的混乱，说道，“这情形我先前不知道。贝塞尔先生出去了。他疯了！”

他接着告诉文西先生，大约半小时前——也就是贝塞尔先生现身于文西先生房间的那个时候——这位失踪的先生从奥尔巴尼的大门冲了出去，奔进了维戈街（Vigo Street），没戴帽子，头发凌乱，朝邦德街（Bond Street）的方向消失了。“他打我身边过去的时候，”看门人说，“笑了起来——那种喘着粗气的笑，张着嘴，瞪着眼——我跟您说，先生，他可把我吓坏了！——就这么笑。”

===Original===
According to his imitation it was anything but a pleasant laugh. “He waved his hand, with all his fingers crooked and clawing—like that. And he said, in a sort of fierce whisper, ‘*Life!*’ Just that one word, ‘*Life!*’ ”

“Dear me,” said Mr. Vincey. “Tut, tut,” and “Dear me!” He could think of nothing else to say. He was naturally very much surprised. He turned from the room to the porter and from the porter to the room in the gravest perplexity. Beyond his suggestion that probably Mr. Bessel would come back presently and explain what had happened, their conversation was unable to proceed. “It might be a sudden toothache,” said the porter, “a very sudden and violent toothache, jumping on him suddenly-like and driving him wild. I’ve broken things myself before now in such a case—” He thought. “If it was, why should he say ‘*Life*’ to me as he went past?”

===Chinese===
从他的模仿来看，那笑声半点儿也说不上悦耳。“他挥着手，五根指头全弯着，像要抓人似的——就这样。他还恶狠狠地低声说了一句：‘*生命！*’就这一个词：‘*生命！*’”

“哎呀，”文西先生说，“啧啧，”又说“哎呀！”他想不出别的话可说。他自然是大为惊讶。他在屋子和看门人之间来回转过身去，困惑到了极点。除了他提议说贝塞尔先生也许很快就会回来、把事情解释清楚之外，他们的谈话便再也无法推进。“说不定是突然牙疼，”看门人说，“一阵来势极猛的牙疼，猛地一下发作起来，把他折腾得发了狂。我自己以前牙疼的时候也砸坏过东西——”他思索着。“可要是牙疼，他打我身边过的时候，干嘛要对我说‘*生命*’呢？”

===Original===
Mr. Vincey did not know. Mr. Bessel did not return, and at last Mr. Vincey, having done some more helpless staring, and having addressed a note of brief inquiry and left it in a conspicuous position on the bureau, returned in a very perplexed frame of mind to his own premises in Staple Inn. This affair had given him a shock. He was at a loss to account for Mr. Bessel’s conduct on any sane hypothesis. He tried to read, but he could not do so; he went for a short walk, and was so preoccupied that he narrowly escaped a cab at the top of Chancery Lane; and at last—a full hour before his usual time—he went to bed. For a considerable time he could not sleep because of his memory of the silent confusion of Mr. Bessel’s apartment, and when at length he did attain an uneasy slumber it was at once disturbed by a very vivid and distressing dream of Mr. Bessel.

He saw Mr. Bessel gesticulating wildly, and with his face white and contorted. And, inexplicably mingled with his appearance, suggested perhaps by his gestures, was an intense fear, an urgency to act. He even believes that he heard the voice of his fellow experimenter calling distressfully to him, though at the time he considered this to be an illusion. The vivid impression remained though Mr. Vincey awoke. For a space he lay awake and trembling in the darkness, possessed with that vague, unaccountable terror of unknown possibilities that comes out of dreams upon even the bravest men. But at last he roused himself, and turned over and went to sleep again, only for the dream to return with enhanced vividness.

===Chinese===
文西先生不知道。贝塞尔先生没有回来。文西先生终于又无助地张望了一阵，留下一张简短询问的便条，放在写字台上显眼的位置，便带着满心困惑回到了斯特普尔律师学院自己的住处。这件事给了他一个不小的惊吓。他无法用任何合乎情理的假设来解释贝塞尔先生的行为。他想读书，却读不进去；他出去散了一小会儿步，心不在焉得险些在大法官巷（Chancery Lane）的尽头被一辆马车撞上；终于，比平时早了整整一个小时，他便上了床。有相当长一段时间他都无法入睡，因为脑子里一直浮现着贝塞尔先生那间屋子死一般的混乱；待他好不容易进入不安的浅睡，马上又因一个异常真切而令人痛苦的、关于贝塞尔先生的梦而惊扰。

他看见贝塞尔先生疯狂地比划着，脸色惨白，五官扭曲。而在他那模样里，又难以言喻地交织着——或许是借他那手势传达出来的——一种强烈的恐惧，和一种急于行动的迫切。他甚至相信自己听见了这位实验伙伴凄苦地呼唤他的声音，尽管当时他以为那只是一种错觉。文西先生醒来后，那鲜活的印象仍挥之不去。有一会儿，他在黑暗中醒着，浑身颤抖，被那种从梦中涌出、即便最勇敢的人也难免的、对未知可能性那说不清道不明的恐怖攫住了。可他终于振作了一下，翻了个身，又睡了过去，结果那梦却以更加强烈的真切感卷土重来。

===Original===
He awoke with such a strong conviction that Mr. Bessel was in overwhelming distress and need of help that sleep was no longer possible. He was persuaded that his friend had rushed out to some dire calamity. For a time he lay reasoning vainly against this belief, but at last he gave way to it. He arose, against all reason, lit his gas, and dressed, and set out through the deserted streets—deserted, save for a noiseless policeman or so and the early news carts—towards Vigo Street to inquire if Mr. Bessel had returned.

But he never got there. As he was going down Long Acre some unaccountable impulse turned him aside out of that street towards Covent Garden, which was just waking to its nocturnal activities. He saw the market in front of him—a queer effect of glowing yellow lights and busy black figures. He became aware of a shouting, and perceived a figure turn the corner by the hotel and run swiftly towards him. He knew at once that it was Mr. Bessel. But it was Mr. Bessel transfigured. He was hatless and dishevelled, his collar was torn open, he grasped a bone-handled walking-cane near the ferrule end, and his mouth was pulled awry. And he ran, with agile strides, very rapidly. Their encounter was the affair of an instant. “Bessel!” cried Vincey.

===Chinese===
他醒来时，怀着一种强烈的确信——贝塞尔先生正陷于灭顶般的危难之中、急需救助——以至于再也无法入睡。他认定他的朋友是奔向某种可怕的灾祸去了。有一阵子他躺着，徒劳地拿道理来反驳这个念头，但终归还是屈服了。他全然不顾理智地爬起来，点亮煤气灯，穿好衣服，出门穿过那些空寂的街道——所谓空寂，其实也还有一两个无声无息的警察和送早报的货车——往维戈街去，打听贝塞尔先生是否已经回来。

可他始终没能走到那里。他正沿着朗埃克（Long Acre）往下走时，一股说不清道不明的冲动让他从那条街拐了出去，转向考文特花园（Covent Garden），那里才刚刚醒转，开始它夜里的营生。他看见市场就在眼前——一片奇异的景象：暖黄的灯火憧憧，黑色的身影忙碌穿梭。他听见一阵叫喊，接着看见一个身影从旅馆那边的街角拐过来，飞快地朝他跑来。他一眼就认出，那是贝塞尔先生。可那是一个完全变了样的贝塞尔先生。他没戴帽子，蓬头散发，衣领被扯开了，手里倒提着一根骨柄手杖——攥的是靠近金属箍的下端——嘴角也扯歪了。他步履矫健，跑得飞快。两人这一打照面，不过是瞬间的事。“贝塞尔！”文西喊道。

===Original===
The running man gave no sign of recognition either of Mr. Vincey or of his own name. Instead, he cut at his friend savagely with the stick, hitting him in the face within an inch of the eye. Mr. Vincey, stunned and astonished, staggered back, lost his footing, and fell heavily on the pavement. It seemed to him that Mr. Bessel leapt over him as he fell. When he looked again Mr. Bessel had vanished, and a policeman and a number of garden porters and salesmen were rushing past towards Long Acre in hot pursuit.

With the assistance of several passersby—for the whole street was speedily alive with running people—Mr. Vincey struggled to his feet. He at once became the centre of a crowd greedy to see his injury. A multitude of voices competed to reassure him of his safety, and then to tell him of the behaviour of the madman, as they regarded Mr. Bessel. He had suddenly appeared in the middle of the market screaming “*Life! Life!*” striking left and right with a bloodstained walking-stick, and dancing and shouting with laughter at each successful blow. A lad and two women had broken heads, and he had smashed a man’s wrist; a little child had been knocked insensible, and for a time he had driven everyone before him, so furious and resolute had his behaviour been. Then he made a raid upon a coffee stall, hurled its paraffin flare through the window of the post office, and fled laughing, after stunning the foremost of the two policemen who had the pluck to charge him.

===Chinese===
那个奔跑的人既没认出文西先生，也没对自己的名字作出任何反应。相反，他抡起手杖凶狠地朝朋友劈去，正打在脸上，离眼睛不过一寸。文西先生又惊又懵，踉跄着往后退，脚下一滑，重重地摔在了石板路上。他觉得，自己倒下时贝塞尔先生是从他身上一跃而过的。他再抬眼看时，贝塞尔先生已没了踪影，一名警察和好几个市场的搬运工、伙计正从他身边蜂拥而过，朝朗埃克方向穷追不舍。

靠着几个路人的搀扶——整条街转眼间满是奔跑的人——文西先生挣扎着站了起来。他随即成了人群的中心，那些人都急于一睹他的伤势。七嘴八舌争先恐后地安慰他安然无恙，随即又告诉他——在他们眼中的疯子贝塞尔先生——方才的所作所为。他突然出现在市场正中，尖声叫着“*生命！生命！*”，挥舞着一根血迹斑斑的手杖左右劈打，每打中一下便手舞足蹈、放声大笑。一个小伙子和两个女人的头被打破了，一个男人的手腕被他砸碎；一个小孩被打得不省人事；有一阵子他把所有人都打得节节败退，其势之猛、其心之决，可见一斑。接着他又扑向一个卖咖啡的摊子，把摊上那盏石蜡灯甩进邮政局的窗子里，在打晕了两个敢于上前抓他的警察中靠前那一个之后，大笑着扬长而去。

===Original===
Mr. Vincey’s first impulse was naturally to join in the pursuit of his friend, in order if possible to save him from the violence of the indignant people. But his action was slow, the blow had half stunned him, and while this was still no more than a resolution came the news, shouted through the crowd, that Mr. Bessel had eluded his pursuers. At first Mr. Vincey could scarcely credit this, but the universality of the report, and presently the dignified return of two futile policemen, convinced him. After some aimless inquiries he returned towards Staple Inn, padding a handkerchief to a now very painful nose.

He was angry and astonished and perplexed. It appeared to him indisputable that Mr. Bessel must have gone violently mad in the midst of his experiment in thought transference, but why that should make him appear with a sad white face in Mr. Vincey’s dreams seemed a problem beyond solution. He racked his brains in vain to explain this. It seemed to him at last that not simply Mr. Bessel, but the order of things must be insane. But he could think of nothing to do. He shut himself carefully into his room, lit his fire—it was a gas fire with asbestos bricks—and, fearing fresh dreams if he went to bed, remained bathing his injured face, or holding up books in a vain attempt to read, until dawn. Throughout that vigil he had a curious persuasion that Mr. Bessel was endeavouring to speak to him, but he would not let himself attend to any such belief.

===Chinese===
文西先生的第一反应自然是想加入追捕朋友的队伍，以便尽可能把他从愤怒的人群的暴力下救出来。可他动作迟缓——那一棍子已把他打得半懵——就在这还不过是心思一动的时候，人群中便传开了喊话：贝塞尔先生甩掉了追他的人。文西先生起初几乎不肯相信，可众人言之凿凿，再加上不久两名徒劳无功的警察一本正经地折了回来，他便信了。他又漫无目的地打听了一阵，便折回斯特普尔律师学院去，一路用手帕捂着此刻痛得厉害的鼻子。

他又气又惊又困惑。在他看来，贝塞尔先生必然是在做思想传感实验的过程中猛然发了疯，这是毋庸置疑的；可这又为什么会让贝塞尔先生带着凄惨发白的脸出现在文西先生的梦里，却似乎是个无从解答的难题。他绞尽脑汁也无法解释此事。到末了他甚至觉得，不仅是贝塞尔先生，恐怕连万物的秩序本身都发了疯。可他又想不出该怎么办。他把自己仔细地锁在屋里，生了火——那是一只装着石棉砖的煤气炉——又怕上床会再做噩梦，便一直或拿凉东西敷着受伤的脸，或举着书徒劳地想读上几行，直到天明。整个守夜的过程中，他总有一种古怪的感觉，觉得贝塞尔先生正竭力想对他说话，可他不愿让自己理会这种念头。

===Original===
About dawn, his physical fatigue asserted itself, and he went to bed and slept at last in spite of dreaming. He rose late, unrested and anxious, and in considerable facial pain. The morning papers had no news of Mr. Bessel’s aberration—it had come too late for them. Mr. Vincey’s perplexities, to which the fever of his bruise added fresh irritation, became at last intolerable, and, after a fruitless visit to the Albany, he went down to St. Paul’s Churchyard to Mr. Hart, Mr. Bessel’s partner, and, so far as Mr. Vincey knew, his nearest friend.

He was surprised to learn that Mr. Hart, although he knew nothing of the outbreak, had also been disturbed by a vision, the very vision that Mr. Vincey had seen—Mr. Bessel, white and dishevelled, pleading earnestly by his gestures for help. That was his impression of the import of his signs. “I was just going to look him up in the Albany when you arrived,” said Mr. Hart. “I was so sure of something being wrong with him.”

===Chinese===
将近黎明时分，身体的疲倦占了上风，他上了床，尽管仍做梦，总算睡过去了。他起得迟，歇息不过来，心事重重，脸上的伤又痛得厉害。晨报上没有贝塞尔先生发疯的任何消息——这事发生得太晚，赶不上当天的报纸。文西先生的种种困惑，因淤伤发起的低烧又添了几分焦躁，终于到了无法忍受的地步。他白跑了一趟奥尔巴尼之后，便赶到圣保罗教堂墓地，去找贝塞尔先生的合伙人——就文西先生所知，也是他最亲近的朋友——哈特先生（Mr. Hart）。

却没想到，哈特先生虽对这桩变故一无所知，却也受到了一次幻象的惊扰——正是文西先生所见的那一个：贝塞尔先生面色惨白、头发散乱，那手势分明是在热切地求救。这是他对那些手势含义的印象。“您到的时候，我正要去奥尔巴尼找他呢，”哈特先生说，“我太确信他是出事了。”

===Original===
As the outcome of their consultation the two gentlemen decided to inquire at Scotland Yard for news of their missing friend. “He is bound to be laid by the heels,” said Mr. Hart. “He can’t go on at that pace for long.” But the police authorities had not laid Mr. Bessel by the heels. They confirmed Mr. Vincey’s overnight experiences and added fresh circumstances, some of an even graver character than those he knew—a list of smashed glass along the upper half of Tottenham Court Road, an attack upon a policeman in Hampstead Road, and an atrocious assault upon a woman. All these outrages were committed between half-past twelve and a quarter to two in the morning, and between those hours—and, indeed, from the very moment of Mr. Bessel’s first rush from his rooms at half-past nine in the evening—they could trace the deepening violence of his fantastic career. For the last hour, at least from before one, that is, until a quarter to two, he had run amuck through London, eluding with amazing agility every effort to stop or capture him.

But after a quarter to two he had vanished. Up to that hour witnesses were multitudinous. Dozens of people had seen him, fled from him or pursued him, and then things suddenly came to an end. At a quarter to two he had been seen running down the Euston Road towards Baker Street, flourishing a can of burning colza oil and jerking splashes of flame therefrom at the windows of the houses he passed. But none of the policemen on Euston Road beyond the Waxwork Exhibition, nor any of those in the side streets down which he must have passed had he left the Euston Road, had seen anything of him. Abruptly he disappeared. Nothing of his subsequent doings came to light in spite of the keenest inquiry.

===Chinese===
两位先生商量的结果是，决定去苏格兰场（Scotland Yard）打听失踪朋友的消息。“他迟早得让人逮住，”哈特先生说，“那个速度可撑不了多久。”可警方并没有逮住贝塞尔先生。他们证实了文西先生昨夜的种种遭遇，又补充了几桩新的情况，有些性质比他所知的更为严重——托特纳姆法院路（Tottenham Court Road）北段沿路一长串被砸碎的玻璃、在汉普斯特德路（Hampstead Road）袭击一名警察、对一名妇女下了毒手。这些暴行都发生在凌晨十二点半到一点三刻之间，而在那几个小时里——其实从当晚九点半贝塞尔先生第一次冲出房门那一刻起——他们就能追溯出他那荒诞行径中节节升级的暴烈。至少在最后一个钟头里——也就是从一点之前，到一点三刻——他在伦敦横冲直撞、大发淫威，以惊人的身手躲过了每一次阻拦和缉捕。

可一点三刻之后，他就不见了。到那个钟点为止，目击者多如牛毛。成打的人见过他、躲过他、追过他，然后事情戛然而止。一点三刻时有人看见他顺着尤斯顿路（Euston Road）往贝克街（Baker Street）方向跑去，手里挥舞着一只烧着的菜籽油（colza oil）油罐，一边跑一边从里面甩出一团团火焰，打在他经过的房屋窗子上。但在蜡像馆（Waxwork Exhibition）那一头尤斯顿路上的警察，以及那些他若离开尤斯顿路便必定经过的小巷里的警察，谁也没有看见他。他一下子便消失了。尽管侦查极为卖力，他此后的行踪却再无半点线索可寻。

===Original===
Here was a fresh astonishment for Mr. Vincey. He had found considerable comfort in Mr. Hart’s conviction: “He is bound to be laid by the heels before long,” and in that assurance he had been able to suspend his mental perplexities. But any fresh development seemed destined to add new impossibilities to a pile already heaped beyond the powers of his acceptance. He found himself doubting whether his memory might not have played him some grotesque trick, debating whether any of these things could possibly have happened; and in the afternoon he hunted up Mr. Hart again to share the intolerable weight on his mind. He found Mr. Hart engaged with a well-known private detective, but as that gentleman accomplished nothing in this case, we need not enlarge upon his proceedings.

All that day Mr. Bessel’s whereabouts eluded an unceasingly active inquiry, and all that night. And all that day there was a persuasion in the back of Vincey’s mind that Mr. Bessel sought his attention, and all through the night Mr. Bessel with a tear-stained face of anguish pursued him through his dreams. And whenever he saw Mr. Bessel in his dreams he also saw a number of other faces, vague but malignant, that seemed to be pursuing Mr. Bessel.

===Chinese===
这对文西先生来说，又是一桩新的骇异之事。哈特先生那句断言“他迟早得让人逮住”曾让他大得安慰，凭着这份宽心，他得以暂且放下心中的困惑。可眼下每一点新的进展，似乎都注定要在这本已超出他承受能力的怪事堆上，再添上几桩更不可能的勾当。他不禁怀疑起自己的记忆是不是跟他开了什么荒诞的玩笑，反复掂量这些事是否真有可能发生过；到了下午，他又去找哈特先生，好分一分心头那不堪重负的压力。他发现哈特先生正与一位赫赫有名的私家侦探商量着，不过那位先生在这案子里一无所获，我们也就无须赘述他的作为了。

整整一天，整整一夜，贝塞尔先生的下落始终躲过了一刻不息的积极追查。而那一整天，文西先生心底总有一种感觉，觉得贝塞尔先生在设法引起他的注意；那一整夜，泪痕满面、满脸痛苦的贝塞尔先生都在梦里追着他。而每当他梦见贝塞尔先生，便也看见另外一些面孔，模糊却狰狞，似乎正在追逐贝塞尔先生。

===Original===
It was on the following day, Sunday, that Mr. Vincey recalled certain remarkable stories of Mrs. Bullock, the medium, who was then attracting attention for the first time in London. He determined to consult her. She was staying at the house of that well-known inquirer, Dr. Wilson Paget, and Mr. Vincey, although he had never met that gentleman before, repaired to him forthwith with the intention of invoking her help. But scarcely had he mentioned the name of Bessel when Doctor Paget interrupted him. “Last night—just at the end,” he said, “we had a communication.”

He left the room, and returned with a slate on which were certain words written in a handwriting, shaky indeed, but indisputably the handwriting of Mr. Bessel!

“How did you get this?” said Mr. Vincey. “Do you mean—?”

===Chinese===
就在第二天，也就是星期天，文西先生想起了当时正初次在伦敦引起轰动的灵媒布洛克夫人（Mrs. Bullock, the medium）的一些奇闻。他决意去请教她。她借住在那位知名研究者威尔逊·佩吉特博士（Dr. Wilson Paget）家中。文西先生虽与这位博士素未谋面，也立刻赶了去，想求她相助。可他刚一提到贝塞尔这个名字，佩吉特博士便打断了他。“昨夜——恰是在最后，”他说，“我们收到了一则讯息。”

他走出房间，回来时手里拿着一块石板，上面写着几行字——字迹虽颤抖，却毫无疑问是贝塞尔先生的手笔！

“您这是怎么得来的？”文西先生说，“您是说——？”

===Original===
“We got it last night,” said Doctor Paget. With numerous interruptions from Mr. Vincey, he proceeded to explain how the writing had been obtained. It appears that in her séances, Mrs. Bullock passes into a condition of trance, her eyes rolling up in a strange way under her eyelids, and her body becoming rigid. She then begins to talk very rapidly, usually in voices other than her own. At the same time one or both of her hands may become active, and if slates and pencils are provided they will then write messages simultaneously with and quite independently of the flow of words from her mouth. By many she is considered an even more remarkable medium than the celebrated Mrs. Piper. It was one of these messages, the one written by her left hand, that Mr. Vincey now had before him. It consisted of eight words written disconnectedly: “George Bessel… trial excavn… Baker Street… help… starvation.” Curiously enough, neither Doctor Paget nor the two other inquirers who were present had heard of the disappearance of Mr. Bessel—the news of it appeared only in the evening papers of Saturday—and they had put the message aside with many others of a vague and enigmatical sort that Mrs. Bullock has from time to time delivered.

When Doctor Paget heard Mr. Vincey’s story, he gave himself at once with great energy to the pursuit of this clue to the discovery of Mr. Bessel. It would serve no useful purpose here to describe the inquiries of Mr. Vincey and himself; suffice it that the clue was a genuine one, and that Mr. Bessel was actually discovered by its aid.

===Chinese===
“昨夜得到的。”佩吉特博士说。他不时被文西先生打断，详细解释了这些字迹是如何得来的。据说，布洛克夫人在她的降神会（séance）上会进入一种通灵状态（trance）：双眼怪异地在眼皮底下往上翻，全身僵直。随后她便开始飞快地说起话来，所用通常并非她本人的嗓音。与此同时，她的一只手或双手也会活动起来；若备有石板和铅笔，这两只手便会写下讯息，与她口中所说的话同时进行，却彼此全不相干。许多人认为，她是一位比那位大名鼎鼎的派珀夫人（Mrs. Piper）还要了得的灵媒。文西先生此刻面前的，正是这样一则讯息——由她的左手写下的那一条。那上面断断续续写着八个词：“乔治·贝塞尔（George Bessel）……试掘（excavn）……贝克街……救命……挨饿。”说来也巧，佩吉特博士和在场的另外两位研究者都未听说过贝塞尔先生失踪的事——这事要等到星期六的晚报才见报——他们便把这则讯息同布洛克夫人时常传达的许多含糊费解的讯息一道，搁置在一旁。

佩吉特博士听完文西先生的讲述，立刻精神抖擞地投入追查这条寻找贝塞尔先生的线索。在此赘述他和文西先生的种种查访并无益处；只需说一句：这条线索是真的，贝塞尔先生确是循着它被找到了。

===Original===
He was found at the bottom of a detached shaft which had been sunk and abandoned at the commencement of the work for the new electric railway near Baker Street Station. His arm and leg and two ribs were broken. The shaft is protected by a hoarding nearly 20 feet high, and over this, incredible as it seems, Mr. Bessel, a stout, middle-aged gentleman, must have scrambled in order to fall down the shaft. He was saturated in colza oil, and the smashed tin lay beside him, but luckily the flame had been extinguished by his fall. And his madness had passed from him altogether. But he was, of course, terribly enfeebled, and at the sight of his rescuers he gave way to hysterical weeping.

In view of the deplorable state of his flat, he was taken to the house of Dr. Hatton in Upper Baker Street. Here he was subjected to a sedative treatment, and anything that might recall the violent crisis through which he had passed was carefully avoided. But on the second day he volunteered a statement.

===Chinese===
他被发现时，正跌落在贝克街车站附近新修电气铁路工程动工时开凿又废弃的一口独立竖井之底。他的一只胳膊、一条腿和两根肋骨折了。竖井四周围着将近 20 英尺高的板墙；令人难以置信的是，贝塞尔先生这样一个身材壮实的中年绅士，竟然是从这堵板墙上方爬过去，才跌进竖井的。他浑身浸透了菜籽油，那只砸扁的铁罐就躺在他身边，但万幸那一跤把火摔灭了。而他的疯症已彻底退去了。当然，他已虚弱到了极点，一见到来救他的人，便情不自禁地歇斯底里地哭了起来。

鉴于他那套住所一团糟的凄惨状况，他被送到了上贝克街哈顿博士（Dr. Hatton）的宅子里。在那里他接受了镇静治疗，凡是可能勾起他回想那场暴烈变故的事物，都被小心翼翼地避开了。但到第二天，他主动说出了一席话。

===Original===
Since that occasion Mr. Bessel has several times repeated this statement—to myself among other people—varying the details as the narrator of real experiences always does, but never by any chance contradicting himself in any particular. And the statement he makes is in substance as follows.

In order to understand it clearly it is necessary to go back to his experiments with Mr. Vincey before his remarkable attack. Mr. Bessel’s first attempts at self-projection, in his experiments with Mr. Vincey, were, as the reader will remember, unsuccessful. But through all of them he was concentrating all his power and will upon getting out of the body—“willing it with all my might,” he says. At last, almost against expectation, came success. And Mr. Bessel asserts that he, being alive, did actually, by an effort of will, leave his body and pass into some place or state outside this world.

The release was, he asserts, instantaneous. “At one moment I was seated in my chair, with my eyes tightly shut, my hands gripping the arms of the chair, doing all I could to concentrate my mind on Vincey, and then I perceived myself outside my body—saw my body near me, but certainly not containing me, with the hands relaxing and the head drooping forward on the breast.”

===Chinese===
自那以后，贝塞尔先生曾好几次复述过这番话——除旁人外，也对我说过——像所有讲述亲身经历的人一样，细节每次都有出入，但任何一处都不曾自相矛盾。他所述的内容，大体如下。

要把这事看个明白，还得回过头去看他在那场奇异的变故之前与文西先生一道做的那些实验。读者想必记得，贝塞尔先生在与文西先生合作的实验中，最初几次尝试自我投射都未成功。但每一次，他都把全部心神和意志集中在“出窍”这件事上——用他自己的话说，是“拼尽全力地想要”。终于，几乎出乎意料地，他成功了。贝塞尔先生断言：他这个活人，确确实实凭借意志之力，离开了身体，进入了某个在此世之外的地方或状态。

他断言，这一解脱是瞬息之间的事。“前一刻我还坐在椅子里，双眼紧闭，双手紧紧攥着椅子的扶手，拼命把心思集中在文西身上；下一刻，我便察觉自己已经在身体之外了——我看见我的身体就在近旁，可它里面装的显然已不再是我，那双手正松弛下来，脑袋向前垂到了胸前。”

===Original===
Nothing shakes him in his assurance of that release. He describes in a quiet, matter-of-fact way the new sensation he experienced. He felt he had become impalpable—so much he had expected, but he had not expected to find himself enormously large. So, however, it would seem he became. “I was a great cloud—if I may express it that way—anchored to my body. It appeared to me, at first, as if I had discovered a greater self of which the conscious being in my brain was only a little part. I saw the Albany and Piccadilly and Regent Street and all the rooms and places in the houses, very minute and very bright and distinct, spread out below me like a little city seen from a balloon. Every now and then vague shapes like drifting wreaths of smoke made the vision a little indistinct, but at first I paid little heed to them. The thing that astonished me most, and which astonishes me still, is that I saw quite distinctly the insides of the houses as well as the streets, saw little people dining and talking in the private houses, men and women dining, playing billiards, and drinking in restaurants and hotels, and several places of entertainment crammed with people. It was like watching the affairs of a glass hive.”

Such were Mr. Bessel’s exact words as I took them down when he told me the story. Quite forgetful of Mr. Vincey, he remained for a space observing these things. Impelled by curiosity, he says, he stooped down, and, with the shadowy arm he found himself possessed of, attempted to touch a man walking along Vigo Street. But he could not do so, though his finger seemed to pass through the man. Something prevented his doing this, but what it was he finds it hard to describe. He compares the obstacle to a sheet of glass.

===Chinese===
任何东西都动摇不了他对那次解脱的确信。他以一种平静而就事论事的口吻，描述自己所体验到的那种崭新感觉。他感到自己变得无形无质——这一点他早有预料；可他没有料到自己会变得硕大无朋。然而，情形似乎正是如此。“我成了一大团云——倘若可以这么比方的话——仍系在我的身体上。起初我仿佛发现了一个更为宏大的‘自我’，而我脑子里那个有意识的存在，不过是其中极小的一部分。我看见奥尔巴尼、皮卡迪利、摄政街（Regent Street），还有那些宅子里所有的房间和角落，极其细小、明亮而清晰，像从气球上俯瞰一座小城一样铺展在我脚下。时不时有些像飘荡烟缕般的模糊影子，叫眼前的景象略微模糊几分，但起初我也没大理会。最叫我惊奇——至今仍叫我惊奇——的是，我不但看得见街道，还能清清楚楚地看进那些房子的内部：看见小人们在私宅里吃饭、谈话，男男女女在餐馆和旅馆里用餐、打台球、喝酒，还有好几处娱乐场所里挤满了人。那景象，就像在看一只玻璃蜂巢里的营生。”

这便是贝塞尔先生给我讲故事时，我逐字记下的原话。他把文西先生忘得一干二净，有一阵子就那么观察着这些景象。据他说，出于好奇，他俯下身去，用他发觉自己所拥有的那条虚影般的手臂，想去碰一碰一个正走在维戈街上的人。可他办不到，尽管他的手指似乎穿过了那人的身体。有什么东西挡住了他，不让他这么做；但那究竟是什么，他觉得很难形容。他把那障碍比作一面玻璃。

===Original===
“I felt as a kitten may feel,” he said, “when it goes for the first time to pat its reflection in a mirror.” Again and again, on the occasion when I heard him tell this story, Mr. Bessel returned to that comparison of the sheet of glass. Yet it was not altogether a precise comparison, because, as the reader will speedily see, there were interruptions of this generally impermeable resistance, means of getting through the barrier to the material world again. But, naturally, there is a very great difficulty in expressing these unprecedented impressions in the language of everyday experience.

A thing that impressed him instantly, and which weighed upon him throughout all this experience, was the stillness of this place—he was in a world without sound.

===Chinese===
“我那种感觉，”他说，“大约就像一只小猫第一次伸出爪子去拍镜子里自己的倒影。”在我听他讲这个故事的那一次，贝塞尔先生三番五次回到那面玻璃的比喻。然而这比喻并不十分贴切，因为——读者很快便会明白——这层通常不可逾越的阻隔，偶尔也有中断之时，存在着重新穿越屏障、回到物质世界去的法子。不过，要把这些前所未有的感受用日常经验的语言表达出来，自然是有极大的难处。

有一件事立刻便给了他极深的印象，并在整个这一番经历中始终压在他心头——那就是这地方的寂静：他置身于一个没有声响的世界。

===Original===
At first Mr. Bessel’s mental state was an unemotional wonder. His thought chiefly concerned itself with where he might be. He was out of the body—out of his material body, at any rate—but that was not all. He believes, and I for one believe also, that he was somewhere out of space, as we understand it, altogether. By a strenuous effort of will he had passed out of his body into a world beyond this world, a world undreamt of, yet lying so close to it and so strangely situated with regard to it that all things on this Earth are clearly visible both from without and from within in this other world about us. For a long time, as it seemed to him, this realisation occupied his mind to the exclusion of all other matters, and then he recalled the engagement with Mr. Vincey, to which this astonishing experience was, after all, but a prelude.

He turned his mind to locomotion in this new body in which he found himself. For a time he was unable to shift himself from his attachment to his earthly carcass. For a time this new strange cloud body of his simply swayed, contracted, expanded, coiled, and writhed with his efforts to free himself, and then quite suddenly the link that bound him snapped. For a moment everything was hidden by what appeared to be whirling spheres of dark vapour, and then through a momentary gap he saw his drooping body collapse limply, saw his lifeless head drop sideways, and found he was driving along like a huge cloud in a strange place of shadowy clouds that had the luminous intricacy of London spread like a model below.

===Chinese===
起初，贝塞尔先生的心境只是一种不带情绪的惊奇。他满脑子想的几乎全是：自己究竟在哪里。他出窍了——至少是脱离了他的肉身——但这还不是全部。他相信——我也是相信的一个——他到了某个全然超出我们所理解的空间之外的地方。凭借一股顽强的意志，他脱离了自己的身体，进入了一个在此世之外的世界——一个做梦也想不到的世界，却又与此世挨得那么近，两者的相对位置又如此奇异，以至于这世上的一切事物，从我们身边这另一个世界里、无论从外还是从内去看，都看得一清二楚。仿佛有很长一段时间，这一领悟占满了他的心，把其他一切念头都挤了出去；然后他才想起与文西先生的约定——而这段惊人的经历，说到底不过是那约定的一段开场白罢了。

他把心思转到了如何用这具新身体移动上来。有一阵子，他没法让自己摆脱与那具尘世躯壳的牵系。有那阵子，他这具新奇古怪的云雾之身，随着他挣脱的努力，只是摇摆、收缩、膨胀、蜷曲、扭动；然后突然之间，那条系住他的纽带啪地断了。有一瞬，一切都被看似旋转的黑色气团遮蔽住了；随后，透过一道短暂的缝隙，他看见自己那垂着的身体软软地瘫倒，看见那颗没有生气的脑袋歪向一侧，而他自己已像一大团云似的，在一个云影幢幢的奇异之地向前飘行；那地方底下，铺展着灯火玲珑、宛如模型的伦敦。

===Original===
But now he was aware that the fluctuating vapour about him was something more than vapour, and the temerarious excitement of his first essay was shot with fear. For he perceived, at first indistinctly, and then suddenly very clearly, that he was surrounded by *faces*! that each roll and coil of the seeming cloud-stuff was a face. And such faces! Faces of thin shadow, faces of gaseous tenuity. Faces like those faces that glare with intolerable strangeness upon the sleeper in the evil hours of his dreams. Evil, greedy eyes that were full of a covetous curiosity, faces with knit brows and snarling, smiling lips; their vague hands clutched at Mr. Bessel as he passed, and the rest of their bodies was but an elusive streak of trailing darkness. Never a word they said, never a sound from the mouths that seemed to gibber. All about him they pressed in that dreamy silence, passing freely through the dim mistiness that was his body, gathering ever more numerously about him. And the shadowy Mr. Bessel, now suddenly fear-stricken, drove through the silent, active multitude of eyes and clutching hands.

So inhuman were these faces, so malignant their staring eyes, and shadowy, clawing gestures, that it did not occur to Mr. Bessel to attempt intercourse with these drifting creatures. Idiot phantoms, they seemed, children of vain desire, beings unborn and forbidden the boon of being, whose only expressions and gestures told of the envy and craving for life that was their one link with existence.

===Chinese===
可现在他发觉，身边那翻涌的雾气并非只是雾气，初次冒险那股子胆大包天的兴奋里，便掺进了恐惧。因为他先是模糊地、继而突然极为清晰地察觉——自己竟被无数张脸包围着！那看似云雾的一团一团、一圈一圈，竟都是一张张脸。而那是些怎样的脸啊！是稀薄如影的脸，是薄如气体的脸。是那些脸——就像在梦魇的时辰里，带着难以忍受的诡异、直瞪着睡眠中人的那些脸。一双双恶毒而贪婪的眼睛，满含着觊觎的好奇；一道道眉头紧锁，嘴唇狞笑；当他经过时，那些模糊的手便朝他抓来，而他们身体的其余部分，不过是些难以捕捉的、拖曳着的黑色残影。他们半句话也不说，那些似乎在喋喋而语的嘴里，也发不出一点声响。就在那梦一般的寂静中，他们朝他四面八方挤拢过来，随意地穿过他那雾蒙蒙的身体，越聚越多。而此时已陡然被恐惧攫住的、虚影般的贝塞尔先生，便从那一群默然躁动的眼睛与乱抓的手中间，穿了过去。

这些脸是如此非人，那直瞪的眼和虚影般乱抓的手势又是如此狰狞，贝塞尔先生压根儿就没想过要同这些飘来荡去的生灵打交道。它们仿佛是些痴愚的幻影，是虚妄欲望的产儿，是未曾降生、也得不到存在的恩准的东西——它们全部的表情和手势，只诉说着一件事：对生命的妒羡与渴求，而这，便是它们与“存在”之间唯一的牵连。

===Original===
It says much for his resolution that, amidst the swarming cloud of these noiseless spirits of evil, he could still think of Mr. Vincey. He made a violent effort of will and found himself, he knew not how, stooping towards Staple Inn, saw Vincey sitting attentive and alert in his armchair by the fire.

And clustering also about him, as they clustered ever about all that lives and breathes, was another multitude of these vain voiceless shadows, longing, desiring, seeking some loophole into life.

For a space Mr. Bessel sought ineffectually to attract his friend’s attention. He tried to get in front of his eyes, to move the objects in his room, to touch him. But Mr. Vincey remained unaffected, ignorant of the being that was so close to his own. The strange something that Mr. Bessel has compared to a sheet of glass separated them impermeably.

===Chinese===
在这群无声的恶灵密密匝匝地围拥之下，他心里还能想着文西先生——这足见他的意志之坚。他猛地一用意志，便发觉自己——他也说不清是怎么回事——正向着斯特普尔律师学院俯冲下去，看见文西正机警专注地坐在炉边的安乐椅里。

而簇拥在他身边的——正如它们永远簇拥着一切有生命、会呼吸的事物——是另外一大群这样的虚妄无声的影子，它们渴慕着、企望着、寻觅着某条钻进生命里去的门路。

有一阵子，贝塞尔先生徒劳地想要引起朋友的注意。他试着凑到他眼前去，试着挪动他屋里的物件，试着去触碰他。可文西先生毫无反应，全然不知有一个存在正紧贴着自己。那贝塞尔先生比作一面玻璃的某种奇怪东西，不可通透地把两人隔开了。

===Original===
And at last Mr. Bessel did a desperate thing. I have told how that in some strange way he could see not only the outside of a man as we see him, but within. He extended his shadowy hand and thrust his vague black fingers, as it seemed, through the heedless brain.

Then, suddenly, Mr. Vincey started like a man who recalls his attention from wandering thoughts, and it seemed to Mr. Bessel that a little dark-red body situated in the middle of Mr. Vincey’s brain swelled and glowed as he did so. Since that experience he has been shown anatomical figures of the brain, and he knows now that this is that useless structure, as doctors call it, the pineal eye. For, strange as it will seem to many, we have, deep in our brains—where it cannot possibly see any earthly light—an eye! At the time this, with the rest of the internal anatomy of the brain, was quite new to him. At the sight of its changed appearance, however, he thrust forth his finger, and, rather fearful still of the consequences, touched this little spot. And instantly Mr. Vincey started, and Mr. Bessel knew that he was seen.

And at that instant it came to Mr. Bessel that evil had happened to his body, and behold! a great wind blew through all that world of shadows and tore him away. So strong was this persuasion that he thought no more of Mr. Vincey, but turned about forthwith, and all the countless faces drove back with him like leaves before a gale. But he returned too late. In an instant he saw the body that he had left inert and collapsed—lying, indeed, like the body of a man just dead—had arisen, had arisen by virtue of some strength and will beyond his own. It stood with staring eyes, stretching its limbs in dubious fashion.

===Chinese===
末了，贝塞尔先生做出了一件孤注一掷的事。前面已经说过，他能以某种奇异的方式，不仅如我们平常所见那样看到一个人的外表，还能看进他的内部。他伸出那只虚影般的手，把自己那模糊黑色的手指，似乎径直插进了那毫不觉察的脑子。

随即，文西先生猛地一惊，像一个把涣散的心思收回来的人；与此同时，贝塞尔先生觉得，文西先生脑子正中那个暗红色的小东西，随着这一下，胀大并亮了起来。那次经历之后，有人给他看了脑部解剖图，他如今才知道，那就是被医生们称为无用构造的“松果眼”（pineal eye）。因为——尽管在许多人听来匪夷所思——我们的脑子深处，竟有一只眼睛！在那儿它绝无可能看见尘世的任何一丝光亮。在当时，这一点——连同脑部的其余内部解剖——对他来说都还是闻所未闻的新鲜事。然而，一见它那变了的模样，他便伸出手指，怀着对后果仍有些惴惴不安的心情，碰了碰那个小小的亮点。文西先生当下便是一惊；贝塞尔先生知道：自己被看见了。

就在那一刹那，贝塞尔先生猛地想到：自己的身体出事了！看哪！一阵大风刮过那整个幽影之国，把他卷走了。这念头如此强烈，他再也顾不上文西先生，当即掉头回去；那无数张脸也跟着他一齐涌了回去，像大风前的落叶。可他回来得太迟了。一转眼之间，他看见自己留下的那具瘫软无力的身体——那确实像一具刚刚断气的人的身体——已经站了起来，凭借某种外在于他的力量和意志，站了起来。它两眼直瞪着，犹犹豫豫地伸展着四肢，立在那里。

===Original===
For a moment he watched it in wild dismay, and then he stooped towards it. But the pane of glass had closed against him again, and he was foiled. He beat himself passionately against this, and all about him the spirits of evil grinned and pointed and mocked. He gave way to furious anger. He compares himself to a bird that has fluttered heedlessly into a room and is beating at the windowpane that holds it back from freedom.

And behold! the little body that had once been his was now dancing with delight. He saw it shouting, though he could not hear its shouts; he saw the violence of its movements grow. He watched it fling his cherished furniture about in the mad delight of existence, rend his books apart, smash bottles, drink heedlessly from the jagged fragments, leap and smite in a passionate acceptance of living. He watched these actions in paralysed astonishment. Then once more he hurled himself against the impassable barrier, and then with all that crew of mocking ghosts about him, hurried back in dire confusion to Vincey to tell him of the outrage that had come upon him.

But the brain of Vincey was now closed against apparitions, and the disembodied Mr. Bessel pursued him in vain as he hurried out into Holborn to call a cab. Foiled and terror-stricken, Mr. Bessel swept back again, to find his desecrated body whooping in a glorious frenzy down the Burlington Arcade…

===Chinese===
他惶急万分地看了一会儿，然后朝它俯冲下去。可那面玻璃又在他面前合上了，他扑了个空。他拼命地朝这层屏障撞去，身边那些恶灵都在咧嘴、指点、讥笑。他陷入了狂怒。他把自己比作一只莽撞地飞进屋里、此刻正扑打着那扇将它与自由隔开的窗玻璃的鸟。

看哪！那具曾经属于他的小小身躯，此刻正欢喜得手舞足蹈。他看见它在呐喊，虽则他听不见那喊声；他看见它的动作愈发暴烈。他眼睁睁看着它在那“活着”的疯狂欢欣中，把他珍爱的家具乱摔乱扔，把他的书撕得粉碎，砸烂瓶酒，从那参差的碎玻璃碴里不管不顾地喝酒，又蹦又跳又打又砸，狂热地领受着“活着”这件事。他浑身瘫软地、惊骇地，看着这一切。随后他又一次朝那道不可逾越的屏障撞去，接着，在那一群讥嘲的鬼影的簇拥下，慌慌张张地赶回文西那里，要把自己横遭的这桩变故告诉他。

可文西的脑子此刻已对一切幽影关上了门；出窍的贝塞尔先生一路追着他赶到霍尔本（Holborn）去叫马车，却终究是徒劳。贝塞尔先生既扑空又惊恐，又卷了回去，却只看见他那被亵渎的身体，正以一种得意忘形的狂热，沿着伯灵顿商场（Burlington Arcade）一路欢呼怪叫……

===Original===
And now the attentive reader begins to understand Mr. Bessel’s interpretation of the first part of this strange story. The being whose frantic rush through London had inflicted so much injury and disaster had indeed Mr. Bessel’s body, but it was not Mr. Bessel. It was an evil spirit out of that strange world beyond existence, into which Mr. Bessel had so rashly ventured. For twenty hours it held possession of him, and for all those twenty hours the dispossessed spirit-body of Mr. Bessel was going to and fro in that unheard-of middle world of shadows seeking help in vain. He spent many hours beating at the minds of Mr. Vincey and of his friend Mr. Hart. Each, as we know, he roused by his efforts. But the language that might convey his situation to these helpers across the gulf he did not know; his feeble fingers groped vainly and powerlessly in their brains. Once, indeed, as we have already told, he was able to turn Mr. Vincey aside from his path so that he encountered the stolen body in its career, but he could not make him understand the thing that had happened: he was unable to draw any help from that encounter…

All through those hours the persuasion was overwhelming in Mr. Bessel’s mind that presently his body would be killed by its furious tenant, and he would have to remain in this shadowland forevermore. So that those long hours were a growing agony of fear. And ever as he hurried to and fro in his ineffectual excitement, innumerable spirits of that world about him mobbed him and confused his mind. And ever an envious applauding multitude poured after their successful fellow as he went upon his glorious career.

For that, it would seem, must be the life of these bodiless things of this world that is the shadow of our world. Ever they watch, coveting a way into a mortal body, in order that they may descend, as furies and frenzies, as violent lusts and mad, strange impulses, rejoicing in the body they have won. For Mr. Bessel was not the only human soul in that place. Witness the fact that he met first one, and afterwards several shadows of men, men like himself, it seemed, who had lost their bodies even it may be as he had lost his, and wandered, despairingly, in that lost world that is neither life nor death. They could not speak because that world is silent, yet he knew them for men because of their dim human bodies, and because of the sadness of their faces.

===Chinese===
读到这里，细心的读者便开始明白贝塞尔先生对这桩奇事的前半段所作的解释了。那个在伦敦横冲直撞、造成那么大伤害与祸患的存在，所用的确实是贝塞尔先生的身体，可它并不是贝塞尔先生。它是一个恶灵，来自贝塞尔先生如此莽撞地闯入的那个“存在”之外的奇异世界。它占据了他整整二十个钟头；在这二十个钟头里，被夺去躯壳的贝塞尔先生的灵魂之身，在那个前所未闻的幽影中间世界里来回奔走，求告无门。他花了许许多多个钟头，去敲文西先生和他朋友哈特先生的心智之门。正如我们所知，他凭着这一番努力，把每一个人都惊动了。可那种能把自己的处境隔着这道鸿沟传达给这些救助者的“语言”，他却不会；他那无力的手指在他们的脑子里徒劳而无效地摸索着。确实有一次——前面我们已经讲过——他设法让文西先生拐离了原路，结果便与那具被盗的身体在其狂奔途中撞了个正着，可他还是无法让他明白究竟发生了什么事：他没能从那场相遇里得到任何帮助……

在那许多个钟头里，贝塞尔先生心里始终有一种压倒一切的预感：他的身体不久就要被那个狂暴的占据者折腾死了，而他则将永远困在这个幽影之国。于是那漫长的几个钟头，便成了一场与日俱增的恐惧的煎熬。而每当他心急如焚、徒劳地来回奔波时，身边那个世界的无数灵体便围上来裹挟他，搅乱他的心神。与此同时，总有一群妒羡而喝彩的灵众，涌在那位得意的同类身后——他正干着他那辉煌的事业呢。

因为，看来这便是那些无形无体的东西——在这个作为我们世界之影的世界里——所过的生活了。它们永远虎视眈眈，觊觎着钻进一具凡人肉身的门路，以便借之现身为暴怒与癫狂、暴烈的情欲与种种怪诞疯狂的冲动，在抢到手的身体里得意洋洋。因为贝塞尔先生并非那个地方唯一的人类灵魂。为证——他先后遇见一个、后来又遇见好几个人的影子，那些人似乎和他一样，也失去了自己的身体——说不定失去的方式就和他相同——正绝望地游荡在那个既非生、亦非死的失落世界里。因为那个世界是无声的，他们也无法说话；可从他们那隐约的人形，从他们脸上那份悲戚，他还是认出他们是人。

===Original===
But how they had come into that world he could not tell, nor where the bodies they had lost might be, whether they still raved about the Earth, or whether they were closed forever in death against return. That they were the spirits of the dead neither he nor I believe. But Doctor Wilson Paget thinks they are the rational souls of men who are lost in madness on the Earth.

At last Mr. Bessel chanced upon a place where a little crowd of such disembodied silent creatures was gathered, and thrusting through them he saw below a brightly-lit room, and four or five quiet gentlemen and a woman, a stoutish woman dressed in black bombazine and sitting awkwardly in a chair with her head thrown back. He knew her from her portraits to be Mrs. Bullock, the medium. And he perceived that tracts and structures in her brain glowed and stirred as he had seen the pineal eye in the brain of Mr. Vincey glow. The light was very fitful; sometimes it was a broad illumination, and sometimes merely a faint twilight spot, and it shifted slowly about her brain. She kept on talking and writing with one hand. And Mr. Bessel saw that the crowding shadows of men about him, and a great multitude of the shadow spirits of that shadowland, were all striving and thrusting to touch the lighted regions of her brain. As one gained her brain or another was thrust away, her voice and the writing of her hand changed. So that what she said was disorderly and confused for the most part; now a fragment of one soul’s message, and now a fragment of another’s, and now she babbled the insane fancies of the spirits of vain desire. Then Mr. Bessel understood that she spoke for the spirit that had touch of her, and he began to struggle very furiously towards her. But he was on the outside of the crowd and at that time he could not reach her, and at last, growing anxious, he went away to find what had happened meanwhile to his body. For a long time he went to and fro seeking it in vain and fearing that it must have been killed, and then he found it at the bottom of the shaft in Baker Street, writhing furiously and cursing with pain. Its leg and an arm and two ribs had been broken by its fall. Moreover, the evil spirit was angry because his time had been so short and because of the painmaking violent movements and casting his body about.

===Chinese===
至于他们是怎样来到这个世界的，他说不上来；他们丢掉的那些身体又在何处，是仍在尘世间疯疯癫癫地四处乱跑，还是已永远地被死亡封闭、无法回归，他也无从得知。至于说他们是死者的亡灵——这一点他和我都不信。不过威尔逊·佩吉特博士认为，他们是那些在尘世间陷入疯狂之人的理性灵魂。

末了，贝塞尔先生偶然撞见一处地方——一小群这般无声的脱壳生灵聚在那里，他挤过他们，看见底下有一间灯光明亮的房间，里面坐着四五个安静的先生和一位妇人；那妇人身形微胖，身着黑色绷纱衣裳，别扭地坐在椅子里，头向后仰着。他从画像上认出，她便是那位灵媒布洛克夫人。他发觉，她脑中有些区域和构造正如他先前看见文西先生脑子里的松果眼那样，亮着、动着。那光很是不稳：有时是一片大块的明亮，有时只是个幽暗如薄暮的小点，在她脑中缓缓游移。她不停地讲着，一只手也不停地写着。贝塞尔先生看见，身边簇拥着的那许多人影，还有那幽影之国里许许多多的影子灵体，全都在挤挤挨挨、争先恐后地想去触碰她脑中那些亮着的区域。这一个挤进了她的脑子，或是那一个被挤开了，她的嗓音和手上写出的字便随之而变。是以她说出的话大多杂乱无章：忽而是这一个灵魂讯息的片段，忽而是那一个的；间或又咿咿呀呀地说着那些虚妄欲望之灵的疯话。至此贝塞尔先生才明白：她是替那触到她的灵体说话——他便开始拼命朝她挤过去。可他在人群外圈，一时挤不到她跟前；末了，他焦躁起来，便先离开一下，去看看这段时间里他的身体怎么样了。他来回找了很久都找不到，只怕是已经死了；后来总算在贝克街那口竖井底下找到了它——它正痛苦万分地扭动着、咒骂着。它那跌下的一跤，摔断了一条腿、一只胳膊和两根肋骨。而且，那恶灵正在恼怒——一来因为它所占的时间已所剩无几；二来因为疼痛，它正在狂暴地乱动，把那身体乱摔乱掷。

===Original===
And at that Mr. Bessel returned with redoubled earnestness to the room where the séance was going on, and so soon as he had thrust himself within sight of the place he saw one of the men who stood about the medium looking at his watch as if he meant that the séance should presently end. At that a great number of the shadows who had been striving turned away with gestures of despair. But the thought that the séance was almost over only made Mr. Bessel the more earnest, and he struggled so stoutly with his will against the others that presently he gained the woman’s brain. It chanced that just at that moment it glowed very brightly, and in that instant she wrote the message that Doctor Wilson Paget preserved. And then the other shadows and the cloud of evil spirits about him had thrust Mr. Bessel away from her, and for all the rest of the séance he could regain her no more.

So he went back and watched through the long hours at the bottom of the shaft where the evil spirit lay in the stolen body it had maimed, writhing and cursing, and weeping and groaning, and learning the lesson of pain. And towards dawn the thing he had waited for happened, the brain glowed brightly and the evil spirit came out, and Mr. Bessel entered the body he had feared he should never enter again. As he did so, the silence—the brooding silence—ended; he heard the tumult of traffic and the voices of people overhead, and that strange world that is the shadow of our world—the dark and silent shadows of ineffectual desire and the shadows of lost men—vanished clean away.

He lay there for the space of about three hours before he was found. And in spite of the pain and suffering of his wounds, and of the dim damp place in which he lay; in spite of the tears—wrung from him by his physical distress—his heart was full of gladness to know that he was nevertheless back once more in the kindly world of men.

===Chinese===
贝塞尔先生一听，便以加倍的热切赶回降神会正在进行的那间屋子。他刚挤到能看见那地方的位置，就看见围在灵媒身边的一个男人正看着表，似乎意思是降神会马上就要结束了。当下，那一大批原本在使劲的影子都绝望地作势转身离去。可一想到降神会快要结束，贝塞尔先生反而愈发急切；他凭着意志与旁人奋力相争，终于，他挤进了那妇人的脑子。恰好那一刻，她脑中那块区域亮得格外分明；就在这一刹那，她写下了那条威尔逊·佩吉特博士所保存的讯息。紧接着，旁的影子和身边那一团恶灵便把贝塞尔先生从她身边挤开了；整个降神会余下的时间，他再也没能回到她那里。

于是他折回去，在竖井底下守了那漫长的几个钟头，看那恶灵躺在它自己所残害的、偷来的身体里，扭动着、咒骂着，哭泣着、呻吟着，领受着痛苦这一课。将近黎明时，他苦等的那一幕发生了：那脑子亮了起来，恶灵走了出来，贝塞尔先生便重新钻进了他原以为再也回不去的身体。他一进去，那寂静——那沉沉笼罩的寂静——便结束了；他听见头顶上车水马龙的喧嚣，听见人们的说话声；而那个作为我们世界之影的奇异世界——那些无能的欲望留下的暗而无声的影子，还有那些失落之人留下的影子——便一下子消失得干干净净。

被发现之前，他在那里躺了大约三个钟头。尽管他伤痕累累、疼痛难当，又躺在一个昏暗潮湿的地方；尽管肉体的苦楚榨出了他的眼泪——他的心头仍然满是欢喜，因为他毕竟又回到了那温情脉脉的人间。

## The Story of the Inexperienced Ghost / 没经验的鬼的故事

===Original===
The scene amidst which Clayton told his last story comes back very vividly to my mind. There he sat, for the greater part of the time, in the corner of the authentic settle by the spacious open fire, and Sanderson sat beside him smoking the Broseley clay that bore his name. There was Evans, and that marvel among actors, Wish, who is also a modest man. We had all come down to the Mermaid Club that Saturday morning, except Clayton, who had slept there overnight—which indeed gave him the opening of his story. We had golfed until golfing was invisible; we had dined, and we were in that mood of tranquil kindliness when men will suffer a story. When Clayton began to tell one, we naturally supposed he was lying. It may be that indeed he was lying—of that the reader will speedily be able to judge as well as I. He began, it is true, with an air of matter-of-fact anecdote, but that we thought was only the incurable artifice of the man.

===Chinese===
克莱顿（Clayton）讲他最后一则故事时的那一幕场景，至今仍极为鲜明地浮现在我脑海里。大半个晚上，他都坐在那宽敞的壁炉旁、那张正宗的老式高背长椅的角落里，桑德森（Sanderson）坐在他身边，抽着那支刻着他名字的布罗斯利陶土烟斗。在场的还有埃文斯（Evans），以及那位演员之中的奇才威什（Wish）——他同时是个谦逊的人。那个星期六的早上，我们全都下到了美人鱼俱乐部（the Mermaid Club），只有克莱顿是头天夜里就睡在那儿的——这恰恰给了他一个引出故事的由头。我们打高尔夫一直打到看不见球为止；我们吃过晚饭，正处于那种宁静而和善的心境之中，男人在这种心境下才肯耐着性子听人讲故事。所以当克莱顿开口讲起来的时候，我们自然而然地以为他在编瞎话。说不定他确实在编瞎话——这一点，读者很快就能和我一样作出判断。诚然，他一开头的口气活像在讲一桩确有其事的轶闻，可我们觉得那不过是这个人改不掉的故弄玄虚罢了。

===Original===
“I say!” he remarked, after a long consideration of the upward rain of sparks from the log that Sanderson had thumped, “you know I was alone here last night?”

“Except for the domestics,” said Wish.

“Who sleep in the other wing,” said Clayton. “Yes. Well—” He pulled at his cigar for some little time as though he still hesitated about his confidence. Then he said, quite quietly, “I caught a ghost!”

“Caught a ghost, did you?” said Sanderson. “Where is it?”

And Evans, who admires Clayton immensely and has been four weeks in America, shouted, “*Caught* a ghost, did you, Clayton? I’m glad of it! Tell us all about it right now.”

Clayton said he would in a minute, and asked him to shut the door.

He looked apologetically at me. “There’s no eavesdropping of course, but we don’t want to upset our very excellent service with any rumours of ghosts in the place. There’s too much shadow and oak panelling to trifle with that. And this, you know, wasn’t a regular ghost. I don’t think it will come again—ever.”

“You mean to say you didn’t keep it?” said Sanderson.

“I hadn’t the heart to,” said Clayton.

And Sanderson said he was surprised.

We laughed, and Clayton looked aggrieved. “I know,” he said, with the flicker of a smile, “but the fact is it really *was* a ghost, and I’m as sure of it as I am that I am talking to you now. I’m not joking. I mean what I say.”

===Chinese===
“我说！”他开口了，盯着桑德森捣过的那根木柴向上飞溅的火星看了好半天之后才说道，“你们知道我昨晚是一个人在这儿的吧？”

“除了那些佣人。”威什说。

“他们都睡在另一翼。”克莱顿说，“是了。那么——”他又抽了好一会儿雪茄，似乎还在犹豫要不要吐露。然后他十分平静地说：“我抓住了一个鬼！”

“抓住了一个鬼，是吗？”桑德森说，“它在哪儿呢？”

埃文斯一向极佩服克莱顿，又刚从美国待了四个星期回来，这时大嚷道：“*抓住*了一个鬼，是吗，克莱顿？我太高兴了！快，原原本本讲给我们听听。”

克莱顿说一会儿就讲，叫他先把门关上。

他带点歉意地看了看我。“当然不会有偷听的，可我们也不想因为这儿闹鬼的传闻，搅了我们这顶呱呱的服务。这地方阴影太多，橡木镶板太多，可经不起这种事儿的折腾。再说，你们知道，这也不是一只正规的鬼。我想它不会再来了——永远不会再来了。”

“你是说，你没把它留下？”桑德森说。

“我下不了那个手。”克莱顿说。

桑德森说他听了真吃惊。

我们都笑了，克莱顿一脸委屈。“我知道，”他说，嘴角闪过一丝笑意，“可事实是，它确实*是*一个鬼，这件事我敢肯定，就像我敢肯定我现在在跟你们说话一样。我不是开玩笑。我是认真的。”

===Original===
Sanderson drew deeply at his pipe, with one reddish eye on Clayton, and then emitted a thin jet of smoke more eloquent than many words.

Clayton ignored the comment. “It is the strangest thing that has ever happened in my life. You know, I never believed in ghosts or anything of the sort, before, ever; and then, you know, I bag one in a corner; and the whole business is in my hands.”

He meditated still more profoundly, and produced and began to pierce a second cigar with a curious little stabber he affected.

“You talked to it?” asked Wish.

“For the space, probably, of an hour.”

“Chatty?” I said, joining the party of the sceptics.

===Chinese===
桑德森深深吸了一口烟斗，一只略带红色的眼睛盯着克莱顿，随后喷出一缕细细的烟气，比千言万语都更有说服力。

克莱顿不理会这个无声的评语。“这是我这辈子遇到过的最离奇的事。你们知道，我从前可从来不信鬼，什么都不信，从来没有过；可这一回呢，我竟在一个角落里逮住了一只；整桩事儿就捏在我手里。”

他又更深沉地沉思起来，摸出一支雪茄，用一支他偏爱的别致小戳针戳了起来。

“你跟它说话了？”威什问。

“大概说了一个钟头的话吧。”

“聊得挺欢？”我说，加入了怀疑者的一边。

===Original===
“The poor devil was in trouble,” said Clayton, bowed over his cigar-end and with the very faintest note of reproof.

“Sobbing?” someone asked.

Clayton heaved a realistic sigh at the memory. “Good Lord!” he said; “yes.” And then, “Poor fellow! yes.”

“Where did you strike it?” asked Evans, in his best American accent.

“I never realised,” said Clayton, ignoring him, “the poor sort of thing a ghost might be,” and he hung us up again for a time, while he sought for matches in his pocket and lit and warmed to his cigar.

“I took an advantage,” he reflected at last.

===Chinese===
“那可怜虫正烦着呢。”克莱顿弓着身子对着雪茄头说，口气里带着极轻微的责备意味。

“在抽泣？”有人问。

克莱顿想起那一幕，逼真地叹了口气。“老天爷！”他说，“是的。”接着又说，“可怜的家伙！是的。”

“你在哪儿撞见它的？”埃文斯用他最地道的美国口音问。

“我从来没意识到，”克莱顿说，没理他，“一只鬼会是多么寒碜的一件东西。”他又让我们等了一会儿，一边在口袋里摸火柴，把雪茄点上，慢慢抽出味儿来。

“我占了便宜。”他终于边想边说。

===Original===
We were none of us in a hurry. “A character,” he said, “remains just the same character for all that it’s been disembodied. That’s a thing we too often forget. People with a certain strength or fixity of purpose may have ghosts of a certain strength and fixity of purpose—most haunting ghosts, you know, must be as one-idea’d as monomaniacs and as obstinate as mules to come back again and again. This poor creature wasn’t.” He suddenly looked up rather queerly, and his eye went round the room. “I say it,” he said, “in all kindliness, but that is the plain truth of the case. Even at the first glance he struck me as weak.”

He punctuated with the help of his cigar.

===Chinese===
我们谁也不着急。“一个人，”他说，“即便已经没了肉身，性情还是那副性情。这一点我们太容易忘记。意志有一定力量、或者目标有一定专一的人，化作鬼之后，那力量和专一也还在——你们知道，最会缠人的鬼，必定得像偏执狂一样心思单一，又得像骡子一样倔强，才能一次又一次地回来。这个可怜虫可不是这样。”他突然古怪地抬起头来，眼睛在屋里转了一圈。“我说这话，”他说，“全是出于好意，可这就是这件事的实情。头一眼我就觉得他窝囊。”

他用雪茄比划着作标点。

===Original===
“I came upon him, you know, in the long passage. His back was towards me and I saw him first. Right off I knew him for a ghost. He was transparent and whitish; clean through his chest I could see the glimmer of the little window at the end. And not only his physique but his attitude struck me as being weak. He looked, you know, as though he didn’t know in the slightest whatever he meant to do. One hand was on the panelling and the other fluttered to his mouth. Like—*so*!”

“What sort of physique?” said Sanderson.

“Lean. You know that sort of young man’s neck that has two great flutings down the back, here and here—so! And a little, meanish head with scrubby hair—And rather bad ears. Shoulders bad, narrower than the hips; turndown collar, ready-made short jacket, trousers baggy and a little frayed at the heels. That’s how he took me. I came very quietly up the staircase. I did not carry a light, you know—the candles are on the landing table and there is that lamp—and I was in my list slippers, and I saw him as I came up. I stopped dead at that—taking him in. I wasn’t a bit afraid. I think that in most of these affairs one is never nearly so afraid or excited as one imagines one would be. I was surprised and interested. I thought, ‘Good Lord! Here’s a ghost at last! And I haven’t believed for a moment in ghosts during the last five-and-twenty years.’”

===Chinese===
“我撞见他，你们知道，是在那条长长的走廊里。他背朝着我，我先看见的是他的背影。我一下子就认出他是个鬼。他是半透明的，泛着白光；透过他的胸膛，我能清清楚楚看见走廊尽头那扇小窗透进来的微光。不仅他的身架，连他的姿态都让我觉得窝囊。他那模样——你们知道——仿佛压根儿不知道自己接下来要干什么。一只手搭在护墙板上，另一只手颤巍巍地举到嘴边。像——*这样*！”

“什么样的身架？”桑德森问。

“瘦。你们知道那种年轻人的脖子，后头有两道深深的凹槽，这儿，还有这儿——这样！一颗小脑袋，略带猥琐，头发稀稀拉拉——耳朵也不大好。肩膀不行的，比胯骨还窄；翻领领子，现成的短外套，裤子松垮垮的，裤脚后跟处有点磨边。他给我的就是这么个印象。我蹑手蹑脚地走上楼梯。我没拿灯，你们知道——蜡烛都搁在楼梯口的桌上，还有那盏灯——我穿着绒毡拖鞋，一边上楼一边就看见他了。我当场站住了——打量着他。我一点也不怕。我觉得在这种事儿里头，人往往远没有自己想象的那样害怕、那样激动。我只是又惊又觉得有趣。我心想：‘老天爷！到底碰见一个鬼了！这二十五年来我可是一刻都没信过鬼的。’”

===Original===
“Um,” said Wish.

“I suppose I wasn’t on the landing a moment before he found out I was there. He turned on me sharply, and I saw the face of an immature young man, a weak nose, a scrubby little moustache, a feeble chin. So for an instant we stood—he looking over his shoulder at me and regarded one another. Then he seemed to remember his high calling. He turned round, drew himself up, projected his face, raised his arms, spread his hands in approved ghost fashion—came towards me. As he did so his little jaw dropped, and he emitted a faint, drawn-out ‘Boo.’ No, it wasn’t—not a bit dreadful. I’d dined. I’d had a bottle of champagne, and being all alone, perhaps two or three—perhaps even four or five—whiskies, so I was as solid as rocks and no more frightened than if I’d been assailed by a frog. ‘Boo!’ I said. ‘Nonsense. You don’t belong to *this* place. What are you doing here?’

===Chinese===
“嗯。”威什说。

“我到了楼梯口还没站一会儿，他就发现我了。他猛地转过身来，我看见一张还没长开的年轻人的脸，鼻子软塌塌的，一小撮稀疏的髭须，下巴颏儿也没劲儿。就这样我们对峙了那么一瞬间——他扭过头从肩膀上头看着我，我们俩彼此打量。接着他似乎想起了自己崇高的使命。他转过身来，挺直腰板，往前探出脸，举起双臂，按鬼的标准姿势张开双手——朝我走过来。他这么走着，那张小嘴张开了，发出一声微弱的、拖长了的‘噗’。不，一点也不——一点也不可怕。我吃过晚饭了。我喝了一瓶香槟，又因为独自一个，大概还喝了两三杯——说不定四五杯——威士忌，所以我稳如磐石，被他这么一吓，就跟被一只青蛙袭击了差不多。‘噗！’我说，‘胡扯。你不是*这*地方的人。你在这儿干什么？’

===Original===
“I could see him wince. ‘Boo-oo,’ he said.

“‘Boo—be hanged! Are you a member?’ I said; and just to show I didn’t care a pin for him I stepped through a corner of him and made to light my candle. ‘Are you a member?’ I repeated, looking at him sideways.

“He moved a little so as to stand clear of me, and his bearing became crestfallen. ‘No,’ he said, in answer to the persistent interrogation of my eye; ‘I’m not a member—I’m a ghost.’

“‘Well, that doesn’t give you the run of the Mermaid Club. Is there anyone you want to see, or anything of that sort?’ and doing it as steadily as possible for fear that he should mistake the carelessness of whisky for the distraction of fear, I got my candle alight. I turned on him, holding it. ‘What are you doing here?’ I said.

“He had dropped his hands and stopped his booing, and there he stood, abashed and awkward, the ghost of a weak, silly, aimless young man. ‘I’m haunting,’ he said.

“‘You haven’t any business to,’ I said in a quiet voice.

“‘I’m a ghost,’ he said, as if in defence.

“‘That may be, but you haven’t any business to haunt here. This is a respectable private club; people often stop here with nursemaids and children, and, going about in the careless way you do, some poor little mite could easily come upon you and be scared out of her wits. I suppose you didn’t think of that?’

“‘No, sir,’ he said, ‘I didn’t.’

“‘You should have done. You haven’t any claim on the place, have you? Weren’t murdered here, or anything of that sort?’

“‘None, sir; but I thought as it was old and oak-panelled—’

“‘That’s *no* excuse.’ I regarded him firmly. ‘Your coming here is a mistake,’ I said, in a tone of friendly superiority. I feigned to see if I had my matches, and then looked up at him frankly. ‘If I were you I wouldn’t wait for cockcrow—I’d vanish right away.’

===Chinese===
“我看得见他往后缩了一下。‘噗——噗，’他说。

“‘噗——去你的！你是会员吗？’我说；为了表示我压根儿不把他放在眼里，我从他身子的一角穿了过去，去点我的蜡烛。‘你是会员吗？’我又问了一遍，斜眼看他。

“他挪了挪，好让我从他身上穿过去时不致受阻，那姿态十分气馁。‘不是，’他在我目光的逼问下答道，‘我不是会员——我是个鬼。’

“‘这可不能让你随便出入美人鱼俱乐部。你有什么人要见，或者诸如此类的事吗？’我尽可能稳当地把话说完，生怕他把我因威士忌而来的大大咧咧，错当成因害怕而失态，一面把蜡烛点着了。我举着蜡烛，转向他。‘你在这儿干什么？’我说。

“他已垂下双手，也不再‘噗’了，就那么站着，又窘又笨——一个软弱的、愚蠢的、漫无目的的年轻人的鬼魂。‘我在作祟，’他说。

“‘你可没这个资格，’我平静地说。

“‘我是个鬼，’他说，像是在辩解。

“‘也许是吧，可你没资格在这儿作祟。这是一家体面的私人俱乐部；常常有人带着保姆和孩子在这儿歇脚，你这么大大咧咧地到处晃荡，万一哪个可怜的小娃娃撞见了你，吓掉了魂儿怎么办。我猜你没想到这一层吧？’

“‘没有，先生，’他说，‘我没想。’

“‘你本该想到的。你对这地方没有什么渊源吧？没在这儿被人谋杀过，或者那一类的事？’

“‘没有，先生；不过我想这儿又老又镶着橡木板——’

“‘那*不*成理由。’我坚定地打量着他。‘你到这儿来是个错误，’我用一种友善而居高临下的口气说。我假装看看自己有没有火柴，然后坦然地抬头看他。‘我要是你，就不等到鸡啼——我干脆立刻消失。’

===Original===
“He looked embarrassed. ‘The fact *is*, sir—’ he began.

“‘I’d vanish,’ I said, driving it home.

“‘The fact is, sir, that—somehow—I can’t.’

“‘You *can’t*?’

“‘No, sir. There’s something I’ve forgotten. I’ve been hanging about here since midnight last night, hiding in the cupboards of the empty bedrooms and things like that. I’m flurried. I’ve never come haunting before, and it seems to put me out.’

“‘Put you out?’

“‘Yes, sir. I’ve tried to do it several times, and it doesn’t come off. There’s some little thing has slipped me, and I can’t get back.’

“That, you know, rather bowled me over. He looked at me in such an abject way that for the life of me I couldn’t keep up quite the high, hectoring vein I had adopted. ‘That’s queer,’ I said, and as I spoke I fancied I heard someone moving about down below. ‘Come into my room and tell me more about it,’ I said. ‘I didn’t, of course, understand this,’ and I tried to take him by the arm. But, of course, you might as well have tried to take hold of a puff of smoke! I had forgotten my number, I think; anyhow, I remember going into several bedrooms—it was lucky I was the only soul in that wing—until I saw my traps. ‘Here we are,’ I said, and sat down in the armchair; ‘sit down and tell me all about it. It seems to me you have got yourself into a jolly awkward position, old chap.’

===Chinese===
“他显得很为难。‘实情是，先生——’他开口道。

“‘我干脆消失，’我说，把这话钉死。

“‘实情是，先生，我——不知怎的——消失不了。’

“‘你*消失不了*？’

“‘是的，先生。有件事我给忘了。我从昨天半夜起就一直在这一带转悠，躲在那些空卧室的衣橱里，还有诸如此类的地方。我心里乱得很。我从没作过祟，这事儿让我心慌。’

“‘让你心慌？’

“‘是的，先生。我试了好几回，都不成。有个小关键我给忘了，我就回不去了。’

“这一下，你们知道，倒真把我唬住了。他望着我，那模样可怜极了，我怎么也没法子维持刚才那副高高在上、盛气凌人的腔调。‘这倒怪了，’我说，说着说着，我恍惚听见楼下有人在走动。‘到我房里来，再多跟我讲讲，’我说，‘我当然不明白这是怎么回事，’说着我想去挽他的胳膊。可——那还用说——你想抓住一缕烟都还容易些！我大概把自己房间的号码忘了；反正我记得我进了好几间卧室——幸好那一翼就我一个人——这才看见自己的行李。‘就是这儿，’我说，在扶手椅里坐下，‘你坐下，原原本本讲给我听。我看你这处境可真是够尴尬的，老兄。’

===Original===
“Well, he said he wouldn’t sit down! he’d prefer to flit up and down the room if it was all the same to me. And so he did, and in a little while we were deep in a long and serious talk. And presently, you know, something of those whiskies and sodas evaporated out of me, and I began to realise just a little what a thundering rum and weird business it was that I was in. There he was, semitransparent—the proper conventional phantom, and noiseless except for his ghost of a voice—flitting to and fro in that nice, clean, chintz-hung old bedroom. You could see the gleam of the copper candlesticks through him, and the lights on the brass fender, and the corners of the framed engravings on the wall—and there he was telling me all about this wretched little life of his that had recently ended on Earth. He hadn’t a particularly honest face, you know, but being transparent, of course, he couldn’t avoid telling the truth.”

===Chinese===
“那么，他说他不坐！他说如果我没意见，他宁愿在屋里来回飘。于是他就这样做了，不一会儿我们便深入地进行了一番又长又认真的交谈。渐渐地，你们知道，那些威士忌苏打的酒劲儿从我身上蒸发掉了一些，我也开始稍稍意识到，我正置身于怎样一桩骇人听闻、稀奇古怪的事儿里。他就在那儿，半透明的——一个规规矩矩、合乎标准的幽灵，除了那一缕鬼嗓音之外毫无声息——在那间雅洁的、挂着印花棉布帘幔的旧卧室里来回飘荡。你可以透过他看见铜烛台的光泽，看见黄铜壁炉栏上的反光，看见墙上那些装框版画的边角——而他就在那儿，向我娓娓讲述着他那刚刚在人间结束了的、可悲可鄙的小小一生。他的相貌不算特别诚实，你们知道，可既然他是透明的，自然就没法不说真话。”

===Original===
“Eh?” said Wish, suddenly sitting up in his chair.

“What?” said Clayton.

“Being transparent—couldn’t avoid telling the truth—I don’t see it,” said Wish.

“*I* don’t see it,” said Clayton, with inimitable assurance. “But it *is* so, I can assure you nevertheless. I don’t believe he got once a nail’s breadth off the Bible truth. He told me how he had been killed—he went down into a London basement with a candle to look for a leakage of gas—and described himself as a senior English master in a London private school when that release occurred.”

“Poor wretch!” said I.

===Chinese===
“啊？”威什猛地在椅子上坐直了说。

“怎么了？”克莱顿说。

“透明的——就没法不说真话——我看不出其中的道理。”威什说。

“*我*也看不出，”克莱顿带着无可仿效的笃定说，“可事实就是如此，我向你保证。我相信他连一指甲盖的谎都没偏离过《圣经》那样的真相。他告诉我他是怎么送命的——他举着一根蜡烛下到伦敦一处地下室的楼梯，去查一个煤气漏点——又说在那场解脱降临之前，他是伦敦一所私立学校里的高年级英文教师。”

“可怜虫！”我说。

===Original===
“That’s what I thought, and the more he talked the more I thought it. There he was, purposeless in life and purposeless out of it. He talked of his father and mother and his schoolmaster, and all who had ever been anything to him in the world, meanly. He had been too sensitive, too nervous; none of them had ever valued him properly or understood him, he said. He had never had a real friend in the world, I think; he had never had a success. He had shirked games and failed examinations. ‘It’s like that with some people,’ he said; ‘whenever I got into the examination-room or anywhere everything seemed to go.’ Engaged to be married of course—to another oversensitive person, I suppose—when the indiscretion with the gas escape ended his affairs. ‘And where are you now?’ I asked. ‘Not in—?’

“He wasn’t clear on that point at all. The impression he gave me was of a sort of vague, intermediate state, a special reserve for souls too nonexistent for anything so positive as either sin or virtue. *I* don’t know. He was much too egotistical and unobservant to give me any clear idea of the kind of place, kind of country, there is on the other side of things. Wherever he was, he seems to have fallen in with a set of kindred spirits: ghosts of weak Cockney young men, who were on a footing of Christian names, and among these there was certainly a lot of talk about ‘going haunting’ and things like that. Yes—going haunting! They seemed to think ‘haunting’ a tremendous adventure, and most of them funked it all the time. And so primed, you know, he had come.”

===Chinese===
“我也是这么想的，他越说我越这么想。他活着没有目标，死了也没有目标。他提起父亲、母亲、老师，以及这世上所有曾经对他有过一点意义的人，口气都刻薄。他说自己太敏感、太神经质，那些人从来没有真正看重过他、理解过他。我想他这辈子没交过一个真正的朋友；他从来没有过一回得意的事。他逃避游戏，考试屡屡不及格。‘有些人就是这样的，’他说，‘我一进考场或者什么地方，什么都好像要从脑袋里溜走。’自然是订过婚的——又是一个过于敏感的人，我猜——直到那桩因查煤气而起的糊涂事断送了他的一切。‘那么你现在在哪儿呢？’我问，‘不在——？’

“这一点他根本说不清楚。他给我的印象，是一种模模糊糊的中间状态，一个专为那些过于虚无、既够不上善也够不上恶的灵魂而设的特别收容所。*我*不知道。他太自我中心，又太不留心周遭，根本没法给我讲清楚，在那一边究竟是怎样一个地方、怎样一个国度。无论他在哪儿，他似乎都结交了一帮同类：都是些软弱的伦敦腔年轻人的鬼魂，彼此以教名相称，凑在一起东拉西扯，‘去作祟’之类的话谈了不少。是——去作祟！他们似乎把‘作祟’看作一场惊天动地的冒险，可大多数人又都怕得要命。他正是在这些鼓动之下，你们知道，才跑来的。”

===Original===
“But really!” said Wish to the fire.

“These are the impressions he gave me, anyhow,” said Clayton, modestly. “I may, of course, have been in a rather uncritical state, but that was the sort of background he gave to himself. He kept flitting up and down, with his thin voice going talking, talking about his wretched self, and never a word of clear, firm statement from first to last. He was thinner and sillier and more pointless than if he had been real and alive. Only then, you know, he would not have been in my bedroom here—if he *had* been alive. I should have kicked him out.”

“Of course,” said Evans, “there *are* poor mortals like that.”

“And there’s just as much chance of their having ghosts as the rest of us,” I admitted.

“What gave a sort of point to him, you know, was the fact that he did seem within limits to have found himself out. The mess he had made of haunting had depressed him terribly. He had been told it would be a ‘lark’; he had come expecting it to be a ‘lark,’ and here it was, nothing but another failure added to his record! He proclaimed himself an utter out-and-out failure. He said, and I can quite believe it, that he had never tried to do anything all his life that he hadn’t made a perfect mess of—and through all the wastes of eternity he never would. If he had had sympathy, perhaps—He paused at that, and stood regarding me. He remarked that, strange as it might seem to me, nobody, not anyone, ever, had given him the amount of sympathy I was doing now. I could see what he wanted straight away, and I determined to head him off at once. I may be a brute, you know, but being the only real friend, the recipient of the confidences of one of these egotistical weaklings, ghost or body, is beyond my physical endurance. I got up briskly. ‘Don’t you brood on these things too much,’ I said. ‘The thing you’ve got to do is to get out of this get out of this—sharp. You pull yourself together and *try*.‘ ‘I can’t,’ he said. ‘You try,’ I said, and try he did.”

===Chinese===
“真有这等事！”威什对着炉火说。

“不管怎样，这就是他给我的印象，”克莱顿谦逊地说，“我当时的判断力当然可能不够缜密，可这就是他给自己描绘的那个背景。他不住地飘来飘去，那细细的嗓音絮絮叨叨，讲的全是他那可悲的自我，自始至终没说过一句清楚、坚定的话。他比真实地活着时更单薄、更愚蠢、更没有意义。只不过，你们知道，假如他活着的话，就不会在我的卧室里——假如他*真*活着，我早把他踢出去了。”

“那自然，”埃文斯说，“世上*确实*有这种可怜的凡人。”

“他们会有鬼魂的机会，倒也和我们其余人一样多。”我承认。

“给他添了那么一点意思的，你们知道，是这样一件事：他似乎在一定的限度之内，看清了自己。他把作祟搞砸了，这把他打击得够呛。有人告诉他那是桩‘乐子’；他满心以为那是桩‘乐子’才来的，可如今呢，不过是他的劣绩记录上又添了一桩失败罢了！他自称是个彻头彻尾、不折不扣的失败者。他说——我也完全相信——他这辈子不论试着做什么，没有一回不搞得一塌糊涂的——而穿过永恒的荒原，他也永远搞不好。当初要是有人同情他，也许——他顿了一下，站在那儿看着我。他说，尽管我也许觉得奇怪，可从来、从来没有任何人，给过他像我此刻这样多的同情。我一眼就看穿了他要的是什么，便当即打定主意岔开话题。我也许算个狠心人，你们知道，可给这种自我中心的软骨头——不管是鬼是人——做唯一的朋友、当知心人，我可消受不了。我一下子站起身来。‘你别老往这些事儿上想，’我说，‘你现在该做的是从这儿出去——出去——赶紧。你振作精神，*试试*看。’‘我不成，’他说。‘你试试，’我说，于是他试了。”

===Original===
“Try!” said Sanderson. “*How?*”

“Passes,” said Clayton.

“Passes?”

“Complicated series of gestures and passes with the hands. That’s how he had come in and that’s how he had to get out again. Lord! what a business I had!”

“But how could *any* series of passes—?” I began.

“My dear man,” said Clayton, turning on me and putting a great emphasis on certain words, “you want *everything* clear. *I* don’t know *how*. All I know is that you *do*—that *he* did, anyhow, at least. After a fearful time, you know, he got his passes right and suddenly disappeared.”

===Chinese===
“试！”桑德森说，“*怎么试？*”

“手法，”克莱顿说。

“手法？”

“一连串复杂的手势和手上的手法。他就是这样进来的，也得这样才能出去。老天爷！我可费了老鼻子劲了！”

“可是——*任何*一连串的手法又怎么能——？”我刚开口。

“我亲爱的老兄，”克莱顿转过身来对我说，把重音落在几个字上，“你什么都要问个明白。*我*不知道*怎么*回事。我只知道*确实*是这样——至少*他*确实是这样的。过了一段要命的时间，你们知道，他终于把手法比划对了，然后一下子就不见了。”

===Original===
“Did you,” said Sanderson, slowly, “observe the passes?”

“Yes,” said Clayton, and seemed to think. “It was tremendously queer,” he said. “There we were, I and this thin vague ghost, in that silent room, in this silent, empty inn, in this silent little Friday-night town. Not a sound except our voices and a faint panting he made when he swung. There was the bedroom candle, and one candle on the dressing-table alight, that was all—sometimes one or other would flare up into a tall, lean, astonished flame for a space. And queer things happened. ‘I can’t,’ he said; ‘I shall never—!’ And suddenly he sat down on a little chair at the foot of the bed and began to sob and sob. Lord! what a harrowing, whimpering thing he seemed!

“‘You pull yourself together,’ I said, and tried to pat him on the back, and… my confounded hand went through him! By that time, you know, I wasn’t nearly so—massive as I had been on the landing. I got the queerness of it full. I remember snatching back my hand out of him, as it were, with a little thrill, and walking over to the dressing-table. ‘You pull yourself together,’ I said to him, ‘and try.’ And in order to encourage and help him I began to try as well.”

===Chinese===
“你，”桑德森慢悠悠地说，“留意到那些手法了吗？”

“留意了，”克莱顿说，似乎陷入思索。“真是离奇极了，”他说，“我俩就在那儿——我和这个瘦弱的、模糊不清的鬼魂——在那间寂静的屋子里，在这家寂静的、空荡荡的客栈里，在这个寂静的小小的、礼拜五夜晚的小镇上。除了我们的说话声，再就是他每次挥动手臂时发出的一点轻微喘息，再没有一丝声响。屋里点着床头蜡烛，梳妆台上还点着一支，就这些——有时这一支或那一支会突然窜起一道又高又瘦、惊愕似的火苗，烧上一会儿。还发生了些怪事。‘我不成，’他说，‘我永远——！’他忽然在床脚一张小椅子上坐下，抽抽搭搭地哭起来，哭了又哭。老天爷！他那时看上去多么揪心、多么像呜咽的一团东西啊！

“‘你振作起来，’我说，想拍拍他的背，于是……我那只该死的手竟从他身上穿了过去！到了那时，你们知道，我已经远不像在楼梯口时那么——那么稳如磐石了。那股子怪味儿整个儿地漫上了我。我记得我像是打了个激灵，把手从他身上抽回来，走到梳妆台前。‘你振作起来，’我对他说，‘试试看。’为了鼓励他、帮帮他，我自己也开始比划起来。”

===Original===
“What!” said Sanderson, “the passes?”

“Yes, the passes.”

“But—” I said, moved by an idea that eluded me for a space.

“This is interesting,” said Sanderson, with his finger in his pipe-bowl. “You mean to say this ghost of yours gave away—”

“Did his level best to give away the whole confounded barrier? *Yes.*”

“He didn’t,” said Wish; “he couldn’t. Or you’d have gone there too.”

“That’s precisely it,” I said, finding my elusive idea put into words for me.

“That *is* precisely it,” said Clayton, with thoughtful eyes upon the fire.

For just a little while there was silence.

“And at last he did it?” said Sanderson.

“At last he did it. I had to keep him up to it hard, but he did it at last—rather suddenly. He despaired, we had a scene, and then he got up abruptly and asked me to go through the whole performance, slowly, so that he might see. ‘I believe,’ he said, ‘if I could *see* I should spot what was wrong at once.’ And he did. ‘*I* know,’ he said. ‘What do you know?’ said I. ‘*I* know,’ he repeated. Then he said, peevishly, ‘I *can’t* do it if you look at me—I really *can’t*; it’s been that, partly, all along. I’m such a nervous fellow that you put me out.’ Well, we had a bit of an argument. Naturally I wanted to see; but he was as obstinate as a mule, and suddenly I had come over as tired as a dog—he tired me out. ‘All right,’ I said, ‘*I* won’t look at you,’ and turned towards the mirror, on the wardrobe, by the bed.

“He started off very fast. I tried to follow him by looking in the looking-glass, to see just what it was had hung. Round went his arms and his hands, so, and so, and so, and then with a rush came to the last gesture of all—you stand erect and open out your arms—and so, don’t you know, he stood. And then he didn’t! He didn’t! He wasn’t! I wheeled round from the looking-glass to him. There was nothing, I was alone, with the flaring candles and a staggering mind. What had happened? Had anything happened? Had I been dreaming?… And then, with an absurd note of finality about it, the clock upon the landing discovered the moment was ripe for striking *one*. So!—Ping! And I was as grave and sober as a judge, with all my champagne and whisky gone into the vast serene. Feeling queer, you know—confoundedly *queer*! Queer! Good Lord!”

He regarded his cigar-ash for a moment. “That’s all that happened,” he said.

===Chinese===
“什么！”桑德森说，“比划那些手法？”

“对，那些手法。”

“可是——”我说，被一个一时抓不住的念头驱使着。

“这就有意思了，”桑德森把手指插进烟斗钵里说，“你是说，你这只鬼竟然把——”

“把他妈的整道关卡和盘托出？*是的。*”

“他不会的，”威什说，“他不能。不然你也到那边去了。”

“正是此理，”我说，发现我那个抓不住的念头被人代我说了出来。

“正*是*此理，”克莱顿说，若有所思地凝视着炉火。

一时大家都静了下来。

“最后他做到了？”桑德森说。

“最后他做到了。我不得不狠命地逼着他，可他终究做到了——做得相当突然。他绝望过，我们有过一场波折，后来他猛地站起来，请我把整套从头到尾、慢慢地做一遍给他看。‘我相信，’他说，‘要是我能*看清楚*，我就能立刻找出哪儿不对。’他果然看出来了。‘*我*知道了，’他说。‘你知道什么？’我说。‘*我*知道了，’他重复。然后他气呼呼地说：‘你盯着我看，我*做*不来——我真*做*不来；这一部分，从头到尾，就是这个缘故。我这人神经衰弱得厉害，你一盯着我，我就慌了神。’我们争论了一番。我自然要看；可他倔得像头骡子，而我又忽然疲倦得像条狗——他把我累坏了。‘好吧，’我说，‘*我*不看你，’便转身对着床头衣橱上、床边那面镜子。

“他开始比划得飞快。我想从镜子里跟着他，看看究竟卡在哪儿。他的胳膊和手转着圈儿，这样，这样，又这样，然后一气冲到最后那个动作——你挺直身子，把双臂大大张开——就这样，你们知道，他站定在那儿。然后他就不在了！他不在了！他没了！我从镜子前猛地转过身看他。什么都没有，我只身一人，对着窜起的烛火和一片晕眩的脑子。发生了什么？到底发生了什么没有？我一直在做梦吗？……就在这时，带着一种滑稽的终结意味，楼梯口那座钟觉得时候已到，敲响了*一点*。嗒！——铛！而我又像法官一样清醒、一样冷静了，所有的香槟和威士忌都消融在那片广袤的宁静里。只觉得古怪，你们知道——古怪*得要命*！古怪！老天爷！”

他对着雪茄灰看了一会儿。“事情就是这样。”他说。

===Original===
“And then you went to bed?” asked Evans.

“What else was there to do?”

I looked Wish in the eye. We wanted to scoff, and there was something, something perhaps in Clayton’s voice and manner, that hampered our desire.

“And about these passes?” said Sanderson.

“I believe I could do them now.”

“Oh!” said Sanderson, and produced a penknife and set himself to grub the dottel out of the bowl of his clay.

“Why don’t you do them now?” said Sanderson, shutting his penknife with a click.

“That’s what I’m going to do,” said Clayton.

“They won’t work,” said Evans.

“If they do—” I suggested.

“You know, I’d rather you didn’t,” said Wish, stretching out his legs.

“Why?” asked Evans.

“I’d rather he didn’t,” said Wish.

“But he hasn’t got ’em right,” said Sanderson, plugging too much tobacco in his pipe.

“All the same, I’d rather he didn’t,” said Wish.

We argued with Wish. He said that for Clayton to go through those gestures was like mocking a serious matter. “But you don’t believe—?” I said. Wish glanced at Clayton, who was staring into the fire, weighing something in his mind. “I do—more than half, anyhow, I do,” said Wish.

“Clayton,” said I, “you’re too good a liar for us. Most of it was all right. But that disappearance… happened to be convincing. Tell us, it’s a tale of cock and bull.”

He stood up without heeding me, took the middle of the hearthrug, and faced me. For a moment he regarded his feet thoughtfully, and then for all the rest of the time his eyes were on the opposite wall, with an intent expression. He raised his two hands slowly to the level of his eyes and so began…

===Chinese===
“后来你就上床睡了？”埃文斯问。

“不睡还能干什么？”

我直视威什的眼睛。我们本想嘲笑一番，可不知怎的——也许是克莱顿的声调、神态里有什么——叫我们嘲讽不起来。

“那些手法呢？”桑德森说。

“我想我现在还能比划出来。”

“哦！”桑德森说，掏出一把小刀，动手去挖他那陶土烟斗钵里的烟灰。

“那你现在干嘛不比划一下？”桑德森啪地合上小刀说。

“我就打算比划。”克莱顿说。

“比了也不灵。”埃文斯说。

“万一灵了呢——”我提了一句。

“你们知道，我倒宁愿你别比划。”威什说着，伸了伸腿。

“为什么？”埃文斯问。

“我宁愿他别比划。”威什说。

“可他比划得不对。”桑德森说，往烟斗里塞了太多的烟丝。

“我还是宁愿他别比划。”威什说。

我们跟威什争了起来。他说让克莱顿去比划那些手势，就如同拿一桩严肃的事开玩笑。“可你并不信——？”我说。威什瞟了克莱顿一眼，后者正盯着炉火，心里在掂量着什么。“我信——至少信了一大半。”威什说。

“克莱顿，”我说，“你撒谎的本事太大，我们可骗不过。故事大半都没问题。可那一段消失……偏偏让人信了。你就直说吧，这是无稽之谈。”

他不理我，站起身，走到炉前毯的正中，对着我。他低头若有所思地看了看自己的脚，然后眼睛就一直盯着对面的墙，神情专注。他慢慢把双手抬到与眼齐平，就这样开始了……

===Original===
Now, Sanderson is a Freemason, a member of the lodge of the Four Kings, which devotes itself so ably to the study and elucidation of all the mysteries of Masonry past and present, and among the students of this lodge Sanderson is by no means the least. He followed Clayton’s motions with a singular interest in his reddish eye. “That’s not bad,” he said, when it was done. “You really do, you know, put things together, Clayton, in a most amazing fashion. But there’s one little detail out.”

“I know,” said Clayton. “I believe I could tell you which.”

“Well?”

“This,” said Clayton, and did a queer little twist and writhing and thrust of the hands.

“Yes.”

“That, you know, was what *he* couldn’t get right,” said Clayton. “But how do *you*—?”

“Most of this business, and particularly how you invented it, I don’t understand at all,” said Sanderson, “but just that phase—I do.” He reflected. “These happen to be a series of gestures—connected with a certain branch of esoteric Masonry. Probably you know. Or else—*how*?” He reflected still further. “I do not see I can do any harm in telling you just the proper twist. After all, if you know, you know; if you don’t, you don’t.”

“I know nothing,” said Clayton, “except what the poor devil let out last night.”

“Well, anyhow,” said Sanderson, and placed his churchwarden very carefully upon the shelf over the fireplace. Then very rapidly he gesticulated with his hands.

“So?” said Clayton, repeating.

“So,” said Sanderson, and took his pipe in hand again.

“Ah, *now*,” said Clayton, “I can do the whole thing—right.”

===Chinese===
要知道，桑德森是个共济会会员（Freemason），隶属于“四王分会”（the lodge of the Four Kings），该分会专心钻研并阐释古往今来共济会的一切奥秘，成绩斐然，而在该分会的会员之中，桑德森绝非等闲之辈。他用那只略带红色的眼睛，怀着一种异乎寻常的兴趣，盯着克莱顿的一举一动。“还不错，”整套做完之后他说，“克莱顿，你这套东西拼到一起，真是有板有眼，神乎其神。只是有一个小细节不对。”

“我知道，”克莱顿说，“我相信我能告诉你错在哪。”

“嗯？”

“就是这个，”克莱顿说着，做了一个古怪的小扭动、小翻转，双手一推。

“对。”

“那一下，你们知道，正是*他*比划不对的地方，”克莱顿说，“可*你*又是怎么——？”

“这桩事的大部分，尤其是你是怎么编出来的，我一点也搞不明白，”桑德森说，“可单是这一段——我懂。”他想了想。“这碰巧是一连串手势——与共济会某一支秘传的仪式有关。想必你知道。不然——*怎么会*？”他又想了想。“我想，告诉你那个正确的扭法，也无妨。毕竟，知道就是知道；不知道就是不知道。”

“我什么都不知道，”克莱顿说，“全是那可怜虫昨夜漏出来的。”

“好吧，无论如何，”桑德森说着，把他那只长柄烟斗小心翼翼地搁到壁炉上方的架子上。然后他飞快地用双手比划了几下。

“这样？”克莱顿跟着比划了一遍。

“对，”桑德森说，重新拿起烟斗。

“啊，*这下*，”克莱顿说，“我能把整套都做出来——做对了。”

===Original===
He stood up before the waning fire and smiled at us all. But I think there was just a little hesitation in his smile. “If I begin—” he said.

“I wouldn’t begin,” said Wish.

“It’s all right!” said Evans. “Matter is indestructible. You don’t think any jiggery-pokery of this sort is going to snatch Clayton into the world of shades. Not it! You may try, Clayton, so far as I’m concerned, until your arms drop off at the wrists.”

“I don’t believe that,” said Wish, and stood up and put his arm on Clayton’s shoulder. “You’ve made me half believe in that story somehow, and I don’t want to see the thing done!”

“Goodness!” said I, “here’s Wish frightened!”

“I am,” said Wish, with real or admirably feigned intensity. “I believe that if he goes through these motions right he’ll *go*.”

“He’ll not do anything of the sort,” I cried. “There’s only one way out of this world for men, and Clayton is thirty years from that. Besides… And such a ghost! Do you think—?”

Wish interrupted me by moving. He walked out from among our chairs and stopped beside the tole and stood there. “Clayton,” he said, “you’re a fool.”
