Clayton, with a humorous light in his eyes, smiled back at him. “Wish,” he said, “is right and all you others are wrong. I shall go. I shall get to the end of these passes, and as the last swish whistles through the air, Presto!—this hearthrug will be vacant, the room will be blank amazement, and a respectably dressed gentleman of fifteen stone will plump into the world of shades. I’m certain. So will you be. I decline to argue further. Let the thing be tried.”

“*No*,” said Wish, and made a step and ceased, and Clayton raised his hands once more to repeat the spirit’s passing.

By that time, you know, we were all in a state of tension—largely because of the behaviour of Wish. We sat all of us with our eyes on Clayton—I, at least, with a sort of tight, stiff feeling about me as though from the back of my skull to the middle of my thighs my body had been changed to steel. And there, with a gravity that was imperturbably serene, Clayton bowed and swayed and waved his hands and arms before us. As he drew towards the end one piled up, one tingled in one’s teeth. The last gesture, I have said, was to swing the arms out wide open, with the face held up. And when at last he swung out to this closing gesture I ceased even to breathe. It was ridiculous, of course, but you know that ghost-story feeling. It was after dinner, in a queer, old shadowy house. Would he, after all—?

===Chinese===
他在渐渐暗下去的炉火前站起身，冲我们大家笑了笑。可我觉得，他那一笑里多少带着点犹豫。“我要是开始——”他说。

“我劝你别开始。”威什说。

“没事儿！”埃文斯说，“物质是不灭的。你以为这点装神弄鬼的小把戏，就能把克莱顿拽到阴曹地府去吗？想得美！你要试就试吧，克莱顿，就我而言，随你试到两只手腕子都掉下来。”

“我才不信那套，”威什说着站起身，把一只手搭在克莱顿肩上。“你这故事不知怎么的让我信了一半，我可不想看你把这套做出来！”

“老天爷！”我说，“威什这是害怕了！”

“我是害怕，”威什说，那神情不管是真是假，都装得惟妙惟肖。“我相信，要是他把这一套动作做对了，他就*走*了。”

“他才不会出那种事呢，”我叫道，“人离开这世上的路只有一条，克莱顿离那条路还有三十年呢。再说……再说是这么一只鬼！你以为——？”

威什不等我说完，已经动了。他从我们这些椅子中间走出来，走到那只彩绘铁皮箱旁站住。“克莱顿，”他说，“你是个傻瓜。”

克莱顿眼里闪着诙谐的光，对他笑回去。“威什，”他说，“说得对，你们其他人都错了。我要走了。我要做完这一整套手法，等最后那一下嗖地划过空中，倏忽之间——这块炉前毯就空了，这间屋子就只剩一片目瞪口呆，一位衣冠楚楚、体重十五英石的绅士，就噗通一声掉进阴曹地府。我对此确信不疑。你们也将会这样。我拒绝再多辩。试一下吧。”

“*不要*，”威什说着，迈出一步又停住，而克莱顿已再次抬起双手，要重做那幽灵的过界手法。

到了这时候，你们知道，我们大家都紧张起来——多半是因为威什的反常举止。我们坐着，眼睛都盯着克莱顿——至少我觉得自己浑身紧绷绷的、僵僵的，仿佛从后脑勺一直到大腿中部，整个身体都化成了钢。就在那儿，克莱顿带着一种不可动摇的庄严，在我们面前鞠躬、摇摆、挥动着他的双臂和双手。随着他接近尾声，人不禁一层层往上提着气，牙齿都跟着发麻。最后那个动作，我已说过，是把双臂大大张开，脸仰起来。当他终于摆出这最后一个姿势时，我连气都不敢出了。这当然荒唐，可你们都懂得那种鬼故事的味道。这是晚饭之后，在一间古怪的、阴影重重的老屋里。他到底会不会——？

===Original===
There he stood for one stupendous moment, with his arms open and his upturned face, assured and bright, in the glare of the hanging lamp. We hung through that moment as if it were an age, and then came from all of us something that was half a sigh of infinite relief and half a reassuring “*No!*” For visibly—he wasn’t going. It was all nonsense. He had told an idle story, and carried it almost to conviction, that was all!… And then in that moment the face of Clayton, changed.

===Chinese===
他在那儿站了一个惊人的瞬间，双臂张开，脸仰着，笃定而明亮，在那盏吊灯的强光里。我们悬在那个瞬间里，仿佛过了一个世纪，然后我们不约而同地发出一声，一半是无限的释然，一半是互相宽慰的“*不！*”因为分明可见——他并没有要走的意思。全是无稽之谈。他不过讲了一则闲话，又差点儿讲得人信以为真，如此而已！……可就在那一瞬间，克莱顿的脸，变了。

===Original===
It changed. It changed as a lit house changes when its lights are suddenly extinguished. His eyes were suddenly eyes that were fixed, his smile was frozen on his lips, and he stood there still. He stood there, very gently swaying.

That moment, too, was an age. And then, you know, chairs were scraping, things were falling, and we were all moving. His knees seemed to give, and he fell forward, and Evans rose and caught him in his arms…

It stunned us all. For a minute I suppose no one said a coherent thing. We believed it, yet could not believe it… I came out of a muddled stupefaction to find myself kneeling beside him, and his vest and shirt were torn open, and Sanderson’s hand lay on his heart…

Well—the simple fact before us could very well wait our convenience; there was no hurry for us to comprehend. It lay there for an hour; it lies athwart my memory, black and amazing still, to this day. Clayton had, indeed, passed into the world that lies so near to and so far from our own, and he had gone thither by the only road that mortal man may take. But whether he did indeed pass there by that poor ghost’s incantation, or whether he was stricken suddenly by apoplexy in the midst of an idle tale—as the coroner’s jury would have us believe—is no matter for my judging; it is just one of those inexplicable riddles that must remain unsolved until the final solution of all things shall come. All I certainly know is that, in the very moment, in the very instant, of concluding those passes, he changed, and staggered, and fell down before us—dead!

===Chinese===
那脸变了。那变化，就像一幢亮着灯的屋子，灯火突然间全数熄灭。他的两眼忽然变成了一双定了神的眼睛，微笑冻结在嘴角，他就那么站着，一动不动。他站在那儿，轻轻地摇晃着。

那个瞬间也像一个世纪那样漫长。接着，你们知道，椅子在刮擦，东西在掉落，我们一齐动起来。他的膝盖似乎一软，整个人朝前倒下去，埃文斯站起，把他抱进了怀里……

我们都惊呆了。大概有一分钟，谁也没说出一句囫囵话来。我们信，可又不能信……我从一阵混沌的麻木中醒过来，发现自己已跪在他身旁，他的背心和衬衫都已被撕开，桑德森的一只手按在他的心脏上……

唉——摆在我们面前的这个简单的事实，大可以等我们方便了再去领会；它并不着急。它在那个地方躺了一个钟头；至今它仍横亘在我的记忆里，黑压压的，叫人惊骇。克莱顿确确实实已走进了那个离我们这般近、又这般远的世界，他所走的，是凡人所能走的唯一的一条路。至于他究竟是不是借那只可怜鬼的咒语走过去的，还是像验尸陪审团所要我们相信的那样，在一则闲话的半中间忽然中了风——这就不是我所能论断的了；这不过是那些说不清的谜团之一，要一直悬着，直到万事万物最终揭晓的那一天。我所确知的只是：在比划完那一整套手法的那个瞬间、那个刹那，他变了脸色，踉跄了一下，倒在我们面前——死了！

## The Story of the Late Mr. Elvesham / 已故埃尔弗沙姆先生的故事

===Original===
I set this story down, not expecting it will be believed, but, if possible, to prepare a way of escape for the next victim. He, perhaps, may profit by my misfortune. My own case, I know, is hopeless, and I am now in some measure prepared to meet my fate.

My name is Edward George Eden. I was born at Trentham, in Staffordshire, my father being employed in the gardens there. I lost my mother when I was three years old, and my father when I was five, my uncle, George Eden, then adopting me as his own son. He was a single man, self-educated, and well-known in Birmingham as an enterprising journalist; he educated me generously, fired my ambition to succeed in the world, and at his death, which happened four years ago, left me his entire fortune, a matter of about five hundred pounds after all outgoing charges were paid. I was then eighteen. He advised me in his will to expend the money in completing my education. I had already chosen the profession of medicine, and through his posthumous generosity and my good fortune in a scholarship competition, I became a medical student at University College, London. At the time of the beginning of my story I lodged at 11A University Street in a little upper room, very shabbily furnished and draughty, overlooking the back of Shoolbred’s premises. I used this little room both to live in and sleep in, because I was anxious to eke out my means to the very last shillings-worth.

===Chinese===
我写下这个故事，并不指望有人会相信，只盼着——如果可能的话——为下一个受害者铺一条逃生之路。他也许能从我的不幸中获益。我知道自己已无指望，如今也算多少做好了面对命运的思想准备。

我叫爱德华·乔治·伊登（Edward George Eden），出生在斯塔福德郡（Staffordshire）的特伦特姆（Trentham），父亲在那里的花园里做事。我三岁丧母，五岁丧父，由叔父乔治·伊登（George Eden）收为己子。他是个独身汉，自学成才，在伯明翰（Birmingham）是个颇有魄力的新闻记者，颇为知名；他慷慨地供我读书，点燃我出人头地的雄心，四年前他去世时，把全部财产留给了我——扣尽各项支出之后，大约五百镑。那时我十八岁。他在遗嘱里劝我把这笔钱用来完成学业。我早已选定医学这一行，靠着他的遗泽和我在奖学金考试中的好运气，我成了伦敦大学学院（University College, London）的医科学生。故事开始之时，我寄宿在大学街（University Street）十一号A一个小小的顶楼房间里，陈设寒酸，四面透风，窗子正对着舒尔布雷德（Shoolbred’s）店铺的后院。我既在这间小屋里住，也在这里睡，因为我恨不得把每一个先令都掰开来使。

===Original===
I was taking a pair of shoes to be mended at a shop in the Tottenham Court Road when I first encountered the little old man with the yellow face, with whom my life has now become so inextricably entangled. He was standing on the kerb, and staring at the number on the door in a doubtful way, as I opened it. His eyes—they were dull grey eyes, and reddish under the rims—fell to my face, and his countenance immediately assumed an expression of corrugated amiability.

“You come,” he said, “apt to the moment. I had forgotten the number of your house. How do you do, Mr. Eden?”

I was a little astonished at his familiar address, for I had never set eyes on the man before. I was a little annoyed, too, at his catching me with my boots under my arm. He noticed my lack of cordiality.

===Chinese===
我正拿着一双鞋去托特纳姆法院路（Tottenham Court Road）的一家铺子修补，就在这时，我头一回遇见了那个黄脸的小老头——如今我的命已与他难解难分地缠在一起。我推开门时，他正站在马路牙子上，犹犹豫豫地盯着门上的门牌号。他的眼睛——一双暗淡的灰眼睛，眼眶下带着红丝——落到我脸上，他脸上的神情立刻变成一种皱巴巴的和蔼。

“你来得，”他说，“正是时候。我忘了你家的门牌号。你好啊，伊登先生？”

他这样熟络的招呼叫我有些吃惊，因为我从没见过这个人。而且，被他撞见我腋下夹着靴子，我也有些不自在。他注意到了我的冷淡。

===Original===
“Wonder who the deuce I am, eh? A friend, let me assure you. I have seen you before, though you haven’t seen me. Is there anywhere where I can talk to you?”

I hesitated. The shabbiness of my room upstairs was not a matter for every stranger. “Perhaps,” said I, “we might walk down the street. I’m unfortunately prevented—” My gesture explained the sentence before I had spoken it.

“The very thing,” he said, and faced this way, and then that. “The street? Which way shall we go?” I slipped my boots down in the passage. “Look here!” he said abruptly; “this business of mine is a rigmarole. Come and lunch with me, Mr. Eden. I’m an old man, a very old man, and not good at explanations, and what with my piping voice and the clatter of the traffic—”

He laid a persuasive skinny hand that trembled a little upon my arm.

I was not so old that an old man might not treat me to a lunch. Yet at the same time I was not altogether pleased by this abrupt invitation. “I had rather—” I began. “But I had rather,” he said, catching me up, “and a certain civility is surely due to my grey hairs.”

And so I consented, and went with him.

===Chinese===
“纳闷我究竟是谁，是吧？放心，是个朋友。我以前见过你，只不过你没见过我罢了。有什么地方可以跟你谈谈吗？”

我犹豫了。楼上那间寒酸的屋子，可不是给每个陌生人看的。“也许，”我说，“我们可以沿街走走。可惜我不太方便——”我的手势在我话出口之前就把意思说明了。

“再好不过，”他说，朝这边望望，又朝那边望望。“上街？往哪边走？”我把靴子悄悄塞进门厅里。“听着！”他突然说，“我这档子事说来话长。来，跟我一块儿吃午饭去，伊登先生。我是个老头子，一个很老很老的老头子，不善言辞，再加上我这尖细的嗓门，街上车子又喧——”

他把一只瘦骨嶙峋、微微发颤的说服性的手搭在我胳膊上。

我还没老到一个老头子不能请我吃顿午饭。可与此同时，我对这突如其来的邀请也不大乐意。“我倒宁愿——”我开口道。“可我倒宁愿，”他抢过我的话，“而且对我这满头白发，多少总该有点礼数吧。”

于是我便应允了，跟他一同前去。

===Original===
He took me to Blavitiski’s; I had to walk slowly to accommodate myself to his paces; and over such a lunch as I had never tasted before, he fended off my leading question, and I took a better note of his appearance. His clean-shaven face was lean and wrinkled, his shrivelled, lips fell over a set of false teeth, and his white hair was thin and rather long; he seemed small to me—though indeed, most people seemed small to me—and his shoulders were rounded and bent. And watching him, I could not help but observe that he too was taking note of me, running his eyes, with a curious touch of greed in them, over me, from my broad shoulders to my suntanned hands, and up to my freckled face again. “And now,” said he, as we lit our cigarettes, “I must tell you of the business in hand.

“I must tell you, then, that I am an old man, a very old man.” He paused momentarily. “And it happens that I have money that I must presently be leaving, and never a child have I to leave it to.” I thought of the confidence trick, and resolved I would be on the alert for the vestiges of my five hundred pounds. He proceeded to enlarge on his loneliness, and the trouble he had to find a proper disposition of his money. “I have weighed this plan and that plan, charities, institutions, and scholarships, and libraries, and I have come to this conclusion at last,”—he fixed his eyes on my face—“that I will find some young fellow, ambitious, pure-minded, and poor, healthy in body and healthy in mind, and, in short, make him my heir, give him all that I have.” He repeated, “Give him all that I have. So that he will suddenly be lifted out of all the trouble and struggle in which his sympathies have been educated, to freedom and influence.”

===Chinese===
他把我带到布拉维茨基餐馆（Blavitiski’s）；我得放慢脚步迁就他的步子；在那顿我从未尝过的丰盛午餐席上，他避开了我最想问的那个问题，我则趁机把他的相貌看得更仔细了些。他那张刮得干干净净的脸又瘦又皱，干瘪的嘴唇包着一副假牙，白发稀疏而略长；我觉得他个子很小——其实大多数人在我看来都算小——双肩圆削佝偻。看着他，我也不由得察觉，他也在打量我，一双眼睛带着几分奇异的贪婪，从我的宽肩膀扫到我那晒黑的手，又抬到我那长着雀斑的脸上。“现在，”我们点起香烟时他说，“我得跟你讲讲正事了。

“那么我得告诉你，我是个老人，一个很老很老的老人。”他略略一顿。“恰巧我有一笔钱，不久就要撇下它走，可我从来没有一个孩子可以继承。”我想到了那种骗人钱财的把戏，暗自决定要盯紧我那五百镑。他接着大谈自己的孤独，以及为这笔钱找一个妥当去处所费的周折。“我权衡过这个方案、那个方案，慈善机关、公共机构、奖学金、图书馆，最后我得出了这样一个结论，”——他直盯着我——“我要找个年轻人，有志气、心地纯洁、穷困，身体健康、心智健全，总之，让他做我的继承人，把我所有的一切都给他。”他又重复一遍，“把我所有的一切都给他。好让他一下子脱离他一向习得同情与挣扎的苦境，跃升到自由与势力的地位。”

===Original===
I tried to seem disinterested. With a transparent hypocrisy I said, “And you want my help, my professional services maybe, to find that person.”

He smiled, and looked at me over his cigarette, and I laughed at his quiet exposure of my modest pretence.

“What a career such a man might have!” he said. “It fills me with envy to think how I have accumulated that another man may spend—

“But there are conditions, of course, burdens to be imposed. He must, for instance, take my name. You cannot expect everything without some return. And I must go into all the circumstances of his life before I can accept him. He *must* be sound. I must know his heredity, how his parents and grandparents died, have the strictest inquiries made into his private morals.”

===Chinese===
我竭力做出一副不动声色的样子。我带着一眼就能看穿的虚伪说：“那您是需要我帮忙，也许是请我用职业上的方便，替您找这样一个人了。”

他微微一笑，隔着香烟望着我，我那点谦虚的做作被他轻轻一戳穿，我也只好跟着笑了。

“这样的人将会有多么辉煌的前程啊！”他说，“一想到我苦苦积攒，只为让另一个人去挥霍，我心里便满是嫉妒——

“当然是有条件的，有要他承担的义务。比方说，他得改用我的姓氏。你不能指望什么都不付出便得到一切。而我对他生平的一切情形，也得细细查考清楚，才能定下来。他*务必*身心健康。我必须知道他的遗传，他的父母祖父母是怎样去世的，对他的私德要做最严格的调查。”

===Original===
This modified my secret congratulations a little.

“And do I understand,” said I, “that I—”

“Yes,” he said, almost fiercely. “You. *You.*”

I answered never a word. My imagination was dancing wildly, my innate scepticism was useless to modify its transports. There was not a particle of gratitude in my mind—I did not know what to say nor how to say it. “But why me in particular?” I said at last.

He had chanced to hear of me from Professor Haslar; he said, as a typically sound and sane young man, and he wished, as far as possible, to leave his money where health and integrity were assured.

===Chinese===
这话叫我心里那份暗喜打了个折扣。

“那么我是否可以理解为，”我说，“我——”

“是的，”他说，几乎是恶狠狠地。“你。*你。*”

我一个字也答不上来。我的想象早已疯狂地飞舞，我天生的怀疑精神对这股狂喜也无可奈何。我心里没有一丝一毫的感激——我不知道该说什么，也不知道该怎么说。“可为什么偏偏是我？”我终于问道。

他是偶然从哈斯拉尔教授（Professor Haslar）那里听说我的，他说，把我当作一个典型的身心俱健的青年，而他但愿尽可能把钱留到一个健康和品行都靠得住的地方。

===Original===
That was my first meeting with the little old man. He was mysterious about himself; he would not give his name yet, he said, and after I had answered some questions of his, he left me at the Blavitiski portal. I noticed that he drew a handful of gold coins from his pocket when it came to paying for the lunch. His insistence upon bodily health was curious. In accordance with an arrangement we had made I applied that day for a life policy in the Loyal Insurance Company for a large sum, and I was exhaustively overhauled by the medical advisers of that company in the subsequent week. Even that did not satisfy him, and he insisted I must be reexamined by the great Doctor Henderson.

It was Friday in Whitsun week before he came to a decision. He called me down, quite late in the evening—nearly nine it was—from cramming chemical equations for my Preliminary Scientific examination. He was standing in the passage under the feeble gas-lamp, and his face was a grotesque interplay of shadows. He seemed more bowed than when I had first seen him, and his cheeks had sunk in a little.

His voice shook with emotion. “Everything is satisfactory, Mr. Eden,” he said. “Everything is quite, quite satisfactory. And this night of all nights, you must dine with me and celebrate your—accession.” He was interrupted by a cough. “You won’t have long to wait, either,” he said, wiping his handkerchief across his lips, and gripping my hand with his long bony claw that was disengaged. “Certainly not very long to wait.”

===Chinese===
这就是我与那小老头的第一次见面。他自己的事讳莫如深；他说暂时还不肯报上姓名，我回答了他几个问题之后，他便在布拉维茨基餐馆门口与我作别。我注意到付账时他从口袋里掏出一把金币。他对身体健康的执拗颇为古怪。按我们事先的约定，那天我便向忠诚保险公司（Loyal Insurance Company）投保了一笔数目不小的人寿险，随后一周里被该公司的医务顾问们做了彻头彻尾的体格检查。即便如此他仍不放心，坚持要我再由大名鼎鼎的亨德森医生（Doctor Henderson）复查一次。

直到圣灵降临周（Whitsun week）的那个礼拜五，他才拿定主意。那天夜深——将近九点了——他从我埋头死记化学方程式以备初级科学考试（Preliminary Scientific examination）的苦读中把我叫下楼来。他站在门厅里那盏昏暗的煤气灯下，脸上的阴影交错成一副怪诞的样子。他似乎比我头一回见他时更佝偻了，两颊也微微凹陷了些。

他的声音因激动而发颤。“一切都很令人满意，伊登先生，”他说，“一切都十分、十分令人满意。而偏偏今晚，您一定要与我共进晚餐，庆祝您的——就任。”他被一阵咳嗽打断。“您也不会等太久了，”他说着，用手帕擦了擦嘴唇，又用那只空出来的、瘦骨嶙峋如爪子般的手紧紧握住我的手。“的确不会等太久。”

===Original===
We went into the street and called a cab. I remember every incident of that drive vividly, the swift, easy motion, the vivid contrast of gas and oil and electric light, the crowds of people in the streets, the place in Regent Street to which we went, and the sumptuous dinner we were served with there. I was disconcerted at first by the well-dressed waiter’s glances at my rough clothes, bothered by the stones of the olives, but as the champagne warmed my blood, my confidence revived. At first the old man talked of himself. He had already told me his name in the cab; he was Egbert Elvesham, the great philosopher, whose name I had known since I was a lad at school. It seemed incredible to me that this man, whose intelligence had so early dominated mine, this great abstraction, should suddenly realise itself as this decrepit, familiar figure. I daresay every young fellow who has suddenly fallen among celebrities has felt something of my disappointment. He told me now of the future that the feeble streams of his life would presently leave dry for me, houses, copyrights, investments; I had never suspected that philosophers were so rich. He watched me drink and eat with a touch of envy. “What a capacity for living you have!” he said; and then with a sigh, a sigh of relief I could have thought it, “it will not be long.”

“Ay,” said I, my head swimming now with champagne; “I have a future perhaps—of a passing agreeable sort, thanks to you. I shall now have the honour of your name. But you have a past. Such a past as is worth all my future.”

===Chinese===
我们走到街上叫了一辆马车。那趟车行的每一个细节我都记得清清楚楚：那迅捷平稳的行驶，煤气灯、油灯和电灯之间鲜明的光影交错，街上熙攘的人群，我们去的摄政街（Regent Street）上的那家餐馆，以及在那里端上来的那一席丰盛的晚宴。起初，衣着讲究的侍者朝我那身粗布衣裳投来的目光令我局促不安，橄榄的核也叫我手忙脚乱，可几杯香槟下肚，热血一涌，我的胆气又回来了。起初老头子谈他自己。在马车上他已经把名字告诉了我；他就是埃格伯特·埃尔弗沙姆（Egbert Elvesham），那位大哲学家，我从做学童时就熟知这个名字。这个人的智慧如此之早地支配过我的头脑，这样一位伟大的抽象存在，竟忽然以这样一个衰颓的、熟络的身影出现在我面前——我觉得简直不可思议。每一个突然间跻身名流之侧的年轻人，大概都体会过我这种失望。他此刻向我描绘他那行将枯竭的生命之流即将为我腾出的未来：宅邸、版权、投资——我从没想到哲学家竟这般富有。他带着一丝嫉妒看我饮酒吃菜。“你的生命力真旺盛啊！”他说；随即一声叹息——我几乎要认为那是一声如释重负的叹息——“不会太久了。”

“是啊，”我说，我的头此刻已被香槟冲得发飘，“我也许会有一个前程——一种还算过得去的惬意前程，多亏了您。我此后便有荣幸顶用您的大名。可您有一个过去。那样的过去，抵得过我全部的未来。”

===Original===
He shook his head and smiled, as I thought, with half sad appreciation of my flattering admiration. “That future,” he said, “would you in truth change it?” The waiter came with liqueurs. “You will not perhaps mind taking my name, taking my position, but would you indeed—willingly—take my years?”

“With your achievements,” said I gallantly.

He smiled again. “Kummel—both,” he said to the waiter, and turned his attention to a little paper packet he had taken from his pocket. “This hour,” said he, “this after-dinner hour is the hour of small things. Here is a scrap of my unpublished wisdom.” He opened the packet with his shaking yellow fingers, and showed a little pinkish powder on the paper. “This,” said he—“well, you must guess what it is. But Kummel—put but a dash of this powder in it—is Himmel.”

His large greyish eyes watched mine with an inscrutable expression.

It was a bit of a shock to me to find this great teacher gave his mind to the flavour of liqueurs. However, I feigned an interest in his weakness, for I was drunk enough for such small sycophancy.

He parted the powder between the little glasses, and, rising suddenly, with a strange unexpected dignity, held out his hand towards me. I imitated his action, and the glasses rang. “To a quick succession,” said he, and raised his glass towards his lips.

===Chinese===
他摇摇头笑了，我觉得那笑容里带着一半感伤的领情，谢我的恭维。“那个未来，”他说，“你果真愿意换吗？”侍者端来利口酒。“你也许不介意借用我的名字、我的地位，可你愿意——心甘情愿地——接受我的年纪吗？”

“连同您那些成就一起，”我豪爽地说。

他又一笑。“库梅尔（Kummel）——两杯都来，”他对侍者说，然后转过身去摆弄一个从口袋里掏出来的小纸包。“此时，”他说，“这餐后之时，是属于小事的时辰。这儿是我一点未刊智慧的零头。”他用发抖的蜡黄手指打开纸包，纸上现出一点淡粉色的粉末。“这东西，”他说——“嗯，你得猜猜它是什么。可库梅尔——只要掺上这么一撮粉末——便是天赐（Himmel）。”

他那双灰白色的大眼睛以一种深不可测的神情望着我。

发现这位大思想家竟然分心于利口酒的滋味，我颇有些吃惊。不过我还是装作对他的这点嗜好很感兴趣，因为我已醉得足以奉承这点小事了。

他把粉末分到两只小酒杯里，然后忽然带着一种出人意料的庄重站起身，向我伸出手。我也学着他的样子，两只杯子碰出一声脆响。“祝速继，”他说着，把杯子举到唇边。

===Original===
“Not that,” I said hastily. “Not that.”

He paused with the liqueur at the level of his chin, and his eyes blazing into mine.

“To a long life,” said I.

He hesitated. “To a long life,” said he, with a sudden bark of laughter, and with eyes fixed on one another we tilted the little glasses. His eyes looked straight into mine, and as I drained the stuff off, I felt a curiously intense sensation. The first touch of it set my brain in a furious tumult; I seemed to feel an actual physical stirring in my skull, and a seething humming filled my ears. I did not notice the flavour in my mouth, the aroma that filled my throat; I saw only the grey intensity of his gaze that burnt into mine. The draught, the mental confusion, the noise and stirring in my head, seemed to last an interminable time. Curious vague impressions of half-forgotten things danced and vanished on the edge of my consciousness. At last he broke the spell. With a sudden explosive sigh he put down his glass.

“Well?” he said.

“It’s glorious,” said I, though I had not tasted the stuff.

My head was spinning. I sat down. My brain was chaos. Then my perception grew clear and minute as though I saw things in a concave mirror. His manner seemed to have changed into something nervous and hasty. He pulled out his watch and grimaced at it. “Eleven-seven! And tonight I must—Seven-twenty-five. Waterloo! I must go at once.” He called for the bill, and struggled with his coat. Officious waiters came to our assistance. In another moment I was wishing him goodbye, over the apron of a cab, and still with an absurd feeling of minute distinctness, as though—how can I express it?—I not only saw but *felt* through an inverted opera-glass.

“That stuff,” he said. He put his hand to his forehead. “I ought not to have given it to you. It will make your head split tomorrow. Wait a minute. Here.” He handed me out a little flat thing like a seidlitz-powder. “Take that in water as you are going to bed. The other thing was a drug. Not till you’re ready to go to bed, mind. It will clear your head. That’s all. One more shake—Futurus!”

I gripped his shrivelled claw. “Goodbye,” he said, and by the droop of his eyelids I judged he too was a little under the influence of that brain-twisting cordial.

He recollected something else with a start, felt in his breast-pocket, and produced another packet, this time a cylinder the size and shape of a shaving-stick. “Here,” said he. “I’d almost forgotten. Don’t open this until I come tomorrow—but take it now.”

It was so heavy that I well-nigh dropped it. “All ri’!” said I, and he grinned at me through the cab window as the cabman flicked his horse into wakefulness. It was a white packet he had given me, with red seals at either end and along its edge. “If this isn’t money,” said I, “it’s platinum or lead.”

I stuck it with elaborate care into my pocket, and with a whirling brain walked home through the Regent Street loiterers and the dark back streets beyond Portland Road. I remember the sensations of that walk very vividly, strange as they were. I was still so far myself that I could notice my strange mental state, and wonder whether this stuff I had had was opium—a drug beyond my experience. It is hard now to describe the peculiarity of my mental strangeness—mental doubling vaguely expresses it. As I was walking up Regent Street I found in my mind a queer persuasion that it was Waterloo Station, and had an odd impulse to get into the Polytechnic as a man might get into a train. I put a knuckle in my eye, and it was Regent Street. How can I express it? You see a skilful actor looking quietly at you, he pulls a grimace, and lo!—another person. Is it too extravagant if I tell you that it seemed to me as if Regent Street had, for the moment, done that? Then, being persuaded it was Regent Street again, I was oddly muddled about some fantastic reminiscences that cropped up. “Thirty years ago,” thought I, “it was here that I quarrelled with my brother.” Then I burst out laughing, to the astonishment and encouragement of a group of night prowlers. Thirty years ago I did not exist, and never in my life had I boasted a brother. The stuff was surely liquid folly, for the poignant regret for that lost brother still clung to me. Along Portland Road the madness took another turn. I began to recall vanished shops, and to compare the street with what it used to be. Confused, troubled thinking is comprehensible enough after the drink I had taken, but what puzzled me were these curiously vivid phantasm memories that had crept into my mind, and not only the memories that had crept in, but also the memories that had slipped out. I stopped opposite Stevens’, the natural history dealer’s, and cudgelled my brains to think what he had to do with me. A bus went by, and sounded exactly like the rumbling of a train. I seemed to be dipping into some dark, remote pit for the recollection. “Of course,” said I, at last, “he has promised me three frogs tomorrow. Odd I should have forgotten.”

===Chinese===
“不是这个，”我赶忙说。“不是这个。”

他端着酒杯停在齐下巴处，一双眼睛灼灼地盯着我。

“祝长寿，”我说。

他迟疑了一下。“祝长寿，”他说，猝然发出一阵短促的笑声，我们彼此对视着，把小杯倾入口中。他的眼睛直直望进我的眼睛，我把那酒饮尽时，感到一种奇异而强烈的感觉。那酒一沾唇，我的脑中便如翻江倒海；我似乎真能感到颅骨之内有一种物理上的搅动，耳朵里灌满了沸腾般的嗡嗡声。我尝不出嘴里的滋味，也辨不出喉间的香气；我看见的只有他那灰色的、灼人的目光。那口酒，那脑中的纷乱，那头里的喧嚣与搅动，似乎持续了无穷无尽的时间。一些似曾相识又似是而非的模糊印象，在我意识的边缘舞动又消逝。终于他打破了这道魔咒。他猛地一声爆破般的叹息，放下了杯子。

“怎么样？”他说。

“好极了，”我说，其实我根本没尝出那酒的滋味。

我头昏目眩。我坐下来。脑子里乱成一团。随后我的知觉变得异常清晰而纤毫毕现，仿佛我是从一面凹面镜里看东西。他的神态似乎也变得有些紧张仓皇。他掏出怀表，看了一眼，做了个苦脸。“十一点零七分！可今晚我还得——七点二十五。滑铁卢（Waterloo）！我得马上走。”他叫人结账，手忙脚乱地穿外衣。殷勤的侍者上来帮忙。转眼间，我便隔着马车的挡布与他道别，心里仍带着那种荒唐的纤毫毕现之感，仿佛——叫我怎么说呢？——我不仅看见，而且*感觉*到一切都是从一架倒过来的观剧镜里看出来的。

“那东西，”他说。他伸手按住额头。“我不该给你喝的。明天它叫你头疼欲裂。等一等。拿着。”他递给我一个扁平的小东西，像一包塞德利茨散剂（seidlitz-powder）。“临睡前用水冲服。先前那个是药。要等你准备上床了才吃，记住。它能清你的脑子。就这样。再握一下——向未来（Futurus）！”

我握住他那干瘪如爪的手。“再见，”他说，从他那眼皮耷拉的样子我判断，他也多少受了那扭曲头脑的烈酒的几分影响。

他猛地想起什么，在胸前的口袋里摸了摸，又掏出一个纸包来，这一回是一个圆筒，大小形状都像一把剃须膏。“拿着，”他说，“我差点忘了。等我明天来了再打开——不过现在先收下。”

那东西沉甸甸的，我险些脱手。“好吧！”我说，车夫把马抖醒时，他隔着车窗朝我咧嘴一笑。他给我的是一个白色的纸包，两头和沿边都封着红蜡。“这要不是钱，”我说，“就是白金或者铅块。”

我煞费苦心地把它塞进口袋，脑子里一团眩晕，穿过摄政街上闲逛的人群和波特兰路（Portland Road）那边漆黑的后街小巷走回家去。那一路的感受我记得分外真切，尽管它们离奇古怪。我神志还勉强算是我自己，能注意到自己那古怪的精神状态，心里纳闷我喝下去的那玩意儿是不是鸦片——一种我从未见识过的毒品。如今很难描述我精神上那种古怪的特性——“精神的重影”勉强可以表达。我沿摄政街走着时，脑子里忽然冒出一个古怪的念头，认定那是滑铁卢车站，还有一种莫名其妙的冲动想走进综合技术馆（Polytechnic），就像人上火车那样。我用指节揉了揉眼睛，又是摄政街了。这叫我怎么说呢？你看见一个出色的演员静静地望着你，他做了一个怪脸，瞧！——另一个人。如果我告诉你，在我看来摄政街那一刻也做了同样的事，这不算太离谱吧？等到我又认定它是摄政街之后，我又被一些冒出来的荒唐回忆搅得一塌糊涂。“三十年前，”我想，“我就是在这儿跟我兄弟吵翻的。”接着我哈哈大笑起来，叫一群夜游的人又惊又受鼓舞。三十年前我根本还不存在，我这一辈子也从未有过什么兄弟。那东西准是液体的疯狂，因为对那个失去的兄弟那种锥心的惋惜，竟还紧紧攫住我不放。沿波特兰路走去，这种癫狂又变了花样。我开始追忆那些早已消失的店铺，把这条街跟它从前的样子比较起来。喝下那杯酒之后，心思混乱烦扰，原也说得过去，可叫我迷惑的是那些悄悄钻进我脑海里的、异常鲜明的幻影般的记忆，不仅钻进来的记忆古怪，溜出去的记忆也同样古怪。我在自然历史商人史蒂文斯店（Stevens’）门前停下，绞尽脑汁地想他与我有何干系。一辆公共汽车驶过，那声音竟和火车隆隆的声响一模一样。我仿佛是从某个幽暗遥远的深坑里打捞回忆。“当然，”我终于说，“他答应明天给我三只青蛙。怪不得我会忘。”

===Original===
Do they still show children dissolving views? In those I remember one view would begin like a faint ghost, and grow and oust another. In just that way it seemed to me that a ghostly set of new sensations was struggling with those of my ordinary self.

I went on through Euston Road to Tottenham Court Road, puzzled, and a little frightened, and scarcely noticed the unusual way I was taking, for commonly I used to cut through the intervening network of back streets. I turned into University Street, to discover that I had forgotten my number. Only by a strong effort did I recall 11A, and even then it seemed to me that it was a thing some forgotten person had told me. I tried to steady my mind by recalling the incidents of the dinner, and for the life of me I could conjure up no picture of my host’s face; I saw him only as a shadowy outline, as one might see oneself reflected in a window through which one was looking. In his place, however, I had a curious exterior vision of myself, sitting at a table, flushed, bright-eyed, and talkative.

“I must take this other powder,” said I. “This is getting impossible.”

I tried the wrong side of the hall for my candle and the matches, and had a doubt of which landing my room might be on. “I’m drunk,” I said, “that’s certain,” and blundered needlessly on the staircase to sustain the proposition.

At the first glance my room seemed unfamiliar. “What rot!” I said, and stared about me. I seemed to bring myself back by the effort, and the odd phantasmal quality passed into the concrete familiar. There was the old glass still, with my notes on the albumens stuck in the corner of the frame, my old everyday suit of clothes pitched about the floor. And yet it was not so real after all. I felt an idiotic persuasion trying to creep into my mind, as it were, that I was in a railway carriage in a train just stopping, that I was peering out of the window at some unknown station. I gripped the bed-rail firmly to reassure myself. “It’s clairvoyance, perhaps,” I said. “I must write to the Psychical Research Society.”

I put the rouleau on my dressing-table, sat on my bed, and began to take off my boots. It was as if the picture of my present sensations was painted over some other picture that was trying to show through. “Curse it!” said I; “my wits are going, or am I in two places at once?” Half-undressed, I tossed the powder into a glass and drank it off. It effervesced, and became a fluorescent amber colour. Before I was in bed my mind was already tranquillised. I felt the pillow at my cheek, and thereupon I must have fallen asleep.

===Chinese===
现在还给孩子们看那种“溶解画片”吗？我记得那种画片里，一幅画面会像一个淡淡的幽灵般起头，渐渐长大，把另一幅挤走。在我看来，正是一整套幽灵般的新感觉在与我平常那些感觉搏斗。

我顺着尤斯顿路（Euston Road）走到托特纳姆法院路，心里又迷惑又有些害怕，几乎没注意自己走的竟是一条不寻常的路——平时我多半抄后街小巷的近道。拐进大学街，才发现自己把门牌号也忘了。我费了好大劲才记起十一号A，可即便那时，我还觉得那是一件某个被遗忘的人告诉我的事。我竭力回想晚宴上的种种情景来稳住神，可怎么也没法在脑中唤出主人那张脸的形象；我只看见他一个影影绰绰的轮廓，就像人隔着玻璃窗看自己映在窗上的影子那样。然而，在他的位置上，我倒有了一个古怪的外视景象——看见我自己坐在桌旁，满脸通红，目光发亮，滔滔不绝。

“我得把另一包药吃了，”我说，“这可不行了。”

我在门厅里摸错了放蜡烛和火柴的那一边，还对自己房间究竟在哪一层也起了疑。“我是醉了，”我说，“这没跑了，”还在楼梯上无谓地绊了一跤以印证这一论断。

头一眼看去，我的屋子似乎很陌生。“胡扯！”我说着，四下张望。我似乎凭着使劲把自己拉了回来，那种古怪的幻影感便化作了具体而熟悉的一切。旧镜子还在，镜框角上插着我那些关于蛋白照片的笔记，我那套平日穿的旧衣裳东一件西一件地扔在地板上。可到底不那么真切。我感到一种愚蠢的念头正想钻进我脑子里——仿佛我正坐在一列刚刚停下的火车车厢里，正从车窗里向外张望某个陌生的车站。我紧紧抓住床栏杆来给自己壮胆。“也许是千里眼，”我说，“我得给心灵研究学会（Psychical Research Society）写信。”

我把那卷钱放在梳妆台上，坐在床沿上开始脱靴子。仿佛我此刻感觉的这幅图画，是画在另一幅正想透出来的图画之上。“见鬼！”我说，“要么是我的神智出了毛病，要么就是我一个人同时分在两个地方了？”脱了一半衣裳，我把那包药粉扔进一只杯子里，一饮而尽。它嘶嘶地冒着泡，变成一种荧光般的琥珀色。还没上床，我的心已经安定下来。我感到枕头贴在脸颊上，随后我必定就那么睡着了。

---

===Original===
I awoke abruptly out of a dream of strange beasts, and found myself lying on my back. Probably everyone knows that dismal, emotional dream from which one escapes, awake indeed, but strangely cowed. There was a curious taste in my mouth, a tired feeling in my limbs, a sense of cutaneous discomfort. I lay with my head motionless on my pillow, expecting that my feeling of strangeness and terror would pass away, and that I should then doze off again to sleep. But instead of that, my uncanny sensations increased. At first I could perceive nothing wrong about me. There was a faint light in the room, so faint that it was the very next thing to darkness, and the furniture stood out in it as vague blots of absolute darkness. I stared with my eyes just over the bedclothes.

It came into my mind that someone had entered the room to rob me of my rouleau of money, but after lying for some moments, breathing regularly to simulate sleep, I realised this was mere fancy. Nevertheless, the uneasy assurance of something wrong kept fast hold of me. With an effort I raised my head from the pillow, and peered about me at the dark. What it was I could not conceive. I looked at the dim shapes around me, the greater and lesser darknesses that indicated curtains, table, fireplace, bookshelves, and so forth. Then I began to perceive something unfamiliar in the forms of the darkness. Had the bed turned round? Yonder should be the bookshelves, and something shrouded and pallid rose there, something that would not answer to the bookshelves, however I looked at it. It was far too big to be my shirt thrown on a chair.

Overcoming a childish terror, I threw back the bedclothes and thrust my leg out of bed. Instead of coming out of my truckle-bed upon the floor, I found my foot scarcely reached the edge of the mattress. I made another step, as it were, and sat up on the edge of the bed. By the side of my bed should be the candle, and the matches upon the broken chair. I put out my hand and touched—nothing. I waved my hand in the darkness, and it came against some heavy hanging, soft and thick in texture, which gave a rustling noise at my touch. I grasped this and pulled it; it appeared to be a curtain suspended over the head of my bed.

===Chinese===
我从一场满是怪兽的梦中猛然惊醒，发现自己仰面躺着。大概人人都做过那种阴郁、动情的梦，醒来时人确实是醒了，却莫名地心绪颓丧。我嘴里有一种古怪的滋味，四肢发软，皮肤有一种说不出的不适。我头不动地枕在枕头上躺着，指望那种陌生和恐惧的感觉会自行过去，然后我又能迷迷糊糊睡去。可非但如此，那种诡异的感觉反倒越来越强。起初我察觉周围并没有什么不对。房间里有一丝微光，微得简直只差没有就是一片漆黑，家具在光里现成一团一团绝对漆黑的模糊影子。我把眼睛露在被褥外面盯着看。

我忽然想到，是不是有人进了屋要偷我那卷钱，但我平躺着呼吸均匀地装睡了一会儿之后，便意识到这只是胡思乱想。尽管如此，那种“有什么不对”的不安却紧紧攫住我不放。我使劲把头从枕头上抬起来，在黑暗中四下张望。到底是什么，我说不上来。我望着周围那些朦胧的形状，那些或深或浅的暗影——它们该是窗帘、桌子、壁炉、书架之类。接着我开始发觉那些暗影的形状里有些陌生的东西。是床转了个方向吗？那边本该是书架，可那儿立着一个蒙着布、苍白的东西，无论我怎么端详，它都对不上书架。它也太大了，不可能是我扔在椅子上的衬衣。

我压下一种孩子气的恐惧，掀开被褥，把一条腿伸下床。我本该从我的小滚轮床上一脚踩到地板，可我发现我的脚几乎够不到床沿。我又迈了一步似地，在床沿坐起来。我床边该是蜡烛，火柴该在那张破椅子上。我伸手一摸——什么也没有。我在黑暗中挥动手臂，碰到一幅沉重的、柔软而厚实的悬挂物，我一碰它就发出窸窣的声响。我抓住它一拉，那似乎是悬在我床头上方的一幅帘子。

===Original===
I was now thoroughly awake, and beginning to realise that I was in a strange room. I was puzzled. I tried to recall the overnight circumstances, and I found them now, curiously enough, vivid in my memory: the supper, my reception of the little packages, my wonder whether I was intoxicated, my slow undressing, the coolness to my flushed face of my pillow. I felt a sudden distrust. Was that last night, or the night before? At any rate, this room was strange to me, and I could not imagine how I had got into it. The dim, pallid outline was growing paler, and I perceived it was a window, with the dark shape of an oval toilet-glass against the weak intimation of the dawn that filtered through the blind. I stood up, and was surprised by a curious feeling of weakness and unsteadiness. With trembling hands outstretched, I walked slowly towards the window, getting, nevertheless, a bruise on the knee from a chair by the way. I fumbled round the glass, which was large, with handsome brass sconces, to find the blind cord. I could not find any. By chance I took hold of the tassel, and with the click of a spring the blind ran up.

I found myself looking out upon a scene that was altogether strange to me. The night was overcast, and through the flocculent grey of the heaped clouds there filtered a faint half-light of dawn. Just at the edge of the sky the cloud-canopy had a bloodred rim. Below, everything was dark and indistinct, dim hills in the distance, a vague mass of buildings running up into pinnacles, trees like spilt ink, and below the window a tracery of black bushes and pale grey paths. It was so unfamiliar that for the moment I thought myself still dreaming. I felt the toilet-table; it appeared to be made of some polished wood, and was rather elaborately furnished—there were little cut-glass bottles and a brush upon it. There was also a queer little object, horseshoe shape it felt, with smooth, hard projections, lying in a saucer. I could find no matches nor candlestick.

===Chinese===
此刻我完全清醒了，开始意识到自己置身于一间陌生的屋子。我困惑不解。我试着回想昨夜的情形，发现它们——说来也怪——此刻在我记忆里格外鲜明：那顿晚餐，我接过那几个小纸包，我纳闷自己是不是喝醉了，我慢慢脱衣，凉枕头贴在我滚烫的脸上。我心里忽然涌起一股不信任。那是昨夜，还是前夜？无论如何，这间屋子对我来说是陌生的，我无法想象自己是怎么进来的。那朦胧苍白的轮廓越来越淡，我看出那是一扇窗子，一个椭圆形梳妆镜的黑色剪影映在百叶帘透进来的那一线微弱的晨曦上。我站起身，竟被一种古怪的虚弱和摇晃之感吓了一跳。我伸出颤抖的双手，慢慢朝窗子摸去，中途却被一把椅子撞青了膝盖。我在一面大镜子周围摸索，那镜子镶着华丽的铜烛台，我想找百叶帘的拉绳。怎么也找不到。我无意中捏住了那流苏，咔哒一声，弹簧一弹，百叶帘便卷了上去。

我发觉自己正眺望着一片全然陌生的景象。夜空乌云密布，从层层叠叠的云团那絮状的灰白里，漏下一线朦胧的曙光。天边尽处的云盖镶着一道血红的边。下面，一切都是幽暗朦胧的，远处有影影绰绰的山峦，一大片参差错落的建筑群尖顶林立，树木像泼洒的墨迹，窗下是黑灌木与浅灰小径交织成的花纹。这一切如此陌生，一时间我以为自己仍在梦中。我摸了摸梳妆台，似乎是某种抛光的木料做的，陈设颇为讲究——上面摆着几只小小的割花玻璃瓶和一把刷子。还有一件古怪的小物件，摸上去像是马蹄铁形状，上面有光滑坚硬的凸起，盛在一只碟子里。我找不到火柴，也找不到烛台。

===Original===
I turned my eyes to the room again. Now the blind was up, faint spectres of its furnishing came out of the darkness. There was a huge curtained bed, and the fireplace at its foot had a large white mantel with something of the shimmer of marble.

I leant against the toilet-table, shut my eyes and opened them again, and tried to think. The whole thing was far too real for dreaming. I was inclined to imagine there was still some hiatus in my memory, as a consequence of my draught of that strange liqueur; that I had come into my inheritance perhaps, and suddenly lost my recollection of everything since my good fortune had been announced. Perhaps if I waited a little, things would be clearer to me again. Yet my dinner with old Elvesham was now singularly vivid and recent. The champagne, the observant waiters, the powder, and the liqueurs—I could have staked my soul it all happened a few hours ago.

And then occurred a thing so trivial and yet so terrible to me that I shiver now to think of that moment. I spoke aloud. I said, “How the devil did I get here?”… *And the voice was not my own.*

===Chinese===
我把目光转回室内。百叶帘卷上去了，屋里陈设的淡淡幽灵便从黑暗中显了出来。有一张挂着帷幔的大床，床脚处的壁炉有一道白色的大炉台，带着几分大理石般的光泽。

我倚着梳妆台，闭上眼睛，又睁开，试着想点什么。这一切实在太真切了，不可能是做梦。我倾向于想象，我的记忆里仍有某段空白，是那杯奇异的利口酒所致；也许我已经继承了那份遗产，忽然间把好运宣布之后的一切都忘了个干净。也许等上一阵，事情便会重新清晰起来。然而我与老埃尔弗沙姆那顿晚餐，此刻却异常鲜明、仿佛近在眼前。香槟、目光犀利的侍者、那撮粉末、那些利口酒——我敢拿灵魂打赌，这一切就发生在几个钟头之前。

紧接着发生了一件事，本身微不足道，于我却可怕至极，如今想起那一刻我仍不寒而栗。我开口说出声来。我说：“我究竟是怎么到这儿来的？”……*而那声音不是我的。*

===Original===
It was not my own, it was thin, the articulation was slurred, the resonance of my facial bones was different. Then, to reassure myself I ran one hand over the other, and felt loose folds of skin, the bony laxity of age. “Surely,” I said, in that horrible voice that had somehow established itself in my throat, “surely this thing is a dream!” Almost as quickly as if I did it involuntarily, I thrust my fingers into my mouth. My teeth had gone. My fingertips ran on the flaccid surface of an even row of shrivelled gums. I was sick with dismay and disgust.

I felt then a passionate desire to see myself, to realise at once in its full horror the ghastly change that had come upon me. I tottered to the mantel, and felt along it for matches. As I did so, a barking cough sprang up in my throat, and I clutched the thick flannel nightdress I found about me. There were no matches there, and I suddenly realised that my extremities were cold. Sniffing and coughing, whimpering a little, perhaps, I fumbled back to bed. “It is surely a dream,” I whispered to myself as I clambered back, “surely a dream.” It was a senile repetition. I pulled the bedclothes over my shoulders, over my ears, I thrust my withered hand under the pillow, and determined to compose myself to sleep. Of course it was a dream. In the morning the dream would be over, and I should wake up strong and vigorous again to my youth and studies. I shut my eyes, breathed regularly, and, finding myself wakeful, began to count slowly through the powers of three.

But the thing I desired would not come. I could not get to sleep. And the persuasion of the inexorable reality of the change that had happened to me grew steadily. Presently I found myself with my eyes wide open, the powers of three forgotten, and my skinny fingers upon my shrivelled gums, I was, indeed, suddenly and abruptly, an old man. I had in some unaccountable manner fallen through my life and come to old age, in some way I had been cheated of all the best of my life, of love, of struggle, of strength, and hope. I grovelled into the pillow and tried to persuade myself that such hallucination was possible. Imperceptibly, steadily, the dawn grew clearer.

===Chinese===
那不是我的声音，它又细又弱，咬字含混，我面部骨骼的共鸣也不同了。接着，为了给自己壮胆，我一只手在另一只手上抚过，触到了松弛的皮褶，触到了老年的那种骨节松垮。“想必，”我用那不知怎地占据了喉咙的可怕声音说，“想必这是梦！”几乎是不假思索地，我把手指伸进嘴里。我的牙齿没了。我的指尖在那一排干瘪牙龈松软的表面上划过。我又是惊骇又是恶心。

我接着生出一股热烈的渴望，想看看自己，想一下子彻底领教降临到我身上那骇人变化的全貌。我踉跄地走到炉台前，沿着它摸火柴。摸着摸着，喉咙里忽然爆出一阵犬吠似的咳嗽，我紧紧揪住身上那件厚法兰绒睡衣。那里没有火柴，我忽然发觉自己的四肢冰凉。我抽着鼻子咳着嗽，也许还哼唧着，摸索着回到床上。“想必是梦，”我爬回去时悄声对自己说，“想必是梦。”那是老朽的反复絮叨。我把被褥拉过肩头，拉过耳朵，把干枯的手塞到枕头底下，决心强迫自己入睡。这当然是梦。到了早晨，梦就会过去，我又会强壮矫健地醒来，回到我的青春和学业里。我闭上眼睛，规律地呼吸，发现仍睡不着，便开始慢慢地背三的幂来数数。

可我盼望的事偏偏不来。我睡不着。而那“这场变化是无可挽回的真实”的信念，却越来越坚决。不久我发觉自己睁大了眼睛，三的幂早已忘到九霄云外，干瘦的手指正按在干枯的牙龈上——我确确实实是猛然间一下子成了一个老人。我不知怎地竟从我的一生里跌了下去，落到了垂暮之年，我这一生最美好的东西——爱情、奋斗、力量与希望——竟这样被人骗走了。我把脸埋进枕头里，竭力说服自己这样的幻觉是可能的。不知不觉地，稳步地，天色越来越亮。

===Original===
At last, despairing of further sleep, I sat up in bed and looked about me. A chill twilight rendered the whole chamber visible. It was spacious and well-furnished, better furnished than any room I had ever slept in before. A candle and matches became dimly visible upon a little pedestal in a recess. I threw back the bedclothes, and, shivering with the rawness of the early morning, albeit it was summertime, I got out and lit the candle. Then, trembling horribly, so that the extinguisher rattled on its spike, I tottered to the glass and saw—*Elvesham’s face!* It was none the less horrible because I had already dimly feared as much. He had already seemed physically weak and pitiful to me, but seen now, dressed only in a coarse flannel nightdress, that fell apart and showed the stringy neck, seen now as my own body, I cannot describe its desolate decrepitude. The hollow cheeks, the straggling tail of dirty grey hair, the rheumy bleared eyes, the quivering, shrivelled lips, the lower displaying a gleam of the pink interior lining, and those horrible dark gums showing. You who are mind and body together, at your natural years, cannot imagine what this fiendish imprisonment meant to me. To be young and full of the desire and energy of youth, and to be caught, and presently to be crushed in this tottering ruin of a body…

But I wander from the course of my story. For some time I must have been stunned at this change that had come upon me. It was daylight when I did so far gather myself together as to think. In some inexplicable way I had been changed, though how, short of magic, the thing had been done, I could not say. And as I thought, the diabolical ingenuity of Elvesham came home to me. It seemed plain to me that as I found myself in his, so he must be in possession of *my* body, of my strength, that is, and my future. But how to prove it? Then, as I thought, the thing became so incredible, even to me, that my mind reeled, and I had to pinch myself, to feel my toothless gums, to see myself in the glass, and touch the things about me, before I could steady myself to face the facts again. Was all life hallucination? Was I indeed Elvesham, and he me? Had I been dreaming of Eden overnight? Was there any Eden? But if I was Elvesham, I should remember where I was on the previous morning, the name of the town in which I lived, what happened before the dream began. I struggled with my thoughts. I recalled the queer doubleness of my memories overnight. But now my mind was clear. Not the ghost of any memories but those proper to Eden could I raise.

===Chinese===
终于，我不再指望能再睡着，便坐起身来四下张望。清冷的微光使整间屋子都隐约可见。屋子很宽敞，陈设讲究，比我睡过的任何一间屋子都强。在一个壁龛里的小台座上，隐约看得见一支蜡烛和几根火柴。我掀开被褥，冻得直哆嗦——虽是夏天，清晨的寒意却透骨——下了床，点着了蜡烛。然后，我抖得厉害，连烛罩都在烛插上咔咔作响，我踉跄着走到镜前，看见了——*埃尔弗沙姆的脸！*虽然我早隐隐怕着这一点，可亲眼看见仍不啻骇人。从前我觉得他这副身体就已经够虚弱可怜的了，可如今亲眼所见，只穿着一件粗法兰绒睡衣，衣襟敞开露出那青筋盘结的脖颈，又亲眼所见作为我自己的身体——它那荒凉的衰败，我简直无法描摹。那凹陷的双颊，那一束稀稀拉拉的肮脏灰发，那一双泪眼昏花的眼，那颤抖干瘪的嘴唇——下唇微微张开，露出一线粉红色的内里——还有那可怕的漆黑牙龈。你们这些身心合一、正当其年的人，无法想象这种恶魔般的囚禁对我意味着什么。明明年轻，满心都是青春的欲望与精力，却被捕获，而且不久便要被这具摇摇欲坠的躯壳压碎……

可我偏离了故事的主线。面对降临到我身上的这一变化，我必有片刻是惊呆了的。等我稍稍定神能思考时，天已大亮。我确确实实被人掉了包，然而除非是巫术，这事究竟是怎么做成的，我说不上来。而我越想，越领略到埃尔弗沙姆那魔鬼般的精巧。在我看来，事情一清二楚：既然我在他的身体里，那他必定占着*我的*身体，也就是说，占着我的气力和我的未来。可怎么证明呢？接着，我越想越觉得这事连我自己也难以置信，脑子里一阵天旋地转，我不得不掐掐自己，摸摸自己那没牙的牙龈，照照镜子，再摸摸身边的东西，才能稳住神面对事实。难道人的一生都是幻觉吗？难道我真的是埃尔弗沙姆，而他是我？难道我昨夜梦见的那个伊登只是个梦？难道真有什么伊登吗？可如果我真的是埃尔弗沙姆，那我该记得昨天早上在哪里，该记得我所住的城镇叫什么名字，该记得做梦之前发生过什么事。我与自己的念头苦苦搏斗。我回想昨夜那种古怪的记忆双重性。可此刻我的头脑是清楚的。除了属于伊登的记忆之外，我再也唤不起任何别的一丝记忆的影子。

===Original===
“This way lies insanity!” I cried in my piping voice. I staggered to my feet, dragged my feeble, heavy limbs to the washhand-stand, and plunged my grey head into a basin of cold water. Then, towelling myself, I tried again. It was no good. I felt beyond all question that I was indeed Eden, not Elvesham. But Eden in Elvesham’s body!

Had I been a man of any other age, I might have given myself up to my fate as one enchanted. But in these sceptical days miracles do not pass current. Here was some trick of psychology. What a drug and a steady stare could do, a drug and a steady stare, or some similar treatment, could surely undo. Men have lost their memories before. But to exchange memories as one does umbrellas! I laughed. Alas! not a healthy laugh, but a wheezing, senile titter. I could have fancied old Elvesham laughing at my plight, and a gust of petulant anger, unusual to me, swept across my feelings. I began dressing eagerly in the clothes I found lying about on the floor, and only realised when I was dressed that it was an evening suit I had assumed. I opened the wardrobe and found some more ordinary clothes, a pair of plaid trousers, and an old-fashioned dressing-gown. I put a venerable smoking-cap on my venerable head, and, coughing a little from my exertions, tottered out upon the landing.

===Chinese===
“这条路通向疯癫！”我用尖细的声音喊道。我挣扎着站起来，拖着那软弱沉重的四肢走到洗脸架前，把这颗苍白的头浸进一盆冷水里。然后我擦着脸，再试一次。没有用。我毫无疑问地感觉到，我确是伊登，不是埃尔弗沙姆。但我是困在埃尔弗沙姆身体里的伊登！

我若是活在别的时代，也许便认命了，当作自己中了邪。可在这怀疑的年头，神迹是行不通的。这不过是某种心理把戏。一剂药、一道凝视能做到的事，一剂药、一道凝视，或类似的治疗手段，定然也能拆穿。从前也有过丧失记忆的人。可像换伞一样交换记忆！我笑了。哎呀！那不是健康的笑，而是喘着粗气的老朽痴笑。我恍惚觉得老埃尔弗沙姆正在嘲笑我的窘境，一阵平日里不属于我的愠怒掠过我的心头。我急切地把地上散落的衣裳套上身，穿好了才发现自己套上的是一套晚礼服。我打开衣橱，找出几件寻常些的衣裳，一条格纹裤，一件老式的晨衣。我给这颗德高望重的脑袋戴上一顶德高望重的吸烟帽，因为费力而咳了几声，踉踉跄跄地走出房门，来到楼梯口。

===Original===
It was then, perhaps, a quarter to six, and the blinds were closely drawn and the house quite silent. The landing was a spacious one, a broad, richly-carpeted staircase went down into the darkness of the hall below, and before me a door ajar showed me a writing-desk, a revolving bookcase, the back of a study chair, and a fine array of bound books, shelf upon shelf.

“My study,” I mumbled, and walked across the landing. Then at the sound of my voice a thought struck me, and I went back to the bedroom and put in the set of false teeth. They slipped in with the ease of old, habit. “That’s better,” said I, gnashing them, and so returned to the study.

The drawers of the writing-desk were locked. Its revolving top was also locked. I could see no indications of the keys, and there were none in the pockets of my trousers. I shuffled back at once to the bedroom, and went through the dress suit, and afterwards the pockets of all the garments I could find. I was very eager, and one might have imagined that burglars had been at work, to see my room when I had done. Not only were there no keys to be found, but not a coin, nor a scrap of paper—save only the receipted bill of the overnight dinner.

A curious weariness asserted itself. I sat down and stared at the garments flung here and there, their pockets turned inside out. My first frenzy had already flickered out. Every moment I was beginning to realise the immense intelligence of the plans of my enemy, to see more and more clearly the hopelessness of my position. With an effort I rose and hurried hobbling into the study again. On the staircase was a housemaid pulling up the blinds. She stared, I think, at the expression of my face. I shut the door of the study behind me, and, seizing a poker, began an attack upon the desk. That is how they found me. The cover of the desk was split, the lock smashed, the letters torn out of the pigeonholes, and tossed about the room. In my senile rage I had flung about the pens and other such light stationery, and overturned the ink. Moreover, a large vase upon the mantel had got broken—I do not know how. I could find no cheque-book, no money, no indications of the slightest use for the recovery of my body. I was battering madly at the drawers, when the butler, backed by two women-servants, intruded upon me.

===Chinese===
那时大约是差一刻六点，百叶帘都紧紧拉着，整所宅子寂然无声。楼梯口很宽敞，一道宽阔的、铺着厚地毯的楼梯通向下面前厅的黑暗中，我面前一扇半掩的门里，露出一张写字台、一只旋转书架、一张书房座椅的椅背，以及一排排装帧精美的书，一架一架。

“我的书房，”我咕哝着，穿过楼梯口。随后听到自己的声音，我心里一动，便折回卧室，把那副假牙装了进去。它们像旧日习惯那样轻巧地滑了进去。“这就好些了，”我咔咔地咬着牙说，便回到书房里。

写字台的抽屉都锁着。它的旋转台面也锁着。我看不出钥匙放在哪里，裤兜里也摸不着。我立刻拖着脚步回到卧室，翻遍了那套晚礼服，又翻遍了能找到的所有衣裳的口袋。我急不可耐，翻完之后这屋子看上去倒像是遭了贼。不仅没有钥匙，连一个硬币、一片纸也没有——只有昨夜那顿晚餐的账单，上面盖着“已收讫”的戳。

一种古怪的倦意涌了上来。我坐下来，盯着东一件西一件扔着的、口袋被翻了个底朝天的衣裳。我最初那阵狂热已经消退了。我每时每刻都更清楚地认识到敌人的计划何等精密，更清楚地看到自己的处境何等无望。我挣扎着站起来，一瘸一拐地又赶回书房。楼梯上一个女佣正在拉百叶帘。我想她被我脸上的神情吓了一跳。我把书房门一关，抄起一根拨火棍，便朝写字台砸去。他们便是这般发现我的：台面被劈开了，锁被砸烂了，信件被从格子里扯出来，扔得满屋都是。我那老朽的狂怒把笔和别的轻巧文具摔得四处都是，还打翻了墨水。此外，炉台上一只大花瓶也碎了——我不知道是怎么打的。我找不到支票簿，找不到钱，找不到任何一点有助于我夺回身体的东西。我正疯狂地砸着抽屉，管家带着两个女仆闯了进来。

---

===Original===
That simply is the story of my change. No one will believe my frantic assertions. I am treated as one demented, and even at this moment I am under restraint. But I am sane, absolutely sane, and to prove it I have sat down to write this story minutely as the things happened to me. I appeal to the reader, whether there is any trace of insanity in the style or method, of the story he has been reading. I am a young man locked away in an old man’s body. But the clear fact is incredible to everyone. Naturally I appear demented to those who will not believe this, naturally I do not know the names of my secretaries, of the doctors who come to see me, of my servants and neighbours, of this town (wherever it is) where I find myself. Naturally I lose myself in my own house, and suffer inconveniences of every sort. Naturally I ask the oddest questions. Naturally I weep and cry out, and have paroxysms of despair. I have no money and no cheque-book. The bank will not recognise my signature, for I suppose that, allowing for the feeble muscles I now have, my handwriting is still Eden’s. These people about me will not let me go to the bank personally. It seems, indeed, that there is no bank in this town, and that I have an account in some part of London. It seems that Elvesham kept the name of his solicitor secret from all his household. I can ascertain nothing. Elvesham was, of course, a profound student of mental science, and all my declarations of the facts of the case merely confirm the theory that my insanity is the outcome of overmuch brooding upon psychology. Dreams of the personal identity indeed! Two days ago I was a healthy youngster, with all life before me; now I am a furious old man, unkempt, and desperate, and miserable, prowling about a great, luxurious, strange house, watched, feared, and avoided as a lunatic by everyone about me. And in London is Elvesham beginning life again in a vigorous body, and with all the accumulated knowledge and wisdom of threescore and ten. He has stolen my life.

===Chinese===
我这番变化的经过，便是如此。没有人会相信我那些疯话。我被当作一个疯子，此刻我也正被看管着。可我是清醒的，绝对清醒，为了证明这一点，我坐下来，把发生在我身上的事一五一十地写成这个故事。我请问读者，在您方才读到的这篇故事的笔法和脉络里，可有一丝一毫疯癫的痕迹？我是一个被锁在老人躯壳里的年轻人。可这明白的事实，谁都难以置信。自然，在那些不肯相信此事的人眼里，我显得癫狂；自然，我不知道那些秘书的名字，不知道来看我的医生们的名字，不知道仆人、邻居的名字，不知道我所在的这座城镇（管它在哪里）的名字；自然，我在自家的宅子里也会迷路，受各种各样的不便；自然，我问出最古怪的问题；自然，我哭泣喊叫，一阵阵地绝望。我没有钱，也没有支票簿。银行不认我的签字，因为我想，我如今腕力虽弱，笔迹却仍是伊登的。我身边的人不肯放我亲自去银行。事实上，这座城镇似乎根本没有银行，我的账户开在伦敦某处。埃尔弗沙姆似乎把他律师的姓名瞒着家里所有的人。我什么都查不出来。埃尔弗沙姆当然是精神科学的渊博学者，我所说的这一切事实，只不过是证实了那种说法——我的癫狂是过多地冥想心理学所致。个人同一性的妄想！两天前我还是个健康的少年，整个人生还在前头；如今我是个暴躁的老人，蓬头垢面，绝望而凄惨，在一所阔大、奢华、陌生的宅子里踱来踱去，身边每一个人都把我当疯子一样地监视、害怕、躲避。而在伦敦，埃尔弗沙姆正借着一具壮健的躯体重新开始人生，还揣着七十年岁月积累下来的全部知识和智慧。他偷走了我的人生。

===Original===
What has happened I do not clearly know. In the study are volumes of manuscript notes referring chiefly to the psychology of memory, and parts of what may be either calculations or ciphers in symbols absolutely strange to me. In some passages there are indications that he was also occupied with the philosophy of mathematics. I take it he has transferred the whole of his memories, the accumulation that makes up his personality, from this old withered brain of his to mine, and, similarly, that he has transferred mine to his discarded tenement. Practically, that is, he has changed bodies. But how such a change may be possible is without the range of my philosophy. I have been a materialist for all my thinking life, but here, suddenly, is a clear case of man’s detachability from matter.

One desperate experiment I am about to try. I sit writing here before putting the matter to issue. This morning, with the help of a table-knife that I had secreted at breakfast, I succeeded in breaking open a fairly obvious secret drawer in this wrecked writing-desk. I discovered nothing save a little green glass phial containing a white powder. Round the neck of the phial was a label, and thereon was written this one word, “*Release.*” This may be—is most probably—poison. I can understand Elvesham placing poison in my way, and I should be sure that it was his intention so to get rid of the only living witness against him, were it not for this careful concealment. The man has practically solved the problem of immortality. Save for the spite of chance, he will live in my body until it has aged, and then, again, throwing that aside, he will assume some other victim’s youth and strength. When one remembers his heartlessness, it is terrible to think of the ever-growing experience that… How long has he been leaping from body to body?… But I tire of writing. The powder appears to be soluble in water. The taste is not unpleasant.

===Chinese===
究竟发生了什么，我并不清楚。书房里有几卷手写的笔记，大多是关于记忆心理学的，还有几部分不知是计算还是密码，用的符号我全然看不懂。有几处迹象表明他也涉猎数学哲学。我猜，他已把全部记忆——构成他整个人格的那一堆积淀——从他那颗枯萎的老脑搬进了我的脑里，相应地，也把我的搬进了他丢弃的那副皮囊里。也就是说，实际上他换了身体。可这样的转换何以可能，已超出我的哲学所能理解的范围。我整个思想生涯都是唯物论的，可忽然间，这里就有一个明明白白的例子，证明人与肉体可以分离。

我要做一个孤注一掷的试验。我坐在这里写下这些，是着手之前的事。今早，靠着早餐时偷藏的一把餐刀，我成功地撬开了这张被砸烂的写字台里一个颇为显眼的暗抽屉。我只找到一只小小的绿色玻璃瓶，里面装着白色粉末。瓶颈上缠着一张标签，上面写着这么一个词：“*解脱（Release）*。”这也许是——极可能就是——毒药。我能理解埃尔弗沙姆把毒药放在我手边，若不是这般小心藏匿，我本该断定他的用意正是借此除掉唯一能指证他的活口。这个人实际上已经解决了长生不死的问题。若非命运作对，他将活在我的身体里直到它衰老，然后再把它抛开，换上另一个受害者的青春和气力。想起他的冷酷无情，那不断累积的经验……实在可怕。他从一具身体跳到另一具身体，已经跳了多久？……可我写累了。那粉末似乎溶于水。味道倒不难喝。

---

===Original===
There the narrative found upon Mr. Elvesham’s desk ends. His dead body lay between the desk and the chair. The latter had been pushed back, probably by his last convulsions. The story was written in pencil and in a crazy hand, quite unlike his usual minute characters. There remain only two curious facts to record. Indisputably there was some connection between Eden and Elvesham, since the whole of Elvesham’s property was bequeathed to the young man. But he never inherited. When Elvesham committed suicide, Eden was, strangely enough, already dead. Twenty-four hours before, he had been knocked down by a cab and killed instantly, at the crowded crossing at the intersection of Gower Street and Euston Road. So that the only human being who could have thrown light upon this fantastic narrative is beyond the reach of questions. Without further comment I leave this extraordinary matter to the reader’s individual judgment.

===Chinese===
在埃尔弗沙姆先生书桌上发现的那篇手记到此为止。他的尸首横在书桌和椅子之间。椅子被推开了，大约是他最后抽搐时推开的。故事是用铅笔写的，字迹潦草凌乱，全然不似他平日蝇头小楷的工整。此外只剩两桩古怪的事实需要交代。无可争辩的是，伊登与埃尔弗沙姆之间确有某种牵连，因为埃尔弗沙姆的全部财产都遗赠给了这个年轻人。可他始终未能继承。埃尔弗沙姆自杀之时，说来奇怪，伊登早已不在人世——早二十四个钟头，他就在高尔街（Gower Street）与尤斯顿路交汇处那处人潮拥挤的道口，被一辆马车撞倒，当场毙命。如此一来，唯一能为这篇离奇手记作证的人，已无从问起了。不再赘言，我把这桩非同寻常的事交由读者各自判断。

## The Temptation of Harringay / 哈林盖的诱惑

===Original===
It is quite impossible to say whether this thing really happened. It depends entirely on the word of R. M. Harringay, who is an artist.

Following his version of the affair, the narrative deposes that Harringay went into his studio about ten o’clock to see what he could make of the head that he had been working at the day before. The head in question was that of an Italian organ-grinder, and Harringay thought—but was not quite sure—that the title would be the “Vigil.” So far he is frank, and his narrative bears the stamp of truth. He had seen the man expectant for pennies, and with a promptness that suggested genius, had had him in at once.

===Chinese===
这件事究竟是否真发生过，实在是说不准。一切全凭 R·M·哈林盖（R. M. Harringay）的一面之词——他是个画家。

按他自己的说法，事情是这样的：十点钟左右，哈林盖走进画室，想看看前一天一直在画的那幅头像还能再弄出点什么名堂。那幅头像画的是个意大利手摇风琴师，哈林盖打算给它取名叫《守候》——不过他也不太有把握。说到这里他还是坦诚的，叙述也带有真实的印记。他先前曾看见这人正眼巴巴地盼着过路人施舍几个便士，便以一种近乎天才的果决，当场就把他请进了画室。

===Original===
“Kneel. Look up at that bracket,” said Harringay. “As if you expected pennies.”

“Don’t *grin*!” said Harringay. “I don’t want to paint your gums. Look as though you were unhappy.”

Now, after a night’s rest, the picture proved decidedly unsatisfactory. “It’s good work,” said Harringay. “That little bit in the neck… But.”

He walked about the studio and looked at the thing from this point and from that. Then he said a wicked word. In the original the word is given.

“Painting,” he says he said. “Just a painting of an organ-grinder—a mere portrait. If it was a live organ-grinder I wouldn’t mind. But somehow I never make things alive. I wonder if my imagination is wrong.” This, too, has a truthful air. His imagination *is* wrong.

“That creative touch! To take canvas and pigment and make a man—as Adam was made of red ochre! But this thing! If you met it walking about the streets you would know it was only a studio production. The little boys would tell it to ‘Garnome and git frimed.’ Some little touch… Well—it won’t do as it is.”

===Chinese===
“跪下。朝那块托架上看，”哈林盖吩咐道，“就像你在盼着便士掉下来。”

“别*咧嘴笑*！”哈林盖道，“我可不想画你的牙床。你要一副愁苦的样子。”

谁知过了一夜，这幅画在第二天的光线下显得十分不能令人满意。“手艺是好的，”哈林盖说，“就是脖子那一小块……唉。”

他在画室里来回踱步，从这个角度瞧瞧，从那个角度瞄瞄。然后他骂了一句脏话。原话这里照录不讳。

“一幅画罢了，”据他说他当时这么自言自语，“不过是一幅手摇风琴师的画——一张普普通通的肖像。要是真是个活生生的风琴师，我倒也不在乎。可不知怎的，我从来都不能把东西画活。我怀疑是不是我的想象力出了毛病。”这话听上去也确有几分真实。他的想象力*确有*毛病。

“那一笔创造的神奇啊！取来画布与颜料，便造出一个活人——就像亚当是用赭红土捏成的那样！可这玩意儿！就算它在街上走来走去，碰见你的人也会一眼看出它不过是画室里炮制出来的。连街上的小孩子都会冲它嚷：‘回家去，你该进画框里待着啦’〔此句原文 ‘Garnome and git frimed’ 是模仿伦敦土腔小孩口齿不清念 ‘Go home and get framed’〕。就差那么一点点……唉——照这样是不行的。”

===Original===
He went to the blinds and began to pull them down. They were made of blue Holland with the rollers at the bottom of the window, so that you pull them down to get more light. He gathered his palette, brushes, and mahl stick from his table. Then he turned to the picture and put a speck of brown in the corner of the mouth; and shifted his attention thence to the pupil of the eye. Then he decided that the chin was a trifle too impassive for a vigil.

Presently he put down his impedimenta, and lighting a pipe surveyed the progress of his work. “I’m hanged if the thing isn’t sneering at me,” said Harringay, and he still believes it sneered.

The animation of the figure had certainly increased, but scarcely in the direction he wished. There was no mistake about the sneer. “Vigil of the Unbeliever,” said Harringay. “Rather subtle and clever that! But the left eyebrow isn’t cynical enough.”

He went and dabbed at the eyebrow, and added a little to the lobe of the ear to suggest materialism. Further consideration ensued. “Vigil’s off, I’m afraid,” said Harringay. “Why not Mephistopheles? But that’s a bit *too* common. ‘A Friend of the Doge,’—not so seedy. The armour won’t do, though. Too Camelot. How about a scarlet robe and call him One of the Sacred College’? Humour in that, and an appreciation of Middle Italian History.”

“There’s always Benvenuto Cellini,” said Harringay; “with a clever suggestion of a gold cup in one corner. But that would scarcely suit the complexion.”

===Chinese===
他走到窗帘跟前，动手把它们往下拉。那是用蓝色荷兰亚麻布做的，卷轴装在窗框下端，往下拉反而能让室内更亮些。他从桌上取来调色板、画笔和支腕杖。然后他转向那幅画，在嘴角点了一点棕色，又把注意力移到眼睛的瞳孔上。接着他断定，要表现“守候”之情，下巴未免太木然了一些。

过了一会儿他把这一摊家伙放下，点上一斗烟，审视起自己这番功夫的进度。“真该死，这玩意儿简直在嘲笑我，”哈林盖说——至今他仍坚持它当时确是嘲笑了。

那人物的神气确实活泼了些，可惜不大往他所希望的方向发展。那一抹讥讽的笑意是错不了的。“《不信者的守候》，”哈林盖说，“这题目既微妙又巧妙！不过左边那条眉毛还不够愤世嫉俗。”

他走过去在那条眉毛上抹了几笔，又在耳垂上加了一点东西，以显出几分唯物主义色彩。再想了想，又说：“《守候》怕是不成了。改作梅菲斯托费勒斯（Mephistopheles）如何？可这题材未免*太*俗。《总督之友》——倒没那么寒酸。可这身铠甲不行。太像卡米洛（Camelot，亚瑟王宫廷）那一套排场了。改成一身猩红长袍，称他为‘枢机团之一’，怎么样？这里头有点幽默，也算是对意大利中期历史的一种品鉴。”

“当然还有本韦努托·切利尼（Benvenuto Cellini），”哈林盖说，“可以在画面一角巧妙地暗示一只金杯。可那肤色不大配。”

===Original===
He describes himself as babbling in this way in order to keep down an unaccountably unpleasant sensation of fear. The thing was certainly acquiring anything but a pleasing expression. Yet it was as certainly becoming far more of a living thing than it had been—if a sinister one—far more alive than anything he had ever painted before. “Call it ‘Portrait of a Gentleman,’” said Harringay;—“A Certain Gentleman.”

“Won’t do,” said Harringay, still keeping up his courage. “Kind of thing they call Bad Taste. That sneer will have to come out. That gone, and a little more fire in the eye—never noticed how warm his eye was before—and he might do for—? What price Passionate Pilgrim? But that devilish face won’t do—*this* side of the Channel.”

“Some little inaccuracy does it,” he said; “eyebrows probably too oblique,”—therewith pulling the blind lower to get a better light, and resuming palette and brushes.

The face on the canvas seemed animated by a spirit of its own. Where the expression of diablerie came in he found impossible to discover. Experiment was necessary. The eyebrows—it could scarcely be the eyebrows? But he altered them. No, that was no better; in fact, if anything, a trifle more satanic. The corner of the mouth? Pah! more than ever a leer—and now, retouched, it was ominously grim. The eye, then? Catastrophe! he had filled his brush with vermilion instead of brown, and yet he had felt sure it was brown! The eye seemed now to have rolled in its socket, and was glaring at him an eye of fire. In a flash of passion, possibly with something of the courage of panic, he struck the brush full of bright red athwart the picture; and then a very curious thing, a very strange thing indeed, occurred—if it *did* occur.

*The diabolified Italian before him shut both his eyes, pursed his mouth, and wiped the colour off his face with his hand.*

Then the *red eye* opened again, with a sound like the opening of lips, and the face smiled. “That was rather hasty of you,” said the picture.

===Chinese===
他后来描述自己当时这样絮絮叨叨，无非是想压下心头一股说不清道不明的恐惧。那东西脸上的神情，确实一点也不讨人喜欢了。然而同样确实的是，它正变得前所未有的栩栩如生——虽说带着邪气——比他以往画过的任何东西都活灵活现。“那就叫《绅士肖像》吧，”哈林盖说，“——《某绅士》。”

“不行，”哈林盖说，仍鼓着劲儿，“这是人家所说的趣味低俗。那一抹讥讽的笑非去掉不可。去掉了它，再把眼神弄得再炽烈一些——从前竟没留意他的眼神有多暖——那他也许能充作——？《热情的朝圣者》如何？可这一脸魔鬼相也不行——*海峡*这一边是不行的。”

“只要略加点失真就成了，”他说，“怕是眉毛画得太斜了些”——一边把窗帘又往下拉了拉，好让光线更足，一边重新拿起调色板和画笔。

画布上那张脸，仿佛被某种属于自己的精灵所驱使。那一脸魔鬼般邪气的神情究竟从何处而来，他实在找不出来。看来非得做一番试验不可。是眉毛——总不至于是眉毛吧？可他还是改了改。不对，并不见佳；倘若真有什么变化，倒仿佛越发邪门了。是嘴角？呸！越发像是一抹淫邪的怪笑——如今一经重描，竟带上了一种不祥的阴狠。那么，是眼睛？大祸临头！他笔上蘸的分明是朱砂红，而不是棕色——可他方才还一口咬定是棕色！那只眼睛此刻似乎已在眼眶里转了转，正怒目圆睁，像一团烈火般瞪着他。一刹那的怒火，或许还掺着一股临危时的胆气，他把蘸满鲜红的画笔，狠狠地向画面横扫过去——接着便发生了一件十分古怪的事，一件真正匪夷所思的事——倘若它真发生过的话。

*眼前这个中了邪的意大利人，把两只眼睛都闭上了，抿紧了嘴，伸出手来，把脸上的颜料一抹而尽。*

随后，那只*红色的眼睛*重新睁开——发出一声像嘴唇开启那样的轻响——那张脸笑了。“你这未免太鲁莽了些，”那幅画开口道。

===Original===
Harringay states that, now that the worst had happened, his self-possession returned. He had a saving persuasion that devils were reasonable creatures.

“Why do you keep moving about then,” he said, “making faces and all that—sneering and squinting, while I am painting you?”

“I don’t,” said the picture.

“You *do*,” said Harringay.

“It’s yourself,” said the picture.

“It’s *not* myself,” said Harringay.

“It *is* yourself,” said the picture. “No! don’t go hitting me with paint again, because it’s true. You have been trying to fluke an expression on my face all the morning. Really, you haven’t an idea what your picture ought to look like.”

“I have,” said Harringay.

“You have *not*,” said the picture: “You *never* have with your pictures. You always start with the vaguest presentiment of what you are going to do; it is to be something beautiful—you are sure of that—and devout, perhaps, or tragic; but beyond that it is all experiment and chance. My dear fellow! you don’t think you can paint a picture like that?”

===Chinese===
据哈林盖说，最坏的事情既已发生，他反倒镇定下来。他始终抱着一个救命的念头：魔鬼毕竟是有理性的生灵。

“那你为什么老动来动去，”他说，“做鬼脸，又是讥笑，又是斜眼——我正画着你呢？”

“我没动，”那幅画说。

“你*明明*在动，”哈林盖说。

“是你自己，”那幅画说。

“才*不是*我自己，”哈林盖说。

“*就是*你自己，”那幅画说，“哎！别再拿颜料摔我啦，我说的是实话。你整个上午都在那儿碰运气，想在我脸上凑出个神情来。说真的，你这幅画该是个什么样子，你自己心里一点谱都没有。”

“我有，”哈林盖说。

“你*没有*，”那幅画说，“你*从来*没有过。你总是怀着一种最朦胧的预感动手；只是觉得要画一件美的东西——这一点你倒是笃定——或许还要虔诚，或许还要悲壮；可再往下就全凭试验和运气了。亲爱的老兄！你该不是当真以为，这样就能画出一幅画来吧？”

===Original===
Now it must be remembered that for what follows we have only Harringay’s word.

“I shall paint a picture exactly as I like,” said Harringay, calmly.

This seemed to disconcert the picture a little. “You can’t paint a picture without an inspiration,” it remarked.

“But I *had* an inspiration—for this.”

“Inspiration!” sneered the sardonic figure; “a fancy that came from your seeing an organ-grinder looking up at a window! Vigil! Ha, ha! You just started painting on the chance of something coming—that’s what you did. And when I saw you at it I came. I want a talk with you!”

“Art, with you,” said the picture—“it’s a poor business. You potter. I don’t know how it is, but you don’t seem able to throw your soul into it. You know too much. It hampers you. In the midst of your enthusiasms you ask yourself whether something like this has not been done before. And—”

“Look here,” said Harringay, who had expected something better than criticism from the devil. “Are you going to talk studio to me?” He filled his number twelve hoghair with red paint.

“The true artist,” said the picture, “is always an ignorant man. An artist who theorises about his work is no longer artist but critic. Wagner… I say!—What’s that red paint for?”

“I’m going to paint you out,” said Harringay. “I don’t want to hear all that Tommy Rot. If you think just because I’m an artist by trade I’m going to talk studio to you, you make a precious mistake.”

===Chinese===
这里必须记住，下面这一段，我们仍然只有哈林盖的一面之词。

“我就照我喜欢的样子画一幅画，”哈林盖平静地说。

这话似乎让那幅画有点发窘。“没有灵感，是画不出一幅画的，”它说。

“可我*确曾*有过一次灵感——为这幅画。”

“灵感！”那讥讽的人物冷笑道，“你不过是看见一个手摇风琴师抬头望着某扇窗子，动了那么个念头罢了！《守候》！哈哈哈！你只是图侥幸，随手画下去，盼着能画出点什么来——就是这样。我一见你这般光景，便来了。我要跟你谈一谈！”

“艺术之于你，”那幅画说，“实在是一门可怜的营生。你只是磨磨蹭蹭。不知怎的，你仿佛没法把整个灵魂投进去。你懂得太多。这反而束住了你的手脚。你正热衷于某件事的时候，便会自问：这般那般，是否已经有人做过了呢？而且——”

“我说，”哈林盖道——他本指望从魔鬼那里听到些比批评更高明的东西——“你打算跟我谈画室里的行话吗？”他往十二号猪鬃笔上蘸满了红颜料。

“真正的艺术家，”那幅画说，“永远是无知的人。一个对自己作品大发理论的人，已经不再是艺术家，而是评论家了。瓦格纳（Wagner）……喂！——那红颜料是要做什么？”

“我要把你涂掉，”哈林盖说，“我可不想听你那一堆胡言乱语。你要是以为我既是靠卖画吃饭的，就会陪你扯什么画室里的行话，那你就大错特错了。”

===Original===
“One minute,” said the picture, evidently alarmed. “I want to make you an offer—a genuine offer. It’s right what I’m saying. You lack inspirations. Well. No doubt you’ve heard of the Cathedral of Cologne, and the Devil’s Bridge, and—”

“Rubbish,” said Harringay. “Do you think I want to go to perdition simply for the pleasure of painting a good picture, and getting it slated. Take that.”

His blood was up. His danger only nerved him to action, so he says. So he planted a dab of vermilion in his creature’s mouth. The Italian spluttered and tried to wipe it off—evidently horribly surprised. And then—according to Harringay—there began a very remarkable struggle, Harringay splashing away with the red paint, and the picture wriggling about and wiping it off as fast as he put it on. “*Two* masterpieces,” said the demon. “Two indubitable masterpieces for a Chelsea artist’s soul. It’s a bargain?” Harringay replied with the paint brush.

For a few minutes nothing could be heard but the brush going and the spluttering and ejaculations of the Italian. A lot of the strokes he caught on his arm and hand, though Harringay got over his guard often enough. Presently the paint on the palette gave out and the two antagonists stood breathless, regarding each other. The picture was so smeared with red that it looked as if it had been rolling about a slaughterhouse, and it was painfully out of breath and very uncomfortable with the wet paint trickling down its neck. Still, the first round was in its favour on the whole. “Think,” it said, sticking pluckily to its point, “two supreme masterpieces—in different styles. Each equivalent to the Cathedral—”

“*I* know,” said Harringay, and rushed out of the studio and along the passage towards his wife’s boudoir.

===Chinese===
“等一等，”那幅画说，显然慌了，“我想跟你做一笔交易——一笔正经的交易。我方才说的都是实话。你缺乏灵感。这个嘛——你一定听说过科隆大教堂（the Cathedral of Cologne），还有魔鬼桥（the Devil’s Bridge），还有——”

“胡说八道，”哈林盖说，“你以为我只为画一幅好画、再被人臭骂一顿的乐趣，就肯下地狱吗？吃我一笔。”

他的血性被激了起来。他说，那番凶险反倒更激出了他的胆气。于是他在那张怪物嘴上狠狠抹了一道朱砂。那意大利人呸呸地吐着，想把它擦掉——显然惊骇万分。接着——据哈林盖说——便开始了一场异乎寻常的搏斗：哈林盖拿着红颜料连连挥洒，那幅画则扭来扭去，他前一笔刚落下，后一笔就被擦掉。“*两幅*杰作，”那恶魔道，“两幅毫无疑义的杰作，换一个切尔西（Chelsea）画家的灵魂。成交？”哈林盖用画答回答了他。

好几分钟里，除了画笔的挥动声、那意大利人的吐唾沫声和惊呼声外，什么也听不见。他的手臂和手掌替他挡下了不少笔，虽说哈林盖屡屡能从他的防守中钻过去。不久，调色板上的颜料见了底，两个对手都气喘吁吁地停了下来，彼此对视。那幅画被红颜料抹得浑身都是，仿佛刚在屠宰场里打过滚似的，上气不接下气，颜料顺着脖子往下淌，难受得了不得。不过总的算来，第一回合他还是占了上风。“你想一想，”它说，仍硬着头皮坚持自己的立场，“两幅至高无上的杰作——风格各异。每一幅都抵得上一座大教堂——”

“*我*明白，”哈林盖说着，冲出画室，沿着走廊直奔他妻子的化妆间。

===Original===
In another minute he was back with a large tin of enamel—Hedge Sparrow’s Egg Tint, it was, and a brush. At the sight of that the artistic devil with the red eye began to scream. “*Three* masterpieces—culminating masterpieces.”

Harringay delivered cut two across the demon, and followed with a thrust in the eye. There was an indistinct rumbling. “*Four* masterpieces,” and a spitting sound.

But Harringay had the upper hand now and meant to keep it. With rapid, bold strokes he continued to paint over the writhing canvas, until at last it was a uniform field of shining Hedge Sparrow tint. Once the mouth reappeared and got as far as “Five master—” before he filled it with enamel; and near the end the red eye opened and glared at him indignantly. But at last nothing remained save a gleaming panel of drying enamel. For a little while a faint stirring beneath the surface puckered it slightly here and there, but presently even that died away and the thing was perfectly still.

Then Harringay—according to Harringay’s account—lit his pipe and sat down and stared at the enamelled canvas, and tried to make out clearly what had happened. Then he walked round behind it, to see if the back of it was at all remarkable. Then it was he began to regret he had not photographed the Devil before he painted him out.

This is Harringay’s story—not mine. He supports it by a small canvas (24 by 20) enamelled a pale green, and by violent asseverations. It is also true that he never has produced a masterpiece, and in the opinion of his intimate friends probably never will.

===Chinese===
不到一分钟他便回来了，手里提着一大罐瓷漆——颜色是“树篱麻雀蛋”色——还有一支刷子。那个长着火眼、深谙艺术的魔鬼一看见这玩意儿，便尖叫起来。“*三幅*杰作——登峰造极的杰作。”

哈林盖朝那恶魔横扫了第二下，紧接着又朝它眼睛直戳过去。底下传来一阵含混的咕噜声：“*四幅*杰作”——还伴着一声吐唾沫的声响。

可哈林盖这会儿占了上风，决意要保住这份上风。他运笔如飞，大胆地一道道涂过去，覆盖住那扭动不停的画布，直到整幅画终于变成一片均一而发亮的“麻雀蛋”色。有一次，那张嘴重新露了出来，刚喊到“五幅杰——”就被他用瓷漆堵了回去；将近末了的时候，那只火眼又睁开，愤怒地瞪了他一眼。但最终，剩下的只是一方亮闪闪、正在阴干的瓷漆板。有一阵子，漆面底下隐约还有些躁动，把漆皮顶得起些微皱褶，但不久连这也平息下去，那东西便一动不动了。

随后，哈林盖——按哈林盖自己的说法——点上烟斗，坐下来，盯着那块上了瓷漆的画布，想理清楚方才到底发生了什么。然后他绕到画布背后，看看背面有没有什么特别之处。直到这时，他才开始后悔，没在把魔鬼涂掉之前，先给他拍一张照片。

这就是哈林盖的故事——可不是我的。他所能拿来作证的，只是一幅小小的画布（24×20），上面涂着一层淡绿色的瓷漆，以及他那一连串激烈的赌咒发誓。同样确凿的是，他从未创作出过一幅杰作；而据他几位挚友看来，他大概永远也创作不出来。

## The Treasure in the Forest / 森林中的宝藏

===Original===
The canoe was now approaching the land. The bay opened out, and a gap in the white surf of the reef marked where the little river ran out to the sea; the thicker and deeper green of the virgin forest showed its course down the distant hill slope. The forest here came close to the beach. Far beyond, dim and almost cloudlike in texture, rose the mountains, like suddenly frozen waves. The sea was still save for an almost imperceptible swell. The sky blazed.

The man with the carved paddle stopped. "It should be somewhere here," he said. He shipped the paddle and held his arms out straight before him.

The other man had been in the fore part of the canoe, closely scrutinising the land. He had a sheet of yellow paper on his knee.

"Come and look at this, Evans," he said.

Both men spoke in low tones, and their lips were hard and dry.

===Chinese===
独木舟此刻正渐渐驶近陆地。海湾豁然开朗，珊瑚礁白色浪花中的一道缺口，标出了那条小河入海的去处；原始森林那更为浓密深邃的绿色，勾勒出它从远处山坡蜿蜒而下的走向。这一带的森林直逼海滩。再往远处，群山升起，朦胧一片，质地几乎如云似雾，宛若骤然冻结的波涛。海面纹丝不动，只有几乎觉察不到的微波荡漾。天空烈日如焚。

那个握着刻花桨的人停下手来。"应该就在这附近什么地方，"他说。他把桨收进舱内，双臂向前伸得笔直。

另一个人原本一直待在独木舟的前部，细细打量着那片陆地。他膝上摊着一张发黄的纸。

"过来看看这个，埃文斯（Evans），"他说。

两人说话都压低了嗓音，嘴唇干硬。

===Original===
The man called Evans came swaying along the canoe until he could look over his companion's shoulder.

The paper had the appearance of a rough map. By much folding it was creased and worn to the pitch of separation, and the second man held the discoloured fragments together where they had parted. On it one could dimly make out, in almost obliterated pencil, the outline of the bay.

"Here," said Evans, "is the reef, and here is the gap." He ran his thumbnail over the chart.

"This curved and twisting line is the river—I could do with a drink now!—and this star is the place."

"You see this dotted line," said the man with the map; "it is a straight line, and runs from the opening of the reef to a clump of palm-trees. The star comes just where it cuts the river. We must mark the place as we go into the lagoon."

===Chinese===
那个叫埃文斯的人一路摇晃着沿独木舟走过来，直到能从同伴肩头探看过去。

那张纸看上去像是一张粗略的地图。因反复折叠，它已被折痕磨得几欲裂开，第二个人把已经断开处的褪色碎片拼拢在一起。纸上能用几乎褪尽的铅笔痕隐约辨认出海湾的轮廓。

"这儿，"埃文斯说，"是珊瑚礁，这儿是那个缺口。"他用拇指甲在图上划过。

"这条弯弯曲曲的线就是那条河——这会儿我真想喝上一口！——而这个星号就是那个地方。"

"你看见这条虚线了吧，"拿地图的那个人说；"它是一条直线，从珊瑚礁的缺口通向一片棕榈树。星号就在它与河流相交的地方。我们驶进泻湖的时候，得把这个位置记下来。"

===Original===
"It's queer," said Evans, after a pause, "what these little marks down here are for. It looks like the plan of a house or something; but what all these little dashes, pointing this way and that, may mean I can't get a notion. And what's the writing?"

"Chinese," said the man with the map.

"Of course! *He* was a Chinee," said Evans.

"They all were," said the man with the map.

They both sat for some minutes staring at the land, while the canoe drifted slowly. Then Evans looked towards the paddle.

===Chinese===
"奇怪，"埃文斯顿了顿说，"下边这些小记号是做什么用的。看起来像是房子的图纸什么的；可这些东一点西一点的小短划到底什么意思，我实在想不出。还有那字写的是什么？"

"中文，"拿地图的那个人说。

"那是当然！*他*本就是个中国佬，"埃文斯说。

"他们都是，"拿地图的那个人说。

两人都坐着盯了那片陆地好几分钟，独木舟缓缓地漂着。随后埃文斯朝那支桨看了看。

===Original===
"Your turn with the paddle now, Hooker," said he.

And his companion quietly folded up his map, put it in his pocket, passed Evans carefully, and began to paddle. His movements were languid, like those of a man whose strength was nearly exhausted.

Evans sat with his eyes half closed, watching the frothy breakwater of the coral creep nearer and nearer. The sky was like a furnace, for the sun was near the zenith. Though they were so near the treasure he did not feel the exaltation he had anticipated. The intense excitement of the struggle for the plan, and the long night voyage from the mainland in the unprovisioned canoe had, to use his own expression, "taken it out of him." He tried to arouse himself by directing his mind to the ingots the Chinamen had spoken of, but it would not rest there; it came back headlong to the thought of sweet water rippling in the river, and to the almost unendurable dryness of his lips and throat. The rhythmic wash of the sea upon the reef was becoming audible now, and it had a pleasant sound in his ears; the water washed along the side of the canoe, and the paddle dripped between each stroke. Presently he began to doze.

He was still dimly conscious of the island, but a queer dream texture interwove with his sensations. Once again it was the night when he and Hooker had hit upon the Chinamen's secret; he saw the moonlit trees, the little fire burning, and the black figures of the three Chinamen—silvered on one side by moonlight, and on the other glowing from the firelight—and heard them talking together in pigeon-English—for they came from different provinces. Hooker had caught the drift of their talk first, and had motioned to him to listen. Fragments of the conversation were inaudible, and fragments incomprehensible. A Spanish galleon from the Philippines hopelessly aground, and its treasure buried against the day of return, lay in the background of the story; a shipwrecked crew thinned by disease, a quarrel or so, and the needs of discipline, and at last taking to their boats never to be heard of again. Then Chang-hi, only a year since, wandering ashore, had happened upon the ingots hidden for two hundred years, had deserted his junk, and reburied them with infinite toil, single-handed but very safe. He laid great stress on the safety—it was a secret of his. Now he wanted help to return and exhume them. Presently the little map fluttered and the voices sank. A fine story for two, stranded British wastrels to hear! Evans' dream shifted to the moment when he had Chang-hi's pigtail in his hand. The life of a Chinaman is scarcely sacred like a European's. The cunning little face of Chang-hi, first keen and furious like a startled snake, and then fearful, treacherous, and pitiful, became overwhelmingly prominent in the dream. At the end Chang-hi had grinned, a most incomprehensible and startling grin. Abruptly things became very unpleasant, as they will do at times in dreams. Chang-hi gibbered and threatened him. He saw in his dream heaps and heaps of gold, and Chang-hi intervening and struggling to hold him back from it. He took Chang-hi by the pigtail—how big the yellow brute was, and how he struggled and grinned! He kept growing bigger, too. Then the bright heaps of gold turned to a roaring furnace, and a vast devil, surprisingly like Chang-hi, but with a huge black tail, began to feed him with coals. They burnt his mouth horribly. Another devil was shouting his name: "Evans, Evans, you sleepy fool!"—or was it Hooker?

===Chinese===
"这回轮到你划了，胡克（Hooker），"他说。

他的同伴不声不响地把地图折好，揣进口袋，小心地侧身从埃文斯身边过去，开始划桨。他的动作有气无力，像一个气力几乎耗尽的人。

埃文斯半闭着眼坐着，望着珊瑚礁那泛着泡沫的防波堤般的外缘一点点逼近。天空如同一座熔炉，因为太阳已近天顶。虽说离宝藏这么近，他却并没有感到原先预想的那种亢奋。争夺那张图纸时的极度紧张，加上从未备粮的独木舟上从大陆渡来的漫长一夜，用他自己的话来说，已经把他"掏空了"。他试着把心思转到那些中国人说过的金砖上去，好打起精神来，可思绪就是不肯停留在那上面；它一往无前地回到那条河里潺潺流动的甘甜清水的念头上，回到嘴唇和喉咙那几乎难以忍受的干渴上。海浪拍打珊瑚礁的有节奏的涛声此刻已能听见，在他耳中颇为悦耳；水沿着独木舟的船身冲刷过去，每划一桨之间，桨叶滴下水珠。不多久他便打起盹来。

他仍隐隐约约地意识到那座岛屿的存在，可一种古怪的梦境纹理已交织进他的种种知觉。那又是他和胡克撞破那几个中国人秘密的那个夜晚；他看见月光下的树木、燃烧着的小小火堆，还有那三个中国人的黑色身影——一侧被月光镀上银色，另一侧被火光映得通红——听见他们用洋泾浜英语（pigeon-English）交谈——因为他们来自不同的省份。胡克先听出了他们话里的门道，便招手让他也来听。谈话有的片断听不真切，有的片断听不明白。一艘来自菲律宾（Philippines）的西班牙大帆船（Spanish galleon）绝望地搁浅，船上的宝藏被埋藏起来以待他日返取——这是整个故事的底色；遇险的船员被疫病削减，又因一两场争执和维系纪律的需要而死掉一些，最后登上小艇出海，从此再无音讯。再后来，常熙（Chang-hi），就在仅仅一年前，在岸上游荡时偶然撞见了那些埋藏了二百年的金砖，便抛下了他的中国帆船，以无穷的辛劳独自一人将它们重新掩埋，虽是单枪匹马，却做得万无一失。他对那份安全格外强调——那是他的一个秘密。如今他想要人帮忙，好回去把它们重新挖出来。不多时那张小地图飘动了一下，说话声也低了下去。对于两个走投无路的英国浪子来说，这可真是一桩妙极了的传闻！埃文斯的梦转到了他一手攥住常熙辫子的那一刻。一个中国人的性命，毕竟不像一个欧洲人的性命那般神圣。常熙那张狡黠的小脸——先是机敏凶狠如受惊的蛇，继而惊惶、阴险、可怜兮兮——在梦里变得异常清晰、压倒一切。到末了，常熙咧嘴笑了起来，那是一种全然费解、令人心惊的笑。陡然间事情变得极其不妙，正如梦境里有时会出现的那样。常熙叽里咕噜地说着，威胁他。他在梦里看见一堆又一堆的黄金，常熙横插进来，拼命拦着不让他靠近。他一把抓住常熙的辫子——这黄皮肤的畜生块头可真大，他挣扎得多厉害，笑得多厉害！他还不停地越长越大。随后那一堆堆闪亮的黄金化作一座轰鸣的熔炉，一个巨大的魔鬼——出奇地像常熙，却拖着一条又粗又黑的尾巴——开始往他嘴里喂煤。烧得他嘴里的滋味可怕极了。另一个魔鬼正大喊着他的名字："埃文斯，埃文斯，你这瞌睡虫！"——还是那是胡克的声音？

===Original===
He woke up. They were in the mouth of the lagoon.

"There are the three palm-trees. It must be in a line with that clump of bushes," said his companion. "Mark that. If we, go to those bushes and then strike into the bush in a straight line from here, we shall come to it when we come to the stream."

They could see now where the mouth of the stream opened out. At the sight of it Evans revived. "Hurry up, man," he said, "or by heaven I shall have to drink sea water!" He gnawed his hand and stared at the gleam of silver among the rocks and green tangle.

Presently he turned almost fiercely upon Hooker. "Give *me* the paddle," he said.

So they reached the river mouth. A little way up Hooker took some water in the hollow of his hand, tasted it, and spat it out. A little further he tried again. "This will do," he said, and they began drinking eagerly.

===Chinese===
他醒了过来。他们已经进了泻湖的口子。

"那三棵棕榈树就在那儿。它必定和那一丛灌木成一条直线，"他的同伴说。"把那个位置记牢。要是我们先到那丛灌木那儿，再从这儿照着直线一头扎进林子，等我们走到那条小溪边上，就能找到它了。"

这会儿他们能看见那条小溪的入海口了。一见这个，埃文斯精神一振。"快点，老兄，"他说，"不然老天在上，我可要喝海水了！"他啃咬着自己的手，瞪着礁石与层层绿蔓之间那一闪一闪的银光。

不多时他几乎蛮横地朝胡克转过身去。"把桨给*我*，"他说。

他们就这样到了溪口。往上走了一小段，胡克用手心捧了些水，尝了尝，又吐掉。再往上一点他又试了一回。"这儿的能喝了，"他说，于是两人便急切地喝了起来。

===Original===
"Curse this!" said Evans suddenly. "It's too slow." And, leaning dangerously over the fore part of the canoe, he began to suck up the water with his lips.

Presently they made an end of drinking, and, running the canoe into a little creek, were about to land among the thick growth that overhung the water.
